1. Scope of the Reference Set

This is a working reference on welding engineering across the full range of industrial joining processes. It covers process mechanics, the components of each process and what each component does, material weldability, joint and procedure decisions, defects and their diagnosis and correction, qualification and quality frameworks, inspection, automation, and the economics of process choice.

It is written to answer four kinds of question:

| Question type | Example | Where answered |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How does it work? | What does constricting a tungsten arc through an orifice actually buy? | The process chapters |
| When do I use it? | Which processes remain available for 2 mm aluminium, one-sided access, high volume? | Chapters 51, 55, 68, 73 |
| What went wrong, and why? | What does clustered porosity indicate that uniform porosity does not? | Chapters 36, 47, 54, 74 |
| What must I do, in what order? | How is a preheat temperature actually decided? | The procedure sections of each chapter |

It contains no welding parameters, no acceptance limits, no cost figures and no product or vendor names. The reasons are set out in Chapter 78, which states the boundaries of the set in full.

2. How the Set Is Organized

Every chapter follows the same structure, so that a reader who knows one chapter knows how to navigate all of them.

| Element | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Title and lede | What the chapter covers, in one sentence |
| In This Chapter | Numbered section list, used as the chapter's own index |
| Numbered sections | Mechanism first, then components, then decisions, then execution |
| Decision tables | Selection and comparison presented as tables, not prose |
| Setup and execution procedure | Numbered before/during/after steps, in every process chapter |
| Failure or defect catalogue | Symptom, mechanism, discriminator, corrective action |
| Worked example | One real scenario carried end to end |
| Known gaps | What the chapter does not settle, and where to go instead |
| Sources | Numbered citations, resolved to the standard or publication |

The format is chosen per concept, not per chapter. Material selection appears as decision tables; defect resolution as symptom-to-action tables with discriminators; procedures as numbered steps; comparisons as matrices; mechanisms as prose. A concept that is genuinely a decision is never written as a paragraph.

# Chapter 1 — Fundamentals and Physics of Resistance Spot Welding

What resistance spot welding is, why it works, and the governing physical relationships an operator, programmer or engineer relies on every time a schedule is set.

## In This Chapter

1. Definition and process classification

2. Why the process works: the resistance distribution

3. The weld cycle: squeeze, weld, hold, release

4. Governing physical relationships (Q = I²Rt and dynamic resistance)

5. The weldability lobe / process window

6. Design rules with numeric, sourced values

7. Main process variables and what each one controls

8. Quality outcomes and common misconceptions

9. Core terminology quick reference

10. Sources referenced in this chapter

# 1. Definition and Process Classification

Resistance spot welding (RSW) is a resistance-welding process that produces a weld at the faying (contacting) surfaces between overlapping parts, using heat obtained from the resistance to the flow of welding current through the parts, combined with the application of mechanical force through the electrodes [S9]. It belongs to the pressure-welding family: unlike arc or laser welding, no filler metal is added and no arc is struck. The joint forms entirely from localized resistive heating under clamping force, which is why the process is sometimes described to newcomers as "welding by squeezing and cooking," a simplification that is directionally correct even though it skips the electrical detail that actually governs weld quality.

RSW is assigned process reference number 21 in the ISO nomenclature system, with 211 (indirect spot welding) and 212 (direct spot welding) as its sub-variants. Resistance seam welding is numbered 22 and projection welding is numbered 23 in the same scheme [S1]. "Direct" spot welding means both electrodes contact the stack directly opposite one another on either face; "indirect" spot welding passes current through one electrode into the stack and returns it through a shunt or an adjacent point rather than through a mirrored electrode. The distinction is not academic: indirect welding produces asymmetric current density through the stack and is materially more prone to shunting losses, so a procedure written for direct welding cannot be assumed to transfer to an indirect configuration without re-qualification.

| ISO 4063 Code | Process | Electrode Arrangement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 21 | Resistance spot welding (general) | Localized nugget at overlapping faying surfaces |
| 211 | Indirect spot welding | Current returns through a shunt or adjacent point, not a mirrored electrode |
| 212 | Direct spot welding | Electrodes directly opposite each other on either face of the stack |
| 22 | Resistance seam welding | Continuous or intermittent linear weld, typically rotating wheel electrodes |
| 23 | Projection welding | Weld localized by a pre-formed projection, embossment or intersection |

# 2. Why the Process Works: The Resistance Distribution

The total electrical resistance in a spot-welding circuit is the sum of several resistances in series: the bulk resistance of each sheet, the contact resistance at each sheet-to-sheet (faying) interface, and the contact resistance at each electrode-to-sheet interface. For structural steels, the electrical and thermal conductivity of the workpiece is far lower than that of the copper-alloy electrodes, so under Joule heating (Q = I²Rt) the heat is generated disproportionately at the sheet interfaces rather than in the electrodes or the bulk of the sheet [S13]. This is the entire reason spot welding of steel works efficiently with copper tooling: copper carries the current with low loss, and the workpiece itself becomes the resistive heating element at the one location — the faying interface — where heat is actually wanted.

A second, self-reinforcing effect drives nugget growth once heating starts. As the steel at the interface heats, its electrical resistivity rises further relative to the still-cool copper electrodes, which concentrates additional heating at the same location. Because of this positive-feedback heating and the small thermal mass involved, a steel spot-weld nugget can form in on the order of one-fifth of a second under production conditions [S13]. This is also why resistance spot welding is compatible with high-volume, high-cycle-rate automotive and appliance production: the fusion event itself is extremely fast, and cycle time in a robotic cell is dominated by gun approach, squeeze and hold time — not by the weld pulse.

| Material Note — Aluminum Is Different Aluminum is treated separately in the Specialized Processes chapter because its electrical and thermal conductivity are much closer to copper's own. The same physics does not concentrate heat as efficiently at the faying interface, so roughly three times the current and about one-third the weld time (versus an equivalent steel joint) are commonly needed, together with a much narrower usable process window [S14]. A schedule philosophy built around steel behavior should never be applied to aluminum by simple parameter scaling. |

# 3. The Weld Cycle: Squeeze, Weld, Hold, Release

Every RSW cycle — regardless of controller make or naming convention — passes through the same functional stages. Vendor documentation and different controller families name these stages slightly differently (see Chapter 16, Weld Sequence and Program Structure, for how these functional stages map onto a specific controller's program-block naming), but the underlying physical requirement at each stage is universal and grounded in ISO 17677-1 terminology.

| Stage | What Physically Happens | What the Control System Must Ensure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Squeeze | Electrodes close and force ramps up to the target electrode force before current starts | Force is stable and contact is established; premature current with unstable force is a leading cause of expulsion and inconsistent nugget size |
| Weld | Current flows for the programmed weld time (in cycles of line frequency, or milliseconds under MFDC); may be a single pulse or several pulses with cooling intervals between them | Current tracks the programmed target (open-loop) or a regulated current/voltage/resistance target (closed-loop adaptive control — Chapter 11) |
| Hold | Current stops but electrode force is maintained | The molten nugget solidifies under continued force/containment before the electrodes release; releasing force too early is a classic cause of internal porosity/shrinkage voids and, in the worst case, expulsion after current-off |
| Off / Release | Electrodes separate | Part or gun can move to the next weld point without disturbing the still-warm joint |

Some schedules add an explicit upslope — a gradual current ramp at the start of the weld pulse, used to reduce initial expulsion on high-resistivity or coated surfaces — and a downslope, a gradual current ramp-down used on hardenable/AHSS grades to control cooling rate and reduce the risk of a brittle, crack-prone nugget. Both are configurable sub-stages of the weld stage itself, not separate cycle stages.

# 4. Governing Physical Relationships

The commonly cited simplified heat-generation relationship for resistance welding is:

Q = I² R t

where Q is heat energy in joules, I is welding current in amperes, R is the effective resistance of the circuit at the joint in ohms, and t is weld time in seconds [S18]. Two consequences of this formula matter directly for engineering judgment and are frequently misunderstood on the shop floor:

- Current enters as a squared term. A given percentage change in current produces roughly double that percentage change in heat input, all else equal — a 10% current increase raises heat input by roughly 21%, not 10%. This is why current is the most sensitive and most consequential parameter to adjust casually.

- Resistance is not constant during the weld — this is dynamic resistance. At the start of the pulse, contact resistance at the faying surface dominates and is sensitive to surface condition (oxide, coating, contamination) and force. As heating proceeds, contact area grows, softens, and can partially collapse, while the bulk resistivity of the heated steel rises. The resistance-versus-time curve for a healthy steel weld typically shows an initial value, a drop as asperities collapse and true contact area grows, then a rise as the heated zone's resistivity increases — a shape used diagnostically by modern monitoring controllers (Chapter 11).

# 5. The Weldability Lobe / Process Window

The relationship between current, time, force and weld quality is characteristically visualized as a weldability lobe, also called a weld lobe or process window: a plot, usually of current against time at a fixed force, showing the region of parameter combinations that produce acceptable welds, bounded on the low side by insufficient fusion (a nugget too small, or a stuck weld) and on the high side by expulsion or excessive electrode indentation [S13]. ISO 14327 is the ISO standard that specifically defines procedures for experimentally determining this lobe for resistance spot, projection and seam welding [S5]. It does not publish universal lobe values, because the lobe is specific to the material, coating, thickness, electrode geometry and equipment in use — which is exactly why a lobe determined for one stack-up and tooling combination cannot be assumed to transfer to another without re-qualification.

ISO 14327 is in fact the weldability-lobe determination procedure described above, not a certification scheme [S5], [S20]. This correction is stated here so the error is not repeated. |
| --- |

Engineering practice generally targets the center of the lobe, not an edge, because production variation — tip wear, force fluctuation, minor material variation, line-voltage sag — will always push the actual weld somewhat away from its nominal setpoint. A process that is only marginally inside the acceptable region at nominal settings will drift out of it in production.

# 6. Design Rules With Numeric, Sourced Values

These are commonly published design and estimation rules. They are useful for sizing a first trial or sanity-checking a program, but every one of them must be confirmed by actual destructive testing and, for production use, by procedure qualification under the applicable standard (Chapter 8, WPS and Qualification). None of them is a substitute for a qualified WPS.

| Design Quantity | Rule | Source / Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Electrode (contact face) diameter | d_e = 5√t (mm), t = thickness of thinnest sheet in the stack, mm | ISO 14373 guidance for spot welding low-carbon steel [S6] |
| Minimum acceptable weld-nugget diameter | 4√t to 5√t (mm), t in mm — the same scaling as the electrode-face rule, so a correctly sized electrode is capable of a code-minimum nugget when current/time/force are correctly set | Widely used rule of thumb [S18] |
| Minimum spacing between adjacent spot welds | not less than 16t (t in mm), preferably greater, ±10% tolerance | ISO 14373 [S6] |
| Minimum edge distance | not less than 1.25 × d_w, where d_w is the weld (nugget) diameter | ISO 14373 [S6] |
| Rough first-trial estimate, mild steel (imperial) | Force (lbf) ≈ 6000 × ΣT; weld time (60 Hz cycles) ≈ 100 × ΣT; current (A) ≈ 100,000 × ΣT; reduce ~20% if ΣT > 0.080 in | Commonly published shop rule of thumb [S18] |

| Not a Production Setpoint The imperial first-trial estimate above is explicitly described by its own source as a starting point for trial-and-error setup on scrap material, not a validated production schedule. Spacing too tight causes current shunting — a portion of the welding current diverts through a previous, already-welded, lower-resistance spot instead of concentrating at the new weld location, weakening the new weld — which is the physical reason the 16t spacing rule exists. |

# 7. Main Process Variables and What Each One Controls

- Current — the dominant heat-generation variable (heat scales with I²); also the variable most responsible for expulsion if increased without corresponding attention to force and time.

- Weld time — total duration of current application; may be a single pulse or multiple pulses with defined cooling intervals between them. Interacts strongly with current — more time at lower current, or less time at higher current, can reach the same total heat input, but with different peak temperatures and different resulting metallurgy/heat-affected zone.

- Electrode force — controls contact resistance (higher force generally lowers contact resistance and current density for a given electrode face area), mechanical containment of the softened/molten zone (resists expulsion), and, together with tip geometry, the effective current density.

- Electrode face geometry/diameter — sets the effective contact area and therefore current density for a given current; wears over the life of the tip, which is why tip dressing and tip-life tracking are process-control activities, not merely maintenance housekeeping (Chapter 13).

- Material stack-up — sheet count, individual thickness, grade and coating; changes the resistance distribution and thermal behavior even at identical current/time/force settings (Chapter 2).

- Cooling — removes heat from electrodes, gun and transformer between and during welds; directly affects electrode life and, at high production rates, cumulative thermal drift of the whole process (Chapter 7).

- Sequence and spot spacing — determine thermal accumulation (heat left over from a nearby recent weld) and electrical shunting risk, per the 16t spacing rule above.

# 8. Quality Outcomes and Common Misconceptions

A production-acceptable spot weld is defined by the applicable product specification, customer requirement, WPS and inspection method — there is no single generic pass/fail number that applies across all applications. That said, several misconceptions recur often enough to be worth stating plainly, and each is grounded in the physics above rather than being an arbitrary rule.

- Higher current is not automatically better. Because heat scales with I², a modest increase can push a marginal weld from "acceptable, small nugget" straight past "good" into "expulsion and electrode damage," with very little current margin in between on a thin, high-conductivity stack.

- More electrode force is not automatically better. Increasing force increases the electrical contact area, which, all else equal, reduces current density and contact resistance at a given current — potentially reducing heat input even while it improves mechanical containment. Force and current are coupled variables, not independent knobs.

- A controller "OK"/"pass" indication is not proof of mechanical weld quality. Most controllers validate that measured current/voltage/time stayed within a programmed monitoring band; that is evidence the electrical process behaved as expected, not direct proof of nugget size or joint strength, which is why destructive and non-destructive testing (Chapter 10) remains necessary.

- A parameter set that works for one material stack does not automatically transfer to a different stack, even one that looks similar on paper — same nominal grade with a different coating, or the same total thickness split across a different number of sheets (Chapter 2).

# 9. Core Terminology Quick Reference

A full alphabetical glossary is provided in Chapter 15. The entries below are the small set of terms needed to read the rest of this chapter and are quoted, where marked, from ISO 17677-1:2021, the standard that actually governs resistance-welding vocabulary [S9].

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Nugget | "Zone in spot, projection or seam weld where the metal has been melted" [S9]. |
| Electrode | "Component of the electrical circuit that supplies electrical power and applies electrode force to the workpiece" [S9]. |
| Resistance spot welding | "Resistance welding process producing a weld at the faying surfaces between overlapping parts by the heat obtained from resistance to the flow of welding current" [S9]. |
| Projection welding | "Resistance welding in which the resulting welds are localized at predetermined points by projections, embossments or intersections" [S9]. |
| Seam welding | "Resistance welding in which force is applied continuously and current is applied continuously or intermittently to produce a linear weld" [S9]. |
| Dynamic resistance | Time-varying effective resistance of the weld circuit during the current pulse, as contact area and material state change. |
| Expulsion | Ejection of molten metal from the weld zone, generally indicating heat input exceeded what the joint geometry and force could contain. |
| Shunting | Current diversion through an unintended lower-resistance path (typically an adjacent, already-made weld), reducing effective current at the intended weld. |

# 1. What "Weldability" Formally Means

ISO 18278-1 supplies the formal framework this reference set uses for the word "weldability." It specifies procedures for assessing the generic weldability for resistance welding of uncoated and coated metals, and it does so for four distinct purposes: comparing metallurgical weldability across different metals, assessing the weldability of varying component designs, investigating the effect of changing welding parameters, and comparing the performance of different resistance-welding equipment [S10]. That four-purpose scope is worth reading carefully, because it means "weldability" is never a single yes/no property of a material sample sitting on a bench — it is always a statement relative to a design, a parameter set, or a piece of equipment as well as to the metal itself.

The standard frames weldability as governed jointly by material, design and production factors, corresponding respectively to metallurgical, operative and constructional weldability [S10]. In practice this means "is this material weldable" decomposes into three separable questions: can the metallurgy itself form a sound fused bond under resistance heating (metallurgical weldability); can the actual joint and component geometry be reached and clamped by available electrodes and tooling (operative weldability); and can the production system reliably reproduce that result, weld after weld, across a real production run (constructional weldability). A change that affects one of these three does not automatically affect the other two — a material can be metallurgically capable of an excellent nugget and still be a poor production choice because access geometry or electrode life makes constructional weldability unacceptable, and conversely a well-tooled, well-fixtured joint can still fail metallurgically if the alloy itself is not tolerant of the required thermal cycle.

ISO 18278-1 further ties this framework to two measurable functional capabilities rather than leaving "weldability" as a qualitative impression: the welding current range, which quantifies the ability to make an acceptable weld at all — in effect, how wide the weldability lobe is for that material and geometry — and electrode wear/life, which quantifies the ability to keep making acceptable welds over a production run without the process drifting out of that lobe [S10]. This second criterion is easy to underweight: a material or coating can be "weldable" in the narrow sense of forming a nugget on a lab coupon and still be a poor production choice if it collapses electrode life to the point that the process cannot be held inside its lobe across a realistic production run without excessive intervention.

ISO 14327 is the companion standard that defines the actual experimental procedure for determining the weldability lobe itself — for spot, projection and seam welding alike (Chapter 1, Fundamentals and Physics, covers what a lobe is and why its center, not its edge, is the sound engineering target). ISO 18278-1 supplies the conceptual framework for what weldability means and how to compare it across materials and equipment; ISO 14327 supplies the procedure for actually drawing the lobe once that framework is applied to a specific case.

# 2. Why Material Matters at the Physics Level

Resistance-welding behavior is governed by electrical resistivity, thermal conductivity, mechanical strength at elevated temperature, surface condition, and metallurgical response to rapid heating and cooling. None of these properties is captured by thickness alone. Two materials of identical thickness can therefore require substantially different current, time and force even though they look interchangeable on a thickness-only specification sheet — which is precisely why the sections below treat coating, grade family and base metal as independent variables rather than as footnotes to a thickness table.

# 3. Coated Steel

Coatings — most commonly hot-dip zinc, galvannealed (an iron-zinc alloy coating), or aluminum-based coatings on structural and body-in-white steels — change the initial contact resistance and heating behavior relative to bare steel. The coating itself has a different resistivity from the base steel and often a distinctly lower melting point, and it is present at exactly the location — the faying interface — where heat needs to concentrate for the process to work efficiently (Chapter 1). Coating composition and thickness also affect electrode life directly: zinc in particular is prone to alloying with and pitting the copper electrode face over repeated welds, which is a major driver of tip-dressing frequency on galvanized-steel production lines (Chapter 3, Electrodes and Tooling, covers this wear mechanism and the dressing response to it in detail).

Because the coating sits precisely at the location where the process is most sensitive to contact-resistance variation, this reference set states the following as a hard constraint rather than a suggestion: the same nominal steel grade with a different coating, or a different coating weight, should never be assumed to share a qualified schedule. A schedule qualified on 1.2 mm galvannealed steel is not automatically valid on 1.2 mm hot-dip-galvanized steel of the same base grade, even though a specification sheet that lists only grade and thickness would make the two stacks look identical.

ISO 14373 — the standard governing the spot-welding procedure itself for low-carbon steels — has a defined scope worth stating precisely, because its boundaries determine what it can and cannot be cited for: it applies to sheet thicknesses of 0.4 mm to 3 mm, uncoated and metallic-coated (including hot-dip zinc, galvannealed, and aluminum-coated) low-carbon steel, welded by pedestal welders, gun welders, automatic equipment, multi-welders and robotic systems; it explicitly excludes organic-coated or primer-coated steels [S6]. It also requires steels to be free from harmful imperfections and requires pre-weld surfaces to be free of grease, scale, rust, paint, dirt or excessive pitting [S6]. That last clause matters more than it might first appear: surface-condition control is stated as a normative requirement of the procedure standard itself, not offered as optional good housekeeping practice layered on top of it.

A weld-shop assumption that "the standard covers coated steel, so it covers this coated steel" is not automatically safe — the coating chemistry has to be checked against the standard's actual metallic-coating scope, not against the word "coated" in isolation. |

# 4. Advanced and Ultra-High-Strength Steel (AHSS/UHSS)

Higher-strength and multiphase steel grades — dual-phase, TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity), martensitic, and press-hardened steels among them — are weldable by resistance spot welding, but they generally require a narrower, more carefully qualified process window than mild steel of the same thickness. The reason is metallurgical: their alloy content and microstructure make weld-zone hardness, cooling rate, and hydrogen-related cracking risk considerably more sensitive to the exact thermal cycle than a plain low-carbon steel is. A schedule that tolerates a wide range of current and time on mild steel may have a materially narrower band of acceptable settings on an AHSS grade of the same nominal thickness.

A schedule qualified for a mild-steel stack should never be transferred to an AHSS stack of nominally the same thickness without independent qualification. This follows directly from the metallurgical-weldability distinction drawn by ISO 18278-1 above: a change in metallurgical weldability (the alloy's tolerance for the thermal cycle) is not a change that operative or constructional weldability testing on the mild-steel stack would ever have surfaced. This is also the same reasoning that AWS D8.1M (the automotive resistance-spot-weld-quality specification) and AWS D8.9M (the associated recommended test-method practice for evaluating resistance-spot-welding behavior of automotive sheet steel) are built around for automotive sheet steel [S11][S12]. Chapter 9, Standards and Compliance Reference, and Chapter 8, WPS and Qualification, cover how these two standards are actually applied to a qualification program.

# 5. Stack-Up: Multi-Sheet Joints

The stack-up describes sheet count, individual thickness, material and coating for each layer, in order — it is a complete description of the joint, not a single number. For a three-sheet stack, welding current passes through two faying interfaces plus the bulk of the center sheet, and the heat generated (and the resulting nugget) is not necessarily symmetric between the two interfaces, particularly when the two outer sheets differ from one another in thickness, grade or coating.

The "thin-thick-thin" or asymmetric-stack case is a well-known challenge case in production spot welding for exactly this reason: achieving adequate fusion at the interface adjacent to the thicker or higher-conductivity member, without over-welding the thinner member, requires a narrower process window than a symmetric two-sheet joint of the same total thickness would. This is not a defect of the process — it is a direct consequence of the resistance-distribution physics covered in Chapter 1: heat generation at each interface depends on the local resistance and thermal mass on each side of it, and an asymmetric stack has, by definition, unequal conditions on the two sides.

# 6. Steel vs. Aluminum: A Concrete, Sourced Comparison

Aluminum alloys are increasingly used alongside or instead of steel for lightweighting, and they behave differently enough from steel in resistance welding that the comparison deserves its own treatment rather than being folded in as "just another material" on a thickness table.

| Factor | Steel | Aluminum |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Conductivity relationship to copper electrodes | Conductivity much lower than copper — the favorable "resistive workpiece / conductive tooling" asymmetry that makes steel RSW efficient (Chapter 1) | Electrical and thermal conductivity close to the copper-alloy electrodes themselves [S14] — this asymmetry is largely absent, so heat does not concentrate at the faying interface nearly as readily |
| Current and time (typical comparison) | Baseline case for the process | Commonly cited comparison: roughly 3× the current and about 1/3 the weld time of an equivalent steel joint [S14] — high current for a short duration, rather than steel's more moderate current over a comparatively longer pulse |
| Plastic range / process window | Comparatively wide plastic temperature range | Significantly narrower plastic range than steel [S14], which directly narrows the acceptable current/time window between "insufficient fusion" and "expulsion" — inherently less forgiving of parameter drift |
| Surface oxide layer | Not a dominant factor in the same way | Tenacious, rapidly-reforming oxide layer of variable thickness/composition [S14]; raises contact resistance (helping initial heating) but its part-to-part inconsistency is a major source of weld-to-weld variability. Over-aggressive current intended to "punch through" the oxide instead promotes electrode sticking (aluminum alloying into the copper tip) and accelerated electrode wear [S14] |
| Dynamic resistance behavior | Resistance rises measurably through the pulse — a self-reinforcing heating effect (Chapter 1) | Resistivity increases only slightly with temperature, so the resistance-vs-time curve is comparatively flat [S14] — the self-reinforcing heating effect steel benefits from is largely absent, so schedules rely more on tightly controlled current/force profiles than on "the process helping itself" |
| Thermal expansion | Baseline case | Roughly 3× the thermal-expansion coefficient of steel [S14], increasing the mechanical driving force for expulsion and for solidification defects (porosity, cracking) if the thermal cycle or force profile is not well matched to the alloy |

The practical consequence for procedure and equipment selection is direct: aluminum resistance spot welding generally needs a higher-current-capable power system (Chapter 4, Power Systems), tighter force control — which favors servo-actuated guns (Chapter 5, Servo Guns and Gun-Drive Systems) — and its own qualified WPS family. A steel WPS is never an acceptable substitute for an aluminum joint, and equipment sized for typical steel body-shop currents may not even be electrically capable of delivering a given aluminum schedule. Chapter 14, Specialized Processes, carries the aluminum-specific process notes and micro-spot-welding treatment forward from this comparison in more operational detail; this chapter's purpose is to establish why the two materials cannot share a schedule philosophy in the first place.

# 8. Scope: Metallic Materials Only

A scope boundary is worth stating plainly rather than leaving implicit: resistance spot welding, as covered throughout this reference set, applies to electrically conductive metal sheet materials — the entire process depends on Joule heating generated by resistance to current flow through the workpiece (Chapter 1), which requires a conductive metal stack in the first place. Plastics, composites and other non-metallic materials are joined by fundamentally different processes — for example ultrasonic, vibration, or adhesive bonding — that rely on entirely different physical mechanisms (frictional/vibrational heating, chemical adhesion) rather than resistive electrical heating. Those processes are outside the scope of resistance spot welding and are not covered in this reference set; nothing in this corpus should be read as a claim about how any specific plastic-joining process works, its parameters, or its equipment, since none of that material was researched or sourced for this package.

# 9. Questions a Practitioner Should Be Able to Answer From This Chapter

The following questions are a useful self-check for whether the material above has actually been internalized rather than skimmed; each is answerable directly from the sections above without introducing any fact beyond what has already been stated and cited.

- Why can changing one sheet from 1.0 mm to 1.2 mm require a different schedule, even at "the same" nominal current setting? Because the electrode-diameter design rule (d_e = 5√t) and the minimum-nugget-diameter rule (4√t–5√t) both scale with the thinnest sheet thickness, and because contact resistance, heat balance, and the required minimum current-time combination all shift with thickness (Chapter 1).

- Which inputs must be rechecked after a coating change, even if the base steel grade and thickness are unchanged? Contact resistance and the expected dynamic-resistance curve shape, electrode wear rate and dressing interval, and whichever WPS explicitly lists coating type/weight as an essential variable (Chapter 8, WPS and Qualification).

- Why can identical current/time/force settings produce different results on steel vs. aluminum stacks of the same nominal thickness? Because the underlying conductivity, plastic range, oxide behavior and dynamic-resistance behavior are fundamentally different, as summarized in Section 6 above — not because of an equipment fault.

- What evidence should support a claim that two material grades are interchangeable for a given WPS? Only a documented requalification per the applicable qualification standard — ISO 15614-12 or the customer's equivalent (Chapter 8) — never visual similarity or matching nominal thickness alone.

# 1. Electrodes Are a Process-Control Element, Not Just a Maintenance Item

Electrodes are simultaneously electrical conductors, mechanical clamps, heat sinks and current-density shapers — four functions performed by one piece of copper, all at once, every cycle. Because current density is set by the electrode face area at the point of contact, electrode condition changes the effective process parameters even when the controller's programmed current, time and force targets are left completely untouched. A tip that has mushroomed since the last dressing presents a larger face area to the same programmed current, which lowers the actual current density delivered to the joint — the controller reports that it delivered the programmed current, and it did, but the process the workpiece actually experienced has drifted.

This is why electrode wear tracking belongs in the same category as current, force and time as a controlled process variable, not in a separate "housekeeping" category to be handled whenever convenient. A maintenance philosophy that treats tip dressing as janitorial upkeep, disconnected from process engineering, will eventually be surprised by a quality trend that the controller's own pass/fail indication never flagged — because, as Chapter 1 notes, a controller "OK" indication is evidence the electrical process behaved as programmed, not direct proof of nugget size or joint strength.

# 2. Governing Standards: ISO 5182 and ISO 5821

Two ISO standards govern electrode hardware directly, and a third — already introduced in Chapters 1 and 2 — governs the design rule that ties electrode geometry to the material being welded. Precision about what each standard actually covers matters here specifically because at least one public secondary source in circulation cites a standard designation, "ISO 5826," that does not correspond to any real ISO standard under that description; this reference set uses only the verified designations below.

| Standard | Edition / Status | Published Scope | What It Actually Covers | How It Is Used |

| ISO 5182:2016 | Current edition | "Resistance welding — Materials for electrodes and ancillary equipment" | Specifies the materials used for electrodes and ancillary current-carrying/force-transmitting equipment in resistance welding [S2]. This is the standard that actually governs electrode/ancillary-equipment materials; it is not to be confused with the non-existent "ISO 5826" designation that appears on at least one secondary web source (Chapter 2 corpus correction; Sources and Bibliography). | Cited as the material-specification standard whenever an electrode alloy family (Group A/B/C, below) is discussed; the qualitative class descriptions in Section 3 are understood to sit under this standard's materials scope even though this corpus does not reproduce its full numeric table from a licensed copy. |

This is the rule that makes electrode selection a function of the joint being made rather than a single generic tip size chosen once and left alone — a stack-thickness change is, by this rule, also an electrode-sizing decision.

# 3. Electrode Material Classes: The RWMA/AWS System

Electrode alloys are conventionally organized by the RWMA (Resistance Welder Manufacturers' Association) classification system, now maintained under AWS (the American Welding Society, which absorbed RWMA). The full numeric specification for this classification lives in AWS C1.1 and the associated RWMA Bulletin 16 resistance-welding manual, neither of which this reference set reproduces from a licensed copy. Instead, the qualitative class structure below is well corroborated across independent public sources — Class 1 is the highest-conductivity, softest alloy family, and each subsequent class trades some conductivity for strength or hardness — while the exact %IACS conductivity and hardness figures come from two secondary industry sources that report those figures somewhat differently.

| 2 | Copper alloy stronger than Class 1 (commonly copper-chromium) | 99.2% Cu / 0.8% Cr; 62 ksi UTS (forged); ~82% IACS | ~75% IACS; ~75 HRB |

Practical selection guidance implied by the class structure: Class 1/2-type alloys (high conductivity) are the default choice for standard low-carbon-steel body-panel spot welding, where minimizing electrode-side resistive loss and heat buildup is the priority. Higher-class (harder, lower-conductivity) alloys are selected instead when mechanical wear resistance, resistance to mushrooming under high force, or resistance to alloying/pickup from an aggressive coating (for example aluminum-coated or heavily galvanized steel) outweighs the conductivity penalty of moving up the class ladder. This is a trade-off decision made deliberately for a specific application, not a default that should be assumed correct without checking against the material and coating actually being welded (Chapter 2).

# 4. Common Electrode Attributes to Track as Controlled Data

The following attributes should be treated as controlled, traceable process data — the same status given to programmed current, time and force — rather than as incidental hardware facts nobody records:

- Electrode material/alloy family and class (Group A/B/C and the numbered class within it, Section 3 above).

- Cap or tip geometry — dome, truncated cone, flat, pointed or offset. Geometry shape is itself a process variable that affects current density and force distribution, not purely a mechanical-access choice made for clearance reasons.

- Face diameter/profile, tied directly to the d_e = 5√t design rule above.

- Cooling-channel design and position relative to the face — affects how effectively heat is removed from the tip between and during welds (Chapter 7, Cooling and Utilities).

- Holder/adaptor interface and taper (per ISO 5821's 1:10 / 1:9.6 taper ratios where applicable).

- Dressing condition and remaining life/wear limit (Sections 5–6 below).

- Coolant flow rate and temperature. A thermally marginal electrode shows current or quality drift that tracks coolant/ambient temperature rather than any deliberate parameter change — a useful diagnostic discriminator (Chapter 4).

- Replacement identity/lot , where full material traceability is required by the applicable quality system (Chapter 17, Traceability and Digital Thread).

# 5. Tip Wear Mechanisms

Repeated welding heats the electrode tip and produces wear through several distinguishable mechanisms, often acting together:

- Mushrooming — plastic deformation of the tip face that increases the effective face diameter, which reduces current density for a given programmed current. This is the dominant wear mode on bare steel.

- Material pickup/alloying — coating material, especially zinc from galvanized steel or aluminum from aluminum-silicon-coated steel, transferring onto and alloying with the copper face. This is a dominant wear mode on coated steel and on aluminum welding itself (Chapter 2).

- Surface contamination, cracking, and dimensional drift of the taper/seating surface, each of which changes how the cap seats on its adaptor or how current actually transfers across the face.

As the contact face geometry changes through any of these mechanisms, current density and pressure distribution both change together — which is exactly why weld quality can degrade gradually, as a loss of process margin, well before a dramatic and obviously visible defect appears. A worn but not yet visibly "broken" electrode is often the least visually obvious and most process-relevant failure mode in the entire electrode life cycle, precisely because nothing about it looks wrong to a quick visual check.

# 6. Tip-Dressing Equipment and Procedure

Tip dressing removes a controlled amount of material from the electrode face to restore a specified face geometry. The equipment used to do this — the tip dresser — is a rotary cutter or abrasive dressing head, mechanically integrated into many production cells so that dressing can occur in place on the gun without removing the electrode, though standalone bench-mounted dressers are also in service. Whichever form it takes, the tip dresser's function is the same: to remove a controlled, repeatable amount of material from the tip face and restore a defined target profile (dome, truncated cone, flat, or whatever geometry the design calls for), not simply to "clean up" the tip by eye.

A robust dressing strategy defines, in advance and as controlled data, each of the following: the dressing trigger (a weld count, a resistance/quality-trend threshold, or a fixed schedule), how much material is removed per dressing pass, how the resulting geometry is verified, and — critically — the point at which the tip must be replaced rather than dressed again, since each dressing pass reduces total electrode length and cooling-channel proximity, and there is a hard limit on how many times a given cap or tip can be dressed before it must be retired. Dressing parameters (feed rate, cutter geometry, target diameter) are equipment- and consumable-specific and must come from the tooling manufacturer's data for the exact cap/dresser combination in use — never from a generic number applied across different tooling.

The generic dressing sequence that this strategy implies, stage by stage, is as follows:

- Confirm that the defined dressing trigger has actually been reached — a weld count against the documented interval for this material/coating, a resistance or quality-trend signal crossing its threshold, or a scheduled maintenance point — rather than dressing on an ad hoc or purely visual basis.

- Bring the welding equipment to a safe, de-energized state per the equipment's own lockout/energy-isolation procedure before any manual intervention at the electrode (Chapter 4 states this safety principle for the power system generally; it applies equally here).

- Inspect the existing tip condition before cutting — face diameter, evidence of mushrooming, material pickup/alloying, cracking, or taper/seating wear — and record it as the pre-dressing baseline.

- Engage the tip dresser to remove material per the tooling manufacturer's specified feed, cutter geometry and target diameter for the exact cap/dresser combination in service; do not substitute a generic dressing parameter for a different consumable.

- Verify the resulting face geometry against the specified target profile — typically with a gauge or diameter check — before returning the electrode to production.

- Log the dressing event: weld count at dressing, material removed (or resulting diameter), and the running total of dressing passes against that cap/tip's documented dressing-count limit.

- Compare the running dressing-pass count to the documented replacement limit for this cap/tip; if the limit has been reached, replace the tip rather than dressing it again, regardless of how the face currently looks.

- Resume production and monitor the next several welds' process signals — dynamic-resistance curve shape and any quality-monitoring output (Chapter 11) — as confirmation that the dressing actually restored the expected process behavior, not merely the expected geometry.

# 7. Electrode-Related Troubleshooting and Predictive Reasoning

The table below collects the electrode-related observations most often reported on a production floor, alongside their likely cause and the evidence that actually discriminates between candidate causes rather than merely confirming a guess.

| Observation | Likely Cause | Evidence to Collect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Weld strength trending down over a production run | Tip wear (mushrooming) or coating pickup/contamination | Weld-quality trend, tip face diameter measurement, dressing/replacement history |
| Expulsion increasing after many welds without a program change | Contact-area/current-density drift from wear, or a thermal-state change | Current/resistance trace shape, tip face photo or measurement, coolant flow and temperature |
| Indentation depth increasing | Current density, force or heat-input change relative to the qualification baseline | Force feedback trace, tip geometry measurement, part surface inspection |
| Uneven welds between left and right electrode (or gun) on a symmetric joint | Gun/electrode alignment, mismatched tip wear between the two electrodes, or unequal force distribution | Mechanical alignment check, tip seating inspection, force balance measurement |

The most useful diagnostic statement built from this table is never "tip worn" offered as an isolated, standalone conclusion — it is a composite one. For example: "tip wear likely, because weld count since last dressing has exceeded the normal dressing interval for this material/coating, the dynamic-resistance curve has shifted in the direction consistent with increased contact area, and destructive test results from the same period show a nugget-diameter trend downward toward the 4√t minimum." Each of those three data types — usage count, process-signal trend, and destructive-test result — is individually weak evidence on its own; together, they support a specific, actionable conclusion in a way that no single one of them could alone. This composite-evidence habit is the same reasoning pattern Chapter 12, Troubleshooting and Diagnostics, applies at the whole-process level.

# 1. The Power Chain, Generically

A production resistance-welding installation delivers energy along a single path, regardless of manufacturer: incoming plant power, into the controller/power-stage (a transformer, or an inverter feeding a transformer), through secondary conductors (busbar or cable, gun arms, electrode holders), across the electrode-to-workpiece interface, and back along a return path. Every element in that chain contributes some impedance and some loss. The entire goal of equipment design and of ongoing maintenance is the same: keep the useful heat concentrated at the workpiece interface, where the process actually needs it (Chapter 1), and minimize loss everywhere else along the circuit.

Secondary-circuit loss contributors are worth listing in the rough order in which they actually turn out, in practice, to be the true cause of an "unexplained" current or quality problem — because the most common cause is rarely the most dramatic-sounding one:

- Busbar/cable connection resistance — loose or corroded joints are extremely common and are easy to miss on a purely visual inspection, since a joint can look intact while its actual contact resistance has drifted upward substantially.

- Transformer internal losses.

- Gun-arm resistance.

- Electrode-holder and electrode contact resistance (Chapter 3 covers electrode condition as a process variable in its own right).

- Unintended shunting paths — current diverting through an adjacent, already-made weld rather than concentrating at the intended new weld location (the 16t spacing rule, Chapter 1).

This ordering is itself a diagnostic tool: when a current or quality problem appears with no obvious programmatic cause, checking connection resistance first — before assuming a transformer or controller fault — reflects how often the fault actually turns out to live there in practice.

# 2. AC vs. MFDC: A Real Technical Comparison

Two fundamentally different power-stage architectures are in production use today, and it is worth being honest about the limits of any single comparison between them: the original training material this reference set replaces deliberately avoided declaring one architecture universally "better," and that caution was correct in the sense that neither is universally superior for every application. What can and should be stated precisely, however, is the underlying technical difference between the two, which is well documented and does not require picking a winner to describe accurately.

| Aspect | Single-Phase AC | MFDC (Medium/Mid-Frequency DC) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Basic architecture | Delivers current at line frequency (60 Hz in the US, 50 Hz in much of the rest of the world) directly through a transformer [S19] | First rectifies and inverts three-phase AC input up to a medium frequency — commonly cited in the 400–4,000 Hz range — feeds that into the welding transformer, then rectifies the transformer's output to deliver true DC to the secondary circuit [S19] |
| Output waveform / heating continuity | A sine wave that crosses zero twice per cycle; the weld actually cools momentarily every time the current crosses zero [S19] — heating is inherently pulsed at line frequency, not continuous | True DC output rather than a zero-crossing sine wave, so heating is continuous through the weld pulse rather than momentarily interrupted every half-cycle |
| Inductive losses | Present at line-frequency levels | Nearly eliminated compared with AC, because of the DC output [S19] — an MFDC system can deliver equivalent heat to the joint using less input power than a comparable AC system |
| Transformer size/weight for a given power rating | Larger/heavier for an equivalent power rating | Because the transformer operates at a much higher frequency, it can be built physically smaller and lighter for the same power rating [S19] — this is specifically why MFDC is the dominant choice for robot-carried, servo-actuated guns, where the transformer is often mounted directly on the gun arm and its mass matters for robot payload and dynamics |
| Control resolution | Adjusted in whole AC half-cycles | Current/time can be adjusted in millisecond increments rather than whole AC half-cycles, giving finer process control [S19] |
| Current industry practice | Remains specified and in service in many existing and simpler installations [S19]; an AC installation qualified for a given application remains a legitimate qualified process for that application | Has become the default choice in most automated/robotic welding [S19] |

| A Statement of Practice, Not a Categorical Claim The "current industry practice" row above is stated honestly as a description of prevailing practice, not as a categorical claim that AC is obsolete or unsuitable [S19]. A properly qualified AC installation for a given application remains a legitimate qualified process for that application; the comparison above exists to make an informed architecture choice, not to declare one architecture universally correct. |

# 3. Weld Controllers: Core Responsibilities, Generically

Regardless of vendor, a resistance-welding controller's core responsibilities are the same functional set. Stating them generically, in the order a weld cycle typically exercises them:

- Accept a weld-program selection and a trigger command.

- Validate readiness/interlock conditions before allowing current to flow.

- Generate the electrical welding schedule — either open-loop, or closed-loop/adaptive (Chapter 11, Process Monitoring and Adaptive Control, covers the closed-loop case in detail).

- Monitor the actual current, voltage and/or derived resistance signal during the pulse.

- Report a completion/result status.

- Raise alarms/diagnostic codes on abnormal conditions — Chapter 12, Troubleshooting and Diagnostics, covers why the specific alarm-code naming for this step is controller/vendor-specific even though the underlying functional need to flag an abnormal condition is universal.

- On modern systems, store or transmit weld-result data for traceability (Chapter 17, Traceability and Digital Thread).

# 4. Controller Product Families: A Generic Pattern

Controller product families are not one-size-fits-all, even within a single manufacturer's own catalog. Commercial weld-controller ranges typically span several distinct families with materially different capability, organized around distinct application needs rather than simply around price tiers of the same underlying product. The pattern below is described generically, as the corpus underlying this reference set frames it, without naming any specific manufacturer or product line.

| Family Pattern | Typical Application Focus | Distinguishing Characteristic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| High-current, general-purpose family | High-volume robotic/automotive and structural welding lines | Sized for the highest routine current demand in a product range; the baseline family most catalogs are organized around |
| Quality-monitoring-focused variant | High-volume production where online weld verification is a priority | Built around quality monitoring and online verification capability specifically, layered on top of the same basic weld-control function |
| General-purpose, I/O-flexible unit | Installations needing integration flexibility across different plant-floor architectures | Supports multiple fieldbus standards, prioritizing integration flexibility over any single specialized capability |
| Legacy line with a retrofit path | Existing installed base still in service | An earlier-generation product line that may still be in service, sometimes with a documented in-place hardware/firmware upgrade path that changes its capability without changing its outward model designation |
| Low-voltage/precision unit | Micro-strand splice welding, sensor contacting, battery welding | Runs at a higher control-loop cycle rate than a general body-shop controller, sometimes with an integrated servo function that removes the need for a separate PLC/motion controller |

| Identify the Product Family Before Diagnosing Selecting or diagnosing "the weld controller" for a real installation without first identifying which specific product family, and which firmware/hardware revision, is actually installed is a category error. This matters most acutely for alarm-code interpretation, where the same underlying functional condition (Chapter 1's squeeze/weld/hold/off stages, in ISO 17677-1 terms) can be surfaced under different fault names and code numbers by different controller families and firmware revisions — see Chapter 12, Troubleshooting and Diagnostics, and Chapter 16, Weld Sequence and Program Structure, for how these functional stages map onto a specific controller's program-block naming. |

# 5. Transformers: Sizing, Duty Cycle, Regulation, and Mounting Architecture

The welding transformer converts available primary electrical input into the low-voltage, high-current secondary output the welding circuit actually needs. Commercial medium-frequency transformer lines are typically offered across several power classes and multiple secondary-voltage classes, with air-cooled and water-cooled variants and options for different primary voltages — the intent being that a transformer can be matched to the current/duty-cycle demand of a specific application, rather than one size being expected to serve every installation equally well. This section goes beyond that general statement into the four specific engineering decisions that actually define a transformer's selection and behavior: duty-cycle rating, thermal role, voltage-regulation method, and physical mounting architecture.

## Duty-cycle rating: what "50%" actually means and why it exists

Duty cycle is fundamentally a heat rating, not a power rating in the everyday sense — its purpose is to protect the transformer's winding insulation from thermal damage, not to describe how "strong" the transformer is [S22]. Because resistance welding is inherently an intermittent process — current flows only during the brief weld pulse, then stops for the remainder of the cycle — industry practice standardizes transformer ratings against a 50% duty cycle measured over a one-minute integrating period: the transformer's rated capacity assumes it conducts current for a total of 30 seconds within any 60-second window, with the remaining 30 seconds available for cooling [S22]. In real production practice, most installations run at roughly 20% duty cycle or lower, which is why a transformer nameplate-rated for 50% duty typically has meaningful thermal margin in an actual welding cell rather than running at its rated limit continuously.

The direct consequence for equipment selection and troubleshooting is this: a transformer that is asked to run at a duty cycle meaningfully higher than its rating — for example, a high-throughput cell with unusually short idle time between welds — will generate more average heat than its insulation system was rated to dissipate, and the resulting thermal stress shows up as exactly the kind of slow, ambient/coolant-correlated current or quality drift already described in the paragraph above, not as an instantaneous fault. Duty cycle is formally defined as the percentage of a one-minute period during which the transformer actually conducts current, and — while the standard nameplate convention is 50% — a given application can be specified anywhere up to and including 100% continuous duty if the application genuinely requires it [S23]. AC and MFDC transformers are evaluated against this same convention using different calculation methods appropriate to their respective waveforms — a continuous DC output versus a pulsed sine-wave output are not thermally equivalent for a given RMS-equivalent current, which is why the two architectures use different duty-cycle formulas rather than one shared calculation applied to both [S23].

This chapter states the concept and its consequence honestly and points to the underlying source rather than reconstructing a formula from memory that could not be verified character-for-character. |

## Voltage regulation: tap switching versus electronic (stepless) control

Coarse output regulation on a transformer-based welding power stage is traditionally achieved with a tap switch — a switch installed on the transformer's primary-side windings that changes the effective turns ratio between primary and secondary [S24]. Changing taps does not directly adjust the primary voltage the transformer receives from the plant supply; instead, changing the turns ratio changes the voltage induced in the secondary winding — the lowest tap produces the lowest available secondary voltage, and the highest tap produces the highest secondary voltage and the transformer's maximum available kVA [S24]. Tap switching is a coarse, discrete-step mechanism: it selects among a fixed number of turns-ratio positions, and finer regulation within a selected tap is then handled electronically by the weld controller's own current/time regulation (Section 3 above), not by further transformer adjustment.

This two-layer regulation pattern — coarse mechanical tap selection for the broad operating range, fine electronic regulation within it — is a real, generic architectural pattern across commercial resistance-welding power stages, described here without attributing it to any specific manufacturer's product. Some modern power-stage designs move more of this regulation into the electronic domain (sometimes described as "stepless" control), reducing reliance on discrete mechanical taps; this reference set states that such designs exist as a category without asserting a specific product's exact regulation range or resolution, since that detail is genuinely product-specific.

## Mounting architecture: remote transformer versus gun-mounted ("transgun") configuration

Beyond the AC-vs-MFDC size/weight comparison already covered in Section 2, transformers built specifically for robotic gun-mounted service — sometimes described in industry literature as a "transformer gun" or "transgun" configuration — are engineered to be relatively light and compact for a given power rating specifically so they can be mounted directly on the robot arm at the gun itself, commonly available across a range of power classes and typically water-cooled given their compact size and duty [S25]. Mounting the transformer at the gun rather than remotely in a control cabinet eliminates the long run of high-current secondary cable that a remote-transformer architecture requires, which directly reduces secondary-circuit electrical losses (Section 1's loss-contributor list) and reduces the resistance/impedance variability that a long, flexed, robot-carried secondary cable would otherwise introduce over its service life.

The tradeoff this architecture accepts is robot payload and dynamics: the transformer's mass now travels with the gun through every motion the robot makes, rather than sitting stationary in a cabinet, which is precisely why light weight for a given power rating is the defining design goal of this transformer category rather than an incidental marketing point. This is also why MFDC's smaller-transformer-for-equivalent-power advantage (Section 2) and the gun-mounted architecture reinforce each other in practice: a smaller, lighter transformer is easier to justify carrying on a robot arm in the first place, which is a meaningful part of why MFDC has become the default choice for automated/robotic welding specifically (Section 2's "current industry practice" row).

Thermal management is critical for any welding transformer regardless of manufacturer or mounting architecture, because both resistive losses and repetitive high-duty-cycle operation generate heat that must be continuously removed (Chapter 7, Cooling and Utilities, covers the utility side of this requirement). A transformer that is thermally marginal for its actual duty cycle will show current or quality drift that tracks ambient or coolant temperature rather than tracking any deliberate parameter or tooling change — which makes this a genuinely useful diagnostic discriminator: a quality trend that correlates with time-of-day or coolant temperature, rather than with a specific tooling event, points toward the transformer's thermal state rather than toward the program or the electrodes.

# 6. Secondary-Circuit Troubleshooting Quick Reference

The following symptom/cause/first-check table is organized the same way as the electrode-troubleshooting table in Chapter 3 — as a starting discrimination tool, not a replacement for the equipment's own diagnostic procedure.

| Symptom | Possible Source | First Checks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Current below expected/commanded value | High circuit resistance (loose connection, worn cable) or a power-stage fault | Resistance/continuity check of the secondary path; power-stage self-diagnostics |
| Uneven or inconsistent current behavior | Connection quality, calibration drift, or a secondary-circuit geometry change (e.g., after a repair) | Verify physical circuit condition, recalibrate current measurement, compare against a known-good baseline |
| Excessive heating in the secondary circuit or transformer | High resistive losses somewhere in the path, or a cooling deficiency | Thermal inspection (thermography if available); verify coolant flow and temperature |
| Quality loss that appears only after a hardware swap (gun, cable, or transformer replacement) | The replacement part has different impedance/geometry than the original, even if nominally "the same part number" | Requalify rather than assume equivalence; compare secondary resistance before and after the swap |

That last row is worth dwelling on: a replacement part carrying the same nominal part number is not proof of equivalent electrical behavior in the installed circuit. Secondary resistance before and after a swap is cheap to measure and directly answers the question that a part-number match alone cannot.

# 1. Generic Architecture and Why Servo Actuation Exists

A servo welding gun positions and closes its electrodes using an electric servo motor and drive rather than a pneumatic cylinder acting against a fixed regulated pressure. The generic functional chain, regardless of manufacturer, is the same: a servo controller/drive commands a motor, the motor drives a mechanical transmission (typically a ballscrew or an equivalent linear-motion mechanism), the transmission moves the gun arm/electrode holder, and the electrode makes contact with the part. A position sensor — and, on some designs, a force sensor — closes the loop back to the drive, so the system knows in real time where the electrode actually is and, in force-sensing designs, how hard it is actually pressing, rather than only what was commanded.

The reason this architecture displaced the simple pneumatic gun in high-value applications is directly tied to the physics established in Chapter 1, Fundamentals and Physics. Electrode force is not a fixed mechanical constant of the equipment; it is a coupled process variable that interacts with current and time to determine heat input, contact resistance and containment of the softened weld zone. A pneumatic gun can only apply the fixed pressure its regulator is set to, uniformly, for every weld in a program — changing it means physically re-adjusting a regulator, which is not something a robot program can do weld-to-weld. A servo gun, by contrast, can command and hold an arbitrary, programmable position and force (or a force profile that changes shape across the weld cycle), and can apply a different qualified force target to different weld points or different stack-ups within the same production program without any hardware adjustment. This makes electrode force a true program variable for the first time, on par with current and time, rather than a plant-wide mechanical setting.

A second, independent benefit follows from programmable positioning rather than from programmable force. Because the gun's closing stroke is commanded rather than fixed, it can adapt to part-to-part variation in access and fit-up without any hardware change, and it can actively compensate for known, predictable geometric change over time — most importantly, electrode wear. As an electrode is dressed (Chapter 13, Preventive Maintenance and Electrode Life), its face is shortened by a small, repeatable amount each time; some servo-gun systems retract the gun's closing stroke automatically to compensate for that shortened electrode, so the electrode continues to reach the same physical contact point without a separate mechanical adjustment after every dressing cycle. Neither of these capabilities — programmable force and automatic geometric compensation — is available from a fixed-pressure pneumatic cylinder, which is the underlying engineering reason servo actuation has become the default choice for high-value, high-precision robotic spot-welding applications even though it costs more and is mechanically more complex than a pneumatic gun.

| Not a Universal Replacement Servo actuation is a superior capability set for programmable, precision force/position control, not a universal replacement for pneumatic actuation in every application. Simpler pneumatic weld guns, clamps and fixtures remain legitimate, qualified equipment for many production contexts, particularly where cost, mechanical simplicity, or a lower-precision process window make the added capability unnecessary (see Section 8 of this chapter for how production context and material drive this choice, and Chapter 7, Cooling and Utilities, on how pneumatic-system health affects any pneumatic actuator regardless of what drives the weld current). |
