# 2. Gun States Through a Weld Cycle (A Vendor-Neutral Model)

A servo gun's controller tracks a small set of functional states as it moves through a weld. The exact state names, exact transition logic and exact fault taxonomy are product-family- and firmware-specific, but the underlying functional states below are a generically applicable model any trainee can use to reason about a real gun regardless of the exact vendor terminology displayed on a pendant or HMI screen.

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Not ready | A safety or self-diagnostic condition does not permit motion or welding |
| Ready | Power, communications and required interlocks are healthy |
| Approaching | The gun is in motion toward the joint |
| Closing | The electrodes are converging on contact |
| Force/position reached | The application-specific readiness condition (commanded force and/or position) is satisfied |
| Welding | The electrical schedule is active |
| Holding | The electrodes remain closed under force per the hold-stage requirement (Chapter 1) |
| Opening | The electrodes are releasing |
| Faulted | Motion or welding is inhibited pending fault resolution |

# 3. Diagnosing "Gun Reaches Position but Weld Does Not Start"

This is a recurring, easy-to-misdiagnose production symptom precisely because it looks like a single failure to an operator watching the cell, when it actually sits at the boundary between two entirely different subsystems: the servo-gun motion system, which is responsible only for getting the electrodes into physical contact at the commanded force/position, and the weld controller, which is responsible for actually deciding whether and when to fire the electrical schedule. A gun that has correctly closed and reached its commanded force tells you nothing about whether the weld controller has independently decided the interlocks, program selection and trigger conditions required to start current are also satisfied.

The correct diagnostic order therefore walks the full readiness chain in sequence, rather than assuming every stalled weld is a welding-parameter problem:

- Confirm the robot (or fixed-gun transfer mechanism) is actually in the commanded position.

- Confirm the gun has closed and reports "closed," not merely "in motion."

- Confirm the force/position readiness condition is actually satisfied and reported to the controller, not just physically true at the tooling.

- Confirm the weld controller itself reports ready (no active fault, no pending self-check).

- Confirm all safety interlocks required for this station and this motion are satisfied.

- Confirm the correct weld program/schedule is actually selected for this part, variant and weld point.

- Confirm the weld trigger command was actually issued and actually accepted by the controller (a trigger can be sent by upstream logic and still be rejected at the controller for a reason not visible upstream).

This ordering matters operationally because the failure modes at each link require completely different corrective actions, even though several of them look identical to an operator as simply "nothing happened." A safety-interlock fault and a wrong-program-selected fault, for example, produce the same visible symptom — the gun sits closed and no weld occurs — but one is a safety-system issue requiring interlock diagnosis and the other is a sequencing/logic issue requiring program-selection diagnosis; treating the two as the same problem wastes time and can mask a genuine safety condition. See Chapter 6, Automation, PLC, Robot and Safety Integration, for how this readiness chain maps onto the cell's layered control architecture, and Chapter 12, Troubleshooting and Diagnostics, for the broader diagnostic-graph discipline this pattern is one instance of.

# 4. Integrated Pressure/Time/Current Control and Gun-Mounted Electronics

Older resistance-welding equipment commonly treats pneumatic pressure as a fixed, unmonitored input and controls only current and time electrically. Some commercial servo-gun systems instead manage pressure (force), time and current together as a single integrated process, which is a materially different control philosophy: rather than the weld controller assuming force is whatever the regulator happens to be delivering, the system actively monitors and manages force through the cycle as a first-class controlled variable, alongside current and time. Described control functions in this class of system typically include electrode grinding (dressing) management, geometric parameter detection (electrode condition and workpiece thickness), workpiece-thickness detection, pressure regulation through the welding cycle, and robot-motion monitoring, with compensation functions such as electrode-pressure calibration, friction compensation, and electrode-rod-length adjustment — the same tip-dressing compensation behavior introduced in Section 1. A representative operating sequence for this class of system is: clamp closure, soft-contact establishment, geometric monitoring, pressure application at the set value, and controlled gun (tong) opening after welding.

Servo-gun platforms of this kind are also commonly built with machine-safety functionality integrated directly into the servo drive itself — safety functions such as safe torque off or safely limited speed, of the type standardized generically by the EN/ISO 13849 (or equivalent) machine-safety family — rather than relying solely on a separate, central safety-relay chain to make the gun's motion safe. This is a real, current servo-gun design consideration, not a theoretical one: distributing safety functions to the drive level changes how a "motion inhibited" fault should be diagnosed, because the inhibiting condition can originate in the drive itself rather than only in an external safety PLC (Chapter 6 develops this point at the cell level).

## Gun-mounted data/identity modules and vendor-naming discipline

Commercial gun systems increasingly include gun-mounted electronics that digitize process signals directly at the gun and store the gun's own configuration/identity data locally. This reduces cabling and lets the wider system recognize which physical gun is actually connected at a given robot or station — a meaningful capability on lines where guns are swapped between robots for maintenance or changeover. Product literature sometimes refers to this class of module by names such as "gun data module" or "measuring gun data module," and separately, some equipment lines use a name pattern along the lines of "weld interface controller" or "weld interface bus" for a dedicated, real-time communication link specifically between the weld controller and gun-mounted sensors/actuators, kept separate from the general factory-automation network (Chapter 6, Automation, PLC, Robot and Safety Integration, discusses this same dedicated real-time bus concept from the cell-communications side). The rest of this subsection goes one level deeper than a name and a one-line description: what this class of hardware actually does, mechanically and electrically, and why each of its design choices exists.

### What actually travels on a dedicated gun-interface bus

A servo gun carries several sensors and actuators that a controller needs to read or command many times within a single weld cycle: a position/encoder sensor on the servo drive (Section 1, Section 2 — this is what tells the system the electrodes have reached "closing" and then "force/position reached"), a force-related signal (either a dedicated force/load-cell sensor on gun designs that have one, or a force estimate derived from motor current/torque on designs that infer force rather than measuring it directly), and, on some gun and process-monitoring designs, a temperature signal from the gun structure or cooling circuit. In the outbound direction, the same link commonly carries the drive/valve command signals the controller issues back to the gun — the commanded position or force setpoint for a servo drive, or a valve-actuation command on a hybrid pneumatic-assist design. The mechanistic point worth being explicit about is where the analog-to-digital conversion physically happens: rather than running each of these signals as a separate, full-length analog wire from the gun all the way back to a remote controller cabinet, the gun-mounted electronics convert them to digital data immediately at the gun, and a single digital bus cable then carries all of them, multiplexed, back to the controller. This is a fundamentally different cabling topology from an older architecture where every sensor is its own dedicated analog run — it collapses many parallel, noise-susceptible analog conductors (each vulnerable to signal degradation over the length of a robot-carried cable and to electrical noise from the welding transformer's own high secondary current) into one digital link, which is the direct physical reason for the cabling reduction, not merely a marketing description of it.

### What class of cycle time this operates at, and why it has to be fast

Force and position are closed-loop control variables (Section 1): the drive commands a target, reads back the actual measured position/force, and continuously corrects the difference throughout the approach, closing and hold stages of a weld cycle that, in total, is typically measured in a fraction of a second to at most a few seconds per weld. A closed loop is only as good as how often it gets a fresh measurement and can issue a fresh correction; a feedback update that arrives too slowly relative to the mechanical dynamics it is trying to control produces exactly the kind of force instability and position overshoot that a monitoring system (Chapter 11, Process Monitoring and Adaptive Control) would otherwise read as unexplained weld-to-weld variation. This is the underlying engineering reason a dedicated gun-interface bus exists as a physically and logically separate link from the general factory-automation fieldbus described in Chapter 6: a general-purpose industrial Ethernet segment carrying diagnostics, program selection and other supervisory traffic is not built to guarantee the same fast, deterministic update rate a real-time force/position control loop needs, and mixing time-critical control traffic onto a shared, best-effort network risks exactly the kind of intermittent, load-dependent timing jitter that a control loop cannot tolerate. Put qualitatively, and without asserting a number this chapter cannot verify for equipment in general: this class of link is fast and deterministic by design, not merely fast in the way a modern factory Ethernet segment is generally fast — deterministic here means the controller can rely on a bounded, predictable time between one measurement and the next, which is the property a closed-loop drive actually needs, independent of whatever raw bandwidth the link happens to carry.

At least one publicly documented commercial product family states that its dedicated weld-interface link runs at a 1 kHz cycle rate — that is, a fresh exchange of sensor and command data roughly every millisecond. This specific figure is stated here only because it is the one number this reference set could verify against a real, currently published commercial specification, and it is reported strictly as an example of the class of cycle time this kind of link operates at, not as a general figure that applies to every dedicated gun-interface bus on the market; a different product family's equivalent link may run faster, slower, or on a different update scheme entirely.

### What the gun-mounted data module stores, and why that matters mechanically

Beyond digitizing live process signals, the same class of gun-mounted electronics commonly stores a small set of data locally, at the gun itself, rather than only in the station's central controller configuration. Three categories recur across how this concept is described in commercial equipment: (1) the gun's own identity — enough information for the controller to recognize which specific physical gun has just been connected, rather than assuming whatever gun is plugged into a given robot arm is the one the station was configured for; (2) calibration and scaling data — the specific conversion factors that translate this individual gun's raw sensor signal (a raw encoder count, a raw force-sensor or motor-current reading) into a correct engineering-unit position or force value, which is properly a property of the specific physical gun and its specific sensors, not a generic constant that applies equally to every gun of the same model; and (3) wear/usage counters — accumulated counts such as weld count or dressing count that support the tip-life and preventive-maintenance tracking already discussed in Chapter 13, Preventive Maintenance and Electrode Life, and the weld-event traceability discussed in Chapter 17, Traceability and Digital Thread.

The mechanical/functional reason this matters is a direct consequence of where that data physically lives. If a gun's calibration and identity data are stored only in a station's central controller configuration file, then swapping a gun onto a different robot, or replacing a faulted gun with a spare, requires someone to manually locate and re-enter that specific gun's calibration at the new station before it can be trusted to weld correctly — a manual step that is slow, is a real source of production error if skipped or entered incorrectly, and does not scale well on a line where guns move between robots for maintenance or changeover. Storing identity, calibration and usage data locally on the gun instead means the data travels physically with the hardware: when the gun is connected to any compatible robot or controller, the controller reads that stored data directly from the gun over the same digital link described above and can immediately apply the correct calibration and recognize the correct usage/wear state, without a manual re-entry step. This is the concrete mechanism behind the commonly stated "reduces cabling and enables faster tool change" benefit — it is not that the module makes tool change fast in some abstract sense, but specifically that it eliminates a manual, error-prone data-re-entry step that would otherwise have to happen every time a gun physically moves.

| Neither Name, Nor the Bus Protocol, Nor the Cycle Rate, Is a Standardized Term — Read the Nameplate Everything in this subsection — "what travels on the bus," "what class of cycle time it runs at," and "what the module stores" — describes a real, generic, mechanistic pattern confirmed against real commercial product documentation during research for this reference set, not a speculative or invented architecture. But neither "gun data module" nor "weld interface controller/bus" is standardized industry vocabulary (Chapter 15, Glossary of Terms, "Vendor-specific acronyms"), and none of the following is safe to assume equally across every manufacturer or product line: the exact name displayed on a nameplate, configuration screen or alarm; the exact communication protocol used on the dedicated bus; the exact cycle rate it runs at (the 1 kHz figure above is documented for one specific product family, not a general industry constant); or the exact set of data fields the module stores and how they are labeled. Different manufacturers — and sometimes different product lines from the same manufacturer — use closely related but not necessarily identical names, protocols and data models for what is, underneath, a similar underlying concept. The correct action when a real alarm, part number, or configuration screen uses one of these terms is to identify the exact product family and firmware/hardware revision from the equipment's own nameplate or configuration screen and consult that unit's specific manual — never assume one manufacturer's or product line's definition, protocol, or cycle rate applies identically to another's similarly named feature. |

# 5. Servo Motor Types: Synchronous vs. Asynchronous

Everything in Sections 1–4 describes what a servo gun's control architecture does — command and monitor position and force in a closed loop. None of it depends on which physical motor technology sits inside the servo drive. That choice is itself an engineering decision with real consequences for the precision, dynamics and cost of the gun's force/position control, and it is worth treating explicitly because the underlying corpus for this reference set does not otherwise address it.

Industrial servo motors are built on two broadly different rotor technologies. A synchronous servo motor, in the form most common in modern high-performance motion control, uses a permanent-magnet rotor: the rotor turns in exact lock-step ("synchronism") with the rotating magnetic field set up by the stator's supply frequency, with no slip between the two. An asynchronous (induction) motor instead induces current in its rotor electromagnetically, which requires the rotor to run slightly behind — to "slip" relative to — the stator's field in order to generate torque at all; that slip is inherent to how an induction motor produces torque, not a defect.

Reputable industrial-automation and motion-control references converge on several qualitative differences that follow from this distinction, though the sources consulted for this section frame the comparison slightly differently and neither source publishes a rigorous, apples-to-apples quantitative benchmark, which is stated plainly rather than papered over with an invented number:

- Speed/positioning precision. Because a permanent-magnet synchronous motor tracks supply frequency with no slip, it maintains constant, precisely controllable speed largely independent of load changes, which industrial-automation references describe as making synchronous designs well suited to applications "requiring high precision" and "exact positioning and movement" [S22]. An induction (asynchronous) motor's inherent slip means there is always some discrepancy between the electrical supply frequency and actual rotor speed, which the same source describes as making asynchronous designs "less precise in speed control compared to synchronous motors" [S22]. A separate industrial-automation source frames the comparison differently — as permanent-magnet motors generally versus AC induction motors generally, rather than specifically as "servo" sub-types — and states plainly that permanent-magnet designs are "less accurate than servomotors" while conventional AC induction motors can still achieve high accuracy in the right application [S21]; the two sources do not use identical category boundaries, which is exactly the kind of terminology inconsistency this reference set flags rather than silently resolves (see the note below).

- Torque/speed characteristics and power density. Permanent-magnet designs are described as offering "excellent torque for its size" in a compact package [S21], while conventional AC induction motors are described as having lower speed range and power density compared with permanent-magnet motors [S21]. Neither source consulted here gives a specific, verifiable percentage figure for the torque-density gap, so none is stated.

- Efficiency and duty cycle. Synchronous (permanent-magnet) designs are described as generally more efficient than induction designs, "especially at lower speeds," while induction designs are described as "less efficient at lower speeds where the occurrence of slip...can lead to increased energy consumption" [S22]; a separate source similarly describes permanent-magnet designs as "more compact and energy efficient, leading to low operating costs" versus induction designs having "higher operating costs over time" with "reduced efficiency at low loads" [S21]. This matters for a weld-gun duty cycle specifically because a servo gun's motor is repeatedly accelerating, holding, and decelerating over a very short cycle (approach, squeeze, hold, release, repeated every few seconds) rather than running continuously at a steady operating speed — a duty cycle dominated by low-speed, high-torque-demand intervals is exactly where both sources agree the efficiency and torque-density gap between the two technologies is largest.

- Cost. Both sources agree, in direction if not in exact figure, that induction (asynchronous) motors are the lower-cost option and permanent-magnet (synchronous) designs carry a cost premium: one source calls induction motors "cost-effective" against synchronous designs' "higher cost and complexity" [S22], and the other independently states that induction motors "tend to be the least expensive to purchase" while permanent-magnet motors are "more expensive than induction motors" [S21]. No specific price ratio is published by either source, so none is stated here.

What this implies for weld-gun force/position control and welding "protocol" — i.e., the achievable squeeze-time control, force-feedback precision and duty-cycle behavior discussed throughout this reference set — follows directly from the precision and dynamic-response characteristics above, reasoned from first principles rather than from a source that specifically tested a resistance-welding gun: a servo gun spends its entire duty cycle in exactly the low-speed, high-precision, frequently-reversing regime where a permanent-magnet synchronous motor's no-slip speed/position tracking and superior low-speed efficiency are most valuable, and where an induction motor's inherent slip works directly against the tight, repeatable squeeze-position and force-ramp control a qualified weld schedule depends on (Chapter 1, Section 4, on why force is a coupled, not fixed, process variable). A drive that cannot hold a precisely repeatable position/force trajectory at low speed will show up, in production, as weld-to-weld force variation that a monitoring system (Chapter 11) would read as unexplained process drift rather than as a known equipment-selection tradeoff.

Readers should treat the paragraph above as informed engineering reasoning grounded in sourced motor characteristics, not as a sourced fact about what motor type any particular commercial gun contains — that detail, like the gun-mounted-module naming question in Section 4, is a product-family-specific fact to confirm from the equipment's own documentation. # 6. Servo-Gun Parameters Relevant to Procedure Eligibility

A weld procedure is qualified for a specific combination of material, equipment and settings (Chapter 8, WPS and Qualification). Because a servo gun is itself a programmable piece of equipment with its own health and capability state, several gun-specific parameters must be verified — not merely assumed — before a given qualified procedure can be trusted to run correctly on a specific physical gun.

| Parameter | Why Procedure Selection Depends on It |
| --- | --- |
| Gun type/family | Sets the mechanical envelope and force/motion capability the gun can physically deliver |
| Maximum/nominal force | Must cover the qualified force target for the procedure being requested |
| Stroke | Must reach the joint and allow safe electrode separation afterward |
| Force calibration status | Absolute commanded force is only trustworthy if calibration is current |
| Position/encoder calibration and health | Squeeze/contact position and closed-loop control depend on trustworthy feedback |
| Speed/motion profile | Affects approach and squeeze-phase timing and repeatability |
| Compensation features enabled (e.g., electrode-length/tip-wear compensation) | Some qualified procedures assume a specific compensation behavior is active |
| Cooling interface | Thermal stability of the electrode/tooling depends on it, same as the transformer (Chapter 7, Cooling and Utilities) |

# 7. Typical Servo-Gun Fault Classes and First Diagnostic Branch

| Fault Class | Representative Causes | First Diagnostic Branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Encoder/position fault | Cable/connector fault, sensor fault, drive electronics fault | Inspect connections; compare commanded vs. actual position |
| Overcurrent (drive) | Mechanical jam, obstruction, or commanded acceleration too aggressive for the load | Mechanical inspection first, then drive diagnostics |
| Force deviation | Calibration drift, mechanical wear/friction, obstruction, feedback-sensor fault | Force-trace comparison against baseline; mechanical inspection |
| Home/reference fault | Reference sensor fault or lost calibration | Run the equipment's approved homing/reference procedure; verify position repeatability afterward |
| Communication fault (drive bus) | Network/cable fault or configuration mismatch | Network and drive-bus diagnostics |

A weld controller can output an electrically correct, in-tolerance current program and still produce inconsistent welds if gun force is wrong or unstable. This is why servo-gun health belongs in the same diagnostic graph as the electrical power path, not in a separate "mechanical-only" category (Chapter 12, Troubleshooting and Diagnostics) — a force-deviation fault and a current-deviation fault can produce visually identical weld defects, and only checking both domains in the same investigation avoids mis-attributing a mechanical problem to the electrical schedule or vice versa.

# 9. Core Terminology Quick Reference

A full alphabetical glossary is provided in Chapter 15, including the "Vendor-specific acronyms" caution referenced throughout this chapter. The entries below are the small set of terms specific to servo-gun discussion.

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Servo gun | A resistance-welding gun that positions and closes its electrodes using an electric servo drive rather than (or in addition to) pneumatic actuation, typically enabling programmable position and/or force control. |
| Synchronous (permanent-magnet) servo motor | A servo motor whose rotor tracks the stator's supply frequency with no slip, commonly associated with high precision and good low-speed efficiency [S22]. |
| Asynchronous (induction) servo motor | A servo motor whose rotor is driven by induced current and inherently runs at a slight slip relative to the stator's supply frequency, commonly associated with lower cost and lower precision at low speed [S22]. |
| Weld interface controller/bus | A vendor-naming pattern (not a standardized term) for a dedicated, real-time communication link between a weld controller and gun-mounted sensors/actuators, separate from the general factory network. See Chapter 15, Glossary of Terms. |
| Gun data module | A vendor-naming pattern (not a standardized term) for gun-mounted electronics that digitize process signals at the gun and store the gun's own identity/configuration data locally. See Chapter 15, Glossary of Terms. |
| Force/position readiness | The generic functional condition — regardless of exact controller wording — confirming the gun has both reached its commanded position and established its commanded force before the weld controller may be permitted to fire. |

# 1. Control Hierarchy in a Typical Robotic Spot-Welding Cell

A production spot-welding cell is layered, and correct diagnostic reasoning respects that layering rather than jumping straight to "the welding parameters" for every symptom the moment something goes wrong. Each layer has a distinct responsibility, its own fault domain, and its own diagnostic tools, and a fault that presents identically to an operator at the cell door can originate in any one of them.

- Business/production layer — the manufacturing execution system (MES) or production database: order context and part genealogy. This layer decides what should be built next, not how any individual weld is made.

- Cell supervisory layer — the PLC and safety PLC: overall sequence logic, interlocks, and safe-state management. This is where the cell decides whether it is safe and correct to proceed to the next step.

- Motion layer — the robot controller and servo-gun drive: position, force, and motion state (Chapter 5, Servo Guns and Gun-Drive Systems, covers the gun side of this layer in detail).

- Welding layer — the weld controller and power stage: program selection, current/voltage delivery, and result reporting (Chapter 4, Power Systems: Transformers and Controllers).

- Physical process — the electrodes, sheets and fixture: where the actual weld forms (Chapter 1, Fundamentals and Physics).

- Monitoring layer — current/voltage/force/displacement/cooling sensors: the evidence that connects layers 2 through 5 to a quality outcome (Chapter 11, Process Monitoring and Adaptive Control).

The practical value of thinking in these six layers is that it turns a vague symptom ("the cell stopped," "the weld looked bad") into a specific question about which layer's responsibility failed, which in turn points to which subsystem's own diagnostics should be consulted first — a discipline developed further in Chapter 12, Troubleshooting and Diagnostics.

# 2. Typical Production Sequence

A representative sequence through one weld cycle at the cell level, expressed generically enough to apply regardless of the specific PLC, robot or weld-controller product in use:

- Load or detect the part.

- Verify part presence and fixture state.

- Select the correct robot and weld programs for this part, variant and station.

- Move to the weld position.

- Check safety and readiness conditions.

- Close the servo gun and verify the required readiness condition (force/position — Chapter 5).

- Trigger the weld controller.

- Receive the weld result.

- Store the result and update traceability (Chapter 17, Traceability and Digital Thread).

- Continue, reject, or stop according to the site's validated logic.

Every step in this sequence is itself a small readiness check that must be satisfied before the next step is permitted — this is exactly the structure Chapter 5, Section 3 walks through in the specific case of "gun reaches position but weld does not start," and the same discipline of naming and checking each individual condition, rather than inferring it from elapsed time, applies to the whole cell sequence, not only to the gun.

# 3. Interlocks: Why They Must Be Explicit Signals, Not Timing Assumptions

Interlocks exist specifically to prevent unsafe or invalid sequencing. To do that reliably, they should be explicit, individually named signals with a documented meaning — "robot in position," "gun ready," "weld controller ready," "cooling healthy," "safety circuit healthy," "correct program selected" — rather than implicit assumptions baked into a fixed timing delay.

| Why "It Usually Works" Is Not the Same as "It Is Correctly Interlocked" A cell where "gun ready" is inferred from an elapsed-time delay rather than an actual feedback signal will eventually produce an intermittent, hard-to-reproduce fault exactly when the timing assumption breaks down — for example, a slightly slower-than-usual gun stroke on a cold morning. The fault will appear rare and confusing precisely because the timing assumption is usually close enough to correct; it is only wrong at the margins, which is exactly when a genuine safety or quality risk is most likely to be missed rather than caught. An explicit, monitored feedback signal does not have this failure mode: it is either true or it is not, regardless of ambient conditions. |
| --- |

# 4. Communications: Two Distinct Tiers With Different Timing Requirements

A modern cell typically layers several kinds of communication on top of each other: hardwired I/O for simple, often safety-related handshakes; industrial Ethernet fieldbus protocols for diagnostics, program selection and general data exchange; a dedicated robot-controller-to-weld-controller interface for the weld trigger/result handshake; and, where higher-level traceability or analytics are implemented, OPC UA or a database gateway.

A typical real-world layering of this communication is worth stating precisely because it explains why a cell's network diagram usually contains at least two distinct communication tiers with very different timing requirements. Commercial resistance-welding controllers commonly support a general factory-automation fieldbus — Ethernet-based industrial protocols, at 10/100 Mbit/s or faster, often with an embedded web server, and/or legacy fieldbus types still found on older installations — alongside discrete 24V digital I/O and serial connections, for supervisory data, program selection and diagnostics. Separately, some platforms implement a purpose-built, dedicated real-time communication bus, documented in at least one commercial product family as running at a 1 kHz cycle rate, specifically for the weld-controller-to-gun/sensor communication path, rather than routing that time-critical traffic over the general-purpose factory network.

| Naming Caution — "Weld Interface Controller/Bus" Is Not a Standard Term This dedicated real-time link is sometimes referred to in product literature by a name pattern such as "weld interface controller" or "weld interface bus." That is a vendor naming pattern, not standardized industry vocabulary — the exact name, protocol and cycle rate are product-specific and must be confirmed from the exact product family and firmware/hardware revision installed, never assumed from a generic description (Chapter 15, Glossary of Terms, "Vendor-specific acronyms"; Chapter 5, Section 4, discusses the same concept from the gun side). What is universal, and safe to rely on generically, is the underlying architectural pattern: a general-purpose supervisory fieldbus for cell-level data, and a separate, faster, dedicated bus for the time-critical weld process itself. |
| --- |

# 5. Safety Architecture, Generically

A resistance-welding cell's safety system typically includes a safety PLC or safety-rated logic managing e-stops, guard interlocks and light curtains; safety-rated I/O modules; and, on modern servo-driven equipment, safety functions integrated directly into the servo drive itself — safe torque off, safely limited speed, and similar functions, of the type standardized generically by the IEC/ISO 13849 or IEC 61508 family of machine-safety standards (Chapter 5, Section 4, discusses this same drive-integrated safety pattern from the gun side).

Commercial resistance-welding I/O catalogs commonly include a dedicated safety-zone monitoring module for safety devices, alongside general-purpose fieldbus I/O modules — some rated for harsh physical/environmental conditions — a subset of which are offered in explicitly safety-rated variants (safety digital-input and safety digital-output modules). This reflects a real, common pattern worth stating explicitly: safety functions distributed across drive-level and I/O-level hardware, not concentrated solely in a single central safety PLC.

| A Diagnostic Consequence of Distributed Safety Because safety functions can live at the drive level, the I/O-module level, or the central safety-PLC level, a "motion inhibited" fault can legitimately originate from any of the three, and each requires different diagnostic access — a central safety-PLC fault log, a zone-monitoring module's own diagnostics, or the servo drive's own internal safety-function status. Assuming the central safety PLC is always the source of a motion-inhibit fault, simply because it is the most familiar place to look, will send a technician to the wrong subsystem exactly as often as the real cause happens to sit elsewhere (Chapter 12, Troubleshooting and Diagnostics). |
| --- |

# 6. ISO 10218-1 and ISO 10218-2: Robot and Robot-System Safety Requirements

Everything in Sections 3 through 5 describes cell-level interlocks and safety architecture in generic, functional terms. The specific international standards family that governs the safety design of the industrial robot itself, and of the robot cell it is integrated into, is ISO 10218, published in two parts. Both parts were most recently republished as new editions in February 2025, superseding their respective 2011 editions, so any procedure or purchasing specification that still cites the 2011 edition by number should be checked against the current edition before being relied on.

The reason a robot-safety standards series belongs in the same chapter as PLC and fieldbus architecture is straightforward: nearly every safety concept already introduced generically in Sections 3 through 5 of this chapter — safety-rated stop functions integrated into the drive, guard interlocks and light curtains managed by the safety PLC, and the overall discipline of layered, explicit interlocking rather than timing assumptions — is exactly the category of requirement that ISO 10218-1 places on the robot manufacturer and ISO 10218-2 places on the cell integrator. A spot-welding cell's robot is, in the vocabulary of this standards series, the motion-layer hardware described in Section 1 of this chapter, and the cell built around it is squarely what ISO 10218-2 calls a "robot cell."

# 8. The Correct AI/Decision-Support Boundary in This Architecture

An automated decision-support or diagnostic-assistance function should advise, retrieve evidence and explain — it should not independently bypass a safety interlock, silently change a qualified welding parameter, reset a safety-relevant fault, or release a nonconforming product for shipment. Any of those actions must remain inside the organization's approved automation and quality-control mechanisms, with a human or an explicitly authorized system-of-record making the actual change.

This is a basic industrial-safety and quality-governance principle, not a hedge specific to any one vendor or software system, and it follows directly from the layered architecture described in this chapter: the cell supervisory layer, welding layer and safety architecture each have a defined authority to change cell state, and a decision-support function sits logically outside that chain of authority no matter how confident its analysis is. The correct role for such a function is the same one this chapter's own diagnostic tables and readiness checklists play — helping a qualified person find the right answer faster — never substituting its own judgment for the interlock, qualification or release decision itself.

# 1. Why Utilities Are a Process Variable, Not Just Plant Infrastructure

Resistance welding is a high-power, repetitive process, and the equipment that delivers it depends on three utilities that are easy to take for granted precisely because they usually just work in the background: cooling water (or air, on smaller equipment), compressed air, and electrical supply. All three influence thermal stability, actuator performance and equipment health directly, and none of them is merely facilities plumbing that sits outside the welding process itself.

The reason this matters at the level of process validity, not just equipment maintenance, is that several of the quantities this reference set has already established as process-critical are themselves temperature-sensitive: tip life and wear rate (Chapter 13, Preventive Maintenance and Electrode Life), transformer thermal margin (Chapter 4, Power Systems: Transformers and Controllers), and even the shape of the dynamic-resistance curve during the weld itself (Chapter 1, Fundamentals and Physics) all respond to how well heat is actually being removed from the equipment between and during welds. A weld schedule was qualified under specific utility conditions, and it cannot be treated as still valid independent of those conditions merely because no parameter in the controller changed.

| A Schedule Can Silently Stop Being Valid Without Anyone Touching the Controller A schedule that was qualified with a chiller supplying 18°C water, and is later run against a chiller struggling to hold 28°C, is not automatically still a validated process — even though no current, time, or force parameter in the weld controller changed at all. This is a genuinely counter-intuitive point worth stating explicitly: from the controller's point of view, and from a casual glance at the program screen, nothing is different. The equipment's actual thermal state, and therefore its actual behavior, can be materially different anyway. Utility drift is exactly the kind of "the program didn't change but quality did" root cause that a purely parameter-focused investigation will miss. |
| --- |

# 2. The Cooling Circuit, Generically

The cooling path in a typical installation runs from a chiller or plant-water source, through a supply/return manifold, through hoses and fittings, through filters/strainers, through flow monitoring and temperature monitoring, through heat exchangers, and finally into the actual cooling passages inside the gun, transformer and electrodes. It is worth walking through why each stage in that chain matters on its own, because every stage is a potential single point of failure for the whole line's thermal margin, and understanding why each exists is what lets a technician reason about a new failure mode rather than only recognizing ones already seen before.

- Chiller or plant-water source — sets the coolant's starting temperature, which is the single biggest lever on the whole circuit's available thermal margin. Everything downstream can only remove heat as effectively as the supply temperature allows; a chiller that is undersized for the installed welding load, or that is simply degrading with age, quietly erodes margin everywhere else in the circuit even if every other component is in perfect condition.

- Supply/return manifold — distributes coolant to multiple guns, transformers or electrode circuits from a common source and collects the warmed return flow. A manifold problem (a partially closed valve, an imbalanced distribution) can starve one branch of the cell while every other branch reads normally, which is why flow and temperature are worth checking per branch, not only at the manifold header.

- Hoses and fittings — carry the coolant the last distance to the actual equipment. They are also the most mechanically exposed part of the circuit — subject to flexing, abrasion, heat and, on a robot-carried gun, continuous motion — so they are a common site for the leaks discussed in Section 3.

- Filters/strainers — remove particulate and scale before it can reach and block the narrow cooling passages inside the gun, transformer and electrodes. A neglected filter does not fail dramatically; it fails by slowly restricting flow, which is exactly the kind of gradual, easy-to-miss degradation that scheduled inspection exists to catch.

- Flow monitoring — exists specifically to catch a developing restriction or loss before it becomes an outright cooling failure, rather than relying on a technician to notice reduced performance after the fact.

- Temperature monitoring — confirms that the flow being measured is actually removing heat effectively, not merely that fluid is moving; a circuit can have nominal flow with degraded temperature performance if the coolant itself is too warm or a heat exchanger is fouled.

- Heat exchangers — transfer heat out of the coolant loop to the plant's ultimate heat rejection (ambient air, plant chilled water, or an external cooling tower depending on installation). Fouling here reduces the whole circuit's effective capacity even when every downstream reading looks locally normal.

- Cooling passages inside the gun, transformer and electrodes — are where the heat removal actually has to happen, at the exact locations generating or accumulating the most heat: the electrode tips (Chapter 3, Electrodes and Tooling), the transformer core and windings (Chapter 4), and, on a servo gun, the drive and mechanical assembly itself (Chapter 5).

# 3. Cooling Fault Patterns

| Condition | Effect | Diagnostic Clue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Low flow | Poor heat removal from electrodes/gun/transformer | Flow-switch alarm, or a rising temperature trend without an alarm if the flow sensor itself has failed |
| High inlet (supply) temperature | Reduced thermal margin even at nominal flow | Trend deviation against the historical baseline for the same ambient/production conditions |
| Blocked passage (scale, debris) | Localized overheating even though overall circuit flow looks adequate | Localized temperature or flow abnormality restricted to one branch/electrode |
| Leaks | Loss of flow, and a direct equipment/electrical-safety risk | Pressure or flow change, or a visible leak |

Reading this table against Section 2's chain is itself a diagnostic technique: because each fault condition has a distinct set of chain stages that could plausibly cause it, knowing which stage a given symptom is consistent with narrows the physical inspection considerably before any tooling is opened up.

# 4. A Specific Diagnostic Case: A Low-Flow Alarm With Confirmed Adequate Flow

One diagnostic case is worth stating explicitly and in full, because it is genuinely counter-intuitive and because getting it wrong has a real safety and equipment-damage cost.

| Symptom | The weld controller (or cooling monitoring system) reports a low-flow alarm, but physical inspection confirms coolant flow at the affected point is actually adequate. |
| --- | --- |
| Category | Cooling / instrumentation — a sensor or wiring fault, not a genuine cooling-circuit loss. |
| Likely Causes | • Flow sensor or flow-switch failure • A wiring or connector fault between the sensor and the monitoring system • Sensor fouling, drift, or miscalibration |
| Diagnostic Steps | 1. Physically verify actual coolant flow at the affected branch/electrode, independent of the alarm indication. 2. Compare the confirmed physical flow reading against what the alarm is reporting. 3. If flow is confirmed adequate while the alarm persists, treat the sensor or its wiring as the fault under investigation, not the cooling circuit itself. 4. Inspect and, as needed, repair or replace the flow sensor and its connections rather than the cooling hardware. |
| Safety Note | Never suppress or bypass a cooling alarm simply to keep producing, even once the sensor is suspected as the actual fault. A genuine future cooling loss would then go undetected by a system the line has been trained to distrust, and can damage electrodes, the gun, or the transformer, in addition to degrading weld quality in ways that may not surface until much later. |
| Escalation | If the sensor or wiring fault cannot be found and corrected promptly, escalate to maintenance/controls engineering and keep the alarm active and respected rather than operating the line on an alarm the crew has started to ignore. |

# 5. Pneumatics

Where pneumatic actuation is still used — clamps, fixtures, non-servo dressers, or simpler pneumatic weld guns (Chapter 5, Section 8, discusses when pneumatic actuation remains an appropriate choice) — pressure stability, air quality (moisture and particulate content) and valve condition affect repeatability even when the welding schedule itself is completely unchanged. This is worth stating plainly because it is a common source of a confusing investigation: a slow pneumatic-pressure drift is a classic cause of a "the program didn't change but quality did" investigation that turns out to have nothing to do with the weld controller, the electrodes, or the material at all. Pneumatic force in this context behaves like a hidden process variable in exactly the way Chapter 5 describes electrode force behaving on a pneumatic gun generally: fixed by a regulator setting rather than actively monitored, so a slow drift in supply pressure, moisture content, or valve response is not something the weld controller has any visibility into at all.

# 6. Electrical Supply Quality

The plant power feeding the welding equipment must match the equipment's electrical requirements: voltage, phase balance, harmonic content, and short-circuit/inrush capacity. This last consideration matters particularly for MFDC inverter-based systems, since inverters are inherently more sensitive to input-side power quality than a simple line-frequency transformer is (Chapter 4, Power Systems: Transformers and Controllers, describes why MFDC systems rectify and invert the incoming supply before it ever reaches the welding transformer — every one of those additional power-electronic stages is another place input-side power quality can matter).

Voltage instability, phase imbalance, harmonics, or an undersized supply relative to the installed welding load can cause controller faults or reduced process availability that, looking at the weld-quality data alone, present exactly like a mechanical or parameter problem. This is precisely the same investigative trap described for cooling drift and pneumatic-pressure drift above: the weld controller's own program did not change, so a technician who only checks the program will not find the cause, even though the actual root cause sits entirely outside the welding schedule.

| Exact Electrical Requirements Are Equipment-Specific Exact electrical requirements — voltage tolerance, inrush current, required supply capacity — are equipment- and product-family-specific and must come from that specific controller/transformer's own technical data, not from a general rule of thumb (Chapter 4, Power Systems: Transformers and Controllers, on why product-family identification matters before consulting a spec at all). No specific voltage-tolerance or inrush-current figure is stated in this chapter for that reason: stating one here, detached from a specific product family, would itself be exactly the kind of unverified generalization this reference set is built to avoid. |
| --- |

Taken together, the three sections above make the same point from three different utilities: cooling, pneumatics and electrical supply quality all sit upstream of the weld controller's own program, all can drift independently of anything an operator or programmer touches, and all three are common, genuine root causes of a quality investigation that looks — from the weld data alone — like a welding-parameter or equipment problem. Treating utility health as part of the process, and not merely as facilities infrastructure that either works or doesn't, is what lets that root cause actually be found.

# 1. What a WPS Is, and What It Is Not

A Welding Procedure Specification (WPS) is a controlled engineering document that specifies a qualified — or otherwise formally approved — set of welding conditions, together with the scope of parts, materials and equipment to which those conditions apply [S7]. It is a quality-system document before it is anything else: it exists to record what has been proven to work, under what conditions, and it carries the approval, revision and traceability metadata needed to answer "is this the currently valid procedure for this joint" at any later point. That last requirement — resolvability at any later point — is why a WPS cannot be treated as a one-time engineering artifact that is written once and then referred to loosely; it has to survive audits, root-cause investigations and customer reviews years after it was first approved.

This chapter is one of the most consequential in the whole reference set, because the distinction it draws is the single most common source of confusion between engineering, quality and controls disciplines on a real production floor: a WPS is not the same thing as a machine (controller) program, and the two must never be conflated, filed as the same document, or assumed to update in lockstep.

| Aspect | WPS (Engineering / Quality Document) | Machine / Controller Program (Chapter 16) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | A controlled document stating qualified conditions and their scope of applicability | An executable machine configuration — literal current/time/force values and pulse structure loaded into a specific controller |
| Where it lives | Quality-system document control (paper or electronic), independent of any one machine | On the weld controller (or its program-management system) at a specific station |
| What it contains | Material/joint scope, qualification basis, essential-variable ranges of validity, approval and revision metadata, required inspection | The numeric schedule itself — current, time, force, pulse pattern, stage/step configuration for one station |
| Cardinality | One WPS may legitimately correspond to multiple machine programs, across multiple stations, as long as each stays within the WPS’s stated validity | One program serves one station/controller configuration; several programs may all trace to the same WPS |
| What it lacks on its own | Not an executable configuration by itself — cannot be "loaded" into a controller | Typically lacks the material/joint scope statement, the qualification basis, and the revision/approval metadata a WPS carries — a program alone is not sufficient to constitute a WPS |
| Who changes it and how | Changed only through engineering/quality change control, against essential-variable limits | Can be changed at the controller by a programmer or technician — which is exactly why an uncontrolled program edit can silently take production outside the qualified WPS without anyone updating a document |

| Why This Distinction Is Not Academic Because a machine program can be edited directly at a controller’s interface, it is entirely possible for the executing schedule at a station to drift away from what the approved WPS actually authorizes without any document being revised at all. The WPS is the reference that says what is allowed; the program is what is actually running. A functioning quality system depends on a change-control link between the two so that no program edit reaches production without being checked against the WPS it claims to implement — this link is exactly what the traceability schema in Chapter 17, Traceability and Digital Thread, is built to preserve. |
| --- |

# 2. The Governing Standards: ISO 15609-5 and ISO 15614-12

Two ISO standards, read together, define the whole WPS-and-qualification discipline for resistance welding. They answer two different questions: one specifies what a WPS document must contain, and the other specifies how a procedure earns the right to be written into a WPS in the first place.

| Standard | Edition / Status | Published Scope | What It Actually Covers | How It Is Used |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ISO 15609-5 | 2011 | Specification and qualification of welding procedures for metallic materials — Welding procedure specification — Part 5: Resistance welding | Specifies the required content of a WPS for resistance welding: it identifies the variables that can influence weld dimensions, nugget dimensions, weld-pattern positioning, mechanical properties and joint geometry, which an organization must translate into its own controlled WPS template and quality system. | Governs the format and mandatory content fields of every resistance-welding WPS discussed in this chapter |
| ISO 15614-12 | 2021 (previously 2014, 2004) | Specification and qualification of welding procedures for metallic materials — Welding procedure test — Part 12: Spot, seam and projection welding | Specifies the tests used to qualify a WPS for spot, seam and projection welding, and defines the conditions for carrying out those tests and the resulting limits of validity (essential variables and their approved ranges). | Governs the qualification test program that must be completed and passed before a WPS can be approved for production use |

Neither standard publishes a single universal numeric checklist that applies to every application — this corpus does not assert one either, because none exists. ISO 15614-12 specifies the qualification test structure and the concept of essential variables and validity limits; the exact route (which tests, how many samples, what constitutes a pass) is determined by the applicable edition of the standard together with the customer specification and the organization’s own quality system. This is stated plainly rather than smoothed over, because inventing a generic checklist where the standard deliberately leaves the decision to the applicable governing document would itself be a compliance risk.

# 3. The WPS Data Groups a Compliant Document Must Contain

ISO 15609-5 does not prescribe a rigid form layout, but it does specify the categories of content that must be present so that anyone reading the WPS later — an auditor, a new engineer, a customer reviewer — can determine exactly what was qualified and where its boundaries lie. The following table lays out the suggested data groups and the specific fields each should carry, organized the way a real resistance-welding WPS template is structured in practice.

| Data Group | Suggested Fields | Why It Matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Identification | WPS number, revision, approval status, date | The unique key every downstream record (program, inspection report, weld-event record) must reference to resolve which procedure applied |
| Process | Process name and ISO 4063 reference number (e.g. 21 for resistance spot welding; see Chapter 9, Standards and Compliance Reference) | Unambiguously identifies the welding process itself, independent of any vendor terminology |
| Parent materials | Grades, thicknesses, coatings | Material and coating changes are classic essential-variable triggers for requalification (Chapter 2, Materials, Coatings and Weldability) |
| Joint | Lap/stack-up configuration, weld-point location, pitch/spacing, access constraints | Joint geometry directly determines current path, shunting risk and electrode access, all of which the qualification tested |
| Electrodes | Type, material/RWMA class, geometry, dressing rule | Electrode face geometry sets current density; a different electrode family or dressing rule can invalidate a qualified schedule (Chapter 3, Electrodes and Tooling) |
| Machine | Controller product/family, transformer, gun, secondary-circuit configuration | Equipment capability (e.g. AC vs. MFDC, transformer rating) is part of what was actually qualified, not an incidental detail |
| Parameters | Force, current, time, pulse pattern, and their qualified tolerance bands — not just nominal targets | A WPS states a validated range of validity, not a single point value; the range is what a machine program must stay inside |
| Utilities | Cooling and air-supply requirements | Utility conditions were part of the qualified process envelope and affect repeatability (Chapter 7, Cooling and Utilities) |
| Monitoring | Monitoring limits and pass/warn/reject result logic | Defines how in-process electrical/mechanical monitoring is meant to catch a weld drifting outside the qualified envelope (Chapter 11, Process Monitoring and Adaptive Control) |
| Inspection | Required tests, frequency, acceptance criteria | Ties the WPS to the actual verification regime, including destructive peel/chisel testing (Chapter 10, Testing and Quality Verification) |
| Traceability | Program and result linkage | Connects the paper procedure to the executing machine program and to every weld-event record produced under it (Chapter 17, Traceability and Digital Thread) |

Note the deliberate ordering logic in this table: identification and process come first because everything else is meaningless without knowing which document and which process is being described; parameters sit in the middle as the technical heart of the document; and traceability comes last because it is the field that ties the static document back into the live production and data systems described later in this reference set. A WPS missing any one of these groups is, functionally, an incomplete engineering record even if it happens to contain correct numbers.

## A Practical Compliance Checklist

Restated as a working checklist, a compliant resistance-welding WPS document should be able to answer every one of the following questions without the reader needing to consult a separate document:

- Does it carry a unique WPS number, current revision letter/number, approval status and approval date?

- Does it state the process by name and its ISO 4063 reference number?

- Does it state every parent material grade, thickness and coating the procedure is qualified for, and no others?

- Does it fully describe the qualified joint configuration — stack-up order, weld-point pitch and location tolerance, and any access constraint?

- Does it identify the qualified electrode type, material/RWMA class, face geometry and dressing rule?

- Does it identify the qualified machine class — controller family, transformer, gun and secondary-circuit configuration — rather than assuming "any machine will do"?

- Does it state force, current, time and pulse pattern as qualified ranges of validity (tolerance bands), not single nominal numbers presented as if they were exact?

- Does it state the required cooling and air-supply conditions the qualification assumed?

- Does it define the monitoring limits and the pass/warn/reject logic expected of the controller’s process-signal monitoring?

- Does it state the required inspection methods, sampling frequency and numeric/qualitative acceptance criteria?

- Does it provide a clear field or mechanism for linking to the executing machine program(s) and to production weld-event records?

# 4. Essential Variables, Ranges of Validity, and Why They Exist

A qualified WPS is not a single-point recipe; it is a validated range of validity. The qualification test program proves that the process behaves acceptably across a defined envelope of the essential variables — the parameters whose change is judged capable of affecting weld dimensions, nugget dimensions, weld-pattern positioning, mechanical properties or joint geometry enough to require requalification if exceeded. This is exactly why a WPS records tolerance bands for its parameters rather than nominal-only values: a machine program running anywhere inside that band is understood to be covered by the existing qualification, while a program drifting outside it is, by definition, running an unqualified condition even if every individual weld still happens to look acceptable that day.

Changes that potentially require requalification include: changes to essential variables as defined by the governing qualification standard/scheme, a material or coating change, a major equipment change, an electrode configuration change, an altered joint geometry, or a significant change to the welding schedule.

| There Is No Universal Trigger List The exact essential-variable trigger list and the exact validity range around each variable is standard- and application-specific. The correct action when this question arises for a real procedure is to retrieve the governing WPS/qualification document and read its stated essential variables and their limits, never to assume a generic rule applies. This is the same principle applied throughout this corpus wherever a specific numeric threshold does not have a citable universal source: state the reasoning and point at where the authoritative answer lives, rather than inventing a number. |
| --- |

# 5. Qualification: What It Actually Establishes

ISO 15614-12:2021 specifies the tests used to qualify a welding procedure specification for spot, seam and projection welding, and defines the conditions for carrying out those tests and the resulting limits of validity [S8]. What qualification actually establishes, precisely stated, is this: under the specific tested conditions — material, thickness, joint configuration, equipment class, electrode configuration and welding schedule — the process reliably produces welds meeting the applicable acceptance criteria, and this holds across the range of validity the test program defines around each essential variable. It does not establish that the process will work under conditions outside that range, and it does not, by itself, prove that every future production weld will be acceptable — routine production verification (below) exists precisely because qualification is a point-in-time proof of capability, not an ongoing guarantee.

# 6. The Qualification Lifecycle

A typical qualification effort moves through a defined sequence, each stage feeding the next with progressively more validated information:

- Define the intended joint and production process.

- Select representative materials, stack-up and equipment.

- Develop preliminary welding conditions — trial-and-error against the design rules covered in Chapter 1, Fundamentals and Physics, refined empirically.

- Run controlled trials.

- Select stable conditions and the acceptance tests that will be used to prove them.

- Create the qualification record.

- Approve the WPS under the organization’s quality process.

- Deploy the production recipe with traceability linkage.

- Manage all future changes against the qualified procedure’s stated validity limits.

Every stage in this sequence produces something that the next stage consumes: preliminary conditions from step 3 become the trial matrix in step 4, which becomes the evidence base for step 5’s test selection, and so on. Skipping a stage — for example, moving straight from a development trial to production deployment without a formal qualification record — breaks that chain and leaves the organization unable to answer, later, exactly what was proven and under what conditions.

# 7. Evidence a Qualification Record Must Retain

A qualification record is only as useful as what it retains. At minimum, a resistance-welding qualification record should retain each of the following, because each answers a specific question an auditor, customer or root-cause investigator will eventually ask:

- Test-piece identification — so a specific physical sample can be traced back to the record that describes it.

- Material and thickness records — confirming exactly what was tested, not just what was intended.

- The exact equipment configuration used — controller, transformer, gun and secondary-circuit configuration as actually run.

- Welding parameters actually run (not just targeted) — the measured, executed values, which can differ from the programmed nominal values.

- Electrode information — type, material/class and geometry as used in the qualification trials.

- Test method and results — which inspection/test method was used and what it found.

- Observed failure modes — e.g. button pull-out versus interfacial failure (Chapter 10, Testing and Quality Verification).

- Measurements and the acceptance decision — the actual numbers and the pass/fail determination made against them.

- Approvals/signatures — who authorized the qualification and when.

- The revision/change history — so later readers can see how the qualified condition arrived at its current state.

| Actually Run, Not Just Targeted The distinction between "parameters targeted" and "parameters actually run" is stated explicitly in the source material because it is a common and consequential gap: a qualification record that only lists the programmed nominal setpoints, without the measured executed values, cannot demonstrate what the process really did during the qualifying welds — which is precisely the evidence a later audit or investigation needs. |
| --- |

# 8. Development Trial vs. Procedure Qualification vs. Routine Production Verification

These are three related but genuinely distinct activities, and conflating them is a common and consequential mistake — one that shows up repeatedly in informal shop-floor language, where "we ran it and it worked" can get treated as equivalent to "it is qualified," which it is not.

| Activity | What It Is | What It Is Not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Development trial | Exploratory work to find a candidate process window | Not yet a qualified procedure and not evidence of production readiness by itself |
| Procedure qualification | The formal test program (per ISO 15614-12 or the applicable customer/industry equivalent) that establishes a WPS is acceptable for defined production use, with a defined validity range | Not a one-time check that can be skipped once a development trial looks promising |
| Routine production verification | Ongoing in-process monitoring and periodic destructive/non-destructive sampling that confirms production welds continue to conform to the already-qualified WPS | Does not by itself qualify a new procedure or justify extending validity beyond what was qualified |

| A Passing Production Sample Is Not a Requalification Because routine production verification only confirms conformance to an already-qualified procedure, a run of good production samples under a schedule that has quietly drifted outside the WPS’s stated validity range is not evidence that the drifted condition is qualified — it may simply mean the drift has not yet produced a failing sample. The correct response to a suspected essential-variable change is always formal requalification against the governing standard, never an informal "it’s still passing" judgment. |
| --- |

# 9. Digital Record and Versioning Discipline

Because a weld result can be perfectly acceptable under one WPS/program revision and non-conforming under a different one, resolving which revision was in effect at the time of the event is essential for root-cause work, not an administrative nicety. This is the reasoning behind adopting a defined status model for every procedure record rather than relying on informal version labels like "latest" or a bare date.

A useful minimum status model for a procedure record moves through the following states, in order:

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| DRAFT | Under development; not yet evaluated or approved for any use |
| TRIAL | Under engineering evaluation; development-trial stage, not yet a qualified procedure |
| QUALIFIED | Formally approved for a defined scope, following a completed qualification test program |
| ACTIVE | Currently allowed for production use |
| SUSPENDED | Temporarily blocked from production use, without necessarily being permanently retired |
| SUPERSEDED | Replaced by a newer revision; no longer the currently active procedure, but retained as historical record |
| RETIRED | No longer valid for any use |

Every weld-result record should carry enough identifying data — procedure ID, revision, station, program — to resolve unambiguously which status applied at the moment that specific weld was made. This requirement connects directly to the weld-event data schema covered in Chapter 17, Traceability and Digital Thread, which is built specifically to make that resolution possible after the fact rather than relying on memory or informal notes.

# 10. A Worked Example: From WPS to Machine Program to Production Record

The following linkage illustrates how the WPS/machine-program distinction and the versioning discipline above actually connect in a real production setting, tying every concept in this chapter together into one coherent chain of custody:

- WPS-RSW-017 Rev C is approved for a defined material stack-up.

- Controller Program P103 on Station S12 implements the approved electrical/mechanical schedule.

- The station configuration also identifies which gun (G12) and transformer (T12) are qualified for that program.

- Production result records reference Program P103, WPS-RSW-017 Rev C, and the station identity together.

- Any revision of Program P103 must trigger a change-control review against the WPS before it is used in production.

Read this chain from the bottom up and its purpose becomes clear: the final step is the one that actually protects the plant from the exact risk described in Section 1 — a program edit reaching production without ever being checked against the WPS. Every field in the earlier sections of this chapter (identification, machine, parameters, traceability) exists so that this specific review can be performed quickly and unambiguously rather than requiring an investigator to reconstruct the linkage after the fact from scattered records.

Understanding this division is what allows a reader to correctly guess which standard governs a question they have not looked up yet.

# 3. Why Edition Tracking Matters (a Real Example, Not a Hypothetical)

The same standard title can exist in withdrawn and current editions simultaneously in the field. ISO 10447 has existed as the 2006, 2015 and 2022 editions, each with potentially different clause numbering, thickness ranges or referenced normative documents. ISO 5821:2009 was withdrawn and superseded by ISO 5821:2025, which also retitled the standard specifically to "Female electrode caps" — a scope narrowing, not merely a cosmetic rename. ISO 14373 and ISO 15614-12 have each gone through three tracked editions in this corpus alone (2006/2015/2024 and 2004/2014/2021 respectively).

The reason this matters for a real WPS is direct and unavoidable: a WPS that cites "ISO 10447" without an edition is not fully specified, because the exact clause numbering, thickness ranges and referenced normative documents can change between editions, and an auditor or customer reviewer verifying compliance needs to know which edition’s clauses the WPS actually satisfied. Any compliance answer must state which edition it is referring to and, ideally, retrieve the edition actually specified by the applicable contract, customer WPS or internal quality procedure — never rely on an unqualified general memory of "the peel-test standard" or "the vocabulary standard," because that memory has no way of encoding which edition’s content is meant.

| Edition Discipline Is Not Optional Detail This is why every WPS field for a cited standard should include an edition/year, and why the "Identification" and "Process" fields on the WPS data-group table in Chapter 8, WPS and Qualification, are listed ahead of "Parameters" — a WPS that gets the standard right but the edition wrong is still, functionally, referencing the wrong governing document. |

# 5. The Compliance Evidence Hierarchy

Not every source carries the same authority when answering a real compliance question. This reference set — including this chapter — sits deliberately near the bottom of that hierarchy, and the hierarchy itself is worth stating explicitly so a reader knows how much weight to place on any given document, from highest to lowest authority:

- Primary controlled source — the approved internal WPS, the OEM equipment manual for the exact installed unit, or the licensed current edition of the applicable standard.

- Validated record — a qualification report or inspection report tied to the specific procedure/equipment in question.

- Approved work instruction — an operator or maintenance instruction derived from (and traceable to) a primary source.

- Historical record — a superseded revision or a closed nonconformance report; useful as context, not as current authority.

- Generic knowledge — a textbook explanation, an industry blog, or a general reference like this corpus itself; useful for education and orientation, never sufficient by itself to prove compliance.

# 6. The Compliance Lifecycle

Standards do not enforce themselves; an organization enforces them through a repeatable lifecycle that translates a requirement into controlled practice and keeps it that way as conditions change:

- Identify the applicable requirement.

- Translate it into controlled engineering criteria.

- Implement it in equipment/procedure.

- Verify through inspection/test/record.

- Monitor continued compliance in production.

- Control any change through the organization’s change-control process.

- Retain objective evidence for the required retention period.

This lifecycle connects directly back to Chapter 8’s WPS status model (DRAFT through RETIRED) and to Chapter 17’s traceability schema: "verify through inspection/test/record" and "retain objective evidence" are precisely the activities that only work if the underlying weld-event and procedure-revision data is actually linked and resolvable, not merely collected.
