# 1. Testing Answers Different Questions Depending on Method

Testing verifies whether a produced weld meets a defined requirement, but "testing" is not one activity — it is several genuinely different activities that happen to converge on the same physical weld. Visual inspection, mechanical destructive testing, process-signal monitoring, and dimensional measurement each answer a different question, and they are complementary rather than interchangeable. A weld that passes one layer of testing has not thereby passed the others; a controller’s electrical "pass" indication in particular is not proof of any of the three inspection-based layers, a point important enough that this chapter returns to it explicitly in Section 7.

This distinction matters practically because a quality plan built around only one layer — commonly, relying on the controller’s own pass/fail signal alone because it is the cheapest and fastest data already being collected — leaves the other questions unanswered. A production system that never destructively samples a weld, for instance, has evidence that the electrical process behaved as expected, but no direct evidence about the mechanical strength the joint actually developed.

# 2. The Four Testing Layers

| Layer | Question Answered | Example Method |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Visual | Is the surface appearance/process behavior plausible? | Indentation depth, expulsion marks, discoloration |
| Mechanical destructive | Did the joint actually develop the required physical strength and failure behavior? | Peel test, chisel test |
| Process signal | Did the electrical/mechanical process stay within its validated behavior envelope during the weld? | Current/voltage/force/displacement trace vs. reference curve (Chapter 11, Process Monitoring and Adaptive Control) |
| Dimensional | Is the weld positioned and sized correctly relative to the part geometry? | Coordinate/fixture measurement, nugget-diameter measurement against the 4√t–5√t rule |

Read down this table and a useful mental model emerges: visual inspection is the cheapest and least conclusive layer; mechanical destructive testing is the most conclusive about actual joint strength but destroys the sample and cannot be run on every production part; process-signal monitoring is continuous and non-destructive but only ever proves that the electrical process behaved as expected, not that the resulting joint is strong; and dimensional inspection catches a different class of defect entirely — a weld that is metallurgically sound but simply in the wrong place, or the wrong size, relative to the part drawing. A mature quality plan (Section 6) deliberately combines layers rather than substituting one for another.

# 3. Peel and Chisel Testing Under ISO 10447

The mechanical destructive layer for resistance spot and projection welding is governed by a single standard, and it is worth covering in full detail because it is the layer that most directly answers "how strong is this joint, actually."

| Standard | Edition / Status | Published Scope | What It Actually Covers | How It Is Used |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ISO 10447 | 2022 (previously 2015, 2006) | Resistance welding — Testing of welds — Peel and chisel testing of resistance spot and projection welds | Specifies the procedure and recommended tooling for peel and chisel testing of resistance spot and projection welds, applicable to sheet-thickness combinations from 0.5 mm to 3.0 mm, for two distinct purposes: as a destructive test to determine weld size and failure type/mode, and as a non-destructive verification test usable directly on production parts. | The governing test-method standard for every destructive/semi-destructive spot-weld test described in this chapter |

## Peel testing

Peel testing separates the two sheets at the weld by applying a peeling force — by hand tool or fixture, depending on part size and access — until the joint fails, then inspects the resulting failure. A button of base metal pulled cleanly out of one sheet, leaving a hole with the nugget still attached to the other sheet, is commonly called button pull-out or a ductile/plug failure, and it is generally the preferred failure mode because it demonstrates the weld is at least as strong as the surrounding base metal — the joint did not fail; the surrounding sheet metal did, at a location away from the weld itself. An interfacial failure — the two sheets separating cleanly at the original faying surface, with no button pull-out — generally indicates an undersized or metallurgically poor nugget, and it is precisely the failure mode that acceptance criteria are designed to screen for and reject [S4].

## Chisel testing

Chisel testing drives a chisel or wedge tool at the edge of the weld to attempt to separate the joint. It is primarily used as a non-destructive or semi-destructive field/production verification method where full peel testing is impractical — for example, on a large assembly where the joint cannot be physically pulled apart with a peel fixture, or where destroying the sample entirely is not acceptable [S4], [S17]. It answers a related but slightly coarser version of the same question peel testing answers: whether the joint resists a defined mechanical separation attempt without failing at the interface, without necessarily fully characterizing the failure mode the way a full peel test does.

# 4. Failure Modes to Recognize

A quality inspector, engineer or investigator needs to recognize the following failure modes on sight, because each points toward a different upstream cause and a different corrective action:

- Interface failure or otherwise insufficient nugget size/strength — the joint separates at the original faying surface without button pull-out; the core failure mode acceptance criteria exist to screen for.

- Button pull-out — generally the preferred, ductile failure mode where specified by the applicable acceptance criteria; base metal fails away from the weld itself, demonstrating the joint is at least as strong as the surrounding sheet.

- Expulsion-related discontinuity — porosity or voids left by material lost during the weld, typically from excessive heat input relative to the containment the joint geometry and force could provide (Chapter 1, Fundamentals and Physics).

- Excessive electrode indentation — a cosmetic concern and, past a threshold, a structural/sealing concern.

- Cracking or other unacceptable metallurgical condition — a particular concern on AHSS and other crack-sensitive grades (Chapter 2, Materials, Coatings and Weldability).

- A weld that is simply missed or misplaced relative to its specified location — a dimensional failure rather than a mechanical/metallurgical one, but no less a quality failure for that.

| Every Failure Mode Points to a Different Root Cause The value of naming these failure modes precisely, rather than recording only "pass/fail," is diagnostic: an interfacial failure trend points toward insufficient heat input, tip wear, or a coating/material change (Chapter 12, Troubleshooting and Diagnostics); an expulsion-related discontinuity points toward excessive heat input or unstable force; excessive indentation points toward force or electrode-geometry issues (Chapter 13, Preventive Maintenance and Electrode Life); and cracking points toward a metallurgical or cooling-rate issue on hardenable grades. Recording only a bare pass/fail result discards exactly the information a root-cause investigation needs. |
| --- |

# 5. Connecting Destructive Testing Back to the Design Rules

The minimum acceptable nugget diameter — commonly the 4√t to 5√t (mm) rule referenced in Chapter 1, Fundamentals and Physics [S18] — is what a peel or chisel test is actually measuring against. This connection is worth stating explicitly because it links the design-rule chapter and the testing chapter into a single coherent loop: the design rule sets the target nugget size, and destructive testing is the method by which that target is confirmed to have actually been achieved in a specific weld.

A button diameter measured after peel testing that is trending toward that minimum — even while every individual weld still nominally "passes" — is meaningful leading-indicator evidence of drift: tip wear, a coating change, or a cooling degradation, per Chapter 3, Electrodes and Tooling, and Chapter 7, Cooling and Utilities. Such a trend should trigger the same investigation a hard failure would, just earlier, before the trend actually crosses the acceptance threshold. Treating a shrinking-but-still-passing button diameter as a non-event, simply because no individual weld has yet failed, discards exactly the early warning the measurement was designed to provide.

# 6. Quality-Plan Structure

The four testing layers above are only useful within a structured quality plan that decides what to measure, how often, and what happens when a result is out of specification. The structure below is generic and applies regardless of which specific acceptance criteria (a customer specification such as AWS D8.1M, an internal standard, or the applicable ISO qualification record) govern a given part — see Chapter 9, Standards and Compliance Reference, for how those specific documents relate to one another.

- Define the characteristics to be controlled.

- Define the inspection/test method for each.

- Define the sampling frequency.

- Define the numeric or qualitative acceptance criteria.

- Define the reaction plan for a nonconformance.

- Record every result with full traceability.

- Periodically review trends and trigger improvement actions before trends become nonconformances.

The final two steps are what turn a quality plan from a static inspection checklist into an active feedback system: recording every result with full traceability is what makes the drift-detection use in Section 5 possible at all, and it is exactly the kind of record that depends on the weld-event schema and lineage discipline covered in Chapter 17, Traceability and Digital Thread. Without that traceability link, a trend like a shrinking button diameter cannot be connected back to which station, electrode, or WPS revision produced it.

# 7. Why a Controller "Pass" Is Not Proof of Weld Quality

This point is made in Chapter 1, Fundamentals and Physics, and it is worth restating here in its testing-specific form because it is the single most common misunderstanding this chapter exists to correct: most controllers validate that measured current, voltage, and time stayed within a programmed monitoring band. That is evidence the electrical process behaved as expected — the process-signal layer in Section 2’s table — and nothing more. It is not direct proof of nugget size, joint strength, or the absence of an interfacial failure, which is exactly why destructive and non-destructive mechanical testing, per ISO 10447, remains necessary even in a production line equipped with sophisticated in-process monitoring.

| Process-Signal Monitoring and Destructive Testing Are Not Substitutes for Each Other A production system that relies solely on controller "pass" signals, with no periodic destructive or non-destructive mechanical verification, has no direct evidence about actual weld strength — only evidence that the electrical process ran within its programmed envelope. Conversely, periodic destructive testing alone, without continuous process-signal monitoring, cannot catch every out-of-envelope weld between samples. A sound quality plan uses both, as the four-layer table in Section 2 lays out, because each layer closes a gap the others leave open. |

# 1. What "Adaptive Control" Means, Generically

Chapter 1 (Fundamentals and Physics) established that the resistance at the weld interface is not constant during the pulse — it is dynamic resistance, and its shape over time depends on material, coating, tip condition and contact quality. A controller that only regulates current has no way to detect, let alone compensate for, changes in that underlying resistance: it can hold current to a commanded value and still deliver a weld that is metallurgically wrong, because the same current at a different resistance produces a different heat input. Adaptive control is the direct control-system answer to that gap. It observes measured process signals — current, voltage, and/or a derived resistance or energy value calculated from them — during the weld itself, and adjusts a controllable variable, typically current, in real time to keep the process inside a defined target, rather than simply outputting a fixed pre-programmed current regardless of what the workpiece is actually doing.

The practical distinction worth holding onto is between open-loop and closed-loop control of the electrical process. An open-loop schedule commands a current and a time and trusts that the resulting weld will be acceptable because it was acceptable during qualification. A closed-loop, adaptive schedule measures what is actually happening at the joint during the pulse and adjusts the commanded variable to compensate for what it sees — the same functional split that Chapter 1's weld-cycle table draws between an open-loop "weld" stage and a regulated current/voltage/resistance target under adaptive control.

# 2. What This Looks Like in Real, Currently Marketed Equipment

Commercial adaptive resistance-welding controllers, as a documented product category, typically offer some combination of the capabilities described below. It is worth being explicit about their evidentiary status: these are real, currently shipping capabilities in commercial equipment — confirmed during the research behind this reference set against public product documentation — not speculative or invented ones. They are described here in generic form, without naming any manufacturer or product, because the underlying concept and its engineering rationale are what matter for understanding the process; which company sells which trade name for a given feature is not.

- Adaptive current/voltage control — the controller measures current and voltage during the weld and calculates resistance and energy from them, using that calculated behavior — not just the commanded current — as the basis for real-time regulation.

- Reference curves — a stored, expected process trajectory (of current, voltage, resistance and/or force/displacement, depending on the platform) against which each production weld's actual trace is compared. Curves are built from accepted, stable welds under a defined, controlled setup procedure, and a production weld's deviation from its reference curve — more than its raw pass/fail status alone — is the primary drift-detection signal. Some platforms automate recording these curves from accepted setup welds.

- Dynamic squeeze-time control — reduces the hold-off time before current start based on measured force and position feedback, rather than using a fixed conservative squeeze time for every cycle. This is a productivity feature enabled by having real force/position feedback, which is why it is practical mainly on servo-actuated guns (Chapter 5, Servo Guns and Gun-Drive Systems).

- Adaptive spatter reduction — automatically adjusts weld parameters in real time to optimize quality against spatter rate, targeting a behavior operators would otherwise tune manually.

- Consolidated stability/quality indicators — some systems compute named, consolidated monitoring variables to summarize process stability and weld quality respectively, intended to give a single trackable number rather than requiring an operator to interpret a raw current/voltage trace on every weld.

- Configurable reaction to repetitive faults — user-configurable system reactions to repeated faults of the same type, such as automatically holding production after a defined number of consecutive same-type rejects.

- Gun-mounted signal recording — some systems record mechanical signals in addition to the classic electrical signals directly at the gun, feeding disturbance detection and process adaptation.

- Shop-floor analytics layers — cloud- or edge-deployed analytics combining statistical/machine-learning analysis with access to controller data across the shop floor, aimed at quality-pattern detection beyond single-weld monitoring.

| What Is Deliberately Not Stated Here None of the numeric behavior of these features — exact tolerance bands, exact adjustment ranges or limits — is asserted in this reference set. Those parameters live in the product's own configuration/engineering manual for the exact installed platform and firmware revision, which is outside the scope of this corpus. Treat every feature above as a real, generic capability category, never as a specific vendor's numeric configuration. |
| --- |

# 3. The Reference-Curve Lifecycle

A reference curve is only as trustworthy as the discipline used to build it. Because production welds are judged against it, a curve built carelessly does not merely fail to help — it actively misleads, by making a drifting process look nominal simply because the drift is baked into the target it is being compared against. The lifecycle below is a generic best-practice model, not a specific platform's exact menu sequence, and it is deliberately sequential: skipping a step (most commonly, skipping the review-before-activation step because a curve "looked fine" on the first pass) is how a bad reference curve enters production.

- Verify the exact qualified procedure and hardware configuration before recording a curve.

- Weld representative sample parts, or use the platform's defined setup method.

- Ensure electrodes are in a known, controlled condition — not mid-life-wear.

- Record multiple stable welds rather than building a curve from one noisy trace.

- Review the recorded traces for outliers or abnormal signatures before accepting them.

- Build the reference curve from the accepted samples per the platform's own rule.

- Define monitoring tolerance bands around the curve.

- Associate the curve with its procedure, weld point, tool and electrode state.

- Activate the curve for production only after review/approval — never automatically the moment it is recorded.

| Guardrail — A Reference Curve Is Not Self-Validating Automated or semi-automated reference-curve creation should only draw from welds already classified as good by the quality workflow, and should explicitly reject traces recorded during a known fault, a setup change, abnormal force, inadequate cooling, excessive tip wear, or uncertain part identity. A reference curve built from a mix of good and marginal welds is itself a source of false confidence, because subsequent welds will be judged against a target that already contains some of the drift they should be flagged for. |
| --- |

# 4. Reading Deviation Patterns

Once a reference curve is active, the diagnostic value of adaptive monitoring comes almost entirely from the shape of the deviation, not merely the fact that a deviation occurred. A trained reader of these traces treats the pattern of the mismatch as evidence pointing toward a specific subsystem, in the same way a physician reads the shape of a waveform rather than only its pass/fail flag. The table below associates the most common deviation shapes with their most probable causes and the correct first place to look — deliberately keeping the causes generic, because the exact numeric signature of any one of these patterns is platform- and configuration-specific.

| Pattern | Possible Causes | Recommended Path |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entire curve shifted uniformly | Material/coating change, or wrong procedure/program loaded | Verify part identity and procedure identity first |
| Early-cycle resistance peak changed shape | Contact condition or electrode-face-surface change | Inspect tip condition and material surface |
| Late-cycle drift | Electrode heating/wear, or cooling degradation | Check tip life (Chapter 3, Electrodes and Tooling) and coolant condition (Chapter 7, Cooling and Utilities) |
| Force/displacement trace mismatched to current/voltage trace | Gun mechanics or alignment issue | Check servo-gun diagnostics and mechanical alignment (Chapter 5, Servo Guns and Gun-Drive Systems) |
| Noisy trace overall | Measurement/cabling/environmental interference | Check sensor wiring and signal acquisition, not the weld process itself |

Notice the internal logic of the table: each row routes attention to a different subsystem, and the routing is what actually saves diagnostic time. Chasing a "late-cycle drift" pattern by adjusting the weld schedule, when the real cause is coolant degradation, produces exactly the failure mode Chapter 12 (Troubleshooting and Diagnostics) warns about generally — masking a physical root cause with a parameter change that only appears to fix it.

# 5. Three Different Views of the Same Production Data

Monitoring systems generally expose the same underlying weld data through at least three distinct views, and conflating them is a common source of missed defects. Each view answers a different question, and none of them substitutes for the others.

- Last-weld record — the detailed data for one specific weld event. This is the right tool for immediate diagnosis of "what just happened" at a single weld point.

- Weld protocol — the full traceable event log over time, connecting individual weld events into the part- and shift-level history (see also Chapter 17, Traceability and Digital Thread).

- Histogram — summarizes the distribution of a chosen variable — current, resistance, force, spatter events, and so on — over many welds. This is the right tool for detecting drift or increasing variability across a population of welds, but it can hide a genuine isolated bad event inside an otherwise-normal-looking distribution.

| Why a Rejected Weld Still Needs Its Own Record Checked A rejected weld with a "normal-looking" histogram still needs its own last-weld record examined rather than being dismissed because the aggregate statistics look fine. The histogram describes the population; it does not clear any individual member of that population of suspicion, and an isolated bad weld is, by construction, exactly the kind of event a population-level summary is least equipped to flag. |
| --- |

# 6. Spatter as a Measured Metric, Not a Fixed Constant

Spatter, or expulsion, should be recorded as an observed event metric — a binary event tied to a specific weld ID, or a rate expressed as events per 100 or 1,000 welds — rather than treated as a fixed physical constant that either is or is not present in some universal sense. Acceptable spatter thresholds are application-, customer- and quality-system-specific, which is why this reference set does not publish a single generic spatter-rate target: doing so would misrepresent something that is properly set by the governing WPS and customer specification (Chapter 8, WPS and Qualification), not by a general reference document.

The correct optimization framing, illustrated by the adaptive spatter-reduction concept described above, is constrained optimization rather than free optimization: minimize spatter, energy, cycle time and tool wear as secondary objectives, while treating validated weld quality as a hard constraint that is never traded away to improve one of the secondary objectives. A controller or operator practice that reduces spatter at the cost of nugget integrity has not actually improved the process — it has simply moved the defect somewhere less visible.

# 1. Core Principle: Move From the Largest Prerequisite Down to the Smallest Failed Layer

Troubleshooting a weld cell should determine, in order, whether a problem is a safety, sequence, motion, energy-delivery, process-quality, utility, or data issue — in roughly that order — before touching any welding parameter. This ordering is not an arbitrary checklist habit; it exists because the functional layers described in Chapter 6 (Automation, PLC, Robot and Safety Integration) are prerequisites for each other. There is no point investigating weld current if the weld controller never even received a valid trigger because a safety interlock was open. A technician who jumps straight to adjusting current or force on a "no weld" symptom is, in effect, guessing at layer six of a seven-layer stack before confirming layers one through five are even satisfied.

The discipline this implies is uncomfortable in a production environment under schedule pressure, because the earliest layers — safety and sequence — are often the least glamorous to check and can feel like a waste of time when "obviously" the fault is electrical. Experience across the fault taxonomy later in this chapter shows the opposite is common: a stalled weld that looks electrical is very often a sequence or interlock condition that never let the electrical stage begin at all.

# 2. The Diagnostic Decision Sequence

The following sequence operationalizes the core principle above as an ordered set of questions. Each question should be answered — not assumed — before moving to the next, and a "no" answer at any step means the investigation stops at that layer rather than continuing downward.

- Is the cell safe and enabled? If not, resolve the safety/interlock condition first — never bypass it to continue diagnosing.

- Is the robot/PLC sequence actually progressing? If not, inspect sequence logic before anything else.

- Is the gun physically reaching the intended position? If not, inspect motion (Chapter 5, Servo Guns and Gun-Drive Systems).

- Is the gun reaching the required force/position readiness state? If not, inspect the servo/gun subsystem specifically, not the weld electronics.

- Is the weld controller ready and actually receiving the trigger? If not, inspect the controller interface, not the welding parameters.

- Is the power stage producing the expected process signal (current/voltage as commanded)? If not, inspect the inverter/transformer/secondary circuit (Chapter 4, Power Systems: Transformers and Controllers).

- Is the weld result poor despite otherwise-normal execution through steps 1–6? Only now inspect electrodes, materials, shunting, cooling and the validated parameters themselves.

- Is the result simply missing from the database despite an apparently normal weld? Inspect communications and traceability (Chapter 6, Automation, PLC, Robot and Safety Integration), not the weld process.

Read as a whole, this sequence is a filter: each step that answers "yes" removes an entire category of possible cause from consideration, so that by the time a technician reaches step 7, the search space has already been narrowed from "the entire cell" down to "the electrode/material/process domain specifically." Skipping steps does not save time on average — it only feels faster on the calls where the guess happens to be right.

# 3. Case-Pattern Quick Reference

The table below captures five recurring symptom patterns, the probable first branches to investigate for each, and — just as importantly — the specific wrong assumption each pattern tends to invite. The "do not assume" column exists because these are exactly the shortcuts an experienced technician is most tempted to take, precisely because they are usually right; the cases where they are wrong are the ones that cause a fix to fail or a symptom to recur.

| Case | Probable First Branches | Do Not Assume |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No weld at all | Safety → sequence → controller-ready → trigger-received | Do not immediately increase current — the process may never have started |
| Weak welds only after a long production run | Electrode wear/dressing history → cooling trend → process-signal drift | Do not assume the WPS itself is wrong; cumulative wear is far more common than a bad procedure that "suddenly" fails |
| Expulsion suddenly increases | Force → tip condition → current/time settings → material surface condition | Do not assume only the current setting changed — force and tip condition are equally likely culprits |
| One specific weld-point position is consistently weak | Gun/electrode alignment at that point → local shunting to a nearby weld → local fit-up | Do not assume the entire recipe is bad because one location is failing |
| Random, non-repeating controller alarms | Communication quality → power-supply quality → thermal condition → intermittent harness/connector fault | Do not treat every alarm as a welding-parameter issue |

# 4. The FMEA-Style Reasoning Pattern

A disciplined explanation of a fault follows a specific chain, borrowed conceptually from failure-mode-and-effects reasoning: symptom → possible failure mode(s) → plausible causes for each → evidence that would discriminate between those causes → the safe/approved corrective action for the confirmed cause → a verification test proving the fix worked → a traceability/record update. The step most often skipped under time pressure is the discrimination step: jumping straight from symptom to a corrective action based on the single most common cause is how a genuinely different root cause gets missed and the same symptom recurs after the "fix."

### Worked example from the corpus: "Welds are getting weaker only after several hundred spots."

A disciplined answer considers, in combination rather than in isolation: electrode wear/mushrooming, tip contamination — especially on coated steel or aluminum (Chapter 2, Materials, Coatings and Weldability, and Chapter 3, Electrodes and Tooling) — whether the dressing interval has been exceeded, and whether cooling has degraded over the same period (Chapter 7, Cooling and Utilities). The correct next step is to pull the actual trend data — weld count since dressing, dynamic-resistance/current trend, coolant temperature trend — before recommending a schedule change, because if the true cause is cumulative tip wear, changing the schedule instead of dressing or replacing the tip will mask the symptom temporarily while the underlying wear keeps progressing. The schedule change and the tip replacement can look, on the very next weld, like equally valid fixes; only the trend data tells you which one actually addresses the mechanism.

# 5. Why Alarm and Error Codes Cannot Be Interpreted From the Numeric Code Alone

This is the single most important discipline in this chapter, and it is stated here at full length deliberately — it is not a hedge, and it is not a disclaimer added for legal caution. It reflects how real weld-controller error systems are actually built, and getting it wrong leads directly to a wrong corrective action being applied with confidence.

The core fact is this: the same numeric or short alphanumeric code is frequently reused across different product families, and sometimes across different firmware or hardware revisions of the same product family, with a different meaning each time. Chapter 4 (Power Systems: Transformers and Controllers) describes exactly the structural reason this risk exists: a single equipment manufacturer's catalog commonly spans several distinct controller families — a high-current general-purpose line, a quality-monitoring-focused variant, an I/O-flexible general-purpose unit, a legacy line (sometimes with a documented in-place hardware/firmware retrofit path that changes behavior on an otherwise identical-looking unit), and a dedicated low-voltage/precision unit — each with its own alarm/parameter model. A code that means one specific condition on the high-current general-purpose line can mean an entirely different condition on the quality-monitoring variant, even if the two units sit side by side on the same production line and share a similar enclosure.

The practical consequence follows directly: any error-code knowledge base — whether it is a shop-floor reference sheet, a maintenance database, or a person's memory of "what that code usually means" — must key its lookup on vendor, product family, hardware revision, and firmware/software revision together, never on the code text alone. A knowledge base, or a person, asked to interpret a code without that identifying information should refuse to guess and should instead ask for it, or state plainly that the generic diagnostic category cannot be established from the code alone. This is a discipline of intellectual honesty as much as a technical procedure: a plausible-sounding wrong answer is more dangerous here than an honest "I need the equipment identity first," because it is likely to be acted on.

| Why This Matters More Than It Sounds Like It Should Acting on a guessed code meaning does not merely waste time if the guess is wrong — it can send the diagnostic effort in exactly the wrong direction (for example, chasing an electrical fault when the code actually indicates a mechanical or safety condition on that particular product family), while the real underlying condition continues unaddressed. In a safety- or interlock-related family specifically, guessing wrong and “clearing” what looks like a nuisance alarm is how an actual unresolved hazard condition gets bypassed rather than fixed. |
| --- |

# 6. The Universal, Code-Independent Diagnostic Workflow

Because the exact meaning of a specific code cannot be assumed, the workflow below is deliberately code-independent: it applies regardless of vendor, and it is the correct starting sequence even when the exact code meaning is not yet known, or never becomes fully known outside the vendor's own documentation.

- Capture the exact error code, its displayed text, the timestamp, and the weld point/station it occurred at.

- Determine whether it is a fault (process/equipment stopped), a warning (process continued, flagged), or a quality rejection (the weld itself failed monitoring, not the equipment).

- Check the safety state first; never bypass an interlock to continue diagnosing.

- Record the machine state immediately before the fault, if the system retains it.

- Identify the affected layer using the hierarchy above: PLC, robot, gun/servo, weld controller, power stage, sensor, utility, or data/traceability.

- Check recent changes: program edits, maintenance actions, tip dressing/replacement, tooling changes, software/firmware updates, or a material change.

- Inspect the simplest physical conditions first — connectors, hoses, obstructions, visible electrode condition — before deep electronic diagnostics.

- Use the equipment's own diagnostics to verify sensor, drive and controller status against expected values.

- Compare actual measured values against the expected/commanded state.

- Apply the specific corrective action approved for the confirmed cause, from the exact vendor manual for that product family/revision, once identified.

- Re-run a controlled verification weld/cycle and confirm the fault condition is actually cleared, not just silenced.

- Record the root cause, the supporting evidence, and the corrective action taken — this record is what lets the same fault be recognized faster next time.

# 7. Generic Fault-Family Taxonomy

This taxonomy groups fault categories by function and gives each family a priority. It is deliberately generic — a category list, never a substitute for the exact vendor alarm table for the equipment actually in front of you. Its purpose is to help a technician quickly classify a code once its meaning is known, and to make clear that the safety/interlock family always sits at the top of the priority order regardless of what else is happening in the cell.

| Family | Representative Examples | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Safety/interlock | E-stop active, guard open, safety chain not ready | Highest — never bypass |
| Servo/gun | Not home, force deviation, encoder/drive fault | High |
| Cooling/thermal | Low water flow, high temperature | High |
| Electrical/power stage | Power-stage fault, current unavailable | High |
| Welding process/monitoring | Current limit exceeded, monitoring curve out of tolerance | High |
| Communication | Fieldbus lost, device unreachable | High |
| Configuration | Program missing, parameter invalid | Medium |
| Data/traceability | Part ID or result-storage failure | Medium |
| Maintenance | Tip life exceeded, service interval due | Medium |

# 8. Minimum Evidence Package for Any Real Fault Investigation

Regardless of the fault family, a minimum evidence package is worth collecting before the investigation branches into equipment-specific detail. Collecting it up front avoids the common failure mode of reaching step 10 of the workflow above only to discover that the one piece of context needed to identify the correct corrective action was never captured and is now gone (an alarm that has since cleared, or a machine state that has since changed).

- Alarm code and timestamp.

- Station and equipment identity, including product family and firmware/hardware revision, per the discipline in Section 5 above.

- The active program/WPS revision.

- The current/voltage trace, if available.

- The force/position trace, if available.

- Electrode age and dressing count.

- Cooling flow/temperature at the time.

- Material/part identification.

- Any recent maintenance or configuration change.

# 9. The Weld Defect Catalog (Real, Standardized Defect Types)

Sections 5 through 8 above are deliberately strict about one thing: a controller's numeric alarm/error code cannot be interpreted without knowing the exact vendor, product family and firmware revision, because the same code means different things on different platforms. That discipline is correct and does not change. But it leaves a real gap if "errors" is read only as "controller alarm codes" — because there is a second, entirely different category of "error" in resistance spot welding that genuinely is standardized across the industry: the physical weld defect itself, independent of which controller made it. A peel test, a chisel test, or a cross-section does not care which brand of controller ran the weld; it reveals the same handful of recognized failure types regardless. This section catalogs those defect types properly, each grounded in the same sourced material already cited in Chapter 10 (Testing and Quality Verification) and Chapter 1 (Fundamentals and Physics), so this chapter's error coverage is not limited to "ask the vendor manual" — for the physical defect side of "error," real, sourced, standardized answers exist and are given here in full.

| Defect | How It Is Detected | Likely Cause(s) | Corrective Action | Source Basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Interfacial failure / undersized or metallurgically poor nugget | Peel or chisel test: the two sheets separate cleanly at the original faying surface with no button pull-out | Insufficient heat input (current × time too low for the resistance present), excessive contamination/coating resistance not compensated, low electrode force raising contact resistance unpredictably, tip wear reducing effective current density | Verify the schedule sits inside the qualified weldability lobe (Chapter 1, Section 5); check tip condition and dressing status (Chapter 3, Chapter 13); re-qualify if the material/coating changed | ISO 10447 [S4]; TestResources restatement [S17] |
| Button pull-out / plug (ductile) failure | Peel or chisel test: a button of base metal is pulled cleanly out of one sheet, remaining attached to the nugget on the other sheet | This is the preferred, ductile outcome, not a defect — recorded here as the acceptance benchmark the other rows are measured against | No corrective action needed when this is the observed mode and the button diameter meets the applicable minimum-diameter acceptance criterion (Chapter 1, Section 6; Chapter 10) | ISO 10447 [S4] |
| Expulsion-related discontinuity (porosity/voids from lost material) | Visual: spatter marks/ejected metal at the joint; process signal: a recorded spatter event on the current/voltage trace (Chapter 11) | Heat input too high for the available force/geometry to contain (current, time, or both set too high relative to the qualified lobe); force too low; poor fit-up/gap; surface contamination | Reduce current or increase force while staying inside the qualified lobe; verify fit-up and tip face condition; do not simply lower current without checking force and tip condition first (Chapter 1, Section 8, on force/current being coupled variables) | AHSS Guidelines [S13]; design-rule basis [S18] |
| Excessive electrode indentation | Visual/dimensional: indentation depth measured against the applicable acceptance limit | Excess force or weld time; worn or incorrectly dressed electrode face reducing effective contact area; wrong electrode-face diameter for the sheet thickness | Check force calibration and electrode face geometry against the d_e = 5√t design rule (Chapter 1, Section 6); verify dressing profile (Chapter 3) | ISO 14373 electrode-geometry rule [S6] |
| Cracking / unacceptable metallurgical condition | Metallographic cross-section or, in some programs, surface visual on crack-prone grades | Excessive cooling rate on a hardenable/AHSS grade without a controlled downslope or temper pulse; heat input far outside the qualified window | Apply/verify the downslope or temper-pulse sub-stage the qualified procedure calls for (Chapter 1, Section 3); this is a particular concern on AHSS/UHSS grades (Chapter 2) | AHSS material behavior [S14]; cycle-stage basis (Chapter 1) |
| Missed or misplaced weld | Dimensional/coordinate check against the specified weld-point location | Fixturing error, program/offset error, gun access/reach issue, part variation outside fixture tolerance | Verify program coordinates and fixture/part location before assuming a process-parameter cause; re-teach the position under the equipment's approved procedure | General quality-plan discipline (Chapter 10) |
| Nugget diameter trending toward the minimum (a drift indicator, not yet a hard failure) | Trend of peel/chisel button diameters over time, even while individual welds still nominally pass | Progressive tip wear, a gradual coating/material change, or slow cooling degradation — the same mechanisms as the FMEA worked example in Section 4 | Treat as a leading indicator and investigate immediately (Chapter 13's tip-life model) rather than waiting for a hard failure to occur | Chapter 10's design-rule linkage; [S18] |

| This Catalog Is About the Weld, Not the Controller Every row above is a property of the physical joint, verifiable by peel/chisel/cross-section testing or by the process-signal trace, independent of controller brand — which is exactly why it can be stated in standardized, sourced form here, unlike a controller alarm code. It complements, rather than replaces, Sections 5–8: a controller alarm tells you the equipment stopped or flagged something; this catalog tells you what the joint itself actually looks like once you test or inspect it. A production quality plan needs both. |

# 11. Worked Example: Sequence Inhibit Active, Cell Will Not Weld

This section walks the diagnostic decision sequence and the universal workflow above through a single, fully worked case, chosen because it sits at the very top of the diagnostic hierarchy: a permissive/interlock condition that prevents the sequence from ever reaching the point where a weld could be attempted. Before working through it, one terminology point has to be stated plainly, because it governs how the whole example should be read.

| Terminology Caveat — Read This Before the Error Card "Sequence inhibit" is used in this worked example as a generic, representative label for an interlock/permissive-type condition — a state in which one or more prerequisite conditions the sequence logic requires have not yet been satisfied, so the sequence is deliberately prevented from advancing to a weld attempt. It is not presented here as a universally standardized fault name. The underlying functional concept — a sequence that will not advance to welding until its prerequisite conditions are confirmed — is real and grounded in ordinary PLC/robot sequence-permissive logic (the same logic Chapter 6, Automation, PLC, Robot and Safety Integration, and the servo-gun readiness chain in Chapter 5 describe generically). But the exact name, the exact code or bit, and the exact set of conditions that set or clear it are controller/PLC-program specific, and vary by product family, cell design and even the specific program written for that cell. This corpus does not claim to know, and does not assert, that any specific real controller uses the literal term "sequence inhibit" for a specific documented fault code — it is used here purely as an illustrative, representative name for the diagnostic method that follows, which is what generalizes, not the label itself. |
| --- |

With that caveat in place, the diagnostic reasoning itself is genuinely general: any interlock/permissive condition of this type sits in the safety/interlock family from the taxonomy above, which the taxonomy marks as the highest priority category specifically because the correct response is never to work around it. Per the decision sequence in Section 2, a condition in this family stops the investigation at step 1 until it is actually resolved — the technician does not proceed to check sequence logic, motion, or the weld controller as if the interlock were simply background noise, because until the permissive is satisfied, none of those downstream layers can be meaningfully evaluated: whatever they report is happening (or not happening) underneath a sequence that has already been told not to proceed.

| Symptom | Sequence inhibit is active/turned on; the cell will not initiate a weld. |
| --- | --- |
| Category | Safety/interlock — sequence-permissive family. This is the generic taxonomy category from Section 7 above, and it carries the highest diagnostic priority: never bypass it to continue diagnosing further down the hierarchy. (Reminder: "sequence inhibit" is used here as an illustrative label for this category, not as a claim about a specific vendor's exact fault name — see the terminology caveat above.) |
| Likely Causes | • An upstream safety device — a guard, an E-stop, a light curtain, or an equivalent protective device — is not in its required ready state. • A required prior sequence step has not yet been confirmed complete, so the logic correctly refuses to advance to the next step. • A part-present or part-identity check has not been satisfied — the sequence logic is designed not to proceed to welding against an unconfirmed or unexpected part. • A cell-mode mismatch, such as the cell being left in manual mode when automatic-mode operation was expected, or vice versa. • A communication or handshake signal from an upstream station has not been received, so the receiving station's sequence logic correctly treats the prerequisite as unmet. |
| Diagnostic Steps | 1. Confirm the cell is actually safe and enabled before anything else, per the decision sequence in Section 2 — do not proceed past this step by assumption. 2. Determine whether the inhibit is a fault, a warning, or a normal permissive state that is simply not yet satisfied (Section 6, step 2 of the universal workflow) — a permissive that has not yet been met is not necessarily an equipment failure. 3. Identify exactly which upstream condition the sequence logic is waiting on: safety-device state, prior-step completion, part-present/identity confirmation, cell mode, or an upstream communication handshake, using the categories listed under Likely Causes above. 4. Check recent changes — a program edit, a maintenance action, a tooling change, or a mode change made shortly before the symptom appeared — since a newly introduced condition is a more common cause than a sudden, unexplained equipment failure. 5. Inspect the simplest physical conditions first: is the guard actually closed, is the E-stop actually released, is the part actually present and correctly seated, before moving to deeper electronic or program-logic diagnostics. 6. Use the equipment's own diagnostics — the PLC/robot program's own status or fault display — to identify exactly which input or step the sequence is waiting on, rather than guessing from the inhibit indication alone. 7. Compare the actual measured/reported state of that specific input against its expected state for normal, ready-to-weld operation. 8. Once the specific unmet condition is identified, apply the corrective action for that actual condition — resolve the guard, safety device, part-presence check, mode setting, or communication link — never a generic "reset" or bypass of the inhibit itself. 9. Re-run a controlled verification cycle and confirm the sequence actually advances to and completes a weld attempt, not merely that the inhibit indication has cleared. 10. Record the root cause, the supporting evidence, and the corrective action taken, per the general evidence-package discipline in Section 8. |
| Safety Note | Never bypass or force a sequence inhibit, or any interlock/permissive condition, to continue production. The correct action is always to resolve the actual condition the interlock is protecting against — bypassing it does not remove the hazard or the unmet prerequisite; it only removes the system's ability to tell you about it. |
| Escalation | Once the affected station and layer are identified, consult the exact cell's PLC/robot program documentation and the equipment's own alarm/interlock list for that specific installation, since the exact bit-level meaning of any sequence-permissive condition is program-specific and cannot be reliably inferred from this or any other generic reference. If the documentation does not resolve it, escalate to whoever maintains that cell's program logic rather than continuing to guess at the meaning of the indication. |

It is worth restating the point of this example plainly, in prose, once the mechanics of the card have been worked through: the value of this worked example is entirely in the method it demonstrates — treat an interlock/permissive condition as the highest-priority layer, identify the actual unmet prerequisite rather than guessing, resolve that specific condition, and verify the fix — not in any claim that "sequence inhibit" is itself a standardized, universal fault name across controllers. A reader who encounters a real cell reporting an actual condition with that name, or a differently named but functionally equivalent one, should apply exactly this reasoning while treating the exact bit-level meaning as something to be confirmed from that cell's own documentation, never assumed from this chapter.

## Servo/gun family

| Symptom | Gun does not reach the commanded open or closed position ("gun not opened/closed"). |
| --- | --- |
| Category | Servo/gun. High priority per the Section 7 taxonomy — the weld controller cannot be meaningfully evaluated until the gun's motion state is confirmed correct (Section 2, step 3–4). |
| Likely Causes | • The controller's open/close command was issued but the servo drive is not enabled to act on it. • A mechanical obstruction is physically preventing the electrodes from reaching the commanded position. • Encoder/position feedback fault — the drive may be moving correctly but reporting an incorrect position, or not moving at all despite a plausible-looking command. • A force-release interlock is holding the sequence if the design requires force to be released before the gun is allowed to open. • A safety or drive fault (Chapter 5, Section 4's discussion of drive-integrated safety functions) is inhibiting motion at the drive level, not the sequence level. |
| Diagnostic Steps | 1. Verify the controller's open or close command was actually issued, not merely intended. 2. Check whether the servo drive is enabled; a disabled drive will not act on a valid command. 3. Inspect for mechanical obstruction along the gun's travel path. 4. Compare actual measured position against the commanded target using the drive's own diagnostics. 5. Inspect encoder/feedback status for a fault or plausibility failure. 6. Check the force-sensor/force-derived state if the sequence requires a force release before opening. 7. Confirm no safety or drive-level fault is inhibiting motion, distinct from a cell-level sequence inhibit (Section 11). 8. Only re-home the axis under the equipment's approved service procedure — never force the gun mechanically while it is energized. |
| Safety Note | Never force a gun mechanically while it is energized, and never override a drive-level safety function to "get it moving" — a drive-integrated safety fault exists for the same reason a cell-level interlock does. |
| Escalation | If the drive reports a specific fault code, that code's exact meaning is product-family and firmware-revision specific (Section 5) — consult the exact equipment documentation rather than assuming based on this or any other generic description. |

## Cooling/thermal family

| Symptom | Controller reports low cooling flow or high temperature on a monitored channel. |
| --- | --- |
| Category | Cooling/thermal. High priority — sustained operation with inadequate cooling risks both electrode/tooling life (Chapter 13) and, at the extreme, equipment damage. |
| Likely Causes | • A genuinely reduced flow: a closed or partially closed valve, a blocked filter, a kinked or degraded hose, or a failing pump/chiller. • A flow or temperature sensor fault or miscalibration reporting a condition that is not physically present. • A chiller running outside its capacity for current production rate/ambient conditions (Chapter 7). • A recently changed hose routing or fitting introducing a new restriction. |
| Diagnostic Steps | 1. Check the specific reported channel — cooling circuits are commonly multi-channel and the fault is usually localized to one. 2. Check the flow-switch state directly against the physical flow condition, if it can be verified independently. 3. Inspect inlet/outlet condition, hose routing, filters and valve state for a physical restriction. 4. Check chiller status and supply/return temperature. 5. If flow is physically confirmed adequate but the controller still reports low flow, treat the fault as a sensor/wiring problem, not a cooling problem. |
| Safety Note | Do not suppress or disable a cooling alarm to keep producing, even after confirming the current instance is a sensor fault — fix the sensor, because a real future cooling loss would otherwise go undetected (Chapter 7, Cooling and Utilities). |
| Escalation | Persistent thermal faults with confirmed adequate flow and a confirmed-good sensor should be escalated to review chiller capacity against current production duty cycle (Chapter 4's duty-cycle discussion, Chapter 7). |

## Electrical/power stage family

| Symptom | Controller reports a power-stage fault, or that commanded current is unavailable/not achieved. |
| --- | --- |
| Category | Electrical/power stage. High priority — this family sits downstream of safety, sequence and motion in the decision sequence (Section 2, steps 1–4 must already be satisfied before this layer is meaningfully evaluated). |
| Likely Causes | • A genuine power-stage hardware fault (inverter/SCR/rectifier fault, depending on AC or MFDC architecture — Chapter 4). • Secondary-circuit degradation: loose connections, worn shunts, or degraded flexible leads increasing circuit resistance beyond what the power stage can compensate for. • Incoming electrical-supply quality issues — voltage sag or an inadequate supply for the demanded weld current (Chapter 7's electrical-supply-quality discussion). • A transformer operating beyond its rated duty cycle, causing thermal derating (Chapter 4's expanded transformer-sizing discussion). |
| Diagnostic Steps | 1. Confirm the fault is a power-stage report and not a downstream process-monitoring rejection (Section 7's taxonomy separates these two families). 2. Check the controller's own power-stage diagnostics for a specific reported condition. 3. Inspect the secondary circuit — connections, shunts, cables — for visible degradation. 4. Compare commanded current/voltage against actually delivered values using the controller's own trace, where available. 5. Check incoming supply quality and whether recent load changes elsewhere in the facility coincide with the fault. 6. Check whether the fault correlates with high production rate, suggesting a duty-cycle/thermal-derating condition rather than a hard fault. |
| Safety Note | High-current secondary-circuit and power-stage components carry hazardous energy even when a weld is not actively in progress; service work here should only be performed per the equipment's approved lockout/isolation procedure. |

| Symptom | Weld-monitoring system flags a weld as out of tolerance against its reference curve. |
| --- | --- |
| Category | Welding process/monitoring. High priority for quality, though not a stop-the-line safety condition by itself. |
| Likely Causes | • A genuine process deviation: material/coating change, tip wear, force instability, or a shunting condition (Chapter 1, Chapter 11). • The wrong procedure/program was loaded for the part actually being welded. • A sensor/measurement fault — e.g., a miscalibrated voltage sensor — producing an out-of-tolerance flag on an otherwise acceptable weld. • A reference curve that was itself built from a marginal or mixed sample set (Chapter 11's reference-curve guardrail). |
| Diagnostic Steps | 1. Check the procedure/program ID actually loaded against the part/material identity intended for that station. 2. Check electrode state (dressing count, visible wear) and recent maintenance history. 3. Compare the current/voltage/force traces against the reference curve and identify which part of the trace deviates (Chapter 11's deviation-pattern table). 4. Distinguish a genuine process deviation from a sensor/measurement fault before concluding the weld itself is bad. 5. If multiple consecutive welds show the same deviation pattern, treat it as a systematic process shift, not an isolated event. |
| Safety Note | A monitoring "pass" is evidence the electrical process behaved as expected, not direct proof of joint strength (Chapter 1, Section 8) — do not treat a monitoring pass as a substitute for the destructive/NDE testing cadence in Chapter 10. |

| Symptom | Fieldbus link lost, or a device on the network is reported unreachable. |
| --- | --- |
| Category | Communication. High priority — a lost link can silently stop a station or cause it to run on stale data, depending on the platform's fail-safe design. |
| Likely Causes | • A physical cabling/connector fault, which is by far the most common cause of an intermittent (as opposed to permanent) communication fault. • A device (robot, PLC, weld controller, gun-mounted electronics) powered down, reset, or in a fault state and therefore not responding. • Electrical noise coupling onto the network segment, particularly relevant near high-current welding equipment (Chapter 5, Section 4's discussion of why the dedicated gun-interface bus is kept physically separate from the general factory network). • A network configuration change (address, switch configuration) that was not fully verified before being put into production. |

Identify whether the fault affects one device or the whole segment — a single-device fault points at that device, a segment-wide fault points at the network infrastructure itself. 3. Check whether the fault is permanent or intermittent; an intermittent fault under vibration or near welding operation suggests a physical/noise cause over a configuration cause. 4. Verify the affected device's own status independently of the network report — it may be the device, not the link. 5. Review any recent network configuration change against the time the fault first appeared. |
| Safety Note | Never assume a station is safe to approach because its network link is down — a communication fault does not by itself remove hazardous energy or motion capability; verify the actual safety state independently (Section 2, step 1). |
| Escalation | A recurring, unexplained communication fault on the dedicated real-time weld-interface link specifically (as opposed to the general factory fieldbus) should be escalated with both segments' identities clearly distinguished, since they are different physical/logical networks with different timing requirements (Chapter 6, Section 4). |

| Symptom | Controller reports a missing program, or an invalid/out-of-range parameter. |
| --- | --- |
| Category | Configuration. Medium priority — typically stops a single station's cycle rather than indicating a hazard, but still prevents production until resolved. |

| Diagnostic Steps | 1. Identify the exact program/schedule ID the controller believes is loaded, and compare it against the qualified WPS/program intended for the part actually being run (Chapter 8). 2. Check whether any parameter was recently edited, by whom, and whether the edit was within the qualified procedure's approved range. 3. Check for a recent software/firmware update coinciding with the fault's first appearance. 4. Verify how the program-selection signal is propagated from upstream (part identification, cell-level selection logic) to this station. |
| Safety Note | Never manually force a parameter into range to clear this fault without confirming the forced value is still within the qualified procedure's approved range — an unqualified parameter combination is a process-quality risk even when it does not trip a safety interlock. |
| Escalation | A configuration fault traced to a firmware/software update should be escalated to whoever manages that update, since the exact valid-range behavior is product-family and revision specific (Section 5's discipline applies here too). |

| --- | --- |

# Chapter 13 — Preventive Maintenance and Electrode Life

Why maintenance is a quality activity, not just a schedule activity — the asset-by-asset maintenance model, the configuration items that must be version-controlled, and a first-class lifecycle model for electrode tip condition.

## In This Chapter

1. The maintenance-to-quality linkage

2. Asset-by-asset maintenance focus

3. Configuration items that must be backed up and version-controlled

4. Post-maintenance validation sequence

5. Electrode tip-life as a first-class production variable

6. Sources referenced in this chapter

# 1. The Maintenance-to-Quality Linkage

Preventive maintenance in a resistance-welding cell should be explicitly linked to quality risk, rather than run as a schedule-only activity disconnected from process data. Treating maintenance as purely calendar-driven — replace this part every N weeks, dress this tip every N welds, regardless of what the process data is actually showing — misses the fact that most degradation in this process is gradual and leaves an electrical signature well before it becomes an outright failure.

The canonical example, developed in full in Chapter 3 (Electrodes and Tooling), is tip wear: increasing tip wear typically appears first as a slow shift in process signals — a dynamic-resistance or current trend, exactly the kind of pattern discussed under adaptive monitoring in Chapter 11 (Process Monitoring and Adaptive Control) — and only later as an actual increase in destructive-test failures. By the time a wear-driven quality failure shows up on a destructive test, the underlying condition has typically been visible in the process data for some time already. This is the entire argument for connecting maintenance records to quality data rather than keeping them apart: a maintenance system that stores service events alongside weld-quality results in the same timeline enables that kind of leading-indicator analysis, catching the slow signal before it becomes a hard failure. A maintenance log kept separately from quality data cannot do this — at best it can explain a failure after the fact; it cannot help predict one.

| Leading Indicator vs. Lagging Indicator A dynamic-resistance/current trend is a leading indicator of tip wear — it moves before quality is affected. A destructive-test failure rate is a lagging indicator — it moves after quality has already been affected. A maintenance program built entirely around lagging indicators will always be reacting to problems that have already happened; the value of the maintenance-to-quality linkage described here is specifically in shifting maintenance decisions toward the leading indicator. |
| --- |

# 2. Asset-by-Asset Maintenance Focus

Different subsystems in a weld cell degrade in different ways and require different maintenance attention. The table below organizes the major asset classes by their principal maintenance focus and the leading indicators most useful for anticipating a problem before it affects production. Several of these assets and their diagnostics are developed at greater length in their own dedicated chapters, referenced in the table.

| Asset | Maintenance Focus | Useful Leading Indicators |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Servo gun | Mechanics, encoder, force calibration | Cycle count, force deviation trend, position repeatability |
| Electrodes | Dressing/replacement schedule | Weld count since dressing, face-geometry measurement, weld-quality trend |
| Weld controller | Cooling fans, configuration integrity, diagnostics | Fault-history rate, internal temperature, parameter-integrity checks |
| Transformer | Cooling and electrical health | Temperature trend and service history |
| Cooling system | Flow, filtration, temperature, leak detection | Flow and temperature trend against baseline |
| Robot | Mechanical condition, dress-pack/cabling | Position errors, alarm rate, service-interval status |
| PLC/network | Communication integrity, configuration change control | Packet-loss/diagnostic-event rate, change history |

A recurring pattern across every row of this table is worth naming explicitly: in every case, the useful leading indicator is a trend, not a single reading. A single elevated temperature reading, a single force-deviation sample, or a single fault event is much weaker evidence than the same measurement moving steadily in one direction over time. This is why the maintenance-to-quality linkage in Section 1 depends on storing data over time in the first place — a snapshot-only maintenance system, even one that captures the right variables, cannot show the trend that actually carries the diagnostic value.

# 3. Configuration Items That Must Be Backed Up and Version-Controlled

"The program" is the item most people think of when they think of backing up a weld cell, but it is only one of several configuration items that need the same discipline. Losing any one of the following, or letting it silently drift out of sync with what is actually running in production, creates a gap between what the organization believes is qualified and running and what is actually welding parts.

- WPS revisions.

- Controller programs.

- Robot programs.

- PLC configuration.

- Servo-drive parameters.

- Network configuration.

- Calibration data.

- The alarm/error dictionary for the exact installed product/firmware revision (Chapter 12, Troubleshooting and Diagnostics, explains why this specific item matters — the same code can mean different things across product families and firmware revisions).

- Maintenance counters themselves — dressing counts, weld counts.

| A Real, Non-Obvious Failure Mode Worth Guarding Against Losing counter state on a controller replacement or firmware update can silently reset tip-life tracking to zero on a tip that is actually mid-life. The equipment will then behave as though a well-worn electrode is brand new, which defeats every leading-indicator and lifecycle-state protection described later in this chapter — not because the physics changed, but because the record of the tip's actual history was lost. This is exactly the kind of failure that a version-controlled, backed-up configuration discipline is meant to prevent, and it is worth explicitly checking during any equipment swap rather than assuming counters carry over automatically. |
| --- |

# 4. Post-Maintenance Validation Sequence

Returning equipment to production after any maintenance event should follow a defined validation sequence rather than an informal "looks fine, put it back in service" judgment. The sequence below is generic and sequential; each step depends on the one before it, so the sequence should not be reordered or partially skipped even under schedule pressure.

- Confirm the replacement/serviced hardware's identity and revision matches what is expected.

- Confirm calibration where required — force, position, current/voltage measurement.

- Load the controlled/approved configuration, not a default or a technician's working copy.

- Verify cooling and utility supply is restored and healthy.

- Run the defined set of test welds.

- Perform the quality verification the site's procedure requires for a post-maintenance release.

- Release the equipment to production only under the organization's change-control procedure, with the maintenance event recorded against the asset's history.

Notice that "run the defined set of test welds" and "perform the quality verification" are separate, sequential steps — producing a test weld is not itself proof the weld met requirements, echoing the same distinction Chapter 1 draws between a controller's "OK" indication and actual proof of mechanical weld quality. Skipping straight from a successful test weld to production release, without the defined quality-verification step, reintroduces exactly the gap that verification testing (Chapter 10, Testing and Quality Verification) exists to close.

# 5. Electrode Tip-Life as a First-Class Production Variable

Because the same controller program can behave differently at different points in a tip's life (Chapter 3, Electrodes and Tooling), tip-life state deserves a defined lifecycle model rather than a single "worn/not worn" flag. Treating tip condition as binary hides exactly the information a well-run maintenance and quality system most needs: how much usable margin remains before the process starts to drift. The table below defines a six-state lifecycle model and the action appropriate to each state.

| State | Meaning | Appropriate Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NEW | Fresh, qualified geometry | Use the approved setup/verification procedure before full production |
| IN-SERVICE | Within normal life limits | Monitor condition and process-signal trend |
| DRESS-DUE | Approaching the maintenance threshold | Schedule dressing and/or verify remaining margin |
| DRESSED | Geometry just restored | Reset/record the counter per the site's controlled procedure; consider a verification weld before resuming full production |
| LIMIT | Beyond the approved life/dressing count | Block automatic production continuation; require an authorized action |
| FAILED | Physical damage or misalignment detected | Stop and inspect before any further welding |

The lifecycle model also has a direct consequence for how a system should treat procedure selection near the end of a tip's life: a tip-life-aware procedure-selection policy should apply a risk factor at the boundary. A recipe with very tight process margin should not automatically run when the tip is near its permitted end of life, even if that recipe is technically still qualified for the material — because "qualified" describes the nominal process, not the reduced margin available from a nearly-worn-out electrode. In other words, qualification status and remaining process margin are two different questions, and a mature maintenance system needs to be able to answer both before allowing a tight-margin recipe to proceed on a tip that is close to its LIMIT state.

| Why This Is Framed as a Production Variable, Not a Maintenance Housekeeping Item Framing tip-life state as a first-class production variable — something the controller and quality system actively reason about, alongside current, time and force — rather than as a maintenance department's private housekeeping record, is what makes the risk-factor policy above possible at all. If tip-life state lives only in a paper log or a maintenance technician's memory, no automated or semi-automated system can apply the boundary-condition logic described here, and the organization is left relying on an individual remembering to be cautious near end of tip life rather than on the system enforcing it. |
| --- |
