# 1. Projection Welding (ISO Process Code 23)

Projection welding concentrates current and force at predetermined points using projections, embossments, or the natural intersection of parts, rather than relying on the electrode face geometry alone to define the weld location. This is the ISO 17677-1 definition, worth quoting directly because it precisely states what distinguishes the process from conventional spot welding: "resistance welding in which the resulting welds are localized at predetermined points by projections, embossments or intersections" [S9]. ISO 4063 codes it as 23 — indirect projection welding is 231 and direct projection welding is 232, paralleling the direct/indirect distinction Chapter 1 (Fundamentals and Physics) established for conventional spot welding [S1].

The practical significance of this definition is that it relocates control of weld location from the tooling (the electrode face) to the part design itself. In conventional spot welding, the electrode face geometry and its alignment with the workpiece largely determine where and how the weld forms. In projection welding, that responsibility shifts to the projection, embossment or intersection built into the part. Because the current-concentration point is designed into the part geometry rather than into the electrode, projection-weld quality is unusually sensitive to the projection itself: its height, shape and formation quality are as much a controlled variable as current, time and force are for conventional spot welding. A collapsed, undersized, or poorly formed projection changes the effective current path and contact area in ways a controller cannot compensate for electrically — no amount of adaptive current or voltage regulation (Chapter 11, Process Monitoring and Adaptive Control) can fix a joint whose current path was already wrong at the mechanical level before the pulse even started.

# 2. Nut and Fastener Welding

Nut welding onto sheet metal is a common industrial application of projection welding: projections on the nut, or on the mating sheet, concentrate force and current at defined points, and heating softens and collapses those projections to form multiple localized joints simultaneously. This "multiple simultaneous joints" characteristic is the key difference from a single conventional spot weld, and it drives most of what makes nut welding a distinct quality discipline rather than simply "projection welding applied to a nut."

Because the joint depends on multiple simultaneous projection welds rather than one, alignment — the electrode/gun axis relative to the nut — and presence/orientation verification before welding are first-order quality factors, not secondary checks. A nut welded slightly off-axis does not fail by producing "a slightly weaker weld" evenly across all of its projections; it can instead fail by producing an uneven mix of well-formed and poorly-formed projections, which shows up as spinning or low torque-out strength rather than a uniform strength reduction. This distinction matters for inspection strategy: a uniform strength reduction might be caught by a strength-only spot check, while an uneven mix of good and bad projections on the same nut can pass an inconsistent inspection while still being functionally unreliable.

| A Nut-Welding Procedure Is Not Reducible to Current/Time/Force Alone A nut-welding procedure is properly specified by the full combination of nut family, material stack, exact projection geometry, sheet thickness, electrode geometry, gun capability and controller program together — changing any one of those without requalifying the combination is not a safe substitution, even when the current/time/force numbers look similar to an already-qualified recipe. This follows the same logic Chapter 2 (Materials, Coatings and Weldability) applies to conventional stack-ups: superficial similarity in the numbers is not evidence of interchangeability. |
| --- |

# 3. Micro-Spot Welding

Micro-spot welding is resistance welding performed on very small parts, thin foils/tabs, fine conductors, or components where the energy scale and weld-zone size are substantially smaller than conventional structural sheet-metal welding. Typical applications include battery-tab welding, sensor and electrical-contact welding, and precision electronics assembly — cases where the parts being joined are foil-gauge or wire-gauge rather than structural sheet-gauge, and where the joint itself may be only a few tenths of a millimeter across.

Several of the general-physics relationships established in Chapter 1 (Fundamentals and Physics) still apply at this scale — heat still scales with I²Rt, dynamic resistance still evolves through the pulse, and force is still a coupled process variable rather than an independent knob — but their sensitivity is substantially amplified when the part and weld-zone dimensions shrink. The corpus identifies five specific ways this sensitivity shows up in practice:

- Surface condition dominates proportionally more. Small contact areas make surface condition — oxide, contamination, handling residue — proportionally far more influential on the result than on a large sheet-metal weld, because a given absolute amount of surface contamination represents a much larger fraction of the already-small contact area.

- Electrode geometry changes have amplified effect. A given absolute change in electrode geometry produces a much larger relative change in current density, because the baseline contact area is already small — a fraction of a millimeter of electrode-face wear matters far more here than the same absolute wear would on a structural-scale electrode.

- Timing margin is compressed. Lower thermal mass makes the process more sensitive to timing — the margin between insufficient fusion and overheat/expulsion, expressed in time, is compressed relative to a structural-scale weld.

- Measurement quality becomes a limiting factor. Sensor resolution and noise become a proportionally larger fraction of the measured signal, so the controller's own measurement quality is itself a limiting factor on process control at this scale, in a way it typically is not for a large automotive weld.

- Fixturing can dominate over the electrical schedule. Fixture accuracy and part cleanliness can dominate repeatability more than the electrical schedule does — a well-chosen current/time/force setpoint cannot compensate for a part that is not held consistently from cycle to cycle.

## Why the Process Window and Equipment Differ From Standard-Gauge Steel Spot Welding

These five sensitivities together explain why micro-spot equipment and process windows look qualitatively different from a structural-steel spot-welding setup, not merely scaled down. First, the process window itself narrows: because timing margin is compressed and surface-condition sensitivity is amplified, the band of current/time/force combinations that produce an acceptable joint is narrower, in relative terms, than the equivalent band for a structural steel weld — which is why the corpus is explicit that there is no universal micro-weld current, time or force setpoint, and why a correctly qualified micro-weld procedure for one material/thickness/electrode combination should never be assumed to transfer to a superficially similar one, such as a different tab thickness or a different battery-cell design, without its own qualification trial.

Second, this narrowed window forces equipment differences at two specific points: finer current and time resolution, and smaller electrode geometry. Because the acceptable band is narrower, the controller needs to resolve current and, especially, time in much finer increments than a structural-steel controller would ever need — a weld pulse measured in single-digit to low-double-digit milliseconds leaves very little room for a control system that only resolves time in coarse increments, since a resolution step that would be a rounding error on a structural weld can represent a meaningful fraction of the entire micro-weld pulse. Electrode geometry follows the same logic in reverse: because contact area is already small and current density is correspondingly sensitive to it (as established above), micro-spot electrodes are built with correspondingly small, precisely formed contact geometries rather than the larger, more tolerant face diameters used on structural-steel electrodes (Chapter 3, Electrodes and Tooling) — a mismatch between electrode scale and part scale reproduces, in miniature, exactly the current-density sensitivity problem this section describes.

A concrete, peer-reviewed illustration of this equipment and process-window shift comes from an academic evaluation of micro-resistance spot welding used to attach nickel tabs to lithium-ion battery cells. That study reported weld currents in the roughly 1,400–2,400 A range and weld times of roughly 8–12 milliseconds, applied through electrodes with a 3.0 mm domed contact face — figures reported for that specific tab/cell material combination, not as universal micro-spot values [S21]. Two things about those figures are worth pointing out for how they illustrate the process-window and equipment argument above, rather than as setpoints to copy: the weld-time figures are an order of magnitude shorter than a typical structural steel weld pulse (Chapter 1 cites nugget formation on the order of one-fifth of a second, i.e. roughly 200 milliseconds, for structural steel), which is exactly the compressed timing margin described above translated into a concrete number; and the electrode force reported in that same study — about 2,300 grams-force applied to each electrode — is far below a typical structural-steel electrode force, consistent with the general observation, also reported in the same study, that micro-resistance spot welding usually requires both lower weld current and lower electrode force than conventional resistance spot welding [S21].

| These Numbers Are an Illustration, Not a Setpoint The current, time, force and electrode-diameter figures above are quoted from one specific published study of one specific nickel-tab-to-battery-cell joint, cited in full at the end of this chapter as [S21]. They are reproduced here to make the "finer resolution, smaller electrode geometry, narrower window" argument concrete with real, sourced numbers — not as a general micro-spot-welding setpoint. The corpus is explicit, and this chapter repeats the point deliberately: there is no universal micro-weld current, time or force setpoint, and a procedure qualified for one material/thickness/electrode combination should never be assumed to transfer to a different one without its own qualification trial. |
| --- |

The same academic source also underscores why micro-spot welding is often chosen specifically for temperature-sensitive assemblies such as battery cells: because the process concentrates a short, low-energy pulse at the joint rather than a longer, higher-energy one, the surrounding component can be kept below a temperature threshold that would otherwise risk damaging heat-sensitive internal materials [S21]. This is a direct, scale-specific consequence of the same physics — small thermal mass, short pulse, compressed timing margin — described earlier in this section, applied to a case where limiting collateral heating is itself a process requirement, not merely a byproduct to be tolerated.

# 4. Low-Heat / Low-Mark Projection Concepts for Appearance-Critical Joints

Some applications combine projection-style current concentration with a shorter, more intense pulse specifically to limit overall heat spread and visible surface marking. This is useful where a structural joint is required at a visually prominent location — an exterior body panel, for example — and a standard spot-weld electrode indentation would be a cosmetic defect rather than merely a process signature.

The tradeoff is that these processes are, if anything, more sensitive to projection geometry, tool alignment and force-path consistency than a standard structural projection weld, precisely because the process is deliberately operating with less thermal margin to achieve the low-mark result. A system evaluating whether to use such a process for a given joint should confirm the part design actually contains the required projection/joint geometry, and that a procedure has actually been qualified for the exact material stack in question — the appearance requirement is a reason to consider the process, not a justification for selecting it without a qualified procedure behind it.

# 5. Aluminum-Specific Process Notes

Aluminum resistance spot welding deserves restating in this specialized-process context, expanding on the treatment already given in Chapter 2 (Materials, Coatings and Weldability), because it is functionally a different process from steel RSW even though both are called "resistance spot welding." Chapter 2 develops the underlying physical reasons for this in detail — conductivity, plastic-range width, oxide-layer behavior, dynamic-resistance shape and thermal-expansion coefficient — and the summary relevant here is the practical consequence for process and equipment selection: roughly three times the current, roughly a third of the weld time, a much narrower process window, and materially different equipment demands, generally favoring higher instantaneous current capability, tighter force control, and MFDC power delivery with servo-actuated force control over simpler AC/pneumatic combinations [S14].

The equipment implication is worth connecting explicitly to Chapter 5's (Servo Guns and Gun-Drive Systems) treatment of hardware selection: a servo-gun parameter table there lists gun type/family, maximum/nominal force, force-calibration status and compensation features as the specific factors that determine whether a given gun can physically deliver a qualified procedure. Aluminum's narrower process window and tighter force-control requirement make several of those same factors — particularly force-calibration status and available force headroom — a harder constraint for aluminum procedures than for an equivalent steel procedure of similar nominal thickness, which is one concrete reason equipment sized for typical steel body-shop currents may not even be electrically or mechanically capable of a given aluminum schedule.

Steel and aluminum implementations require entirely separate qualified procedure families; a dissimilar steel-to-aluminum joint is its own distinct qualification case and should never be approached by extrapolating from either material's individual steel-only or aluminum-only procedure. This is the same principle Chapter 8 (WPS and Qualification) applies more generally: a change to any essential variable — and material family is as essential a variable as exists — requires its own qualification, not an assumption of transferability.

# Chapter 15 — Glossary of Terms

An alphabetical reference to the vocabulary used throughout this set, marked to show exactly which definitions come from the governing vocabulary standard and which are cross-checked industry usage.

## In This Chapter

1. How to use this glossary

2. Alphabetical glossary

# 1. How to Use This Glossary

This glossary is meant to be read alongside the chapters that introduce each term in context, not as a stand-alone dictionary to be memorized in isolation. Every other chapter in this set links back here for a precise definition, and this chapter links forward to the chapter where each term is actually put to work — so treat it as the hub, not the whole wheel.

The single most important thing to notice in the table below is which entries carry the [S9] marking. An entry marked [S9] is quoted or closely paraphrased from ISO 17677-1:2021, Resistance welding — Vocabulary — Part 1: Spot, projection and seam welding, which is the standard that actually governs this terminology — the definition is a normative one, not a house convention, and it can be relied on to mean the same thing in any document that also cites ISO 17677-1. Every other entry — unmarked — is standard industry usage that has been cross-checked across the sourced material listed in this chapter's Sources section, but it is not a standards-body quotation, and a different organization's internal glossary could phrase the same concept somewhat differently without being wrong. This distinction matters most at the exact moment a reader is tempted to treat a convenient plain-language description as if it carried the authority of a cited standard: it does not, unless it is marked [S9].

The glossary is organized alphabetically by term, followed by a separate short subsection on vendor-specific acronym patterns — terms that recur across commercial equipment but are not standardized industry vocabulary at all, and must always be confirmed against the specific product's own documentation before being relied on.

# 2. Alphabetical Glossary

Cross-references in the right-hand column point to the chapter in this set where the term is developed in full context.

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Adaptive control | Closed-loop control that adjusts a welding variable (typically current) in real time based on measured process response (current, voltage, resistance), rather than outputting a fixed pre-programmed value regardless of workpiece behavior. See Chapter 11, Process Monitoring and Adaptive Control. |
| Chisel test | A wedge/chisel-tool-based test method, often used as a non-destructive production verification, standardized in ISO 10447 [S4]. |
| Contact resistance | Resistance localized at an interface in the electrical path (electrode-to-sheet or sheet-to-sheet); contributes disproportionately to local heating because it is concentrated at the point where the weld is wanted. |
| Dynamic resistance | The time-varying effective resistance of the weld circuit during the current pulse, as contact area, surface condition and material state change through the cycle. See Chapter 1, Fundamentals and Physics. |
| Electrode | "Component of the electrical circuit that supplies electrical power and applies electrode force to the workpiece" [S9]. |
| Electrode cap | Replaceable electrode contact element used in many gun designs, dimensionally governed for spot welding by ISO 5821 [S3]. See Chapter 3, Electrodes and Tooling. |
| Electrode force | The mechanical force applied through the electrodes at the workpiece interface; controls contact resistance, current-density distribution, and containment of the heated/softened zone. |
| Expulsion | Ejection of molten material from the weld region, generally indicating heat input exceeded what the available force/geometry could contain; also called spatter. |
| Faying surface | The interface between the overlapping parts being joined; the location where resistance heating is meant to concentrate. |
| Nugget | "Zone in spot, projection or seam weld where the metal has been melted" [S9]; the primary fused region associated with joint strength. |
| Peel test | Destructive test method in which the joint is pulled apart to expose the failure mode, standardized (for resistance spot/projection welds) in ISO 10447 [S4]. See Chapter 10, Testing and Quality Verification. |
| Procedure qualification | The formal test program, per a standard such as ISO 15614-12, establishing that a defined welding procedure meets applicable requirements over a stated range of validity. See Chapter 8, WPS and Qualification. |
| Projection welding | "Resistance welding in which the resulting welds are localized at predetermined points by projections, embossments or intersections" [S9]. ISO 4063 code 23 [S1]. |
| Reference curve | A stored expected process trajectory (current/voltage/resistance/force) used by a monitoring or adaptive-control system to compare against actual weld behavior. See Chapter 11, Process Monitoring and Adaptive Control. |
| Resistance spot welding (RSW) | "Resistance welding process producing a weld at the faying surfaces between overlapping parts by the heat obtained from resistance to the flow of welding current" [S9]. ISO 4063 code 21 [S1]. |
| Seam welding | "Resistance welding in which force is applied continuously and current is applied continuously or intermittently to produce a linear weld" [S9]. ISO 4063 code 22 [S1]. |
| Secondary circuit | The high-current path from the welding transformer's secondary winding through the busbar/cable, gun arms, electrode holders and electrodes to the workpiece and back. See Chapter 4, Power Systems: Transformers and Controllers. |
| Servo gun | A resistance-welding gun that positions and closes its electrodes using an electric servo drive rather than (or in addition to) pneumatic actuation, typically enabling programmable position and/or force control. See Chapter 5, Servo Guns and Gun-Drive Systems. |
| Shunting | Current diverted through an unintended path — typically an adjacent, already-completed weld of lower resistance — reducing the effective current reaching the intended weld location. Governed practically by minimum-spacing design rules (e.g. ISO 14373's ≥16t rule, Chapter 1) [S6]. |
| Tip dressing | Controlled removal of material from an electrode face to restore a specified geometry, addressing wear (mushrooming) and contamination pickup. See Chapter 13, Preventive Maintenance and Electrode Life. |
| Weld controller | The control unit that executes a welding schedule and monitors process conditions; product-family- and firmware-revision-specific for any exact behavior or alarm-code claim. See Chapter 4, Power Systems: Transformers and Controllers, and Chapter 12, Troubleshooting and Diagnostics. |
| Weldability | Per ISO 18278-1, the suitability of a material/component design/production system combination for resistance welding, formally decomposed into metallurgical, operative and constructional weldability [S10]. See Chapter 2, Materials, Coatings and Weldability. |
| Weldability lobe / weld lobe / process window | The region of current/time (typically, at a given force) that produces acceptable welds; the experimental procedure for determining it is standardized in ISO 14327 [S5]. See Chapter 1, Fundamentals and Physics. |
| Welding Procedure Specification (WPS) | The controlled engineering document defining a qualified/approved welding procedure and its scope of applicability; content requirements for resistance welding are specified in ISO 15609-5 [S7]. Distinct from a machine/controller program — see Chapter 8, WPS and Qualification, and Chapter 16, Weld Sequence and Program Structure. |

# 3. Vendor-Specific Acronyms (Not General Industry Vocabulary)

Real equipment manufacturers commonly use their own internal acronyms and names for concepts that are not standardized across the industry. Two are worth knowing about specifically, because they recur in production troubleshooting and because this same naming discipline is exactly the principle Chapter 16, Weld Sequence and Program Structure, applies to controller program-structure terminology such as "weld block" or "sequence block."

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Weld interface controller / weld interface bus | A name pattern used by at least one commercial equipment line for a dedicated, real-time communication link specifically between the weld controller and gun-mounted sensors/actuators, separate from the general factory-automation network. The exact name, protocol and cycle rate are product-specific. |
| Gun data module | A name pattern used across commercial product lines for gun-mounted electronics that digitize process signals at the gun and store the gun's own identity/configuration data locally, reducing cabling. Different manufacturers, and sometimes different product lines from the same manufacturer, use closely related but not necessarily identical names and data models for this concept. (Also seen as "measuring gun data module" and similar variants.) |

| Confirm Against the Nameplate, Never Against This Book In both cases above, the correct action for a real installation is to read the exact term off the equipment's own nameplate or configuration screen and consult that specific product's documentation — never assume one manufacturer's or product line's definition applies to another's identically- or similarly-named feature. This glossary can tell a reader that a naming pattern exists and roughly what functional role it plays; it cannot and does not claim to tell a reader what any specific real product calls the feature or how that product's firmware actually implements it. |

# Chapter 16 — Weld Sequence and Program Structure

How the universal squeeze / weld / hold / off model of Chapter 1 becomes an executable program on a real controller — and an honest account of why terms like "weld block" cannot be treated as one industry-wide standard.

## In This Chapter

1. The universal functional model: squeeze, weld, hold, off

2. How a controller organizes a schedule into structural units — and why the exact names vary

3. A generic, illustrative worked model (not a real controller's block structure)

4. Why the distinction matters in practice

5. Sources referenced in this chapter

# 1. The Universal Functional Model: Squeeze, Weld, Hold, Off

Chapter 1, Fundamentals and Physics, establishes that every resistance spot welding cycle — regardless of controller make, product family or firmware revision — passes through the same functional stages: squeeze (electrodes close and force ramps to target before current starts), weld (current flows for the programmed weld time, as a single pulse or several pulses with cooling intervals between them), hold (current stops but force is maintained while the nugget solidifies), and off/release (electrodes separate). Some schedules add an explicit upslope (a gradual current ramp at the start of the weld pulse) and downslope (a gradual current ramp-down), configured as sub-stages of the weld stage rather than as separate cycle stages. This stage vocabulary — squeeze, weld, hold, off — is grounded in ISO 17677-1 terminology and is not this reference set's own invention [S9].

This chapter does not re-derive that physics; it exists to answer a different, narrower question that Chapter 1 deliberately defers: once those four universal stages are settled, how does a real weld controller actually organize them, along with everything else a production weld point needs (which parameter set to load, what tolerance band counts as acceptable, when the cell is even allowed to fire), into something that can be selected, stored, sequenced and monitored as an executable program? The answer to that question is where terminology gets genuinely inconsistent across the industry — and this chapter's job is to be honest about exactly where that inconsistency starts and where it stops.

| Read This Chapter as "How the Stages Get Organized," Not "What the Stages Are" If a reader arrives at this chapter looking for the physical definition of squeeze, weld, hold and off time, that material lives in Chapter 1 and is not repeated here in full. This chapter picks up exactly where Chapter 1 leaves off: those four stages are universal and settled; how a specific controller platform packages them into a stored, selectable, monitored program is not. |
| --- |

# 2. How a Controller Organizes a Schedule Into Structural Units — and Why the Exact Names Vary

A production weld point needs more configured around it than just a current/time/force triple for the weld stage itself. At minimum, a real installation needs, functionally:

- A stored parameter set for that weld point — the squeeze/weld/hold/off timing values, the target current (and, on force-controlled equipment, the target force profile), any upslope/downslope, and which of several stored programs applies to this specific weld point on this specific part variant.

- A monitoring/tolerance-band configuration — the acceptance limits (current, voltage, resistance, energy, and on some platforms force/displacement) that a production weld's measured trace is compared against, typically relative to a stored reference curve (Chapter 11, Process Monitoring and Adaptive Control).

- Sequencing/interlock logic — the conditions that must be true before the weld point is allowed to fire at all: robot or gun in position, part presence confirmed, correct program selected for this part/variant, safety circuit healthy, upstream permissives satisfied (Chapter 6, Automation, PLC, Robot and Safety Integration).

Every commercial resistance-welding controller has to represent these three functional needs somehow, because a cell simply cannot run without all three being configured. Where the terminology genuinely diverges is in what these configured units are called, how their boundaries are drawn, and how many distinct named unit-types a given platform exposes to the person programming it.

## What fresh research for this chapter actually found

This chapter was written after a dedicated research pass specifically aimed at the phrase pattern "weld block / sequence block / monitor block," because that is genuinely useful terminology to a reader who has encountered it and wants to know how solid it is. The finding is that this is not one industry-wide, standardized naming convention:

- A publicly available resistance-welding fundamentals reference, aimed at operators and setup personnel, describes a weld schedule using only "squeeze time," "weld time," "hold time," "off time," force and current — no "block" naming of any kind — and directly points to AWS C1.1 and the RWMA Resistance Welding Manual as the underlying authority for schedule data [S21], [S22].

- Two independently reviewed real controller instruction manuals organize their programming around the terms "weld schedule," "sequence," "function," and, on one platform, a per-schedule "stepper" concept used for current-density compensation across multiple schedules — again, not "weld block," "sequence block," or "monitor block" [S23], [S24]. Neither manual subdivides a schedule into a set of named, hierarchical "block" types of the kind the phrase implies.

That is a negative finding about three specific real sources, not proof that no controller platform anywhere uses "block" as a structural term — firmware terminology across the whole installed base of resistance-welding controllers, across decades of product generations, is not something any single literature review can exhaustively rule out. What the research does support, confidently, is the general pattern this chapter is built around: controller platforms genuinely do organize a schedule's parameter data, its monitoring/tolerance configuration, and its sequencing/interlock logic into named structural units for configuration purposes — that functional need is real and universal — but the specific names given to those units, where their boundaries fall, and how many distinct unit-types exist are controller-family- and firmware-revision-specific, not one industry-wide standard.

| Caveat — Do Not Treat "Block" Naming as a Universal Standard Terms such as "weld block," "sequence block" or "monitor block" are examples of the kind of structural/functional naming pattern that some controller platforms use for the configuration units described above — a stored parameter set, a monitoring/tolerance configuration, and sequencing/interlock logic. They are not confirmed, by the research behind this chapter, to be one universal, standardized naming convention used consistently across the industry. This is exactly the same discipline Chapter 15's Glossary already applies to vendor-specific acronyms such as "weld interface controller/bus" and "gun data module": a real, recurring functional pattern is described generically, while the exact name, boundary and count of structural units is stated to be product-specific and must be confirmed against that exact platform's own documentation before being relied on. Never assert one vendor's or one platform's naming as if it were the one universal standard — for either the acronyms in Chapter 15 or the structural terms in this chapter. |
| --- |

# 3. A Generic, Illustrative Worked Model (Not a Real Controller's Block Structure)

The table below is a teaching model only. It illustrates, in deliberately generic language, how the three functional needs from Section 2 commonly relate to one another conceptually on a modern controller — it is not a claim about any specific real product's exact block structure, naming, or firmware behavior, and a reader should never quote it as if it described a particular platform.

| Illustrative Structural Unit | What It Would Typically Hold | Cross-Reference for the Underlying Concept |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Parameter/schedule unit | The squeeze/weld/hold/off timing values, target current and (on force-controlled equipment) target force profile for a given weld point or part variant, plus any upslope/downslope sub-stage settings | Chapter 1, Fundamentals and Physics (the physical stages themselves) |
| Monitoring unit | Acceptance tolerance bands (current, voltage, resistance, energy and, on some platforms, force/displacement) compared against a stored reference curve built from accepted, stable production welds | Chapter 11, Process Monitoring and Adaptive Control (reference-curve lifecycle and deviation patterns) |
| Sequence/interlock unit | The conditions gating whether this weld point is allowed to fire: robot/gun in position, part presence and identity confirmed, correct program selected, safety circuit and cell permissives satisfied | Chapter 6, Automation, PLC, Robot and Safety Integration (interlocks and cell control hierarchy) |

Read this table as a conceptual map from "what a weld point functionally needs" to "the three kinds of configuration a controller has to represent somehow" — not as a literal inventory of named objects on any particular screen. # 4. Why the Distinction Matters in Practice

The practical consequence of everything above is a simple habit of mind, not a complicated rule: a technician, programmer or engineer reading a real controller's documentation should map its exact terms onto the universal squeeze/weld/hold/off model from Chapter 1 first, and only then learn that specific platform's own names for how it packages parameters, monitoring and sequencing — rather than assuming that a term learned on one platform (or the illustrative "parameter/schedule unit," "monitoring unit," "sequence/interlock unit" labels used in Section 3 of this very chapter) applies unchanged on a different platform.

This matters for several concrete reasons that recur throughout this reference set:

- Cross-training and job transfer. A technician who learned "weld schedule" and "sequence" terminology on one controller family and then encounters "block" terminology on a different one (or vice versa) has not necessarily encountered a different underlying architecture — they may be looking at the same three functional needs from Section 2, packaged and labeled differently. Recognizing the universal squeeze/weld/hold/off stages and the three functional needs underneath the label is what transfers between platforms; the label itself often does not.

- Troubleshooting and documentation literacy. Chapter 12, Troubleshooting and Diagnostics, and Chapter 15's Glossary both already establish that vendor-specific alarm codes and acronyms must be read off the exact equipment and confirmed against that product's own documentation, never inferred from a superficially similar name on different equipment. Program-structure terminology is subject to exactly the same discipline, for the same reason: a name that looks familiar is not evidence that the underlying object model is the same.

- Procurement and specification writing. A specification or training document that names a specific "block" structure as if it were a universal requirement risks being unintentionally vendor-specific — silently steering equipment selection toward whichever platform happens to use that naming, or creating confusion when a qualified alternative platform organizes the same functional content differently but is otherwise fully capable.

- Writing and reading a WPS. Chapter 8, WPS and Qualification, is explicit that a Welding Procedure Specification is a controlled engineering document distinct from a machine/controller program. A WPS should state the qualified squeeze/weld/hold/off values and the qualified range of validity in the universal, controller-independent vocabulary of Chapter 1 — not in one specific platform's internal block or schedule naming — precisely so that the WPS remains valid evidence even if the shop later requalifies or replaces the controller it was originally written against.

None of this is a criticism of any specific naming convention. A controller vendor is free to organize its own configuration model however serves its firmware architecture and its own users best. The discipline this chapter asks for runs the other way: the reader, not the vendor, is responsible for keeping the universal physical model and the platform-specific packaging of that model mentally separate, so that a lesson learned on one controller transfers correctly instead of being silently mis-applied to the next.

# Chapter 17 — Traceability and Digital Thread

Why a weld result is only diagnostically meaningful when linked to its full context, what a minimum weld-event data schema must contain, and how good traceability turns individual results into organization-wide analytics.

## In This Chapter

1. Why traceability is what makes diagnosis possible at all

2. The minimum useful weld-event schema

3. Data lineage: from answer back to controlled source

4. Useful analytics enabled by good traceability

5. Digital-record versioning links directly to procedure governance

6. What a weak traceability system cannot answer

7. Sources referenced in this chapter

# 1. Why Traceability Is What Makes Diagnosis Possible at All

A single weld result — one pass/fail flag, one current trace, one nugget-diameter measurement — is only diagnostically meaningful when it is connected to its full context. In isolation, a result answers almost nothing useful: it cannot say whether a measured current was normal for that station, whether the procedure in effect that day was actually the currently approved one, or whether a similar result appeared on a neighboring station at the same time. Every one of those questions requires linking the result to other records, which is exactly what a traceability system exists to make possible.

Almost every diagnostic and quality-verification technique described elsewhere in this reference set depends on exactly this kind of linked context. Comparing a weld’s process signal to a reference curve (Chapter 11, Process Monitoring and Adaptive Control) requires knowing which reference curve applies to that station, material and program. Correlating an alarm with electrode age (Chapter 12, Troubleshooting and Diagnostics) requires knowing how many welds that electrode has made since its last dressing. Resolving which WPS revision was actually in effect at the moment a specific weld was made (Chapter 8, WPS and Qualification) requires a timestamp-resolvable link between the weld event and the procedure’s revision history. None of these techniques works on an unlinked, standalone result — they all depend on a weld-event record carrying enough linked context to answer the question every real investigation eventually asks: "compared to what, under what conditions, per which approved procedure."

| Traceability Is Infrastructure, Not a Reporting Feature It is worth stating plainly that traceability is not an add-on reporting convenience layered on top of "real" process control — it is the infrastructure that every other diagnostic and quality technique in this reference set is built on top of. A production system with excellent process monitoring but poor traceability linkage still cannot answer many of the questions an auditor or root-cause investigator will actually ask, because the individual data points it collects are not connected to each other. |
| --- |

# 2. The Minimum Useful Weld-Event Schema

The following is a minimum useful schema for a single weld-event record — the set of fields a weld-event record needs at a minimum in order to support the diagnostic and analytic uses described later in this chapter. It is presented generically, as a conceptual data model, not as a specification of any particular database, software platform or vendor implementation; any system capable of capturing and linking these fields, in whatever concrete technical form, satisfies the underlying requirement.

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| weld_event_id | Unique event identifier |
| timestamp | Execution time |
| part_id | Part or assembly identity/genealogy reference |
| station_id | Cell/station identity |
| robot_id | Motion-system identity |
| gun_id | Gun identity (and, where the equipment supports it, the gun’s own onboard data-module identity — see Chapter 5, Servo Guns and Gun-Drive Systems) |
| controller_id | Weld-controller identity, including product family and firmware/hardware revision |
| program_id / program_revision | Executed machine program and its configuration revision |
| wps_id | Linked engineering procedure and revision (Chapter 8, WPS and Qualification) |
| material_stack_id | Material/stack-up reference |
| spot_id | Logical weld-point location |
| measured_signals | Current, voltage, force, displacement, etc., as available |
| result | Pass/warning/reject/fault classification |
| alarm | Fault or warning code, if present, with the vendor/product/revision context needed to interpret it |
| maintenance_context | Recent relevant service events (tip dressing count, last calibration, etc.) |

Two design choices in this schema deserve explicit comment. First, several fields carry both an identity and a revision component — program_id / program_revision, and wps_id (which implies its own revision) — rather than identity alone; this is deliberate and is explored fully in Section 5, because identity without revision cannot answer whether a specific historical weld was made under a currently valid procedure. Second, the alarm field explicitly requires vendor/product/revision context rather than a bare code, because — as covered in Chapter 12, Troubleshooting and Diagnostics — fault-code naming and numbering is controller/vendor-specific and varies by product family and firmware revision; an alarm code recorded without that context becomes uninterpretable the moment it is read back outside the context of the exact controller that produced it.

| Naming Conventions Are Not Universal As elsewhere in this reference set, the underlying functional need for each field above is universal and grounded in real production requirements, but the exact field names, data types and storage technology used to implement this schema are vendor- and platform-specific and vary widely across commercial systems. Present the concept as real; never present one vendor’s specific implementation as if it were a universal standard. |
| --- |

# 3. Data Lineage: From Answer Back to Controlled Source

Every retrieval-backed answer — whether generated by a person querying a database, a report, or an automated analytics or AI system built on top of this data — should be traceable through an unbroken chain: from the answer, to the specific retrieved record or data chunk that supports it, to that record’s document ID and revision, to the original controlled source file. This chain is what allows "why do you say that" to be answered with an actual, checkable document reference rather than an unattributed general impression.

This matters most exactly where it is hardest to enforce casually: compliance and quality questions. It is easy, in an informal production environment, for an answer like "that stack-up normally runs fine" to circulate as accepted wisdom without anyone being able to point to the specific qualification record, inspection report, or WPS revision that actually supports it. A functioning digital thread makes that lineage explicit and retrievable, so that a compliance or quality claim can always be walked backward to its controlled source rather than resting on institutional memory.

# 4. Useful Analytics Enabled by Good Traceability

Once weld-event records are consistently captured with the linked schema in Section 2, a range of analyses becomes possible that are simply unavailable from unlinked, standalone results. Each of the following depends on the same underlying capability — correlating many individual weld-event records across a shared dimension (time, station, procedure revision, or component identity):

- Drift detection — a slow trend in a monitored variable, visible only across many linked events, not from any single reading (Chapter 11, Process Monitoring and Adaptive Control; Chapter 10, Testing and Quality Verification, for the button-diameter trend example).

- Station-to-station comparison — isolating whether a quality issue is process-wide or specific to one gun/controller/station, which is only possible if station and equipment identity are consistently linked to every result.

- Gun/electrode life estimation — tying quality trend to weld count and dressing history (Chapter 13, Preventive Maintenance and Electrode Life).

- Alarm clustering — finding that several apparently unrelated alarms share a common upstream cause, for example a cooling or power-quality issue triggering several different downstream fault codes (Chapter 7, Cooling and Utilities; Chapter 12, Troubleshooting and Diagnostics).

- Parameter-change impact analysis — before/after comparison across a controlled program change, which depends on program_revision being recorded consistently on every event, not just at the moment of the change.

- Defect root-cause analysis — tracing a specific defect pattern back through station, procedure, material and maintenance context to its actual originating condition.

- Maintenance-effectiveness tracking — confirming whether a maintenance action (a tip dressing, a calibration) actually improved the quality trend that followed it.

- Weld-quality prediction from leading indicators — using early, non-failing trend signals (again, the shrinking-but-passing button diameter is the canonical example from Chapter 10) to anticipate a nonconformance before it occurs.

None of these analyses is possible from an unlinked collection of individual pass/fail flags. What makes each one possible is precisely the linkage the schema in Section 2 is designed to preserve: without station_id, station-to-station comparison cannot exist; without program_revision, before/after impact analysis cannot exist; without maintenance_context, maintenance-effectiveness tracking cannot exist. The analytics are a direct, mechanical consequence of which fields the underlying schema chose to capture and link — they are not a separate capability bolted on afterward.

# 5. Digital-Record Versioning Links Directly to Procedure Governance

Every analytic use described in Section 4 assumes the weld-event record correctly identifies which WPS/program revision was active at the moment of that specific weld. This is exactly the status model established in Chapter 8, WPS and Qualification: DRAFT, TRIAL, QUALIFIED, ACTIVE, SUSPENDED, SUPERSEDED, RETIRED. A traceability system that stores only an unqualified identity — for example, "program P103" with no revision — cannot actually answer the question a real root-cause investigation frequently needs answered first: was this specific historical weld made under a currently valid, qualified procedure?

| What Is Recorded | What It Can Answer | What It Cannot Answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Program identity only ("P103") | Which program family executed this weld | Whether P103 had been revised since this weld was made, or whether that revision was ever checked against its WPS |
| Program identity + revision, no timestamp resolution | Which specific revision of the program is nominally linked | Whether that specific revision was actually the one active at the exact moment of this weld, if the program has since changed |
| Program identity + revision + timestamp-resolvable link to the WPS status history | Whether this specific historical weld was made under a currently valid, qualified procedure at the time it was made | (this is the level of resolution a real investigation actually needs) |

| This Is the Question Investigations Actually Ask First A traceability system that stores only "program P103" without the revision, or without a timestamp-resolvable link to which revision of P103 was active at that moment, cannot actually answer "was this specific historical weld made under a currently valid procedure" — which is frequently the exact question a real root-cause investigation needs answered first, before any technical analysis of the weld data itself even begins. |
| --- |

# 6. What a Weak Traceability System Cannot Answer

It is useful to close this chapter by restating, plainly, the practical cost of under-investing in traceability, because the cost is easy to underestimate until an investigation actually needs the missing link. A production system that captures process signals and pass/fail results but does not consistently link station, equipment, program revision, WPS revision and maintenance context to each event will, sooner or later, face a question it cannot answer from its own data: which stations were affected, which procedure revision was in effect, whether a specific maintenance action actually helped, or whether a historical weld was made under a currently valid procedure at all. None of these gaps is visible day to day, because routine production does not usually need to ask them — they become visible exactly when a nonconformance, audit or customer complaint forces the question, which is the worst possible time to discover that the answer is unrecoverable.

The corrective principle is the same one this reference set applies throughout: build the linkage discipline — consistent identifiers, revision tracking, and timestamp resolution — into the weld-event schema from the start, rather than treating it as something that can be reconstructed after the fact from scattered records once it turns out to matter.

# 1. What This Reference Set Is

This is a 20-chapter, long-form reference set on resistance spot welding (RSW), written for an expert audience — the technician, engineer, quality specialist or programmer who needs precise, citable, working knowledge rather than an introductory overview. Each chapter is a self-contained document: every factual claim, standard scope, or design rule carries a citation tag resolved in full in that chapter's own Sources section, so any single chapter can be read, shared or referenced on its own without requiring the rest of the set to be open at the same time.

The set covers the physics of the process, materials and weldability, tooling, power systems and controllers, servo guns, automation and safety integration, cooling and utilities, procedure qualification, standards and a full compliance-verification checklist, testing, process monitoring, troubleshooting (including a standardized weld-defect catalog and a hardware-to-fault-category map), maintenance, specialized processes, terminology, program structure, traceability, an end-to-end production weld execution procedure that ties every component together, a material-and-thickness parameter selection guide, and — in this chapter — how to navigate the whole set. No equipment manufacturer, product, or brand name appears anywhere in it; every equipment-level concept is described generically, as something true of a category of equipment, because the engineering concept is what a reader needs, not a trade name that may not match the equipment actually in front of them.

# 2. Why It Was Built This Way

This set replaces an earlier, considerably shallower package that covered the same general subject area across a much larger number of files. That earlier package was reviewed in full before this one was written. Its structural problem was not a lack of ambition in scope — it touched most of the right topics — but a lack of depth and evidence underneath each topic: every file followed an identical template, with the same disclaimer language and the same short, generic citation block repeated verbatim across dozens of files regardless of what that specific file was actually about, and most sections were placeholder headings with little or no real content beneath them. No real numeric parameters, formulas, or standard scopes appeared anywhere in a form a reader could act on or verify. That structure teaches a reader (or a model trained on it) to produce confident-sounding hedges, not knowledge — which is the opposite of what an expert reference is supposed to do.

This set was built from a fresh, from-scratch research pass instead: real formulas and design rules stated with their numeric values and sources (electrode diameter, minimum nugget size, weld spacing, edge distance); real, verified standard scopes and current editions, with specific factual errors found in one public reference site's own standards list documented rather than silently repeated; real equipment architecture and control concepts described generically and confirmed, during research, to be actual currently shipping capabilities in commercial equipment rather than invented ones; a distinct structure per chapter instead of one repeated template; and — running through the whole set — an explicit habit of flagging rather than hiding the places where public sources disagree, where a number is a rule of thumb rather than a normative value, or where a piece of terminology is not standardized industry-wide. Chapter 16, Weld Sequence and Program Structure, and this chapter's own closing section are two direct examples of that habit in practice.

| What Was Deliberately Not Done No standard's paywalled full text is reproduced anywhere in this set — only scope statements quoted from each standard's own free preview page, plus independently verified catalog metadata (title, number, edition, status). No numeric welding parameter for a specific material/thickness is presented as a ready-to-use production setpoint; every such number is either a widely published design/estimation rule explicitly labeled as such, or a documented example tied to its specific cited scope. This restraint is intentional: it is safer for a reader to be told plainly that a number is a starting estimate than to be handed a confident-looking number that turns out not to be qualified for their exact application. |

# 5. Known Gaps, Stated Plainly

Consistent with the honesty discipline that runs through this whole set, the gaps below are stated directly rather than glossed over. None of them is an oversight to be quietly fixed later without comment — each one is a boundary of what a public, vendor-neutral literature review can responsibly claim to know, and each is already flagged at the point in the set where it matters most.

- No production-ready current/time/force schedule for any specific material stack. Chapter 1's design rules and rough starting estimates are exactly that — starting points for trial-and-error setup or sanity-checking, not qualified production values. Producing a real schedule requires actual destructive testing and procedure qualification (Chapter 8) against the specific material, coating, thickness, electrode and equipment combination in use; no public-source literature review can substitute for that.

- No vendor alarm-code table for any controller. Alarm and fault codes live in licensed, manufacturer-specific service manuals and are firmware- and hardware-revision-specific. Chapter 12, Troubleshooting and Diagnostics, explains in more detail why this set is right not to invent or guess at one, and Chapter 16 applies the identical discipline to program-structure naming such as "weld block."

# Why This Chapter Exists

Every other chapter in this reference set explains one component, one standard, or one concept in isolation: Chapter 3 explains electrodes, Chapter 5 explains servo guns, Chapter 8 explains the WPS, Chapter 11 explains monitoring, Chapter 12 explains diagnosis. That isolation is necessary for depth, but it leaves an honest gap — a reader can understand every part and still not see how they fit together into the thing a production operator or engineer actually does: run a weld, correctly, on a real part, right now. This chapter closes that gap. It introduces no new facts beyond what the rest of this reference set already establishes; its entire purpose is correlation — showing, as one continuous, numbered sequence, exactly where the gun, the tip, the transformer, the WPS, the monitoring system, and the error-handling discipline each enter the picture, and in what order, and why that order is not arbitrary.

Read this chapter alongside Chapter 12's decision sequence (Section 2 there) and Chapter 6's control hierarchy — this chapter is what those two look like when walked forward, start to finish, for one weld, rather than backward from a fault.

# Step 1 — Pre-Production Setup

Before any part reaches the weld station, the station has to be running the correct procedure for the correct part. This sounds trivial and is, in practice, one of the most common sources of a "the weld looked fine but wasn't qualified" problem — not because the weld itself misbehaved, but because the wrong procedure was running against the right-looking part.

- Confirm the part/product identity actually queued at this station (by part number, routing, or an automated identification read where the cell has one — Chapter 17, Traceability and Digital Thread).

- Resolve which WPS revision governs this exact joint, material, coating and thickness combination for this part — not a WPS for "a similar part" (Chapter 8, WPS and Qualification, Section 1's WPS/program distinction and Section 9's status model: only an ACTIVE-status revision is valid for production use).

- Confirm the machine/controller program ID actually loaded at this station matches the program the resolved WPS authorizes for this station (Chapter 8, Section 10's worked WPS-to-program-to-record chain).

- If the WPS or program was recently revised, confirm the revision has cleared change control and is not still in DRAFT or TRIAL status (Chapter 8, Section 9).

- Confirm the material lot/coating actually on hand matches what the WPS specifies, using the material-family and thickness-band guidance in Chapter 2 (Materials, Coatings and Weldability) and Chapter 20 (Material and Thickness Parameter Guide) as the reference point for what "matches" means.

| Symptom | The program/WPS actually loaded at the station does not match what the part routing calls for. |
| --- | --- |
| Category | Configuration fault, caught at Step 1 before any weld is attempted — see Chapter 12, Section 7's Configuration family and Section 12's worked Configuration-family card for the full diagnostic treatment. |
| Likely Causes | • An upstream part-identification/routing signal did not correctly select the program for this specific part variant. • A manual program selection was left at a previous part's setting after a changeover. • The WPS was revised but the station program was not updated to match (Chapter 8, Section 1's core warning). |
| Diagnostic Steps | 1. Do not weld the part. Resolving this mismatch always comes before Step 2. 2. Identify the correct WPS/program pairing for the part actually present, per Chapter 8, Section 10. 3. Correct the station configuration and re-verify before proceeding to Step 2. |
| Safety Note | Welding a part against the wrong procedure is a quality escape, not merely an inconvenience — treat a caught mismatch as a near-miss worth recording, not a nuisance to clear silently. |
| Escalation | A recurring mismatch pattern at a specific station should be escalated as a routing/configuration investigation (Chapter 12, Configuration family), not repeatedly corrected by hand without addressing the root cause. |

# Step 2 — Gun and Tooling Readiness

With the correct procedure identified, the next question is whether the physical hardware assigned to execute it is actually in a state capable of doing so. A perfectly correct WPS running through a gun with the wrong tip, or a tip past its dressing life, does not produce a qualified weld — it produces a weld that merely looks like the qualified one was supposed to.

- Confirm the correct gun is assigned for this joint's geometry and access requirements (Chapter 5, Servo Guns and Gun-Drive Systems, Section 6's procedure-eligibility parameters) — a gun capable of a different joint's reach/access is not automatically capable of this one.

- Confirm the electrode/tip currently mounted matches the type, material/RWMA class and face geometry the WPS specifies (Chapter 3, Electrodes and Tooling; Chapter 8, Section 3's "Electrodes" data group).

- Check the tip's dressing count/weld count against its configured life limit before starting production (Chapter 13, Preventive Maintenance and Electrode Life's tip-life lifecycle model) — this is a scheduled check, not an optional one, precisely because tip wear is the single most common slow-drift cause in Chapter 12's FMEA worked example (Section 4 there).

- If gun-mounted identity/calibration data is available on this platform, confirm it reports the expected gun identity and current calibration state before trusting its force/position readings (Chapter 5, Section 4's discussion of what a gun-mounted data module stores and why).

- Confirm the gun's force calibration and position/encoder calibration are both current (Chapter 5, Section 6) — absolute commanded force and squeeze/contact position are only trustworthy if both are true.

| If This Check Fails... | Do Not | Do Instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tip is past its configured dressing/life limit | Run "just this one more part" past the limit to avoid a changeover delay | Dress or replace the tip per Chapter 13's model before starting the run — the defect risk (Chapter 12, Section 9's Weld Defect Catalog) rises exactly where this shortcut is most tempting |
| Wrong gun/tip family mounted for this joint | Assume "close enough" because the part still fits in the fixture | Correct the tooling assignment; a joint qualified for one electrode geometry is not automatically qualified for another (Chapter 1, Section 6's d_e = 5√t rule) |
| Force or position calibration is not current | Trust the displayed force/position reading anyway | Recalibrate per the equipment's approved procedure before relying on closed-loop force/position control (Chapter 5, Section 4) |

# Step 3 — Parameter Load and Verification

Only once the correct procedure is identified (Step 1) and the correct, capable hardware is confirmed ready (Step 2) does it make sense to look at the parameters themselves — loading correct current/time/force values onto the wrong gun, or against the wrong material, does not produce a correct weld.

- Confirm the loaded current, time and force values fall within the qualified WPS's stated range of validity (Chapter 8, Section 4's essential-variables discussion) — not merely that some plausible-looking numbers are present.

- Cross-check the loaded parameters against the material-family and thickness-band guidance in Chapter 20 (Material and Thickness Parameter Guide) as a sanity check, remembering that Chapter 20's figures are calculated first-trial estimates, not a substitute for the actual qualified WPS values (Chapter 20, Section 2).

- If the schedule includes upslope/downslope sub-stages (Chapter 1, Section 3), confirm they are actually enabled and configured as the WPS specifies — an omitted downslope on a hardenable/AHSS grade is a direct path to the cracking defect entry in Chapter 12's Weld Defect Catalog (Section 9 there).

- Confirm the monitoring tolerance bands loaded match those the WPS specifies (Chapter 8, Section 3's "Monitoring" data group; Chapter 11's reference-curve concept) — a monitoring system with the wrong tolerance band will not correctly flag Step 6's quality decision below.

# Step 4 — Cell and Safety Readiness

This step is deliberately placed after Steps 1–3, not before them, for a specific reason: Steps 1–3 establish what should happen; Step 4 confirms the cell is actually allowed to let it happen. Per Chapter 12's decision sequence (Section 2 there), safety and sequence readiness sit at the very top of the diagnostic hierarchy precisely because none of the downstream layers can be meaningfully evaluated until this step is satisfied.

- Confirm all safety devices — guards, E-stops, light curtains and equivalent protective devices — report their required ready state (Chapter 6, Automation, PLC, Robot and Safety Integration, Section 5).

- Confirm the PLC/robot sequence is not held on a permissive/interlock condition of the kind worked through in Chapter 12's sequence-inhibit example (Section 11 there) — if it is, resolve that condition per Chapter 12's method before proceeding; never bypass it.

- Confirm part-presence/identity confirmation for the specific part now at the station is satisfied, consistent with Step 1's identity check.

- Confirm the cell is in the correct operating mode (automatic vs. manual) for the intended production run.

# Step 5 — Weld Execution With Real-Time Monitoring

With Steps 1–4 satisfied, the weld itself executes through the squeeze/weld/hold/off cycle described in Chapter 1, Section 3. What makes this step "production" rather than merely "a weld happened" is that the execution is measured, not just performed.

## What is actually being monitored, and why

Chapter 11 (Process Monitoring and Adaptive Control) establishes the real, sourced concept behind this step: the controller measures current and voltage (and, on many platforms, force/position) throughout the pulse, derives resistance/energy from them, and compares the resulting trace against a stored reference curve built from previously accepted, stable welds. This reference set does not assert a specific "IoT" protocol or a specific data-acquisition architecture beyond what Chapter 11 and Chapter 17 already establish as real, generic, sourced concepts — what matters operationally is the function, not a specific communications standard:

- Current/voltage/resistance trace against the reference curve, to catch a process-quality deviation while it is still happening rather than only after destructive testing later (Chapter 11).

- Force/position trace on platforms with real force feedback, to catch a mechanical/servo-side deviation distinct from a purely electrical one (Chapter 5, Chapter 11's deviation-pattern table).

- Spatter/expulsion events recorded as a discrete event tied to a specific weld ID, or as a rate over many welds — never treated as a fixed physical constant (Chapter 11's "Spatter as a measured, not universal, metric" section).

- The resulting record is what becomes the weld-event data described in Chapter 17 (Traceability and Digital Thread) — this is the same data that Step 8 below commits to the traceability system, not a separate data stream.

| This Reference Set States the Real, Sourced Concept — Not an Invented Protocol Chapter 11 documents, generically and without naming a manufacturer, that commercial controllers capable of this kind of monitoring are a real, currently shipping equipment category — adaptive current/voltage control, reference-curve comparison, and shop-floor analytics layers are confirmed real capabilities. This chapter reuses that same sourced material rather than inventing a specific sensor protocol, update rate, or dashboard technology that no source in this reference set actually verifies. |

# Step 6 — In-Process Quality Decision

The monitoring data from Step 5 has to resolve to an actual decision before the part moves on. This step is where Chapter 11's tolerance-band concept and Chapter 12's "a monitoring pass is not proof of joint strength" caution both apply directly.

- Compare the completed weld's trace against the loaded reference curve and tolerance bands (Step 3, Step 5).

- Classify the result: pass, warn (flagged but within an accepted secondary band, if the platform supports one), or reject.

- On a reject or warn, do not simply re-weld the same location without first checking whether the cause is a genuine process deviation or a sensor/measurement fault (Chapter 12, Section 12's Welding process/monitoring worked card) — re-welding blind treats the symptom, not the cause.

- Record the classification against the part identity, regardless of outcome — a "pass" result still needs to be recorded, because Step 8's traceability commit depends on every weld having a resolvable record, not only the failures.

# Step 7 — Error-Handling Loop

If any step above — not only Step 6's quality decision, but any of Steps 1 through 6 — surfaces a fault, this step is where that fault gets resolved before production resumes. This is not a separate procedure from the rest of this chapter; it is what happens when any of the numbered checks above returns "no" instead of "yes."

- Identify which step (1–6 above) the fault actually occurred at — this alone often narrows the affected hardware layer immediately, per this chapter's own structure.

- Cross-reference the fault against Chapter 12's Hardware Component to Fault Category table (Section 10 there) to identify the physical subsystem most likely responsible.

- Apply Chapter 12's universal, code-independent diagnostic workflow (Section 6 there) and the matching fault-family worked example (Section 11 for safety/interlock, Section 12 for the other eight families).

- Resolve the actual identified condition — never bypass an interlock or force a result to "get production moving" (Chapter 12's safety notes apply without exception here).

- Re-verify: re-run the specific step that failed (not the whole sequence from Step 1, unless the fault could plausibly have affected an earlier step too) and confirm it now passes before resuming.

- Record the root cause and corrective action, per Chapter 12's evidence-package discipline (Section 8 there), before considering the fault closed.

| --- | --- |
| Category | This is itself a diagnostic starting point, not a dead end — the ambiguity usually resolves quickly once the affected layer is identified. |
| Likely Causes | • The fault display shows a downstream symptom (e.g., a monitoring rejection) whose actual root cause sits at an earlier step (e.g., a Step 2 tip-wear condition that was never checked). • Multiple near-simultaneous conditions make the first-reported fault misleading about where the chain actually broke. |
| Diagnostic Steps | 1. Apply Chapter 12's core principle (Section 1 there): move from the largest prerequisite down to the smallest failed layer, which in this chapter's terms means checking Step 4 (safety/sequence) before Step 6 (quality), even if the displayed fault looks like a Step 6 issue. 2. # Step 8 — Post-Weld Verification and Traceability Commit

A weld that passed Step 6's in-process check still participates in the broader quality system described in Chapter 10 (Testing and Quality Verification) and Chapter 9's Compliance Verification Checklist (Section 7 there). This step is what actually closes the loop from "this specific weld" back to "this part's compliance record."

- Confirm the weld-event record — parameters achieved (not just targeted, per Chapter 8, Section 7's "actually run, not just targeted" distinction), monitoring result, timestamp, station and equipment identity — was successfully written to the traceability system (Chapter 17).

- If this part falls within the destructive/NDE sampling plan's current frequency (Chapter 10's quality-plan structure; Chapter 9's Compliance Verification Checklist, Testing row), route it for that testing rather than treating an in-process pass as sufficient by itself.

- If the traceability write itself fails despite a normal weld (Chapter 12, Section 12's Data/traceability worked card), resolve that separately from the weld-quality question — a missing record and a bad weld are two different problems with two different urgencies.

- Confirm the part's identity and this weld's record are correctly linked before the part leaves the station, since resolving this after the part has moved on is far more costly than confirming it now.

At this point the sequence returns to Step 1 for the next part. The reason this chapter presents all eight steps as one numbered sequence, rather than eight separate chapters' worth of unconnected advice, is exactly the point the user feedback behind this chapter raised: a gun is not "ready" in the abstract, a parameter set is not "correct" in the abstract, and a monitoring system is not "working" in the abstract — each is ready, correct or working only in relation to the specific part, procedure and station in front of it at that moment, and that relation is what Steps 1 through 8 make explicit.

# 1. Purpose and Scope of This Chapter

Chapter 1 (Fundamentals and Physics) sets out the governing physical relationships and a short list of commonly published design and estimation formulas: electrode face diameter, minimum nugget diameter, minimum weld spacing, minimum edge distance, and a rough imperial-unit starting estimate for force, time and current. Chapter 2 (Materials, Coatings and Weldability) sets out why material family and coating change process behavior even when thickness is held constant. Neither chapter, by itself, answers the question a programmer or process engineer actually asks first when a new part arrives on the bench: "this part is 1.2 mm galvanized steel — what force, current and time do I even start with?"

This chapter exists to close exactly that gap, and only that gap. It does not derive any new physics and it does not introduce any formula beyond what Chapter 1 already cites. What it does is apply those cited formulas arithmetically across a representative sweep of sheet-thickness bands and material families, so the arithmetic that would otherwise be left as an exercise for the reader is shown explicitly, band by band. Every number in every table below traces back to one of the formulas in Chapter 1's design-rules section, and every number is presented with the same qualification this reference set has used from Chapter 1 onward: it is a calculated first-trial estimate for sizing tooling and sanity-checking a program, not a validated production setpoint, and it does not replace destructive weldability-lobe testing per ISO 14327 or procedure qualification per ISO 15614-12 [S5][S8].

# 2. How the Numbers in This Chapter Are Produced

Two independent sets of formulas from Chapter 1 are combined here, and it is worth being explicit about which is which, because they use different units and different definitions of "thickness":

- The metric geometry rules (electrode face diameter, minimum nugget diameter, minimum spacing, minimum edge distance) are all functions of t, the thickness of the thinnest sheet in the stack, in millimeters, per ISO 14373's guidance for low-carbon steel [S6]. These rules describe tooling and joint-layout geometry — they do not by themselves specify current, force or time.

- The imperial first-trial estimate (force, time, current) is a function of ΣT, the sum of all sheet thicknesses in the stack, in inches — not the single thinnest-sheet value used by the geometry rules [S18]. This chapter therefore has to state, for every thickness band, what stack it is assuming ΣT represents, so the arithmetic is reproducible rather than a black box.

For every band in this chapter, the representative case modeled is a symmetric two-sheet stack of equal-thickness sheets: both the geometry rules' t and half of the imperial formula's ΣT use the same representative thickness value drawn from the midpoint of the band (for example, the 0.8–1.2 mm band is represented by t = 1.0 mm, giving ΣT = 2.0 mm for the imperial calculation). This is a modeling choice made explicit here so the arithmetic can be checked and re-derived for a different stack composition — Section 7 below (Stack-Up Considerations) addresses what changes for an unequal or three-sheet stack, where this simplification no longer applies directly.

| Thickness Band | Representative Sheet Thickness, t | Representative ΣT (2-sheet equal stack) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.5–0.8 mm | 0.65 mm | 1.30 mm (0.0512 in) |
| 0.8–1.2 mm | 1.0 mm | 2.00 mm (0.0787 in) |
| 1.2–1.6 mm | 1.4 mm | 2.80 mm (0.1102 in) |
| 1.6–2.0 mm | 1.8 mm | 3.60 mm (0.1417 in) |
| 2.0–3.0 mm | 2.5 mm | 5.00 mm (0.1969 in) |

The thinnest band in this chapter (0.5–0.8 mm) sits inside that scope but close to its lower edge; a stack thinner than roughly 0.4–0.5 mm is approaching the boundary where conventional-scale design rules and the micro-spot-welding treatment in Chapter 14 (Specialized Processes) begin to overlap — see Section 8 below. |

# 3. Thickness-Driven Electrode and Joint Geometry Across the Sweep

The four geometry rules from Chapter 1 — electrode face diameter, minimum nugget diameter, minimum spacing, and minimum edge distance — are all driven by thickness alone in their published form, not by material family. They are stated in Chapter 1 as ISO 14373 guidance developed for low-carbon steel [S6], and this chapter applies them here as a common starting geometry for the steel family (mild/low-carbon, HSLA, AHSS/UHSS, and zinc-coated variants of low-carbon steel all fall within, or close to, ISO 14373's coated/uncoated low-carbon-steel scope). Aluminum is addressed separately at the end of this section, because the specific numeric coefficient in these formulas is sourced for low-carbon steel and this corpus does not carry an independently sourced coefficient for aluminum.
