| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0.5–0.8 mm | 0.65 mm | 5√0.65 ≈ 4.0 | 3.2 – 4.0 | ≥ 10.4 | ≈ 4.0 – 5.0 |
| 0.8–1.2 mm | 1.0 mm | 5√1.0 = 5.0 | 4.0 – 5.0 | ≥ 16.0 | ≈ 5.0 – 6.3 |
| 1.2–1.6 mm | 1.4 mm | 5√1.4 ≈ 5.9 | 4.7 – 5.9 | ≥ 22.4 | ≈ 5.9 – 7.4 |
| 1.6–2.0 mm | 1.8 mm | 5√1.8 ≈ 6.7 | 5.4 – 6.7 | ≥ 28.8 | ≈ 6.7 – 8.4 |
| 2.0–3.0 mm | 2.5 mm | 5√2.5 ≈ 7.9 | 6.3 – 7.9 | ≥ 40.0 | ≈ 7.9 – 9.9 |

Reading the first row as a worked example: at t = 0.65 mm, d_e = 5√t → 5 × √0.65 = 5 × 0.806 ≈ 4.0 mm. The minimum nugget diameter range uses the same square-root scaling with coefficients 4 and 5 in place of the electrode rule's coefficient of 5, giving 4 × 0.806 ≈ 3.2 mm to 5 × 0.806 ≈ 4.0 mm. Minimum spacing is linear in t: 16 × 0.65 = 10.4 mm. Minimum edge distance is linear in the nugget diameter, 1.25 × d_w, so it is evaluated at both ends of the nugget-diameter range: 1.25 × 3.2 ≈ 4.0 mm and 1.25 × 4.0 = 5.0 mm. The remaining rows follow the identical arithmetic at their respective t values.

| Aluminum Electrode Geometry Is Not Covered by This Specific Formula The 5√t electrode-diameter coefficient and the 4√t–5√t nugget-diameter coefficients are sourced from ISO 14373 guidance and a widely used rule of thumb, both developed around low-carbon steel [S6][S18]. Chapter 2 and Chapter 1 both establish that aluminum's conductivity, plastic range and dynamic-resistance behavior are fundamentally different from steel's [S14], and this corpus does not carry an independently sourced numeric electrode-diameter coefficient for aluminum. Aluminum electrode-face sizing should be treated as governed by the same general concept — contact area must be matched to current density and thickness — but the specific 5√t coefficient above should not be applied to an aluminum stack as if it were validated for that material; aluminum tooling geometry is an equipment- and alloy-specific determination (Chapter 3, Electrodes and Tooling; Chapter 14, Specialized Processes). |

# 4. Indicative Force, Time and Current — Mild/Low-Carbon Steel Baseline

The imperial first-trial estimate from Chapter 1 is: force (lbf) ≈ 6000 × ΣT; weld time (60 Hz cycles) ≈ 100 × ΣT; weld current (A) ≈ 100,000 × ΣT, with the current figure reduced roughly 20% when total stack thickness ΣT exceeds 0.080 in [S18]. Applying this formula to the representative ΣT values from Section 2 gives the mild/low-carbon steel baseline below. This is the steel-family baseline referred to throughout the rest of this chapter; Section 6 addresses how HSLA, AHSS/UHSS and zinc-coated steel are expected to relate to it.

| Thickness Band | ΣT (in) | Force ≈ 6000×ΣT (lbf) | Weld Time ≈ 100×ΣT (cycles) | Current ≈ 100,000×ΣT (A) | >0.080 in? ~20% Reduction Applied |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0.5–0.8 mm | 0.0512 | ≈ 307 | ≈ 5.1 | ≈ 5,120 | No |
| 0.8–1.2 mm | 0.0787 | ≈ 472 | ≈ 7.9 | ≈ 7,870 | No (at threshold) |
| 1.2–1.6 mm | 0.1102 | ≈ 661 | ≈ 11.0 | ≈ 8,820 (reduced from ≈11,020) | Yes |
| 1.6–2.0 mm | 0.1417 | ≈ 850 | ≈ 14.2 | ≈ 11,340 (reduced from ≈14,170) | Yes |
| 2.0–3.0 mm | 0.1969 | ≈ 1,181 | ≈ 19.7 | ≈ 15,750 (reduced from ≈19,690) | Yes |

Worked example for the 1.2–1.6 mm band: ΣT = 0.1102 in (two 1.4 mm sheets). Force ≈ 6000 × 0.1102 ≈ 661 lbf. Weld time ≈ 100 × 0.1102 ≈ 11.0 cycles at 60 Hz. Current before reduction ≈ 100,000 × 0.1102 ≈ 11,020 A; because ΣT (0.1102 in) exceeds the 0.080 in threshold, the source's ~20% reduction applies, giving 11,020 × 0.80 ≈ 8,820 A as the indicative first-trial current. The same three-step arithmetic — multiply ΣT by the stated coefficient, then apply the reduction only above 0.080 in — produces every other row in the table.

# 7. Stack-Up Considerations

## 7.1 Why the thinnest sheet governs electrode sizing

Chapter 1's electrode-diameter rule is explicitly stated as a function of t, the thickness of the thinnest sheet in the stack, not the total stack thickness and not the thickest member. The reasoning carries over directly from the physics in Chapter 1 and Chapter 2: the thinner sheet has less thermal mass and a smaller tolerance for excess heat input before it either melts through, distorts, or drives expulsion at its own faying interface, so it is the thinner member — not the assembly as a whole — that sets the ceiling on how large an electrode face (and therefore how wide a current path) the joint can tolerate. An electrode sized to the thickest sheet in an unequal stack would oversize the effective contact area relative to what the thin sheet can safely absorb, pushing that interface toward insufficient fusion even while the thick-sheet interface might still be within its own acceptable range.

## 7.2 Equal vs. unequal sheet-thickness ratio within a stack

A symmetric stack — two (or, for a three-sheet joint, an outer pair of) sheets of equal or near-equal thickness and similar material/coating — is the case the design-rule formulas in this chapter model most directly, because the heat generated at the single faying interface (two-sheet case) or at each of the two faying interfaces (three-sheet case) is not being pulled toward two different thermal-mass targets at once. As the thickness ratio between the thinnest and thickest sheet in the stack widens, the process window narrows for the reason given in 7.1: the schedule has to deliver enough heat at the thin-sheet interface to meet the minimum nugget-diameter rule without exceeding what the thin sheet itself can contain, while still generating adequate fusion on the thicker side. Chapter 2 identifies the "thin-thick-thin" case as a well-known challenge configuration for exactly this reason. This corpus does not carry a single universally cited numeric thickness-ratio limit beyond which a stack is categorically unweldable by conventional RSW — that boundary is equipment-, material- and geometry-specific and is properly established by weldability-lobe testing (ISO 14327) for the actual combination in question, not read off a table [S5].

| No Universal Thickness-Ratio Limit Is Asserted Here It would be easy to publish a specific maximum thin:thick ratio (for example "3:1") as if it were a universal design rule. This chapter deliberately does not do that, because no such ratio is stated in the corpus sources behind this reference set. What is sourced, and stated above, is the direction and mechanism of the effect — wider thickness ratio narrows the window and requires more careful qualification — not a numeric ceiling. Any specific ratio limit used in production should come from that stack's own lobe-testing or procedure-qualification record, not from this or any other general reference. |
| --- |

## 7.3 Two-sheet vs. three-sheet stacks: current path and heat balance

A two-sheet stack has one faying interface: essentially all of the resistive heat this chapter's formulas are describing is generated at that single interface, bounded on either side by the two sheets' bulk resistance and by the electrode contact resistance at the two outer faces. A three-sheet stack is a materially different electrical and thermal problem, not simply "the same thing with more metal": current passes through two faying interfaces in series plus the bulk of the center sheet, and Chapter 2 is explicit that the heat generated — and the resulting nugget — is not necessarily symmetric between those two interfaces, particularly when the two outer sheets differ from one another in thickness, grade or coating.

The practical consequence for parameter selection is that the ΣT-based imperial estimate in Section 4 (and its aluminum-multiplier extension in Section 5) gives a starting total-current/time/force figure for the stack as a whole, but it says nothing about how that total resolves into two separate interface conditions inside a three-sheet joint. A three-sheet stack — especially an asymmetric one — needs its adequacy checked at each interface independently (via lobe testing and, ultimately, destructive sectioning per Chapter 10, Testing and Quality Verification) rather than assumed adequate simply because the whole-stack ΣT falls inside a comfortable range. This is the same "thin-thick-thin" mechanism as 7.2, restated for the specific case of current path rather than thickness ratio alone.

# 8. When a Stack-Up Falls Outside Standard RSW's Practical Range

The design rules and the imperial estimate in this chapter are built around, and bounded by, the same practical range the rest of this reference set assumes: sheet-metal-scale steel and aluminum stacks within roughly the thickness band this chapter sweeps, welded on conventional or servo-actuated RSW equipment. Two situations recur where a stack-up should be recognized as falling outside that practical range and routed to Chapter 14 (Specialized Processes) rather than parameter-sized from this chapter's tables:

- Very thin, micro-scale stacks. ISO 14373's own low-carbon-steel scope begins at 0.4 mm [S6], and this chapter's thinnest band (0.5–0.8 mm) sits close to that boundary. Foils, tabs and fine conductors thinner than this range — battery-tab welding, sensor and electrical-contact welding, and precision electronics assembly are the typical applications — move into micro-spot welding, where Chapter 14 is explicit that there is no universal current, time or force setpoint at that scale and where the general-physics relationships this chapter is built on still apply in principle but their sensitivity is amplified well beyond what a shop rule of thumb sized for structural sheet metal can responsibly estimate.

- Aluminum stacks needing specialized equipment capability. Section 5 above shows the aluminum indicative currents in this sweep reaching well past the typical 8–15 kA steel production range [S13], consistent with Chapter 2's statement that equipment sized for typical steel body-shop currents may not even be electrically capable of a given aluminum schedule. Once a stack's indicative aluminum current or force demand is at or beyond what the intended power system (Chapter 4, Power Systems) and gun (Chapter 5, Servo Guns and Gun-Drive Systems) are actually rated for, the decision is not "push the setpoint higher" — it is to route to the aluminum-specific process notes in Chapter 14, which carry the aluminum treatment forward from Chapter 2's comparison in more operational detail, and to confirm equipment capability before any trial weld is attempted.

Its purpose is only to make explicit, at the point where a practitioner is most likely to reach for this chapter's tables, when the right move is to stop sizing from this chapter and go read Chapter 14 instead. |

1. Why Process Identity Is the First Engineering Decision

Every other decision in this reference set — filler metal, shielding gas, preheat, position, inspection method, acceptance criteria, welder qualification range — is conditioned on which process is being used. A carbon-steel fillet weld is not one engineering problem; it is at least six different engineering problems depending on whether it is made with a covered electrode, a solid wire under active gas, a flux-cored wire, a tungsten electrode, submerged arc, or a laser. The consumable classification systems are different, the defect populations are different, the qualification essential variables are different, and the economics are different by an order of magnitude.

This is why process identity is treated in the codes as an essential variable rather than a descriptive label. Changing the process invalidates a welding procedure qualification outright in every major system — there is no "similar process" allowance that lets a procedure qualified with one process be used with another. A shop that qualifies a procedure on 135 and then runs production on 138 has, in the strict reading of every code discussed in Chapter 31, no qualified procedure for what it actually welded, regardless of how similar the two look on the shop floor and regardless of whether the resulting welds pass inspection.

The practical consequence is that a person or a system reasoning about welding has to be able to do three things reliably: recognize which process a document is describing, recognize when two documents are describing the same process under different names, and recognize when a number or an acronym is ambiguous enough that it must be clarified before any downstream advice is given. This chapter builds that capability. It is deliberately placed first in this volume because every chapter that follows assumes it.

2. The Two Naming Systems in Daily Use

Two systems dominate, and they do not map onto each other cleanly.

The ISO system assigns each process a numeric reference number, defined in ISO 4063 [S1]. The number is hierarchical: the first digit identifies a broad process group, the second digit narrows it, and the third digit identifies a specific variant. A procedure specification written to European or international practice will typically carry this number in a field labelled "process" or "welding process reference number," often with no words next to it at all — the number is expected to be sufficient.

The AWS system assigns each process a letter designation defined in AWS A3.0, the standard welding terms and definitions document. These are the acronyms most fabricators speak in daily: SMAW, GMAW, FCAW, GTAW, PAW, SAW, RSW, EBW, LBW, FSW. A procedure written to AWS or ASME practice will typically name the process by these letters and will not carry a numeric reference at all.

Neither system is a superset of the other. ISO 4063 subdivides some processes far more finely than the AWS acronyms do — the AWS acronym GMAW covers at least six distinct ISO reference numbers, and the distinctions ISO draws between them (inert against active gas, solid against flux-cored against metal-cored electrode) are exactly the distinctions that matter for consumable selection and fume behaviour. Conversely, AWS distinguishes some things by separate acronyms where ISO uses one number with a variant digit.

The correct working habit is to treat both as incomplete on their own. A process statement of "GMAW" without a wire type and gas type is under-specified. A process statement of "131" without an edition of ISO 4063 is under-specified in a different way (see Section 15). A well-written procedure carries both, plus the actual consumable classification, and a system reading welding documents should expect to have to reconstruct the missing half.

3. How an ISO 4063 Reference Number Is Constructed

The numbering is hierarchical and is read left to right, from general to specific. The first digit is the process group:

| First digit | Process group |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Arc welding |
| 2 | Resistance welding |
| 3 | Gas welding |
| 4 | Welding with pressure (solid-state processes) |
| 5 | Beam welding |
| 6 | Welding of plastics |
| 7 | Other welding processes |
| 8 | Cutting and gouging |
| 9 | Brazing, soldering and braze welding |

Adding a second digit narrows the group — 13 is gas-shielded metal arc welding within group 1, 14 is gas-shielded arc welding with a non-consumable electrode. Adding a third digit identifies the specific process — 131 is MIG welding with a solid wire electrode, 135 is MAG welding with a solid wire electrode.

A shorter number is not a different process; it is a less specific statement about the same process. Writing "13" on a procedure is not wrong in the way that writing the wrong number is wrong, but it is under-specified: it commits to gas-shielded metal arc welding without saying whether the gas is inert or active or whether the electrode is solid, flux-cored or metal-cored. Since those three choices drive the filler classification, the fume generation, the slag behaviour and the position capability, "13" is rarely sufficient on a production document.

| Read the Number, Then Read What Is Missing The hierarchy means an under-specified number is silently under-specified — it looks like a complete answer. A procedure that says "13" or "14" has not stated the gas or the electrode form, and those are the variables that determine what consumable to buy and what defects to expect. Treat a two-digit process number on a production document as an open question, not as a specification. |

First, 131 against 135 is the inert-gas against active-gas distinction. 131 uses argon or argon-helium with no oxidizing component; 135 uses a mixture containing carbon dioxide or oxygen. Because unalloyed and low-alloy steel is essentially always welded under an active mixture and aluminium is essentially always welded under a pure inert gas, the number often functions as a proxy for the material — but it is not a material statement, and treating it as one goes wrong on stainless and nickel work, where both appear.

They are classified under different filler-metal specifications, generate different fume, and require different post-weld cleaning. Chapter 40 treats both in detail.

Also worth noting: 114 is self-shielded flux-cored welding and sits outside the 13x family entirely, because it uses no external shielding gas at all. This is a real structural distinction, not a numbering accident — a self-shielded wire is a chemically different consumable that carries its own deoxidizers and denitriders, and its behaviour in wind is the reason it exists.

Group 6 covers welding of thermoplastics — electrofusion, hot gas, hot plate, heated wedge, socket and saddle fusion, extrusion welding, and related processes. It sits inside the same nomenclature standard as metal welding because the standard's scope is welding as a class of joining operations, not welding of metals specifically.

This reference set does not cover polymer welding in technical depth. It is named here for one specific reason: a reader or a system encountering a 6xx reference number should recognize immediately that it is outside the metallic-welding domain and should not attempt to answer it with metallic-welding reasoning. Hot plate welding of polyethylene pipe (661) and electrofusion (611) are large, well-standardized industrial disciplines with their own qualification, inspection and defect frameworks. Recognizing the boundary is the useful knowledge here; pretending to competence past it is not.

11. Groups 8 and 9 — Cutting, Brazing and Soldering

Group 8 covers thermal cutting and gouging: oxy-fuel cutting, arc cutting, plasma cutting, laser cutting, and the gouging variants of each. These are not joining processes, but they belong in a welding engineer's scope for a concrete reason — cut quality determines joint preparation quality, and joint preparation quality determines root fusion, which is one of the most common causes of rejectable weld defects. Chapter 64 covers them from that angle.

Group 9 covers brazing, soldering and braze welding. These are distinct from welding by definition: the parent metal is not melted, and the joint is made by a filler that melts below the parent's melting range and is distributed by capillary action (in brazing and soldering) or deposited like a weld bead without parent fusion (in braze welding). The dividing line between brazing and soldering is conventionally the 450 °C liquidus of the filler — above it is brazing, below it is soldering. Chapters 66 through 68 cover the family and, more usefully, cover when to recommend it instead of welding.

13. The Six-Attribute Process Fingerprint

Numbers and acronyms are labels. What actually determines how a process behaves — and therefore what a person needs to reason about when choosing or troubleshooting one — is a small set of physical attributes. Any welding process can be fingerprinted on six:

1. Energy source. Electric arc, resistance heating, chemical flame, friction/deformation, focused beam, or induced current. This determines power density, which determines heat-affected zone width and distortion more than any other single factor.

2. Shielding mechanism. External gas, flux-generated gas and slag, self-shielding consumable chemistry, vacuum, submerged flux blanket, or none needed because the process never melts anything. This determines the porosity and oxidation failure modes.

3. Filler delivery. Continuously fed consumable electrode, hand-fed rod with a non-consumable electrode, no filler at all, or filler that is the parent metal displaced by force. This determines deposition rate and therefore economics.

4. Pressure requirement. Whether the joint is made under applied force. Every group 2 and group 4 process requires it; almost no group 1, 3 or 5 process does.

5. Joint access requirement. Whether the process needs access from one side, both sides, or full enclosure. This is frequently the constraint that eliminates an otherwise ideal process.

6. Automation coupling. Whether the process is inherently manual, inherently mechanized, or capable of both. Some processes exist only as machine processes because the control tolerances are outside human capability.

This fingerprint is the working basis of the process-selection framework in Chapter 73. Its value here is diagnostic: when a process behaves unexpectedly, the fault almost always lies in one of these six attributes, and naming which one narrows the search immediately.

14. Why Misnaming a Process Invalidates Qualification

In every qualification system covered in Chapter 31, the welding process is an essential variable — meaning a change to it requires requalification rather than merely a revised procedure document. This is not bureaucratic conservatism. Three concrete mechanisms sit behind it:

Different processes deposit different metal. A 111 electrode and a 136 wire nominally matched to the same base metal will not produce identical weld-metal chemistry, because the flux systems, deoxidizer packages and dilution behaviour differ. Mechanical properties follow chemistry, and a qualification test proves mechanical properties.

Different processes produce different thermal cycles. Heat input per unit length, and therefore cooling rate through the transformation range, differs substantially between processes at nominally similar travel speeds. The hardness and toughness of the heat-affected zone follow the cooling rate (Chapter 22), so a qualification result obtained with one process does not predict the result with another.

Different processes fail differently. The defect population of 141 is dominated by tungsten inclusions and oxidation; that of 111 by slag inclusions and arc strikes; that of 135 by lack of fusion in short-circuit mode and by porosity from lost shielding. An inspection plan calibrated to one process's failure modes is miscalibrated for another's.

The practical rule that follows is uncomfortable but simple: if the process reference on the procedure does not match the process actually used in the shop, the correct answer is that the work is unqualified, not that it is "probably fine because the welds look good." Chapter 31 develops what to do about it.

15. Edition Drift: The Trap of Quoting a Number Without an Edition

ISO 4063 has been revised several times, and the numbering has not been perfectly stable across revisions. Reference numbers have been added, and subdivisions have been introduced where earlier editions used a single number. The 2023 edition, for example, presents the resistance spot welding entries as 211 (indirect) and 212 (direct), where older practice and much surviving shop documentation simply says "21."

This creates a specific, avoidable failure. A procedure written years ago against an earlier edition, read today against the current edition, can be misread — either by treating a two-digit legacy number as though it were deliberately under-specified when it was in fact fully specific under its own edition, or by assuming a three-digit number carries the meaning it has in the current edition when the document predates that subdivision.

The discipline that prevents this is to record the edition alongside the number on any document that will outlive a standards revision cycle, and to treat an undated process number on an old document as a question to be resolved against the edition in force when the document was written — not against the edition in force today. This is the same discipline Volume 1 applies to controller alarm codes and for the same underlying reason: a code without its context is not self-interpreting.

16. Worked Example: Decoding 135 Against 138 on an Incoming Procedure

A fabrication shop receives a customer-supplied welding procedure specification for a structural fillet weld in S355-class steel. The process field reads 138. The shop's existing qualified procedure for this joint reads 135. The shop's welding engineer is asked whether the existing qualification can be used.

Step 1 — Resolve both numbers precisely. 135 is MAG welding with a solid wire electrode. 138 is MAG welding with a metal cored electrode [S1]. Both use an active shielding gas; both are gas metal arc welding in AWS terms; both would be described by a welder as "MIG welding."

Step 2 — Identify what physically differs. The electrode form differs. A metal-cored wire is a tubular sheath filled with metallic powder and arc stabilizers. Compared to a solid wire at the same current, it typically deposits faster, runs with a broader arc cone, and produces a different fusion profile. It is also classified under a different filler-metal specification, so the consumable purchased against a 138 procedure is not the consumable purchased against a 135 procedure.

Step 3 — Test against the essential-variable rule. Process is an essential variable, and 135 and 138 are different processes under the nomenclature. A change of consumable classification is independently an essential variable in most systems. Two independent grounds therefore point the same way.

Step 4 — State the conclusion honestly. The existing 135 qualification does not cover 138 work. The shop's options are to qualify a new procedure for 138, to ask the customer whether 135 is acceptable for the application (a commercial and engineering question, not a documentation one), or to decline the work. What the shop must not do is run 138 wire under a 135 procedure on the grounds that "it's all MIG."

Step 5 — Note the trap that was avoided. Had the process field read "13" on both documents, the two procedures would have looked identical and the difference would have been invisible until someone compared the consumable classifications. This is precisely why Section 3 warns against accepting two-digit process numbers on production documents.

1. A Weld Is a Moving Thermal Event, Not a Static Joint

Almost every persistent misunderstanding in welding engineering comes from picturing a weld as a static thing — a bead of metal sitting in a groove — instead of as the frozen record of a thermal event that moved along the joint. The bead is what remains after a small volume of molten metal travelled the length of the joint at a defined speed, dragging a steep temperature gradient behind it and leaving every point it passed with a permanent thermal history.

That reframing pays for itself immediately. It explains why travel speed is a metallurgical variable and not just a productivity variable. It explains why the same current and voltage produce different results on 6 mm plate than on 40 mm plate — the surrounding metal is the heat sink, and a thicker heat sink extracts heat in three dimensions instead of two. It explains why the last 20 mm of a weld behaves differently from the middle, why a weld made on a preheated plate has different properties from an identical weld on a cold one, and why the region that fails is so often not the weld metal at all but a band of parent metal a few millimetres to the side of it that nobody deposited, inspected, or thought about.

Every fusion process in Volumes 3, 5 and 7 is a different way of delivering that moving thermal event. The delivery mechanisms differ enormously; the consequences of the event are governed by the same physics in all of them. This chapter states that physics once.

2. Power Density: The Attribute That Orders the Processes

If a single number had to be chosen to characterize a welding heat source, it would be power density — the rate of energy delivery per unit area of the surface it acts on, conventionally expressed in W/mm².

Power density orders the processes into a spectrum that predicts most of their observable behaviour. An oxy-fuel flame spreads its energy over a large area at low intensity. An electric arc concentrates it far more. A focused laser or electron beam concentrates it by several further orders of magnitude. The consequences follow directly and consistently:

• Low power density means the heat has time to conduct sideways before the metal beneath it melts, so a large volume is heated to make a small weld. This produces a wide heat-affected zone, high total heat input per unit of joint made, and substantial distortion.

• High power density means the metal melts — and vaporizes — faster than heat can conduct away, so a very small volume is heated. This produces a narrow heat-affected zone, low total heat input, minimal distortion, and deep narrow welds.

This single relationship explains why oxy-fuel welding distorts thin sheet badly and laser welding does not; why electron beam welding can make a 50 mm deep weld in one pass while arc welding needs many passes to do it; and why high power density processes are unforgiving of joint fit-up — a beam that concentrates energy into a fraction of a millimetre cannot bridge a gap that a broad arc would fill without complaint.

It also explains a trade-off worth stating plainly, because it recurs throughout this reference set: the same property that makes a high power density process precise makes it intolerant. Precision and forgiveness are opposite ends of one axis, not independent virtues to be optimized separately.

3. Heat Input: The Formula, the Efficiency Factor, and the Honest Uncertainty in It

Heat input is the energy delivered per unit length of weld. For arc processes it is calculated as:

Heat input (kJ/mm) = (Arc voltage × Welding current × 60) ÷ (Travel speed in mm/min × 1000)

So a weld run at 28 V and 260 A at 350 mm/min gives (28 × 260 × 60) ÷ (350 × 1000) = 1.25 kJ/mm.

This quantity is called arc energy in some standards and heat input in others, and the distinction between the two is not cosmetic. Arc energy is the raw electrical energy per unit length as calculated above. Heat input proper is arc energy multiplied by a thermal efficiency factor that accounts for the fraction of that energy actually entering the workpiece rather than being lost to radiation, convection, and spatter ejection.

Commonly cited efficiency factors, which vary between published sources and should be treated as approximate:

| Process | Typical thermal efficiency factor |
| --- | --- |
| Submerged arc (SAW) | ~0.95–1.0 — the flux blanket returns most losses to the joint |
| Shielded metal arc (SMAW) | ~0.75–0.85 |
| Gas metal arc / flux cored (GMAW, FCAW) | ~0.75–0.85 |
| Gas tungsten arc (GTAW) | ~0.6–0.7 — significant radiative and convective loss from an open arc |
| Plasma arc (PAW) | ~0.6–0.8 depending on configuration |

Two honesty points belong here. First, published efficiency factors differ between sources, and a calculation that matters — a qualification record, a customer submittal, a cracking investigation — should use the factor prescribed by the governing standard rather than a textbook value. Second, the formula assumes steady-state travel. It does not correctly describe weaving, stitch welding, pulsed waveforms with high peak currents, or any situation where the instantaneous power differs substantially from the average the meter reports. For pulsed processes in particular, the arithmetic mean of a rapidly varying current is not a reliable stand-in for its thermal effect, and standards addressing pulsed welding specify how the equivalent value must be derived.

| Why Heat Input Is Controlled in Both Directions Novices treat heat input as something to keep below a limit. Experienced practice recognizes it is often bracketed on both sides. Too high, and the heat-affected zone coarsens, toughness falls, and quenched-and-tempered or thermomechanically processed steels lose the properties their processing route gave them. Too low, and the cooling rate rises far enough to form hard, crack-susceptible martensite in the heat-affected zone. Duplex stainless steel (Chapter 24) is the clearest case: it has a genuine window with a floor and a ceiling, and violating either end degrades the joint by a different mechanism. |

4. The Thermal Cycle at a Point, and the t8/5 Concept

Consider a single point in the parent metal 3 mm from the fusion line. As the arc approaches, that point heats rapidly — hundreds of degrees per second is normal. It reaches a peak temperature determined by its distance from the heat source. Then, as the arc passes, it cools, initially very fast and then progressively more slowly as the temperature difference driving the heat flow diminishes.

Three features of that curve determine what happens metallurgically:

1. Peak temperature determines which metallurgical changes are possible at all. A point that reached 1400 °C has been fully austenitized and its grains have grown; a point that only reached 600 °C has not transformed at all but may have been tempered.

2. Time above a critical temperature determines how far diffusion-driven processes proceed — grain growth, carbide precipitation, dissolution of strengthening particles.

3. Cooling rate through the transformation range determines which microstructure forms from the austenite present at high temperature.

Because the third is the most consequential for steel, it is given a standardized measure: t8/5, the time in seconds for the point to cool from 800 °C to 500 °C. That interval is chosen because it brackets the transformation range in which austenite decomposes into ferrite, pearlite, bainite or martensite in most structural steels.

A short t8/5 — a fast cool — favours hard, brittle martensite. A long t8/5 — a slow cool — favours softer, tougher structures but, taken too far, produces coarse grains with poor toughness of a different kind. t8/5 is governed by heat input, plate thickness, joint geometry, preheat temperature and interpass temperature acting together, which is why none of those variables can be adjusted in isolation.

5. Forces Inside the Weld Pool and the Penetration Profile They Produce

The weld pool is not a passive puddle. At least four forces act on it simultaneously, and the balance between them determines the shape of the weld — which in turn determines whether it fuses the joint faces properly and whether it cracks.

Surface tension and the Marangoni effect. Surface tension varies with temperature, and the direction of that variation determines whether the surface flow carries hot metal from the centre outward (producing a wide shallow pool) or from the edge inward and down (producing a narrow deep pool). Trace elements — sulphur and oxygen in particular, at concentrations measured in tens of parts per million — reverse the sign of this gradient. This is the mechanism behind the notorious cast-to-cast variation in gas tungsten arc welding of stainless steel: two plates of identical specification, from different heats, welded with identical parameters, can produce visibly different penetration because their residual sulphur differs. It is not an equipment fault and no amount of parameter adjustment diagnoses it; the fix is to control the material specification or add a flux (Chapter 41).

Arc pressure. The plasma jet impinges on the pool surface and depresses it. At high current this depression becomes deep enough that the arc acts partly on the depressed surface, increasing penetration further. Excessive arc pressure on thin material blows through; on thick material it contributes to the finger-shaped penetration profile characteristic of spray transfer.

Electromagnetic (Lorentz) force. Current flowing through the molten metal in a diverging path generates an inward and downward body force. This is a significant contributor to deep penetration at high current and to the droplet detachment mechanism in consumable-electrode processes.

Buoyancy. Hot metal at the pool centre is less dense and rises; this circulates the pool but is weak compared to the other three in most arc welding.

The practical consequence is that penetration is not a simple function of current. It is the outcome of a force balance that trace chemistry, shielding gas composition, polarity and pool size all perturb — which is why penetration is a qualified, tested outcome rather than something calculated with confidence from settings alone.

6. Solidification Structure and Where It Goes Wrong

Weld metal solidifies epitaxially: the first solid forms on the existing grains at the fusion boundary and continues their crystallographic orientation. There is no nucleation barrier to overcome, so the weld metal grain structure is seeded directly by the parent grain structure at the fusion line.

Growth then proceeds competitively — grains oriented favourably relative to the steepest thermal gradient outgrow their neighbours — producing the coarse columnar grains that run from the fusion boundary toward the weld centreline in almost every fusion weld. The direction those columns take is set by the shape of the trailing pool boundary, which is set by travel speed. A slow weld has a roughly elliptical pool and columnar grains that curve gently to meet at the centreline; a fast weld has a teardrop-shaped pool and columnar grains that meet the centreline head-on in a straight, continuous plane.

That straight central plane is a metallurgical weakness. As grains grow inward from both sides they push impurities ahead of them, and the last liquid to solidify — enriched in sulphur, phosphorus and other low-melting constituents — is trapped exactly along it. This is the mechanism of centreline solidification cracking, and it explains a rule that otherwise looks arbitrary: excessive travel speed causes centreline cracking. The speed does not crack the weld; the teardrop pool shape it produces concentrates the segregated liquid into a continuous plane instead of dispersing it.

The related geometric rule concerns the depth-to-width ratio of the weld bead. A deep, narrow bead solidifies from both side walls toward a central plane and is therefore susceptible for the same reason; a wider, shallower bead is not. This is why a cracked root pass in a deep narrow groove is often cured by widening the groove or reducing the current rather than by changing the consumable.

7. The Heat-Affected Zone and Its Sub-Zones

The heat-affected zone is the band of parent metal that was not melted but was heated enough to change. It is where a large fraction of service failures actually originate, and it is invisible to visual inspection.

For a plain carbon-manganese steel, it subdivides by peak temperature:

| Sub-zone | Approximate peak temperature | What happens there |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Coarse-grained HAZ | ~1100 °C to melting | Full austenitization with substantial grain growth; on rapid cooling this is where martensite forms and where toughness is normally lowest |
| Fine-grained HAZ | ~900–1100 °C | Full austenitization without significant grain growth; often the toughest region in the joint |
| Intercritical HAZ | ~723–900 °C | Partial austenitization; a mixed structure of transformed and untransformed regions with mixed properties |
| Subcritical HAZ | ~500–723 °C | No transformation, but tempering of any pre-existing hardened structure and, in some steels, strain-age embrittlement |

Two consequences deserve emphasis. First, the coarse-grained heat-affected zone is usually the critical region for toughness and for hydrogen cracking, and it is a band typically well under a millimetre to a few millimetres wide immediately adjacent to the fusion line. Impact-test sampling positions in qualification testing are specified where they are precisely to interrogate it.

Second, in steels that derive their properties from a prior heat treatment or thermomechanical processing route — quenched and tempered steels, thermomechanically controlled processed steels, and the advanced high-strength steels of Chapter 23 — the subcritical heat-affected zone can end up softer than the parent metal, because the weld thermal cycle tempers a structure the mill deliberately created. This HAZ softening is not a defect in any inspection code's vocabulary; it will pass every non-destructive test. It shows up only as a strength shortfall or as a failure location in service, which is why the process chapters treat heat input limits on these steels as a design constraint rather than a preference.

8. Cooling Rate, Microstructure and Hardness

For steel, the relationship between cooling rate and resulting structure is captured by continuous-cooling-transformation behaviour. The practical summary:

• Very fast cooling produces martensite: hard, strong, low in toughness, and — critically — the microstructure most susceptible to hydrogen-induced cracking (Chapter 23).

• Intermediate cooling produces bainite: a reasonable compromise of strength and toughness, and the target structure for many modern weld metals.

• Slow cooling produces ferrite and pearlite: soft and tough, but at very slow rates accompanied by grain coarsening that reduces toughness again.

Hardness in the heat-affected zone is the routine proxy measurement for this, because it is quick, cheap and correlates with martensite content. Codes and specifications commonly impose HAZ hardness ceilings — typically expressed in HV10 — chosen to limit both cracking susceptibility during fabrication and, in sour service, susceptibility to environmental cracking in operation. The applicable ceiling is always a property of the specification in force, not a universal number, and Chapter 34 addresses how preheat is used to achieve it.

The variables that lengthen cooling time, and therefore lower hardness, are: higher heat input, higher preheat, higher interpass temperature, thinner section, and joint geometry that conducts heat in two dimensions rather than three. These are not independent knobs — they combine, which is why the hydrogen-control preheat calculations in Chapter 34 take all of them as inputs simultaneously.

9. Dilution

Dilution is the proportion of the weld metal that came from the melted parent metal rather than from the filler:

Dilution (%) = (Area of melted parent metal ÷ Total weld cross-sectional area) × 100

It matters because the composition of the weld metal — and therefore its strength, corrosion resistance and cracking susceptibility — is a mixture of filler and parent, not the filler's own analysis. A filler chosen correctly on paper can produce unacceptable deposit chemistry at high dilution.

Dilution is high in processes with deep penetration and low filler addition (autogenous GTAW is 100 % dilution by definition; submerged arc and laser welding are typically high), and low in processes that deposit a great deal of filler for the penetration achieved (SMAW at moderate current, and deliberately buttered or weave-deposited passes).

Three places where dilution is the whole engineering problem: corrosion-resistant cladding, where the surface layer must meet a chemical specification and excess dilution from the carbon-steel substrate fails it; dissimilar-metal joints (Chapter 27), where dilution determines whether a brittle intermetallic forms; and root passes in high-alloy pipe, where the root is the most diluted pass in the joint and is often the one that must resist the service environment.

10. Residual Stress: Why It Exists and How Large It Gets

Weld metal and the surrounding heated material expand when heated and contract when cooled. Because they are restrained by the surrounding cold structure, that contraction cannot happen freely, and the result is a locked-in stress field that persists after the weld has cooled to ambient temperature.

The magnitude of longitudinal residual stress along a weld commonly approaches the yield strength of the material. This is not an unusual worst case; it is the normal condition of an as-welded joint. Three consequences follow, and all three are frequently underestimated:

1. Any applied service stress adds to a field that already sits near yield, which is a large part of why weld toes are fatigue initiation sites.

2. Residual stress is one of the three ingredients of hydrogen cracking (Chapter 23) and one of the drivers of stress-corrosion cracking in susceptible material/environment combinations.

3. Machining or cutting a welded assembly redistributes the field, so a component that was dimensionally correct as welded can move measurably when material is removed. Fabricators who machine after welding without a stress-relief step discover this as an unexplained dimensional drift.

Post-weld heat treatment (Chapter 34) is the principal engineered remedy, reducing the peak residual stress by allowing localized creep relaxation at temperature. Mechanical methods — vibratory treatment, peening, proof loading — are used in specific contexts and have their own qualification requirements.

11. The Six Distortion Patterns and How to Control Them

Distortion is residual stress that was free to move. The classical patterns:

| Pattern | Description | Principal driver |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Longitudinal shrinkage | Shortening along the weld axis | Contraction of the weld and adjacent HAZ along its length |
| Transverse shrinkage | Narrowing across the joint | Contraction across the weld; increases with groove volume |
| Angular distortion | Plates rotate about the weld axis, closing or opening the included angle | Non-uniform contraction through thickness — more weld metal at the top of a V-groove than at the root |
| Bowing / longitudinal bending | The whole member curves | Weld placed away from the neutral axis of the section |
| Buckling | Out-of-plane waviness in thin panels | Compressive residual stress in thin sheet exceeding its stability limit |
| Rotational distortion | Plate edges swing in or out ahead of and behind the arc | Thermal expansion running ahead of the moving heat source |

Control methods, in rough order of how often they are the right answer:

• Reduce total heat input. Distortion scales with the heat put in; a faster process or a smaller weld distorts less. Oversized fillet welds are the single most common avoidable cause of distortion in general fabrication, and specifying a fillet larger than the design requires increases weld volume roughly with the square of leg length.

• Balance the welding about the neutral axis. Alternating sides, using back-step or skip sequences, and welding symmetrically all exploit the fact that opposing contractions cancel.

• Pre-set and pre-bend. Deliberately assemble with an offset that the weld's own contraction removes. Cheap, effective, and dependent on repeatable process parameters.

• Restrain with fixturing. Effective for dimensions but it converts distortion into residual stress; on crack-sensitive material, heavy restraint increases cracking risk rather than eliminating a problem.

• Sequence to leave the most restrained joints for last where possible, and avoid welding into a fully closed, fully restrained configuration.

| The Restraint Trade-Off, Stated Plainly Restraint does not remove contraction; it converts it from movement into stress. On a low-carbon steel of modest thickness, that trade is usually acceptable. On a thick, high-strength, hydrogen-sensitive material, heavy restraint plus inadequate preheat is one of the most reliable ways to produce a cracked joint that was dimensionally perfect the moment it left the fixture and cracked hours later. Restraint and preheat decisions belong together, not in separate conversations. |
| --- |

12. What the Second Pass Does to the First

In multi-pass welding, each pass imposes a new thermal cycle on everything deposited before it. This is not merely repetition — it is a real metallurgical mechanism with predominantly beneficial effects that codes and consumable designers actively exploit:

• Grain refinement. A subsequent pass reheats part of the previous weld metal above the transformation temperature, recrystallizing coarse columnar grains into finer equiaxed ones. Multi-pass weld metal is generally tougher than single-pass weld metal of the same composition for this reason.

• Tempering. Regions of previously formed martensite are tempered by later passes, reducing hardness and improving toughness.

• Hydrogen escape. Time at elevated temperature between passes allows diffusible hydrogen to escape, which is part of why maintaining interpass temperature matters and why the last pass and the root pass — one never reheated, one most restrained — are the two most crack-prone locations in a multi-pass joint.

The corresponding negative is cumulative heat: interpass temperature rises through a multi-pass joint unless it is controlled, extending t8/5 and coarsening structure. This is why specifications routinely set a maximum interpass temperature as well as a minimum, and why the maximum is the one most often violated in production, since nothing visible happens when it is exceeded.

13. Arc Physics: Polarity, Arc Pressure and Arc Blow

Polarity determines where the heat goes. In direct-current welding, the electron flow deposits more energy at the anode than at the cathode for most configurations. With the electrode negative (DCEN, "straight polarity"), more heat goes into the work — favoured for gas tungsten arc welding on steel, where the tungsten must be kept cool. With the electrode positive (DCEP, "reverse polarity"), more heat goes to the electrode — which is what most consumable-electrode processes want, since melting the electrode is the point, and which is why DCEP gives deeper penetration in gas metal arc welding through its effect on droplet transfer.

Alternating current alternates between the two, and on aluminium this is exploited deliberately: the electrode-positive half-cycle provides cathodic cleaning, breaking up the tenacious aluminium oxide film, while the electrode-negative half-cycle provides penetration. Modern equipment allows the balance between the two halves to be adjusted, trading cleaning action against penetration (Chapter 41).

Arc blow is the deflection of the arc by magnetic fields, and it is a direct-current phenomenon — alternating current suffers from it far less. The field arises from the welding current's own path through the workpiece and from residual magnetism in the material. It is worst near the ends of a joint, near abrupt changes in section, close to the earth return connection, and on heavily magnetized material such as pipe that has been handled with magnetic lifting equipment or previously magnetic-particle inspected. Its symptoms are erratic arc behaviour, undercut on one side, porosity, lack of fusion, and heavy spatter. Remedies: reposition or split the earth return, weld toward the earth connection or use a run-off tab, reduce current, switch to alternating current where the process permits, or demagnetize the material.

14. Spatter as a Physical Phenomenon

Spatter — molten metal ejected from the arc and pool that does not become part of the weld — is treated in this reference set as a first-class subject rather than a cosmetic nuisance, because it is simultaneously a productivity cost, a quality indicator and, in some applications, a rejectable condition in its own right. It is classified in the international imperfection system as reference 602 within the group of miscellaneous imperfections [S3].

The physics behind it is straightforward. Spatter is produced whenever molten metal receives a momentum impulse larger than the surface tension holding it to the electrode tip or the pool:

• Short-circuit rupture. In short-circuiting metal transfer, the electrode touches the pool, current rises, and the resulting electromagnetic pinch severs the bridge. If the current rise rate is too aggressive — inductance set too low, or voltage set too low forcing violent shorts — the bridge ruptures explosively and throws metal [S4][S5].

• Globular droplet repulsion. In the globular transfer range, a droplet larger than the electrode diameter hangs on the tip and is acted on by arc forces that can repel it upward and away from the joint rather than transferring it. This is the highest-spatter operating region of gas metal arc welding, and the fact that it sits between two low-spatter regions is precisely why parameter selection in Chapter 39 is framed as "get out of the globular zone" [S4][S5].

• Gas evolution. Carbon dioxide dissociates in the arc and recombines exothermically, raising arc force; carbon-dioxide-rich shielding is consistently more spattery than argon-rich mixtures for that reason [S5]. Contamination — rust, mill scale, zinc coating, oil, moisture — generates gas inside the pool and ejects metal as it escapes.

• Arc instability from the wire feed path. A worn liner, incorrect drive-roll pressure, or a worn contact tip modulates the wire feed speed. Arc length then oscillates, and spatter rises before any other symptom becomes visible [S5].

• Arc blow, per Section 13.

Why it matters beyond appearance:

1. It is lost deposit. Metal ejected is metal paid for and not deposited; heavy spatter measurably degrades deposition efficiency.

2. It costs labour. Removal is manual and slow, and on coated or architectural work it is frequently the dominant post-weld labour cost.

3. It damages equipment. Spatter accumulation in the gas nozzle disturbs shielding gas flow, which causes porosity — so unmanaged spatter causes a second, more serious defect.

4. It is a leading indicator. A sudden rise in spatter on a stable production weld is one of the earliest observable signs that something has changed: gas supply, wire feed, contact tip, material surface condition or earth connection. Treating it as noise discards a free diagnostic signal.

5. It can be rejectable. Acceptance depends on function rather than appearance: adherent spatter is judged on whether it impairs coating adhesion, fatigue performance, hygiene in food and pharmaceutical work, or subsequent machining [S5]. Coating-critical and fatigue-loaded work commonly requires complete removal; general static structures often tolerate light spatter.

Control measures are collected process by process in Volume 3, and the master defect index in Chapter 74 indexes them together.

15. Decision Reference: What Changing Each Variable Actually Does

| If you increase… | Heat input | Penetration | Cooling rate (t8/5) | Distortion | Typical risk introduced |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Current | Up | Up | Slower | Up | Burn-through on thin section; undercut; excess dilution |
| Voltage (arc length) | Up | Slightly down, bead widens | Slower | Up | Porosity from lost shielding; undercut; spatter at extremes |
| Travel speed | Down | Down | Faster | Down | Lack of fusion; centreline cracking from teardrop pool shape |
| Preheat temperature | Unchanged | Unchanged | Slower | Can increase | Excess softening of Q&T steels; personnel exposure |
| Plate thickness | Unchanged | Unchanged | Faster (3-D heat flow) | Down per unit heat | Higher hardness and cracking risk at same parameters |
| Interpass temperature | Unchanged | Unchanged | Slower | Up | Exceeding a specified maximum; coarsened structure; loss of strength in Q&T and duplex |

The table's real lesson is in its columns rather than its rows: no variable moves one outcome only. Current cannot be raised to fix lack of fusion without simultaneously raising dilution, distortion and burn-through risk. This coupling is the reason welding parameters are qualified as complete sets rather than tuned individually in production.

16. Worked Example: Heat Input and Cooling Time on a Structural Fillet

Situation. An 8 mm fillet weld is to be made on 20 mm structural steel plate using a flux-cored wire. The fabricator's draft procedure specifies 290 A, 29 V, 400 mm/min. The material specification imposes a maximum heat-affected zone hardness and the steel supplier's guidance calls for a minimum t8/5. The question posed to the welding engineer is whether the parameters are acceptable.

Step 1 — Calculate arc energy. (29 V × 290 A × 60) ÷ (400 mm/min × 1000) = 1.26 kJ/mm.

Step 2 — Apply the efficiency factor. Using a factor of 0.8 for flux-cored arc welding, heat input ≈ 1.26 × 0.8 ≈ 1.01 kJ/mm. Which of arc energy or heat input the governing standard requires must be checked; quoting the wrong one is a common submittal error, and the two differ here by twenty percent.

Step 3 — Recognize what the number alone does not settle. Heat input does not determine cooling rate by itself. The 20 mm thickness means three-dimensional heat flow, which extracts heat faster than the two-dimensional flow of thin plate at the same heat input. The joint is a fillet, so the heat sink is larger than for a butt weld of the same thickness — a T-joint conducts heat into three plate legs. Both effects shorten t8/5 relative to what the heat-input figure alone would suggest.

Step 4 — Identify the actual decision. If a hardness ceiling is the binding constraint, the levers are preheat (Chapter 34), higher heat input, or a leaner steel. Preheat is usually the correct first lever because it lengthens t8/5 without increasing weld volume, distortion or HAZ width, whereas raising heat input achieves the same cooling change at the cost of a coarser heat-affected zone.

Step 5 — Check the other end of the window. If the steel is thermomechanically processed or quenched and tempered, there will also be a maximum heat input, and raising heat input to slow cooling could violate it. Where both limits exist, preheat is not merely preferable — it may be the only available lever.

Step 6 — State what must be verified rather than calculated. Heat input arithmetic bounds the problem; it does not prove the result. A procedure qualification with hardness survey and impact testing on the actual material is what demonstrates acceptability, and Chapter 31 covers what that test must include.

17. Known Gaps

• Thermal efficiency factors in Section 3 are approximate and vary between published sources. Where a calculation is contractual, the factor prescribed by the governing standard must be used rather than the values tabulated here.

• No t8/5 calculation is given. Standardized methods exist that combine heat input, thickness, joint type and preheat into a t8/5 estimate; they are published in standards this chapter does not reproduce. The concept is explained here; the calculation belongs to the governing standard.

• Sub-zone temperature boundaries in Section 7 are typical values for plain carbon-manganese steel. They shift with composition and do not transfer to stainless, aluminium or nickel alloys, which have entirely different sub-zone structures — Chapters 24 through 26 treat each separately.

• Residual stress magnitudes are stated qualitatively. Measured values depend on geometry, restraint and material, and no general numeric claim would be defensible.
