1. Weldability Is a System Property, Not a Material Property

"Weldability" is used loosely to mean a quality a steel possesses, as though it were tensile strength. It is not. A steel that welds without difficulty at 6 mm thickness in a warm shop with dry low-hydrogen consumables can crack reliably at 40 mm thickness in an unheated yard in winter with the same consumables stored badly. Nothing about the steel changed.

The useful definition is that weldability is the property of a combination: material composition, section thickness, joint restraint, hydrogen level of the process, heat input, preheat, and ambient conditions. Every serious cracking investigation ends up examining that whole set, and the ones that go wrong are the ones that stopped at the first item.

This matters for how advice is given. A question of the form "is this steel weldable?" cannot be answered responsibly with yes or no. It can be answered with: under what conditions, with what controls, and what happens if any of those controls is missing. That framing is the one this chapter uses throughout.

2. The Steel Families and Where Each Becomes Difficult

| Family | Typical carbon content | Principal welding difficulty |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Low-carbon / mild steel | Up to ~0.15 % C | Generally minimal; difficulty arises only at heavy thickness or high restraint |
| Medium-carbon steel | ~0.15–0.30 % C | Hardenable heat-affected zone; preheat commonly required |
| High-carbon steel | Above ~0.30 % C | Strongly hardenable; preheat and post-weld heat treatment usually mandatory |
| High-strength low-alloy (HSLA) | Low C, microalloyed | Good weldability by design, but heat input limits protect the microalloyed structure |
| Quenched and tempered (Q&T) | Low-to-medium C, alloyed | Both a preheat floor and a heat input ceiling; the HAZ can be softened by welding |
| Thermomechanically controlled processed (TMCP) | Very low C, low CE | Excellent cold-cracking resistance; strict heat input ceiling to preserve properties |
| Creep-resistant Cr-Mo steels | Low C, Cr and Mo alloyed | Preheat, mandatory post-weld heat treatment, and reheat-cracking susceptibility |
| Advanced high-strength steels (AHSS) | Low C, multiphase | HAZ softening; narrow process windows; addressed for resistance welding in Volume 1 |

The single most useful generalization is that carbon content drives hardenability, and hardenability drives cold cracking risk — but that generalization is exactly what the carbon equivalent formulas exist to make quantitative, because alloying elements other than carbon contribute too.

3. Carbon Equivalent: The Formulas, Their Disagreements, and Their Limits

Carbon equivalent converts a multi-element composition into a single number expressing hardenability, so that steels of different chemistry can be compared on one scale.

The IIW form, the most widely quoted, is conventionally written:

CE(IIW) = C + Mn/6 + (Cr + Mo + V)/5 + (Ni + Cu)/15

AWS D1.1 Annex B presents an IIW-type formula that also includes silicon in the manganese term [S2]:

CE = C + (Mn + Si)/6 + (Cr + Mo + V)/5 + (Ni + Cu)/15

This is a real, documented difference between published forms of "the IIW carbon equivalent," and it is worth stating plainly rather than glossing: a calculation performed with the silicon term and compared against a threshold derived without it is not a like-for-like comparison. Anyone using a carbon equivalent in a contractual context must state which formula was used.

The Pcm form (critical metal parameter) weights carbon much more heavily and includes boron, and is the more appropriate measure for modern low-carbon steels, conventionally below about 0.18 % C, where the IIW form tends to overestimate risk [S2]:

Pcm = C + Si/30 + (Mn + Cu + Cr)/20 + Ni/60 + Mo/15 + V/10 + 5B

Three honest limitations:

1. A carbon equivalent is a hardenability index, not a preheat prescription. It says how readily the steel forms martensite on cooling; it says nothing on its own about hydrogen level, restraint or thickness, which are equally necessary ingredients of cracking.

2. Threshold values quoted in general literature are not universal. Guidance of the type "below 0.40 is readily weldable, 0.40–0.60 requires preheat" circulates widely and is a reasonable orientation, but the codes do not generally work that way. AWS D1.1 Annex B, for instance, does not apply a single carbon equivalent cutoff; it uses composition, thickness, hydrogen level and restraint together in a calculation that outputs a preheat temperature [S2]. Treat quoted thresholds as orientation, and the governing code's own method as the answer.

3. It requires a real analysis. A carbon equivalent computed from the maximum permitted composition of a specification is a worst case, not the actual value; one computed from a mill certificate is specific to that heat. Which is appropriate depends on whether the mill certificate for the material actually being welded is in hand.

4. Hydrogen-Induced Cold Cracking: Four Conditions, All Required

Hydrogen-induced cold cracking — also called cold cracking, delayed cracking, underbead cracking or hydrogen-assisted cracking — is the dominant fabrication failure mechanism in carbon and low-alloy steel welding. It requires four conditions simultaneously:

1. Diffusible hydrogen in the weld metal, from any source (Section 5).

2. A susceptible microstructure, in practice martensite or hard bainite, produced by rapid cooling of a hardenable steel.

3. Tensile stress, which in an as-welded joint is present by default at levels near yield (Chapter 22, Section 10), amplified by restraint.

4. A temperature range roughly between ambient and about 150 °C, in which hydrogen is mobile enough to diffuse to stress concentrations but the structure is not warm enough for it to escape harmlessly.

Every one of those is necessary. Remove any one and the mechanism cannot operate — which is precisely why fabrication controls target them individually: low-hydrogen consumables attack condition 1, preheat attacks conditions 2 and 4, joint design and sequence attack condition 3, and post-weld hydrogen soak attacks conditions 1 and 4 together.

The characteristic that causes the most operational trouble is delay. Because the mechanism depends on hydrogen diffusing to a stress concentration, cracking occurs after welding — hours to days later, in the temperature window above. A joint can pass visual inspection at the end of a shift and be cracked the next morning. This is not a rare pathology; it is the normal behaviour of the mechanism, and it is why codes commonly require a delay before final inspection on higher-strength or thicker material, and why "it looked fine when I welded it" carries no evidential weight in a cracking investigation.

Cracks from this mechanism are typically found in the coarse-grained heat-affected zone parallel to the fusion boundary (underbead cracking), at the weld toe, or at the weld root — the three locations combining peak hardness with peak stress concentration.

5. Where the Hydrogen Comes From and How It Is Controlled

Sources, in rough order of how often they are the actual cause:

• Moisture in consumable coverings or fluxes. Basic covered electrodes and submerged arc fluxes are hygroscopic. An electrode that meets a low-hydrogen classification when it leaves the factory does not meet it after a day in humid air.

• Moisture, oil, grease, rust and paint on the joint surfaces. Hydrocarbons and hydrated oxides dissociate in the arc.

• Moisture in the shielding gas or in gas lines, particularly after a line has been opened or a new cylinder connected.

• Water leaks onto the joint from cooling circuits.

• The consumable's own chemistry, which is what the classification designators quantify.

The consumable's hydrogen level is designated by an H-number giving the maximum diffusible hydrogen in millilitres per 100 g of deposited weld metal: H4, H8, H16 and so on, where H4 means not more than 4 ml/100 g. Lower is better, and the difference is consequential — code preheat requirements are stated against these categories, and a lower-hydrogen consumable can legitimately reduce the required preheat temperature [S3].

Practical controls that actually work:

• Purchase to the required H-designation and hold the certification.

• Store hermetically sealed consumables sealed until use; once opened, hold at the manufacturer's specified holding-oven temperature.

• Re-bake exposed basic electrodes only per the manufacturer's specified schedule, and only where re-baking is permitted — some coatings cannot be recovered.

• Use quivers on the shop floor with a genuine time limit on exposure, enforced rather than nominal.

• Clean the joint and the adjacent surfaces of rust, scale, oil and moisture; remove condensation with gentle preheat before welding on cold material even where preheat is not otherwise required.

• Post-weld hydrogen release ("hydrogen soak"): holding the joint at a moderate elevated temperature for a period after welding accelerates hydrogen escape before it can do damage. This is a recognized control for thick, restrained, higher-strength joints and is specified as such in codes.

| The Cheapest Control Is Almost Always Consumable Handling In cracking investigations across general fabrication, consumable exposure and joint surface condition account for a large share of root causes — not exotic metallurgy. A shop that cannot demonstrate controlled electrode storage has an open hydrogen source regardless of what its procedures say about preheat, and no preheat temperature fully compensates for an uncontrolled hydrogen input. |
| --- |

6. Preheat: What It Does and the Three Ways It Is Decided

Preheat is heating the joint and the surrounding material before welding. It achieves three things at once:

1. It slows cooling, lengthening t8/5 and reducing the proportion of martensite formed (Chapter 22).

2. It holds the joint above the temperature range in which hydrogen cracking operates for longer, giving diffusible hydrogen time to escape while the metal is still warm.

3. It removes surface moisture, eliminating one hydrogen source.

There are three recognized routes to a preheat value, and confusing them is a common source of argument between fabricator and inspector:

Route 1 — The prescriptive table. AWS D1.1 provides a table of minimum preheat and interpass temperatures organized by steel category and thickness, with the categories distinguished by strength level and by the hydrogen designation of the filler metal permitted [S3]. Its virtue is simplicity and its availability for prequalified procedures; its cost is conservatism, because a table cannot know the actual chemistry of the heat in front of you.

Route 2 — Hardness control. Calculate the preheat needed to keep heat-affected zone hardness below a target by controlling cooling rate. In AWS D1.1's annex treatment this route is limited in application — notably to fillet welds — because the assumptions behind it do not hold generally [S2][S3].

Route 3 — Hydrogen control. Calculate the preheat needed to keep the joint's hydrogen level and stress state below the cracking threshold, taking as inputs the actual steel composition, the filler metal's diffusible hydrogen level, the combined thickness at the joint, and the restraint level [S2][S3]. This is the most defensible route technically and generally produces lower preheat temperatures than the prescriptive table for modern clean steels with H4 or H8 consumables — a genuine cost and cycle-time saving that is frequently left unclaimed because the table is easier [S3].

Practical execution points that determine whether preheat works at all:

• Measure on the correct surface. Preheat is verified on the face opposite the heating source, or after a soak time sufficient for the temperature to equalize through thickness. Measuring the surface a torch just played on measures the torch.

• Heat a wide enough band. Common practice heats a band extending a specified distance either side of the joint, because a hot line in a cold plate cools almost as fast as a cold plate.

• Preheat is a minimum to be maintained, not an event. It must be present at the start of welding and maintained throughout, including between passes and across interruptions. A joint that was preheated, then left while the welder went to lunch, is a cold joint.

• Combined thickness matters, not plate thickness. At a T-joint, three plate legs conduct heat away; the appropriate thickness input is the combined thickness of all members at the joint.

7. Interpass Temperature, Controlled in Both Directions

Interpass temperature is the temperature of the joint immediately before the next pass is deposited.

The minimum interpass temperature is normally the same as the preheat temperature, and for the same reasons — the cracking mechanism does not care whether the metal is cold because it was never heated or cold because it was allowed to cool between passes.

The maximum interpass temperature exists for a different reason and is more often violated, because nothing visible happens when it is exceeded. Excessive interpass temperature extends t8/5 far enough to coarsen the microstructure and degrade toughness; on quenched and tempered steels it over-tempers the parent metal; on duplex stainless (Chapter 24) it destroys the phase balance. A production sequence that welds joints back-to-back without a cooling check will exceed a maximum interpass limit routinely, and only mechanical testing will ever reveal it.

8. Solidification (Hot) Cracking in Steel

Distinct from cold cracking in every respect: it happens at high temperature, during solidification, and is visible immediately rather than after a delay.

Mechanism. As the weld solidifies, low-melting-point constituents — principally iron sulphides and phosphides — are rejected ahead of the growing solid and concentrate in the last liquid, which sits in a continuous film between the columnar grains. Contraction stress across that still-liquid film tears it.

Contributing factors:

• Sulphur and phosphorus content in the parent metal or in dilution from it. Free-machining steels with deliberately high sulphur are notoriously prone.

• Bead geometry. A deep, narrow bead with a depth-to-width ratio above roughly one solidifies from both sides into a central plane and concentrates segregated liquid there (Chapter 22, Section 6).

• Excessive travel speed, producing a teardrop-shaped pool with a straight central solidification plane.

• High restraint, supplying the stress.

• Crater termination. A crater is the extreme case — a shrinking pool solidifying inward from all sides with the last liquid at its centre — which is why crater cracks are so common and why crater-fill routines exist.

Manganese-to-sulphur ratio is the classical control: manganese forms manganese sulphide, which is far less damaging than iron sulphide, so a high Mn:S ratio suppresses the mechanism. Weld metal formulations for crack-sensitive applications are designed around this.

Corrective actions: reduce dilution from a high-sulphur parent; widen the bead or reduce penetration to bring the depth-to-width ratio down; reduce travel speed; reduce restraint or change sequence; use a filler with a controlled Mn:S ratio; use crater-fill or run-off tabs to eliminate crater terminations.

9. Lamellar Tearing

A distinct mechanism that occurs in the parent plate, not the weld, and only under a specific loading geometry.

Mechanism. Rolled plate contains non-metallic inclusions — principally manganese sulphides and silicates — that are flattened into planes parallel to the rolled surface. The plate is therefore weaker in the through-thickness direction than in the rolling direction. When a weld imposes contraction stress in the through-thickness direction, these flattened inclusions decohere and link, producing a stepped, terrace-like crack running parallel to the plate surface below the weld.

Where it happens: T-joints, corner joints and cruciform joints in thick plate where the weld shrinkage pulls perpendicular to the plate surface. It does not occur in butt welds, where the contraction is in-plane.

Recognition: the characteristic stepped appearance, located in the parent plate below the heat-affected zone rather than in it, and typically found by ultrasonic testing rather than surface methods.

Prevention:

• Specify plate with guaranteed through-thickness properties (commonly designated by a Z-quality grade with a specified through-thickness reduction of area), and with low sulphur.

• Redesign the joint so contraction is not carried in the through-thickness direction — this is the most reliable remedy and belongs at the design stage.

• Buttering: deposit a layer of low-strength, ductile weld metal on the plate surface first, then weld to the buttered layer, so the shrinkage strain is absorbed by ductile weld metal rather than by the susceptible plate.

• Reduce weld volume and restraint; use lower-strength consumables where design permits, since the strain is imposed by the weld's own contraction.

10. Reheat Cracking in Creep-Resistant Steels

Also called stress-relief cracking. It occurs during post-weld heat treatment or during high-temperature service, not during welding.

Mechanism. In creep-resistant steels containing strong carbide formers — chromium, molybdenum, vanadium, niobium — the coarse-grained heat-affected zone is left after welding with those elements in solution. On reheating to stress-relief temperature, fine carbides precipitate inside the grains, strengthening the grain interiors relative to the grain boundaries. Residual stress then relaxes preferentially by sliding at the weakened boundaries, and intergranular cracks form in the coarse-grained heat-affected zone.

Susceptible materials: Cr-Mo and Cr-Mo-V creep-resistant steels, some stainless grades stabilized with niobium, and some nickel alloys.

Controls: minimize coarse-grained HAZ width by controlling heat input; use weld toe dressing to reduce local stress concentration; follow the material supplier's qualified heat treatment schedule including heating and cooling rate limits; avoid excessive restraint; and, on the most susceptible grades, use the specific weld metal and PWHT combination the material specification prescribes rather than a generic one.

11. Advanced High-Strength and Thermomechanically Processed Steels

Modern low-carbon high-strength steels achieve their strength not from carbon but from processing — controlled rolling, accelerated cooling, microalloy precipitation, and multiphase microstructures. This inverts the traditional welding problem in a way that catches out practitioners trained on older steels.

Their cold-cracking resistance is generally excellent, because carbon equivalent is low. The naive conclusion — that they are easy to weld — is wrong, because the failure mode has moved:

• The weld thermal cycle destroys the processing route's product. The strengthening structure was created by a specific cooling history at the mill; welding imposes a different one, and the affected material reverts toward a lower-strength condition. This shows up as heat-affected zone softening, most pronounced in the subcritical region where tempering occurs without re-transformation.

• Softening is invisible to every non-destructive method. It passes radiography, ultrasonics, penetrant and visual inspection because it is not a discontinuity. It is a property loss, detectable only by hardness traverse or by mechanical testing.

• The controlling variable is a heat input ceiling, specified by the steel producer. Exceeding it does not produce a defect; it produces a joint weaker than the design assumed.

The engineering consequence is that on these steels the welding procedure is protecting a property, not preventing a discontinuity — a genuinely different mental model, and one that makes the maximum heat input and maximum interpass temperature the critical controlled variables rather than preheat.

12. Quenched and Tempered Steels

Q&T steels combine both problems: they are hardenable enough to require preheat against cold cracking, and heat-treated enough that excessive heat input over-tempers the heat-affected zone and loses strength.

This gives a bracketed window — a preheat floor and a heat input ceiling — and the two are not independent, since preheat and interpass temperature both act to slow cooling in the same direction as high heat input. A procedure that satisfies the preheat minimum by running very hot may violate the heat input maximum without anyone noticing.

Additional controls typically applied: strict maximum interpass temperature, low-hydrogen consumables mandated without exception, matching or under-matching filler chosen deliberately (over-matching increases restraint stress on the parent), and often a requirement that the joint be allowed to cool below the maximum interpass temperature before the next pass rather than welded continuously.

15. Worked Example: A Delayed Crack Found on Monday Morning

Situation. A fabricator welds 30 mm thick S460-class plate into a heavily restrained node using flux-cored wire. The welds are made Friday afternoon, pass visual inspection at the end of the shift, and are found cracked by magnetic particle inspection on Monday. The cracks lie in the heat-affected zone, parallel to the fusion boundary. Shop temperature over the weekend was about 8 °C.

Step 1 — Classify the mechanism from the evidence available. Delay of days, location in the coarse-grained heat-affected zone, parallel to the fusion line, in a hardenable steel at heavy thickness under high restraint. Every one of those points to hydrogen-induced cold cracking rather than solidification cracking, which would have appeared immediately and would sit in the weld metal.

Step 2 — Test the four conditions rather than guessing at one. Susceptible microstructure: 30 mm section, S460-class chemistry, three-dimensional heat flow — plausible. Tensile stress: heavily restrained node — present by design. Temperature window: the joint sat between ambient and 150 °C for the entire weekend — satisfied for the full duration. Hydrogen: to be established, and it is the only one of the four that is not already obviously present.

Step 3 — Investigate the condition that is actually variable. The questions worth asking are: what H-designation was the wire purchased to, how was it stored, was the spool left on the machine over a humid period, was the joint preheated and to what temperature, was preheat maintained across passes and interruptions, and was the plate surface free of rust and moisture. In practice this is where the answer usually lies.

Step 4 — Check whether preheat was decided or assumed. If preheat was taken from a prescriptive table, verify that the correct steel category and the correct combined thickness at the node were used — a node has more than two members, and using single-plate thickness understates the heat sink substantially. If preheat was calculated by the hydrogen-control route, verify that the hydrogen level used in the calculation matches the consumable actually used and stored, not the one specified.

Step 5 — Decide the repair, not just the diagnosis. Cracked material must be excavated fully — a crack left in place will propagate under the repair weld's own contraction — and the repair welded with verified preheat, verified low-hydrogen consumable and a maintained interpass temperature. The repair is more restrained than the original joint, so the repair conditions should be at least as conservative as the original, never less.

Step 6 — Fix the system, not the joint. If the cause was consumable exposure, one repaired node does not address the other joints made that week with the same spool. The corrective action is a consumable handling control with an enforced exposure limit, plus a review of every joint made under the same conditions. This is the step most often skipped.

Step 7 — Reconsider the inspection timing. Inspecting immediately after welding did not detect a mechanism that operates over hours to days. On material and thickness of this class, a specified delay before final inspection is not a formality; it is what makes the inspection capable of finding the defect that this material is most likely to have.

16. Known Gaps

• No preheat temperatures are tabulated in this chapter. The values are code-specific and thickness-specific, and reproducing a table from a purchased code would be both a copyright problem and an accuracy risk if the edition changed. The three decision routes are explained; the numbers belong to the code in force.

• The published forms of the IIW carbon equivalent disagree over the silicon term. Section 3 states both. No attempt is made here to declare one correct — the correct one is the one the governing document specifies.

• Threshold values for carbon equivalent are not endorsed. Widely circulated bands are noted as orientation only, and the code's own calculation is identified as the answer.

• Hardness limits are not stated numerically. They are set by the application specification — structural, pressure, sour service and offshore practice all differ — and no general value would be safe.

• Steel designations are referred to by family rather than by national grade. Cross-referencing national grade systems is outside this chapter's scope, and a grade name without its standard is ambiguous.

1. Five Families, Five Different Problems

"Stainless steel" names a corrosion-resistance property, not a metallurgical family, and the five families grouped under it behave so differently at the arc that treating them as one material is the root of most stainless welding failures.

| Family | Structure | Typical examples | Dominant welding problem |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Austenitic | Face-centred cubic, non-magnetic | 304/304L, 316/316L, 321, 347, 310 | Sensitization; hot cracking if ferrite-free; heavy distortion |
| Ferritic | Body-centred cubic, magnetic | 409, 430, 439, 444 | Grain growth and embrittlement in the HAZ |
| Martensitic | Hardenable, magnetic | 410, 420, 440 | Hydrogen cracking; requires preheat and PWHT |
| Duplex | ~50/50 ferrite and austenite | 2205, 2507, lean grades | Phase imbalance; intermetallic precipitation; both a heat input floor and a ceiling |
| Precipitation-hardening | Age-hardenable | 17-4PH, 15-5PH | Property loss unless the full solution/age cycle is respected |

An engineer who knows only that a material is "stainless" knows almost nothing about how to weld it. The grade is the minimum useful information, and for duplex and PH grades even the grade is insufficient without the delivered heat-treatment condition.

2. What Makes Stainless Behave Differently From Carbon Steel at the Arc

Four physical properties, all of them of the austenitic family in particular, change how the process behaves before any metallurgy is considered:

Thermal expansion is substantially higher than carbon steel — on the order of fifty percent higher for austenitic grades. More expansion on heating means more contraction on cooling, which means more distortion and more residual stress from an identical weld. Fixturing, sequencing and tack spacing that are adequate for carbon steel are frequently inadequate here.

Thermal conductivity is substantially lower — roughly a third that of carbon steel for austenitics. Heat does not run away from the joint; it stays local. The practical consequences are a narrower but hotter affected region, a tendency to overheat if carbon-steel parameters are copied across, and a real risk of burn-through on thin material at settings that would be conservative on mild steel. As a rule of thumb, austenitic stainless is welded at lower current than carbon steel of the same thickness.

Electrical resistivity is higher, which matters for consumable-electrode processes: a long electrode extension heats more, so stick-out control has a larger effect than on carbon steel.

The oxide is tenacious and the metal is oxygen-sensitive. Chromium oxide forms readily and is far more refractory than the base metal. On the weld face the shielding gas handles it; on the back of the joint it must be handled deliberately (Section 10), which is why root purging is a routine requirement on stainless and not on carbon steel.

3. Austenitic Grades: Sensitization and Intergranular Corrosion

This is the defining metallurgical hazard of the most-used stainless family, and it is a corrosion failure produced by welding rather than a weld defect in the inspection sense.

Mechanism. Austenitic stainless resists corrosion because dissolved chromium forms a passive film. When the material is held in a temperature range of roughly 425–815 °C, chromium and carbon combine and precipitate as chromium carbides at the grain boundaries. Chromium diffuses slowly at these temperatures while carbon diffuses quickly, so the chromium consumed comes from the metal immediately adjacent to the boundary — leaving a narrow chromium-depleted band along every grain boundary. That depleted band is no longer stainless. In a corrosive environment it is attacked preferentially, and grains fall out of the surface.

Where it appears. In a band of the heat-affected zone parallel to but set back from the fusion line — the region whose peak temperature fell inside the sensitizing range. The classic field name is weld decay, and its appearance as two parallel lines of attack either side of a weld is diagnostic.

The three controls, in order of how often each is the right answer:

1. Low-carbon grades (the "L" grades). 304L and 316L cap carbon at a low level so there is insufficient carbon to precipitate enough carbide to matter over normal weld thermal cycles. This is the standard modern solution and the reason L grades dominate welded fabrication.

2. Stabilized grades. 321 (titanium-stabilized) and 347 (niobium-stabilized) contain a strong carbide former that preferentially ties up carbon as titanium or niobium carbide, leaving chromium in solution. These are used where service temperature keeps the material in or near the sensitizing range for long periods, where even an L grade would eventually sensitize.

3. Solution annealing after welding. Heating above the carbide dissolution temperature and quenching redissolves the carbides. Metallurgically complete, but often impractical on a fabricated assembly for distortion and furnace-size reasons.

Knife-line attack is the specific failure mode of stabilized grades: a very narrow band immediately adjacent to the fusion line, where the peak temperature was high enough to dissolve the stabilizing carbides, and a subsequent thermal cycle — a later pass, or service exposure — then allowed chromium carbide to precipitate in that band. It is narrow, sharp and easily missed. The control is a stabilization heat treatment where the material specification calls for it, and heat input control to limit the width of the affected band.

Heat input control helps all cases, because sensitization is time-at-temperature dependent: lower heat input means less time in the sensitizing range means less carbide precipitated.

4. Ferrite in Austenitic Weld Metal: The Hot-Cracking Control

Fully austenitic weld metal is notably susceptible to solidification cracking, by the mechanism of Chapter 23 Section 8: impurities segregate to a continuous liquid film between columnar grains and the film tears under contraction stress.

The engineered fix is to make the weld metal solidify with a small amount of ferrite present. Ferrite dissolves sulphur and phosphorus far more readily than austenite, so the impurities are absorbed into the ferrite instead of concentrating in an intergranular liquid film. Ferrite also produces a more tortuous, discontinuous boundary structure that resists crack propagation.

The conventional target for general-purpose austenitic weld metal is roughly 3 to 10 Ferrite Number (FN) — enough to suppress cracking, not so much that the properties the austenitic structure provides are compromised. This target is why standard fillers such as 308L are deliberately formulated with a composition that solidifies with residual ferrite, and why substituting a filler that matches the parent analysis exactly is usually a mistake: matching the parent composition removes the very imbalance the filler was designed to provide.

Where the ferrite target must be reconsidered:

• Cryogenic service. Ferrite is brittle at very low temperature; specifications for cryogenic duty often cap it.

• High-temperature service. Ferrite can transform to brittle sigma phase over long exposure in the roughly 600–900 °C range; specifications for elevated-temperature service often cap it for that reason.

• Non-magnetic requirements. Ferrite is magnetic; applications requiring low magnetic permeability restrict it.

• Severely corrosive service. Ferrite and austenite can corrode at different rates in some media, giving selective attack.

• Fully austenitic grades that cannot form ferrite at all (such as high-nickel grades and 310) must instead be controlled through very low impurity levels, restricted heat input, and bead geometry that avoids a high depth-to-width ratio.

5. Predicting Ferrite: Schaeffler, DeLong and WRC-1992

Ferrite content is predicted from composition using constitution diagrams that plot a chromium equivalent (ferrite-forming elements: Cr, Mo, Si, Nb) against a nickel equivalent (austenite-forming elements: Ni, C, Mn, N).

Three generations exist and they are not interchangeable:

• The Schaeffler diagram is the original and remains useful for a first estimate and for dissimilar-metal dilution problems, where its ability to plot a mixed composition graphically is genuinely convenient (Chapter 27). It does not account for nitrogen.

• The DeLong diagram refined it by including nitrogen, a strong austenite former whose omission caused systematic overprediction of ferrite, and introduced the Ferrite Number scale.

• The WRC-1992 diagram is the current reference for predicting ferrite in austenitic and duplex weld metal and is generally the most accurate of the three.

Two practical cautions. First, predicted ferrite is not measured ferrite: production practice for applications with a ferrite requirement is to measure it, typically with a calibrated magnetic instrument, rather than to rely on the calculation. Second, Ferrite Number and percent ferrite are not the same scale and diverge at higher levels; a specification citing one and a measurement reported in the other is a real and common source of dispute.

6. Duplex Grades: A Window With a Floor and a Ceiling

Duplex stainless achieves its combination of strength and corrosion resistance from a roughly balanced mixture of ferrite and austenite. Everything about welding it follows from the requirement to preserve that balance.

What happens on the weld thermal cycle. At high temperature duplex is fully or nearly fully ferritic. Austenite reforms during cooling, and how much reforms depends on how long the metal spends in the temperature range where that transformation occurs. A fast cool leaves too much ferrite — a joint with excessive ferrite has reduced toughness and reduced corrosion resistance, particularly in the heat-affected zone.

Why the window has a ceiling too. Slow cooling, or excessive time at elevated temperature, allows brittle intermetallic phases to precipitate — sigma and chi phases in a range around 600–1000 °C, and the separate "475 °C embrittlement" mechanism at lower temperatures. Both severely reduce toughness and corrosion resistance.

The result is one of the clearest genuine process windows in welding: too fast is wrong and too slow is wrong, and both ends fail by a different mechanism. In practice this is managed through:

• A specified heat input range with both minimum and maximum values, taken from the material producer's recommendation for the specific grade.

• A specified maximum interpass temperature, commonly enforced strictly, because cumulative heat in a multi-pass joint is the usual way the ceiling gets breached.

• Nitrogen additions to the shielding gas — nitrogen is a strong austenite stabilizer, and adding a small percentage to the shielding gas or the backing gas helps restore austenite in the weld and root region.

• Over-alloyed filler metal, typically higher in nickel than the parent (2209 filler for 2205 parent), specifically so that the weld metal reforms sufficient austenite on cooling despite the fast weld thermal cycle.

• Ferrite measurement as an acceptance activity, with an acceptance band specified by the application standard rather than assumed.

Autogenous welding of duplex is generally discouraged — without the nickel-enriched filler, the weld metal reforms too little austenite. Where an autogenous process is unavoidable (some tube mill and orbital applications), a post-weld solution anneal or a nitrogen-enriched shielding gas becomes necessary rather than optional.

7. Ferritic Grades: Grain Growth and Embrittlement

Ferritic stainless does not transform on heating and cooling the way carbon steel does, so it cannot be grain-refined by a thermal cycle. What it does instead is grow grains, irreversibly, and grain growth in the heat-affected zone is the family's central problem: coarse-grained ferritic stainless has poor toughness and poor ductility, and no post-weld heat treatment restores the fine structure.

Additional mechanisms:

• 475 °C embrittlement — a slow precipitation reaction in a range roughly 350–550 °C causing severe loss of toughness, relevant for both fabrication exposure and service temperature.

• Sigma phase formation on prolonged exposure at higher temperatures in the higher-chromium grades.

• Sensitization is possible in ferritics as well, and in some grades it occurs on cooling rather than on holding, which makes it harder to avoid by thermal management alone; stabilized ferritic grades exist for this reason.

Controls: minimize heat input, which is the single most effective lever because it limits both the peak temperature reached in the HAZ and the time spent at temperature; keep interpass temperature low; use austenitic filler (309L is common) where a tougher, more ductile weld metal is acceptable to the design; and avoid multi-pass deposition where a single pass will do.

8. Martensitic and Precipitation-Hardening Grades

Martensitic grades behave, in welding terms, much more like a hardenable alloy steel than like the other stainless families. They air-harden, forming martensite in the weld metal and heat-affected zone even at modest cooling rates, and they are therefore susceptible to hydrogen cracking by the mechanism of Chapter 23 Section 4. Controls are correspondingly familiar: preheat, controlled interpass temperature, strictly low-hydrogen consumables, and a post-weld tempering treatment that is normally mandatory rather than optional. A common alternative where the design permits is to weld with an austenitic filler, producing a ductile weld metal that tolerates the strain — at the cost of a joint whose properties do not match the parent.

Precipitation-hardening grades derive their strength from a controlled solution-treat-and-age cycle. Welding disturbs that condition locally, and the governing question is the material's condition before welding and the heat treatment applied after. Welding in the solution-treated condition and performing the full age after welding generally gives the best result; welding a fully aged component and not re-treating it leaves a heat-affected zone in an uncontrolled condition. The material producer's specified sequence governs, and deviation from it is a property decision, not a procedural convenience.

Second, for dissimilar joints the filler must survive dilution, which is why 309L rather than 308L is the standard choice for stainless-to-carbon-steel work: it carries enough alloy margin that the diluted deposit still lands in a safe region of the constitution diagram.

10. Root Purging, Heat Tint and Back-Side Oxidation

The chromium oxide that gives stainless its corrosion resistance is beneficial when it forms as a thin passive film at ambient temperature and damaging when it forms as a thick scale at welding temperature. On the back side of a joint, unprotected by shielding gas, the hot root oxidizes.

Sugaring is the severe case: a rough, granular, heavily oxidized root surface with badly degraded corrosion resistance and a surface that traps product. In piping for pharmaceutical, food, semiconductor and high-purity service it is a rejectable condition, and in corrosive service it is a leak waiting to happen.

Root purging prevents it by displacing air from the back of the joint with an inert gas — argon commonly, sometimes with a nitrogen or hydrogen addition where the material and the specification permit — until the joint is complete and cool enough not to oxidize. Practical points that determine success:

• Purge to an oxygen level, not to a time. Specifications for critical work state a maximum residual oxygen (measured with an oxygen analyzer) rather than a purge duration, because duration depends on volume, leakage and gas flow.

• Contain the purge volume. Purge dams, soluble film barriers and purpose-made devices reduce the volume to be displaced, cutting both gas cost and time enormously on large-diameter pipe.

• Maintain the purge until the metal is cool enough, not merely until the arc is off; hot stainless continues to oxidize in air.

• Control flow, not just presence. Excessive purge pressure blows the root out of the joint; insufficient flow fails to displace air.

Heat tint on the outer surface is the same oxidation at lower severity, and the coloured bands either side of a weld are a real, measurable reduction in corrosion resistance rather than a cosmetic feature. Specifications for critical service state an acceptable tint level, often against a colour reference chart, and require removal above it. Removal methods — pickling paste, electropolishing, mechanical cleaning followed by passivation — are chosen against the service condition, and mechanical removal alone leaves a surface that has not re-passivated to the same state.

11. Post-Weld Cleaning, Passivation and Iron Contamination

Iron contamination is the most common self-inflicted corrosion failure on stainless fabrication. Embedded carbon steel particles rust in service and initiate pitting in the stainless beneath. Sources are ordinary shop practice: grinding wheels or wire brushes previously used on carbon steel, contact with carbon steel benches, lifting chains and fixtures, and carbon steel tooling marks.

Controls are simple, cheap and routinely ignored: dedicated stainless-only abrasives and brushes (stainless bristles), segregated work areas and storage, protective covering on benches and rollers, and a passivation or pickling step after fabrication where the specification requires it.

Pickling removes both heat tint and embedded contamination chemically. Passivation restores the protective chromium oxide film. They are different operations with different chemistry, and a specification calling for one is not satisfied by the other. Both generate hazardous waste and require appropriate handling.

| The Corrosion Failure That NDT Will Never Find Sensitization, heat tint and iron contamination all pass radiography, ultrasonics and penetrant testing without comment. They are not discontinuities. A stainless fabrication can be flawless by every weld-inspection standard and still fail in months because the root was not purged, the tint was not removed, or a carbon steel grinding disc was used on it. The inspection plan for stainless has to include the corrosion-relevant checks explicitly, or those failure modes are simply not being looked for. |

14. Worked Example: A 316L Pipe Spool That Failed a Corrosion Test

Situation. A fabricator supplies 316L pipe spools for a chemical process line. The welds pass radiography and visual inspection. A witnessed corrosion test on a sacrificial spool shows attack at the weld root and in narrow bands adjacent to the weld on the inside surface. The fabricator's position is that the welds are sound and the material must be at fault.

Step 1 — Separate weld soundness from corrosion performance. Radiography detects volumetric discontinuities. It cannot detect sensitization, heat tint, root oxidation or iron contamination, none of which are discontinuities. "The welds passed RT" is therefore not evidence about the failure mode observed, and the investigation should not be framed as a challenge to the radiography.

Step 2 — Read the location of the attack. Two distinct locations were reported: at the root, and in narrow bands adjacent to the weld on the inside. These suggest two different mechanisms, and treating them as one would misdiagnose at least one of them.

Step 3 — Root attack: check the purge, first and specifically. The questions are whether a back purge was used at all; whether it was verified to a measured oxygen level or merely run for a nominal time; whether purge dams were used and whether they leaked; whether the purge was maintained until the root cooled; and whether the root surface was inspected internally after welding. Root oxidation is the leading candidate and is confirmable by borescope examination of a retained spool.

Step 4 — Banded attack: check for sensitization, and check the material grade actually supplied. Bands parallel to the weld at a set-back distance are the classic weld decay signature. On a genuine 316L this should be unlikely at normal heat input — which makes the first question not metallurgical but documentary: was the material actually the low-carbon grade, or was 316 supplied against a 316L order? Mill certificates for the actual heats resolve this quickly, and grade substitution is a more common root cause than exotic thermal effects.

Step 5 — If the grade is confirmed correct, examine the thermal history. Heat input above what was qualified, an unenforced maximum interpass temperature, or repeated repair passes over the same region all extend time in the sensitizing range. Repair history is worth checking specifically: a joint repaired twice has had three thermal cycles, not one.

Step 6 — Check the contamination controls independently of both. A ferroxyl or equivalent test on the internal surface establishes whether embedded iron is present. This is worth doing regardless of the outcome above, because it is cheap, it is a frequent contributor, and finding it changes the corrective action.

Step 7 — Frame the corrective action at the system level. If the cause is purging practice, the fix is a purge procedure with a measured oxygen acceptance criterion and a verification record, not a reminder to be careful. If the cause is grade substitution, the fix is incoming material verification. If it is contamination, the fix is tooling segregation. In each case, the population of spools made under the same conditions must be assessed, not only the one that was tested.

15. Known Gaps

• No numeric heat input windows are given for duplex. They are grade-specific and producer-specific, and publishing a general range would invite its misapplication to a grade it does not fit. The producer's recommendation and the application standard govern.

• Ferrite acceptance bands are not stated. They are set by the application standard and vary widely between service categories; the mechanism and the measurement principle are explained here, the acceptance value is not.

• The sensitization range of roughly 425–815 °C is a widely used approximation. Exact limits vary with composition and with the time available at temperature.

• Constitution diagrams are described but not reproduced. They are published, copyrighted figures; the chapter explains what each accounts for and which is current so a reader knows which to consult.

• Filler recommendations in Section 9 are conventional industry practice, not a substitute for the filler specified by the application code or the material producer for a particular service condition.

1. Why Aluminium Is a Different Discipline, Not a Softer Steel

Welders and engineers who arrive at aluminium from a steel background consistently underestimate it, and the reason is that aluminium violates the sensory cues that steel practice is built on.

It does not change colour before it melts. Steel glows through a predictable sequence and an experienced welder reads heat from it. Aluminium goes from solid to collapsed with no visual warning, which is why unsupported thin aluminium falls out of the joint so readily.

Its thermal conductivity is roughly four to six times that of steel. Heat runs out of the joint immediately. This produces the counter-intuitive result that aluminium generally requires higher current than steel of the same thickness despite melting at less than half the temperature — the heat source is competing with a far more effective heat sink. It also means that on a long weld the workpiece heats up progressively, and parameters correct at the start of a seam are too hot at the end.

Its oxide melts at roughly three times the temperature of the metal beneath it. The film has to be removed or disrupted; it will not melt out of the way.

It dissolves hydrogen readily when molten and almost none when solid. That single fact produces the family's characteristic porosity.

It has no ductile-to-brittle transition in the way ferritic steels do, which makes it excellent at cryogenic temperatures, and it loses strength steadily with rising temperature, which makes it poor above a couple of hundred degrees.

Its strength is a product of processing that welding removes locally. This is the deepest difference, and Section 3 develops it.

2. The Alloy Series and What Each Is Made Of

Wrought aluminium alloys are identified by a four-digit designation whose first digit gives the principal alloying element.

| Series | Principal alloying element | Heat-treatable? | Typical uses | Welding character |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1xxx | None (≥99 % aluminium) | No | Electrical, chemical | Very weldable; low strength |
| 2xxx | Copper | Yes | Aerospace structure | Generally poor fusion weldability; crack-sensitive |
| 3xxx | Manganese | No | Sheet, tube, cooking ware | Readily weldable |
| 4xxx | Silicon | Some | Filler metals, castings | Used mostly *as* filler (4043, 4047) |
| 5xxx | Magnesium | No | Marine, structural plate, cryogenic | Readily weldable; the best structural fusion-welding series |
| 6xxx | Magnesium + silicon | Yes | Extrusions, structural sections | Weldable but crack-sensitive without correct filler; strength loss in HAZ |
| 7xxx | Zinc | Yes | High-strength aerospace, some structural | Weldability ranges from difficult to unweldable by fusion depending on grade |
| 8xxx | Other (Li, Fe) | Varies | Specialist | Grade-specific |

The single most useful generalization for fabrication: 5xxx and 6xxx are the workhorse weldable structural series; 2xxx and most 7xxx are the series where fusion welding is either avoided or handled as a specialist qualified process, and where solid-state joining (Chapter 57) is frequently the correct answer instead.

The temper designation that follows the alloy number — -O annealed, -H strain-hardened with digits describing degree, -T thermally treated with digits describing the route (T4, T5, T6, T651 and so on) — is not a footnote. It states the condition that gives the material its strength, and therefore states what welding will take away.

3. Heat-Treatable Against Non-Heat-Treatable: The Property That Welding Destroys

This division governs everything about how a welded aluminium structure is designed.

Non-heat-treatable alloys (1xxx, 3xxx, 5xxx) gain strength from alloying in solid solution and from cold work (strain hardening). Welding anneales the heat-affected zone, so a joint in strain-hardened material loses the cold-work component locally and returns toward the annealed condition. The loss is real but bounded, and the resulting HAZ strength is predictable — which is exactly why design codes for welded aluminium structures commonly require the designer to use annealed-condition properties in the vicinity of a weld.

Heat-treatable alloys (2xxx, 6xxx, 7xxx) gain strength from precipitation hardening: a solution treatment followed by controlled ageing produces fine precipitates that impede dislocation motion. The weld thermal cycle over-ages or dissolves those precipitates in the heat-affected zone. The consequence is a soft band running alongside every weld, typically weaker than both the parent metal and the weld metal, and it is where the joint will fail in a tensile test.

Three consequences follow that are routinely missed:

1. The strength of a welded 6082-T6 joint is not the strength of 6082-T6. Designing to parent properties and welding the structure produces an assembly weaker than the calculation assumed. Aluminium structural codes handle this by specifying reduced allowable stresses adjacent to welds.

2. Some strength recovers over time. In naturally ageing alloys the HAZ regains a portion of its strength over weeks at room temperature. This is real and is accounted for in some codes — but it is partial, alloy-dependent, and never a restoration to the original temper.

3. Post-weld heat treatment is rarely practical. A full solution-treat-and-age cycle would restore properties but requires temperatures near the melting range followed by quenching, which distorts fabricated assemblies severely. It is used on small, high-value components and effectively never on large fabrications.

4. The Oxide Film and How Each Process Defeats It

Aluminium oxide forms instantly on exposed aluminium, is chemically stable, is electrically insulating, and melts at a temperature far above the metal beneath it. It also absorbs moisture, making it a hydrogen reservoir (Section 5).

The film must be dealt with in two separate places, and confusing them causes half of all aluminium porosity problems:

Before welding, mechanically or chemically. Degrease first with a solvent, then remove oxide with a stainless steel wire brush reserved exclusively for aluminium, or by scraping or chemical etching. Order matters: brushing a greasy surface drives contamination into the metal. Time matters too — the film regrows within minutes to hours, so cleaning is done shortly before welding, not the day before.

During welding, by the process itself:

• Alternating-current gas tungsten arc welding provides cathodic cleaning during the electrode-positive half-cycle, in which ion bombardment breaks up the film. This is the classic mechanism, and the ability to adjust the AC balance — the proportion of the cycle spent in each polarity — is a direct trade between cleaning action and penetration.

• Direct-current electrode-positive gas metal arc welding provides continuous cathodic cleaning, which is one of the reasons aluminium GMAW is run on DCEP essentially universally.

• Beam processes vaporize through the film, but its presence still affects coupling and porosity.

• Friction stir welding (Chapter 57) disperses the film mechanically within the stirred zone rather than removing it — which is one of the reasons it produces such consistently low-defect aluminium joints and why it dominates for long structural seams.

5. Hydrogen Porosity: The Characteristic Aluminium Defect

Hydrogen is highly soluble in molten aluminium and almost insoluble in solid aluminium. During solidification the dissolved hydrogen is rejected from the advancing solid, becomes supersaturated in the remaining liquid, and forms bubbles. If the pool solidifies before the bubbles escape, they are trapped as porosity.

This mechanism is unavoidable in principle and controllable in practice. Sources of hydrogen:

• Moisture in the oxide film on the parent metal or on the filler wire — the largest single source in most shops.

• Hydrocarbons: oil, grease, cutting fluid, drawing lubricant residue on filler wire, fingerprints.

• Moisture in the shielding gas or gas lines, and air entrainment through a leaking torch or an excessive gas flow that induces turbulence.

• Condensation on cold material brought into a warm shop.

Controls that work, roughly in order of effectiveness:

1. Clean and degrease immediately before welding; store and handle filler wire so it stays clean and dry, and do not leave a spool exposed on the machine overnight.

2. Verify gas purity and check the whole gas path for leaks — a pinhole draws air in even under positive pressure through venturi action at fittings.

3. Set gas flow high enough to shield and low enough to avoid turbulent air entrainment; correct nozzle size for the joint.

4. Avoid welding condensing-cold material; a gentle warm-through to remove surface moisture is legitimate and is not the same thing as metallurgical preheat.

5. Reduce travel speed slightly where the pool is freezing too quickly for bubbles to escape, within the constraints of Section 6.

6. Solidification Cracking and the Crack-Sensitivity Curve

Aluminium alloys crack during solidification by the general mechanism of Chapter 22 — but with a distinctive and highly useful relationship to composition.

For the major alloying elements, crack sensitivity plotted against alloy content produces a curve with a peak at low-to-intermediate alloy content and lower sensitivity both below and above it. Pure aluminium has a narrow freezing range and does not crack; a small alloying addition widens the freezing range and creates a large, weak mushy zone with just enough liquid to form a continuous film but not enough to backfill tears as they form — the worst case; higher alloy content produces enough eutectic liquid to flow into and heal incipient tears, so sensitivity falls again.

Two engineering consequences follow directly, and they explain almost all aluminium filler selection:

First, the most crack-sensitive compositions are the ones near the peak — which unfortunately includes 6xxx alloys welded autogenously, since their own composition sits close to it. 6xxx alloys should not, as a rule, be welded without filler. An autogenous 6082 or 6061 weld is a textbook crack-sensitivity failure, and the "fix" is not a parameter change; it is filler.

Second, adding filler moves the weld metal composition off the peak. A silicon-rich 4xxx filler moves it well past the peak into the eutectic-rich, crack-tolerant region. A magnesium-rich 5xxx filler moves it in the other direction toward higher magnesium, also away from the peak. Both work, and Section 7 covers when to choose which.

7. Filler Metal Selection as Crack Avoidance

For aluminium, filler selection is a crack-avoidance decision first, a strength decision second, and a corrosion or appearance decision third. That ordering is unusual and it is the point.

| Parent material | Common filler | Reasoning | Trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6xxx (6061, 6082, 6005) | 4043 (Al-Si) | Silicon addition moves composition well off the crack-sensitivity peak; the standard general-purpose choice | Lower strength than 5xxx fillers; anodizes to a dark grey, poor colour match |
| 6xxx where higher strength or better anodized appearance is needed | 5356 (Al-Mg) | Higher strength deposit; anodizes closer to the parent | Higher crack sensitivity than 4043; less forgiving of restraint and fit-up |
| 5xxx (5083, 5086, 5454) | 5356 or matching 5xxx | Magnesium content maintained; strength and marine corrosion resistance retained | 4043 must not be used on high-magnesium 5xxx: silicon and magnesium form brittle Mg₂Si |
| 5xxx for elevated-temperature service | 5554 or as specified | Controlled magnesium level to avoid sensitization to stress-corrosion cracking above ~65 °C | Grade-specific; specification governs |
| 3xxx | 4043 or 5356 | Both work; choose on strength and appearance | — |
| 1xxx | 1100 | Purity retained for electrical or chemical service | Very low strength |
| Castings (Al-Si) | 4043 / 4047 | Compositionally close to common casting alloys | Casting quality and porosity often dominate the result |
| 2xxx, 7xxx | Specialist / often not fusion welded | Crack sensitivity and property loss are severe | Solid-state joining or mechanical fastening frequently preferred |

Two rules that carry disproportionate weight:

• Never use 4043 on high-magnesium 5xxx alloys. The Mg₂Si intermetallic that forms is brittle and reduces ductility badly.

• The choice between 4043 and 5356 on 6xxx is a genuine engineering trade, not a preference: 4043 is more crack-tolerant and easier to run; 5356 is stronger and anodizes to match. A joint with high restraint and a cosmetic anodized finish requirement forces the two considerations into conflict, and the resolution is usually to use 5356 and control restraint and fit-up much more tightly.

8. Preheat: Mostly the Wrong Answer

Preheat is a standard control in steel welding and a frequently harmful one in aluminium.

There is no hydrogen cold-cracking mechanism in aluminium requiring preheat — the mechanism of Chapter 23 does not apply. Modest preheat is legitimately used for two limited purposes: driving off surface moisture on cold or damp material, and helping to establish fusion at the start of a weld in a heavy section where the heat sink is overwhelming.

Against that, excessive preheat causes real harm:

• It increases the width of the softened heat-affected zone in heat-treatable alloys, extending exactly the property loss that Section 3 identifies as the design problem.

• It over-ages precipitation-hardened material further, deepening the strength loss.

• It increases distortion and the risk of collapse on thin material that already gives no visual warning before it melts.

• It can sensitize high-magnesium 5xxx alloys, promoting later stress-corrosion cracking.

Where preheat is used, temperatures are modest and interpass temperature is generally capped rather than floored — the opposite of steel practice. The material producer's guidance governs, and the default assumption for aluminium should be that preheat is not required unless a specific reason applies.

9. Joint Preparation, Cleaning and the Shop Discipline That Actually Matters

Aluminium fabrication quality is determined by shop discipline to a greater extent than by welding technique, and the controls are unglamorous:

• Dedicated tooling. Stainless brushes used only on aluminium; abrasives never previously used on steel; separate storage and handling.

• Degrease before mechanical cleaning, never after.

• Clean shortly before welding, not at the start of the shift.

• Store filler wire sealed, and do not leave a partially used spool exposed on a machine overnight in a humid shop.

• Control the wire feed path. Aluminium wire is soft and deforms rather than driving; U-groove drive rolls, correct roll pressure, PTFE or graphite liners and short, straight torch cable paths are needed. Push-pull or spool-on-gun feeding exists precisely because conventional push feeding of soft wire over any distance produces feed instability, and feed instability produces arc instability, porosity and spatter.

• Manage the workpiece heat build-up on long seams, since conductivity guarantees the part gets hotter as the weld progresses.

• Protect from draughts. The shielding gas requirement is absolute; a lost shield on aluminium produces immediate, gross porosity.

10. Process Selection for Aluminium

| Process | Suitability | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GTAW (141), AC | Excellent for thin material and precision work | Cathodic cleaning via AC balance; slow; high operator skill |
| GTAW, DCEN with helium | Thick sections | Higher heat input; no cathodic cleaning, so pre-cleaning is critical |
| GMAW (131), DCEP pulsed | The production workhorse for structural aluminium | Pulsed transfer gives all-position capability and controlled heat input; feed-path discipline is the limiting factor |
| Laser / hybrid laser-arc (52x) | High-volume, low-distortion seams | Reflectivity and porosity control are the challenges; fit-up must be tight |
| Friction stir welding (43x) | Long structural seams, extrusions, plate | No melting, so no solidification cracking and no hydrogen porosity; superb property retention; needs machine access and rigid clamping |
| Resistance spot welding (21x) | Sheet assembly | Functionally a different process from steel RSW — see Volume 1, Chapter 14 |
| SMAW, oxy-fuel | Rarely appropriate | Flux residues are corrosive and hard to remove; used only for repair where nothing better exists |

The two entries that matter most strategically are the last-line options. Friction stir welding side-steps the two dominant aluminium fusion defects entirely — there is no molten pool, so hydrogen porosity and solidification cracking cannot occur, and the property loss is smaller because peak temperature is lower. Where geometry and volume allow it, it is frequently the correct answer rather than a novelty. And for 2xxx and 7xxx alloys, the honest recommendation is often not to fusion weld at all, but to use mechanical fastening, adhesive bonding or a solid-state process.

13. Worked Example: Cracked 6082 Extrusion Joints on a Production Line

Situation. A fabricator produces welded frames from 6082-T6 extrusions. Corner joints crack along the weld centreline on roughly one assembly in five. Parameters and welder are unchanged from a previous, trouble-free contract in 5083 plate. The proposed fix on the shop floor is to reduce current.

Step 1 — Identify the mechanism from timing and location. The cracks appear immediately, run along the weld centreline, and lie in the weld metal. This is solidification cracking, not hydrogen cracking — aluminium has no hydrogen cold-cracking mechanism, and centreline location in freshly deposited metal is the classic signature.

Step 2 — Ask what changed from the successful contract. The alloy changed from 5083 (non-heat-treatable, magnesium) to 6082 (heat-treatable, magnesium-silicon). This is not a small change: 6082's own composition sits near the crack-sensitivity peak described in Section 6, while 5083's does not.

Step 3 — Establish whether filler is being used, and which. This is the decisive question and it is frequently answered incorrectly on the shop floor, because corner joints in thin extrusion are exactly where a welder is most tempted to fuse the corner without adding wire. An autogenous 6xxx weld will crack, reliably, and no parameter adjustment prevents it. If filler is being used, the next question is which — 5356 carried over from the 5083 job is a plausible and imperfect choice for a highly restrained 6082 corner.

Step 4 — Evaluate the proposed fix honestly. Reducing current addresses heat input, which is a contributing factor to cracking only insofar as it affects pool shape and restraint. It does not address composition, which is the dominant factor here. Reducing current on a high-conductivity alloy is also likely to introduce lack of fusion — trading a visible defect for an invisible one, which is worse.

Step 5 — Apply the correct hierarchy of controls. First, ensure filler is used on every joint, with 4043 as the crack-tolerant default unless strength or anodized appearance forbids it. Second, review joint design and fit-up: a tight, well-fitted corner with a consistent gap distributes strain far better than an inconsistent one, and gap variation is a common hidden cause of intermittent cracking — which fits the observed one-in-five pattern better than a parameter problem, since parameters do not vary between parts but fit-up does. Third, eliminate crater terminations with a downslope or crater-fill routine and run-off tabs. Fourth, reduce restraint by revising the assembly sequence so the corner is not welded into a fully closed frame.

Step 6 — Check the design assumption while the joint is open. 6082-T6 loses substantial strength in the heat-affected zone (Section 3). If the frame was designed to parent-metal properties, correcting the cracking still leaves a structure weaker than the calculation assumed. This is worth raising even though it was not the question asked, because the cracking investigation is the moment the information is available.

Step 7 — Consider the alternative process, honestly. If these corner joints are high-volume, repetitive and accessible, friction stir welding removes the solidification cracking mechanism entirely and retains more strength. That may or may not be economic here, but it should be stated rather than left unmentioned, because a recurring process-limited defect is exactly the situation in which a process change deserves evaluation.

14. Known Gaps

• No parameter values are given. Aluminium parameters depend on alloy, thickness, joint type, process, gas and equipment, and any published number would be a starting point at best. Qualification testing is what produces a usable procedure.

• The crack-sensitivity curve is described qualitatively. Published curves exist for each major alloying element; the shape and its consequences are explained here, the specific compositions at which the peak falls are not.

• The ~65 °C threshold for 5xxx sensitization is an approximate, widely cited figure and is magnesium-content dependent; the material producer's guidance governs for a specific grade.

• 2xxx and 7xxx welding is described only in outline. Both are specialist fields, largely aerospace-driven, governed by specifications outside this reference set's scope.

Chapter 26 — Weldability IV: Nickel Alloys, Titanium, Copper Alloys and Cast Iron

Four material families that each break a rule carried over from steel practice — the sluggish nickel weld pool, titanium's atmospheric contamination limit, copper's heat sink, and cast iron's refusal to tolerate a normal weld thermal cycle.
