1. Why These Four Are Grouped Together

These families are grouped not because they resemble each other but because each one invalidates a different habit that steel practice teaches. A welder or engineer who is competent on steel and stainless will make a specific, predictable mistake on each:

• On nickel alloys, they will weave and travel as if the pool would flow like steel, and produce lack of fusion at the sidewalls.

• On titanium, they will treat shielding as something that only matters while the arc is on, and produce an embrittled joint that passes every dimensional and volumetric check.

• On copper, they will apply steel currents and fail to establish fusion at all, then over-compensate and burn through.

• On cast iron, they will weld it like a steel casting and crack it, sometimes while it is still cooling.

Each section below is organized around the specific habit that must be replaced.

2. Nickel and Nickel Alloys: The Pool Does Not Flow

The single most important practical fact about welding nickel alloys is that the molten weld pool is sluggish and does not wet out. It sits where it is placed. Steel practice relies on a fluid pool that flows into the joint faces and self-corrects a slightly imperfect torch position; nickel alloys give no such assistance.

Consequences that follow directly:

• Penetration is shallow relative to steel at the same current. The weld goes where the arc puts it, and no further.

• Lack of sidewall fusion is the characteristic defect, because the pool will not run up the groove face on its own.

• Joint preparation must be more open than for equivalent steel work — wider included angles and larger root openings — so the arc can be directed at the fusion faces directly rather than relying on the pool to reach them.

• A deliberate weaving or oscillating technique is normally required to place metal against both faces, rather than the stringer-bead discipline preferred on many steels.

• Travel speed must be lower, and the operator must direct the arc at the sidewall rather than at the centre of the pool.

Additional physical characteristics: thermal conductivity is low, so heat concentrates; thermal expansion is high, so distortion is significant; and the alloys retain strength at elevated temperature, so residual stress in a restrained joint is higher than in steel of comparable strength.

3. Nickel Alloys: Hot Cracking and the Contamination That Causes It

Nickel alloys are strongly susceptible to solidification and liquation cracking, and they are unusually sensitive to low-melting-point contaminants. Elements that form low-melting compounds with nickel — sulphur, phosphorus, lead, zinc, tin, bismuth — produce intergranular liquid films at grain boundaries that tear under contraction stress.

The severity of this cannot be overstated and it makes cleanliness a first-order engineering control rather than good housekeeping. Realistic contamination sources in an ordinary workshop:

• Marking crayons, paint sticks and layout dyes containing sulphur or zinc.

• Cutting fluids, lubricants and greases, especially sulphurized cutting oils.

• Fingerprints — skin oils contain sulphur, and this is a genuine, documented cause rather than a fastidious precaution.

• Zinc from galvanized surfaces, fixtures, or adjacent work, including airborne contamination from cutting galvanized material nearby.

• Copper from tooling, backing bars or contact tips, and lead from any leaded alloy in the vicinity.

• Residue from previous work on shared fixtures and benches.

The control is straightforward and must be enforced: degrease with an approved solvent immediately before welding, use only approved marking materials, use dedicated tooling and abrasives, handle with clean gloves, and keep galvanized and leaded materials away from the nickel work area entirely.

Restraint and heat input are the other half of the control. High restraint plus high heat input maximizes both the stress and the liquation. Nickel alloys are therefore welded with controlled, generally low heat input, low interpass temperature, and joint sequencing that limits restraint — with the immediate tension that low heat input on a non-wetting pool increases the risk of lack of fusion. Resolving that tension is what the qualification test exists to do.

Certain precipitation-hardened nickel alloys are additionally susceptible to strain-age cracking during post-weld heat treatment, when age-hardening precipitation occurs while residual stress is still relaxing. Control routes are specified by the alloy producer and typically involve welding in the solution-annealed condition and using a controlled heating rate through the precipitation range.

4. Nickel Filler Selection and Shielding Practice

Nickel alloy fillers are commonly over-alloyed relative to the parent, for the same reason as in stainless practice: the deposit must survive dilution and must resist cracking in a solidification structure it cannot avoid.

| Application | Common filler families | Reasoning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nickel-chromium alloys (600-type) | ERNiCr-3 / ENiCrFe-3 | Niobium addition controls solidification cracking |
| Nickel-chromium-molybdenum (625-type) | ERNiCrMo-3 | High alloy content tolerates dilution; strong corrosion resistance |
| Highly corrosion-resistant (C-276-type) | ERNiCrMo-4 | Matched for severe chemical service |
| Nickel-copper (400-type) | ERNiCu-7 | Matched composition |
| Dissimilar nickel-to-steel and overlay | ERNiCrMo-3, ERNiCr-3 | Alloy margin absorbs iron dilution; also the standard choice for dissimilar joints (Chapter 27) |

Shielding practice: argon is standard for gas tungsten arc welding; helium additions increase heat input where the sluggish pool needs help. Carbon dioxide and oxygen additions are avoided — nickel alloys are sensitive to oxidation, and active gases degrade both corrosion resistance and cracking behaviour. Root purging is required on the same basis as stainless (Chapter 24, Section 10), and the purge must be maintained until the joint is cool.

5. Titanium: Welding Inside a Controlled Atmosphere

Titanium is not difficult to melt and not especially crack-sensitive. It is difficult because it reacts with the atmosphere at welding temperature, and the reaction products embrittle it irreversibly.

Above roughly 400 °C, titanium absorbs oxygen, nitrogen and hydrogen from the air. These dissolve interstitially and raise strength while destroying ductility and toughness. There is no post-weld heat treatment that removes them — the contamination is dissolved in the metal, not a surface scale to be cleaned off. A contaminated titanium weld is scrap.

The engineering response is total atmospheric exclusion over the whole region that exceeds that temperature, not merely the pool:

1. Primary shielding at the torch, argon or argon-helium, at a flow rate and nozzle size sized generously; gas lenses are standard practice for laminar flow.

2. Trailing shields — a gas-fed shoe following the torch that keeps the just-solidified weld and adjacent metal under inert cover until it has cooled below the reaction temperature. This is not optional on open-air titanium welding; it is what makes the process viable.

3. Back purging on any joint with a second side exposed, maintained until cool.

4. Chamber welding — a purged enclosure or glove box — for critical work, where the entire component is under an inert atmosphere and residual oxygen is measured before welding begins.

Additional titanium-specific disciplines:

• Absolute cleanliness. Degrease with an approved non-chlorinated solvent. Chlorinated solvents must not be used, because chloride residues promote stress-corrosion cracking in titanium.

• No contamination from steel tooling. Dedicated brushes, abrasives and fixtures; iron contamination is both a corrosion and an embrittlement problem.

• Handle with clean gloves; skin oils are a hydrogen and contamination source.

• Match filler to grade, using the ERTi-series filler appropriate to the parent grade, and store it clean and dry.

• Hydrogen limits are specified in the material and filler specifications, and are strictly enforced in aerospace and medical work.

6. Titanium: Colour as an Inspection Criterion

Because contamination is invisible to conventional non-destructive testing, titanium welding uses surface colour as a primary acceptance criterion — one of the very few places in welding where appearance is a legitimate proxy for a metallurgical property. The oxide film's thickness determines its interference colour, and its thickness correlates with the degree of atmospheric exposure.

The generally applied progression, from best to worst:

| Colour | Interpretation | Typical disposition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bright silver | Clean weld, effective shielding | Accept |
| Light straw / pale gold | Very light oxidation | Normally accept |
| Dark straw / bronze | Increasing oxidation | Often accept with limits, specification dependent |
| Blue | Significant oxidation | Frequently rejectable; specification dependent |
| Grey / purple-grey | Heavy oxidation | Reject |
| White / powdery | Gross contamination | Reject — remove entirely |

The exact acceptance boundary is set by the applicable specification, and aerospace practice is stricter than general fabrication. The important principle is that a titanium weld that changes colour has told the inspector that shielding failed, and the correct response is to investigate the shielding — flow rate, trailing shield fit, purge integrity, draughts — rather than to polish the discolouration away. Removing the colour removes the evidence, not the contamination.

7. Copper and Copper Alloys: Fighting the Heat Sink

Copper's thermal conductivity is far higher than steel's — higher even than aluminium's. Heat delivered to the joint runs away from it immediately. The practical consequences:

• Preheat is routinely required, and on heavy sections it is substantial. This is the opposite of aluminium practice and is one of the few places where high preheat is genuinely the right answer.

• High heat input processes and helium-rich shielding are favoured, because helium's higher arc voltage and thermal conductivity in the arc column deliver more energy to the joint.

• Starts are the difficult part. Until the surrounding metal has warmed, fusion cannot be established; a weld that runs well after 50 mm can have a lack-of-fusion start.

• Distortion is significant, as thermal expansion is high.

• Copper's high reflectivity makes laser welding difficult at conventional infrared wavelengths, which is why shorter-wavelength (green and blue) laser sources have found a specific role in copper joining for electrical assemblies.

8. Copper Alloys: The Family-by-Family Problems

| Alloy family | Specific problem | Control |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tough-pitch (oxygen-bearing) copper | Contains cuprous oxide; hydrogen from the arc reduces it to steam inside the metal, producing embrittlement and porosity | Use deoxidized or oxygen-free copper for welded work; tough-pitch copper is fundamentally poor for fusion welding |
| Oxygen-free / deoxidized copper | Weldable; heat sink is the main issue | Preheat, helium-rich shielding, high heat input |
| Brasses (Cu-Zn) | Zinc boils well below copper's melting point: it vaporizes, causing porosity, loss of alloy content, heavy fume and a serious health hazard (metal fume fever) | Extraction at source is mandatory; use silicon bronze filler; consider brazing instead of welding |
| Aluminium bronzes | Tenacious aluminium oxide film on the pool | Cathodic cleaning via AC or DCEP; mechanical cleaning; matched filler |
| Silicon bronzes | Among the most weldable copper alloys | Widely used as a filler for dissimilar and brazing-type applications |
| Cupronickels | Good weldability; sensitive to sulphur and lead contamination like nickel alloys | Cleanliness discipline per Section 3; matched filler |
| Beryllium coppers | Beryllium fume is highly toxic | Specialist controlled process with dedicated extraction and monitoring; not general workshop work |

The brass entry deserves emphasis as a safety matter rather than only a quality matter: welding brass generates zinc oxide fume in quantity, and metal fume fever is a real and common occupational illness. Chapter 37 covers the control hierarchy; the summary here is that local exhaust ventilation at the arc is required, not advisable.

9. Cast Iron: Why It Resists Welding At All

Cast iron is the hardest of these four families to weld successfully, and the reasons are structural rather than procedural.

• Very high carbon content — typically 2 to 4 percent — means the heat-affected zone transforms to hard, brittle martensite and iron carbide on any normal weld cooling rate.

• Graphite is present as a separate phase, whose morphology defines the grade: flakes in grey iron, spheroids in ductile (nodular) iron, compacted vermicular forms in CGI. Grey iron's flakes act as internal notches, giving essentially zero ductility, so the material cannot yield to accommodate weld contraction — it cracks instead.

• Low ductility means no strain tolerance. Steel accommodates weld shrinkage by yielding locally; grey cast iron cannot, so the shrinkage stress goes directly into cracking.

• Castings are frequently contaminated in service — oil, fuel, coolant and other fluids soaked into the porous graphite structure over years — and that contamination boils out during welding, causing severe porosity. This is the most common practical cause of failed cast iron repairs, and it is why a "clean-looking" casting can still weld badly.

• Grade identification is often unavailable. A repair is frequently attempted on a casting whose grade nobody knows, which makes filler selection a judgement call.

Ductile (nodular) iron is meaningfully more weldable than grey iron because its spheroidal graphite does not act as a notch array and the material has real ductility. Grey iron is the hardest case, and highly alloyed or chilled irons are harder still.

10. Cast Iron: The Cold and Hot Welding Strategies

Two coherent strategies exist. Mixing them produces the failures.

Cold welding — welding without substantial preheat, using a filler that produces a soft, ductile deposit that absorbs the contraction strain the parent cannot.

• Nickel-based electrodes are the standard: high-nickel types (ENi-CI) give the most machinable deposit; nickel-iron types (ENiFe-CI) give a stronger, tougher deposit and are generally preferred for ductile iron and for higher-stress repairs; nickel-copper types are also used.

• Technique is the control: very short beads — typically a few tens of millimetres — with the deposit peened immediately while hot to plastically stretch it and relieve contraction stress, then allowed to cool to hand-warm before the next bead is deposited. This limits the heat-affected zone and prevents heat accumulation.

• Low current and small electrodes, to limit dilution from the high-carbon parent, which is what makes the deposit brittle.

• Studding is used on heavy sections: threaded steel studs are screwed into the prepared surface and welded over, providing mechanical anchorage so the joint does not rely on the bond to the cast iron alone.

Hot welding — preheating the whole casting substantially (commonly in the range of several hundred degrees Celsius), welding, and then cooling very slowly under insulation or in a furnace. This keeps the casting above the temperature at which the contraction stress becomes damaging and slows cooling enough to avoid martensite and carbide formation. It permits the use of cast-iron filler for a colour- and machinability-matched repair, and it is the approach for large, valuable or highly stressed castings — at the cost of substantial time, energy, furnace capacity and handling risk.

Common preparation steps for either strategy: remove the contaminated surface layer by grinding or by a burn-off heating cycle, drill stop-holes at crack ends, fully excavate the crack rather than welding over it, and prepare a groove wide enough for proper access.

13. Worked Example: Porosity and Cracking on an Inconel 625 Overlay

Situation. A shop applies a corrosion-resistant nickel alloy overlay to a carbon steel vessel nozzle. The first two layers show scattered porosity and, in two locations, fine cracks in the deposit. The shop has previously applied the same overlay successfully on other jobs.

Step 1 — Separate the two symptoms. Porosity and cracking in a nickel deposit have different causes and should not be pursued as one problem. Cracking in nickel points first at contamination and restraint; porosity points first at shielding and surface condition.

Step 2 — On cracking, work the contamination list before anything else. Nickel alloys crack from sulphur, phosphorus, lead and zinc at low concentrations. The questions are concrete and answerable on the shop floor: what marking materials were used on the nozzle; was the surface degreased immediately before welding or earlier; were fixtures or backing bars previously used on galvanized or leaded work; was any galvanized cutting done nearby; were clean gloves used. In a shop with previous success, the useful question is what changed — a new marker, a different bench, a new operator's habits.

Step 3 — Check dilution as the second cracking candidate. An overlay's first layer is heavily diluted by the carbon steel substrate, and excessive iron pickup shifts the deposit composition away from the region the filler was designed for. If parameters were run hotter than qualified — higher current, slower travel, more weave — dilution rises. Measuring the deposit chemistry of the first layer settles this directly, and it is the standard acceptance check for corrosion-resistant overlay work in any case.

Step 4 — On porosity, check the shielding system as a system. Gas purity, flow rate, nozzle condition, gas lens presence, leaks in hoses and fittings, and draughts in the work area. Overlay work on a nozzle often involves awkward torch angles where the shield is easily disturbed, and a nozzle geometry can create a wind channel that is not obvious.

Step 5 — Check the substrate surface. Mill scale, rust, oil and moisture on the carbon steel all produce porosity in the first layer. Overlay preparation is frequently less rigorous than joint preparation because the surface is large and the work feels less critical, which is exactly why this is a common cause.

Step 6 — Address heat input and restraint together. Nickel wants low heat input to limit cracking but the pool does not wet at low heat input, so the operator's instinct under a lack-of-fusion problem is to run hotter — which increases both dilution and cracking. If the shop has been adjusting parameters informally to fix appearance, the procedure is no longer the qualified one. Returning to qualified parameters is the first corrective action, not the last.

Step 7 — Verify the repair, and verify the population. Repaired areas must be re-examined by the same methods, and the deposit chemistry re-checked. If contamination was the cause, every component handled under the same conditions is suspect, not just the two cracked locations.

• Cast iron grade identification is frequently impossible in repair work, and the strategies in Section 10 are described generically for that reason. A repair on an unidentified casting is inherently a judgement, and this chapter does not pretend otherwise.

1. Why a Dissimilar Joint Is a Different Engineering Problem

A dissimilar joint is not the average of two welding problems. It is a third problem, with failure modes that neither parent metal exhibits on its own.

Three things change simultaneously. The weld metal is a new alloy that appears nowhere on any material certificate — a mixture of both parents and the filler, in proportions set by dilution, and its properties must be predicted rather than looked up. The joint contains a property gradient — strength, thermal expansion, conductivity and electrochemical potential all step across a short distance — and gradients concentrate stress and drive corrosion. The joint keeps changing after it is made, because diffusion across the interface continues at service temperature, which means a dissimilar joint can pass every acceptance test and then degrade in operation by a mechanism that inspection never looked for.

That last point is the one that catches organizations out. The most common serious dissimilar-metal failures are not fabrication defects. They are service failures in joints that were correctly made.

2. The Five Incompatibility Mechanisms

1. Brittle intermetallic formation. Many metal pairs form intermetallic compounds — ordered, hard, brittle phases — when melted together. Iron and aluminium are the classic example: the Fe-Al intermetallic layer that forms at the interface is brittle at any thickness and becomes a crack path once it exceeds a few micrometres. Where intermetallics form, the joint's strength is governed by that layer, not by either parent.

2. Thermal expansion mismatch. Austenitic stainless expands roughly fifty percent more than ferritic steel per degree. In a joint that is thermally cycled, this difference generates cyclic strain at the interface for the life of the component, with no external load applied at all. It is a fatigue driver built into the joint by material selection.

3. Galvanic corrosion. Two metals of different electrochemical potential, electrically connected and sharing an electrolyte, form a cell. The less noble metal corrodes preferentially, and the rate depends strongly on the area ratio — a small anode connected to a large cathode corrodes very fast.

4. Carbon migration. At elevated temperature, carbon diffuses from a low-alloy steel toward a high-chromium material, because chromium has a strong affinity for carbon. This decarburizes a band of the low-alloy side (leaving it soft and weak) and carburizes a band on the high-chromium side (leaving it hard and brittle). Section 5 develops this; it is the dominant long-term degradation mechanism in high-temperature dissimilar joints.

5. Melting point and dilution mismatch. Where two parents have very different melting points, the lower-melting one liquates while the higher-melting one has barely softened, making a controlled pool difficult and dilution wildly asymmetric.

3. Predicting the Diluted Weld Composition Before Welding

For iron-based dissimilar joints, the diluted weld metal composition can be estimated graphically using a constitution diagram — the Schaeffler diagram remains the practical tool for this specific job, even though WRC-1992 is more accurate for ferrite prediction in single-material welds (Chapter 24, Section 5), because Schaeffler's axes make the mixing construction straightforward.

The method:

1. Calculate the chromium and nickel equivalents of each parent metal and of the filler, and plot all three points.

2. Draw a line between the two parent points. Mark the point corresponding to the relative proportions of each parent in the joint — for a symmetric joint the midpoint.

3. Draw a line from that point to the filler point. Mark the position corresponding to the expected dilution level — for example, at 30 % total dilution, the weld composition sits 30 % of the way from the filler point toward the parent-mixture point.

4. Read which structural region that final point lands in.

The regions to avoid are the ones the diagram labels for martensite (brittle, crack-prone) and for fully austenitic with no ferrite (hot cracking, per Chapter 24, Section 4). The target for a stainless-to-carbon-steel joint is a small amount of ferrite in an otherwise austenitic deposit.

This construction is the reason that 309L, not 308L, is the standard filler for austenitic stainless to carbon steel. 308L would be adequate if there were no dilution; diluted by carbon steel, its composition moves into the martensitic region and the joint cracks. 309L's higher chromium and nickel content carries enough margin that the diluted composition still lands in the safe region. The filler is chosen for what it becomes, not for what it is.

| The Rule Behind Every Dissimilar Filler Choice Select the filler so that the *diluted* deposit — not the filler as supplied — lands in an acceptable structural region. This single principle explains 309L for stainless-to-carbon, nickel-based fillers for high-temperature dissimilar joints, and the general preference for over-alloyed consumables in dissimilar work. Anyone selecting a dissimilar filler by matching one of the two parents has misunderstood the problem. |
| --- |

4. Carbon Steel to Austenitic Stainless: The Standard Case

This is by far the most common dissimilar joint in industry, and the practice is well established.

Filler: 309L or 309LMo. Where the joint sees elevated temperature or thermal cycling, a nickel-based filler (ERNiCr-3, ERNiCrMo-3) is often specified instead, for the reasons in Section 6.

Dilution control: keep it low. Techniques include lower current, stringer beads rather than heavy weaving, and positioning the arc preferentially on the stainless side so more of the melted parent comes from the higher-alloy material.

Buttering is the more robust approach for critical joints and for joints requiring post-weld heat treatment: deposit a layer of the high-alloy filler onto the carbon steel face first, heat treat the buttered carbon steel component if PWHT is required, then make the closing weld between the buttered layer and the stainless. This isolates the dilution problem into a controlled operation and — importantly — allows PWHT to be performed on the carbon steel side without subjecting the austenitic material to a heat treatment that would harm it.

Post-weld heat treatment is the recurring conflict in these joints. Carbon steel side may require it; austenitic stainless is damaged by it (sensitization, sigma). Buttering resolves the conflict; where it cannot be used, the code's specific provisions for dissimilar joints govern.

5. Carbon Migration and Why the Joint Degrades in Service

Carbon migration is the mechanism that makes an apparently sound dissimilar joint fail years later.

At elevated temperature, carbon in the ferritic or low-alloy steel diffuses toward the chromium-rich material because chromium's affinity for carbon lowers the chemical potential of carbon there. Two damaged bands result, on either side of the interface:

• A decarburized, soft band in the low-alloy steel, weakened and prone to creep deformation.

• A carburized, hard, brittle band in the high-chromium material, prone to cracking.

The rate depends on temperature and time, so it is negligible at ambient temperature and severe in high-temperature service — power plant, refinery and process heater applications in particular.

The engineered control is to use a nickel-based filler rather than a stainless filler. Nickel has a low carbon diffusivity and does not draw carbon the way chromium does, so a nickel-based weld metal acts as a diffusion barrier. This is the technical reason that dissimilar welds in high-temperature service specify nickel fillers, and it is a service-life decision, not a fabrication convenience.

A second consideration in the same applications is thermal expansion: a nickel-based weld metal has an expansion coefficient intermediate between ferritic steel and austenitic stainless, which reduces the cyclic interface strain of mechanism 2.

6. Ferritic to Austenitic in Creep Service

The dissimilar metal weld between a creep-resistant ferritic steel and an austenitic stainless — common where a boiler's lower-temperature ferritic sections meet higher-temperature austenitic sections — is one of the most studied failure locations in power generation.

The failure is typically cracking at or near the interface on the ferritic side, driven by the combination of carbon migration (Section 5), thermal expansion mismatch under cycling, creep strength mismatch across a narrow region, and residual and service stress concentrated there. It occurs after long service rather than during fabrication.

Mitigations applied in practice: nickel-based filler as the diffusion barrier and expansion intermediate; locating the dissimilar joint in a cooler part of the circuit where the mechanism runs more slowly, which is a design decision rather than a welding one and is usually the most effective single measure; and inspection programmes that specifically target these welds with methods capable of finding interface-region damage rather than treating them as ordinary welds in a general inspection sweep.

7. Aluminium to Steel: The Intermetallic Barrier

Aluminium and iron form brittle Fe-Al intermetallic compounds whenever they are melted together. This is not a process fault to be optimized away — it is thermodynamics. Conventional fusion welding of aluminium to steel produces a joint whose strength is set by a brittle layer, and the practical objective in any successful process is to keep that layer thin, typically to a few micrometres, rather than to prevent it.

Routes that work, and why:

• Solid-state processes. Friction stir welding, magnetic pulse welding and explosion welding join below melting, so intermetallic growth is limited by short time at temperature. These are the most reliable routes for a structural aluminium-steel joint.

• Brazing-type processes. Cold metal transfer and related low-heat-input arc processes braze the aluminium filler onto a coated steel surface while fusing on the aluminium side, limiting reaction time. Widely used in automotive body construction.

• Coated steel. Zinc or aluminium-silicon coatings on the steel improve wetting and moderate the reaction.

• Transition inserts. A pre-manufactured bimetallic block (Section 10) lets the fabricator make two similar-metal welds instead of one dissimilar weld.

• Mechanical joining and adhesive bonding. Self-piercing rivets, flow-drill screws and structural adhesives avoid the metallurgical problem entirely and are extensively used in mixed-material vehicle structures.

The honest engineering position: for a load-bearing aluminium-to-steel joint, conventional arc fusion welding is normally the wrong answer, and recommending it without qualification would be a mistake.

8. Aluminium to Copper and Other Electrical Joints

Aluminium-copper joints are ubiquitous in electrical distribution, motors and battery assemblies, and they present the same intermetallic problem as aluminium-steel with an additional constraint: the joint must have low and stable electrical resistance, not merely mechanical strength.

Intermetallic phases at the Al-Cu interface are both brittle and substantially more electrically resistive than either parent. A joint that starts with acceptable resistance can therefore degrade in service as the intermetallic layer thickens, and resistance heating accelerates its own growth — a self-reinforcing failure mode that ends in a hot joint.

The dominant industrial routes are consequently solid-state: ultrasonic welding (Chapter 58) for foils, tabs and thin conductors, and magnetic pulse welding (Chapter 62) for tubular and busbar joints. Laser welding is used with tightly controlled energy input and often with beam oscillation to limit mixing. Resistance and mechanical crimping remain common where a demountable or lower-cost joint is acceptable.

9. Titanium, and Joints That Need a Transition Piece

Titanium forms brittle intermetallics with iron, nickel and copper. Direct fusion welding of titanium to steel is not a viable structural route.

Where such a joint is required — chemical plant, marine, aerospace — the standard solutions are an explosion-welded transition joint (Section 10) or an interlayer of a metal that is compatible with both, such as vanadium or niobium, deposited in a controlled sequence. Both are specialist operations.

Other pairs requiring similar treatment: copper to steel (interlayer or transition joint for structural applications), and any pairing where a phase diagram shows intermetallic compounds across the composition range of interest. Checking the binary phase diagram before proposing a fusion weld is a legitimate five-minute engineering check that prevents a great deal of wasted qualification effort.

10. Transition Joints: What They Are and How They Are Made

A transition joint is a pre-manufactured bimetallic component — a block, ring, or plate — in which the dissimilar interface has already been made under controlled factory conditions by a process capable of joining that pair. The fabricator then makes two similar-metal welds: one to each side.

The dominant manufacturing method is explosion welding (Chapter 59), which drives the two metals together at high velocity so that a metallurgical bond forms with a very thin, controlled reaction layer. Roll bonding and diffusion bonding are also used.

Why this route is often the correct engineering answer:

• The dissimilar interface is made under factory-controlled conditions and is inspected and certified as a component before it reaches the fabrication.

• The fabricator's welders make ordinary similar-metal welds using ordinary qualified procedures, requiring no exotic capability on site.

• Common commercially available combinations include aluminium-to-steel, titanium-to-steel, copper-to-aluminium and copper-to-steel, largely because these are precisely the pairs that fusion welding handles badly.

The constraints are geometric and commercial: the joint must be one the transition piece's shape suits, and a transition insert is a purchased component with lead time and cost.

11. Galvanic Corrosion at the Joint

Where a dissimilar joint sees an electrolyte — seawater, condensate, process fluid, even persistent humidity — galvanic corrosion must be assessed independently of the metallurgy.

The governing factors:

• Potential difference between the two metals in the specific electrolyte. Published galvanic series are electrolyte-specific; the seawater series is the most commonly reproduced and does not transfer to other media.

• Area ratio, which is the factor most often mishandled. A small area of less noble metal connected to a large area of more noble metal corrodes rapidly. The practical rule is to avoid a small anode with a large cathode — for instance, carbon steel fasteners in a stainless structure is a poor arrangement, while stainless fasteners in a carbon steel structure is far more tolerable.

• Electrolyte conductivity and continuity, which determine whether the cell can operate at all.

• The weld metal is a third material in the cell, with its own potential, and can itself be the anode. Preferentially corroding weld metal in an otherwise sound joint is a recognized failure mode, and it is why fillers for corrosive service are often deliberately over-alloyed relative to the parent.

Controls: electrical isolation where the design permits; coating the more noble metal (counter-intuitively — coating the anode leaves small holidays acting as tiny anodes with a huge cathode, which is the worst case); selecting metals closer together in the galvanic series; and designing the joint so the electrolyte drains rather than pools.

12. Compatibility Reference Matrix

| Pair | Fusion weldable? | Preferred route | Governing risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Carbon steel ↔ austenitic stainless | Yes, routinely | 309L filler; nickel filler for elevated temperature; buttering for PWHT conflicts | Dilution to martensite; carbon migration in service; expansion mismatch |
| Carbon steel ↔ duplex | Yes, with care | Nickel-based or over-alloyed duplex filler | Phase balance in the diluted deposit |
| Ferritic creep steel ↔ austenitic | Yes, but a known long-term failure location | Nickel-based filler; locate the joint in a cooler zone by design | Carbon migration; creep and expansion mismatch |
| Austenitic ↔ nickel alloy | Yes | Nickel-based filler | Dilution; hot cracking |
| Carbon steel ↔ nickel alloy | Yes | Nickel-based filler (ERNiCr-3, ERNiCrMo-3) | Dilution; contamination cracking |
| Aluminium ↔ steel | Not by conventional arc fusion | FSW, magnetic pulse, CMT braze, coated steel, transition insert, mechanical/adhesive | Brittle Fe-Al intermetallic layer |
| Aluminium ↔ copper | Not by conventional arc fusion | Ultrasonic, magnetic pulse, controlled laser | Brittle and resistive intermetallics; resistance rise in service |
| Titanium ↔ steel / nickel / copper | No | Explosion-welded transition joint; compatible interlayer | Brittle intermetallics |
| Copper ↔ steel | Marginal | Nickel-based filler, buttering, or transition joint | Cracking; dilution; expansion mismatch |
| Aluminium ↔ magnesium | No | Mechanical or adhesive | Brittle intermetallics |
| Cast iron ↔ steel | Yes, with cast iron practice | Nickel electrode, cast iron technique (Chapter 26) | Cracking; dilution from high-carbon parent |

13. Decision Framework: Choosing a Route for a Dissimilar Joint

Work through these in order. Stopping early is what produces failures.

1. Check the binary phase diagram for intermetallic compounds. If the pair forms them across the relevant composition range, fusion welding is likely inappropriate and the decision moves to solid-state, brazing, transition joint or mechanical routes.

2. Establish the service temperature. Above roughly a few hundred degrees Celsius, carbon migration and expansion mismatch become the governing long-term mechanisms, and nickel-based filler becomes the default rather than an upgrade.

3. Establish whether an electrolyte will be present. If so, assess galvanic corrosion and area ratio explicitly, including the weld metal as a third material.

4. Predict the diluted weld composition using the construction in Section 3, and confirm it lands in an acceptable region.

5. Check for a post-weld heat treatment conflict between the two parents. If one exists, buttering is usually the resolution.

6. Check whether the joint is thermally cycled. Cycling converts an expansion mismatch from a static stress into a fatigue mechanism.

7. Ask whether a transition joint removes the problem. If the geometry allows it, converting one dissimilar weld into two similar welds is frequently cheaper over the life of the project than qualifying and inspecting a dissimilar procedure.

8. Qualify it as its own procedure. A dissimilar joint is never covered by qualifications on either parent individually, and the test coupon must represent the actual pairing, filler and dilution.

14. Defect Catalog: Dissimilar Joints

| Defect | How it is detected | Likely cause(s) | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cracking in the diluted weld metal | PT/MT; RT/UT; sectioning | Diluted composition landed in the martensitic region — filler under-alloyed for the dilution level | Use a higher-alloy filler (309L rather than 308L; nickel-based where required); reduce dilution; butter the carbon steel face |
| Hot cracking in a fully austenitic diluted deposit | Visible immediately; PT | Diluted composition landed in the ferrite-free austenitic region | Adjust filler so the deposit retains a small ferrite content; reduce restraint and heat input |
| Interface cracking after service (high temperature) | UT/PAUT of the interface region; metallography | Carbon migration producing a soft decarburized band and a hard carburized band; expansion mismatch under cycling | Nickel-based filler as a diffusion barrier; relocate the joint to a cooler zone at design stage; targeted in-service inspection |
| Brittle intermetallic layer failure | Low-strength failure at the interface; metallography shows a distinct reaction layer | Aluminium-steel, aluminium-copper or titanium-steel pair joined by fusion | Change process to solid-state, braze-type or transition joint; the layer cannot be inspected away |
| Galvanic attack at the joint | Visual and dimensional loss in service; typically on one side only | Dissimilar potentials plus electrolyte plus unfavourable area ratio | Isolate electrically; coat the more noble side; reselect materials; redesign to drain |
| Preferential weld metal corrosion | Attack confined to the weld bead | Weld metal is anodic to both parents in the service environment | Select an over-alloyed filler with a more noble potential in the specific medium |
| Fatigue cracking at the interface under cycling | Crack initiating at the fusion boundary; found by surface or volumetric NDT | Thermal expansion mismatch generating cyclic strain independent of applied load | Nickel-based filler with intermediate expansion; reduce thermal cycling by design; improve weld profile to lower stress concentration |
| Lack of fusion on the higher-melting side | RT/UT | Asymmetric melting points; arc not biased correctly | Bias the arc toward the higher-melting parent; adjust joint preparation; requalify parameters |
| PWHT damage to one parent | Property loss found in testing | A heat treatment required by one parent was applied to a joint containing a parent it harms | Butter and heat treat the sensitive component separately before the closing weld |

15. Worked Example: A Leaking Stainless-to-Carbon-Steel Nozzle After Two Years

Situation. A process vessel has a 316L nozzle welded to a carbon steel shell. The joint passed radiography and hydrostatic testing at fabrication. Two years into operation, at a service temperature of roughly 400 °C with periodic shutdowns, it develops a leak. The maintenance report describes a crack running close to the fusion boundary on the carbon steel side.

Step 1 — Classify by timing. The joint passed fabrication testing and failed after two years of thermal cycling at elevated temperature. This is a service degradation mechanism, not a fabrication defect that was missed. Framing the investigation as "the radiography must have been inadequate" would send it in the wrong direction from the start.

Step 2 — List the service mechanisms that operate in this specific configuration. At 400 °C with cycling, three of the five mechanisms in Section 2 are active: carbon migration from carbon steel toward the chromium-rich material, thermal expansion mismatch generating cyclic strain at every shutdown and start-up, and — if any condensate is present during shutdowns — the possibility of a galvanic contribution. Crack location on the carbon steel side near the fusion boundary is consistent with the first two acting together.

Step 3 — Establish what filler was used. This is the decisive question. If the joint was made with 309L, it is metallurgically correct for fabrication but provides no diffusion barrier against carbon migration and has an expansion coefficient closer to austenitic than to ferritic. If a nickel-based filler had been used, both mechanisms would have been substantially slower. In practice, dissimilar nozzles are frequently welded with 309L because the fabricator's procedure was written for room-temperature service and reused.

Step 4 — Confirm metallographically rather than by inference. A section through the failed region should show, if carbon migration is the mechanism, a decarburized band on the carbon steel side and a carburized, harder band on the stainless side. A hardness traverse across the interface is the quick version of the same check and is usually available faster than metallography.

Step 5 — Separate the repair from the fix. Repairing the crack with the same filler reproduces the same joint and the same service life. If the mechanism is confirmed, the repair should use a nickel-based filler, and the buttering approach should be considered so that the carbon steel side can receive any required post-weld heat treatment without exposing the austenitic material to it.

Step 6 — Widen the scope to the population. If this vessel has other dissimilar nozzles made to the same procedure at similar temperature, they share the mechanism and the same elapsed time. The corrective action is an assessment of all of them, with targeted inspection of the interface region, not a single repair.

Step 7 — Feed it back to design. The most effective long-term control for this failure is to locate dissimilar joints in cooler parts of the system. That is a design decision, and a service failure is the moment at which the design feedback is credible. Recording it as a materials-engineering lesson rather than a maintenance event is what prevents the next one.

16. Known Gaps

• No galvanic series is reproduced. Published series are specific to an electrolyte, and reproducing a seawater series risks its application to a chemical process fluid where it does not hold. The governing factors are explained; the series must be sourced for the actual medium.

• The constitution-diagram construction is described but the diagrams are not reproduced. They are published copyrighted figures. The method and the reasoning behind 309L are given so that a reader knows what to consult and why.

• No temperature threshold for carbon migration is stated. The mechanism is diffusion-controlled and therefore continuous with temperature and time; there is no sharp onset, and any single threshold value would be misleading.

• Intermetallic layer thickness limits are referred to qualitatively. Acceptable thickness is application- and process-specific and is set by the qualification of the specific joining process.

• Filler recommendations reflect conventional industrial practice, not the requirements of any particular code. Where a code governs a dissimilar joint, its provisions take precedence over the general practice described here.

1. Joint Type and Weld Type Are Two Different Decisions

These two terms are used interchangeably in conversation and they mean different things. The joint type is the geometric arrangement of the parts — how the two pieces of metal are placed relative to each other. The weld type is what is deposited into that arrangement.

The distinction is practical rather than pedantic: a T-joint can be made with a fillet weld, with a partial-penetration groove weld, with a full-penetration groove weld, or with a combination of groove and fillet. Those four choices have different strengths, different costs, different inspection requirements and different distortion behaviour. Specifying "a T-joint" says nothing about which. Every drawing dispute over welding traces back to one party naming the joint and the other assuming the weld.

2. The Five Joint Types

| Joint type | Arrangement | Typical use | Principal concern |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Butt | Two members in the same plane, edge to edge | Plate, pipe and structural splices | Full penetration and root quality |
| T | One member perpendicular to the surface of another | Stiffeners, brackets, frames | Root fusion at the intersection; lamellar tearing risk in thick plate |
| Corner | Two members meeting at an edge, forming an angle | Box sections, enclosures | Fit-up variability; access to the root |
| Lap | Two members overlapping | Sheet metal, non-critical structure | Crevice corrosion; poor fatigue performance |
| Edge | Two parallel members joined along their common edge | Sheet flanges, sealing joints | Limited strength; used for sealing more than for load |

Two of these deserve a note. Lap joints are cheap and tolerant of fit-up, which is why they dominate sheet fabrication — but they create a crevice that traps electrolyte and they carry load eccentrically, so they perform poorly in both corrosive and fatigue-loaded service. Corner joints are where fit-up variation does the most damage, because a small angular error changes the root geometry substantially.

3. The Weld Types

Groove welds fill a prepared gap between members. The preparation shapes are: square (no preparation, thin material only), single and double V, single and double bevel, single and double U, single and double J, and the flare grooves (flare-V and flare-bevel) formed by the natural radius between curved members such as tube-to-plate.

Groove welds are either complete joint penetration (CJP), where the weld extends fully through the joint thickness, or partial joint penetration (PJP), where it deliberately does not. This is a design decision with real consequences: a PJP weld has an unfused root that acts as a built-in crack-like discontinuity, so PJP welds are unsuitable for joints subject to fatigue loading transverse to the joint, and codes restrict where they may be used.

Fillet welds are triangular in section and deposited into the corner formed by two surfaces without any edge preparation. They are the cheapest weld type per unit of joint made, they need no preparation, and they tolerate fit-up variation. They are also the most common weld in general fabrication by a wide margin.

Other types: plug and slot welds (filling a hole or slot in one member to join it to another beneath); spot and seam welds (Volume 1); edge welds; surfacing welds (Chapter 65); and back or backing welds (deposited on the reverse side of a groove weld, either to complete the root after gouging or to support the root during welding).

4. Groove Geometry: What Each Dimension Actually Controls

Groove design is a small set of dimensions, each controlling something specific. Getting them right is what makes a joint weldable; getting them wrong produces defects that no amount of welder skill corrects.

| Dimension | What it is | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Groove angle / included angle | Total angle between the prepared faces | Access for the electrode or torch to reach the fusion faces; larger angle means better access but more weld metal, more heat, more distortion and more cost |
| Bevel angle | The angle prepared on one member | Half of the included angle in a symmetric preparation |
| Root opening (root gap) | The separation between the members at the root | Root penetration; too small gives incomplete penetration, too large gives burn-through and excessive filler consumption |
| Root face (land) | The unbevelled square portion at the root | Resistance to burn-through; too large prevents full root fusion, too small allows melt-through |
| Groove radius (U and J) | The radius at the bottom of a U or J preparation | Access at the root without the large volume of a wide V |

The governing trade-off is between access and volume. A wide V-groove is easy to weld and expensive to fill; a narrow groove is cheap in filler and difficult to fuse at the sidewalls. This is why U and J preparations are used on thick sections: they provide root access with far less cross-sectional area than a V of the same depth, saving substantial filler metal, welding time and distortion. Their cost is that they require machining rather than simple flame or plasma cutting.

The rule of thumb behind all of it: weld metal volume in a V-groove increases approximately with the square of the thickness, so on heavy sections the choice of preparation is a major cost driver, not a detail.

5. Single-Sided Against Double-Sided, Backing and Back-Gouging

Double-sided preparations (double-V, double-U) halve the weld volume compared to a single-sided preparation of the same thickness and, critically, allow balanced welding — alternating sides so that the angular distortion from each side largely cancels. They require access to both sides, which is often the limiting factor.

Single-sided joints require some way to control the root. Three approaches:

1. Open root, welded by a skilled welder using a process capable of controlling a free root — gas tungsten arc or a downhill-capable technique. Highest skill requirement; used extensively in pipe welding.

2. Backing, permanent or temporary. A backing bar or strip supports the molten root. Permanent steel backing left in place creates a crevice and a stress concentration, so codes restrict its use in fatigue-loaded joints. Ceramic backing is removed after welding and leaves a formed root profile.

3. Consumable insert, a preplaced ring of filler metal fused into the root — used in high-quality pipe work.

Back-gouging is the operation of removing the root of the first side from the reverse before welding the second side, by grinding, arc-air gouging or machining. Its purpose is to reach sound metal: the root of a first pass frequently contains incomplete fusion or entrapped slag, and back-gouging removes it rather than welding over it. Where a code requires complete joint penetration from both sides, back-gouging is normally mandatory, and inspection of the gouged surface before welding is a hold point.

6. Fillet Welds: Sizing, and the Most Expensive Mistake in Fabrication

A fillet weld is specified by its leg length or by its throat thickness, and the relationship between them for a standard equal-leg fillet with a flat face is that the design throat is approximately 0.7 times the leg length.

Two properties of that relationship govern fabrication economics:

The cross-sectional area — and therefore the deposited volume, the arc time, the filler cost and the heat put into the structure — increases with the square of the leg length. A 10 mm fillet is not 25 % more weld than an 8 mm fillet; it is roughly 56 % more. Oversizing fillets is the most common and most expensive avoidable error in general fabrication, and it is committed with the best of intentions by welders who believe a bigger weld is a safer weld. It is not: it costs more, takes longer, distorts more, and puts more heat into the material.

A fillet larger than necessary cannot generally be justified as conservative, because the additional heat and contraction increase distortion and residual stress, and on heat-input-limited materials (Chapter 23) it can violate the procedure outright.

Fillet weld profile matters as well as size. A convex fillet has a sharper toe angle and a higher stress concentration; a flat or slightly concave profile has better fatigue performance. Codes specify acceptable convexity, and for fatigue-critical joints toe dressing is used deliberately to improve the profile.

Intermittent fillet welds — short lengths at a specified pitch — reduce weld volume and distortion substantially and are appropriate for many non-critical, statically loaded joints. They are prohibited in fatigue-loaded and corrosive applications because each weld termination is a stress concentration and each gap is a crevice.

7. Welding Symbols: The Structure of the Symbol

A welding symbol is a compact instruction. Its elements:

• The reference line, horizontal, carrying all the information.

• The arrow, pointing to the joint. The member the arrow touches defines the arrow side; the opposite side is the other side.

• The weld symbol — a small pictograph of the weld type (a triangle for a fillet, a V for a V-groove, and so on) — placed on the reference line, with its position relative to the line indicating which side of the joint the weld goes on.

• Dimensions: size to the left of the weld symbol; length and pitch to the right (for example, `6 – 50 (150)` meaning a 6 mm fillet, 50 mm long, at 150 mm pitch).

• Supplementary symbols: a circle at the junction of arrow and reference line for weld all around; a flag for a field weld; contour and finish symbols for the required surface profile and how it is to be achieved.

• The tail, carrying references that will not fit as symbols — a procedure number, a process designation, an inspection requirement.

Reading order in practice: identify the joint from the arrow, read the weld symbol to find the weld type and which side it belongs on, read the size and length, then check the supplementary symbols and the tail.

8. The Two Symbol Systems and the Trap Between Them

Two standards govern welding symbols internationally: AWS A2.4 and ISO 2553 [S1][S2]. They are similar in structure and different in a way that matters.

In the AWS system, the side convention is carried entirely by position relative to a single reference line: a weld symbol below the reference line indicates the arrow side, and a weld symbol above the line indicates the other side.

ISO 2553 provides two systems. In system A, the reference line is accompanied by a dashed identification line, and the weld symbol's placement relative to the continuous and dashed lines conveys the side. In system B, the convention follows the same arrow-side-below approach as AWS. A drawing prepared under ISO 2553 must indicate which system it uses.

The consequence is a real and dangerous ambiguity: the same symbol can mean opposite sides depending on the standard and system in force. A drawing that does not state its symbol standard is under-specified, and a fabricator who assumes the wrong one puts the weld on the wrong side of the joint — an error that is expensive to discover after assembly and that has occurred often enough to be a recognized cause of rework.

| The Only Safe Habit Establish which symbol standard and, for ISO, which system a drawing uses before interpreting any symbol on it — and if the drawing does not say, treat it as a question for the designer rather than an assumption to be made. A drawing office that issues welding symbols without stating the governing standard has created an ambiguity that the shop cannot resolve on its own. |
| --- |

9. Welding Positions and Their Designations

Position describes the orientation of the joint and the direction of welding relative to gravity. Two designation systems are in common use.

Plate, AWS-style designations:

| Code | Position | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1G / 1F | Flat | Weld deposited from above onto a horizontal surface |
| 2G / 2F | Horizontal | Weld axis horizontal, on a vertical surface |
| 3G / 3F | Vertical | Weld axis vertical; welded upward or downward |
| 4G / 4F | Overhead | Weld deposited from below |

G denotes groove welds, F denotes fillet welds.

Pipe, AWS-style designations:

| Code | Description |
| --- | --- |
| 1G | Pipe horizontal and rotated; welding in the flat position |
| 2G | Pipe vertical, axis vertical; welding in the horizontal position |
| 5G | Pipe horizontal and fixed; welding progresses around the circumference through overhead, vertical and flat |
| 6G | Pipe fixed at 45°; the most demanding standard position, combining all others |
| 6GR | 6G with a restriction ring simulating restricted access; the most demanding test position in common use |

ISO designations use a letter system: PA flat, PB horizontal-vertical (fillet), PC horizontal, PD horizontal overhead, PE overhead, PF vertical upward, PG vertical downward, and H-L045 for the inclined fixed pipe position corresponding to 6G.

The distinction between PF (vertical up) and PG (vertical down) is one of the most consequential in the entire scheme and is examined in the next section.

10. Why Position Governs Process Selection

Position determines whether gravity helps or hinders, and processes differ enormously in their ability to work against it.

The governing factor is the size of the molten pool. A large pool cannot be held in place against gravity out of position; it sags, runs, and falls out. Processes and modes that produce a small, controllable pool work in all positions; those that produce a large pool are restricted to flat and horizontal.

| Process / mode | Position capability | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SMAW (111) | All positions | Small pool; slag supports the pool; electrode classification designates positional capability |
| GMAW short-circuit (135) | All positions | Low heat input, small pool |
| GMAW spray (135) | Flat and horizontal only | Large fluid pool; high deposition |
| GMAW pulsed (135) | All positions | Pulsing gives spray-type transfer at a low average current, so the pool stays small |
| FCAW gas-shielded (136) | All positions with a designated wire | Fast-freezing slag supports the pool out of position |
| GTAW (141) | All positions | Very small, fully controlled pool |
| SAW (121) | Flat and horizontal only | Flux and molten pool both depend on gravity to stay in place |
| ESW (72x) | Vertical only | The process is defined by a vertically rising molten slag pool |

Two further points. First, vertical-up and vertical-down are different processes in practice: vertical-up gives higher heat input, deeper penetration and greater deposit thickness per pass and is used where strength matters; vertical-down is fast, low in penetration, and used on thin material and for cosmetic capping — using it on thick material where penetration is required is a recognized cause of lack of fusion.

Second, consumables are designated for position and the designation must be respected: an electrode classified for flat and horizontal only will not hold a pool overhead regardless of technique.

11. Position and the Qualification Range

Position is an essential variable in welder qualification, and the ranges are not symmetric — qualifying in a harder position generally qualifies the welder for easier ones, and not the reverse.

This is why 6G is the benchmark pipe test: a welder who passes a 6G test has demonstrated capability through flat, vertical, horizontal and overhead in a single weld, and the qualification range that follows is correspondingly broad. It is also why testing everyone in 1G is a false economy: it is the cheapest test to run and it qualifies the narrowest range of work.

The specific ranges are set by the governing standard (ISO 9606 series, ASME Section IX, AWS D1.1) and differ between them — Chapter 32 covers this in detail. The general principle transfers across all of them: the test position determines what the welder may weld in production, and choosing the test position is therefore a production planning decision, not an administrative one.

12. Fit-Up Tolerance and What Happens When It Drifts

A welding procedure is qualified on a joint that was prepared to specified dimensions. Production joints vary, and the variation causes defects that get blamed on the welder or the parameters.

| Fit-up deviation | Consequence |
| --- | --- |
| Root gap too small | Incomplete root penetration; the arc cannot reach the root faces |
| Root gap too large | Burn-through; excessive filler consumption; root sag; increased shrinkage |
| Root face too thick | Incomplete root fusion |
| Root face too thin / knife-edged | Melt-through, root concavity |
| Included angle too small | Lack of sidewall fusion; slag entrapment in the narrow groove |
| Included angle too large | Excess weld volume, cost, distortion |
| Linear misalignment (high-low) | Stress concentration; incomplete fusion on the low side; a rejectable condition in its own right (ISO 6520-1 code 507) |
| Angular misalignment | Distorted final geometry; uneven root gap along the joint |

The engineering point is that fit-up variation is a production control problem, not a welding problem. A shop that finds intermittent root defects on a stable procedure should measure fit-up on a sample of joints before adjusting anything about the welding. Fit-up varies between parts; parameters do not. Intermittency is the signature.

13. Decision Reference: Choosing a Joint Preparation

| Situation | Preparation | Reasoning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Thin plate, full penetration, both sides accessible | Square butt, welded both sides | No preparation cost; thickness allows full fusion without a groove |
| Medium plate, one side access | Single V with backing or open root | Access from one side only; backing controls the root |
| Medium plate, both sides access | Double V | Half the weld volume; balanced welding controls angular distortion |
| Thick plate, both sides access | Double U | Minimum weld volume at large thickness; machining cost repaid in filler, time and distortion |
| Thick plate, one side access, high quality | Single U with back-gouging where possible | Root access with reduced volume |
| T-joint, statically loaded | Fillet welds | Cheapest; no preparation; adequate for the load |
| T-joint, full strength required | Double bevel groove plus reinforcing fillets | Full penetration through the web-to-flange intersection |
| Fatigue-loaded transverse joint | CJP groove, ground flush or toe-dressed | PJP roots and fillet toes are fatigue initiation sites |
| Sheet metal, non-critical | Lap joint with fillet | Tolerant of fit-up; cheap; adequate where corrosion and fatigue are not concerns |

| Defect | ISO 6520-1 reference | How it is detected | Design/fit-up cause | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Incomplete penetration | 402 | RT, UT; visual on accessible roots | Root gap too small; root face too thick; included angle too small; wrong process for the root | Correct the preparation dimensions; verify with a fit-up gauge before welding; consider open-root process capability |
| Lack of sidewall fusion | 4011 | RT, UT | Included angle too small for electrode access; narrow groove with insufficient manipulation | Open the groove angle; change to U preparation for thick sections; correct torch angle |
| Burn-through / melt-through | — | Visual | Root gap too large; root face too thin; excessive current for the root geometry | Control fit-up; use backing; reduce root pass current |
| Linear misalignment (high-low) | 507 | Visual and dimensional | Poor assembly; inadequate tacking; distortion during fitting | Improve fitting fixtures and tack sequence; measure before welding |

15. Worked Example: A Groove Design That Could Not Be Welded

Situation. A drawing specifies a complete-joint-penetration single-V butt weld in 40 mm plate, welded from one side only with permanent backing, with a 30° included angle. The fabricator reports repeated lack of sidewall fusion at mid-thickness and slag entrapment, found by ultrasonic testing. The welders are qualified and the procedure is qualified. The shop's proposed fix is to increase current.

Step 1 — Check the geometry against the access requirement before touching parameters. At 40 mm depth with a 30° included angle, the groove is deep and narrow. At mid-thickness the electrode must reach a sidewall that is far from the opening at a very shallow approach angle. The defect location — mid-thickness, on the sidewalls — matches this geometric limitation precisely, and that match is the diagnosis.

Step 2 — Recognize what raising current would do. More current increases pool volume and heat but does not change the angle at which the electrode can approach the sidewall. It would increase the risk of slag entrapment in the same narrow groove and add heat input and distortion. It addresses a symptom's magnitude, not its cause.

Step 3 — Consider the preparation alternatives properly. A wider V (typically 60° for manual welding on plate of this thickness) restores access, at the cost of substantially more weld metal — and at 40 mm the volume penalty of a wide V is large. A single-U preparation provides root access and sidewall access with far less cross-sectional area than a wide V of the same depth, which is precisely the reason U preparations exist for heavy sections. The trade is machining cost against filler, arc time and distortion, and at 40 mm the U preparation usually wins on total cost even before the rework saved is counted.

Step 4 — Question the single-sided requirement. Single-sided welding of 40 mm plate is a demanding choice. If the second side is accessible, a double-U or double-V preparation halves the weld volume, allows balanced welding to control angular distortion, and removes the deep-groove access problem entirely. Whether both sides are accessible is a question for the designer, and it is worth asking before accepting the constraint.

Step 5 — Examine the backing decision on its own merits. Permanent backing left in a completed joint creates a crevice and a stress concentration at the root. If the joint is fatigue-loaded or in corrosive service, permanent backing may be inappropriate regardless of the welding difficulty, and that is a design conversation the defect has now made necessary.

Step 6 — State the conclusion. This is a joint design problem presenting as a welding problem. Correcting it requires a drawing change, not a parameter change, and the corrective action belongs with the designer. Requalification will be needed for the revised preparation, since joint geometry is a qualification variable.

Step 7 — Record the general lesson. Deep, narrow single-sided grooves in thick plate are a recurring source of exactly this defect pattern. A design review step that checks electrode access at mid-thickness for any groove above about 25 mm depth would have caught it before fabrication started.

16. Known Gaps

• No groove angle, root gap or root face dimensions are prescribed. Prequalified joint details are published in the governing codes with dimensions tied to process, position and thickness; reproducing them here would risk misapplication across codes and editions. The variables and what each controls are explained; the dimensions belong to the code.

• Welding symbols are described structurally, not reproduced graphically. The symbol libraries in AWS A2.4 and ISO 2553 are copyrighted figure sets; this chapter explains how symbols are constructed and read so that a reader knows what to look up.

• The ISO 2553 system A / system B distinction is stated in principle. The precise graphical conventions must be taken from the standard itself.

• Qualification position ranges are not tabulated. They differ between ISO 9606, ASME IX and AWS D1.1, and Chapter 32 addresses the differences.

• Fillet throat-to-leg relationships assume a standard equal-leg, flat-faced fillet. Unequal-leg, deep-penetration and concave profiles are treated differently by the codes.

1. What a Filler Metal Classification Actually Guarantees

A filler metal classification is a contract between the consumable manufacturer and the user. It states that material carrying that designation, deposited under the specific test conditions the specification defines, will meet stated requirements for chemical composition, mechanical properties, and — for some classes — usability characteristics such as positional capability and current type.

Three limits on that guarantee matter in practice, and misunderstanding any of them causes real problems:

The properties are those of the deposit under test conditions, not of your weld. The specification's test assembly has a defined joint geometry, preheat and interpass temperature, and a defined number of passes. A production weld with heavy dilution from the parent metal, different heat input, or a different thermal history will not necessarily reproduce those properties. This is exactly why procedure qualification (Chapter 31) tests the actual joint rather than accepting the consumable certificate as proof.

A classification is a minimum, not a specification of the actual product. Two electrodes of the same classification from different manufacturers both meet the classification and are not identical. Where a specific characteristic matters — toughness at a particular temperature, a particular diffusible hydrogen level, or a specific chemistry within an allowed range — the manufacturer's actual certificate is what settles it, not the classification.

The classification says nothing about the condition the consumable is in when used. A low-hydrogen electrode left exposed on a humid shop floor no longer delivers the hydrogen level the classification promises. The designation describes the product as manufactured (Section 10).
