3. Decoding a Covered Electrode: E7018 and Its Relatives

For carbon steel covered electrodes under A5.1, the designation has the form E XX Y Z:

| Position | Meaning in E7018 |
| --- | --- |
| E | Electrode |
| 70 | Minimum tensile strength of the deposit in thousands of pounds per square inch — here 70 ksi |
| 1 | Positional capability: 1 = all positions; 2 = flat and horizontal fillet only; 4 = all positions including vertical down |
| 8 | Covering type, current type and polarity — here a low-hydrogen potassium covering with iron powder, usable on AC or DCEP |

The last digit is the one that carries the operating character, and the common values in carbon steel practice:

| Last digit | Covering | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 (as in E6010) | Cellulosic sodium, DCEP | Deep penetration, digging arc, fast-freezing; the classic pipe root electrode; not low hydrogen |
| 1 (as in E6011) | Cellulosic potassium | As above but AC capable |
| 3 (as in E6013) | Rutile | Soft arc, good appearance, light penetration; general purpose and sheet work |
| 4 (as in E7014) | Rutile with iron powder | Higher deposition, easier operation |
| 8 (as in E7018) | Low hydrogen with iron powder | The structural workhorse; low hydrogen, good toughness, requires proper storage |

The single most consequential distinction in this table: E6010 and E6011 are cellulosic electrodes that deliberately generate hydrogen as part of their arc-shielding mechanism, and are therefore not low-hydrogen consumables. They are used where their fast-freezing, deep-penetrating characteristics are needed — notably open-root pipe welding — and they are inappropriate where hydrogen cracking is a concern (Chapter 23). E7018 is the low-hydrogen structural default, and it only remains low-hydrogen if it is stored correctly.

Low-alloy electrodes under A5.5 use the same base structure with an added suffix identifying the alloy system — for example a suffix denoting a carbon-molybdenum or chromium-molybdenum deposit for creep-resistant service.

4. Decoding a Solid Wire: ER70S-6

For carbon steel solid wires under A5.18, the form is ER XX S-Y:

| Position | Meaning in ER70S-6 |
| --- | --- |
| ER | Electrode or rod — usable as a continuously fed electrode or as a hand-fed filler rod |
| 70 | Minimum tensile strength of the deposit, 70 ksi |
| S | Solid wire |
| 6 | Chemical composition designator |

The composition designator is where the practical differences sit. In carbon steel practice the two most common are:

• ER70S-3, a general-purpose wire with moderate deoxidizer content.

• ER70S-6, with higher manganese and silicon content. Those additional deoxidizers let it tolerate more surface contamination — mill scale, light rust — and produce a more fluid pool with better wetting. This is why ER70S-6 dominates general fabrication: it is the more forgiving of the two on real-world plate surfaces.

The tolerance of ER70S-6 for scale is a genuine benefit and a genuine trap: it makes marginal surface preparation *work*, which allows a shop to normalize poor cleaning practice until it meets a material or a process that will not tolerate it.

5. Decoding a Tubular Wire: E71T-1

For carbon steel flux cored electrodes under A5.20, the form is E X Y T-Z followed by shielding and supplemental designators:

| Position | Meaning in E71T-1C |
| --- | --- |
| E | Electrode |
| 7 | Minimum tensile strength in tens of ksi — here 70 ksi |
| 1 | Positional capability: 0 = flat and horizontal only; 1 = all positions |
| T | Tubular (cored) electrode |
| 1 | Usability designator — identifies the slag system, shielding requirement, polarity and operating characteristics |
| C | Shielding gas: C = 100 % CO₂; M = mixed gas (typically argon-CO₂) |

The usability designator is the key digit and it is the one most often ignored. It encodes whether the wire is gas-shielded or self-shielded, what polarity it requires, what slag system it uses, and how it behaves out of position [S2]. Some common groupings:

• T-1: rutile slag, gas-shielded, smooth spray-like arc, low spatter, excellent operator appeal, good for all positions in the "1" positional class.

• T-5: basic slag, gas-shielded, better toughness and lower hydrogen, less attractive arc characteristics and more spatter — chosen for properties rather than appearance.

• T-8: self-shielded, all-position, used where no shielding gas is available or wind precludes it.

• T-11: self-shielded, general purpose, widely used in light fabrication.

Two rules that follow directly. First, the shielding designator is not optional information: a wire classified for CO₂ run under an argon mixture, or the reverse, will not reproduce its classified properties, and the change alters both chemistry and arc behaviour. Second, self-shielded and gas-shielded wires are not interchangeable — a self-shielded wire contains its own deoxidizers and denitriders in quantities calculated for operation without gas, and running it under gas produces an over-deoxidized deposit with degraded toughness.

6. Stainless, Aluminium, Nickel and Other Alloy Designations

For most alloy families the designation is built around the alloy identity rather than a strength number.

| Family | Example | Structure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stainless bare (A5.9) | ER308L | ER + AISI-style alloy number + L for low carbon |
| Stainless covered (A5.4) | E308L-16 | E + alloy number + covering/position designator |
| Aluminium (A5.10) | ER4043, ER5356 | ER + the four-digit aluminium alloy number of the deposit |
| Nickel (A5.14) | ERNiCrMo-3 | ER + Ni + principal alloying elements + a sequence number |
| Titanium (A5.16) | ERTi-2 | ER + Ti + grade number |
| Copper (A5.7) | ERCuSi-A | ER + Cu + principal alloying element + variant |
| Cast iron (A5.15) | ENiFe-CI | E + deposit alloy + CI for cast iron |
| Tungsten (A5.12) | EWTh-2, EWLa-1.5 | EW + oxide addition + nominal oxide percentage |

Two notes on the tungsten entries, since they are frequently misread. The designations identify the oxide added to the tungsten: EWP is pure tungsten, EWTh-2 contains roughly 1.7–2.2 % thorium oxide, EWCe-2 roughly 1.8–2.2 % cerium oxide, EWLa-1.5 roughly 1.3–1.7 % lanthanum oxide, and EWZr-1 roughly 0.15–0.40 % zirconium oxide [S3][S4]. Colour codes are applied to identify them — with the important caveat that AWS A5.12 changed the colour code for EWCe-2 from orange to grey, and permits the manufacturer to select any colour for the EWG (unspecified) classification [S3]. An electrode identified by remembered colour alone, from a batch of unknown vintage, is not reliably identified; once the colour band wears off, the electrode cannot be identified without laboratory analysis, and the correct action is to discard it rather than guess [S4].

7. Supplemental Designators: Hydrogen, Toughness and Moisture Resistance

Optional suffixes carry information that is frequently the deciding factor in consumable selection.

Diffusible hydrogen designators state the maximum diffusible hydrogen in the deposit in millilitres per 100 g:

| Designator | Maximum diffusible hydrogen |
| --- | --- |
| H16 | 16 ml / 100 g |
| H8 | 8 ml / 100 g |
| H4 | 4 ml / 100 g |
| H2 | 2 ml / 100 g |

Lower is better, and the practical significance is direct: code preheat requirements are stated against these categories, and using a lower-hydrogen consumable can legitimately reduce the required preheat temperature — a real cost saving that also reduces the cracking risk (Chapter 23, Section 6) [S5].

Toughness designators state the temperature at which the deposit meets a specified impact energy. These matter wherever low-temperature service, offshore, pressure or structural fatigue requirements apply, and a consumable meeting the strength requirement but not the toughness requirement is a common substitution error.

The R designator on covered electrodes indicates enhanced moisture resistance — a covering formulated to absorb less atmospheric moisture, extending permissible exposure time. It does not make the electrode immune to exposure; it widens the window.

8. The ISO Classification System and Its Two Parallel Schemes

The ISO consumable standards cover the same ground with a different structure:

| ISO standard | Covers |
| --- | --- |
| ISO 2560 | Covered electrodes for manual metal arc welding of non-alloy and fine grain steels |
| ISO 14341 | Wire electrodes and deposits for gas-shielded metal arc welding of non-alloy and fine grain steels |
| ISO 17632 | Tubular cored electrodes for gas-shielded and non-gas-shielded metal arc welding of non-alloy and fine grain steels |
| ISO 636 | Rods, wires and deposits for tungsten inert gas welding of non-alloy and fine grain steels |
| ISO 14343 | Wire electrodes, strip electrodes, wires and rods for arc welding of stainless and heat-resisting steels |
| ISO 3581 | Covered electrodes for manual metal arc welding of stainless and heat-resisting steels |

| ISO 18274 | Wires, strips, wire electrodes and rods for welding of nickel and nickel alloys |
| ISO 14171 | Solid wire electrodes, tubular cored electrodes and flux combinations for submerged arc welding |

An ISO designation encodes more information positionally than the AWS equivalent — typically strength level, impact toughness temperature, chemical composition, and the shielding gas group in a single string.

The structural feature that catches people out is that several ISO consumable standards publish two parallel classification systems, A and B. System A follows the European convention; system B is structured to align with the AWS-style approach. The two produce different designations for the same product, and a standard's designation is incomplete without stating which system it uses. A purchase specification or procedure quoting an ISO consumable designation without an A or B indication is ambiguous in exactly the way that a welding symbol without its standard is ambiguous (Chapter 28, Section 8).

The corollary is that AWS and ISO designations are not directly interchangeable. Manufacturers commonly print both on a package, and that dual marking is the reliable cross-reference — not a conversion table, and certainly not an assumption that similar-looking numbers mean the same thing.

9. Matching, Undermatching and Overmatching

Filler strength relative to the parent metal is a deliberate design decision with three possible answers.

Matching — filler strength approximately equal to parent strength — is the default for most structural work and is what prequalified procedures assume.

Undermatching — filler weaker than the parent — is used deliberately in three situations: where the weld is not the critical load path and a lower-strength, more ductile deposit reduces cracking risk; where a lower-strength consumable has lower hydrogen sensitivity on a high-strength parent; and in fillet welds on high-strength steel, where a full-strength fillet is often not required by the design and an undermatched consumable reduces both cost and cracking risk. It requires the designer's agreement, because the joint's capacity is then set by the weld.

Overmatching — filler stronger than the parent — is generally avoided where it is not required. A stronger, less ductile weld metal concentrates strain into the parent or the heat-affected zone rather than distributing it, and it increases the restraint stress the joint imposes on itself. Overmatching is a specific and occasionally correct choice; it is not a safe default, and the intuition that stronger is safer is wrong here in the same way it is wrong for fillet size (Chapter 28, Section 6).

For corrosion service, the equivalent decision is made on chemistry rather than strength: fillers are commonly over-alloyed relative to the parent so that the diluted deposit is at least as corrosion resistant as the parent (Chapters 24 and 27).

10. Storage, Handling and Reconditioning

The classification describes the product as manufactured. Its condition when it reaches the arc is the user's responsibility, and this is where a large share of hydrogen-related failures originate.

Low-hydrogen covered electrodes:

• Supplied in hermetically sealed packaging. Once opened, the covering begins absorbing atmospheric moisture immediately.

• Store opened electrodes in a holding oven at the manufacturer's specified temperature.

• Observe an exposure time limit on the shop floor, enforced with a real control — a quiver with a time record, not an instruction. Permitted exposure depends on the classification, the H-designator and ambient humidity.

• Re-baking to a specified schedule can restore some electrodes; it must follow the manufacturer's schedule, it is permitted only a limited number of times, and it is not permitted at all for some coverings. Re-baking a cellulosic electrode destroys it — its covering depends on retained moisture to function.

Solid wire: store dry and sealed. The risks are surface rust, drawing lubricant residue and moisture; a partially used spool left on a machine over a humid weekend is a routine porosity source.

Flux cored wire: more hygroscopic than solid wire because the core is exposed at the cut end. Reseal partly used spools; observe the manufacturer's storage guidance.

Submerged arc flux: highly hygroscopic; requires heated storage and re-drying to a specified schedule. Recycled flux must be screened and handled per procedure.

Aluminium, nickel and titanium consumables: the risk is surface contamination rather than moisture absorption in the covering sense. Sealed storage, clean handling with gloves, and no exposure to shop contaminants (Chapters 25 and 26).

Traceability applies to all of them: batch identity has to survive from goods-in to the weld, because a consumable problem discovered later is only actionable if the affected welds can be identified. This is a stated requirement of the quality-requirement standards in Chapter 33, not an optional refinement.

11. Decision Reference: Selecting a Filler Metal

Work through in this order:

1. Parent material family and grade. Establishes the alloy system of the deposit. For dissimilar joints, the diluted composition governs (Chapter 27).

2. Process. Determines which specification family applies — a covered electrode, solid wire, cored wire or submerged arc combination.

3. Strength requirement. Matching, undermatching or overmatching per Section 9, and the designer's intent.

4. Toughness requirement. The service temperature and the applicable impact test requirement select the toughness designator.

5. Hydrogen requirement. Set by the cracking risk assessment; drives the H-designator and, in turn, the required preheat.

6. Corrosion requirement. May override strength considerations entirely and push toward an over-alloyed deposit.

7. Position. The positional digit must permit the positions actually to be welded.

8. Shielding gas compatibility. For gas-shielded consumables, the classification is tied to a specific gas or gas group (Chapter 30).

9. Code and procedure constraints. The qualified WPS names a consumable classification; substitution outside it invalidates the qualification.

13. Worked Example: A Toughness Failure Traced to a Consumable Substitution

Situation. A fabricator's procedure qualification for a structural project passes. Six months into production, a routine production test coupon fails Charpy impact testing at the specified temperature. Tensile and bend results pass. Nothing in the WPS parameters has changed and the welders are the same.

Step 1 — Note what passed and what failed. Strength and ductility are acceptable; toughness is not. That pattern points at deposit chemistry or thermal history, not at joint preparation, technique or gross parameter error — those would normally show up in bend or radiographic results too.

Step 2 — Check the consumable actually in use against the WPS. The WPS names a classification including a toughness designator. The question is what is physically on the machine and what the goods-in records show was purchased. Consumable substitution — a "same strength" product from a different supplier, ordered when the specified one was unavailable — is a common cause and is often invisible because both products carry the same strength number.

Step 3 — Check the certificate, not the classification. Even without substitution, two products of identical classification can differ in actual chemistry within the permitted range, and a product at one end of the range may meet the classification's toughness requirement marginally. The manufacturer's certificate for the actual batch is the evidence.

Step 4 — Check the shielding gas against the consumable's shielding designator. For a cored wire, a change from a CO₂-designated product to a mixed-gas-designated one, or a change of the gas supplied without a change of wire, alters deposit chemistry and toughness directly. A gas supply change six months into a project is a realistic and easily overlooked event.

Step 5 — Check heat input and interpass temperature against the qualified range. Toughness is sensitive to thermal history (Chapter 22). If production has drifted toward higher heat input or higher interpass temperature to increase deposition rate, toughness can fall while every other result stays acceptable. Reviewing recorded parameters against the qualified range settles this.

Step 6 — Establish the affected population. If a consumable substitution is confirmed, the affected work is everything welded since the substitution — identified through consumable batch traceability. If traceability is inadequate, the affected population cannot be bounded, and that is itself a finding requiring corrective action at the quality-system level (Chapter 33).

Step 7 — Fix the control, not the coupon. The corrective action is a consumable control that prevents substitution without engineering review: a locked approved-consumable list tied to the WPS, goods-in verification against it, and batch traceability from store to weld. Re-testing a new coupon proves nothing about the material already welded.

14. Known Gaps

• No complete classification tables are reproduced. The AWS A5 and ISO consumable standards are purchased documents containing extensive composition and property tables. This chapter explains the structure of the designations so that a reader can decode and look them up; the tables themselves belong to the standards.

• Usability designators for cored wires are described by common groupings, not exhaustively. The full set with its polarity, slag system and operating characteristics is in AWS A5.20 and A5.29.

• Exposure time limits and re-baking schedules are not stated numerically. They are manufacturer-specific and classification-specific, and using a generic figure would be unsafe.

• AWS and ISO designations are not cross-mapped here. No general conversion is defensible; the manufacturer's dual marking on the product is the reliable cross-reference.

• Tungsten oxide percentages in Section 6 are quoted from a published technical summary of AWS A5.12 and should be confirmed against the standard where an exact figure matters.

1. Shielding Gas Does Four Jobs, Not One

The obvious job of a shielding gas is to displace air and keep oxygen and nitrogen out of the molten metal. That is necessary but it is not why one gas mixture is chosen over another — every inert gas does it. The other three jobs are what drive selection:

It sets the electrical and thermal character of the arc. Ionization potential determines how easily the arc strikes and how stable it is; thermal conductivity in the arc column determines how energy is distributed across the pool and therefore the penetration profile.

It determines the mode of metal transfer. In consumable-electrode processes, whether droplets transfer as a fine spray, as large repelled globules, or by short-circuiting is governed by the gas as much as by the current. This is why the same wire at the same current behaves completely differently under argon-rich and CO₂-rich shielding.

It controls the chemistry of the deposit. Oxidizing components burn out deoxidizers and can alter the alloy content of the deposit; this is why a consumable's classification is tied to a specific gas or gas group (Chapter 29, Section 5), and why changing the gas without changing the wire changes the weld metal properties.

The consequence: shielding gas is a welding variable of the same rank as current and voltage, is an essential variable in procedure qualification, and cannot be changed on the shop floor for availability reasons without engineering review.

2. The Physical Properties That Matter

| Property | What it governs | Practical consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ionization potential | How easily the arc strikes and sustains | Argon's low ionization potential gives easy starting and a stable, quiet arc; helium's high value gives a hotter but harder-to-start arc |
| Thermal conductivity | Heat distribution across the arc column and into the work | Helium and CO₂ spread heat, producing a broader, deeper fusion profile; argon concentrates it, giving the characteristic narrow "finger" penetration |
| Density relative to air | How well the gas blankets the joint | Argon and CO₂ are heavier than air and blanket well in flat position; helium is much lighter and escapes upward, requiring higher flow rates |
| Reactivity | Chemical interaction with the molten metal | Inert gases do not react; oxygen and CO₂ oxidize; hydrogen reduces; nitrogen can stabilize austenite or embrittle, depending on the material |
| Dissociation | Energy absorbed and released by molecular breakdown | CO₂ dissociates in the arc and recombines exothermically at the pool, transferring extra energy and increasing arc force |

The dissociation behaviour of carbon dioxide is the single most consequential entry in that table, because it explains simultaneously why CO₂ gives deep penetration, why it produces a violent arc with heavy spatter, and why it is the cheapest gas in industrial use.

3. The Individual Gases and What Each Contributes

Argon. Inert, heavy, low ionization potential. Gives a stable, easily started arc with good cleaning action on reverse polarity and a narrow, deep central penetration profile. The base gas for almost every mixture. Used pure for aluminium, magnesium, titanium, nickel and copper work, and for gas tungsten arc welding generally.

Helium. Inert, very light, high ionization potential and high thermal conductivity. Produces a hotter arc with a broader, more uniform penetration profile and higher heat input at a given current. Used where extra heat is needed — thick aluminium and copper in particular. Costs more, requires higher flow rates because it escapes upward, and makes arc starting harder, which is why it is usually blended with argon rather than used alone.

Carbon dioxide. Active. Dissociates in the arc, giving deep broad penetration and high arc force. Cheapest of the common gases. Its costs are heavy spatter, a harsher arc, an oxidizing atmosphere that burns out deoxidizers, and no support for spray transfer. Used pure only with wires formulated for it; more commonly as a component of an argon-based mixture.

Oxygen. Active, used in small percentages (typically a few percent) in argon-based mixtures for steel. It lowers the surface tension of the molten droplet and the pool, which stabilizes spray transfer, improves wetting at the toes and reduces undercut. Excess oxygen oxidizes the deposit and degrades toughness.

Hydrogen. Reducing. Added in small percentages to argon for austenitic stainless and nickel gas tungsten arc welding, where it increases heat input, improves wetting and gives a cleaner, brighter bead by reducing surface oxides. It must never be used on ferritic steels (hydrogen cracking, Chapter 23) or on titanium (hydrogen embrittlement, Chapter 26), and it introduces a flammability consideration.

Nitrogen. Behaves differently by material. On austenitic and especially duplex stainless it is a strong austenite stabilizer, and small additions to shielding or backing gas help restore the phase balance (Chapter 24, Section 6). On carbon steel it causes porosity and embrittlement. On copper it is used as a cheap purge. Never used on titanium.

4. The ISO 14175 Classification System

ISO 14175 classifies gases and gas mixtures for fusion welding by main group letter with numbered subgroups [S1][S2]:

| Group | Description |
| --- | --- |
| I | Inert gases and inert gas mixtures — argon, helium, or combinations. Subgroups I1 to I3 distinguish by helium content |
| M1, M2, M3 | Oxidizing mixtures containing oxygen and/or carbon dioxide, in three progressive levels of oxidizing intensity with increasing CO₂ and O₂ ranges |
| C | Highly oxidizing gas and mixtures — pure carbon dioxide, or CO₂-dominant with oxygen |
| R | Reducing gas mixtures containing hydrogen (roughly 0.5–50 %) balanced with inert gas |
| N | Low-reactivity or reducing mixtures containing nitrogen (roughly 0.5–50 %), optionally with hydrogen |
| O | Oxygen (100 %) |
| Z | Mixtures containing components not listed, or outside the listed composition ranges |

A full designation states the standard, the group, the components and the proportions — for example the form ISO 14175 – M25 – ArCO – 6/4, denoting an argon base with 6 % CO₂ and 4 % oxygen, classified in the M2 oxidizing family [S2].

The practical value of the group letters is that consumable specifications and welding procedures frequently specify a gas group rather than a single commercial product, which permits a shop to use any product within the group. Two consequences: a change within a group is generally permissible, and a change between groups is a change of essential variable requiring requalification. Knowing which group a cylinder actually contains — rather than which supplier's trade name is printed on it — is what makes that distinction usable.

5. Carbon Dioxide Content: Penetration, Spatter and the Trade-Off

The proportion of carbon dioxide in an argon-based mixture is the strongest single lever a shop has over arc behaviour on steel, and it trades three things against each other.

Rising CO₂ content gives:

• Deeper and broader penetration, from dissociation energy and increased arc force.

• A wider, less finger-shaped fusion profile, generally more tolerant of slightly imperfect fit-up.

• Lower gas cost.

Rising CO₂ content costs:

• More spatter. CO₂-rich shielding increases arc force and droplet repulsion compared to argon, and this is the dominant reason CO₂-shielded welding is spattery [S3][S4]. It is also the reason the standard first recommendation for a spatter problem on steel is to increase the argon fraction — commonly to at least 80 % argon — and avoid pure CO₂ [S4].

• Loss of true spray transfer. Spray transfer requires a substantially argon-rich atmosphere — conventionally at least about 80 % argon or helium [S3]. Under pure CO₂ the transfer stays globular or short-circuiting no matter how the current is set, which means the high-spatter globular region cannot be escaped by parameter adjustment alone.

• An oxidizing atmosphere, burning out deoxidizers and requiring a consumable formulated to compensate.

• A harsher, noisier arc with poorer operator appeal.

The relationship to metal transfer mode is what makes this decisive rather than merely a preference. The globular range is the highest-spatter operating region in gas metal arc welding, with large droplets transferring erratically, repelled and burst by arc forces [S3][S4]. Escaping it requires either dropping into true short-circuiting or rising into spray — and spray is only available under an argon-rich mixture. A shop welding steel under pure CO₂ and complaining about spatter has, in effect, chosen a gas that removes one of the two escape routes.

| The Standard Spatter Diagnosis Order When spatter rises on a steel MAG weld, work in this order: (1) determine which transfer mode the parameters actually put you in, and get out of the globular range — into short-circuit or spray, or use pulsed transfer; (2) raise the argon fraction of the mixture; (3) set inductance for a softer current rise if welding in short-circuit; (4) inspect the wire feed path — liner, drive rolls, contact tip — since feed instability modulates arc length; (5) reposition the earth return if arc blow is suspected; (6) clean the joint of rust, zinc, oil and moisture [S4]. That sequence addresses cause before symptom, and it is the same order used in the process chapters of Volume 3. |
| --- |

6. Gas Selection by Process and Material

| Process and material | Typical gas | Reasoning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GMAW, carbon steel, short-circuit | Ar-CO₂ mixtures with moderate CO₂, or CO₂ | Short-circuit works under any of these; higher CO₂ gives penetration at the cost of spatter |
| GMAW, carbon steel, spray | Argon-rich mixture (≥ ~80 % Ar), often with a few percent O₂ or CO₂ | Spray transfer requires an argon-rich atmosphere; small O₂ or CO₂ additions stabilize the arc and improve wetting |
| GMAW, carbon steel, pulsed | Argon-rich mixture | Pulsing gives spray-type droplet detachment at low average current; needs the same argon-rich base |
| GMAW, austenitic stainless | Argon with small additions (O₂ or CO₂, often as a tri-mix) | Minimal carbon pickup; enough active component for arc stability and wetting |
| GMAW, aluminium | Pure argon, or argon-helium for thick sections | Inert group only — no oxidizing component; helium adds heat for heavy sections |
| GMAW, nickel alloys | Argon, sometimes with helium | Inert only; nickel is oxidation-sensitive |
| FCAW, gas-shielded | CO₂ or Ar-CO₂ per the wire's shielding designator | The wire's classification is tied to the gas; changing it changes deposit chemistry |
| GTAW, steel and stainless | Argon; argon-helium for more heat; argon-hydrogen for austenitic stainless and nickel | Inert base essential; hydrogen additions only where the material permits |
| GTAW, aluminium | Argon (AC), argon-helium (thick sections) | Cathodic cleaning on AC; helium for heat on heavy sections |
| GTAW, titanium | Argon, high purity, with trailing shield and back purge | Total atmospheric exclusion required (Chapter 26) |
| Plasma arc welding | Argon plasma gas; argon or argon-hydrogen shielding | Plasma gas must be inert and consistent; shielding chosen by material |
| Laser welding | Helium or argon, sometimes nitrogen | Helium suppresses plasma plume better at high power; choice interacts with the source wavelength |

7. Backing and Purging Gases

The back side of a joint needs the same protection as the front on any material that oxidizes badly — stainless, duplex, nickel, titanium, zirconium (Chapters 24 and 26).

Argon is the general-purpose backing gas: inert, heavier than air so it displaces upward-escaping air well in many geometries, universally acceptable.

Nitrogen is used as a cheaper backing gas on austenitic stainless and copper, and is deliberately chosen for duplex stainless where its austenite-stabilizing effect at the root is beneficial. It must not be used on titanium or on carbon steel roots.

Forming gas — nitrogen with a small hydrogen addition — is used on austenitic stainless where its reducing character gives a bright, oxide-free root. Not for ferritic steels or titanium; the hydrogen content introduces a flammability control requirement.

Practical purging discipline, restated here because it is a gas-delivery matter as much as a metallurgical one:

• Purge to a measured residual oxygen level, not to a time, for critical work; a duration is a guess about volume, leakage and flow.

• Reduce the purge volume with dams or soluble barriers on large-diameter pipe — this cuts gas consumption and purge time enormously.

• Control purge pressure. Too much pressure blows the root out or causes root concavity; too little fails to exclude air. A vented, low-pressure flowing purge is the objective, not a pressurized one.

• Maintain until cool. Hot stainless and titanium continue to oxidize after the arc is off.

8. Flow Rate, Nozzle and the Turbulence Trap

More gas is not better shielding, and this is one of the most persistent misconceptions on the shop floor.

Shielding depends on laminar flow — a smooth column of gas displacing air. Above a certain flow rate for a given nozzle, the flow becomes turbulent, and turbulent flow entrains the surrounding air into the shielding column. The result is that increasing flow past that point makes porosity worse, not better. A welder responding to porosity by turning the flowmeter up is a common and self-defeating sequence.

The variables that determine effective shielding:

• Flow rate matched to nozzle size and joint geometry. A larger nozzle needs more flow; a fillet in a corner is better shielded than an outside corner at the same flow.

• Nozzle condition. Spatter build-up inside the nozzle disrupts flow and is the leading mechanical cause of shielding failure — which is precisely why unmanaged spatter causes porosity (Chapter 22, Section 14).

• Gas lens. A diffuser screen that smooths flow and permits greater electrode extension with stable shielding; standard practice on gas tungsten arc welding of reactive materials.

• Nozzle-to-work distance. Excessive stand-off lets air in around the edge of the gas column.

• Draughts. A cross-draught of a few metres per second will strip a shielding column. Doors, fans, extraction systems and adjacent air movers are routine causes; screening the work area is the fix, not more gas.

• Torch angle. Steep angles direct the gas column away from the pool and can aspirate air behind it.

9. Gas Delivery: From Cylinder to Arc

The delivery system between cylinder and arc has more failure modes than the cylinder does, and most gas-related defects originate here:

• Leaks in hoses and fittings. A leaking joint under positive pressure can still admit air by aspiration at the fitting, and a slow leak wastes gas continuously. Leak-checking the whole path is a routine maintenance task that is skipped until porosity appears.

• Permeable or degraded hose. Some hose materials permit atmospheric ingress over time; welding-grade hose exists for a reason and shop-air hose is not a substitute.

• Excess hose volume with solenoid control. A long hose between solenoid and torch delays gas arrival at arc start, producing start porosity even when the flow setting is correct.

• Pre-flow and post-flow settings. Insufficient pre-flow leaves air in the nozzle at arc initiation; insufficient post-flow exposes the still-hot pool and electrode after the arc extinguishes. Both produce localized porosity at the ends of welds — a distinctive and diagnostic pattern.

• Manifold and mixer faults. Central gas systems with on-site mixing can drift out of proportion; the mixture that arrives is not necessarily the mixture that was set.

• Cylinder moisture and contamination. Uncommon with reputable suppliers but not impossible; certificates of analysis exist for critical work.

• Flowmeter type. A flowmeter calibrated for one gas reads incorrectly on another because the reading depends on gas density — using an argon-calibrated meter on helium or CO₂ gives a false reading unless a correction is applied.

10. Fuel Gases for Oxy-Fuel Welding and Cutting

For the oxy-fuel processes (Chapters 63 and 64), the gas is the heat source rather than a shield.

| Fuel gas | Character | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Acetylene | Highest flame temperature of the common fuels; concentrated inner cone; fastest preheat | Welding, cutting, brazing, heating where speed matters |
| Propane | Lower flame temperature; more total heat in the outer envelope | Cutting, heating, brazing; poor for welding steel |
| Propylene | Intermediate between acetylene and propane | Cutting and heating |
| Natural gas | Low temperature, cheap, piped | Heating, some cutting |
| Hydrogen | Clean flame, no carbon | Underwater cutting, specialist applications |

The neutral, oxidizing and carburizing flame settings matter for welding: a neutral flame (balanced oxygen and fuel) is used for steel; an oxidizing flame is used for some copper alloys; a carburizing flame with excess acetylene is used for hardfacing and for some cast iron work. Setting the flame is a skill, and the flame condition is the process control.

11. Gas Safety

Gases used in welding carry hazards independent of the welding itself, and Chapter 37 covers the framework. The gas-specific points:

• Asphyxiation. Argon, CO₂ and nitrogen are heavier than air, are odourless, and displace oxygen. They accumulate in pits, tanks, vessels and low areas. A purged vessel is an oxygen-deficient atmosphere and entering one without testing and a permit has killed people. This is the single most serious gas hazard in welding and it is not perceptible to the person affected.

• Cylinder handling. Cylinders are secured upright, valve caps fitted for transport, never dropped, never lifted by the valve, never used as rollers or supports. A cylinder with a broken-off valve becomes a projectile.

• Acetylene specifics. Acetylene is unstable at elevated pressure and is dissolved in acetone within a porous filler inside the cylinder. Consequences: it must be used within its rated pressure limit (regulator settings for acetylene are strictly limited by the equipment standard and by regulation); cylinders must be used and stored upright, because a cylinder used on its side can deliver liquid acetone into the hose; and there is a maximum withdrawal rate — drawing too fast pulls acetone out with the gas and can cause the cylinder to overheat.

• Oxygen is not a fuel but it makes everything else burn violently. Oil or grease in contact with high-pressure oxygen can ignite spontaneously. Oxygen equipment must be kept free of hydrocarbons, and oxygen must never be used to blow down clothing, ventilate a space, or power tools.

• Flashback arrestors and check valves on both fuel and oxygen lines are standard required equipment on oxy-fuel systems.

• Hydrogen-bearing mixtures introduce flammability control requirements in enclosed spaces and around purge exhausts.

12. Decision Reference: Gas Selection

| Requirement | Choose | Avoid |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lowest spatter on steel GMAW | Argon-rich mixture with pulsed or spray transfer | Pure CO₂; parameters in the globular range |
| Deepest penetration on steel at lowest gas cost | Higher CO₂ content | If spatter or appearance matters |
| Spray transfer capability | At least ~80 % argon | Pure CO₂ — spray is unavailable |
| Thick aluminium or copper | Argon-helium | Pure argon alone if fusion cannot be established |
| Austenitic stainless GTAW, bright clean bead | Argon with a small hydrogen addition | Hydrogen on ferritic steel or titanium |
| Duplex stainless root and shield | Nitrogen-bearing mixtures | Gas without nitrogen where phase balance is marginal |
| Titanium | High-purity argon with trailing shield and purge | Any nitrogen or hydrogen content |
| Cheap backing on austenitic stainless | Nitrogen | Nitrogen on titanium or carbon steel roots |
| Root purge on critical pipe | Argon, purged to a measured oxygen level | Time-based purging without measurement |

| Defect | How it is detected | Gas-related cause | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Porosity, general | RT; surface pores visually | Insufficient flow; turbulent flow entraining air; leak in the gas path; draught; nozzle blocked with spatter; wrong gas | Set flow for the nozzle and joint; leak-check the path; screen from draughts; clean the nozzle; verify the gas group in use |
| Porosity at weld starts | RT; visual at starts | Insufficient pre-flow; long hose between solenoid and torch delaying gas arrival | Increase pre-flow; shorten the solenoid-to-torch hose volume |
| Porosity and crater oxidation at weld ends | Visual at terminations | Insufficient post-flow leaving the hot pool exposed | Increase post-flow; hold the torch over the crater until flow ceases |
| Excessive spatter | Visual | High CO₂ content; parameters in the globular range; incorrect inductance | Increase argon fraction; move to short-circuit, spray or pulsed transfer; set inductance; service the wire feed path [S4] |
| Undercut and poor wetting | Visual; dimensional | Insufficient active component in the mixture for the process (surface tension too high) | Add a small oxygen or CO₂ percentage within the qualified group |
| Loss of toughness in the deposit | Impact testing | Over-oxidizing mixture burning out deoxidizers; gas group changed without changing consumable | Return to the qualified gas group; verify consumable-to-gas designator match (Chapter 29) |
| Root oxidation / sugaring | Visual; borescope | Absent, insufficient, prematurely stopped or leaking back purge | Purge to a measured oxygen level; contain purge volume; maintain until cool |
| Root concavity or blown root | Visual; RT | Excessive purge pressure | Reduce purge pressure; provide a vent so the purge flows rather than pressurizes |
| Nitrogen porosity or embrittlement in steel | RT; impact testing | Nitrogen-bearing backing gas used on a carbon steel root; air entrainment | Use argon backing on carbon steel; correct the shielding failure |
| Hydrogen cracking | Delayed; MT/PT after hold | Hydrogen-bearing shielding or backing gas used on ferritic steel | Never use R-group or hydrogen-bearing forming gas on ferritic steels |
| Titanium discoloration / embrittlement | Surface colour; ductility testing | Shielding failure, inadequate trailing shield, or nitrogen/hydrogen in the gas | High-purity argon only; trailing shield; verify gas certificate |
| Tungsten inclusion | RT | Contaminated or oxidizing gas eroding the electrode | Inert gas only for GTAW; verify no active component has been supplied in error |

14. Worked Example: Intermittent Porosity on One Robot Cell Out of Four

Situation. A fabricator runs four identical robotic GMAW cells welding the same part with the same program, wire and gas mixture from a common manifold. One cell produces intermittent porosity; the other three do not. The cell has been re-taught, the wire spool changed, and the parameters verified against the program. The porosity persists.

Step 1 — Use the comparison that is already available. Four nominally identical cells with one deviating is close to a controlled experiment. Anything common to all four — the gas mixture at the manifold, the wire batch, the part, the program logic — is unlikely to be the cause, because it would affect all four. The investigation should concentrate exclusively on what is *not* shared.

Step 2 — List what is unique to one cell. The gas line from the manifold to that cell and every fitting in it; that cell's solenoid, hose length and internal volume; that cell's torch, nozzle, diffuser and liner; that cell's extraction hood and its air movement; that cell's physical position relative to doors, fans and adjacent equipment; and that cell's pre-flow and post-flow settings if they are stored locally rather than in a shared program.

Step 3 — Read the intermittency as evidence. Intermittent porosity that is not correlated with a parameter change usually means something that varies: a leak that opens and closes with hose movement as the robot articulates, a draught that comes and goes as a door opens, or a nozzle that progressively blocks with spatter and is periodically cleaned. Each of those produces a different pattern in time, and correlating the defective parts against time of day, robot pose or nozzle-cleaning interval will usually distinguish them.

Step 4 — Check the gas path physically. Leak-check from the manifold takeoff to the torch, with the robot moved through its full range so that any leak that only opens at a particular pose is detected. Torch-cable leaks that appear only at articulation extremes are a well-known cause of exactly this pattern and are invisible in a static check.

Step 5 — Check nozzle condition and the spatter loop. If this cell generates more spatter than the others — for any reason, including a worn contact tip or a drive roll issue — spatter accumulates in the nozzle, disrupts gas flow and produces porosity. That makes spatter the cause and porosity the symptom, and cleaning the nozzle more often treats the symptom while the underlying cause persists.

Step 6 — Check the local air movement. An extraction hood positioned differently, a newly installed fan, or proximity to a door can strip shielding on one cell and not the others. This is worth checking physically with a smoke source rather than by inspection, because a draught strong enough to disturb a shielding column is not necessarily strong enough to feel.

Step 7 — Resist the flowmeter. The instinctive response is to increase gas flow on the affected cell. If the flow is already at or above the laminar limit for that nozzle, increasing it entrains more air and makes the porosity worse — and if it appears to help temporarily, that masks the real fault. Flow should be verified as correct for the nozzle and left there while the actual cause is found.

Step 8 — Confirm and close. Once the cause is identified and corrected, run the cell for a defined production quantity with the same inspection level applied to all four cells, so that the comparison that identified the problem also verifies the fix.

15. Known Gaps

• No flow rates are given. Correct flow depends on nozzle size, joint geometry, torch angle and local air movement, and a published number would be applied outside the conditions it was derived for. The variables and the turbulence limit are explained instead.

• ISO 14175 composition ranges are described by group character, not by numeric limits. The numeric ranges are in the purchased standard; the group structure and designation format given here are from a publicly available copy of the standard's classification tables [S2].

• Commercial gas mixture names are not used. Suppliers market proprietary names for products within the same ISO groups; specifying by group and composition is the transferable practice.

• Acetylene pressure and withdrawal-rate limits are described qualitatively. The numeric limits are set by equipment standards and by national regulation and must be taken from those.

• Laser shielding gas selection is stated only in outline, since it interacts with source wavelength, power and process mode; Chapter 52 develops it.

1. Why Welding Requires Qualification When Machining Does Not

A machined dimension can be measured. If a shaft is specified at 50.00 mm ± 0.02 and the micrometer reads 50.01, the part conforms — the verification is complete, direct and cheap.

A weld cannot be verified this way. Its critical properties — tensile strength, ductility, toughness, hardness distribution, freedom from internal discontinuities and resistance to environmental cracking — are not measurable on the finished component without destroying it. Non-destructive testing finds discontinuities; it does not measure toughness, and it says nothing about the microstructure the thermal cycle produced.

This is why welding is formally designated a special process: a process whose result cannot be fully verified by subsequent inspection of the product. The engineering response is to control the process instead of inspecting the product, which requires proving in advance that a defined set of conditions produces acceptable properties, then holding production to those conditions.

That is the entire logic of procedure qualification, and understanding it makes the rest of this chapter follow naturally. Everything a qualification system does — essential variables, ranges of qualification, welder testing, consumable control, records — exists to make the demonstrated result transferable from a test coupon to a production joint.

2. The Document Chain: WPS, pWPS, PQR

Three documents, produced in a specific order:

The pWPS (preliminary Welding Procedure Specification) is the proposed recipe: material, thickness, joint design, process, consumable, gas, position, current and voltage ranges, travel speed, preheat and interpass temperature, post-weld heat treatment, and technique. It is a proposal. Nothing may be produced against it.

The PQR (Procedure Qualification Record) is the evidence. A test coupon is welded following the pWPS; the actual values used are recorded — the values used, not the ranges proposed — and the coupon is tested destructively. The PQR records both what was done and what the tests showed. It is a historical record of a single event and is never revised.

The WPS (Welding Procedure Specification) is the production instruction, issued once the PQR shows acceptable results. It states ranges rather than single values, and those ranges are limited by what the PQR supports.

The relationship in one sentence: the PQR proves what happened once; the WPS states what may be done in production; the range between them is set by the code's essential variable rules.

A fourth document belongs in the chain in ISO practice: the WPQR (Welding Procedure Qualification Record), which serves the same evidential role as the ASME PQR. The terminology differs; the function does not.

3. Essential, Supplementary Essential and Non-Essential Variables

Every qualification system classifies welding variables by how much a change to them affects the properties the test demonstrated.

Essential variables. A change requires requalification — a new coupon and new tests. These are variables that materially affect mechanical properties: the welding process, the base material group, the filler metal group, thickness beyond the qualified range, and (in some systems) preheat reduction or post-weld heat treatment changes.

Supplementary essential variables. These apply only when notch toughness is a requirement of the application. Because toughness is more sensitive to thermal history than strength is, variables that need not be requalified for a strength-only application do require it when impact testing is specified — heat input, position, and progression among them. A shop that adds a toughness requirement to an existing procedure has not merely added a test; it has activated a whole extra class of variables.

Non-essential variables. A change requires only that the WPS be revised — no requalification. Joint detail within limits, and minor technique changes, typically fall here.

The classification is not a matter of opinion. Each system publishes its own tables assigning every variable to a class, per process. The classifications differ between systems, which is why a change that is non-essential under one code can be essential under another, and why "we've always treated that as a minor change" is not a defence when the governing code says otherwise.

4. The ASME Section IX Approach

ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section IX governs welding, brazing and fusing qualification for pressure equipment and is referenced far beyond the pressure sector [S1].

Its structural features:

• No prequalification exists. Every procedure must be supported by a PQR. There is no route by which a procedure may be used without a qualification test behind it.

• Variables are tabulated per process in the QW-250 series, each classified as essential, supplementary essential or non-essential.

• Materials are grouped by P-number, with Group numbers subdividing P-numbers where toughness matters. Qualification on one material generally qualifies others in the same P-number, which is what makes the system economical.

• Filler metals are grouped by F-number (grouped by usability characteristics) and A-number (grouped by deposit chemistry).

• Thickness ranges are defined by tables relating the test coupon thickness to the production thickness range qualified.

• Welder qualification is separate from procedure qualification and is covered in the QW-300 series (Chapter 32).

The system's character is that it is evidence-based and unforgiving of shortcuts — but generous in its grouping, so a modest number of well-chosen qualifications can cover a wide production range. Qualification strategy under ASME IX is a real engineering exercise: choosing test coupon thickness, material and process to maximize the production range covered per test.

5. The ISO 15607 Family and Its Five Qualification Routes

The ISO system is structured as a family of standards rather than a single document, and it offers something the other two do not: more than one route to a qualified procedure [S2].

| Standard | Role |
| --- | --- |
| ISO 15607 | General rules; defines the framework and the available qualification routes |
| ISO 15609 (parts by process) | Content and format of the WPS itself — Part 1 arc, Part 2 gas, Part 3 electron beam, Part 4 laser, Part 5 resistance, Part 6 hybrid laser-arc |
| ISO 15610 | Qualification based on tested welding consumables |
| ISO 15611 | Qualification based on previous welding experience |
| ISO 15612 | Qualification by adoption of a standard welding procedure |
| ISO 15613 | Qualification based on a pre-production welding test |
| ISO 15614 (parts by process) | Qualification by welding procedure test — the principal route |

The five routes, with the practical distinction between them:

1. Welding procedure test (ISO 15614). The full test coupon route, equivalent in principle to an ASME PQR. The most widely used and the most widely accepted.

2. Tested welding consumables (ISO 15610). Relies on the consumable's own certification. Restricted in application, generally to lower-risk work and specific consumable classes.

3. Previous welding experience (ISO 15611). Documented evidence of past production with the same procedure. Requires real records, not assertion.

4. Standard welding procedure (ISO 15612). Adoption of a procedure qualified elsewhere by a qualified body, subject to conditions on the adopting manufacturer.

5. Pre-production welding test (ISO 15613). Used where a standard test coupon cannot represent the production joint — an unusual geometry, a joint that cannot be reproduced as a plate or pipe coupon. The test is made on a representative production-like assembly.

Route 5 is the one most often overlooked and most often the correct answer for complex fabrications. A standard butt-weld coupon does not represent a nozzle-to-shell attachment or a heavily restrained node, and where the joint's real behaviour depends on its geometry, testing that geometry is the technically correct approach.

ISO 15614's own parts follow the process split: Part 1 covers arc and gas welding of steels and nickel alloys, and other parts address aluminium, tube-to-tubesheet joints, beam processes, resistance spot/seam/projection welding, resistance butt and flash welding, and hybrid processes.

6. The AWS D1.1 Approach and the Prequalified Concept

AWS D1.1 governs structural steel welding and introduces a concept the other two systems do not have: prequalification [S3].

A prequalified WPS may be used without a supporting PQR, provided every one of the code's prequalification conditions is met: an approved base metal, an approved filler metal, an approved process, a joint detail taken from the code's prequalified joint details, preheat per the code's table, and all parameters within the code's stated limits.

The logic is that the industry's accumulated evidence for these specific combinations is sufficient, and requiring every fabricator to re-demonstrate them individually adds cost without adding safety.

Its limits are strict and are where fabricators get into trouble:

• Prequalification is all-or-nothing. Departing from any single condition — a different joint detail, a different process, a base metal outside the approved list, a preheat below the table — removes prequalified status entirely, and the procedure then requires qualification by test like any other.

• It does not cover every process or material. Processes and materials outside the code's approved lists must be qualified by test.

• It does not remove the welder qualification requirement. Prequalification applies to the procedure, not to the people.

D1.1 also provides qualification by test for everything outside the prequalified envelope, with its own variable tables and ranges.

7. Where the Three Systems Genuinely Differ

| Aspect | ASME Section IX | ISO 15614 family | AWS D1.1 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Prequalification | Not available | Not available in the same form; ISO 15612 standard procedures are the nearest analogue | Available, subject to strict conditions |
| Alternative qualification routes | Single route: qualification by test | Five routes (ISO 15607) | Prequalified, or qualification by test |
| Material grouping | P-numbers and Group numbers | Material groups per the ISO/TR 15608 grouping system | Approved base metal lists and groups |
| Filler grouping | F-numbers and A-numbers | Consumable classification per the ISO consumable standards | Approved filler metal lists |
| Toughness handling | Supplementary essential variables activate when impact testing is required | Impact testing requirements built into the test coupon requirements | Requirements by application and service category |
| Typical sector | Pressure equipment, piping, boilers | European and international fabrication generally | Structural steel, North American practice |

The most consequential practical difference is the prequalified route in D1.1, because it changes the economics of small structural fabrication entirely — and because a fabricator moving from structural work into pressure work frequently arrives expecting prequalification to exist and finds it does not.

The second most consequential is the range of qualification for a given test, which differs between systems. A procedure qualified under one system is not automatically acceptable under another, and where a project specifies a particular code, qualifications held under a different code generally require review or re-qualification rather than direct transfer.

8. Material Grouping Systems

Grouping exists so that one test can cover many materials. Without it, every grade would require its own qualification and the cost would be prohibitive.

ASME P-numbers group base metals by broadly similar weldability characteristics — composition, weldability and mechanical properties. Group numbers subdivide P-numbers where impact-tested applications demand finer distinction.

ISO material groups, defined in the ISO/TR 15608 grouping system, serve the same purpose with a different structure, organizing steels, aluminium, copper, nickel, titanium and other families into numbered groups and sub-groups.

Two rules govern their use, and both are frequently broken:

1. Qualification on one material in a group generally qualifies others in the same group — but the direction can be restricted. Some systems restrict qualification from a higher-strength to a lower-strength material or vice versa, and the code's own rules govern.

2. Group membership must be established from the material's actual specification, not assumed from a similar name. A grade whose designation resembles another is not necessarily in the same group.

9. Ranges of Qualification: The Four That Matter Most

Thickness. A test coupon qualifies a range of production thicknesses defined by the code's tables, typically extending both above and below the coupon thickness. The rule is asymmetric and non-obvious, which is why the tables exist. Qualification strategy usually involves selecting the coupon thickness that maximizes the qualified range for the production mix.

Diameter (for pipe). Small-diameter coupons generally qualify a limited range; larger coupons qualify more widely, often including all larger diameters. Welding a small-diameter coupon is cheaper and qualifies less.

Position. Positions qualified are determined by the test position, with harder positions qualifying easier ones (Chapter 28, Section 11). This applies to both procedure and welder qualification, with different rules for each.

Heat input (where toughness is required). Where impact testing applies, the heat input used in the test constrains the production range. This is a supplementary essential variable in ASME terms and is the variable most often exceeded in production without anyone noticing, because nothing visible changes.

Two further ranges deserve mention: post-weld heat treatment condition (a procedure qualified with PWHT does not qualify production without it, and the reverse), and preheat (reducing preheat below the qualified value is generally an essential change, while increasing it is usually not — though excessive increase can violate a maximum interpass requirement).

10. The Test Coupon and What Each Test Proves

| Test | What it demonstrates | What it does not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Transverse tensile | The joint's tensile strength meets or exceeds the requirement; identifies the weakest location by where it breaks | Toughness, hardness, or freedom from internal defects elsewhere in the joint |
| Bend test (face, root, side) | Soundness and ductility; opens up lack of fusion, cracks and inclusions on the tension surface | Strength or toughness numerically |
| Impact (Charpy) test | Notch toughness at a specified temperature, at specified notch locations (weld metal, fusion line, HAZ positions) | Behaviour anywhere other than at the notch positions tested |
| Macro examination | Fusion profile, penetration, HAZ extent, and gross discontinuities in one section | Anything outside the plane of that single section |
| Hardness survey | Peak hardness in the weld metal and HAZ against a specified ceiling | Toughness directly, though it correlates |
| Non-destructive testing of the coupon | Absence of detectable discontinuities before destructive testing | Properties of any kind |
| Corrosion testing (where specified) | Resistance to a specific mechanism in a specific medium | General corrosion performance |

The impact test deserves particular attention because of its notch positions. Toughness is tested at specific locations — commonly the weld centreline and one or more positions in the heat-affected zone at defined distances from the fusion line. Those positions are chosen to interrogate the coarse-grained heat-affected zone (Chapter 22, Section 7), which is normally the toughest region to satisfy. A test that samples the wrong location can pass a joint whose critical region would have failed.

11. What Invalidates a Qualification

A qualification ceases to cover production when any of these occur:

• The process changes — including changes that look minor, such as solid wire to metal-cored wire (Chapter 21, Section 16).

• The base material moves outside the qualified group, or a substitution is made without checking group membership.

• The filler metal classification changes outside the qualified group.

• Thickness or diameter moves outside the qualified range.

• Position moves outside the qualified positions.

• The shielding gas group changes.

• Preheat is reduced below the qualified minimum, or PWHT condition changes.

• Heat input exceeds the qualified range, where toughness is a requirement.

• The joint design changes beyond what the code permits as non-essential.

The uncomfortable operational reality is that most of these can happen silently. A gas supply substitution, a consumable substitution during a shortage, a production drift toward higher deposition rates, or a thickness change on a revised drawing — none of them announce themselves, and none of them are visible in the finished weld. This is why the quality-system requirements of Chapter 33 exist, and why they concentrate on controls at the points where those substitutions happen rather than on inspecting welds afterwards.

12. Qualification for Non-Arc Processes

The same framework applies to processes outside arc welding, with process-specific variables:

• Resistance welding (Volume 1, Chapter 8; ISO 15614-12) qualifies current, time, force, electrode geometry and material stack rather than voltage and travel speed.

• Beam processes (ISO 15614-11) qualify beam power, focus position, travel speed, working distance and vacuum condition.

• Friction stir welding of aluminium is qualified under ISO 25239-4, with tool geometry, rotation speed, traverse speed and plunge depth as the controlled variables [S4].

• Brazing is qualified under its own provisions in ASME Section IX and in the ISO brazing standards, with joint clearance, filler, flux, atmosphere and temperature cycle as variables.

The transferable principle across all of them: the qualification controls whatever variables that process uses to deliver energy and control the joint. The variables differ; the logic is identical.

13. Decision Reference: Choosing a Qualification Route

| Situation | Route |
| --- | --- |
| Structural steel, common material and process, standard joint detail, AWS D1.1 governs | Prequalified WPS, if every condition is met without exception |
| Structural steel, anything outside the prequalified envelope | Qualification by test to D1.1 |
| Pressure equipment under ASME | PQR by test; no alternative exists |
| European or international fabrication, standard joint | ISO 15614 welding procedure test |
| Joint geometry that a standard coupon cannot represent | ISO 15613 pre-production welding test |
| Well-documented history of the same procedure in production | ISO 15611 previous experience, if the records genuinely support it |
| Dissimilar metal joint | Qualification by test representing the actual pairing; no grouping shortcut applies |
| New material grade with no group assignment | Qualification by test; establish grouping with the material supplier first |

14. Failure Catalog: Qualification Problems and What They Mean

| Problem | Meaning | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tensile test breaks in the weld metal below requirement | Filler undermatched or deposit chemistry wrong for the requirement | Review filler selection and dilution; verify the consumable actually used |
| Tensile breaks in the HAZ below requirement | HAZ softening — typical of Q&T, TMCP and AHSS material welded above the heat input ceiling | Reduce heat input and interpass; requalify within the producer's limits (Chapter 23) |
| Bend test opens a defect | Lack of fusion, inclusion or crack revealed by the tension surface | Investigate as a welding defect; the procedure as written did not produce a sound joint |
| Impact test fails at the fusion line | Coarse-grained HAZ toughness inadequate at the test temperature | Reduce heat input; reconsider consumable toughness class; check interpass control |
| Hardness exceeds the specified ceiling | Cooling too fast: insufficient preheat, low heat input, heavy section | Increase preheat first; then heat input within limits (Chapter 34) |
| Macro shows incomplete root penetration | Joint preparation or root technique inadequate as specified | Correct the preparation dimensions or root process; requalify (Chapter 28) |
| Production parameters found outside the WPS range | The work is not covered by the qualification | Stop, assess the affected population, decide between requalification and rework; do not retrospectively widen the WPS |
| WPS ranges wider than the PQR supports | The WPS was written beyond its evidence | Correct the WPS to the ranges the code permits from that PQR; reassess work performed under the incorrect ranges |

15. Worked Example: A WPS That Did Not Cover the Work Being Done

Situation. A fabricator holds a qualified WPS for a butt weld in 12 mm plate, qualified by test on a 12 mm coupon in the flat position, with impact testing required by the project. Production drawings are revised and the plate becomes 20 mm. The site supervisor notes the WPS is "for the same material and process" and continues. Two months later a third-party audit questions it.

Step 1 — Establish what the qualification actually covers, from the PQR and the code table, not from the WPS header. The qualified thickness range is set by the code's table against the coupon thickness. Whether 20 mm falls inside that range is a table lookup, and it is the first question — not an opinion about similarity.

Step 2 — Check position separately. The coupon was welded in the flat position. If any production welding on the 20 mm plate was done in another position, the position range is a second, independent question with its own answer, and both must be satisfied.

Step 3 — Check what the toughness requirement activates. Because impact testing is a project requirement, the supplementary essential variables are live. Heat input used in production must lie within what the PQR supports, and on 20 mm plate a welder will naturally use higher currents and more passes than on 12 mm. Recorded production parameters must be compared against the qualified range, and if they were not recorded, that absence is itself a finding.

Step 4 — Check preheat. The heavier section changes the cooling rate, and the preheat requirement for 20 mm may exceed what the 12 mm procedure specified (Chapter 34). A procedure qualified at one preheat does not automatically cover production at a lower one, and the code's preheat requirements are thickness-dependent regardless of the qualification question.

Step 5 — Determine the affected population. Everything welded on the 20 mm material since the drawing revision is potentially uncovered work. Bounding that population requires production records tying joints to dates, WPS references and material. If those records do not exist, the population cannot be bounded and the exposure is the whole period.

Step 6 — Choose between the available responses honestly. There are three: qualify a new procedure covering 20 mm and demonstrate by testing that the work already done meets requirements; perform additional testing on the completed work sufficient to demonstrate acceptability; or remove and rework. Which is appropriate depends on the code, the client and the criticality. What is not available is retrospectively widening the WPS to match what was done — a WPS cannot be amended to cover work already performed outside it.

Step 7 — Identify the control that failed. The technical error was a thickness range check. The system failure is that a drawing revision changed a welding-relevant parameter without triggering a review of the applicable WPS. The corrective action is a change-control step linking drawing revisions to welding procedure review — which is a documented requirement of the quality-requirement standards in Chapter 33, and its absence is the real finding.

16. Known Gaps

• No thickness, diameter or position qualification ranges are tabulated. They are code-specific, edition-specific, and reproducing them here would risk both misapplication across codes and error on revision. The principle and the variables are explained; the tables belong to the code in force.

• P-numbers, F-numbers, A-numbers and ISO material group numbers are described but not listed. These are extensive tables in the purchased codes.

• The ISO 15614 part structure is described in outline. Part numbering and scopes should be confirmed against the current editions, which are revised on their own cycles.

• No comparison is offered on which system is "stricter." They are differently structured and a valid comparison depends on the specific joint, material and application; general claims either way are unreliable.

• Prequalification conditions are not reproduced. They are extensive and cumulative in AWS D1.1, and the code's own text is the only safe source.
