1. Procedure Qualification and Welder Qualification Prove Different Things

These two are constantly confused, and the distinction is simple once stated.

Procedure qualification (Chapter 31) proves that a set of welding conditions produces a joint with the required properties. Its tests are property tests: tensile, impact, hardness, macro. It is welded by a competent welder precisely so that welder skill is not the variable under examination.

Welder qualification proves that a specific person can produce a sound weld using a given process in a given configuration. Its tests are soundness tests: bend tests, radiography, fracture tests. It does not test tensile strength or toughness, because those are properties of the procedure, not of the person.

Both are required. A qualified welder working to an unqualified procedure produces sound welds whose properties are unknown. A qualified procedure welded by an unqualified welder produces welds whose properties would be right if the joint were sound, and nobody has demonstrated that it will be.

2. The Essential Variables for a Welder

A welder qualification covers a defined range, and changes to certain variables take production outside it. Under ISO 9606-1, the variables that trigger requalification include the welding process, the material group beyond the approved scope, the filler metal designation where it affects properties, the shielding gas type for metallurgically sensitive processes, thickness outside the approved band, pipe outside diameter beyond the qualified range, and welding position outside those covered [S2].

The underlying logic is worth understanding rather than memorizing, because it explains what is and is not on the list. The variables that matter for a welder are the ones that change the manual skill required. Position changes the skill; the material's precise alloy content largely does not, which is why materials are grouped broadly for welder qualification. Process changes the skill fundamentally, which is why it is always essential. Backing changes it substantially, because welding an open root without backing is a different skill from filling a groove onto a solid backing bar.

This also explains a distinction that surprises people: welder qualification material grouping is broader than procedure qualification grouping, because the welder is being tested on manipulation rather than on metallurgy.

3. Range of Approval: Thickness

The test coupon thickness determines the production thickness range the welder may weld. Under ISO 9606-1 the ranges are banded by test thickness, with the general pattern that a test on material of thickness *t* qualifies from a stated minimum up to 2t [S2].

For example, a test on a 12 mm plate butt weld gives a range of approval from 3 mm to 24 mm [S2].

Two practical consequences:

Testing thicker qualifies more. A shop that tests everyone on thin material to save consumables and time will find its welders unqualified for the heavier work in the same production mix.

The lower bound is real. A qualification on heavy plate does not automatically extend down to sheet thicknesses, because thin material is a genuinely different manipulation problem — the risk changes from lack of fusion to burn-through.

4. Range of Approval: Pipe Diameter

Pipe qualification adds diameter as a variable, because welding a small-bore pipe is a substantially different manipulation problem from welding a large-diameter one — the torch angle changes continuously around a small circumference and access is restricted.

Under ISO 9606-1 the pattern is that small-diameter tests qualify a limited band around the tested diameter, while tests above a certain diameter qualify without an upper limit [S2]. Larger test pieces therefore qualify more broadly, and the same logic as thickness applies: testing on the smallest available pipe is the cheapest test and the narrowest qualification.

A related rule that catches fabricators out: plate qualification and pipe qualification are not freely interchangeable. Depending on the system and the diameter involved, a pipe test may qualify plate work while the reverse does not, precisely because the pipe test is the harder manipulation.

5. Range of Approval: Position, and Why PE and H-L045 Matter

Position is the variable with the widest leverage, because harder positions qualify easier ones. Under ISO 9606-1 the coverage pattern runs approximately as follows [S2]:

| Test position | Positions covered |
| --- | --- |
| PA (flat) | PA only |
| PB (horizontal-vertical fillet) | PA, PB |
| PC (horizontal butt) | PA, PC |
| PF (vertical up) | PA, PB, PC, PF |
| PE (overhead) | PA, PB, PC, PD, PE |
| H-L045 (fixed inclined pipe) | Full position coverage |

Two conclusions follow directly and they are the practical heart of qualification planning:

PE (overhead) gives the broadest single-test coverage for plate [S2]. A shop testing welders in PA is buying the narrowest possible qualification for the same consumable cost and the same test administration.

H-L045 — the fixed inclined pipe position, corresponding to 6G in the AWS designation system — gives the broadest coverage available. This is why 6G is the benchmark pipe welder test across the industry: a single weld demonstrates capability through flat, vertical, horizontal and overhead in one continuous joint.

The planning conclusion is that choosing the test position is a production planning decision with a direct financial consequence, not an administrative default. The cost difference between testing in PA and testing in PE is small; the difference in what the welder may then legally weld is large.

6. The Other Range Variables: Backing, Progression, Filler and Gas

Backing. Welding with backing and welding an open root without backing are separately qualified in the general case, and the direction matters: a test without backing normally qualifies work with backing, while the reverse does not, because the open root is the harder skill.

Progression. Vertical-up and vertical-down are distinct (Chapter 28, Section 10). A welder qualified vertical-down is not thereby qualified vertical-up, and the two produce different penetration and different deposit thickness per pass.

Filler metal group. Consumables are grouped for welder qualification by their operating characteristics rather than by their exact chemistry — a rutile electrode and a basic low-hydrogen electrode handle differently and are treated as different, while two basic electrodes of slightly different alloy content are not.

Shielding gas. Treated as essential where it materially changes handling or where the material is metallurgically sensitive [S2].

Whether filler is used at all. Welding with filler and welding autogenously are different skills, and qualification in one does not cover the other.

7. How a Qualification Is Tested

The test coupon is welded under supervision, to an approved WPS, and is then examined. Typical examination methods:

• Visual examination first, always. A coupon failing visual acceptance criteria is failed without further testing.

• Bend testing — face, root or side bends depending on thickness and joint type. Bends open lack of fusion, cracks and inclusions on the tension surface, which makes them a direct soundness test.

• Radiographic testing as an alternative to bend testing in many systems, subject to conditions on process and material — radiography is poor at detecting tightly closed planar defects, so its use as a substitute is restricted for processes prone to lack of fusion.

• Fracture testing for fillet weld tests, breaking the joint open to expose the root for examination.

• Macro examination for fillet welds and some configurations, to check root fusion and profile.

The examiner and the examining body matter: qualification is normally witnessed and certified by an independent examiner or an authorized third party, depending on the code and the contract, and a certificate issued without the required witnessing is not valid regardless of the welding.

8. Validity, Continuity and the Certificate That Expired Without Anyone Noticing

This is where most welder qualification non-conformances are found in audits, and the reason is that a certificate carries a printed date while the condition that actually invalidates it is invisible.

Two separate mechanisms operate:

Continuity. A qualification lapses if the welder has not used the process within a defined interval — a documented gap of six months or more without welding activity in the qualified range requires requalification under ISO 9606-1 practice [S2]. The certificate does not change appearance when this happens. Only the continuity record shows it.

Periodic confirmation. Beyond continuity, the systems require periodic confirmation that the welder is still working within the qualified range and producing acceptable work, documented by the employer or the responsible welding coordinator [S2]. The exact interval and the evidence required vary by standard and edition.

The operational consequences:

• A welder returning from extended absence — illness, secondment, a spell in another role — may have lapsed even though the certificate's printed expiry date is a year away.

• A welder who has been welding continuously but in a different process has lapsed in the unused one.

• Continuity evidence must be records, not recollection. A production record showing the welder's identifier against welds in the qualified range is what satisfies it; a supervisor's confirmation that "he's been welding all year" is not.

This is why welder qualification management is a records problem more than a testing problem, and why the quality-requirement standards of Chapter 33 make personnel records an explicit requirement.

9. Welding Operators and Weld Setters: Mechanized and Automatic Work

A person operating a mechanized or automatic welding system is not doing the same job as a manual welder, and is qualified under a different standard: ISO 14732, covering qualification testing of welding operators and weld setters for mechanized and automatic welding of metallic materials [S3].

The distinction the standard draws is between:

• The welding operator, who operates equipment that performs the weld, monitors it, and responds to deviations.

• The weld setter, who sets up and adjusts the equipment but may not operate it during welding.

What is tested is correspondingly different from a manual welder test. The relevant competence is not manipulation of an electrode but the ability to set up the equipment correctly, verify that the settings match the WPS, recognize when the process is deviating, and respond appropriately. For robotic welding this includes program verification and the ability to identify a drift in the process (Chapter 69).

Two implications commonly missed:

1. A qualified manual welder is not automatically a qualified welding operator, and a robot cell staffed by highly skilled manual welders is not thereby staffed by qualified operators.

2. Automation does not remove the personnel qualification requirement; it changes which standard applies. A shop that automates and disbands its welder qualification programme has substituted one requirement for another, not eliminated it.

10. Welding Coordination Personnel

Above the welder and the operator sits the welding coordinator, whose responsibilities are defined in ISO 14731 [S4]. This is a requirement of the quality-requirement standards (Chapter 33) rather than an optional role.

The coordinator's tasks span the entire welding activity: reviewing contract requirements for weldability and feasibility, ensuring materials and consumables are correct and correctly stored, ensuring procedures are qualified and personnel are qualified and current, supervising production welding, and handling non-conformance. The standard defines both the tasks and responsibilities and the technical knowledge levels appropriate to different levels of responsibility.

The practical importance for a fabricator: assigning a responsible welding coordinator with defined, documented tasks and demonstrable technical knowledge is an auditable requirement for organizations working to the comprehensive quality-requirement level, and "the welding supervisor handles that" without documented tasks, competence evidence and delegated authority is a common audit finding.

11. The Three Systems Compared

| Aspect | ISO 9606 series | ASME Section IX | AWS D1.1 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scope | ISO 9606-1 steels; further parts for aluminium, copper, nickel, titanium/zirconium | All materials within one section | Structural steel |
| Test approach | Test coupon, ranges of approval tabulated per variable | Performance qualification with essential variables per process | Test coupon with code-specified ranges |
| Continuity | Documented activity requirement with defined interval; lapse requires requalification | Continuity requirement with periodic use; qualification maintained by documented use | Code-specified; maintained by continued employment and use |
| Operators | ISO 14732 (separate standard) | Covered within Section IX | Covered within the code |
| Coordination personnel | ISO 14731 (separate standard) | Not addressed in the same terms | Addressed through the code's inspection provisions |

Qualifications do not transfer between systems automatically. A welder qualified to ISO 9606-1 is not thereby qualified under ASME Section IX, and a project specifying one system requires qualifications held under it. This is a routine and expensive discovery for fabricators moving between sectors or markets, and it should be established at tender stage rather than at first inspection.

12. Decision Reference: Designing a Qualification Programme

| Objective | Approach |
| --- | --- |
| Maximize plate coverage from one test | Test in PE (overhead), on the heaviest thickness in the production mix |
| Maximize pipe coverage from one test | Test in H-L045 / 6G, on a diameter above the unlimited-coverage threshold |
| Cover both open-root and backed work | Test without backing — it covers backed work, not the reverse |
| Cover both vertical-up and vertical-down | Test both; one does not cover the other |
| Cover multiple processes | Separate qualification per process; no process substitutes for another |
| Minimize requalification churn | Track continuity actively with production records rather than reacting to expiry dates |
| Automate a cell | Qualify operators to ISO 14732; do not assume manual welder qualifications transfer |
| Satisfy a comprehensive quality-requirement level | Appoint and document a responsible welding coordinator per ISO 14731 |

13. Failure Catalog: Welder Qualification Problems

| Problem | Cause | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Certificate in date but qualification invalid | Continuity lapse — six months or more without documented welding in the qualified range | Requalify; institute continuity tracking from production records |
| Welder working outside thickness range | Production thickness above 2t of the test coupon, or below the qualified minimum | Stop; assess affected work; requalify on appropriate thickness |
| Welder working outside position range | Production position not covered by the test position | Stop; assess affected work; retest in a position that covers the production mix |
| Open-root work done on a backed qualification | Backing treated as a non-essential variable | Requalify without backing; assess affected roots specifically, since the root is where the skill difference shows |
| Vertical-down used on a vertical-up qualification | Progression treated as a technique preference | Requalify; check the affected welds for lack of fusion, the characteristic vertical-down defect on thick material |
| Robot cell staffed by unqualified operators | Manual welder qualifications assumed to transfer | Qualify to ISO 14732 |
| No documented welding coordinator | Role assumed rather than assigned | Appoint, document the tasks and responsibilities, and evidence the technical knowledge per ISO 14731 |
| Qualification not accepted on a new project | Held under a different code system than the project specifies | Establish the required system at tender stage; requalify under the specified code |
| Bend test failure at retest | Genuine skill gap, or an unsuitable WPS given to the welder for the test | Distinguish the two before retraining — a coupon welded to a marginal procedure fails for procedure reasons |

14. Worked Example: A Certificate That Did Not Cover the Production Work

Situation. A pressure pipework contractor is audited. A welder's certificate is produced, in date, showing qualification on a 6 mm wall, 60 mm outside diameter pipe butt weld in the PF position, GTAW root with SMAW fill. Production records show the same welder completed joints on 10 mm wall, 200 mm diameter pipe over the preceding three months. The contractor's position is that the certificate is valid and current.

Step 1 — Check thickness first, because it is the simplest calculation. A test at 6 mm gives a range of approval to 2t, or 12 mm [S2]. Production at 10 mm falls inside that. Thickness is satisfied, and establishing this early prevents the investigation from chasing the wrong variable.

Step 2 — Check diameter. The test was on 60 mm outside diameter. Under the ISO 9606-1 diameter banding, a test in the mid-diameter band qualifies from a fraction of the tested diameter upward without an upper limit [S2]. Whether 200 mm production falls inside the range is a table lookup against the specific band — and this is the check that most often passes, since larger diameters are generally easier.

Step 3 — Check position, which is where the problem usually is. The test was PF, vertical up on a fixed pipe. PF covers PA, PB, PC and PF [S2]. A 200 mm fixed pipe joint welded in position requires welding through the overhead sector — PE — which PF does not cover. Unless the production pipe was rotated so that welding was performed in the flat position throughout, the work was outside the qualification.

Step 4 — Establish whether the pipe was rotated. This is a factual question about production practice, and it decides the case. Rotated pipe welding (equivalent to 1G) is genuinely covered by a PF qualification. Fixed pipe welding is not. Production records, fit-up records or interviews with the supervisor should establish it, and the answer determines the scope of the problem.

Step 5 — Check the process combination separately. The certificate covers a GTAW root and SMAW fill combination. If production used a different fill process — flux-cored, for example, introduced for productivity — that is a process change and is essential regardless of everything above.

Step 6 — Check continuity for the period, not just the expiry date. Even where the ranges are satisfied, the qualification requires documented activity in the qualified range within the continuity interval [S2]. Three months of continuous production satisfies it for this period, but the months preceding the certificate's most recent confirmation should be checked as well.

Step 7 — Bound the affected work and choose a response. If the position range was exceeded, every fixed-position joint welded by that welder in the period is affected. The available responses are additional non-destructive testing sufficient to demonstrate acceptability of the completed work, or removal and rework, alongside immediate requalification in a position covering the production mix. Retrospective reinterpretation of the certificate is not available.

Step 8 — Fix the system. The failure is that production allocation did not check the welder's qualified range against the joint being assigned. The corrective action is a control at the point of allocation — a qualification matrix that supervisors check when assigning work — rather than an instruction to be more careful, and it belongs in the welding coordinator's documented responsibilities under ISO 14731 [S4].

15. Known Gaps

• The ranges in Sections 3 to 5 are summarized from published guidance on ISO 9606-1 [S2] and are given to explain the structure and the planning consequences. The exact bands, conditions and exceptions are in the standard itself, which is the only safe source for a specific case.

• Validity and continuity intervals are described in principle. The published guidance used here documents the continuity requirement and the employer confirmation requirement but does not fully resolve the validity period, and the standard's own current edition governs. ISO 9606-1:2012 is the edition on the ISO catalogue, with a revision noted as under preparation by the responsible committee [S1].

• ASME and AWS ranges are not tabulated. They differ from the ISO ranges and from each other, and each code's own tables govern.

• Nothing here addresses examiner or examining body accreditation, which is set by contract, by national regulation and by the applicable scheme.

• Parts of the ISO 9606 series beyond Part 1 are named but not detailed. Aluminium, copper, nickel and titanium/zirconium welder qualification each have their own part with their own ranges.

1. The Special Process Argument, and What Follows From It

A special process is one whose output cannot be fully verified by subsequent inspection or testing of the product. Welding is the textbook example (Chapter 31, Section 1): non-destructive testing finds discontinuities but measures no property, and the properties that matter — toughness, hardness distribution, corrosion resistance, resistance to hydrogen cracking — are only measurable by destroying the joint.

Everything in a welding quality system follows from that single fact. If the product cannot be verified, then confidence has to come from controlling every input that determines the outcome and from evidence that those controls were in force at the time the weld was made. That is why a welding quality system concerns itself with things that appear peripheral to welding — where consumables were stored, whether the calibration of a preheat thermometer is current, whether the person who welded a joint can be identified six months later.

The failure mode this guards against is specific and common: a fabricator with excellent welders and good equipment producing a batch of defective work because one input changed silently, and having no way afterwards to establish which joints were affected. Inspection cannot recover that situation. Records can.

2. The ISO 3834 Family and What Each Part Is For

ISO 3834 sets quality requirements for fusion welding of metallic materials [S1][S2]. It is structured as a family:

| Part | Role |
| --- | --- |
| ISO 3834-1 | Criteria for the selection of the appropriate level of quality requirements |
| ISO 3834-2 | Comprehensive quality requirements |
| ISO 3834-3 | Standard quality requirements |
| ISO 3834-4 | Elementary quality requirements |
| ISO 3834-5 | Documents with which it is necessary to conform to claim conformity to Parts 2, 3 or 4 |
| ISO 3834-6 | Guidance on implementing ISO 3834 |

The three levels are not three different standards; they are three depths of the same requirement set. The comprehensive level (Part 2) requires the full set; the standard level (Part 3) requires a reduced set; the elementary level (Part 4) requires the least. Part 5 is the practical companion, because it lists the other standards a fabricator must also conform to — procedure qualification, welder qualification, welding coordination — in order to claim conformity to any of the three.

A point that is frequently misunderstood: ISO 3834 is not a quality management system standard in the sense that ISO 9001 is. It does not replace a QMS and does not require one. It is a set of welding-specific requirements that can be implemented inside an existing QMS or independently.

3. Choosing a Level: The Selection Criteria

Part 1 provides criteria for the selection [S1], and the choice is a technical judgement rather than a commercial preference. The considerations:

• The extent and significance of safety-critical products. A pressure vessel, a lifting structure or a load-bearing building frame carries consequences that a decorative railing does not.

• The complexity of manufacture. Simple repetitive joints in one material differ from a mixed-material fabrication with many joint types.

• The range of products manufactured, and how often the fabricator moves between materials and processes.

• The range of materials used, and their metallurgical difficulty.

• The extent to which metallurgical problems may occur — crack sensitivity, heat-affected zone property loss, corrosion behaviour.

• The extent to which manufacturing imperfections affect product performance — whether a discontinuity would be an appearance issue or a failure initiation site.

Frequently the level is not chosen by the fabricator at all: a product standard or a contract specifies it (Section 8). Where it is genuinely open, the honest question is what would happen if a joint failed, and the answer usually settles the level quickly.

4. The Requirement Areas in Full

The comprehensive level addresses, in substance, the following areas. Reading them as a list makes clear how much of welding quality lies outside the arc:

| Requirement area | What must be demonstrated |
| --- | --- |
| Review of requirements | The contract's welding requirements were identified and understood before acceptance |
| Technical review | The fabricator assessed feasibility — materials, processes, qualification, capability — against those requirements |
| Sub-contracting | Sub-contracted welding, NDT or heat treatment is controlled and the sub-contractor meets the same requirements |
| Welders and operators | Qualified, current, and working within their range (Chapter 32) |
| Welding coordination personnel | Appointed, with defined tasks, responsibilities and demonstrable technical knowledge |
| Inspection and testing personnel | Qualified to the relevant scheme for the method they perform |
| Equipment | Suitable for the work, listed, and maintained |
| Equipment maintenance | Planned maintenance carried out and recorded, including welding plant and heat treatment equipment |
| Production planning | Sequence, process, procedures and inspection defined before work starts |
| Welding procedure specifications | Available at the workstation, in the right revision, covering the work being done |
| Qualification of welding procedures | Valid qualifications supporting every WPS in use (Chapter 31) |
| Batch testing of consumables | Where required by the contract or the product standard |
| Storage and handling of consumables | Per the manufacturer's requirements, with exposure control for low-hydrogen products (Chapter 29) |
| Storage of parent material | Protected from damage and deterioration, identity maintained |
| Post-weld heat treatment | Procedure, records, calibrated equipment, verified thermal cycle (Chapter 34) |
| Inspection and testing before, during and after welding | Defined, performed at the right stage, and recorded |
| Non-conformance and corrective action | Identified, dispositioned, corrected, and the cause addressed |
| Calibration and validation | Measuring and testing equipment calibrated, including thermometers, flow meters and welding machine instrumentation where used for control |
| Identification and traceability | As required by the contract — see Section 6 |
| Quality records | Retained for the specified period and retrievable |

5. Requirements That Fail Audits Most Often

Across audits, findings cluster in a small number of areas — and they are rarely the technically hardest ones:

Consumable storage and exposure control. Ovens present but no records; quivers with no time limit enforced; opened packets on benches. This is a first-order technical control (Chapter 23, Section 5) that fabricators routinely treat as housekeeping.

Welder continuity records. Certificates in date but no evidence of continued activity in the qualified range (Chapter 32, Section 8).

WPS availability at the workstation. Procedures held in the office, not at the arc, in the wrong revision, or not covering the joint being welded.

Calibration of temperature measurement. Preheat and interpass temperatures controlled with uncalibrated contact thermometers or with indicating crayons whose specification is not recorded.

Welding coordination. The role assumed by a supervisor with no documented tasks, no delegated authority and no evidence of technical knowledge.

Traceability. No means of connecting a completed weld to the welder, the consumable batch, the WPS revision and the heat treatment record.

Technical review evidence. Contract accepted without documented assessment of whether the fabricator could actually meet the welding requirements — which is a real engineering step, not a formality, and its absence is how a shop ends up discovering mid-project that it cannot qualify for what it agreed to do.

6. Traceability: What It Means in Practice

Traceability is the ability to connect a completed weld to the conditions under which it was made. The elements normally required:

• Which welder or operator made the joint.

• Which WPS revision was in force.

• Which consumable batch was used.

• Which parent material heat or cast the joint was made in.

• What heat treatment the joint received, and the record of that cycle.

• What inspection was performed, by whom, and with what result.

Its purpose is bounding. When a consumable batch is found defective, when a welder's qualification is found to have lapsed, when a heat treatment furnace is found to have been out of calibration, the question is always the same: which welds are affected? With traceability, the answer is a list. Without it, the answer is the whole period, and the cost difference between those two answers is the entire business case for traceability.

The level of traceability required is set by the contract and the product standard — it ranges from batch-level for general fabrication to individual weld identification with a marked location on an as-built drawing for pressure and safety-critical work. Volume 1, Chapter 17 develops the equivalent for resistance welding, where the traceability record is generated automatically by the controller.

7. The Relationship to ISO 9001 and to Product Codes

Three documents can apply simultaneously and are frequently confused:

ISO 9001 is a general management system standard. It requires that special processes be controlled but does not say how to control welding specifically.

ISO 3834 supplies the welding-specific requirements. It can be implemented within an ISO 9001 system or standalone. Certification to ISO 3834 is available and is commonly required commercially.

The product code — a pressure code, a structural code, a sector standard — sets the technical requirements for the product: acceptance criteria, qualification requirements, inspection extent. It takes precedence on technical matters.

The clean mental model: the product code says what the weld must be; ISO 3834 says what the organization must have in place to produce it reliably; ISO 9001 says how the organization manages itself generally.

8. Execution Classes and How They Select a Quality Level

In structural steelwork, the quality level is not chosen by the fabricator — it is derived from the execution class assigned to the structure, which is determined at design stage from consequence of failure, service category (static or fatigue-loaded) and production category.

The general pattern in European structural practice is that higher execution classes require higher ISO 3834 levels: the lowest class corresponds to the elementary level, intermediate classes to the standard level, and the higher classes — those covering structures with severe consequences of failure or fatigue loading — to the comprehensive level.

Two consequences for a fabricator:

1. The execution class arrives with the design, and a fabricator quoting work at a class above its certification level is quoting work it cannot legally deliver. This belongs in the technical review at tender stage (Section 4).

2. Moving up an execution class is not a paperwork exercise. It brings additional qualification, inspection extent, traceability and coordination requirements, and the lead time to implement them is measured in months.

9. Welding Coordination as the Load-Bearing Requirement

Among the requirement areas, welding coordination is the one that makes the others work. The coordinator, whose tasks and responsibilities are defined in ISO 14731 (Chapter 32, Section 10), is the person who reviews requirements before acceptance, confirms procedures and personnel are adequate, checks consumables and materials, supervises production, and handles non-conformance.

Where this role is genuinely staffed with defined authority, the other requirements tend to be satisfied because someone owns them. Where it is nominal, the failure pattern is consistent: the technical review is not documented because nobody was responsible for it, consumable control drifts because nobody enforces it, and qualification lapses go unnoticed because nobody tracks them.

The auditable elements are specific: an appointment in writing, a defined task list with delegated authority, evidence of technical knowledge appropriate to the responsibility level, and evidence that the coordinator actually performed the tasks — signatures on technical reviews, on procedure approvals, on non-conformance dispositions.

12. Worked Example: A Fabricator Failing an ISO 3834-2 Surveillance Audit

Situation. A structural fabricator certified to the comprehensive level receives three major findings at surveillance: low-hydrogen electrodes found loose on benches, welder continuity records absent, and one WPS in use at a workstation superseded two revisions earlier. Management's initial response is to issue an instruction to supervisors to be more diligent.

Step 1 — Recognize that the three findings share a cause. Each one is a control that requires someone to own it day to day. Electrode issue and return, continuity tracking, and controlled document distribution are all coordinator functions. Three findings in three different areas with the same character point at the coordination role, not at three independent lapses of diligence.

Step 2 — Assess the technical exposure of each finding, not just the paperwork. Uncontrolled electrode exposure is a live hydrogen-cracking risk on every joint welded in that period (Chapter 23), particularly at heavier thicknesses and higher restraint. Absent continuity records mean qualification status is unknown rather than invalid, but the burden of proof sits with the fabricator. A superseded WPS means work was performed against a procedure that has since been changed, and what changed determines whether the work is acceptable.

Step 3 — Bound each exposure using whatever traceability exists. For the electrodes: which joints were welded with material from the affected period, and of those, which are at thickness and restraint where cracking risk is real. For the WPS: what changed between the revisions — if the change was editorial the exposure is documentation only; if it changed preheat, consumable or heat input, it is technical.

Step 4 — Decide the disposition for the technical exposure honestly. Options are additional inspection targeted at the credible defect (delayed magnetic particle inspection for hydrogen cracking on the affected joints), engineering assessment, or rework. The choice depends on the assessed risk and the client's requirements, and the assessment must be documented.

Step 5 — Reject the proposed corrective action. "Instruct supervisors to be more diligent" addresses none of the three findings' causes and would be rejected by any competent auditor, because it creates no mechanism. The same finding will recur at the next surveillance.

Step 6 — Design controls that work without depending on vigilance. Electrodes issued from a controlled oven against a signed record with a return time; continuity generated automatically from the production weld record rather than compiled manually; WPS distribution replaced with a controlled point-of-use system where superseded revisions are physically withdrawn when a new one is issued.

Step 7 — Address the coordination role explicitly. If three coordinator functions failed simultaneously, the coordinator either lacks the time, the authority or the definition of the role. Reviewing the appointment, the task list and the workload is the corrective action that prevents the pattern rather than the instances.

Step 8 — Verify effectiveness before the next audit. Corrective action is closed when evidence shows the control operating — sampled electrode issue records, a generated continuity report, a documented revision withdrawal — not when the procedure describing it has been written.

13. Known Gaps

• The requirement areas in Section 4 are a substantive summary, not a reproduction of the standard's clauses. The normative text is in the purchased standard, and the exact requirements at each of the three levels differ in ways that only the standard resolves.

• The differences between the comprehensive, standard and elementary levels are described in principle only. ISO 3834-2, -3 and -4 each state their own requirement set, and which requirements are reduced at each level must be taken from them.

• Execution class to quality level mapping is described as a general pattern. The specific mapping is set by the applicable execution standard and its current edition, and it should be confirmed rather than assumed.

• Certification scheme requirements are not addressed. Certification bodies apply their own procedures within the standard's framework.

• Nothing here addresses sector-specific quality regimes — aerospace, nuclear, rail and offshore each add requirements beyond ISO 3834, and those regimes govern where they apply.

1. Three Controls, Three Different Purposes

Preheat, interpass temperature and post-weld heat treatment are frequently treated as one topic called "heat treatment," and they are not.

Preheat acts before and during welding, to control the cooling rate and to keep the joint out of the hydrogen cracking window while hydrogen escapes.

Interpass temperature acts during welding, and is controlled in both directions — as a minimum for the same reasons as preheat, and as a maximum to prevent cumulative heat from degrading the microstructure.

Post-weld heat treatment acts after welding is complete, principally to relieve residual stress and to temper hard microstructures, and it can do neither of the first two jobs.

Confusing them produces real errors, the most common being the belief that a specified PWHT compensates for inadequate preheat. It does not: hydrogen cracking occurs during cooling and in the hours and days after welding, so a joint that cracks on Sunday night is already cracked when it enters the furnace on Monday, and the heat treatment then bakes the crack in.

2. Preheat: The Four Things It Achieves

1. It slows the cooling rate, lengthening t8/5 (Chapter 22, Section 4) and reducing the proportion of hard martensite formed in the heat-affected zone. This is the mechanism most often cited and it is real, but it is not the only one.

2. It holds the joint above the hydrogen cracking temperature window for longer, giving diffusible hydrogen time to escape while the metal is still warm enough for it to diffuse out rather than accumulate at stress concentrations (Chapter 23, Section 4).

3. It removes surface moisture, eliminating one hydrogen source directly.

4. It reduces the thermal gradient between the weld and the surrounding cold metal, which modestly reduces the residual stress the joint locks in and reduces distortion in some configurations.

The second mechanism is the one most often forgotten and it changes practice: it is why preheat must be maintained rather than merely applied, and why maintaining temperature for a period after welding (a hydrogen soak) is a recognized control on thick, restrained, high-strength joints.

3. Deciding a Preheat Temperature

Three legitimate routes, described in Chapter 23, Section 6 and restated here in operational terms:

Route 1 — The prescriptive table. AWS D1.1 provides minimum preheat and interpass temperatures by steel category and thickness, with the categories distinguished by strength level and by the hydrogen designation of the permitted filler metal [S1]. Simple, conservative, and available for prequalified procedures.

Route 2 — Hardness control. Calculate the preheat needed to keep heat-affected zone hardness below a target. In the AWS D1.1 annex treatment this route is limited in application, notably to fillet welds [S1][S2].

Route 3 — Hydrogen control. Calculate the preheat from the actual steel composition, the filler metal's diffusible hydrogen level, the combined thickness at the joint, and the restraint level [S1][S2]. This route generally produces lower preheat temperatures than the prescriptive table for modern clean steels with H4 or H8 consumables, and the saving is real — in fuel, in cycle time and in personnel exposure [S1].

Which route is available is set by the governing code. Where more than one is available, the hydrogen-control route is normally the technically strongest, because it uses the actual material and the actual consumable rather than a worst-case assumption about both.

Two practical points that decide whether the chosen temperature is achieved:

Use combined thickness, not plate thickness. At a T-joint or a node, heat conducts away into every member present. The thickness input to any calculation is the combined thickness of all members at the joint, and using a single plate thickness understates the heat sink substantially — a frequent and consequential error on nodes and heavy attachments.

Preheat is a minimum to be maintained, not an event. It must be present at the start of welding and maintained through the joint, including between passes and across interruptions and shift changes.

4. Combined Thickness, Heated Band and Soak

Heated band width. Heating a narrow line on a cold plate produces a joint that cools almost as fast as an unheated one, because the surrounding cold metal is still the heat sink. Codes specify a heated band extending a defined distance either side of the joint for this reason, and the distance scales with thickness.

Soak time. Applying a torch to one face raises that face's temperature long before the far face responds. The joint is at preheat when it is at temperature through the thickness, which requires either a soak period or measurement on the opposite face (Section 6).

Through-thickness verification matters most on heavy sections, where the difference between surface temperature and mid-thickness temperature during heating can be very large.

5. Heating Methods Compared

| Method | Character | Best for | Limitations |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gas torch | Fast, cheap, portable, manual | Field work, single joints, small assemblies | Very uneven; localized overheating easy; hard to maintain; hard to evidence |
| Electrical resistance pads | Ceramic-bead heating elements strapped to the work with insulation | Controlled preheat and local PWHT on pipe and pressure work | Setup time; needs power; pad and thermocouple layout matters |
| Induction heating | Rapid, efficient, deep and uniform heating; work coil around the joint | Pipe preheat and PWHT, repeat work, thick sections | Capital cost; coil configuration per geometry |
| Furnace | Whole component heated uniformly, closely controlled and recorded | Full PWHT of complete assemblies | Component must fit; distortion under self-weight; handling |
| Flame heating rings / ring burners | Uniform circumferential heating on pipe | Pipe preheat in the field | Fuel supply; less controllable than electrical methods |

The distinction that matters for the record: torch heating is difficult to evidence and easy to get wrong, because it is manual, local and transient. Where a preheat temperature is a code requirement rather than good practice, resistance or induction heating with recorded thermocouple output is what produces defensible evidence.

6. Temperature Measurement, and How the Recorded Number Goes Wrong

The measurement is where preheat control most often fails silently, because a number gets recorded either way.

| Method | Character | Failure mode |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Temperature-indicating crayons | Melt at a rated temperature; cheap and quick | Indicates a threshold, not a value; the rating of the crayon actually used is often not recorded; wrong crayon grabbed from a set |
| Contact pyrometer | Direct surface reading | Requires good contact and dwell; calibration frequently overlooked; reads the surface only |
| Thermocouples attached to the work | Continuous, recordable, the basis of defensible evidence | Attachment quality; placement; requires calibrated recording |
| Infrared thermometer | Non-contact, fast | Emissivity-dependent — readings on bright, oxidized and painted surfaces differ substantially for the same true temperature; unreliable on shiny steel unless emissivity is set and verified |

Three rules that determine whether the recorded number is meaningful:

1. Measure on the face opposite the heat source, or after a soak time sufficient for through-thickness equalization. Measuring the face a torch has just played on measures the torch.

2. Measure at the specified distance from the joint, not on the joint itself, and per the code's requirement — a temperature taken directly in the groove and one taken at the specified offset are different numbers.

3. Calibrate. Uncalibrated temperature measurement is one of the most common quality-system findings (Chapter 33, Section 5), and it means preheat control is unverified rather than merely undocumented.

7. Interpass Temperature: Minimum and Maximum

The minimum is normally the same as the preheat temperature and exists for the same reasons. The mechanism does not care whether the metal is cold because it was never heated or cold because it was allowed to cool between passes.

The maximum exists for entirely different reasons and is violated far more often, because nothing observable happens when it is exceeded:

• On quenched and tempered steels, excessive interpass temperature over-tempers the parent metal and loses strength.

• On thermomechanically processed steels, it extends time at temperature and degrades the properties the mill's processing route created.

• On duplex stainless, it drives intermetallic precipitation and destroys the phase balance (Chapter 24, Section 6).

• On any steel where toughness is specified, it extends t8/5 far enough to coarsen the structure and reduce toughness.

Production sequences that weld joints back-to-back without a cooling check will exceed a maximum interpass limit routinely. The only controls that work are an enforced measurement between passes and a production sequence that allows cooling — which means the maximum interpass requirement has a direct, and often unwelcome, effect on production rate.

8. Post-Weld Heat Treatment: The Six Reasons It Is Specified

PWHT is specified for one or more of six distinct purposes, and knowing which one applies determines the temperature, the time and what damage to watch for:

1. Stress relief. Heating to a temperature at which the material's yield strength falls low enough for residual stress to relax by localized creep. This is the most common purpose, and it reduces susceptibility to brittle fracture, stress-corrosion cracking and distortion during machining.

2. Tempering. Softening hard martensitic structures in the weld metal and heat-affected zone, improving toughness and ductility. Mandatory for martensitic stainless and many alloy steels.

3. Hydrogen release (dehydrogenation). A lower-temperature hold, applied soon after welding and before the joint cools, to drive out diffusible hydrogen before it can cause cracking. This is a preventive treatment against the mechanism of Chapter 23 and must be applied before cracking occurs, not after.

4. Dimensional stability. Relieving stress so that subsequent machining does not release it and move the part.

5. Restoring corrosion resistance. Solution annealing austenitic and duplex stainless to redissolve precipitated phases (Chapter 24).

6. Achieving specified properties. Solution treatment and ageing for precipitation-hardening materials, where the final properties depend on completing a defined cycle.

9. The PWHT Thermal Cycle and Its Controlled Parameters

A PWHT specification controls the whole cycle, not just the peak temperature:

• Heating rate, usually expressed as a maximum in degrees per hour, often scaled inversely with thickness. Heating too fast generates thermal gradients and their own stresses, and can crack a component before it reaches soak.

• Soak temperature, with a tolerance band. Below the band the treatment does not achieve its purpose; above it, the parent metal's own tempering temperature can be exceeded (Section 11).

• Soak time, conventionally scaled with thickness — the widely used convention in pressure work is on the order of one hour per 25 mm of thickness, subject to a stated minimum and the governing code's own table.

• Cooling rate, controlled to a maximum down to a stated temperature, below which free cooling in still air is permitted.

• Thermocouple placement, sufficient in number and position to demonstrate that the whole heated region met the cycle, including the coolest points.

• Heated band and insulation width for local treatment (Section 10).

The record of that cycle — a calibrated chart or data file showing every thermocouple through the whole cycle — is the deliverable. A PWHT with no chart, or with thermocouples whose positions were not recorded, cannot be shown to have been achieved (Chapter 33, Section 11).

10. Local Against Furnace Heat Treatment

Furnace treatment heats the whole component and is the most reliable route: uniform, well-instrumented, easily evidenced. Its constraints are furnace size, handling, cost, and the risk of distortion under the component's own weight at temperature — large thin components can sag, and support arrangements are part of the procedure.

Local treatment heats a band around the joint using resistance pads or induction. It is used where the component cannot be furnace-treated: field pipework, large vessels, repairs on installed equipment. Its critical parameters are:

• Heated band width, which must be wide enough that the soak zone is genuinely at temperature and not merely the middle of a steep gradient.

• Gradient control band beyond the heated band, insulated so the temperature falls gradually rather than sharply. A steep gradient at the edge of a locally heated zone introduces its own thermal stress, which is precisely what the treatment exists to remove.

• Full circumference or full section coverage — heating only the accessible side of a joint produces a through-thickness gradient and an ineffective treatment on the far side.

• Thermocouple placement including the edges of the band, not only the centre.

A recurring failure in local PWHT is a band that is too narrow, well instrumented at its centre, producing an excellent chart and an ineffective treatment.

11. When PWHT Causes Damage

PWHT is not universally beneficial and specifying it by default causes real harm in several cases:

Reheat (stress-relief) cracking. In creep-resistant Cr-Mo and Cr-Mo-V steels and some stabilized stainless and nickel alloys, carbide precipitation during the treatment strengthens grain interiors while boundaries relax, producing intergranular cracking in the coarse-grained heat-affected zone (Chapter 23, Section 10). The treatment intended to make the joint safer cracks it.

Over-tempering of the parent metal. If the PWHT soak temperature approaches or exceeds the tempering temperature used by the steelmaker for a quenched and tempered material, the parent metal loses strength across the whole heated region — not just at the joint. The rule is that PWHT temperature must stay safely below the parent's own tempering temperature, and the material certificate is where that temperature is found.

Sensitization of austenitic stainless. A stress-relief soak in the roughly 425–815 °C range is precisely the sensitizing range (Chapter 24, Section 3). Austenitic stainless is generally not stress-relieved for this reason; where a treatment is required, a solution anneal at much higher temperature followed by rapid cooling is the appropriate cycle.

Intermetallic precipitation in duplex stainless. Duplex must not be given a conventional stress-relief soak; the temperature range overlaps sigma phase formation.

Temper embrittlement. Some low-alloy steels embrittle on slow cooling through a specific range, requiring controlled cooling rather than furnace cooling.

Distortion. A component at stress-relief temperature has greatly reduced yield strength and can deform under its own weight or under fixturing restraint.

Loss of properties in TMCP and AHSS steels, whose properties derive from a processing route that a heat treatment cycle undoes.

12. Alternatives to PWHT

Where PWHT is impractical or harmful, recognized alternatives exist — each with its own qualification requirements:

Temper bead welding (controlled deposition). A deliberately designed bead placement sequence in which each subsequent bead's thermal cycle tempers and grain-refines the heat-affected zone of the previous one. Used extensively for repairs on installed equipment where furnace treatment is impossible. It requires its own qualification demonstrating that the intended tempering is achieved, and bead placement is tightly controlled.

Dehydrogenation soak in place of full PWHT where the concern is hydrogen rather than residual stress — lower temperature, shorter, and it addresses only that mechanism.

Vibratory stress relief. Used in some sectors for dimensional stability. It does not reproduce the metallurgical effects of thermal treatment and is not generally accepted where a code requires PWHT.

Design and consumable choices that avoid the requirement: reducing restraint, using a lower-strength consumable, or selecting a material whose code requirements do not trigger PWHT at the thickness in question.

15. Worked Example: A PWHT That Softened the Parent Metal

Situation. A fabricator welds a pressure component in a quenched and tempered steel and applies PWHT per its standard shop procedure — a soak temperature it has used successfully for years on carbon steel work. Post-treatment testing shows parent metal tensile strength below the material specification, across the whole heated region rather than only at the joint.

Step 1 — Read the location of the property loss. The loss is in the parent metal across the whole heated region, not confined to the weld or heat-affected zone. That immediately distinguishes it from a welding problem: nothing about the arc affects material 300 mm from the joint. Whatever happened, happened to everything that reached soak temperature.

Step 2 — Compare the PWHT soak temperature against the parent's tempering temperature. A quenched and tempered steel derives its properties from a temper at a specific temperature recorded on the material certificate. A PWHT soak at or above that temperature re-tempers the material, and strength falls accordingly. This single comparison usually resolves the case.

Step 3 — Recognize why the shop procedure was wrong here and right before. A soak temperature appropriate for ordinary carbon steel can exceed the tempering temperature of a Q&T grade. The procedure was never validated against this material; it was carried across because the operation looked the same. This is the general failure mode of standard shop procedures applied to a new material.

Step 4 — Establish the extent. Everything within the heated band, on every component treated in that cycle, is affected — not just the tested area. If multiple components shared the furnace load, all are affected.

Step 5 — Assess whether the material can be recovered. For a Q&T steel, restoring properties requires re-quenching and re-tempering the whole component, which is rarely practical on a welded fabrication and would itself require requalification of the joint's properties afterwards. In most cases the honest answer is that the material cannot be restored in situ and the component must be assessed for fitness at its actual properties or replaced.

Step 6 — Check the qualification too. The procedure qualification for the joint was performed with a particular PWHT condition. If production PWHT differed from the qualified condition, the joint's properties are additionally unqualified — a second, independent finding (Chapter 31, Section 11).

Step 7 — Fix the control. The corrective action is a requirement that PWHT parameters be established per material from the material certificate and the applicable code, with a check that the soak temperature sits safely below the parent's tempering temperature, before any heat treatment is released. A standard shop cycle applied by default across materials is the hazard, and removing that default is the fix.

16. Known Gaps

• No preheat, soak or PWHT temperatures are tabulated. They are code-, material- and thickness-specific and are published in the governing codes. The mechanisms, the decision routes and the failure modes are given here; the numbers belong to the code and to the material certificate.

• The one-hour-per-25-mm soak convention is a widely used industry convention, not a universal rule. The governing code's own table takes precedence, and minimum soak times and thickness definitions vary.

• Heated band and gradient band widths are described in principle only. They are specified in the applicable code and scale with thickness and geometry.

• Temper bead welding is described in outline. It requires a qualified procedure with specific bead placement, and the qualification requirements are set by the applicable code.

• The sensitizing range for austenitic stainless (approximately 425–815 °C) is an approximation that varies with composition and exposure time (Chapter 24).

1. Detection Is Physical, Not Procedural

Every inspection method works by a physical mechanism, and that mechanism defines both what it finds and what it cannot find. This is the single most important thing to understand about weld inspection, because most inspection failures are not procedural errors — they are cases where a method was applied to a defect type it was physically incapable of detecting, and the resulting "pass" was recorded as evidence of soundness.

Two properties of a discontinuity determine which methods can find it:

Whether it breaks the surface. Penetrant and magnetic particle testing are surface methods; a subsurface defect is invisible to them regardless of size.

Whether it is volumetric or planar, and how it is oriented. A volumetric defect — a gas pore, a slag inclusion — has measurable extent in all three directions and absorbs radiation differently from the surrounding metal, which makes radiography effective. A planar defect — a crack, a lack of fusion — is a two-dimensional separation that may be only micrometres thick. Radiography detects it only if the beam happens to run nearly parallel to its plane; at other angles it presents almost no absorption difference and is missed. Ultrasonics, by contrast, reflects strongly from a planar face and finds these defects readily.

That difference between planar and volumetric defect detection governs the entire radiography-versus-ultrasonics decision, and it explains why the most dangerous weld defects — cracks and lack of fusion, both planar — are the ones radiography is worst at finding.

2. Visual Testing: The Method That Finds the Most Defects

Visual testing is the cheapest method, it is applied to every weld, and it finds more defects in total than all other methods combined. It is also the most frequently undervalued.

What it detects: surface cracks, undercut, overlap, incomplete fill, excess or insufficient reinforcement, incorrect profile and size, arc strikes, spatter, surface porosity, root concavity and excess penetration on accessible roots, misalignment, and — crucially — evidence of process problems such as discolouration on stainless and titanium (Chapters 24 and 26).

What it is blind to: everything below the surface.

Its requirements are more specific than "look at it," and are set out in ISO 17637 [S2]: adequate illumination at the surface, a defined viewing distance and angle, access to the surface, and appropriate aids — gauges for fillet size and reinforcement, mirrors, borescopes for internal surfaces, magnification where specified.

Direct visual testing requires the eye within a specified distance and angle of the surface. Remote visual testing uses borescopes or cameras and is used where access prevents direct viewing — pipe internals in particular.

The engineering point: visual inspection before and during welding is worth more than visual inspection after it. Checking joint preparation, fit-up, cleanliness, preheat and interpass condition prevents defects; checking the completed weld only finds them. The most effective visual inspection programmes concentrate effort before the arc is struck.

3. Penetrant Testing

Mechanism. A low-viscosity liquid penetrant is applied to a clean surface and drawn into surface-breaking discontinuities by capillary action. Excess penetrant is removed from the surface, and a developer is applied that draws the trapped penetrant back out, producing a visible indication substantially wider than the discontinuity itself.

What it detects: surface-breaking discontinuities in essentially any non-porous material — including non-ferromagnetic ones, which is where it is indispensable. Cracks, laps, porosity breaking the surface.

What it is blind to: anything not open to the surface. A crack filled with paint, oxide or smeared metal from grinding will not take penetrant, which is why surface preparation is part of the method and why grinding immediately before penetrant testing can close the very defect being sought.

Variants: colour-contrast (visible red on white developer) and fluorescent (viewed under ultraviolet light, more sensitive). Removal methods are water-washable, solvent-removable, and post-emulsifiable, in increasing order of sensitivity and cost.

Critical procedural variables: cleanliness of the surface, penetrant dwell time, correct removal without over-washing (which strips penetrant from the defect), and development time. The single most common error is insufficient dwell followed by aggressive removal — producing a clean, defect-free-looking surface that has been washed clean of the evidence.

The governing standard family is ISO 3452, with acceptance levels for welds in ISO 23277 [S6].

4. Magnetic Particle Testing

Mechanism. The component is magnetized, and a discontinuity at or near the surface distorts the magnetic field, causing flux to leak out of the surface. Fine ferromagnetic particles applied to the surface are attracted to the leakage field and accumulate over the discontinuity.

What it detects: surface-breaking and slightly subsurface discontinuities — a real advantage over penetrant testing, which finds only surface-breaking ones. It is faster than penetrant, tolerant of slightly dirty surfaces, and highly sensitive to tight cracks.

What it is blind to: anything in a non-ferromagnetic material. Austenitic stainless, aluminium, copper, titanium and nickel alloys cannot be tested this way, which is a hard constraint on method selection rather than a preference.

The orientation rule: the method detects discontinuities that lie transverse to the magnetic field. A crack parallel to the field produces no leakage and is invisible. This is why the method is always applied in two directions approximately 90° apart — a single-direction examination is capable of missing an entire class of defect orientation, and an inspection report showing a single direction is incomplete.

Magnetization methods: yoke (portable electromagnet, most common for welds), prods (direct current through the part — carries a risk of arc strikes on the surface, which are themselves a defect), coils, and central conductors.

Demagnetization is often required afterwards, particularly where residual magnetism would disturb subsequent welding (arc blow, Chapter 22, Section 13) or interfere with the component's function.

The governing standard is ISO 17638, with acceptance levels in ISO 23278 [S3][S6].

5. Radiographic Testing

Mechanism. Radiation — X-rays from a tube, or gamma rays from an isotope source — passes through the weld and is recorded on film or a digital detector. Regions of lower density or reduced thickness absorb less radiation and appear darker.

What it detects well: volumetric defects — porosity, slag inclusions, incomplete penetration when it presents a genuine gap, and undercut. It produces a permanent, reviewable image, which is a real advantage for records and for third-party review.

What it detects poorly: planar defects not aligned with the beam. A tight lack of sidewall fusion or a crack lying across the beam direction may be entirely invisible. This is the method's fundamental limitation and it is not a matter of technique or operator skill.

Sources: X-ray equipment is controllable and can be switched off, and is generally preferred where power and access allow. Gamma sources (iridium-192, selenium-75, cobalt-60 for heavy sections) are portable and require no power, and are used in field and pipeline work — with the important consequence that they cannot be switched off and present a continuous radiation hazard.

Image quality indicators (penetrameters) are placed on the component and radiographed with it. They demonstrate that the technique achieved the required sensitivity — without an acceptable IQI reading, the radiograph is not evidence of anything, regardless of how clean the image looks.

Digital radiography — computed radiography with imaging plates, and direct digital detectors — is increasingly standard, offering faster processing, lower dose, and image enhancement. The governing standard family is ISO 17636, with parts covering film and digital techniques, and acceptance levels in ISO 10675-1 [S6].

Safety dominates deployment. Radiography requires exclusion zones, controlled areas, dosimetry, and licensed personnel. On a multi-trade site it frequently drives night-shift working because the area must be cleared, and that scheduling consequence is a real project cost that is often underestimated.

6. Ultrasonic Testing

Mechanism. A high-frequency sound pulse is introduced into the material through a couplant. It travels until it meets an interface — a back wall or a discontinuity — and reflects. The time of flight gives depth and the reflected amplitude gives an indication of size.

What it detects well: planar defects — cracks, lack of fusion, lack of penetration — particularly when oriented to reflect toward the probe. It gives depth information, which radiography does not. It penetrates thick sections readily, has no radiation hazard, and requires access from only one side.

What it detects poorly or not at all: very small defects near the surface (masked by the initial pulse), defects in coarse-grained or highly attenuating material — austenitic stainless weld metal in particular scatters ultrasound badly, which is why conventional UT of austenitic welds is difficult and often requires specialized techniques. Rounded volumetric defects reflect less strongly than planar ones and can be under-called.

Angle probes are used for welds because a normal-incidence beam would run parallel to the fusion faces where lack of fusion lives. Beam angle selection is matched to the joint geometry so that the beam strikes the expected defect orientation as close to perpendicular as possible.

Its dependencies: calibration on reference blocks, correct couplant, surface condition adequate for coupling, and — more than any other method — operator skill. Conventional manual ultrasonic testing produces a live interpretation with no permanent image, so the record is the operator's report. Two qualified operators can produce different results on the same weld, and this is a known and quantified characteristic of the method rather than an aberration.

The governing standard is ISO 17640, with acceptance levels in ISO 11666 [S6].

7. Phased Array and Time-of-Flight Diffraction

Phased array ultrasonic testing (PAUT) uses a probe containing many small elements pulsed with controlled time delays, so the beam can be steered and focused electronically without moving the probe. Its advantages over conventional UT: multiple angles from one position, real-time sector imaging, encoded position data producing a permanent reviewable record, and better coverage of complex geometry. It has substantially displaced radiography for thick-section and pipeline girth weld inspection.

Time-of-flight diffraction (TOFD) uses a transmitter and receiver either side of the weld and works from the weak diffracted signals from the tips of a defect rather than from specular reflection off its face. This makes it unusually good at sizing defects through-wall and much less sensitive to defect orientation than pulse-echo methods. Its blind zones near the surfaces are its main limitation, which is why TOFD is normally combined with pulse-echo or phased array coverage rather than used alone.

Together, PAUT and TOFD form the basis of most modern automated ultrasonic testing (AUT) systems, and are what make mechanized inspection of pipeline girth welds practical at production speed. Their combination of orientation-tolerant sizing and permanent encoded records is why fitness-for-service assessment — which needs accurate defect height, not just detection — depends on them.

8. Eddy Current and Other Surface Methods

Eddy current testing induces circulating currents in a conductive material with a coil, and detects the perturbation those currents suffer at a discontinuity. It works on any electrically conductive material — including non-ferromagnetic ones, unlike magnetic particle testing — detects surface and near-surface defects, requires no couplant, and can work through thin non-conductive coatings, which is a substantial practical advantage on painted structures.

Its limitations are shallow penetration, sensitivity to material property and geometry variation (which produces indications unrelated to defects), and interpretation difficulty.

Alternating current field measurement (ACFM) is a related technique widely used for detecting and sizing surface-breaking cracks through coatings, notably on offshore structures underwater.

9. Leak, Pressure and Specialist Testing

Pressure testing — hydrostatic or pneumatic — proves the assembly holds pressure. It is a system test rather than a weld test, and passing it is not evidence that individual welds are free of defects; a joint containing a substantial unfused root can hold a hydrotest comfortably and fail later in fatigue.

Leak testing by bubble, pressure change, halogen or helium mass spectrometry detects through-thickness leakage paths with sensitivity far beyond a pressure test, and is used on vacuum and containment systems.

Acoustic emission testing monitors the stress waves emitted by growing defects during loading. It is a global monitoring method that locates active sources rather than a survey method.

Thermography detects subsurface features by their thermal response and is used in specific applications.

11. Method Selection: How It Is Actually Decided

Selection is governed in international practice by ISO 17635, which provides general rules for the non-destructive testing of welds in metallic materials, including which methods are appropriate and the extent of testing [S1][S5].

The decision inputs, in the order they actually constrain the choice:

1. Material. Ferromagnetic or not — this alone eliminates magnetic particle testing for austenitic stainless, aluminium and most nickel alloys. Coarse austenitic weld metal constrains ultrasonics.

2. Joint type and thickness. Thin material limits ultrasonic access; heavy sections limit radiographic practicality and dose.

3. The defects credibly expected, which follow from the process and the material. A process prone to lack of fusion needs a method that finds planar defects; a process prone to porosity is well served by radiography.

4. Access. Radiography needs both sides; ultrasonics needs one. This decides many field cases outright.

5. The acceptance criteria in force, which are method-specific (Section 14).

6. The consequence of failure, which sets the extent of testing — spot, partial or full coverage.

7. Practical constraints: radiation exclusion zones, shift working, surface temperature, coating condition.

The single most useful heuristic: choose the method by the defect you expect, not by convention. A shop that radiographs everything because it always has will systematically under-detect lack of fusion in its GMAW work.

12. When Inspection Is Performed, and Why Timing Matters

• Before welding: material identity, joint preparation, fit-up, cleanliness, preheat. The cheapest defect prevention available.

• During welding: interpass cleaning and condition, interpass temperature, root pass inspection before it is covered, back-gouged surfaces before the second side is welded. Once a root is buried under fill passes, correcting it costs many times more.

• After welding, immediately: visual, and surface methods where the criteria permit.

• After welding, after a delay: essential where hydrogen cracking is credible. Cracking develops over hours to days (Chapter 23, Section 4), so a surface examination performed straight after welding on a thick, high-strength, restrained joint is looking for something that has not happened yet. Codes specify minimum delay periods for this reason, and treating them as administrative padding defeats the inspection.

• After post-weld heat treatment: where PWHT could introduce reheat cracking (Chapter 34, Section 11), inspection after treatment is what finds it.

13. Personnel Qualification and the Human Factor

Inspection results are only as good as the person producing them, and this is formalized: ISO 9712 certifies NDT personnel by method and level (Level 1 performing under instruction, Level 2 performing and interpreting, Level 3 responsible for the technique and procedures), and equivalent employer-based schemes operate in North American practice.

Beyond certification, probability of detection is a real and measured property of an inspection system — the method, the procedure, the equipment, the person and the conditions together. It is never 100 %. It falls with smaller defects, unfavourable orientation, poor access, awkward positions, fatigue and time pressure.

The engineering consequences are uncomfortable and should be stated: a clear inspection report is evidence, not proof; the extent of inspection should be matched to consequence rather than to habit; and where a defect type is critical, choosing a method with genuinely high detection probability for that specific defect matters more than increasing the coverage percentage of a method that is poor at finding it.

14. Acceptance Criteria Are Separate From the Method

A frequent and consequential confusion: the standard that governs how a method is performed is not the standard that says what is acceptable.

| Function | Example standards |
| --- | --- |
| How to perform the method | ISO 17637 (VT), ISO 3452 (PT), ISO 17638 (MT), ISO 17636 (RT), ISO 17640 (UT) |
| What is acceptable | ISO 23277 (PT), ISO 23278 (MT), ISO 10675-1 (RT), ISO 11666 (UT), and the quality levels of ISO 5817 |
| Which method and how much | ISO 17635 |

An inspection specification that names only a method standard has not stated acceptance criteria, and the inspector cannot report a result. Conversely, a quality level from ISO 5817 (Chapter 36) is not directly applicable to a radiograph without the corresponding acceptance-level standard that translates it into what may be seen on the image.

15. Destructive Testing: What Only It Can Prove

No non-destructive method measures a mechanical property. Where properties must be demonstrated, destructive testing is the only route (Chapter 31, Section 10):

| Test | Proves |
| --- | --- |
| Transverse tensile | Joint strength, and the weakest location by fracture position |
| Bend | Soundness and ductility; opens planar defects on the tension surface |
| Charpy impact | Notch toughness at temperature, at specified notch positions |
| Hardness survey | Peak hardness in weld and HAZ against a ceiling |
| Macro / micro examination | Fusion profile, penetration, HAZ extent, microstructure |
| Fracture (nick-break) | Root fusion and internal condition on fillet welds |
| Corrosion tests | Resistance to a specific mechanism — intergranular attack, pitting — in a specified medium |
| Fillet weld shear | Load capacity of the fillet configuration |

Destructive testing appears in three contexts: procedure and welder qualification, production test coupons welded alongside production work under the same conditions, and failure investigation, where sectioning the failed joint is usually the only way to establish the mechanism.
