17. Failure Catalog: Inspection Failures

| Failure | Cause | Correction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lack of fusion passed by radiography | Planar defect not aligned with the beam — a physical limitation, not an error | Specify UT or PAUT where lack of fusion is credible |
| Crack missed by magnetic particle testing | Examination performed in one direction only; crack parallel to the field | Two directions approximately 90° apart, always |
| Defect missed by penetrant testing after grinding | Grinding smeared metal over the discontinuity and closed it | Etch or otherwise prepare per procedure; avoid smearing surface preparation before PT |
| Hydrogen crack missed | Inspection performed immediately after welding, before the delayed mechanism operated | Apply the specified delay before final surface inspection |
| Austenitic weld "clean" by UT | Coarse austenitic structure scattered the beam; poor penetration and high noise | Use techniques qualified for austenitic material, or an alternative method |
| Radiograph accepted with poor IQI | Sensitivity not demonstrated; the image proves nothing | Reject and re-shoot; IQI acceptance is a prerequisite, not a formality |
| Two inspectors, two different UT results | Inherent operator dependence of manual UT | Use encoded PAUT for a reviewable record where consistency matters |
| Pressure test passed, joint later failed | A pressure test is a system test, not a weld quality test | Do not treat hydrotest success as evidence of weld soundness |
| Acceptance disputes at handover | Method standard specified without an acceptance standard | Specify method, acceptance standard and quality level together |
| Inspection extent adequate on paper, defects still escaping | High coverage of a method with low detection probability for the actual defect type | Reselect the method against the credible defect, then set extent |

18. Worked Example: A Defect That Radiography Could Not Have Found

Situation. A fabricator welds thick-section butt joints using gas metal arc welding in the short-circuit mode for the root and fill. All joints are radiographed to full coverage and accepted. In service, a joint fails. Sectioning the failure shows an extensive lack of sidewall fusion running along the groove face. The client's position is that the radiography must have been performed negligently.

Step 1 — Establish whether the method could have found the defect at all before assessing whether it was performed well. Lack of sidewall fusion is a planar discontinuity lying along the groove face, typically at an angle to the plate surface set by the bevel. Radiography detects a planar defect only when the beam runs closely parallel to its plane. A standard radiographic set-up through the thickness presents the beam at a substantial angle to a bevel face, and a tight lack of fusion under that geometry produces almost no absorption contrast. The method was physically incapable of reliably finding this defect.

Step 2 — Check the radiographs for what they do demonstrate. Acceptable image quality indicator readings demonstrate the technique achieved its required sensitivity for the defects the method can detect. The films are valid evidence of the absence of detectable volumetric defects, and they are not evidence about planar defects at that orientation. Distinguishing these two statements is the whole of the technical case.

Step 3 — Ask why lack of fusion was credible in this work. Short-circuit transfer is a low heat input mode, and its characteristic defect on thick section is precisely lack of fusion — the mode does not deliver enough energy to fuse the groove faces reliably at depth. The defect type was predictable from the process choice, which means the inspection method should have been selected against it (Section 11).

Step 4 — Identify the real failure. The failure is in inspection specification, not in inspection performance. A method that finds volumetric defects was applied to a process whose dominant failure mode is planar. The correct specification would have been ultrasonic or phased array testing, either instead of or alongside radiography.

Step 5 — Consider whether the process choice itself was appropriate. Short-circuit GMAW on thick section is a recognized risk for exactly this defect. If the process was chosen for its out-of-position capability, alternatives exist — pulsed transfer gives all-position capability at higher energy (Chapter 39). The inspection question and the process question are connected, and correcting only the inspection leaves the shop producing the same defects and merely finding them later.

Step 6 — Assess the existing population. Every joint made by the same process and inspected by the same method carries the same risk. Re-inspection with an appropriate method on a risk-prioritized sample is the reasonable response, targeting the joints with the highest consequence and the greatest thickness.

Step 7 — Correct the specification. The inspection plan should be rewritten to select methods against credible defect types by process and material, with the reasoning recorded — which is what ISO 17635 exists to structure [S1][S5]. Recording the reasoning matters as much as the choice, because it is what prevents the plan reverting to habit at the next revision.

19. Known Gaps

• No acceptance criteria are reproduced. Every acceptance standard cited is a purchased document with detailed, quality-level-dependent limits. This chapter identifies which standard governs which function; the limits belong to the standard and the contract.

• No probability-of-detection figures are quoted. Published values are specific to a method, procedure, defect type, material and study, and quoting a general figure would be misleading.

• Method standards are named by number without reproducing their technique requirements. Beam angles, sensitivity settings, dwell times and scanning patterns are specified in the standards and in written procedures qualified against them.

• Radiation safety is not covered here beyond noting its practical consequences. It is governed by national regulation and is outside this reference set's scope.

• Advanced and emerging methods are summarized only. Full matrix capture, guided wave, and in-process monitoring approaches each have substantial literature of their own.

1. Imperfection, Defect and the Distinction That Matters

The two words are not interchangeable in standards language, and the distinction carries real consequences.

An imperfection is any deviation from the ideal weld. Every weld ever made contains imperfections. A weld with no imperfections does not exist, and a report that finds none has either not looked properly or is describing a weld inspected by a method incapable of finding what is there.

A defect is an imperfection that exceeds the acceptance criteria applicable to that weld. It is a judgement made by comparing an observed imperfection against a specified limit.

The practical consequence: the same physical condition can be acceptable on one joint and rejectable on another — not because the inspector's judgement differed, but because the applicable quality level differed. Undercut of a given depth may be perfectly acceptable on a statically loaded general structure and rejectable on a fatigue-loaded one. Arguing about whether something is "a defect" without first establishing the acceptance criteria is a category error, and it is the shape of most inspection disputes.

2. The Classification Structure: Six Groups

ISO 6520-1 classifies geometric imperfections in fusion welding into six groups, each with a numeric reference range [S1][S2]:

| Group | Reference range | Category |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 100–199 | Cracks |
| 2 | 200–299 | Cavities |
| 3 | 300–399 | Solid inclusions |
| 4 | 400–499 | Lack of fusion and penetration |
| 5 | 500–599 | Imperfect shape and dimensions |
| 6 | 600–699 | Miscellaneous imperfections |

The value of the numbering is that it is unambiguous across languages and across documents. "Porosity" means several different things in casual speech; reference 2011 does not. Inspection reports, acceptance standards and procedure documents that use the reference numbers can be compared directly; those that use only descriptive words cannot.

The groups are ordered, roughly, by severity of consequence — cracks first, cosmetic and surface conditions last — and that ordering is a useful default when triaging a set of findings.

3. Group 1 — Cracks

Cracks are the most serious class of imperfection because they are planar, sharp-tipped stress concentrators that propagate under load. In most codes and at most quality levels, cracks are not permitted at any size.

| Reference | Imperfection |
| --- | --- |
| 101 | Longitudinal crack |
| 102 | Transverse crack |
| 104 | Crater crack |
| 106 | Heat-affected zone crack |

Further references within the group cover radiating cracks, branched or grouped cracks, and cracks classified by their location in the weld metal, fusion line, heat-affected zone or parent metal.

The classification is geometric, but the mechanism is what determines the corrective action, and four distinct mechanisms produce cracks that the geometric classification does not distinguish:

| Mechanism | When it occurs | Where | Chapter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Solidification (hot) cracking | During solidification, immediately | Weld metal, usually centreline | 23 §8, 22 §6 |
| Hydrogen-induced (cold) cracking | Hours to days after welding | HAZ, toe or root | 23 §4 |
| Lamellar tearing | During or shortly after welding | Parent plate, stepped, below the joint | 23 §9 |
| Reheat (stress-relief) cracking | During PWHT or high-temperature service | Coarse-grained HAZ, intergranular | 23 §10, 34 §11 |

Identifying which mechanism produced a crack is the first step in any investigation, and the two most useful discriminators are timing (immediate against delayed) and location (weld metal against HAZ against parent plate).

4. Group 2 — Cavities

Gas-filled or shrinkage voids. Generally less severe than cracks because they are rounded and do not concentrate stress as sharply, but they reduce cross-section and can link.

| Reference | Imperfection |
| --- | --- |
| 201 | Gas pore |
| 2011 | Uniformly distributed porosity |
| 2012 | Clustered (localized) porosity |
| 2014 | Elongated cavity (worm hole) |
| 202 | Crater pipe |

Causes across processes: moisture, oil, grease, rust, paint or coating on the joint; damp consumables or flux; loss or contamination of shielding gas; turbulent gas flow entraining air; excessive arc length; nitrogen pickup; and, in aluminium specifically, hydrogen rejected during solidification (Chapter 25, Section 5).

The distribution pattern is diagnostic, and reading it saves investigation time:

• Uniformly distributed porosity across a whole weld suggests a systematic cause — consumable condition, gas purity, or a general surface condition.

• Clustered porosity suggests a local cause — a patch of contamination, a momentary shielding disturbance.

• Porosity at starts suggests inadequate gas pre-flow; at stops, inadequate post-flow (Chapter 30, Section 9).

• Linear porosity along the root suggests a root gap contamination or purge problem.

• Worm holes indicate gas escaping through solidifying metal, generally from a strong, sustained gas source.

5. Group 3 — Solid Inclusions

Foreign solid matter trapped in the weld metal.

| Reference | Imperfection |
| --- | --- |
| 301 | Slag inclusion |
| 3041 | Tungsten inclusion |
| 3042 | Copper inclusion |

The group also covers flux inclusions and oxide inclusions.

Slag inclusions (301) occur in slag-producing processes — shielded metal arc, flux cored, submerged arc. Causes: inadequate interpass cleaning, a groove too narrow for slag to float clear, incorrect electrode angle or travel speed leaving slag ahead of the pool, undercut from a previous pass forming a trap, and irregular bead profiles creating pockets. The most common single cause is inadequate interpass cleaning, and the second is a joint preparation too narrow for the process (Chapter 28, Section 4).

Tungsten inclusions (3041) are specific to gas tungsten arc welding: the electrode contacted the pool or the filler wire, or was eroded by excessive current or an oxidizing gas. They appear as bright spots on a radiograph because tungsten is far denser than steel. Prevention is technique and correct electrode selection and preparation (Chapter 41).

Copper inclusions (3042) come from the contact tip in consumable-electrode processes or from copper backing bars, and indicate either contact tip damage or a backing bar being melted into the joint.

6. Group 4 — Lack of Fusion and Penetration

The most dangerous imperfections after cracks, because they are planar, they are frequently large, and they are poorly detected by radiography (Chapter 35, Section 1).

| Reference | Imperfection |
| --- | --- |
| 401 | Lack of fusion |
| 4011 | Lack of sidewall fusion |
| 402 | Incomplete penetration |

The group further distinguishes lack of fusion between passes and at the root.

Lack of fusion means the weld metal did not fuse with the parent metal or with the previous pass — the two are in contact but not joined. It behaves mechanically like a crack.

Causes: heat input too low for the joint; travel speed too high; incorrect torch or electrode angle directing the arc away from the fusion face; a groove angle too narrow for access (Chapter 28); contamination or oxide on the fusion faces; magnetic arc blow deflecting the arc; and — the archetypal case — short-circuit metal transfer used on thick sections, where the low heat input mode does not fuse the groove faces reliably (Chapter 39).

Incomplete penetration means the weld did not extend through the joint thickness as required. Causes: root gap too small, root face too thick, insufficient root pass current, incorrect electrode size for the root, and travel speed too high.

A distinction worth keeping clear: partial joint penetration by design is not incomplete penetration. A PJP weld's unfused root is intended (Chapter 28, Section 3). Incomplete penetration is failure to achieve the penetration the design required.

7. Group 5 — Imperfect Shape and Dimension

Geometric deviations. Mostly detectable visually, and mostly significant because of the stress concentrations they create rather than because of lost cross-section.

| Reference | Imperfection |
| --- | --- |
| 501 | Undercut |
| 502 | Shrinkage groove |
| 506 | Overlap |
| 507 | Linear misalignment |

The group also covers excess weld metal and excess convexity, excess penetration, incorrect weld toe angle, angular misalignment, sagging, burn-through, incompletely filled groove, excessive fillet asymmetry, irregular width and surface, root concavity, and poor restarts.

The ones that matter most in practice:

Undercut (501) — a groove melted into the parent metal at the weld toe and not filled. It is a stress concentration at exactly the location where fatigue cracks initiate, which is why fatigue-loaded joints have far stricter undercut limits than statically loaded ones. Causes: current too high, travel speed too high, incorrect electrode angle, excessive weaving, wrong shielding gas giving poor wetting.

Overlap (506) — weld metal flowed over the parent surface without fusing to it, producing a sharp notch at the toe. Caused by too low a travel speed, too low an arc energy for the deposition rate, or incorrect technique.

Linear misalignment (507) — the two members are offset. A fit-up problem (Chapter 28, Section 12), it creates a bending stress under axial load and a geometric stress concentration.

Root concavity, burn-through and excess penetration are all root conditions driven by fit-up, root pass parameters and purge pressure.

Poor restarts are a frequent source of localized defects, because a restart combines a cold start, possible slag entrapment and a profile discontinuity in one location.

8. Group 6 — Miscellaneous Imperfections, Including Spatter

| Reference | Imperfection |
| --- | --- |
| 601 | Arc strike |
| 602 | Spatter |

The group also covers torn surfaces, grinding and chipping marks, underflushing where a surface has been ground below the parent contour, and surface discolouration and temper colour.

Arc strikes (601) deserve more attention than their group placement suggests. An arc struck on the parent metal outside the joint produces a small, uncontrolled, unfused melted spot with a very rapid quench into cold surrounding metal. On hardenable steel that produces a hard, brittle, often cracked micro-region with no filler and no controlled cooling. Many codes prohibit arc strikes outright on certain material and service categories and require them to be removed by grinding and the area examined by a surface method — because the crack, not the mark, is the problem.

Surface discolouration and temper colour are cosmetic on carbon steel and are a genuine property statement on stainless and titanium, where colour indicates oxidation and loss of corrosion resistance or atmospheric contamination (Chapters 24 and 26).

9. Spatter in Full: Mechanism, Control and Acceptance

Spatter is classified as imperfection 602 in the miscellaneous group [S1][S2]. Its placement there understates its practical importance, so it is treated at length here and cross-referenced from every process chapter.

Mechanism. Spatter is molten metal ejected from the arc or pool that does not become part of the weld. It occurs whenever a droplet receives a momentum impulse larger than the surface tension retaining it (Chapter 22, Section 14). The specific sources:

1. Violent short-circuit rupture. In short-circuiting transfer, each short is cleared by an electromagnetic pinch. If the current rise rate is too aggressive — inductance set too low, or voltage too low forcing hard shorts — the bridge ruptures explosively and ejects metal [S4][S5].

2. Globular droplet repulsion. In the globular transfer range, droplets larger than the electrode diameter transfer erratically and are repelled and burst by arc forces. This is the highest-spatter operating region in gas metal arc welding [S4][S5].

3. Carbon dioxide arc force. CO₂-rich shielding increases arc force and droplet repulsion relative to argon [S5], which is why the standard first remedy is to raise the argon fraction — commonly to at least 80 % argon on steel — and avoid pure CO₂ [S5].

4. Contamination. Rust, mill scale, zinc coating, oil, paint and moisture generate gas within the pool that ejects metal as it escapes.

5. Wire feed instability. A worn liner, incorrect drive-roll pressure or a worn contact tip modulates wire feed speed, which modulates arc length and produces spatter before any other symptom is visible [S5].

6. Arc blow. Magnetic deflection destabilizes transfer, particularly near joint ends and earth connections [S5] (Chapter 22, Section 13).

7. Excessive current or voltage outside the stable operating envelope for the wire and gas combination.

Why it matters beyond appearance:

• Lost deposit. Ejected metal is purchased filler that did not become weld, directly reducing deposition efficiency.

• Removal labour, which on coated, architectural or hygienic work is frequently the dominant post-weld cost.

• Nozzle blockage, which disturbs shielding gas flow and causes porosity — so unmanaged spatter causes a second, more serious imperfection.

• A leading indicator. A rise in spatter on a stable production weld is among the earliest observable signs that gas supply, wire feed, contact tip, surface condition or earth connection has changed. Treating it as background noise discards a free diagnostic signal.

• Coating and corrosion consequences. Adherent spatter creates coating holidays and crevices.

Acceptance. Acceptance of adherent spatter is judged on whether it impairs the surface function — coating adhesion, fatigue performance, hygiene in food and pharmaceutical applications, or subsequent machining [S5]. In practice: coating-critical work typically requires complete removal; fatigue-loaded structures commonly require removal in stressed zones; general static structures frequently tolerate light spatter [S5]. On stainless steel, removal must be performed with stainless-only tooling, or the removal operation introduces iron contamination and a corrosion problem worse than the spatter (Chapter 24, Section 11).

Control order. Determine which transfer mode the parameters actually produce and get out of the globular range; raise the argon fraction; set inductance for a softer current rise in short-circuit; service the wire feed path; correct earth position for arc blow; clean the joint [S5]. Anti-spatter compounds and nozzle sprays reduce adherence but treat the symptom — they do not reduce the metal being ejected.

10. Quality Levels and How Acceptance Is Decided

ISO 5817 provides quality levels for imperfections in fusion-welded joints in steel, nickel, titanium and their alloys, excluding beam welding [S3]. It defines three levels:

| Level | Character |
| --- | --- |
| B | Stringent — the tightest limits |
| C | Intermediate |
| D | Moderate — the most permissive |

For each imperfection type, the standard states the limit applicable at each level, typically expressed as a function of material thickness or weld size rather than as an absolute dimension.

Three points govern their use:

The level is selected by the application, not by the fabricator. It is set by the design specification, the product standard or the contract, based on consequence of failure, loading type — static or fatigue — and service conditions.

A quality level is not a single pass/fail line but a set of limits per imperfection type. A weld can meet level B for porosity and fail level C for undercut. Reporting must be per imperfection type.

Some imperfections are not permitted at any level. Cracks are the principal case.

Level D is not "poor workmanship" — it is the appropriate level for applications where the consequence of the imperfection is genuinely low, and specifying level B universally is a common and expensive error that generates repairs adding more risk than the imperfections they remove (Section 13).

11. Which Acceptance Standard Applies to What

ISO 5817's scope is specific, and applying it outside that scope is a frequent error:

| Material / process | Acceptance standard |
| --- | --- |
| Fusion welds in steel, nickel, titanium and their alloys (beam welding excluded) | ISO 5817 [S3] |
| Arc welds in aluminium and its alloys | ISO 10042 |
| Electron and laser beam welds | ISO 13919 series |
| Structural steel under AWS practice | The acceptance provisions of AWS D1.1 [S6] |
| Pressure equipment | The applicable pressure code's own criteria |
| Resistance spot, seam and projection welds | The resistance welding standards (Volume 1, Chapter 10) |

Method-specific acceptance levels then translate a quality level into what may be seen by a given inspection method — ISO 10675-1 for radiography, ISO 11666 for ultrasonics, ISO 23277 for penetrant, ISO 23278 for magnetic particle (Chapter 35, Section 14). Specifying a quality level without the corresponding method acceptance level leaves the inspector unable to report a result.

13. Repair: When, How, and When Not To

A repair is a welding operation on a joint that has already been welded, and it is more demanding than the original weld — more restrained, potentially in a confined excavation, with an already thermally cycled heat-affected zone.

The sequence: establish the cause before repairing; define the extent by NDT before excavating; excavate fully to sound metal, confirmed by a surface method on the excavated surface; prepare a groove with proper access rather than a narrow slot; weld to a qualified repair procedure with preheat at least as conservative as the original; re-examine by the same methods and criteria.

Repair is not automatically the right answer. Three considerations argue against it:

1. A repair introduces its own risk. Higher restraint, an additional thermal cycle, and a heat-affected zone that has now been cycled two or three times. Repeated repairs at the same location are recognized as increasingly likely to produce a worse joint than the one being repaired, and many codes limit the number of repairs permitted at a location without engineering assessment.

2. A fitness-for-service assessment may show the imperfection is acceptable for the actual loading and service, even where it exceeds a workmanship acceptance criterion. Workmanship criteria are generally conservative and are not failure predictions.

3. The cause must be fixed regardless. Repairing every joint from a systematic cause while leaving the cause running produces the same defect in the next batch.

14. Decision Reference: Which Imperfections Are Always Unacceptable

| Imperfection | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Cracks of any type | Not permitted at any quality level in general fusion welding practice |
| Lack of fusion in fatigue-loaded joints | Effectively unacceptable — planar and crack-like |
| Incomplete penetration where CJP is specified | Unacceptable by definition |
| Arc strikes on hardenable material in critical service | Commonly prohibited; require removal and examination |
| Undercut in fatigue-loaded joints | Tightly limited; a primary fatigue initiation site |

15. Worked Example: An Acceptance Dispute Over Spatter and Arc Strikes

Situation. A structural fabricator delivers a painted steel assembly. The client's inspector rejects it for spatter across the members and for several arc strikes on the parent metal away from the joints. The fabricator's position is that the welds themselves are sound, all NDT passed, and the findings are cosmetic.

Step 1 — Separate the two findings. Spatter and arc strikes are both in group 6 but are entirely different in consequence, and treating them as one dispute guarantees a wrong outcome on at least one of them.

Step 2 — Assess the arc strikes on their mechanism, not their appearance. An arc strike is a small uncontrolled melt with a very rapid quench into cold parent metal. On hardenable steel it produces a hard, brittle micro-region that may contain cracks. The correct action is to examine each one with a surface method for cracking, then remove by grinding and re-examine. This is not cosmetic, and the fabricator's position is wrong on this point. It is also worth establishing where they came from — a poorly secured earth return connection is a common source and would recur.

Step 3 — Assess the spatter against function, not preference. The governing question is whether the adherent spatter impairs a surface function [S5]. This assembly is painted, so coating adhesion is directly relevant: spatter creates coating holidays where corrosion initiates. If the assembly is also fatigue-loaded, spatter in stressed zones is a further concern. On a purely static, unpainted structure the same spatter would commonly be tolerable.

Step 4 — Establish what the contract actually specified. The dispute is resolvable only against the specified quality level and any surface preparation specification for coating. If the contract specified a quality level and a coating standard, both state requirements that settle the matter. If it specified neither, the dispute is a contractual gap and the fabricator has a stronger position — which is an argument for specifying acceptance criteria at tender, not for arguing afterwards.

Step 5 — Address the cause, since both findings point at process control. Heavy spatter indicates parameters in the globular range, excessive CO₂, or a wire feed problem (Section 9). Arc strikes indicate earth return and handling practice. Both are correctable at source, and correcting them is cheaper than cleaning every subsequent assembly.

Step 6 — Agree the remedy proportionately. Arc strikes: remove and examine, without exception. Spatter: remove where it affects coating adhesion and in fatigue-stressed zones, using tooling appropriate to the material. Reject-and-rebuild would be disproportionate to either finding on this evidence.

Step 7 — Close the specification gap. The lasting fix is that future contracts state the quality level, the applicable acceptance standard, and the surface condition requirement for coating. Most spatter disputes are specification disputes wearing an inspection costume.

16. Known Gaps

• No acceptance limits are reproduced. ISO 5817 states its limits per imperfection type and quality level as functions of thickness and weld size; the standard is a purchased document and the limits belong to it.

• The reference numbers listed are those confirmed from a published summary of ISO 6520-1 [S2]. The standard contains many more sub-references than are listed here, and where an exact reference number matters it should be taken from the standard itself. Where this chapter describes an imperfection without printing a number, that reflects the limits of the summary used, not the absence of a number.

• ISO 5817's exclusion of beam welding and of aluminium is significant and is stated in Section 11; applying it outside its scope is a common error this chapter flags rather than resolves.

• Fitness-for-service assessment is named but not developed. It is governed by its own standards and requires fracture mechanics analysis outside this chapter's scope.

• Repair limits — how many repairs are permitted at one location — are code-specific and are not stated here.

1. The Hazard Inventory, and Which Hazards Actually Cause Harm

Welding presents an unusually broad hazard profile: electrical, optical, respiratory, thermal, chemical, mechanical, acoustic and atmospheric hazards all present simultaneously at one workstation.

The distribution of actual harm is not the distribution of perceived risk, and this is worth stating plainly at the outset:

• Burns and eye injuries are the most frequent injuries, and are mostly minor to moderate.

• Fire and explosion cause the largest single-event losses, often involving people who were not welding.

• Fume exposure causes the greatest total burden of serious harm, but the harm is chronic and delayed, so it is systematically under-perceived by the people exposed.

• Confined space asphyxiation causes the highest proportion of fatalities per event, and it is entirely imperceptible to the person affected.

Two of those four — fume and asphyxiation — give the person no useful warning at the time. That is precisely why they need engineered controls rather than vigilance.

2. Electric Shock

Welding equipment presents two distinct electrical hazards, and the more dangerous one is the one workers respect less.

Primary circuit shock. The mains supply to the welding machine — several hundred volts. Contact is usually fatal or seriously injurious. Guarded by conventional electrical safety practice: qualified installation, enclosure integrity, isolation before maintenance.

Secondary circuit shock. The welding circuit itself. Voltage is low during welding, but the open-circuit voltage present between electrode and work before the arc is struck is substantially higher. It is normally survivable, and that is the problem: it is treated as harmless until conditions change.

The conditions that make secondary shock dangerous:

• Moisture. Sweat, rain, condensation and wet clothing dramatically reduce skin resistance. A voltage that is a mild shock dry can be fatal wet.

• Confined and cramped positions, where the welder's body is in contact with the workpiece or with earthed structure over a large area and cannot recoil.

• Damaged insulation on cables, electrode holders and torches.

• Two machines' circuits in contact, where a welder can be exposed to the sum of two open-circuit voltages.

Controls: keep dry — including gloves and clothing; inspect cables, holders and torches before use and remove damaged equipment from service; never change electrodes with bare hands or wet gloves; connect the work return as close to the weld as practical and to the workpiece itself, not through the building structure; isolate before opening equipment; and use equipment with voltage-reducing devices where the risk assessment calls for it, particularly in damp or confined work.

The earth return connection deserves specific mention because it causes both a safety and a quality problem: a poor return connection produces arcing at the connection point, and a return routed through the building structure can energize unexpected paths and cause arc blow (Chapter 22, Section 13) and arc strikes at remote locations.

3. Arc Radiation and Eye Protection

The arc emits across the spectrum, and three bands cause harm:

Ultraviolet causes photokeratitis — "arc eye" or "welder's flash" — an inflammation of the cornea that appears several hours after exposure, feels like sand in the eyes, and lasts a day or two. It is painful, temporarily disabling and generally recovers fully. UV also causes skin erythema — sunburn — and, with chronic exposure, the same long-term skin risks as any UV source.

Visible light at arc intensity causes glare and, at extremes, retinal damage.

Infrared causes thermal injury to the eye and skin.

Key practical points:

• Filter shade must match the process and current. Shade selection tables exist for exactly this; too dark is a hazard in its own right because the welder cannot see the joint and compensates by lifting the helmet.

• Auto-darkening helmets must be verified as functioning before each use; a failed unit gives no protection at the moment of striking.

• Safety glasses under the helmet are required, not optional — the helmet protects against radiation and the glasses against slag, grinding debris and the flash from an adjacent bay when the helmet is lifted.

• UV reflects. Bright or light-coloured walls, aluminium surfaces and stainless sheet reflect UV effectively, and a bystander several metres away can receive an injurious dose. Welding screens and matt, UV-absorbing surface finishes protect other workers, and screening is a requirement in shared spaces rather than a courtesy.

• Covered skin. Long sleeves, gloves and a covered neck — UV penetrates thin or open-weave clothing, and welders working in hot conditions in short sleeves get burnt.

• Different processes radiate differently. Gas tungsten arc welding produces proportionally more UV than shielded metal arc welding at similar currents, and aluminium work reflects strongly.

4. Welding Fume: What Is Actually In It

Welding fume is not smoke from burning material. It is condensed metal vapour: metal boiled off at arc temperature, oxidized in air, and condensed into extremely fine particles, mixed with gases from the process and from any coating or contamination present.

Two properties determine the harm:

Particle size. Welding fume particles are very fine — well within the respirable range — so they are not filtered out by the upper airway and reach deep into the lungs.

Composition, which comes from three sources: the consumable (usually the largest contributor by mass), the parent metal, and anything on the parent metal — paint, primer, galvanizing, oil, plating.

The last of those is the one that produces the severe acute cases, because a welder can be exposed to a substance that appears nowhere on the material certificate or the consumable data sheet.

The general health effects of mixed welding fume include respiratory irritation, chronic respiratory disease, and increased susceptibility to respiratory infection. Welding fume as a class has been the subject of substantial occupational health scrutiny, and the direction of that scrutiny has consistently been toward tighter control rather than looser.

| Hexavalent chromium | Stainless and chromium-alloy welding, particularly with covered electrodes and flux-cored wire | Carcinogen; respiratory and nasal damage | Requires specific engineered control and exposure assessment; process and consumable choice materially change generation rate |
| Manganese | Present in almost all steel consumables | Neurological effects on chronic exposure | Ubiquitous, so control is about general fume management rather than a special case |
| Nickel | Stainless and nickel alloys | Carcinogen; sensitizer | As hexavalent chromium |

| Beryllium | Beryllium copper | Chronic beryllium disease; extremely low exposure limits | Specialist controlled process only (Chapter 26, Section 8) |
| Fluorides | Basic electrode coverings and some fluxes | Respiratory irritation | General fume control |
| Isocyanates and decomposition products | Welding through paints, primers and coatings | Sensitization, asthma, severe respiratory effects | Remove the coating from the weld zone before welding — this is the control, not respirators |

The general rule that follows: the material certificate does not describe the fume. Coatings, platings and prior surface treatments are frequently the dominant hazard, and identifying them is a pre-job step.

6. Gases Produced by the Process and by Contamination

Distinct from particulate fume, and each with its own mechanism:

Ozone. Formed by ultraviolet radiation acting on atmospheric oxygen. It is a strong respiratory irritant. Generation is highest with high-UV processes — gas metal arc welding of aluminium and gas tungsten arc welding, particularly under argon and at high current. It is a common cause of respiratory complaints in aluminium fabrication.

Nitrogen oxides. Formed by the arc's heating of atmospheric nitrogen and oxygen. Respiratory irritants with delayed effects, meaning symptoms can appear hours after exposure.

Carbon monoxide. Formed by the dissociation of carbon dioxide in the arc — relevant to CO₂ and CO₂-rich shielded welding, and significant in confined spaces where it accumulates.

Phosgene and related decomposition products. This one is specific, severe and insufficiently known: ultraviolet radiation from the arc decomposes chlorinated hydrocarbon vapours into phosgene and other highly toxic gases. Chlorinated solvents — used for degreasing — must therefore be kept entirely away from welding areas, and parts degreased with them must be fully dry and vented before welding. Degreasing baths and welding stations in the same room is a documented, severe hazard, and it produces harm without any visible smoke.

Shielding gases themselves as asphyxiants (Section 9).

7. The Control Hierarchy, Applied Honestly

The hierarchy — elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, personal protective equipment — is universally recited and unevenly applied. Applied to welding fume specifically:

Elimination. Can the joint be made without welding? Mechanical fastening, adhesive bonding or a different design removes the exposure entirely. Rarely available, but it should be asked before it is dismissed.

Substitution. This is the level most often skipped and it has more leverage in welding than in most trades:

• Process substitution. Fume generation rate differs substantially between processes for the same joint — a solid wire under gas-shielded conditions generates less fume than a covered electrode or a self-shielded flux-cored wire for comparable deposition.

• Consumable substitution. Fume generation and composition vary between consumable types meeting the same classification.

• Material substitution. Removing galvanizing or specifying an uncoated material for the weld zone eliminates zinc exposure at source.

Engineering controls. The load-bearing level in practice:

• Local exhaust ventilation capturing at the source — on-torch extraction, movable hoods, downdraft or backdraft benches. Capture at source is far more effective than general dilution ventilation, because it removes fume before it reaches the breathing zone.

• The capture point must actually be near the arc. An extraction hood two metres away is decorative. On-gun extraction works because it is inherently positioned correctly.

• General ventilation dilutes what escapes capture; it is a supplement, not a substitute.

• Positioning. The single most effective free control is to keep the head out of the plume — the fume plume rises, and a welder leaning directly over the arc is in it.

Administrative controls. Job rotation, restricted access, scheduling high-fume work when fewer people are present.

Personal protective equipment. Respiratory protection — from disposable respirators through to powered air-purifying respirators integrated into welding helmets. PPE is last in the hierarchy because it depends on correct selection, correct fit, correct use and correct maintenance, every time, by every person. It is not a substitute for extraction, and where extraction is absent the PPE is compensating for a missing control rather than adding to one.

8. Fire and Explosion

Welding and cutting are the classic hot work hazards, and hot work fires characteristically injure people who were not welding and start in places nobody was watching.

The mechanisms:

• Sparks and spatter travel — a substantial horizontal distance on the flat, and much further when falling from height. They find combustibles through floor openings, wall penetrations, conveyor gaps and cable routes.

• Conduction through the material. The far side of a wall or bulkhead can ignite insulation or stored material, without any spark travelling at all. This is the mechanism behind many serious hot work fires and it defeats a fire watch that only watches the visible side.

• Smouldering. Fires from hot work frequently develop slowly and break out well after work has finished — which is why fire watch requirements extend after the work stops, not just during it.

Controls: a hot work permit system with a genuine authorization step; removal of combustibles from the area, or protection where removal is impossible; covering floor openings and penetrations; a fire watch during work and for a defined period after it; appropriate extinguishing equipment present and known to work; and a check of the far side of any wall, bulkhead, deck or partition being welded.

Containers and vessels that have held flammable material deserve their own treatment, because this is a recurring source of fatal explosions. A drum or tank that "had fuel in it once" can retain enough vapour or residue in seams, scale and linings to explode. The controls are cleaning, purging or inerting, and gas testing, per an established procedure — and the rule that a container of unknown history is treated as dangerous rather than as probably empty.

9. Confined Spaces and Asphyxiation

The highest-lethality hazard in welding, and the one that gives no warning.

The mechanism. Argon, carbon dioxide and nitrogen are odourless, colourless and heavier than air. They displace oxygen and accumulate in low-lying and enclosed spaces — vessel bottoms, pits, trenches, tank interiors, double-bottom compartments. A person entering an oxygen-deficient atmosphere loses consciousness rapidly and without the sensation of suffocation, because the physiological drive to breathe responds to carbon dioxide build-up, not to oxygen absence.

The specific welding contribution: a purged vessel or pipe is an oxygen-deficient atmosphere by design (Chapter 30, Section 7). A pipe spool purged with argon overnight, or a vessel purged for a root pass, is lethal to anyone who puts their head inside it. This has killed people, including experienced ones, and including would-be rescuers.

Controls: confined space entry procedures with permit, atmosphere testing before and continuously during entry, forced ventilation, attendant outside, rescue arrangements established before entry, and — specific to welding — removal or isolation of gas supplies during breaks so that a leaking torch does not fill a space while nobody is watching.

Never enter to rescue without breathing apparatus. A large proportion of confined space fatalities are rescuers, and the instinct to help is precisely what kills them.

10. Noise, Heat, Ergonomics and Electromagnetic Fields

Noise. Air carbon arc gouging and plasma cutting are genuinely high-noise operations requiring hearing protection; most arc welding is not, but the associated grinding and chipping is.

Heat stress. Radiant heat from the arc and the workpiece, plus heavy protective clothing, plus confined or elevated positions. Manageable with work-rest cycles, hydration and cooling, and worth explicit planning in hot climates and in vessel interiors, where heat exhaustion also degrades judgement about every other hazard on this list.

Ergonomics. Sustained awkward postures, overhead work, vibration from grinders and manual handling of cylinders and assemblies. Musculoskeletal disorders are among the most common causes of long-term absence in fabrication.

Electromagnetic fields. Welding currents generate strong fields close to cables and the workpiece. The established precautions are to keep cables together and close to the body's side rather than draped around the torso, avoid coiling cable around the body, and keep the welder's body away from the loop formed by the electrode and return cables. People with implanted medical devices such as pacemakers must obtain specific medical advice before working near welding equipment.

Two of those warrant emphasis because they surprise people: electron beam welding produces X-rays, which is why EBW machines are shielded enclosures rather than open workstations; and grinding thoriated tungsten electrodes produces low-level radioactive dust, which is a genuine reason many shops have moved to lanthanated or ceriated types (Chapter 29, Section 6).

12. Governing Standards

ANSI/AWS Z49.1, Safety in Welding, Cutting, and Allied Processes, is the principal consensus safety standard for the industry and covers ventilation, fire prevention, protective equipment, confined spaces and electrical safety [S1].

OSHA 29 CFR 1910 Subpart Q covers welding, cutting and brazing in United States workplaces, with related provisions for confined spaces, respiratory protection, hazard communication and permissible exposure limits appearing elsewhere in the same part.

International and European standards cover equipment safety, protective clothing, eye protection and fume sampling — including standards for fume sampling in the breathing zone and for the performance of protective equipment.

Exposure limits are set by national regulation, differ between jurisdictions, and change. Any figure quoted from memory is unreliable, and the applicable limit must be taken from the regulation in force in the jurisdiction of the work.

15. Worked Example: A Fume Exposure Problem in a Stainless Fabrication Bay

Situation. A fabricator receives complaints of respiratory irritation from welders in a stainless bay. Local exhaust arms are installed at each bay. Management's response is to issue better respirators.

Step 1 — Establish what is actually in the fume before controlling it. Stainless welding generates hexavalent chromium and nickel — both carcinogens with specific control requirements — plus manganese from the consumable. This is not general fume, and treating it as general fume under-controls it. Any coating, marking or residual contamination on the material adds further substances that neither the material certificate nor the consumable data sheet lists.

Step 2 — Check whether the installed engineering control is being used and is capable. Extraction arms are the most commonly installed and most commonly ineffective control, for a specific reason: they only work if positioned within a short distance of the arc, and repositioning them for every weld is work the welder must repeatedly do. Arms parked out of the way, or left at the last position from an hour ago, provide nothing. This should be observed in production rather than asked about.

Step 3 — Check the welder's position relative to the plume. The plume rises. A welder leaning over the joint puts their breathing zone directly in it, and no extraction arm placed to the side recovers that. Position and, where the joint allows it, part orientation are free controls that are frequently available.

Step 4 — Evaluate the substitution options that were skipped. Different processes and consumable types generate substantially different quantities of fume for the same deposited metal, and process choice is the highest-leverage change available. Whether it is feasible depends on the joint, the position and the quality requirements — but it should be assessed rather than assumed unavailable, and assessing it is an engineering decision, not a safety-officer decision.

Step 5 — Reject respirators as the primary answer. Respiratory protection is last in the hierarchy because it depends on correct selection, fit testing, consistent use and maintenance. Issuing better respirators while leaving an ineffective engineering control in place moves the burden of protection from the building to the individual, every hour of every shift. It is also, in most jurisdictions, not what the regulation requires where engineering control is reasonably practicable.

Step 6 — Measure, since this is a substance with specific limits. For hexavalent chromium and nickel, personal exposure monitoring in the breathing zone establishes what the exposure actually is against the applicable limit. Complaints establish that there is a problem; measurement establishes its size and whether a control has fixed it.

Step 7 — Fix in hierarchy order and verify. Assess process and consumable substitution first; then improve capture at source — on-torch extraction removes the repositioning problem by design, and a moveable hood with a positioning discipline is second best; then address positioning and general ventilation; then select respiratory protection appropriate to the residual exposure, with fit testing. Re-measure afterwards: a control that has not been verified by measurement is an intention.

16. Known Gaps

• No exposure limits are quoted. They vary by jurisdiction and change over time; the regulation in force at the place of work governs.

• No filter shade numbers are tabulated. Shade selection tables are published in the safety standards by process and current, and reproducing values risks their misapplication.

• Spark travel distances and fire watch durations are described qualitatively. Both are specified numerically in hot work standards and in insurers' requirements, and those govern.

• This chapter does not constitute a risk assessment. It identifies hazards and control principles; a risk assessment for actual work must consider the specific materials, coatings, location, ventilation, personnel and emergency arrangements.

• Regulatory frameworks outside the United States are referred to generically. National regulations differ substantially in structure and in duty-holder obligations.

1. Process Overview: ISO 4063 Reference 111

Shielded metal arc welding — reference 111 in the ISO nomenclature, and known universally as stick welding or manual metal arc welding [S1] — strikes an arc between a flux-covered consumable electrode and the workpiece. The electrode melts and is deposited as filler; the covering melts, decomposes and forms both a shielding gas and a slag blanket over the solidifying weld.

The whole process consists of a power source, a cable, an electrode holder, a work return clamp and a box of electrodes. Nothing is fed, nothing is pumped, no gas is supplied. That simplicity is the entire basis of its continued relevance: it works outdoors in wind, at the end of a long cable, on a rusty surface, in any position, on a wide range of materials, with equipment that can be carried.

Its costs are equally clear: the electrode is consumed to a stub and must be changed every minute or two, the slag must be removed between every pass, and the duty cycle — the proportion of working time actually spent with an arc established — is low compared with continuous-wire processes. It is a low-productivity, high-flexibility process.

2. What the Covering Actually Does

The covering is the engineered part of the electrode, and it performs five distinct jobs simultaneously:

1. Generates shielding gas. Covering constituents decompose in the arc to produce a gas envelope that displaces atmospheric oxygen and nitrogen. This is why no external gas supply is needed and why the process tolerates wind that would strip the shielding from a gas-shielded process.

2. Forms slag. Molten covering floats to the surface of the pool and solidifies as a slag layer that protects the weld metal during cooling, slows the cooling rate, and — with fast-freezing formulations — physically supports the pool out of position.

3. Stabilizes the arc. Ionizing agents in the covering lower the effective ionization potential of the arc atmosphere, allowing a stable arc, and in particular allowing operation on alternating current, which would otherwise extinguish at every zero crossing.

4. Adds alloying elements and deoxidizers. The covering carries deoxidizers such as manganese and silicon, and can carry alloying additions, so the deposit's composition is not simply that of the core wire.

5. Shapes the bead and controls penetration. Covering formulation determines arc force and pool fluidity, which determine bead profile and penetration depth.

The design tension in electrode formulation is between jobs 1 and 4. Cellulosic coverings generate a large volume of shielding gas through decomposition — producing a forceful, deeply penetrating arc — but the decomposition products include hydrogen. Basic (low-hydrogen) coverings produce far less hydrogen and better toughness, but a softer arc with less penetration and worse out-of-position handling on the root. That trade is the reason both types survive.

3. Equipment and Components

| Component | Function | Failure consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Power source | Provides a constant-current (drooping) output: current stays approximately constant as arc length and therefore voltage varies | Constant-voltage output is wrong for SMAW; using it makes arc length uncontrollable |
| Output control | Sets welding current; modern inverters also provide arc force and hot start controls | Current outside the electrode's range causes lack of fusion or burn-through and undercut |
| Arc force (dig) control | Momentarily increases current as arc length shortens, preventing the electrode sticking | Without it, low-current root work sticks the electrode repeatedly |
| Hot start | Brief current boost at arc initiation | Poor starting; start porosity and lack of fusion at each restart |
| Electrode holder | Clamps and energizes the electrode; insulated | Damaged insulation is a direct shock hazard; poor clamping causes heating and arc instability |
| Welding cable | Carries current to the holder | Undersized or damaged cable causes voltage drop, heating and unstable arc |
| Work return clamp and cable | Completes the circuit at the workpiece | A poor return connection causes arc instability, arc blow, and arcing at the connection point |
| Chipping hammer and wire brush | Slag removal between passes | Inadequate interpass cleaning is the leading cause of slag inclusions |
| Electrode oven and quiver | Maintains low-hydrogen electrodes at temperature | Without it, low-hydrogen electrodes stop being low-hydrogen (Section 5) |

Polarity is set at the machine. Most low-hydrogen electrodes run on DC electrode positive (DCEP) or AC; cellulosic electrodes are specified per class; some classes are AC-only or DC-only. Running an electrode on a polarity it is not designed for produces an unstable arc and a deposit that does not meet its classification.

4. Consumables: The Electrode Classes and What Each Is For

The classification structure is decoded in Chapter 29, Section 3. The practical selection:

| Class | Covering | Character | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| E6010 | Cellulosic sodium, DCEP | Deep, digging penetration; fast-freezing; not low hydrogen | Open-root pipe welding; work over rust and mill scale; the classic field root electrode |
| E6011 | Cellulosic potassium | As E6010 but AC-capable | Field work with AC machines |
| E6013 | Rutile | Soft arc, shallow penetration, excellent appearance, easy to run | Sheet metal, light fabrication, general purpose |
| E7014 | Rutile with iron powder | Higher deposition than E6013, easy operation | General fabrication where speed matters more than penetration |
| E7018 | Basic, low hydrogen, iron powder | Low hydrogen, good toughness, moderate penetration | The structural workhorse; higher-strength and thicker material; anything with a cracking risk |
| E7024 | Rutile, high iron powder | Very high deposition, flat and horizontal only | Long fillet welds in the flat position |
| Low-alloy classes | Basic, alloyed | Matched to Cr-Mo, high-strength and low-temperature grades | Creep-resistant, high-strength and low-temperature service |
| Stainless classes | Per Chapter 24 | Alloy-matched, ferrite-controlled deposits | Stainless fabrication |
| Nickel classes (cast iron) | ENi-CI, ENiFe-CI | Soft ductile deposits absorbing contraction strain | Cast iron repair (Chapter 26) |

The E6010 / E7018 combination is the most common pairing in pipe welding: a cellulosic root pass for its penetration and pool control on an open root, followed by low-hydrogen fill and cap for their toughness and hydrogen safety. It is worth understanding *why* this apparently contradictory combination is used — the root's hydrogen contribution is small relative to the fill volume and is largely driven off by subsequent passes, while the root's need for a controllable, fast-freezing, penetrating arc is absolute.

5. Electrode Storage and the Hydrogen Discipline

This is the single most consequential operational discipline in the process, and Chapter 29, Section 10 sets out the general rules. The SMAW-specific points:

• Low-hydrogen electrodes are hygroscopic. The covering absorbs atmospheric moisture from the moment the sealed packet is opened, and moisture is a hydrogen source (Chapter 23, Section 5).

• Holding ovens keep opened electrodes at the manufacturer's specified temperature. Quivers — portable heated containers — carry a limited quantity to the work.

• Exposure time on the shop floor must be limited and enforced, and the limit depends on the classification, the hydrogen designator and the ambient humidity.

• Re-baking to the manufacturer's schedule can restore some electrodes, a limited number of times.

• Cellulosic electrodes must never be baked. Their covering depends on retained moisture to generate its shielding gas; drying them destroys their operating characteristics. This is a genuine trap, because a well-intentioned store that bakes everything ruins its E6010 stock.

6. Parameters and What Each One Controls

| Parameter | Set by | Controls | Symptom if wrong |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Current | Machine, within the electrode's stated range | Deposition rate, penetration, heat input | Too low: lack of fusion, slag inclusions, electrode sticking. Too high: undercut, excess spatter, burn-through, covering breakdown and overheating of the electrode |
| Electrode diameter | Selection | Current range available; access into the groove | Too large for the root: cannot reach the fusion faces |
| Arc length | The welder's hand | Arc voltage, and therefore heat and shielding integrity | Too long: porosity, spatter, undercut, arc wander. Too short: sticking, narrow bead, slag entrapment |
| Travel speed | The welder's hand | Heat input per unit length, bead width and profile | Too fast: narrow bead, lack of fusion, undercut, centreline cracking. Too slow: excess deposit, overlap, excessive heat |
| Electrode angle | The welder's hand | Where the arc force is directed; slag control | Wrong angle: slag ahead of the pool, inclusions, uneven profile |
| Polarity | Machine | Heat distribution and arc character | Wrong polarity for the class: unstable arc, non-conforming deposit |

The defining characteristic of SMAW is that three of the six variables are in the welder's hands and are not recorded anywhere. A WPS states current and polarity; it cannot state arc length. This is why welder qualification matters so much more in SMAW than in mechanized processes, and why SMAW production quality tracks welder skill more directly than any other process in this volume.

7. Joint Types and Positions

SMAW is an all-position process, subject to the electrode class permitting it. The positional digit in the classification is not advisory: an electrode classified for flat and horizontal only will not hold a pool overhead.

| Position | Practice |
| --- | --- |
| Flat (PA / 1G, 1F) | Highest deposition; use high-deposition classes such as E7024 where available |
| Horizontal (PC / 2G, 2F) | Slight electrode angle to counter pool sag; smaller electrodes on the upper toe |
| Vertical up (PF / 3G) | Weaving common; higher penetration and deposit thickness; used where strength matters |
| Vertical down (PG) | Fast, low penetration; suitable for thin material and cosmetic passes; a known lack-of-fusion risk on thick material |
| Overhead (PE / 4G, 4F) | Smaller electrodes and lower current; fast-freezing coverings; the position that most demands electrode class discipline |

Joint access requirements follow Chapter 28: the groove angle must allow the electrode — including its covering — to reach the fusion faces at an appropriate angle, which makes SMAW less suited to deep narrow preparations than processes with a smaller physical torch envelope.

8. Setup and Execution Procedure

The following is a general execution sequence. It does not replace a qualified WPS, which governs all parameter values.

Before striking an arc

1. Confirm the WPS covering this joint, material and thickness is available, current, and applies to the work in front of you.

2. Confirm your own qualification covers the process, position, thickness and material group (Chapter 32).

3. Verify the electrode classification and diameter against the WPS, and take electrodes from the oven or quiver, not from an open packet on the bench.

4. Inspect the joint preparation against the WPS: groove angle, root face, root gap, alignment, cleanliness. Reject fit-up outside tolerance rather than compensating for it with technique.

5. Clean the joint and adjacent surfaces of rust, scale, oil, moisture, paint and coating for the distance the specification requires.

6. Verify preheat where required — measured on the correct surface, with a calibrated instrument, over the specified heated band (Chapter 34, Section 6).

7. Set the machine: polarity per the electrode class, current within the WPS range, arc force and hot start as appropriate.

8. Connect the work return to the workpiece, as close to the joint as practical, with a clean contact surface.

9. Check the electrode holder, cable and clamp insulation; confirm dry gloves and clothing.

10. Confirm screens are in place, the extraction is positioned, and the fire watch and hot work permit requirements are satisfied.

Root pass

11. Strike the arc inside the joint or on a run-on tab — never on the parent metal outside the weld, which produces an arc strike (Chapter 36, Section 8).

12. Establish the arc length and hold it: approximately the electrode core diameter is the conventional starting point.

13. Run the root at the specified angle and travel speed, watching the keyhole or root bead formation rather than the arc.

14. At the end of the electrode, break the arc by moving forward slightly then lifting — leaving a taper rather than a crater.

15. Chip and brush the slag completely before restarting. Restarts are a defect-prone location and deserve deliberate attention.

16. Restart ahead of the crater, run back into it to re-establish the pool, then continue forward.

17. Inspect the root visually — and, on a joint where the root will be covered, this is the last opportunity to see it.

Fill and cap

18. Verify interpass temperature against the WPS minimum and maximum before each pass (Chapter 34, Section 7).

19. Remove slag completely between every pass, including from the groove faces and any undercut at the toes.

20. Deposit fill passes with the electrode angle directed at the fusion faces, keeping bead size within the WPS.

21. Watch for and correct any undercut at the toes before it is buried by the next pass — undercut becomes a slag trap.

22. Cap with the specified reinforcement and profile, keeping toe angles smooth.

23. Fill every crater at every termination.

After welding

24. Clean the completed weld of slag and spatter.

25. Perform visual inspection against the acceptance criteria.

26. Observe any specified delay before final non-destructive testing where hydrogen cracking is credible (Chapter 35, Section 12).

27. Record the joint against the welder, the WPS revision, the consumable batch and the heat treatment, per the traceability requirement (Chapter 33, Section 6).

9. Technique: The Four Variables in the Welder's Hands

Arc length. The single most important manual variable. Too long draws air into the arc and produces porosity, spatter and undercut; too short causes sticking and traps slag. The conventional guide is an arc length approximately equal to the electrode core diameter, reduced for low-hydrogen electrodes, which run best short.

Travel angle. The tilt of the electrode along the direction of travel. A drag (backhand) angle is standard for most SMAW, directing arc force into the pool and helping hold the slag behind. Excessive drag traps slag; a push angle reduces penetration.

Work angle. The tilt across the joint. It aims the arc force at the fusion faces and, in fillet welds, controls whether the leg lengths come out equal.

Weaving. Lateral oscillation to widen the bead. It increases heat input and deposit width per pass and helps fusion on the groove faces, particularly vertical-up. It is limited by the WPS, because unlimited weaving increases heat input beyond the qualified range, and excessive weave width is a common cause of slag entrapment at the bead edges.

10. When to Use SMAW and When Not To

| Choose SMAW when | Choose something else when |
| --- | --- |
| Working outdoors or in wind — the covering shields where a gas would be stripped | High deposition rate is the priority — GMAW, FCAW or SAW deposit far faster |
| Access is poor and equipment must be carried in | Long continuous seams in the flat position — SAW is far more productive |
| The work is repair, maintenance or short intermittent welds | Thin sheet — GMAW short-circuit or GTAW give better control |
| Material is rusty, painted or imperfectly prepared — cellulosic classes tolerate it | Aluminium, titanium, or reactive metals — gas-shielded processes are required |
| A wide range of materials must be welded with one machine | Fume generation must be minimized — SMAW generates more than gas-shielded solid wire |
| Power supply is limited or a generator is the only source | Duty cycle and labour cost dominate the economics |
| Open-root pipe welding where E6010 root control is wanted | High-volume repetitive production — any mechanized process wins |

11. Defect Catalog

| Defect | ISO 6520-1 ref | Detection | SMAW-specific causes | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Slag inclusion | 301 | RT | Inadequate interpass cleaning; excessive weave; drag angle too steep pushing slag ahead; undercut from a previous pass trapping slag; groove too narrow | Clean completely between passes; limit weave; correct electrode angle; remove undercut before covering |
| Porosity | 201, 2011 | RT; visual | Damp electrode covering; arc length too long; rust, oil, paint, moisture on the joint; welding over a contaminated restart | Control electrode storage and exposure; shorten arc; clean the joint; brush restarts |
| Lack of fusion | 401, 4011 | UT, PAUT | Current too low; travel too fast; electrode too large for the groove; arc directed at the pool rather than the fusion face | Increase current within range; correct angle and speed; smaller electrode for access |
| Incomplete penetration | 402 | RT, UT | Root gap too small; root face too thick; current too low for the root; electrode too large | Correct fit-up; adjust root parameters; use the specified root electrode class |
| Undercut | 501 | Visual, MT | Current too high; arc too long; excessive weave; incorrect work angle | Reduce current; shorten arc; control weave; correct angle |
| Arc strike | 601 | Visual; MT for cracking | Striking outside the joint; holder or cable contacting the parent metal | Strike inside the joint or on a tab; insulate and secure the holder; grind out and examine any strike |
| Hydrogen crack | 106 | MT/PT after delay; UT | Exposed low-hydrogen electrodes; cellulosic electrodes used where low hydrogen was required; insufficient preheat | Enforce oven and quiver discipline; verify class against the WPS; correct preheat |
| Spatter | 602 | Visual | Arc too long; current too high; damp electrode; wrong polarity for the class; arc blow | Shorten arc; correct current and polarity; verify electrode condition; reposition the earth return |

| Excessive reinforcement | Group 5 | Visual, dimensional | Travel too slow; current too low for the deposition | Increase travel speed; correct current |

12. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Electrode sticking repeatedly

Symptom: the electrode freezes to the work at strike or during low-current work.

Category: parameter / equipment.

Likely causes: current too low for the electrode diameter; arc force control set too low or absent; damp electrode; poor work return connection reducing available current; welder holding too short an arc at strike.

Steps: verify current against the electrode's stated range; check and increase arc force; check the return connection and cable condition; verify electrode condition and storage; check machine output under load rather than at the panel setting.

Card 2 — Arc wanders and undercuts one side

Symptom: the arc pulls consistently to one side; undercut and porosity on that side.

Category: magnetic arc blow.

Likely causes: DC welding with the return connection at one end; residual magnetism in the material; welding near a joint end or an abrupt section change; nearby magnetic lifting equipment or previous magnetic particle inspection.

Steps: reposition or split the earth return; weld toward the return connection; use run-off tabs at joint ends; reduce current; switch to AC where the electrode class and procedure permit; demagnetize the material (Chapter 22, Section 13).

Card 3 — Slag is difficult to remove and inclusions are found

Symptom: slag adheres tightly; radiography shows inclusions.

Category: technique / joint design.

Likely causes: groove angle too narrow for the electrode; excessive weave leaving slag at the bead edges; travel angle pushing slag ahead of the pool; previous pass left undercut at the toes; current too low producing a cold, ropey bead.

Steps: check the groove angle against the electrode diameter; reduce weave width; correct the drag angle; grind out undercut before covering; increase current within the WPS range; confirm interpass cleaning is being done at all rather than partially.

Card 4 — Porosity appearing only on site work

Symptom: shop welds clean, identical site welds porous.

Category: consumable condition / environment.

Likely causes: electrodes carried to site in an unheated container or an opened packet; humidity and condensation; joint surfaces damp or contaminated; no preheat to remove surface moisture.

Steps: verify quiver use and exposure time at the point of work; check whether electrodes were returned to the oven overnight; check joint surface condition and apply a warm-through to remove moisture; verify preheat measurement is being done on site with a calibrated instrument.

Card 5 — Welder produces good caps and rejectable roots

Symptom: consistent root defects, sound fill and cap.

Category: qualification / technique / fit-up.

Likely causes: welder qualified with backing but working open-root; root electrode class wrong for open-root control; root gap inconsistent; root face outside tolerance.

Steps: check the welder's qualification specifically for backing and progression (Chapter 32, Section 6); verify the root electrode class against the WPS; measure fit-up on several joints — intermittency points at fit-up rather than technique.

13. Safety Specifics

Beyond the general framework of Chapter 37:

• Fume generation is higher than gas-shielded solid wire processes for comparable deposition, and basic coverings generate fluorides. Local exhaust at source is required in enclosed spaces and advisable generally.

• Electrode stubs are hot and sharp and are a slip and burn hazard; stub containers at the workstation are standard practice.

• The holder is live whenever the machine is on. Never place a live holder on the workpiece or the bench; use an insulated hanger.

• Slag chipping ejects hot, sharp particles — eye protection under the helmet is not optional.

• Confined-space work combines shock risk from damp conditions with fume accumulation; both controls are required together.

14. Standards and Qualification

• Process reference: ISO 4063 reference 111 [S1].

• Consumables: AWS A5.1 (carbon steel), A5.5 (low alloy), A5.4 (stainless covered), A5.11 (nickel covered), A5.15 (cast iron); ISO 2560 (non-alloy and fine-grain steels), ISO 3581 (stainless).

• Procedure qualification: ASME Section IX, the ISO 15614 family, or AWS D1.1 — including D1.1's prequalified route, for which SMAW with low-hydrogen electrodes on approved base metals is a common qualifying case (Chapter 31).

• Welder qualification: ISO 9606-1 or the applicable code (Chapter 32).

• Acceptance: ISO 5817 quality levels, or the code's own criteria (Chapter 36).

15. Worked Example: Porosity on a Site Repair That Passed in the Shop

Situation. A contractor performs a structural repair on site using E7018. Radiography shows scattered porosity through the fill passes. The identical repair procedure, welded in the shop the previous week on a mock-up, was clean. The welder, the machine and the electrode classification are the same.

Step 1 — Use the shop-versus-site comparison, which is the strongest evidence available. Same welder, same procedure, same classification, different result. The cause is almost certainly something that differs between the two environments, not something intrinsic to the procedure or the person.

Step 2 — Establish what actually differs. Electrode handling and storage; ambient humidity and temperature; joint surface condition on an in-service structure against a clean mock-up; preheat capability and verification on site; the work return connection arrangement; and wind or draught conditions.

Step 3 — Check electrode condition first, because E7018 is hygroscopic and porosity is the symptom it produces. The specific questions: were electrodes taken to site in a heated quiver or in an opened packet in a toolbox; how long were they out of the oven; were they returned to the oven overnight or left in the van; what was the humidity. A day in a damp van is enough to take an E7018 out of its classification.

Step 4 — Check the joint surface. An in-service structure carries paint, primer, grease, rust and possibly moisture. A mock-up does not. Cleaning to the specification's distance either side is frequently curtailed on site because access is awkward, and welding over a coating produces both porosity and, depending on the coating, a serious fume hazard (Chapter 37, Section 5).

Step 5 — Check preheat, which is doing two jobs here. On site, preheat is often applied with a torch and verified with a crayon or not at all. Beyond its metallurgical role, preheat removes surface moisture — so an unverified preheat on a cold, damp structure loses a porosity control as well as a cracking control.

Step 6 — Check arc length as a secondary factor. Site work in awkward positions and restricted access tends to lengthen the arc, which draws air in. This is a real contributor but it should be considered after the material and consumable factors, because it is the hardest to verify and the easiest to blame.

Step 7 — Correct the system rather than the joint. The repair must be excavated and rewelded. The lasting fix is a site consumable control — heated quivers with an enforced exposure limit and a return-to-oven discipline — plus a joint preparation standard for site work with a verified cleaning extent, and calibrated preheat measurement in the site kit. Every one of those is a Chapter 33 requirement that a shop satisfies by default and a site team has to be equipped for explicitly.

16. Known Gaps

• No current ranges are given. They depend on electrode class, diameter, position and material, and are stated on the manufacturer's packaging and in the WPS.

• No electrode oven temperatures or exposure limits are stated. These are manufacturer- and classification-specific.

• Technique guidance in Sections 8 and 9 is generic. It describes the sequence and the variables; it does not substitute for training, and no written description teaches manual arc control.

• Electrode classes are described by their common carbon steel designations. Low-alloy, stainless and nickel classes follow the same structure with alloy suffixes covered in Chapter 29.

• The E6010/E7018 root-and-fill combination is described as established practice; whether it is permitted on a given job is a matter for the governing code and the WPS.
