1. Process Overview: ISO 4063 References 131 and 135

Gas metal arc welding feeds a continuous solid wire electrode through a torch, strikes an arc between the wire and the work, and shields the arc and pool with a gas supplied through the torch nozzle. The wire is both the electrode and the filler.

The ISO nomenclature splits it by shielding gas: 131 is MIG welding with a solid wire electrode, using an inert gas, and 135 is MAG welding with a solid wire electrode, using an active gas mixture [S1]. Both are called GMAW in AWS terminology, and both are called "MIG" in workshop conversation — an imprecision that matters, because the gas determines the transfer mode available and the deposit chemistry (Chapter 21, Section 12).

Its dominance in production fabrication comes from three properties: continuous wire feed with no stopping to change electrodes, no slag to remove between passes, and high deposition rates. Its weaknesses are equally consistent: total dependence on shielding gas, which restricts it in wind; sensitivity to the wire feed path; and — the one that causes the most structural failures — the ease with which it produces lack of fusion when the wrong transfer mode is used.

2. The Four Metal Transfer Modes

Everything else in this chapter follows from this section. The way molten metal crosses the arc from the wire tip to the pool determines the heat input, the position capability, the spatter level and the fusion characteristics of the process. Four modes exist, and they are not settings on a dial — they are physical regimes determined by current, voltage, wire diameter and, critically, shielding gas.

| Mode | Current level | Gas requirement | Positions | Spatter | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Short-circuiting | Lowest | Any, including CO₂ | All | Moderate — controllable | Thin material, open roots, out-of-position |
| Globular | Low-to-medium | Any; unavoidable under CO₂ | Flat, horizontal | Highest | Not deliberately selected |
| Spray | High | ≥ ~80 % argon | Flat, horizontal | Very low | Thick material, high deposition |
| Pulsed spray | Average low, peak high | ≥ ~80 % argon | All | Very low | All-position work needing spray quality |

The most important structural fact in the table: globular transfer sits between short-circuit and spray, and it is the worst operating region on every count. Understanding that the process must be operated *deliberately on one side or the other* of the globular range is the single most useful piece of GMAW knowledge a person can hold.

3. Short-Circuiting Transfer

Mechanism. At low current and voltage, the wire feeds forward until it physically touches the pool. The arc extinguishes, current rises through the short, and the electromagnetic pinch force severs the molten bridge. The arc re-establishes, the wire burns back, and the cycle repeats — at a rate on the order of tens to a couple of hundred times per second [S3].

Characteristics. The lowest heat input of any GMAW mode; a small, fast-freezing pool that can be held in any position; suitable for thin material, for bridging root gaps, and for open-root work; and tolerant of poor fit-up compared with other modes.

The critical limitation, stated plainly: short-circuiting transfer has the lowest heat input of the four modes, and heat input is what fuses the groove faces. On thick section, it is entirely capable of depositing a well-formed, visually excellent bead that has not fused to the sidewall. This is the classic cold lap or lack-of-sidewall-fusion failure, it is planar, it is not reliably detectable by radiography (Chapter 35, Section 1), and it is the mechanism behind a substantial proportion of GMAW structural failures.

The rule that follows: short-circuit transfer is for thin material, roots and out-of-position work — not for filling thick sections. Where thick section must be welded out of position, pulsed transfer is the correct answer, not short-circuit at higher settings, because raising the settings does not stay in short-circuit mode; it moves into globular.

Inductance is the machine parameter that shapes the current rise during each short. Higher inductance gives a slower rise, a softer break, less spatter and a more fluid pool; lower inductance gives a faster rise, a harder break, a colder pool and more spatter. An aggressive current rise makes the bridge rupture explosively and eject metal [S4] — which is why inductance is the first thing to check on a spattery short-circuit weld after the transfer mode itself.

4. Globular Transfer: The Region to Avoid

Mechanism. Above the short-circuit range but below the spray transition, droplets grow on the wire tip until they are larger than the wire diameter, then detach irregularly under gravity and arc forces. Under CO₂ shielding, arc forces actively repel the droplet upward and away from the joint rather than propelling it into the pool [S3][S4].

Characteristics. Erratic transfer, an unstable arc, and the highest spatter of any mode — the published characterization is precisely that large droplets transfer erratically, repelled and burst by arc forces, making it the highest-spatter operating region [S4]. Limited to flat and horizontal positions because the large droplets cannot be controlled against gravity [S3]. Penetration is inconsistent.

Nobody selects globular transfer deliberately. It is where a machine ends up when parameters are set between the two useful regimes, or when the shielding gas will not support spray. This second case is the important one: under pure CO₂, spray transfer is unavailable at any current, because spray requires an argon-rich atmosphere [S3]. A shop welding under CO₂ and pushing the current up to increase deposition therefore moves from short-circuit straight into globular and stays there — which is exactly why CO₂-shielded GMAW has a reputation for heavy spatter.

5. Spray Transfer

Mechanism. Above a threshold known as the globular-to-spray transition current, and in an argon-rich atmosphere, the droplet detachment mechanism changes character: droplets become smaller than the wire diameter and are propelled axially across the arc at a rate from under a hundred to several hundred per second [S3].

The gas requirement is absolute. Spray transfer requires at least approximately 80 % argon or helium [S3]. This is not a preference or a quality refinement — the physics of the transition depends on the arc atmosphere, and under a CO₂-dominant gas the transition does not occur.

Characteristics. Very low spatter, a stable and quiet arc, high deposition rate, deep finger-shaped penetration, and excellent bead appearance. Restricted to flat and horizontal positions because the large, fluid pool cannot be supported against gravity, and unsuitable for thin material because of the high heat input [S3].

The transition current itself depends on wire diameter, wire composition and gas composition — larger diameters and higher CO₂ content raise it. The practical implication is that a procedure written for one wire diameter does not transfer to another without re-establishing where the transition sits.

6. Pulsed Spray Transfer

Mechanism. The power source alternates between a peak current high enough to detach one droplet in spray mode and a background current just sufficient to maintain the arc, at a pulse frequency from a few to several hundred pulses per second [S3].

Why it matters. The result is spray-mode droplet transfer — small droplets, axial, low spatter — at a low average current. That combination resolves the central conflict of the process:

• Spray quality with low heat input.

• All-position capability, because the pool is small enough to control against gravity [S3].

• Reduced distortion on thin and heat-sensitive material [S3].

• Good fusion characteristics, because the peak current does the fusing even though the average is low.

Pulsed transfer is therefore the correct answer to the most common GMAW problem: needing to weld thick or fusion-critical joints out of position. The alternative — short-circuit transfer on thick section — is the lack-of-fusion trap of Section 3. Modern equipment implements pulsed programmes tuned per wire and gas combination, which makes it far more accessible than its reputation for complexity suggests.

It still requires an argon-rich gas, for the same reason as conventional spray.

7. Equipment and Components

| Component | Function | Failure consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Power source | Constant-voltage output: arc length self-corrects because a shortening arc draws more current and burns the wire back faster | Constant-current output is wrong for GMAW; arc length becomes uncontrollable |
| Wire feed unit | Drives the wire at a set speed, which sets the current on a CV machine | Speed variation causes arc length and current variation — spatter, porosity, fusion defects |
| Drive rolls | Grip and push the wire; profile matched to wire type (V-groove for steel, U-groove for aluminium, knurled for cored wire) | Wrong profile or pressure deforms, slips or crushes the wire |
| Liner | Guides the wire through the torch cable | Wrong size, worn, or contaminated liner causes drag, feed variation and birdnesting |
| Contact tip | Transfers current to the wire at a defined point | Wear enlarges the bore, causing arcing inside the tip, erratic current and spatter |
| Gas diffuser | Distributes shielding gas evenly around the wire | Blocked diffuser disturbs the gas envelope and causes porosity |
| Nozzle | Directs the gas column | Spatter build-up inside the nozzle disrupts flow and causes porosity |
| Gas solenoid, pre-flow/post-flow control | Times gas delivery | Insufficient pre-flow gives start porosity; insufficient post-flow gives crater porosity |
| Inductance / arc control | Shapes current rise in short-circuit mode | Incorrect setting causes excessive spatter or a cold, ropey bead |
| Pulse controller | Generates peak/background waveform | Wrong programme for the wire and gas gives unstable transfer |

8. The Wire Feed Path: Where Most Faults Actually Originate

This section is placed prominently because a disproportionate share of GMAW faults blamed on parameters, gas or the welder are actually feed path faults.

The mechanism. On a constant-voltage machine, welding current is determined by wire feed speed. If the wire's actual delivery speed at the contact tip varies — even briefly — the arc length and the current vary with it. The result is an unstable arc, and instability produces spatter, porosity, inconsistent penetration and poor bead appearance. Critically, spatter rises before any other symptom becomes visible [S4], which makes it the early warning signal.

The failure points, in order of frequency:

• Worn or wrong-size liner. A liner sized for a different wire diameter, or worn and full of debris, drags on the wire.

• Contact tip wear. The bore enlarges, contact becomes intermittent, arcing occurs inside the tip, and current delivery becomes erratic.

• Drive roll pressure. Too little and the rolls slip; too much and the wire is deformed or, on soft wire, crushed.

• Wrong drive roll profile for the wire type.

• Torch cable routing. Tight bends and coils multiply drag. This matters enormously on aluminium.

• Spool braking. Too tight adds drag; too loose lets the spool overrun and tangle.

• Wire condition. Rusty, dirty or poorly wound wire adds drag and introduces contamination.

The diagnostic habit worth building: when a GMAW problem appears — spatter, porosity, inconsistent bead, erratic current — check the feed path before the parameters. The parameters are recorded and did not change on their own; the feed path degrades continuously and silently.

9. Consumables and Shielding Gas

Wire. Carbon steel wires under AWS A5.18 (Chapter 29, Section 4), the most common being ER70S-3 and ER70S-6. ER70S-6 carries higher manganese and silicon, which makes it more tolerant of mill scale and light rust and gives better wetting — the reason it dominates general fabrication. Stainless wires under A5.9, aluminium under A5.10, nickel under A5.14.

Gas selection (Chapter 30, Section 6), summarized for GMAW specifically:

| Material and mode | Gas | Reasoning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Carbon steel, short-circuit | Ar-CO₂ mixtures, or CO₂ | Any of these support short-circuit transfer; higher CO₂ gives more penetration and more spatter |
| Carbon steel, spray or pulsed | ≥ ~80 % argon, often with a small O₂ or CO₂ addition | Spray transfer is unavailable below this [S3]; small active additions stabilize the arc and improve wetting |
| Austenitic stainless | Argon with small active additions, commonly a tri-mix | Minimal carbon pickup with enough active component for arc stability |
| Aluminium | Pure argon, or argon-helium for thick sections | Inert group only; helium adds heat for heavy sections |
| Nickel alloys | Argon, sometimes with helium | Oxidation-sensitive; no active component |

The gas is an essential variable in procedure qualification and is tied to the consumable's classification. Substituting a gas for availability reasons changes the deposit chemistry and can change the available transfer mode — it is an engineering decision, not a stores decision.

10. Parameters and What Each One Controls

| Parameter | Controls | Symptom if wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wire feed speed | Current, and therefore deposition rate and penetration | Too low: lack of fusion, unstable arc. Too high: burn-through, excessive reinforcement |
| Voltage | Arc length, bead width, transfer mode | Too low: stubbing, ropey narrow bead, spatter. Too high: wide flat bead, undercut, porosity from a long arc, spatter |
| Contact tip to work distance (stick-out) | Resistive preheating of the wire extension, and therefore burn-off rate and penetration | Too long: reduced penetration, unstable arc, poor gas coverage. Too short: tip burn-back and spatter build-up |
| Travel speed | Heat input per unit length, bead size | Too fast: undercut, narrow bead, lack of fusion. Too slow: excess deposit, overlap, burn-through |
| Gas flow | Shielding integrity | Too low: porosity. Too high: turbulence entrains air — also porosity (Chapter 30, Section 8) |
| Inductance / arc control | Current rise rate in short-circuit | Too low: harsh, spattery break. Too high: fluid, sluggish pool |
| Torch angle | Penetration and gas coverage | Excessive push or drag disturbs shielding and changes penetration |

11. Joint Types and Positions

Position capability is set by transfer mode, not by the process:

| Position | Available modes |
| --- | --- |
| Flat, horizontal | All four modes |
| Vertical, overhead | Short-circuit and pulsed only — spray and globular pools cannot be supported |

Vertical-up and vertical-down both occur. Vertical-down is fast and low-penetration, suitable for thin material and cosmetic passes, and is a recognized lack-of-fusion risk on thick material (Chapter 28, Section 10).

Joint design follows Chapter 28, with one GMAW-specific point: the process's deep, narrow, finger-shaped penetration in spray mode means it is less tolerant of joint misalignment than a broader-profile process, and fit-up control matters correspondingly more.

12. Setup and Execution Procedure

Before welding

1. Confirm the WPS covers this joint, material, thickness and position, and confirm your qualification covers the process, position and thickness.

2. Establish which transfer mode the WPS requires, and confirm the gas on the machine will support it — spray and pulsed require an argon-rich mixture [S3].

3. Verify the wire classification and diameter against the WPS.

4. Inspect and service the feed path: liner size and condition, drive roll profile and pressure, contact tip bore and condition, nozzle clear of spatter, diffuser clear.

5. Check the gas: correct mixture, cylinder content, regulator and flowmeter set for the nozzle and joint, and no leaks in the path.

6. Set pre-flow and post-flow.

7. Inspect the joint preparation and cleanliness; on aluminium, degrease then mechanically clean immediately before welding (Chapter 25, Section 9).

8. Verify preheat where required, measured correctly (Chapter 34, Section 6).

9. Connect the work return to the workpiece close to the joint, on a clean surface.

10. Confirm extraction is positioned and screens are in place.

Establishing the arc

11. Cut the wire to a clean, short stick-out — a balled or spattered wire end causes a poor start.

12. Set wire feed speed and voltage per the WPS, and verify the arc sounds correct for the intended mode: a steady rapid crackle for short-circuit, a smooth hiss for spray, a rhythmic buzz for pulsed. An irregular, popping arc with heavy spatter means globular transfer — stop and correct the parameters or the gas rather than continuing.

13. Run a test bead on a coupon of the same material and thickness where the work permits it.

Welding

14. Hold a consistent contact tip to work distance; this is the most commonly drifting manual variable in GMAW.

15. Maintain the specified torch angle, typically a slight drag for steel to improve gas coverage and penetration visibility.

16. Watch the leading edge of the pool and the fusion at the toes rather than the arc itself.

17. Keep travel speed consistent — GMAW's continuous feed makes speed variation show up immediately as bead width variation.

18. Verify interpass temperature before each pass against both the minimum and the maximum (Chapter 34, Section 7).

19. Between passes, remove silica islands and any spatter from the groove; GMAW produces no slag but deoxidation products do accumulate and can cause inclusions if welded over.

20. Fill every crater; use the crater-fill or downslope function where the machine provides it.

21. Watch spatter level as a live process signal — a rise means something has changed (Section 13).

After welding

22. Clean spatter from the weld and adjacent surfaces, with tooling appropriate to the material.

23. Visual inspection against the acceptance criteria.

24. Record joint, welder, WPS revision and consumable batch per the traceability requirement.

13. Spatter Control in Full

Spatter is classified as imperfection 602 (Chapter 36, Section 9). In GMAW it is both a cost and a diagnostic signal, and it is controllable in a defined order [S4]:

1. Determine which transfer mode the parameters actually produce, and get out of the globular range. This is the first and largest lever. Move down into true short-circuiting or up into spray — or use pulsed transfer, which delivers spray-mode transfer at a low average current [S4].

2. Raise the argon fraction. CO₂-rich shielding increases arc force and droplet repulsion; the standard recommendation is at least 80 % argon for steel and avoiding pure CO₂ [S4]. Raising the argon fraction also makes spray transfer available, which addresses step 1 as well.

3. Set inductance for a softer current rise where welding in short-circuit mode. An aggressive rise ruptures the bridge explosively [S4].

4. Service the wire feed path. A worn liner, slipping rolls or a worn contact tip modulate wire feed speed, destabilizing arc length and producing spatter before any other symptom appears [S4].

5. Correct arc blow. Reposition the work return clamp or adjust the electrode angle where magnetic deflection is destabilizing transfer near edges and earth connections [S4].

6. Clean the joint. Rust, zinc coating, oil and moisture generate gas in the pool that ejects metal [S4].

7. Check stick-out and voltage. Excessive stick-out destabilizes the arc; excessive voltage lengthens it.

Anti-spatter sprays and nozzle compounds reduce adherence and ease cleaning. They do not reduce the metal being ejected, and using them as the primary control masks a process problem that is also costing deposition efficiency and, through nozzle blockage, causing porosity.

14. When to Use GMAW and When Not To

| Choose GMAW when | Choose something else when |
| --- | --- |
| Production volume and deposition rate matter | Working outdoors in wind — the gas shield is stripped; use SMAW or self-shielded FCAW |
| Slag removal time is a significant cost | Material is heavily rusted, painted or contaminated — SMAW tolerates it better |
| Long continuous welds without electrode changes | Very thin, precision or cosmetic work — GTAW gives more control |
| Robotic or mechanized welding is planned — GMAW is the dominant robotic arc process | Thick section out of position without pulsed capability — the short-circuit lack-of-fusion trap applies |
| Aluminium production welding with pulsed transfer | Long flat seams in heavy plate — SAW deposits far faster |
| Thin sheet with short-circuit or pulsed transfer | Reactive metals requiring total atmospheric exclusion — GTAW with trailing shields |

16. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Heavy spatter on a previously clean weld

Symptom: spatter level rises on a job that was running well.

Category: process stability.

Likely causes: parameters drifted into the globular range; gas mixture changed or cylinder swapped; contact tip worn; liner worn or contaminated; drive roll pressure changed; joint surface condition changed (new material batch with heavier scale); earth connection degraded.

Steps: identify the transfer mode from the arc sound and the parameters; verify the gas actually connected against the WPS; inspect the contact tip and liner; check drive roll pressure; check the return connection; check the incoming material surface condition [S4].

Card 2 — Lack of fusion found by ultrasonics on thick section

Symptom: UT finds sidewall lack of fusion; welds look excellent visually and passed radiography.

Category: transfer mode selection.

Likely causes: short-circuit transfer used to fill a thick section, most often because the joint required out-of-position welding; travel speed too high; groove too narrow.

Steps: establish the transfer mode from the recorded parameters; if short-circuit on thick section, this is the known trap of Section 3; move to pulsed transfer for all-position capability at adequate energy, or reposition the work for spray transfer; verify the inspection method is appropriate — radiography does not reliably find this defect (Chapter 35, Section 1).

Card 3 — Porosity that worsens when gas flow is increased

Symptom: porosity present; increasing flow makes it worse.

Category: gas delivery.

Likely causes: flow above the laminar limit for the nozzle, entraining air; nozzle partly blocked with spatter causing turbulence; excessive stick-out; draught.

Steps: return flow to the correct value for the nozzle size; clean the nozzle and diffuser; check stick-out; screen the work area; leak-check the gas path with the torch articulated through its range (Chapter 30, Section 14).

Card 4 — Erratic arc and inconsistent bead width

Symptom: arc surges, bead width varies along the weld.

Category: wire feed.

Likely causes: liner drag or wrong size; drive roll slipping or wrong profile; spool brake too tight; cable coiled tightly; wire rusty or poorly wound; contact tip bore worn.

Steps: run the wire out by hand feel for drag; inspect the liner and replace on condition, not on schedule; check roll profile against wire type and set pressure to the minimum that feeds without slipping; straighten the cable run; replace the contact tip.

Card 5 — Cannot achieve spray transfer whatever the setting

Symptom: increasing current produces heavy spatter, not a spray arc.

Category: shielding gas.

Likely causes: shielding gas is CO₂ or CO₂-dominant, under which spray transfer does not occur at any current [S3].

Steps: verify the gas group actually in use; spray requires at least about 80 % argon [S3]; change gas — and note this is a change of essential variable requiring procedure review, not a shop-floor substitution (Chapter 31, Section 11).

17. Safety Specifics

• Ozone generation is significant on aluminium and on high-current argon-shielded work, from UV acting on atmospheric oxygen (Chapter 37, Section 6).

• UV output is high, and aluminium's reflectivity increases bystander exposure — screening matters more than on steel.

• Fume rate is lower than SMAW or FCAW for comparable deposition, but stainless work still generates hexavalent chromium and nickel requiring specific control.

• Carbon monoxide from CO₂ dissociation accumulates in confined spaces.

• The wire is live whenever the trigger is pulled, and a continuously fed live wire is a shock and burn hazard; never point the torch at anyone while feeding wire.

• Spatter accumulation creates fire risk in the surrounding area and in extraction ducting.

18. Standards and Qualification

• Process references: ISO 4063 references 131 (MIG, inert gas) and 135 (MAG, active gas) [S1].

• Consumables: AWS A5.18 (carbon steel), A5.28 (low alloy), A5.9 (stainless), A5.10 (aluminium), A5.14 (nickel); ISO 14341 (non-alloy and fine-grain steels), ISO 14343 (stainless), ISO 18273 (aluminium).

• Shielding gases: ISO 14175, AWS A5.32 (Chapter 30).

• Procedure qualification: ASME Section IX, ISO 15614 family, AWS D1.1 (Chapter 31). Transfer mode is a qualification consideration — short-circuit transfer is treated with particular caution in structural codes precisely because of the lack-of-fusion risk.

• Welder qualification: ISO 9606-1 or the applicable code; operators of mechanized and robotic GMAW qualify under ISO 14732 (Chapter 32, Section 9).

19. Worked Example: Burn-Through on Thin Sheet After a Gas Change

Situation. A fabricator welds 1.5 mm sheet assemblies with GMAW. The gas supplier changes the delivered mixture after a supply issue. Welders immediately report burn-through and distortion, and the shop's response is to reduce wire feed speed.

Step 1 — Establish exactly what changed. The single known change is the shielding gas. Everything else — wire, machine, welder, part, program — is unchanged. The investigation should start and, if possible, end there.

Step 2 — Identify what the gas change does mechanically. Gas composition determines the transfer mode boundaries and the heat delivered to the work. A change toward higher CO₂ content increases penetration and arc force; a change toward argon-rich shifts the transition current and can move a parameter set that was in short-circuit toward globular or spray. On 1.5 mm sheet, either shift is enough to burn through.

Step 3 — Determine which mode the parameters now produce. The arc sound and the spatter level indicate it directly: a steady rapid crackle is short-circuit; irregular popping with heavy spatter is globular; a smooth hiss is spray. On thin sheet, anything but short-circuit or pulsed is wrong.

Step 4 — Assess the proposed fix. Reducing wire feed speed lowers current and heat, which addresses the symptom. But if the gas change has moved the process out of the mode the procedure was qualified in, the fix leaves the shop running an unqualified process at reduced settings — and it may introduce lack of fusion at the lower energy on the very same joints.

Step 5 — Recognize the qualification issue, which is the real finding. Shielding gas is an essential variable (Chapter 31, Section 11). A delivered gas different from the qualified gas means the work is outside the qualified procedure regardless of whether the welds look acceptable. That is true even if a parameter adjustment restores the appearance.

Step 6 — Take the correct actions in order. Stop; confirm what mixture was actually delivered, by ISO 14175 group rather than by trade name; if it differs from the qualified gas, obtain the correct gas or requalify; assess the parts welded since the change; and only then adjust parameters — within the qualified ranges, not outside them.

Step 7 — Prevent the recurrence. The system failure is that a substituted gas reached the shop floor without an engineering check. The control is a goods-in verification against the approved consumable and gas list tied to the WPS, and it is the same control that prevents consumable substitution (Chapter 29, Section 13). Gas is a consumable, and it is the one most often treated as a utility.

20. Known Gaps

• No transition current values are given. They depend on wire diameter, wire composition and gas composition, and any single figure would be misleading applied to a different combination.

• No parameter values are given. Wire feed speed, voltage and travel speed are joint-, thickness- and equipment-specific, and the WPS governs.

• Gas flow rates are not stated for the reasons in Chapter 30, Section 15.

• Pulsed waveform parameters are equipment-specific. Modern machines carry synergic programmes indexed to wire and gas; the underlying pulse parameters are not generally user-adjustable in production and vary by manufacturer.

• The short-circuit frequency range in Section 3 is quoted from a published technical source [S3] and varies with parameters and equipment.

1. Process Overview: Gas-Shielded and Self-Shielded

Flux cored arc welding feeds a tubular wire — a metal sheath containing a core of flux and alloying compounds — through a torch and strikes an arc as in gas metal arc welding. The core performs the jobs a covered electrode's covering performs in shielded metal arc welding: generating shielding gas, forming a protective slag, stabilizing the arc, and adding deoxidizers and alloys.

The family splits by whether external shielding gas is also supplied, and the ISO nomenclature separates them clearly [S1]:

| Reference | Process |
| --- | --- |
| 136 | MAG welding with flux cored electrode — gas-shielded under an active gas |
| 132 | MIG welding with flux cored electrode — gas-shielded under an inert gas |
| 114 | Self-shielded tubular cored arc welding — no external gas |
| 138 | MAG welding with metal cored electrode (Section 5) |

Note that 114 sits outside the 13x family entirely, which correctly reflects that self-shielded welding is a structurally different process rather than a gas-shielded process with the gas turned off.

2. Why the Tubular Construction Changes the Process

Three consequences follow from putting the flux inside the wire rather than outside a stick electrode:

Deposition rate is high. Current is carried by the thin metal sheath rather than by the full cross-section, so current density in the conducting metal is very high, and burn-off rate rises accordingly. FCAW deposits substantially faster than SMAW and generally faster than solid-wire GMAW at comparable current.

Out-of-position capability is excellent. The slag freezes quickly and physically supports the molten pool against gravity. This is what allows all-position welding at deposition rates that a solid wire could not sustain out of position, and it is the process's principal competitive advantage over GMAW.

The core is exposed at the wire's cut end. Unlike a solid wire, a cored wire can absorb moisture into its core, which makes storage and handling a real hydrogen control rather than a housekeeping matter (Chapter 29, Section 10).

3. Gas-Shielded FCAW

The wire's core provides slag, deoxidizers and arc stabilizers; an external gas — carbon dioxide or an argon-CO₂ mixture — provides the primary shielding.

Characteristics: high deposition rates, excellent all-position capability with a wire classified for it, good tolerance of mill scale and light surface contamination compared with solid wire, good bead appearance, and a smooth arc with a rutile-type core.

Its constraint is the shielding gas, with the same wind sensitivity as GMAW: the shield can be stripped outdoors, and the wire's own core cannot make up the difference because it was formulated on the assumption that gas would be present.

The shielding designator on the classification is binding. A wire classified for CO₂ run under an argon mixture — or the reverse — produces a deposit that does not meet its classification, because the arc atmosphere changes both the oxidation state and the recovery of the deoxidizers and alloys in the core (Chapter 29, Section 5).

4. Self-Shielded FCAW and Why It Works Without Gas

Self-shielded wire generates its entire protective atmosphere from the core, and the chemistry is genuinely different rather than merely more concentrated.

The mechanism. Beyond gas-forming and slag-forming constituents, the core carries strong denitriders and deoxidizers — aluminium in particular — in quantities calculated to scavenge the nitrogen and oxygen that inevitably reach the pool from the surrounding air. The process does not exclude the atmosphere the way a gas shield does; it tolerates partial atmospheric contact and neutralizes the consequences chemically.

Three things follow directly, and all three are frequently violated in practice:

1. Self-shielded wire must never be run under a shielding gas. Doing so removes the oxygen and nitrogen the scavenging chemistry was designed to consume, leaving an over-deoxidized deposit with degraded toughness. The result looks fine and tests badly.

2. Electrode extension (stick-out) is a controlled variable, not a preference. The scavenging reactions depend on the resistive preheating of the wire extension, and self-shielded wires are formulated for a specific, generally long, stick-out range. Running short defeats the chemistry.

3. Some self-shielded wires run DCEN rather than the DCEP typical of gas-shielded wires. Polarity is stated by the classification and is not interchangeable.

Where it wins decisively: outdoor and site work in wind. There is no gas column to strip, which makes it the process of choice for structural steel erection, pipeline external work, shipbuilding on the ways, and heavy field fabrication.

Its costs: the highest fume generation rates in common arc welding (Section 15), generally poorer toughness than an equivalent gas-shielded basic wire, and more spatter and slag.

5. Metal-Cored Wire: The Third Member of the Family

Metal-cored wire — references 138 under active gas and 133 under inert gas [S1] — is tubular like a flux-cored wire, but the core is predominantly metal powder with arc stabilizers rather than slag-forming minerals.

The result behaves like a very high-deposition solid wire: it produces essentially no slag, only small silica islands, so interpass cleaning is minimal; it gives broad, consistent fusion with less of the finger-shaped penetration of solid-wire spray transfer; and it delivers high travel speeds in the flat and horizontal positions.

Its trade against flux-cored wire is positional: without a supporting slag, out-of-position capability depends on pulsed transfer rather than on the consumable. Its trade against solid wire is cost per kilogram against deposition rate and fusion consistency.

It is a distinct process reference and a distinct consumable classification, so substituting metal-cored for flux-cored wire — or for solid wire — is a change of essential variable (Chapter 21, Section 16).

6. Slag Systems: Rutile Against Basic

The core's mineral system determines the operating character in the same way an electrode covering does:

| System | Character | Chosen for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rutile (typified by T-1 usability) | Smooth, spray-like arc; low spatter; excellent bead appearance; easy slag removal; very good all-position handling | Operator appeal, appearance, productivity, general structural work |
| Basic (typified by T-5 usability) | Harsher arc; more spatter; less attractive bead; better toughness and lower diffusible hydrogen | Applications where impact toughness or hydrogen control governs |

The trade is honest and unavoidable: the wire that runs best is not the wire with the best properties. A shop selecting consumables on welder preference will select rutile wires, and where a toughness or hydrogen requirement applies, that preference produces a non-conforming deposit. This is a specification decision, not a shop-floor one.

7. Equipment and Components

Broadly as GMAW (Chapter 39, Section 7), with FCAW-specific differences:

| Component | FCAW-specific requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Drive rolls | Knurled or V-knurled, not smooth V-groove. A cored wire is a tube and is crushed by excessive pressure from smooth rolls — crushing changes the wire's cross-section, its feed behaviour and the core's exposure |
| Drive roll pressure | Set to the minimum that feeds without slipping; over-tightening deforms the tube |
| Contact tip | As GMAW, but wear rates are typically higher |
| Nozzle | Gas-shielded: as GMAW. Self-shielded: no gas nozzle is needed, and a nozzle-free guide with the correct stick-out guide is used |
| Extraction | Higher capacity than GMAW because fume generation is substantially higher |
| Slag removal tools | Required between every pass, as SMAW |

8. Consumables and the Usability Designator

The classification structure is decoded in Chapter 29, Section 5. The usability designator — the digit after the T — is the critical field, encoding the slag system, the shielding requirement, the polarity and the operating characteristics [S2]:

| Designator | Character |
| --- | --- |
| T-1 | Rutile, gas-shielded, smooth spray-like arc, low spatter, good all-position handling |
| T-5 | Basic, gas-shielded, better toughness and lower hydrogen, harsher arc, more spatter |
| T-8 | Self-shielded, all-position, used where gas is unavailable or wind precludes it |
| T-11 | Self-shielded, general purpose, widely used in light fabrication |

The shielding suffix — C for 100 % CO₂, M for a mixed argon-CO₂ gas — states the gas the wire was classified under, and it is binding as described in Section 3.

Storage. Cored wires are more hygroscopic than solid wires because the core is exposed at the cut end. Partly used spools should be resealed or returned to controlled storage; a spool left on a machine over a humid weekend is a documented cause of the worm-hole porosity in Section 17.

9. Parameters, and Why Stick-Out Is Critical Here

| Parameter | Controls | FCAW-specific note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wire feed speed | Current, deposition rate | As GMAW: current follows wire feed speed on a constant-voltage machine |
| Voltage | Arc length, bead width, slag behaviour | Too high gives excessive spatter and can disturb slag coverage; too low gives a ropey bead with slag entrapment |
| Electrode extension (stick-out) | Resistive preheating of the wire; for self-shielded wire, the completion of the shielding chemistry | The most under-controlled variable in FCAW. Self-shielded wires specify a stick-out range and running outside it degrades the deposit chemistry regardless of every other setting |
| Travel speed | Heat input, bead size, slag control | Too slow lets slag run ahead of the pool and become entrapped |
| Travel angle | Slag control and penetration | A drag angle is normal; excessive drag pushes slag ahead of the pool |
| Polarity | Arc character and deposit chemistry | Stated by the classification; some self-shielded wires are DCEN |

The stick-out point deserves restating because it distinguishes FCAW from every other wire process: on solid-wire GMAW, stick-out affects current and penetration. On self-shielded FCAW it affects the metallurgy of the deposit, because the scavenging reactions depend on the wire extension being heated over the specified distance.

10. Joint Types and Positions

All-position welding is available with a wire classified for it — the positional digit in the classification governs, and a flat-and-horizontal-only wire will not hold a pool overhead regardless of technique.

FCAW's fast-freezing slag makes it notably capable in vertical-up work, where it competes directly with SMAW at far higher deposition rates, and this is a large part of its dominance in structural erection.

Joint design follows Chapter 28, with one specific consideration: the slag must be able to float clear and be removed between passes, so grooves that are too narrow for slag release produce inclusions (Chapter 36, Section 5).

11. Setup and Execution Procedure

Before welding

1. Confirm the WPS covers the joint, material, thickness and position, and confirm your qualification covers process, position and thickness.

2. Verify the exact wire classification against the WPS, including the usability and shielding designators. T-1 and T-5 are not interchangeable; C and M shielding designators are not interchangeable; gas-shielded and self-shielded are entirely different consumables.

3. Confirm the polarity required by the classification and set it at the machine.

4. Take the wire from controlled storage; check the spool has not been left exposed.

5. Set drive rolls: knurled profile, minimum pressure that feeds without slipping.

6. Gas-shielded: verify the gas group against the wire's shielding designator, set flow for the nozzle, leak-check the path. Self-shielded: confirm no gas is connected.

7. Set and mark the stick-out, particularly for self-shielded wire; use the manufacturer's stated range.

8. Inspect joint preparation and cleanliness; confirm the groove is wide enough for slag release.

9. Verify preheat where required (Chapter 34).

10. Connect the work return to the workpiece close to the joint.

11. Confirm extraction is positioned — FCAW fume rates make this more important than for GMAW.

Welding

12. Establish the arc on the joint or a run-on tab, never on the parent metal outside the weld.

13. Hold the specified stick-out consistently — this is the variable that drifts most and matters most.

14. Maintain a drag angle appropriate to the wire and position, keeping the slag behind the pool.

15. Watch the fusion at the toes and the slag coverage rather than the arc.

16. Remove slag completely between every pass, including from the groove faces and any undercut. Cored-wire slag can be tenacious, and incomplete removal is the leading cause of inclusions.

17. Check interpass temperature against both the minimum and the maximum before each pass.

18. Fill craters at every termination.

19. Watch spatter level as a live signal of process change (Chapter 39, Section 13).

After welding

20. Remove all slag and spatter; inspect visually against acceptance criteria.

21. Observe any specified delay before final NDT where hydrogen cracking is credible.

22. Record joint, welder, WPS revision and consumable batch.

12. When to Use FCAW and When Not To

| Choose FCAW when | Choose something else when |
| --- | --- |
| High deposition out of position is needed — its defining advantage | Slag removal time is unacceptable — use metal-cored or solid wire |
| Working outdoors in wind (self-shielded) | Fume must be minimized — FCAW generates the most of the common arc processes |
| Material carries mill scale or light surface contamination | Thin sheet — heat input is high; use GMAW short-circuit or GTAW |
| Structural erection, shipbuilding, heavy plate fabrication | Reactive metals or aluminium — not applicable |
| Thick-section fill where SMAW would be too slow | Cosmetic or precision work — GTAW gives control, GMAW gives cleaner appearance |
| Vertical-up welding at production rates | Toughness and hydrogen requirements favour a basic wire the welders dislike — the specification still governs |

| Spatter | 602 | Visual | Basic-slag wires inherently spatter more than rutile; excessive voltage; incorrect polarity for the classification; feed instability; arc blow | Verify polarity and parameters; service the feed path; accept that a basic wire spatters more and plan the cleaning rather than changing the wire |
| Crushed or deformed wire, feed problems | — | Immediate | Smooth V-groove drive rolls or excessive pressure crushing the tube | Fit knurled rolls; set minimum effective pressure |
| Undercut | 501 | Visual, MT | Voltage or travel speed too high; incorrect work angle | Reduce parameters; correct angle |

14. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Worm-hole porosity appearing in cold, damp conditions

Symptom: elongated cavities along the weld, worse on the first welds of the day.

Category: consumable condition.

Likely causes: moisture absorbed into the wire core from humid storage or an exposed spool; condensation on the joint surface; no warm-through applied on cold material.

Steps: check wire storage and whether the spool was left on the machine overnight; check whether partly used spools are resealed; apply a warm-through to remove surface moisture from cold material; confirm the joint is dry before welding.

Card 2 — Deposit fails impact testing on a self-shielded wire

Symptom: toughness below requirement; strength and soundness acceptable.

Category: consumable misuse.

Likely causes: self-shielded wire run under shielding gas, removing the oxygen and nitrogen its scavenging chemistry was formulated to consume; stick-out outside the specified range; wrong polarity.

Steps: confirm no gas is connected when running self-shielded wire; verify stick-out against the manufacturer's range; verify polarity against the classification; check whether the wire actually issued matches the WPS classification.

Card 3 — Slag inclusions found repeatedly in a deep groove

Symptom: RT shows inclusions concentrated at mid-thickness.

Category: joint design and technique.

Likely causes: groove too narrow for slag to float clear; excessive drag angle; incomplete interpass cleaning at the groove faces; undercut at the toes forming traps.

Steps: check the groove angle against the wire diameter and torch access; correct the drag angle; verify interpass cleaning includes the groove faces, not just the bead surface; grind out undercut before the next pass.

Card 4 — Wire feeds erratically and birdnests at the drive

Symptom: feed stops; wire tangles at the rolls.

Category: feed path.

Likely causes: smooth rolls crushing a tubular wire; excessive roll pressure; worn liner; tight cable routing; spool brake too tight.

Steps: fit knurled rolls; reduce pressure to the minimum that feeds; inspect and replace the liner; straighten the cable run; adjust the brake.

Card 5 — Excellent appearance, rejected on toughness

Symptom: welds look outstanding; Charpy results fail.

Category: consumable selection.

Likely causes: a rutile wire was selected for its operating characteristics where a basic wire was specified for toughness.

Steps: verify the classification actually purchased and issued against the WPS; where a toughness requirement exists, the specification governs over operator preference; if the change was made informally, treat the affected production as welded outside the qualified procedure (Chapter 31, Section 11).

15. Safety Specifics: The Highest Fume Rates in Arc Welding

FCAW — and self-shielded FCAW in particular — generates substantially more fume than gas-shielded solid wire processes for comparable deposition. The reasons are inherent: a large mass of flux is vaporized and condensed in the arc, and self-shielded wires operate with partial atmospheric contact by design.

The consequences for control:

• Local exhaust at source is required, not advisable, and the capture device must be near the arc. On-torch extraction exists for FCAW and is effective.

• Confined-space FCAW requires forced ventilation and, commonly, respiratory protection, and it is a situation where process substitution should be considered seriously (Chapter 37, Section 7).

• Stainless and alloy cored wires add hexavalent chromium and nickel to the fume with the same controls as other stainless processes.

• Slag chipping produces flying hot particles; eye protection under the helmet is required.

• Self-shielded arcs are visually harsh, with a bright arc and heavy fume plume that obscures the pool — welders tend to move closer, putting the breathing zone directly in the plume.

16. Standards and Qualification

• Process references: ISO 4063 references 136 (MAG, flux cored), 132 (MIG, flux cored), 114 (self-shielded tubular cored), 138 and 133 (metal cored) [S1].

• Consumables: AWS A5.20 (carbon steel FCAW), A5.29 (low alloy FCAW), A5.22 (stainless flux cored and metal cored), A5.36 (open classification for carbon and low-alloy cored wires); ISO 17632 (non-alloy and fine-grain steels).

• Procedure qualification: ASME Section IX, ISO 15614 family, AWS D1.1 (Chapter 31).

• Welder qualification: ISO 9606-1 or the applicable code; mechanized and robotic operators under ISO 14732.

• Acceptance: ISO 5817 quality levels or the code's criteria.

17. Worked Example: Worm-Hole Porosity on a Structure Welded in Winter

Situation. A steel erection contractor using self-shielded FCAW on site finds elongated worm-hole porosity in radiographs of welds made during a cold, wet week. Welds from the previous month were clean. Same wire specification, same welders, same machines.

Step 1 — Read the defect type as evidence. Worm-hole porosity — elongated cavities rather than round pores — indicates a sustained gas source escaping through metal that is solidifying around it, rather than a momentary shielding disturbance. That points at moisture or contamination present continuously, not at an intermittent shielding failure (Chapter 36, Section 4).

Step 2 — Use the timing. The change coincides with cold, wet weather and nothing else. On site, weather affects three things simultaneously: wire storage conditions, joint surface condition, and whether preheat is applied and verified.

Step 3 — Check wire handling specifically, because cored wire is hygroscopic. The questions: where are spools stored overnight on site; are partly used spools removed and resealed or left on the machine under a tarpaulin; how long has a given spool been open; is there any heated storage on site at all. A spool left on a machine through a wet week has absorbed moisture into an exposed core.

Step 4 — Check the joint surface. Site steel in wet weather carries condensation, and welding over a wet surface produces exactly this defect. A warm-through pass to drive off surface moisture is a legitimate and cheap control that is routinely skipped when preheat is not otherwise required.

Step 5 — Check stick-out, because this is self-shielded wire. Cold, awkward conditions push welders toward a shorter stick-out for better visibility and control. On self-shielded wire, short stick-out defeats the shielding chemistry and produces porosity independently of moisture (Section 9). Two mechanisms may be contributing at once, and confirming stick-out practice on site is quick.

Step 6 — Rule out a gas confusion. It is worth confirming that nobody has connected shielding gas to a self-shielded wire "to help with the porosity" — a well-intentioned intervention that would degrade toughness while doing nothing for the porosity.

Step 7 — Correct at the system level. The immediate action is to excavate and reweld the affected welds. The lasting fix is site consumable storage — a heated or at minimum sealed and dry store, with a discipline for removing and resealing spools at end of shift — plus a written cold-weather procedure covering surface moisture removal, and a stick-out check as part of the site supervisor's routine. Every one of those is a Chapter 33 requirement that a shop meets by default and a site has to be equipped for deliberately.

18. Known Gaps

• No parameter values or stick-out ranges are given. Stick-out in particular is wire-specific and stated by the manufacturer; using a generic value on a self-shielded wire is precisely the error Section 9 warns against.

• Usability designators are described by common groupings [S2], not exhaustively. The full set is in AWS A5.20 and A5.29.

• Fume generation rates are described comparatively, not numerically. Published rates vary by wire, current and measurement method.

• The AWS A5.36 open classification system for cored wires is named but not developed; it classifies by properties achieved with a stated gas rather than by fixed classification, and its structure differs from the fixed-classification system described in Chapter 29.

• Metal-cored wire is introduced here for family completeness but shares more operating characteristics with GMAW (Chapter 39) than with flux-cored welding.

1. Process Overview: ISO 4063 References 141, 142 and 143

Gas tungsten arc welding strikes an arc between a non-consumable tungsten electrode and the work, under an inert gas shield. Filler metal, if used at all, is added separately — hand-fed as a rod or mechanically fed as a wire.

The ISO nomenclature distinguishes by filler [S1]:

| Reference | Process |
| --- | --- |
| 141 | TIG welding with solid filler material |
| 142 | Autogenous TIG welding — no filler |
| 143 | TIG welding with tubular cored filler material |
| 145 / 146 | TIG welding using reducing gas, with solid or cored filler |

The process gives the highest degree of control of any arc process and the lowest deposition rate. Those two facts are the same fact: a small, precisely controlled pool is precisely what cannot be deposited quickly.

2. Why Separating Heat From Filler Changes Everything

In every consumable-electrode process, the electrode is both the heat source and the filler, so current controls both heat and deposition simultaneously — raise the current for more penetration and you also deposit more metal. GTAW breaks that coupling.

The consequences run through everything else in this chapter:

• Heat and deposition are independently controllable. The welder can put heat into the joint without adding metal, or add metal at a rate unrelated to the current.

• Autogenous welding is possible — fusing the joint with no filler at all, which is how thin sheet, tube mill seams and many orbital welds are made.

• The pool can be very small and precisely placed, giving control at thicknesses where any other arc process would blow through.

• The deposit chemistry is exactly the filler's chemistry, diluted by parent — there is no flux or covering contributing elements, which is why GTAW deposits are clean and why the process dominates where deposit chemistry must be controlled precisely.

• There is no slag, so nothing supports the pool out of position and nothing protects the cooling weld — the gas shield must do all of it (Section 8).

3. Polarity: DCEN, DCEP and AC

Polarity determines where the arc's heat is deposited and whether the oxide-removing cleaning action occurs.

| Polarity | Heat distribution | Cleaning action | Electrode capacity | Use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DCEN (electrode negative, "straight") | Majority into the work | None | Highest — the electrode runs coolest | The standard for steel, stainless, nickel, titanium, copper |
| DCEP (electrode positive, "reverse") | Majority into the electrode | Strong | Very low — the electrode overheats rapidly | Rarely used alone; requires a much larger electrode for the same current |
| AC | Alternates | Present on the positive half-cycle | Intermediate | Aluminium and magnesium |

The pattern is a straightforward trade: the polarity that cleans the oxide is the polarity that destroys the electrode. DCEN puts the heat where it is wanted and provides no cleaning; DCEP cleans well and cannot carry useful current without an impractically large electrode. Alternating current resolves it by doing both, alternately — which is why aluminium is welded on AC and steel is not.

4. AC Balance and Cathodic Cleaning on Aluminium

Aluminium's oxide melts far above the metal beneath it and must be disrupted rather than melted (Chapter 25, Section 4). On the electrode-positive half of the AC cycle, ions bombard the workpiece surface and break up the oxide film — the cathodic cleaning effect. On the electrode-negative half, heat goes into the work and provides penetration.

Modern AC power sources allow the balance between the two halves to be adjusted, and this is a direct, continuous trade:

• More electrode-negative time: deeper penetration, faster travel, cooler electrode, narrower cleaned zone.

• More electrode-positive time: wider and more aggressive cleaning, shallower penetration, hotter electrode requiring a larger diameter or a balled tip.

Practical guidance: set the balance to the minimum cleaning that actually removes the oxide for the material condition in front of you. Excess cleaning wastes heat on the electrode, widens the etched zone unnecessarily, and can overheat the tungsten. A heavily oxidized or aged surface needs more cleaning; a freshly cleaned surface needs less — which is another reason mechanical cleaning immediately before welding pays for itself (Chapter 25, Section 9).

Modern square-wave and adjustable-frequency AC sources also allow AC frequency adjustment, which narrows or broadens the arc cone and focuses the energy.

5. Arc Initiation Methods

| Method | Mechanism | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| High-frequency (HF) start | A high-frequency, high-voltage discharge ionizes the gap so the arc strikes without contact | No tungsten contamination; the standard method; generates electromagnetic interference that can disturb nearby electronics and control systems |
| Lift arc / touch start | Electrode touches the work at low current, then is lifted to establish the arc | No HF interference; minimal contamination if performed correctly; standard where electronics are sensitive |
| Scratch start | Electrode is scratched across the work like a match | Contaminates the tungsten and the workpiece; leaves an arc strike; acceptable only on the most basic equipment and never on critical work |

HF is also used continuously on AC in some machines to re-establish the arc at each zero crossing; modern square-wave inverters largely remove that requirement.

6. The Tungsten Electrode: Type, Preparation and Failure

Type selection (Chapter 29, Section 6) [S2][S3]:

| Classification | Oxide addition | Colour | Application |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| EWP | None — 99.5 % tungsten | Green | AC welding of aluminium and magnesium; good arc stability on AC |
| EWTh-2 | ~1.7–2.2 % thorium oxide | Red | DCEN on carbon and stainless steel; the long-standing general-purpose choice; radioactive dust when ground |
| EWCe-2 | ~1.8–2.2 % cerium oxide | Grey (changed from orange in AWS A5.12) | DC at low current; also AC capable; non-radioactive |
| EWLa-1.5 | ~1.3–1.7 % lanthanum oxide | Gold | Similar to ceriated; conductivity resembling thoriated; non-radioactive |
| EWZr-1 | ~0.15–0.40 % zirconium oxide | Brown | AC only — explicitly not recommended for DC welding |

Two points of practical consequence. First, the colour code for EWCe-2 was changed from orange to grey in AWS A5.12, and the manufacturer may select any colour for the unspecified EWG classification [S2] — so colour identification requires knowing the vintage and the classification, and an electrode whose band has worn off cannot be identified without laboratory analysis and should be discarded rather than guessed at [S3]. Second, the move away from thoriated types in many shops is driven by the radioactive dust generated when grinding them, not by welding performance (Chapter 37, Section 11).

Preparation:

• Grind longitudinally, along the electrode axis, never circumferentially. Circumferential grinding marks cause the arc to wander because the electron emission follows the grinding grooves.

• Use a dedicated wheel for tungsten, never one used on steel, and extract the dust.

• Tip geometry: a ground point for DCEN — a sharper point gives a more focused arc and easier starting at low current, a blunter point carries more current and lasts longer. For AC, a balled or truncated tip is conventional, formed deliberately at a controlled current.

• Diameter matched to current. An electrode too small for the current overheats, spits and contaminates the weld; too large gives an unstable, wandering arc at low current.

Failure modes: contact with the pool or filler wire (contamination, tungsten inclusion), current above the electrode's capacity (melting and spitting), oxidizing shielding gas (rapid erosion), inadequate post-flow (the hot electrode oxidizes after the arc stops).

7. Equipment and Components

| Component | Function | Failure consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Power source | Constant-current output; AC/DC capability with balance and frequency control for aluminium | Wrong output type makes current uncontrollable with arc length variation |
| Torch | Holds and cools the electrode, delivers shielding gas | Air-cooled torches are current-limited; water-cooled required for sustained higher current |
| Collet and collet body | Grip the electrode and conduct current | Wrong size or worn collet causes overheating and poor current transfer |
| Gas lens | Screen that converts gas flow to laminar and permits greater electrode extension | Without one, shielding is poorer and stick-out must be short |
| Nozzle (cup) | Directs the gas column; size matched to joint and electrode extension | Too small gives inadequate coverage; too large wastes gas and blocks visibility |
| Foot pedal or torch amperage control | Live current control during welding | Without it, current cannot be tapered at starts and stops |
| Post-flow timer | Maintains gas over the electrode and pool after the arc stops | Insufficient post-flow oxidizes the electrode and the crater |
| Filler wire | Added separately, hand or machine fed | Wrong size or contaminated wire causes defects independent of the arc |
| Trailing shield | Extends gas coverage over the cooling weld | Essential on titanium; useful on stainless and nickel (Section 8) |

8. Shielding, Trailing Shields and Purging

Because GTAW produces no slag, the shielding gas is the only protection for both the pool and the cooling metal behind it. Three levels of coverage:

Primary shielding through the torch nozzle. Argon is standard; argon-helium raises heat input for thicker sections; argon-hydrogen (the R group of ISO 14175) is used on austenitic stainless and nickel for a hotter, cleaner arc and better wetting — and must never be used on ferritic steels or titanium (Chapter 30, Section 3).

Trailing shields — a gas-fed shoe following the torch — keep the just-solidified weld under cover until it cools below its reaction temperature. On titanium this is not optional (Chapter 26, Section 5); on stainless and nickel it reduces heat tint and improves corrosion performance.

Back purging on any joint with an inaccessible reverse side that will oxidize — stainless, duplex, nickel, titanium. Purge to a measured residual oxygen level rather than to a time, contain the purge volume with dams, control pressure so the root is not blown out, and maintain until cool (Chapter 30, Section 7).

Gas lenses matter more here than in any other process, because GTAW frequently requires the electrode to extend well beyond the nozzle to reach into a joint. A gas lens converts the flow to laminar and maintains coverage at that extension; without one, the extension must be short and the shielding degrades quickly.

9. Filler Wire and Technique

Because filler is added by hand in manual GTAW, the technique has specific requirements that do not arise in wire-fed processes:

• Keep the hot end of the filler rod inside the gas envelope. Withdrawing it into air oxidizes the end, and dipping that oxidized end back into the pool introduces oxide inclusions. This is the most common manual GTAW error.

• Feed into the leading edge of the pool, not into the arc, and not onto unfused metal ahead of it.

• Do not touch the tungsten with the filler. Contact contaminates both, requires the electrode to be re-ground and the contaminated weld metal to be removed.

• Match rod diameter to the pool. Too large chills the pool and causes lack of fusion; too small requires excessive feeding and adds arc time.

• Handle filler with clean gloves and store it clean — on aluminium, titanium and nickel this is a first-order control, not housekeeping (Chapters 25 and 26).

10. Pulsed GTAW

Pulsing alternates a peak current that establishes penetration with a lower background current that lets the pool partially solidify. Its advantages:

• Lower average heat input for the same penetration, reducing distortion on thin material.

• Better pool control out of position, since the pool partially freezes between pulses.

• Consistent penetration on varying thickness or fit-up, because the peak does the fusing.

• A characteristic stacked-coin bead appearance in manual work, produced by feeding filler in time with the pulse.

Pulsed GTAW is standard practice in orbital tube welding, aerospace work and thin-section fabrication, where its heat-input control is what makes the joint possible.

11. Cast-to-Cast Variation: The Same Parameters, Different Penetration

This is a real and initially baffling phenomenon that GTAW users on stainless steel meet sooner or later, and it deserves explicit treatment because it is routinely misdiagnosed as an equipment fault.

The observation: two plates of the same specification, from different heats, welded autogenously with identical parameters, produce visibly different penetration — one deep and narrow, the other wide and shallow.

The mechanism is the Marangoni effect (Chapter 22, Section 5). Surface tension varies with temperature, and the sign of that variation depends on trace elements — sulphur and oxygen in particular, at concentrations of tens of parts per million. With sufficient trace sulphur, the surface flow carries hot metal inward and down, giving a deep narrow pool. Without it, the flow runs outward, giving a wide shallow pool.

Why it matters: the difference is large enough to take an autogenous full-penetration weld from acceptable to unacceptable with no change to any controlled parameter. It is a property of the material, not of the machine, and no amount of adjustment diagnoses it.

What to do about it:

• Recognize it — the signature is different penetration between material batches with identical settings.

• Control the material specification where the application demands it, by specifying a trace sulphur range as a purchase requirement.

• Use an activating flux where permitted — a surface-applied flux that alters the surface tension gradient and produces consistent deep penetration regardless of the heat.

• Add filler rather than welding autogenously, where the joint allows it, since filler dominates the pool chemistry.

• Qualify to the worst case, and re-verify penetration when the material batch changes on autogenous full-penetration work.

12. Parameters and What Each Controls

| Parameter | Controls | Symptom if wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Current | Heat input, penetration | Too low: lack of fusion. Too high: burn-through, overheated electrode, excessive HAZ |
| Polarity / AC balance | Heat distribution and cleaning | Wrong polarity: electrode destruction or no cleaning. Excess cleaning: shallow penetration, hot electrode |
| Arc length | Arc voltage, heat concentration, shielding integrity | Too long: wide shallow bead, poor shielding, arc wander. Too short: risk of electrode contact |
| Travel speed | Heat input per unit length | Too fast: lack of fusion, narrow bead. Too slow: excessive heat, burn-through, wide HAZ |
| Filler feed rate | Deposit volume, pool temperature | Too fast: cold, unfused deposit. Too slow: undercut, insufficient fill |
| Gas flow | Shielding | Too low: oxidation and porosity. Too high: turbulence and air entrainment |
| Post-flow time | Protection of the cooling electrode and crater | Too short: oxidized electrode, crater oxidation and cracking |
| Electrode type, size and tip | Arc stability and current capacity | Mismatch: arc wander, spitting, tungsten inclusion |

13. Joint Types and Positions

All-position capable, and one of the few processes fully controllable overhead, because the pool is small and the welder controls current live through a pedal.

Its characteristic applications by joint type:

• Open-root pipe welds, where the pool control and the ability to see the root make it the standard root-pass process across pressure and pipeline work.

• Thin sheet and foil, down to thicknesses no other arc process can handle.

• Tube-to-tubesheet joints, usually mechanized.

• Autogenous seam welds in tube mills and on formed sheet.

• Repair and rework where precision and a small heat-affected zone matter.

14. Setup and Execution Procedure

Before welding

1. Confirm the WPS covers the joint, material, thickness and position; confirm your qualification covers process, position, thickness and — separately — whether filler is used, since autogenous and filler-added welding are different qualifications.

2. Select the tungsten type and diameter per the material and current; grind it longitudinally on a dedicated wheel with extraction.

3. Set the tip geometry: point for DC, balled or truncated for AC.

4. Fit the correct collet, collet body, gas lens and nozzle for the electrode diameter and the required extension.

5. Set electrode extension beyond the nozzle appropriate to the joint access and the gas lens in use.

6. Set polarity — DCEN for steel, stainless, nickel, titanium and copper; AC with an appropriate balance for aluminium and magnesium.

7. Verify the shielding gas against the WPS: inert group for aluminium, nickel and titanium; argon-hydrogen only where the material permits.

8. Set gas flow for the nozzle size, and set post-flow long enough to protect the electrode and crater.

9. Where required, set up trailing shield and back purge; purge to a measured oxygen level for critical work.

10. Clean the joint and the filler wire immediately before welding; on aluminium degrease first, then mechanically clean with a dedicated stainless brush.

11. Verify preheat where required, and confirm fit-up against the WPS.

12. Connect the work return close to the joint on a clean surface.

Welding

13. Initiate the arc by HF or lift-arc — never scratch start on quality work.

14. Establish the pool before adding filler; adding filler to an unestablished pool causes lack of fusion.

15. Hold a short, consistent arc length — arc length is the most influential manual variable in GTAW.

16. Feed filler into the leading edge of the pool, keeping the hot rod end inside the gas envelope at all times.

17. Keep the tungsten clear of the pool and the filler; on contact, stop, re-grind the electrode and remove the contaminated weld metal.

18. Control heat through the pedal or torch control, tapering current at starts and terminations.

19. Fill the crater by tapering current down rather than breaking the arc abruptly.

20. Hold the torch over the crater until post-flow ends — moving away immediately exposes the hot metal and electrode to air.

21. Between passes, check interpass temperature and clean any oxide from the previous bead.

After welding

22. Inspect the weld and — on stainless, duplex and titanium — inspect the colour, both on the face and, where accessible, on the root. Colour is a property statement on these materials (Chapters 24 and 26).

23. Inspect the root through a borescope on pipe where accessible.

24. Record the joint against welder, WPS revision and consumable batch.

15. When to Use GTAW and When Not To

| Choose GTAW when | Choose something else when |
| --- | --- |
| Root passes on pipe requiring precise control | Deposition rate matters — GTAW is the slowest common arc process |
| Thin sheet, foil, tube and precision components | Thick section fill — use GMAW, FCAW or SAW after a GTAW root |
| Reactive metals — titanium, zirconium — needing total atmospheric exclusion | Outdoors in wind — the shield is stripped and there is no slag backup |
| Aluminium where appearance and control matter more than speed | Material is dirty, painted or rusted — GTAW is intolerant of contamination |
| Deposit chemistry must be tightly controlled with no flux contribution | Long production seams where a mechanized high-deposition process fits |
| Autogenous welding is wanted — no other arc process does it as cleanly | An unskilled or partially trained workforce — GTAW has the highest skill ceiling |
| Orbital and mechanized tube welding | Cost per metre is the dominant criterion |
