| Crater crack | 104 | Visual | Arc broken abruptly leaving an unfilled crater | Taper current down; use the pedal or downslope function |
| Root oxidation / sugaring | — | Visual, borescope | Absent, insufficient or prematurely stopped purge | Purge to measured oxygen; maintain until cool |
| Inconsistent penetration between material batches | — | Sectioning, visual on the root | Cast-to-cast trace element variation (Section 11) | Specify trace sulphur; use activating flux where permitted; add filler; requalify per batch on autogenous full-penetration work |
| Electrode spitting / rapid erosion | — | Visual | Current above capacity; oxidizing gas; wrong electrode type; insufficient post-flow | Increase diameter; verify gas; verify electrode type against polarity and current |

17. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Tungsten inclusions found by radiography

Symptom: bright spots on the radiograph.

Category: electrode.

Likely causes: electrode contacting the pool or the filler rod; current above the electrode's rating; electrode diameter too small; oxidizing shielding gas eroding the tip; scratch starting.

Steps: verify electrode diameter and type against the current; verify the gas is inert with no active component; check the arc initiation method — replace scratch starting with HF or lift arc; retrain on rod feeding technique; remove all contaminated weld metal.

Card 2 — Heat tint beyond acceptance on stainless

Symptom: coloured bands either side of the weld exceeding the colour reference.

Category: shielding.

Likely causes: gas flow too low or turbulent; no gas lens; nozzle too small for the extension; no trailing shield; post-flow too short; excessive heat input holding the metal hot longer; back purge failure on the reverse.

Steps: set flow for the nozzle and fit a gas lens; consider a trailing shield; extend post-flow; reduce heat input; check the purge; remove tint per specification by pickling or approved mechanical means followed by passivation (Chapter 24, Section 10).

Card 3 — Arc will not start or starts erratically

Symptom: HF discharge visible but no arc, or repeated failed starts.

Category: initiation and setup.

Likely causes: contaminated or incorrectly ground electrode; excessive arc gap at start; poor work return connection; gas not flowing at start (pre-flow too short); wrong electrode type for the polarity; damaged HF unit or torch cable.

Steps: re-grind the electrode longitudinally to a fresh surface; check the return connection at the workpiece; verify pre-flow; verify electrode type against polarity; check the torch and HF path.

Card 4 — Aluminium welds are dirty and the tungsten balls excessively

Symptom: grey oxide in the weld; electrode melting back and forming a large ball.

Category: AC balance and electrode.

Likely causes: AC balance set with too much electrode-positive time, overheating the electrode; electrode diameter too small for the current; surface not cleaned before welding, forcing excessive cleaning action; wrong electrode type.

Steps: reduce the electrode-positive proportion to the minimum that cleans; increase electrode diameter; clean the joint mechanically immediately before welding so less cleaning action is needed; verify electrode type is suitable for AC.

Card 5 — Weld looks acceptable, root fails inspection on pipe

Symptom: cap acceptable; root concave, oxidized or incompletely fused.

Category: root technique and purge.

Likely causes: purge absent, insufficient or over-pressurized; root gap and root face outside tolerance; current too low for root fusion; filler added before the keyhole was established.

Steps: measure fit-up on several joints — intermittency points at fit-up; verify the purge to a measured oxygen level and check purge pressure; confirm the welder's qualification covers open-root work without backing (Chapter 32, Section 6).

18. Safety Specifics

• High ultraviolet output. GTAW produces proportionally more UV than shielded metal arc welding at similar currents, and the open arc is not obscured by smoke, so radiation exposure to the welder's skin and to bystanders is higher than it appears (Chapter 37, Section 3).

• Ozone generation is significant, particularly on aluminium and at higher currents under argon.

• Grinding thoriated tungsten produces low-level radioactive dust. Use a dedicated wheel with extraction, or select lanthanated or ceriated electrodes, which is the reason many organizations have moved away from thoriated types.

• HF start generates electromagnetic interference that can disturb nearby electronics, control systems and instrumentation; lift-arc starting exists partly for this reason.

• Argon asphyxiation risk in confined spaces and in purged assemblies — a purged pipe spool is an oxygen-deficient atmosphere (Chapter 37, Section 9).

19. Standards and Qualification

• Process references: ISO 4063 references 141 (with solid filler), 142 (autogenous), 143 (cored filler), 145 and 146 (reducing gas) [S1].

• Consumables: AWS A5.18 (carbon steel rods), A5.9 (stainless), A5.10 (aluminium), A5.14 (nickel), A5.16 (titanium), A5.12 (tungsten electrodes) [S2]; ISO 636 (non-alloy and fine-grain steels), ISO 14343 (stainless), ISO 18273 (aluminium), ISO 18274 (nickel).

• Gases: ISO 14175 — inert (I) group for reactive metals; R group hydrogen mixtures only where the material permits.

• Procedure and welder qualification: as Chapters 31 and 32; note that autogenous and filler-added welding are separately qualified, and orbital and mechanized GTAW operators qualify under ISO 14732.

20. Worked Example: Two Plates, One Procedure, Two Penetration Results

Situation. A fabricator makes autogenous full-penetration GTAW seam welds on 2 mm austenitic stainless sheet. A new material batch arrives, of the same specification and from the same supplier. With unchanged parameters, welds on the new batch show incomplete penetration. The operator increases current, which produces excessive width and distortion before achieving full penetration.

Step 1 — Confirm that nothing controlled has changed. Machine settings, gas, electrode, fixture and program are unchanged and verifiable from the records. Only the material batch changed. This narrows the field immediately.

Step 2 — Check the material certificate against the previous batch. Both will meet the specification; the question is where within the permitted ranges each sits. The elements of interest are the trace ones — sulphur in particular — which specifications control only as maxima and which therefore vary substantially between heats while both remain conforming.

Step 3 — Recognize the mechanism. This is cast-to-cast variation through the Marangoni effect (Section 11). Low trace sulphur produces outward surface flow, a wide shallow pool, and reduced penetration at identical parameters. It is a material property, not an equipment fault, and no parameter is "wrong."

Step 4 — Evaluate the operator's response. Increasing current does achieve penetration, but by brute heat rather than by restoring the flow pattern — hence the excessive width and distortion. It also takes the process outside the qualified parameter range, which is a qualification issue independent of the weld's appearance (Chapter 31, Section 11).

Step 5 — Choose among the real options. Specify a trace sulphur range as a purchase requirement, which is the durable fix for repeat production but has a commercial cost and a lead time. Use an activating flux where the specification and the application permit it, which restores deep penetration regardless of the heat. Add filler rather than welding autogenously, where the joint design allows, since filler dominates the pool chemistry. Or qualify the procedure to the worst-case material and accept the resulting parameters on all batches.

Step 6 — Add a batch verification step. For autogenous full-penetration production, a penetration check on a coupon from each new material batch, before releasing it to production, catches this at the point where it costs a coupon rather than a production run.

Step 7 — Record it as material knowledge, not as an incident. This phenomenon recurs. A shop that documents it once — with the mechanism, the evidence and the chosen control — saves itself the same investigation on every future batch change, and gives the next engineer an explanation rather than a mystery.

21. Known Gaps

• No current, gas flow or travel speed values are given. All are material-, thickness- and joint-specific, and the WPS governs.

• Tungsten oxide percentages and colour codes are quoted from published summaries of AWS A5.12 [S2][S3] and should be confirmed against the standard where exactness matters — particularly given the documented colour code change for EWCe-2.

• Tip geometry guidance is qualitative. Included angle recommendations exist in the literature and vary with current and application.

• Activating flux use is application- and specification-dependent and is not permitted universally; it is named as an option rather than recommended generally.

• Trace element thresholds for the Marangoni effect are not quoted. The mechanism is well established; the specific concentration at which the flow reverses depends on the alloy and the other trace elements present.

1. Process Overview: ISO 4063 References 15x

Plasma arc welding is gas tungsten arc welding with the arc constricted through a water-cooled copper orifice. The tungsten electrode is recessed inside a nozzle; plasma gas flows around it and is forced through the orifice, which squeezes the arc column into a narrow, collimated, high-velocity plasma jet. A separate shielding gas flows through an outer cup.

The ISO nomenclature covers the family [S1]:

| Reference | Process |
| --- | --- |
| 153 | Plasma welding with transferred arc — the principal welding configuration |
| 154 | Plasma arc welding with non-transferred arc |
| 155 | Plasma arc welding with partially transferred arc |
| 151 | Plasma MIG welding — a hybrid with a consumable wire |
| 152 | Powder plasma arc welding — powder filler, used extensively for hardfacing |

Everything that distinguishes PAW from GTAW follows from the orifice.

2. What Constriction Does to the Arc

A free GTAW arc spreads as it travels from electrode to work — it is a cone. Forcing it through an orifice produces four changes, and each one has a direct practical consequence:

Higher energy density. The same current is concentrated into a much smaller area, raising power density by roughly an order of magnitude over a free tungsten arc. This gives deeper penetration for the same current and a narrower heat-affected zone.

A collimated, stiff arc. The plasma column is nearly parallel-sided rather than conical, so the arc is directionally stable and resists deflection. Arc wander and magnetic deflection are much reduced.

Standoff tolerance. Because the column is parallel rather than conical, moving the torch closer or further from the work changes the heated area far less than it would in GTAW. Torch height variation of a millimetre or two — which would materially change a GTAW bead — has little effect. This is the property that makes PAW attractive for mechanized work and for manual work by operators of varying skill.

The electrode is protected inside the nozzle. It cannot touch the workpiece or the filler wire, so tungsten inclusions are structurally impossible in normal operation — eliminating one of GTAW's characteristic defects (Chapter 41, Section 16).

3. Transferred, Non-Transferred and Partially Transferred Arcs

| Configuration | Circuit | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Transferred (153) | Arc runs between the electrode and the workpiece, which carries current | Welding of conductive materials; the standard welding configuration; highest efficiency |
| Non-transferred (154) | Arc runs between the electrode and the nozzle; the plasma jet is blown out and carries the heat | Non-conductive materials, spraying, and applications where the work must not carry current |
| Partially transferred (155) | Both circuits operate simultaneously | Powder deposition and some surfacing applications |

A pilot arc — a low-current non-transferred arc — is normally maintained continuously between the electrode and the nozzle. It ionizes the plasma gas so that the main transferred arc can be established instantly and reliably without high-frequency starting at the workpiece. This gives PAW notably better arc-starting reliability than GTAW, which matters for mechanized work with many starts and stops.

4. The Three Operating Regimes: Microplasma, Melt-In and Keyhole

PAW covers an unusually wide current range, and it behaves as three distinct processes across it:

Microplasma, at very low currents — fractions of an ampere up to a few amperes. The constricted arc remains stable and directional at currents where a free GTAW arc would be unstable and wander. This is the regime for foil, fine wire, bellows, instrument diaphragms, medical devices and thermocouple junctions, and it is a genuine capability gap that no other arc process fills.

Melt-in mode, at intermediate currents. The pool is melted from the surface downward, as in GTAW, with better penetration and standoff tolerance. Used for general welding, root passes and thin sheet.

Keyhole mode, at higher currents. The plasma jet fully penetrates the material, forming a hole through it that the molten metal flows around and closes behind (Section 5).

5. Keyhole Mode Explained

Above a threshold of energy density and gas flow, the plasma jet's pressure exceeds the surface tension holding the molten pool, and it displaces the pool entirely, opening a hole through the joint. As the torch travels, molten metal flows around the keyhole and solidifies behind it.

The observable characteristics:

• Full penetration in a single pass, in thicknesses that would require multiple passes with GTAW.

• A visible efflux plume on the underside, which is direct evidence that the keyhole is open — a real-time penetration indicator that most processes do not provide.

• A narrow, nearly parallel-sided weld with a small heat-affected zone and low distortion.

• High travel speeds relative to melt-in welding of the same thickness.

The keyhole is a stability problem, not a setting. It exists in a balance between plasma jet pressure opening it and surface tension closing it. Too little energy or gas and it does not open, or it collapses part-way along the joint, leaving incomplete penetration. Too much and it becomes unstable, cutting rather than welding, or leaving undercut and excess penetration. The keyhole is therefore sensitive to travel speed, current, plasma gas flow, joint gap and — critically — material thickness variation and fit-up.

Keyhole PAW has an upper thickness limit for single-pass welding that varies by material and equipment. Above it, the technique is a keyhole root pass followed by melt-in fill passes, using PAW's own strengths for the hardest part of the joint.

6. Equipment and Components

| Component | Function | Failure consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Power source | Constant-current output, usually with pilot arc supply and current up/down slope control | Without slope control, keyhole opening and closing cannot be managed |
| Plasma torch | Houses the recessed electrode, delivers plasma gas through the orifice, delivers shielding gas through the outer cup | The critical component; alignment of electrode to orifice is essential |
| Constricting nozzle (orifice) | Squeezes the arc; water-cooled; orifice diameter matched to current and mode | A consumable. Orifice erosion changes the arc characteristics progressively; a double-arcing event destroys it |
| Electrode | Tungsten, recessed a defined distance behind the orifice | Setback distance is a set-up variable; wrong setback changes the arc and can cause double arcing |
| Water cooling | Removes heat from the nozzle | Loss of cooling destroys the nozzle rapidly |
| Two independent gas supplies | Plasma gas (through the orifice) and shielding gas (through the cup) | Confusing the two, or setting the wrong flows, changes the mode entirely |
| Wire feed (optional) | Adds filler where required | As GTAW |
| Motion system | Most PAW is mechanized | Keyhole stability depends on consistent travel speed |

Double arcing is the characteristic equipment failure: the arc finds a path from the electrode to the nozzle and from the nozzle to the work, rather than direct to the work. It damages the nozzle immediately. Causes include excessive current for the orifice, insufficient plasma gas, incorrect electrode setback, a contaminated or eroded nozzle, and spatter bridging the orifice.

7. Plasma Gas and Shielding Gas

PAW uses two separate gas streams and the distinction is functional, not redundant:

Plasma gas flows through the orifice and becomes the arc plasma. It is almost always argon, because it ionizes easily and is chemically inert to the tungsten. Its flow rate is a primary process control: it determines the jet's momentum and therefore whether the keyhole opens and stays open. Small changes have large effects.

Shielding gas flows through the outer cup and protects the pool and cooling weld, exactly as in GTAW. It is chosen for the material — argon for general use; argon-hydrogen for austenitic stainless and nickel to raise heat input and improve wetting; argon-helium for thicker sections and higher heat; pure argon for titanium and reactive metals, with the same trailing shield and purge requirements as GTAW (Chapter 41, Section 8).

Because the two are independent, PAW allows the arc character and the pool protection to be optimized separately — a flexibility GTAW does not have, where one gas does both jobs.

8. Parameters and What Each Controls

| Parameter | Controls | Symptom if wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Current | Energy input; determines mode with gas flow | Too low: keyhole will not open. Too high: cutting rather than welding; double arcing |
| Plasma gas flow | Jet momentum; keyhole formation and stability | Too low: keyhole collapses, incomplete penetration. Too high: excessive penetration, undercut, cutting action, blown-out root |
| Orifice diameter | Degree of constriction; current capacity | Too small for the current: double arcing and nozzle destruction |
| Electrode setback | Arc constriction and stability | Too far forward: reduced constriction. Too far back: double arcing risk |
| Travel speed | Heat input; keyhole balance | Too fast: keyhole collapse, incomplete penetration. Too slow: excessive penetration, burn-through |
| Shielding gas flow | Pool and cooling weld protection | Too low: oxidation. Too high: turbulence |
| Current upslope / downslope | Opening and closing the keyhole at start and finish | Abrupt start: no keyhole or blow-out. Abrupt stop: unfilled keyhole leaving a hole |
| Standoff distance | Less critical than GTAW, but still bounded | Extreme values still degrade the arc and shielding |

The two most powerful controls are current and plasma gas flow acting together, and they are coupled: a change to one requires reassessment of the other. This coupling is a large part of why PAW is more demanding to set up than GTAW.

9. Joint Types and Positions

PAW's high energy density and standoff tolerance suit it particularly to:

• Square butt joints without edge preparation in thicknesses where GTAW would require a groove — the keyhole penetrates directly, saving preparation cost and filler.

• Longitudinal and circumferential seam welding, mechanized, in tube and vessel manufacture.

• Root passes in heavier joints, followed by fill by another process.

• Foil, bellows and instrument work using microplasma.

Position capability resembles GTAW for melt-in and microplasma work. Keyhole welding is most stable in the flat position and out-of-position keyholing is demanding, because the keyhole balance now includes gravity acting on the surrounding molten metal.

Fit-up requirements are tighter than GTAW, because the keyhole is intolerant of gap variation — a gap the plasma jet can pass through without forming a proper keyhole produces a hole rather than a weld.

10. Setup and Execution Procedure

Before welding

1. Confirm the WPS covers the joint, material, thickness and mode — melt-in, keyhole or microplasma are effectively different procedures.

2. Select the orifice diameter for the current and mode; inspect the nozzle for erosion or spatter, and replace on condition.

3. Fit the tungsten electrode and set the setback distance per the equipment manufacturer's specification; verify concentricity with the orifice.

4. Confirm water cooling is flowing and at temperature.

5. Set plasma gas and shielding gas independently, per the WPS, and verify both are flowing.

6. Verify fit-up tightly — keyhole welding is intolerant of gap variation.

7. Confirm the motion system's travel speed is set and consistent, and that the fixture holds the joint rigidly.

8. Set current upslope and downslope for keyhole opening and closing.

9. Set up back purge and trailing shield where the material requires it.

Welding

10. Establish the pilot arc and confirm it is stable.

11. Transfer the arc to the work and allow the upslope to open the keyhole; on a mechanized seam, this occurs on a run-on tab or a lead-in.

12. Confirm the keyhole is established — the efflux plume on the underside is the direct indicator.

13. Travel at the set speed, monitoring the keyhole through the joint.

14. Where filler is used, feed into the leading edge of the pool behind the keyhole.

15. At termination, use the downslope to close the keyhole progressively; stopping abruptly leaves an open hole through the joint.

16. Where a run-off tab is available, close the keyhole on the tab rather than in the joint.

After welding

17. Inspect the root for continuous penetration and for oxidation or sugaring where purge was used.

18. Inspect the nozzle for erosion or damage before the next joint, and treat progressive erosion as a controlled consumable replacement rather than a fault.

19. Record joint, operator, WPS revision and consumable batch.

11. PAW Against GTAW: The Honest Comparison

| Factor | GTAW | PAW |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Energy density | Moderate | Roughly an order of magnitude higher |
| Arc stability and directionality | Good; can wander | Excellent — stiff, collimated |
| Standoff sensitivity | High — torch height matters | Low — a major advantage for mechanized and manual work |
| Tungsten inclusion risk | Real | Structurally eliminated — electrode is recessed |
| Low-current stability | Poor below a few amperes | Excellent — microplasma down to fractions of an ampere |
| Single-pass full penetration | Limited | Keyhole capability |
| Heat-affected zone width | Wider | Narrower |
| Equipment cost | Low | Substantially higher |
| Consumable maintenance | Electrode grinding | Orifice nozzle is a consumable; double arcing destroys it |
| Setup complexity | Few variables | Two gases, orifice, setback, upslope/downslope — many more variables |
| Fit-up tolerance | Moderate | Tighter, especially in keyhole mode |
| Operator skill for manual work | Very high | Lower for equivalent results, due to standoff tolerance |

The summary judgement: PAW buys arc quality and capability with equipment cost and setup complexity. It earns its place where the capability is genuinely needed — keyhole penetration, microplasma, mechanized seam welding at speed, or standoff-insensitive manual work — and is over-specified where a GTAW arc would do the job.

12. When to Use PAW and When Not To

| Choose PAW when | Choose something else when |
| --- | --- |
| Single-pass full penetration is wanted on material too thick for GTAW | GTAW can do the job — PAW's cost is not justified by marginal gains |
| Welding foil, fine wire, bellows or instrument components (microplasma) | Deposition rate is the objective — PAW is not a filling process |
| Mechanized longitudinal or circumferential seams at production speed | Fit-up cannot be controlled tightly — keyhole mode is intolerant of gap |
| Torch standoff cannot be held precisely | Equipment budget and maintenance capability are limited |
| Tungsten inclusions are unacceptable and have been a problem | Field or site work with limited support — PAW is a shop process |
| A narrow heat-affected zone and low distortion are required | Thick section fill — use PAW for the root and another process for fill |
| Hardfacing with powder filler (152) | Simple manual work in varied positions |

| Defect | ISO 6520-1 ref | Detection | PAW-specific causes | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Incomplete penetration | 402 | RT, UT; loss of efflux plume during welding | Keyhole collapsed — plasma gas flow too low, current too low, travel too fast, thickness or gap variation | Increase plasma gas flow or current; reduce travel speed; tighten fit-up and thickness control |

14. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Keyhole collapses part-way along a seam

Symptom: efflux plume disappears mid-weld; radiography shows incomplete penetration from that point.

Category: keyhole stability.

Likely causes: plasma gas flow marginal; material thickness increasing along the seam; fit-up gap closing; travel speed drift; progressive nozzle orifice erosion reducing constriction; current drift.

Steps: measure material thickness along the seam; measure the gap along the joint; check nozzle condition and life since replacement; verify travel speed with the motion system rather than the setting; increase plasma gas flow in small increments and re-verify, since it is the most sensitive control.

Card 2 — Repeated nozzle destruction

Symptom: nozzles failing rapidly; arc quality degrading quickly after replacement.

Category: double arcing.

Likely causes: current above the orifice's rating; plasma gas flow too low; electrode setback wrong or electrode not concentric; spatter bridging the orifice; water cooling flow inadequate.

Steps: verify the orifice size against the current per the equipment manufacturer's table; check plasma gas flow at the torch, not just at the flowmeter; re-set electrode setback and check concentricity; check coolant flow and temperature; inspect for spatter on the nozzle face.

Card 3 — Weld looks acceptable, root fails inspection intermittently

Symptom: root penetration intermittent along nominally identical joints.

Category: fit-up variation.

Likely causes: keyhole mode is intolerant of gap and thickness variation, and intermittency is the signature of a variable that changes between parts.

Steps: measure fit-up on a sample of parts rather than one; check upstream forming and cutting tolerances; verify fixture clamping repeatability; if fit-up cannot be controlled, evaluate melt-in mode with filler rather than keyhole.

Card 4 — Cannot establish the keyhole at all

Symptom: melt-in pool forms; no efflux plume; no keyhole.

Category: mode setup.

Likely causes: plasma gas flow too low; current too low for the thickness; orifice too large for the current, giving insufficient constriction; travel speed too high; material thicker than the single-pass capability.

Steps: verify orifice size and current against the equipment data; increase plasma gas flow; reduce travel speed; confirm the thickness is within single-pass keyhole capability for the material — if not, use a keyhole root plus melt-in fill.

15. Safety Specifics

• The pilot arc is live whenever it is running, even between welds, and it is a genuine burn hazard on a manual torch.

• UV output is high — the constricted arc is intense — with the same radiation controls as GTAW plus attention to reflection from the bright plasma column.

• Noise from the plasma jet at higher gas flows can be significant, more so in cutting configurations (Chapter 64).

• Ozone generation from UV acting on atmospheric oxygen, as GTAW.

• High-frequency starting, where used, generates electromagnetic interference.

• Water-cooled torches carry a coolant leak hazard onto a live electrical assembly; leak checking is part of routine maintenance.

• Thoriated tungsten grinding dust applies as in GTAW (Chapter 41, Section 18).

16. Standards and Qualification

• Process references: ISO 4063 references 151, 152, 153, 154 and 155 [S1].

• Consumables: tungsten electrodes to AWS A5.12; filler wires per the material family as in GTAW (Chapter 29).

• Gases: ISO 14175 — argon for plasma gas; shielding gas per the material.

• Procedure qualification: as Chapter 31; note that operating mode (keyhole against melt-in) and both gas flows are process-defining variables that must be recorded on the WPS with the same rigour as current.

• Operator qualification: most PAW is mechanized, so ISO 14732 applies to operators and weld setters (Chapter 32, Section 9).

17. Worked Example: Keyhole Collapse on a Longitudinal Seam

Situation. A manufacturer welds longitudinal seams in 4 mm stainless tube using mechanized keyhole PAW. Production runs well for several hours, then radiography begins showing incomplete penetration over the last portion of each seam. Parameters are unchanged and verified against the WPS.

Step 1 — Note the pattern precisely. The defect appears later in each seam and appears after several hours of production. Two different time-dependences are present, and separating them matters: one is within a weld, one is across a shift.

Step 2 — Consider what changes within a single seam. As welding progresses along a tube, the workpiece heats up. A hotter workpiece needs less energy to reach the same pool condition, which would tend to increase penetration rather than reduce it — so heat build-up does not explain a collapse, and that line can be set aside quickly.

Step 3 — Consider what changes across hours of production. The nozzle orifice erodes. As it enlarges, constriction falls, the plasma jet's velocity and momentum drop, and the keyhole balance shifts toward collapse. This progresses gradually and would first show up at the least favourable point in each weld — which is the end, where the joint has accumulated the most heat and the least margin.

Step 4 — Verify rather than assume. Measure or inspect the orifice on a nozzle removed after several hours and compare with a new one. Check the nozzle's service hours against the manufacturer's expected life. Confirm whether the failures correlate with time since nozzle change rather than with anything else on the line.

Step 5 — Rule out the alternatives that share the pattern. Progressive contamination of the plasma gas supply, a slowly failing gas regulator, coolant temperature rising through the shift and reducing cooling effectiveness, and travel speed drift in the motion system would all produce a similar signature. Each is quickly checked.

Step 6 — Fix it as a consumable management problem, not a parameter problem. If nozzle erosion is confirmed, the correct response is a scheduled nozzle replacement interval set inside the point where keyhole stability degrades, not an increase in plasma gas flow to compensate for a worn nozzle. Compensating masks the wear, drifts the process away from the qualified parameters, and eventually fails anyway.

Step 7 — Add a live indicator to the process. The efflux plume is a direct, real-time indicator that the keyhole is open. Monitoring it — visually on a manual process, or with a sensor on a mechanized one — converts this from a defect found by radiography after the fact into a condition detected during welding. That is a cheaper feedback loop than radiography, and on a repetitive production seam it is worth engineering deliberately (Volume 1, Chapter 11 develops the equivalent argument for resistance welding).

18. Known Gaps

• No current, gas flow or orifice size values are given. These are tightly coupled and equipment-specific; the manufacturer's data and the WPS govern, and generic values would risk nozzle damage.

• Single-pass keyhole thickness limits are not stated numerically. They vary by material, equipment and configuration.

• Electrode setback distances are equipment-specific and must be taken from the torch manufacturer's instructions.

• Plasma MIG (151) and powder plasma (152) are named but not developed. Both are specialist configurations, the latter used predominantly in hardfacing (Chapter 65).

• Out-of-position keyhole welding is described qualitatively. It is done, but the parameter windows narrow considerably and are application-specific.

Chapter 43 — Submerged Arc Welding (SAW)

The highest-deposition arc process — how a granular flux blanket makes an invisible arc possible, why flux type is a metallurgical decision rather than a consumable choice, and how the same properties that make it fast make it dangerous on thin or crack-sensitive material.

1. Process Overview: ISO 4063 References 12x

Submerged arc welding feeds a continuous bare wire electrode into the joint beneath a blanket of granular flux delivered ahead of the arc. The arc burns inside a cavity formed within the molten flux, entirely below the surface of the flux blanket — invisible, and shielded from the atmosphere by the flux itself.

The ISO nomenclature distinguishes by electrode form [S1]:

| Reference | Process |
| --- | --- |
| 121 | Submerged arc welding with solid wire electrode |
| 122 | Submerged arc welding with strip electrode |
| 124 | Submerged arc welding with metal powder addition |
| 125 | Submerged arc welding with tubular cored electrode |
| 126 | Submerged arc welding with cored strip electrode |

Its defining characteristic is deposition rate. Because there is no open arc, there is no radiation to limit the current a welder can stand near, and no spatter to lose — currents far higher than any open-arc process are practical, and the deposition rate scales with them.

2. Why Burying the Arc Changes the Economics

Four consequences follow from the flux blanket, and together they define where the process belongs:

Very high current, and therefore very high deposition. Currents run to levels that would be unusable in an open arc. The flux contains the arc energy and the molten pool, and returns radiated and convected heat to the joint — which is why SAW's thermal efficiency is the highest of the arc processes, commonly quoted near unity (Chapter 22, Section 3).

No arc radiation and no visible arc. Operators need no dark filter, and bystander UV exposure is essentially eliminated. This is a real occupational health advantage and also means the operator cannot see the weld being made — the process is controlled by parameters and by tracking, not by watching the pool.

Almost no spatter and very low fume, because the arc and its products are contained under the flux. This makes SAW the cleanest arc process by a wide margin from a fume perspective.

Gravity is required. The flux blanket and the large fluid pool are both held in place by gravity, which restricts the process to the flat and horizontal positions and makes it a fundamentally mechanized process (Section 9).

3. The Flux: What It Does and How Types Differ

The flux performs the functions a covered electrode's covering performs, plus one more: it physically contains the arc.

Its jobs: shield the arc and pool from the atmosphere; form a slag that protects the cooling weld and shapes the bead; stabilize the arc; contribute or remove alloying elements; and insulate the arc cavity thermally.

Fluxes are classified by manufacturing method and by chemical behaviour, and the two classifications answer different questions:

By manufacturing method:

| Type | Manufacture | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fused | Melted, cooled and crushed | Chemically homogeneous, non-hygroscopic, recyclable easily; cannot carry deoxidizers or alloys, because they would oxidize during melting |
| Bonded / agglomerated | Dry constituents bound with a binder and baked at low temperature | Can carry deoxidizers and alloying elements; lower density so a thicker layer per unit weight; more hygroscopic and requires controlled storage |
| Mixed / mechanically blended | Blends of the above | Used to achieve intermediate characteristics; risk of segregation during handling |

The trade is straightforward: fused fluxes are robust and stable but chemically inert; bonded fluxes can do metallurgy but must be kept dry.

By chemical behaviour — the classification that determines properties (Section 4).

4. Flux Basicity and Its Consequences

Fluxes are described on a scale from acid through neutral to basic, conventionally expressed as a basicity index calculated from the flux's oxide composition.

| Character | Operating behaviour | Weld metal properties |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Acid | Excellent bead appearance, good slag detachability, high welding speeds, tolerant of surface contamination | Higher oxygen content in the deposit; lower toughness |
| Neutral | Balanced; does not significantly change deposit chemistry from the wire | Predictable, general-purpose properties; the reference case for multi-pass welding |
| Basic | Poorer bead appearance and slag detachability, more sensitive to surface condition, lower welding speeds | Lower oxygen, better toughness and lower hydrogen |

The pattern mirrors electrode coverings (Chapter 40, Section 6) and produces the same honest conflict: the flux that runs best is not the flux with the best properties. A production department left to choose will choose the flux that gives the best bead and the easiest slag removal; where impact toughness is specified, that choice fails the test.

The neutral / active distinction carries a specific trap worth stating separately. An active flux deliberately adds deoxidizers — typically manganese and silicon — to the weld metal to improve resistance to porosity on contaminated surfaces. That addition is beneficial in a single pass and cumulative in multi-pass welding: each pass adds more, and by several passes the deposit's manganese and silicon content can exceed the specification. Active fluxes therefore belong on single-pass or two-pass work, and neutral fluxes on multi-pass work. Substituting one for the other because it is what was in the hopper is a real metallurgical error that no visual inspection will find.

5. Wire-Flux Combinations Are Classified Together

This is the structural feature of SAW consumables that distinguishes them from every other process: the wire and the flux are classified as a combination, not separately, because the deposit's chemistry and mechanical properties depend on both.

The classification designates the properties achieved by that specific wire with that specific flux. It follows that:

• Changing the flux while keeping the wire changes the deposit and invalidates the classification.

• Changing the wire while keeping the flux does the same.

• A wire and flux from different manufacturers, both individually reputable, are not a classified combination unless they have been classified together.

• On a WPS, both must be specified, and substituting either is a change of essential variable (Chapter 31, Section 11).

Governing specifications: AWS A5.17 for carbon steel wire-flux combinations, A5.23 for low-alloy combinations, A5.22 for stainless; ISO 14171 for the equivalent combinations.

6. Equipment and Components

| Component | Function | Failure consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Power source | High-current constant-voltage (or constant-current for some configurations), rated for very high duty cycle | Undersized supply cannot hold current at SAW levels |
| Wire feed system | Delivers wire at high, precisely controlled rates | Feed variation directly changes current and deposition |
| Contact assembly | Transfers very high current to the wire | Wear and poor contact cause arcing, heating and unstable current |
| Flux hopper and delivery | Lays a controlled depth of flux ahead of the arc | Too little flux exposes the arc; too much restricts gas escape and roughens the bead |
| Flux recovery system | Vacuum recovery of unmelted flux behind the weld | Recovering slag and debris with the flux contaminates the next weld |
| Travel carriage, boom or column | Moves torch or work at controlled speed | Speed variation changes heat input and bead geometry directly |
| Seam tracking | Keeps the wire on the joint | The operator cannot see the arc; tracking is what prevents a weld running off the joint |
| Backing (flux, copper, ceramic, or a backing weld) | Supports the root on full-penetration single-sided joints | Without adequate backing, the fluid pool falls out of the joint |

The seam tracking point is worth emphasizing. In every open-arc process the welder or operator sees the arc and corrects position continuously. In SAW nothing is visible, so joint tracking must be mechanical or sensor-based, and a joint that wanders relative to the torch produces a weld that misses the joint entirely — which is discovered by inspection, not by observation.

7. Variants: Multi-Wire, Strip, Metal Powder Addition

Multi-wire configurations — twin-wire, tandem, and three or more wires in series — raise deposition further. Tandem arrangements typically use a leading wire on direct current for penetration and a trailing wire on alternating current for fill and bead shape, with the AC arrangement chosen partly to reduce magnetic interaction between arcs.

Strip cladding (122, 126) replaces the round wire with a wide strip electrode, producing a broad, shallow, low-dilution overlay in a single pass. It is the dominant process for corrosion-resistant weld overlay on pressure vessel internals, where low dilution is the whole objective (Chapter 22, Section 9).

Metal powder addition (124) feeds iron or alloy powder into the joint ahead of the arc. The arc's surplus energy melts the powder, so deposition rises without a corresponding rise in heat input and dilution — one of the few ways to increase deposition and reduce dilution simultaneously.

Cored wire (125) gives alloying flexibility with the deposition characteristics of a tubular electrode.

8. Parameters and What Each Controls

| Parameter | Controls | Symptom if wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Current | Penetration, deposition rate | Too high: excessive penetration and dilution, burn-through, undercut. Too low: lack of fusion |
| Voltage | Arc length, bead width, flux consumption | Too high: wide flat bead, excessive flux melted, more alloy pickup from the flux, undercut. Too low: narrow humped bead, poor slag detachability |
| Travel speed | Heat input per unit length, bead size | Too fast: narrow bead, undercut, centreline cracking from a teardrop pool. Too slow: excessive heat, large pool, distortion |
| Flux depth | Arc containment | Too shallow: arc flashes through, spatter, poor bead. Too deep: gas cannot escape, rough bead, slag inclusions |
| Wire extension | Resistive preheating, deposition rate | Longer extension increases deposition and reduces penetration; a deliberate technique but a variable that must be controlled |
| Polarity | Penetration and deposition balance | DCEP gives deepest penetration; DCEN gives higher deposition; AC reduces arc blow in multi-wire |
| Wire diameter | Current density and penetration profile | Larger diameters at the same current give lower penetration |
| Joint tracking | Whether the weld lands on the joint | Any deviation puts the deposit off the joint — invisible to the operator |

Heat input in SAW is high by nature, which drives the two characteristic risks: coarse-grained heat-affected zone with reduced toughness, and — combined with high dilution — a susceptibility to centreline solidification cracking (Section 17).

9. Joint Types, Positions and the Gravity Constraint

Position is flat and horizontal only. The flux blanket must lie on the joint and the pool is large and fluid; neither survives out of position. For circumferential welds, the work is rotated so that welding always takes place at or near top dead centre.

Joint design considerations specific to SAW:

• Square-edge preparations are usable at greater thicknesses than in open-arc processes, because penetration is deep — a genuine cost saving in preparation and filler.

• Backing is essential on single-sided full-penetration joints: flux backing, copper backing, ceramic backing, or a first pass by another process.

• Two-sided welding with back-gouging is standard on heavy plate.

• Run-on and run-off tabs are used, because arc start and stop regions are defect-prone and, given the invisible arc, difficult to assess.

10. Setup and Execution Procedure

Before welding

1. Confirm the WPS covers the joint, material and thickness, and confirm both the wire and the flux designations — the classified combination, not the wire alone.

2. Confirm the flux is the correct type for the number of passes: active flux only where the pass count permits (Section 4).

3. Check flux condition and storage; where re-drying is specified, confirm it was done to the manufacturer's schedule.

4. Inspect the joint preparation, fit-up and cleanliness; SAW's high dilution makes surface condition a metallurgical variable.

5. Confirm the backing arrangement is in place and correctly fitted along the whole joint.

6. Set the machine: current, voltage, travel speed, polarity, wire extension, per the WPS.

7. Set flux depth to cover the arc without excessive burden.

8. Verify the tracking arrangement and dry-run the travel path over the full joint length before striking.

9. Fit run-on and run-off tabs.

10. Verify preheat where required, over the specified band and measured correctly.

Welding

11. Start on the run-on tab so that the unstable start region lies outside the joint.

12. Confirm the flux is feeding continuously and covering the arc — a flash of visible arc means the flux delivery has failed.

13. Monitor current, voltage and travel speed against the WPS during the pass; these are the only real-time process indicators available.

14. Watch the slag formation behind the weld — irregular slag is an early indicator of a parameter or flux problem.

15. Terminate on the run-off tab.

16. Allow the slag to cool, then remove it completely. Well-set SAW slag frequently detaches in a single piece; slag that will not detach is itself diagnostic (Section 14).

17. Verify interpass temperature against both minimum and maximum before the next pass.

18. Inspect the bead visually before covering it with the next pass.

After welding

19. Remove run-on and run-off tabs and dress the ends.

20. Perform NDT per the inspection plan — ultrasonics is normally the primary method on heavy section (Chapter 35, Section 11).

21. Record joint, operator, WPS revision, and both wire and flux batch identities.

11. Flux Handling and Recycling

Flux is bought in bulk, spread in quantity, and largely recovered and reused — which creates control requirements that a consumable used once does not have:

• Storage. Bonded fluxes are hygroscopic and require dry storage; re-drying schedules are specified by the manufacturer and are a genuine hydrogen control, not housekeeping.

• Recovery contamination. Recovered flux contains fused slag particles, mill scale, dust and debris picked up from the plate. Recycling it without screening reintroduces contamination into the next weld.

• Screening and blending. Recovered flux must be screened to remove slag and fines, and blended with new flux in a controlled ratio, because the particle size distribution shifts with each cycle.

• Segregation. Mechanically blended fluxes can segregate by particle size and density during handling and recovery, changing the composition delivered to the arc.

• Hopper contamination. Changing flux type without emptying and cleaning the hopper and delivery system leaves the previous flux in the system — a real cause of unexplained property variation.

12. When to Use SAW and When Not To

| Choose SAW when | Choose something else when |
| --- | --- |
| Long, straight or circumferential seams in heavy plate | Position welding is required — SAW is flat and horizontal only |
| Deposition rate dominates the economics | Thin material — heat input and penetration are far too high |
| Low fume and no arc radiation are valuable (enclosed shops, operator health) | Short, intermittent or irregular joints — set-up time exceeds welding time |
| Corrosion-resistant overlay with low dilution (strip cladding) | Site or field work with poor access — SAW is a shop process |
| Pressure vessel, pipe mill, shipbuilding, structural beam production | Crack-sensitive materials where high heat input and dilution are hazards |
| Consistent, repeatable mechanized welding is required | Joint tracking cannot be assured — the operator cannot see the arc |

14. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Slag will not detach

Symptom: slag adheres firmly and must be chipped; inclusions found in the next pass.

Category: parameters and flux.

Likely causes: voltage too low producing a narrow, deeply-set bead; bead profile too convex; flux type mismatched to the joint; flux depth excessive; groove too narrow; previous pass left undercut at the toes.

Steps: increase voltage within the qualified range; check bead profile and placement; verify the flux type against the WPS; reduce flux depth; check the groove geometry. Note that difficult slag detachment is normally a symptom of bead geometry, not a property of the flux alone.

Card 2 — Porosity appearing after a flux recycling change

Symptom: porosity increases following a change in flux handling.

Category: flux condition.

Likely causes: recovered flux not screened, carrying slag and mill scale; recovered-to-new blending ratio changed; flux exposed to humidity in an open hopper; re-drying schedule not followed; fines accumulating and changing the flux's behaviour.

Steps: check the screening and blending procedure and whether it is actually being followed; check hopper covering and ambient humidity; verify re-drying records; empty and inspect the delivery system.

Card 3 — Deposit chemistry drifting out of specification on multi-pass welds

Symptom: manganese and silicon above specification in the completed joint; single-pass test coupons were fine.

Category: flux type.

Likely causes: an active flux used on multi-pass work, adding deoxidizers cumulatively pass by pass (Section 4).

Steps: verify the flux type — active, neutral or alloying — against the WPS; confirm the classified wire-flux combination; switch to a neutral flux for multi-pass work; assess the deposits already made.

Card 4 — Weld found off the joint centreline

Symptom: radiography or ultrasonics shows the weld deposited to one side; fusion incomplete on the other.

Category: tracking.

Likely causes: seam tracking not set or drifting; joint not straight; workpiece movement during welding; carriage rail alignment.

Steps: dry-run the full path before welding and observe the wire position throughout; check fixture clamping and whether the work moves as it heats; check rail and carriage alignment; on long seams, verify tracking mid-length as well as at the ends.

Card 5 — Centreline cracks on a heavy seam

Symptom: cracks along the bead centreline, visible or found by NDT.

Category: solidification cracking.

Likely causes: depth-to-width ratio too high; travel speed too high producing a teardrop pool; high dilution from a sulphur-bearing parent; high restraint.

Steps: measure the bead's depth-to-width ratio on a macro section; reduce travel speed; increase voltage to widen the bead; reduce current to reduce penetration and dilution; check parent metal sulphur; review restraint and joint sequence (Section 17).

15. Safety Specifics

SAW is the safest common arc process on several counts, and this is a legitimate reason to select it:

• No arc radiation reaches the operator — no arc eye, no skin burns, no bystander exposure. Eye protection is still needed against flux, slag and mechanical hazards.

• Very low fume, because the arc products are contained under the flux. This makes it valuable in enclosed shops and for materials whose fume is hazardous.

• Very low spatter, reducing fire risk from ejected metal.

The hazards it does present:

• Very high currents and correspondingly heavy cables and connections; electrical safety and connection integrity matter more, not less.

• Hot slag in large quantity, removed while still hot.

• Flux dust during handling, filling and recovery — a nuisance dust with a respiratory component, requiring handling controls.

• Molten flux and pool break-out if backing fails on a full-penetration joint: a large volume of molten metal and slag can escape.

• Mechanical hazards from the manipulator, carriage or column-and-boom motion.

• Burns from the invisible arc region — the absence of visible arc misleads people about how hot the area is.

16. Standards and Qualification

• Process references: ISO 4063 references 121, 122, 124, 125, 126 [S1].

• Consumables: wire and flux classified as a combination — AWS A5.17 (carbon steel), A5.23 (low alloy), A5.22 (stainless); ISO 14171 and related combination standards.

• Procedure qualification: as Chapter 31. Note that the flux is an essential variable in its own right, and a wire-flux combination change requires requalification.

• Operator qualification: SAW is mechanized, so ISO 14732 applies to operators and weld setters (Chapter 32, Section 9).

• Acceptance: ISO 5817 quality levels or the applicable code; ultrasonics is normally the primary NDT method on heavy section.

17. Worked Example: Centreline Cracking on a Heavy Structural Seam

Situation. A fabricator welds heavy plate butt joints with single-wire SAW. Production is increased by raising travel speed to meet a schedule, with current increased proportionally to maintain deposition. Cracks appear along the bead centreline on the first joints welded at the new settings.

Step 1 — Classify the crack. The cracks are visible immediately after welding and lie along the weld centreline in the weld metal. That is solidification cracking, not hydrogen cracking — hydrogen cracks are delayed and lie in the heat-affected zone (Chapter 36, Section 3).

Step 2 — Identify what the parameter change did to pool shape. Higher travel speed elongates the weld pool into a teardrop shape, so the columnar grains growing from both sides meet head-on along a straight central plane. Segregated low-melting liquid — sulphur and phosphorus bearing — is concentrated into that plane, and contraction stress tears it (Chapter 22, Section 6).

Step 3 — Identify what the current increase did. Higher current deepens penetration, raising the bead's depth-to-width ratio and increasing dilution from the parent metal. A high depth-to-width ratio solidifies from both sidewalls into a central plane — the same geometry that concentrates segregation. Higher dilution brings more parent sulphur into the weld metal. Both changes push in the same direction as the speed increase.

Step 4 — Recognize that two changes compounded. Neither change alone might have caused cracking; together they moved the joint across the threshold. This is why parameter changes are qualified as sets rather than adjusted individually (Chapter 22, Section 15).

Step 5 — Take a macro section and measure. The depth-to-width ratio is directly measurable and is the strongest single piece of evidence. A ratio above roughly one is the classic warning sign, and it converts a plausible explanation into a confirmed one.

Step 6 — Correct in the right order. Reduce travel speed to restore an elliptical pool; increase voltage to widen the bead and reduce the depth-to-width ratio; reduce current to reduce penetration and dilution. Check parent metal sulphur on the material certificates — if it is at the high end of the specification, the process window is genuinely narrower on this material and the parameters must sit further from the threshold.

Step 7 — Address restraint and sequence. High restraint supplies the stress that opens the crack. Reviewing the joint sequence and the fixturing to reduce restraint attacks the third leg of the mechanism, alongside the two metallurgical ones.

Step 8 — Recognize the qualification consequence. The joints were welded outside the qualified parameters. Requalifying at the new settings is not the answer if those settings crack; the correct sequence is to establish parameters that produce sound welds, then qualify them, then produce. Increasing production rate by moving outside a qualified window is how this failure happens, and the corrective action belongs at the planning level, not on the machine.

18. Known Gaps

• No parameter values are given. SAW currents, voltages and travel speeds are joint-, thickness- and equipment-specific and span a very wide range; the WPS governs.

• Basicity index formulas are not reproduced. Several published forms exist and differ; the flux manufacturer's stated basicity and the classified combination are what matter in practice.

• Flux re-drying schedules are manufacturer-specific and are not stated here.

• Recovered-to-new flux blending ratios are specified by the flux manufacturer and by the fabricator's procedure; no general figure is defensible.

• Multi-wire configurations are described in outline. Tandem and multi-wire parameter development is a specialist activity with strong equipment dependence.

• The depth-to-width ratio guideline of approximately one is a widely used rule of thumb rather than a normative limit.

1. Process Overview: ISO 4063 References 72x and 73

Both processes weld a vertical joint in a single pass, however thick the material, by holding a molten pool between the plate edges with water-cooled copper shoes and progressing upward as the joint fills.

The ISO nomenclature covers electroslag welding by electrode form [S1]:

| Reference | Process |
| --- | --- |
| 721 | Electroslag welding with strip electrode |
| 722 | Electroslag welding with wire electrode |
| 73 | Electrogas welding (in the same general group) |

The configuration is the same for both: the joint is vertical, the edges are usually square with a gap between them, water-cooled copper shoes close the gap on both faces to contain the molten metal, and the assembly rises as the weld progresses.

What differs is the heat source, and that difference is fundamental (Sections 2 and 3).

2. Electroslag Welding: A Process Without an Arc

Electroslag welding is not an arc welding process, despite being grouped with them administratively. After a brief starting arc establishes a pool of molten flux, the arc extinguishes and does not return.

The mechanism. Current passes from the electrode, through a bath of electrically conductive molten slag, to the workpiece. The slag has substantial electrical resistance, so the current passing through it generates heat by resistance — the slag bath itself becomes the heat source, at a temperature above the melting point of the steel. The electrode is fed continuously into the slag bath, where it melts; droplets fall through the slag to the pool of molten metal beneath, and the pool solidifies from the bottom as the assembly rises.

Consequences of having no arc:

• No arc radiation and very little spatter or fume.

• Very high deposition rate, limited by heat extraction rather than by arc stability.

• Any thickness in one pass — the process is used on sections far too thick for any multi-pass approach to be economic.

• A very large molten pool with a very long solidification time, which is the source of the metallurgical problem in Section 8.

• The slag must remain molten and conductive throughout — if it freezes or its composition drifts, the process stops.

3. Electrogas Welding: An Arc Process in the Same Configuration

Electrogas welding uses the same vertical, shoe-contained configuration, but maintains an arc shielded by a gas — either supplied externally or generated by a flux-cored electrode, or both.

Consequences of retaining the arc:

• Heat input is lower than electroslag for the same joint, so the heat-affected zone is narrower and grain coarsening less severe.

• Deposition rate is lower.

• Thickness capability in one pass is lower — electrogas covers the upper end of conventional plate, electroslag goes far beyond it.

• The process behaves more like a very large vertical flux-cored or gas-metal-arc weld than like a casting operation.

4. The Two Compared

| Factor | Electroslag (722) | Electrogas (73) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Heat source | Resistance heating of a molten slag bath — no arc | Electric arc under gas shielding |
| Heat input | Very high | High, but substantially lower |
| Thickness in one pass | Very large — the process's reason for existing | Upper-conventional plate thicknesses |
| Deposition rate | Highest of any fusion welding process | High |
| Heat-affected zone | Very wide, coarse-grained | Narrower |
| Toughness as-welded | Generally poor without post-weld normalizing | Better, but still requires attention |
| Restart after interruption | Difficult — usually requires cutting out and restarting | Easier |
| Typical use | Very heavy plate, ingot moulds, machine bases, heavy structural members | Storage tank vertical seams, shipbuilding, heavy plate |

5. Equipment and Components

| Component | Function | Failure consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Power source | High current, continuous duty, typically constant voltage | Interruption ends the weld and usually the joint |
| Wire or strip feeder | Feeds continuously into the slag bath or arc | Feed interruption collapses the process |
| Oscillating head (thick sections) | Traverses the electrode across the joint width for even melting | Without it, thick joints fuse unevenly at the edges |
| Water-cooled copper shoes (dams) | Contain the molten pool on both faces and chill the weld surfaces | A leaking or badly fitted shoe causes break-out of molten metal — a serious hazard |
| Vertical drive | Raises the head and shoes as the weld fills | Speed mismatch to fill rate causes overflow or slag entrapment |
| Flux delivery (ESW) | Maintains slag bath depth and composition | Bath too shallow: arcing returns. Too deep: unstable and slow |
| Gas supply (EGW) | Shields the arc | Loss of shielding gives porosity through a very large deposit |
| Starting sump and run-off tab | Contains the unstable start and finish regions outside the joint | Without them, start and stop defects lie within the joint |
| Cooling water circuit | Keeps the shoes intact | Loss of cooling destroys the shoes and releases the pool |

6. Consumables

Electroslag uses a solid wire or strip electrode with a granular flux that forms the conductive slag bath. The flux's electrical conductivity when molten is a defining property — it is not interchangeable with a submerged arc flux, whose function is different. Consumable guide tubes are used in some configurations, where a consumable tube conducts the wire into the bath and is itself melted into the joint.

Electrogas uses a flux-cored or solid wire with shielding gas, and consumables resemble those of flux-cored arc welding.

For both, the deposit's toughness depends heavily on the consumable, and consumables intended for these processes are formulated for the slow cooling and coarse structure they produce.

7. Parameters and What Each Controls

| Parameter | Controls | Symptom if wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Current / wire feed speed | Melting rate, heat input, fill rate | Too low: incomplete fusion at the plate edges. Too high: excessive heat, wider HAZ |
| Voltage | Slag bath resistance behaviour and heat distribution (ESW); arc length (EGW) | Too high in ESW: arcing through the slag. Too low: sluggish melting |
| Slag bath depth (ESW) | Whether the process remains arcless | Too shallow: the arc returns and the process becomes something else. Too deep: unstable, poor edge fusion |
| Vertical travel speed | Must match the fill rate | Too fast: pool overflows the shoes or leaves unfilled joint. Too slow: excess heat |
| Oscillation width and dwell | Even fusion across a thick joint | Insufficient dwell at the edges: lack of fusion at the plate faces |
| Root gap | Pool volume and containment | Too narrow: poor edge fusion. Too wide: excess weld volume and heat |
| Shoe fit | Containment | Poor fit: molten metal break-out |

8. The Metallurgical Problem: Grain Structure and Toughness

This is the central engineering issue with both processes, and it is inherent rather than a fault to be tuned out.

What happens. The very high heat input and the very large molten volume give an extremely slow cooling rate. The weld metal solidifies with coarse columnar grains growing inward from the chilled faces toward the centre, and the heat-affected zone is very wide with substantial grain coarsening (Chapter 22, Sections 6 and 7).

Why it matters. Coarse grains in both the weld metal and the coarse-grained heat-affected zone give low notch toughness. In a statically loaded, non-critical application this may be acceptable. In a structure subject to dynamic loading, low temperature service, or where brittle fracture is a design consideration, it is not.

The controls available:

1. Post-weld normalizing. Heating the joint above the transformation temperature and cooling produces a fine equiaxed grain structure, restoring toughness. Metallurgically complete and often impractical on a large fabricated assembly — furnace size and distortion are the constraints.

2. Consumable selection formulated for these processes.

3. Reduce heat input as far as the process permits — favouring electrogas over electroslag where thickness allows, and using oscillation to reduce the electrode current needed.

4. Restrict application. The most common control is simply not to use these processes where toughness governs. Several structural codes have historically restricted or conditioned the use of electroslag welding in dynamically loaded structures for exactly this reason, and where a code permits it, it does so with specific qualification and testing requirements.

The honest summary: these processes are chosen for economics on very heavy section, and the toughness consequence must be addressed explicitly at design stage — by heat treatment, by code-compliant qualification with impact testing, or by not choosing the process. It cannot be addressed by inspection, because coarse grain structure is not a discontinuity.

9. Electroslag Surfacing and Strip Cladding

A distinct and commercially significant application: electroslag strip cladding deposits a wide, shallow, low-dilution corrosion-resistant overlay using a strip electrode in a slag bath, on a horizontal surface rather than in a vertical joint.

Compared with submerged arc strip cladding (Chapter 43, Section 7), electroslag strip gives lower dilution and higher deposition — both advantageous for corrosion-resistant overlay, where dilution from the substrate is the principal quality limit (Chapter 22, Section 9). It is widely used on pressure vessel internals.

10. Setup and Execution Procedure

Before welding

1. Confirm the WPS covers the material, thickness and configuration, including any required post-weld heat treatment.

2. Confirm the toughness requirement and how it will be met — this is a design-level question that must be settled before the joint is welded, not after.

3. Set up the joint vertically with the specified root gap, aligned and rigidly held.

4. Fit and seal the water-cooled shoes on both faces; verify cooling water flow.

5. Fit the starting sump at the bottom and the run-off tab at the top so start and finish regions lie outside the joint.

6. Verify consumable and flux (ESW) or gas (EGW) against the WPS.

7. Verify the vertical drive and, where used, the oscillation settings.

8. Confirm preheat where required.

Welding

9. Start in the sump: establish the arc, build the slag bath (ESW), and confirm the transition to arcless operation before the weld enters the joint.

10. Confirm the slag bath depth is stable and that no arcing is occurring through it (ESW).

11. Match the vertical travel to the fill rate, keeping the pool at the correct level relative to the shoes.

12. Monitor current, voltage and travel continuously — with the pool contained and largely unobservable, these are the process indicators.

13. Maintain oscillation dwell at the plate edges on thick joints, so the plate faces fuse.

14. Do not interrupt. An interrupted electroslag weld normally cannot simply be restarted: the slag bath solidifies and the restart region is defect-prone. Recovery usually means cutting out and re-preparing.

15. Finish in the run-off tab so the terminal shrinkage region lies outside the joint.

After welding

16. Remove the sump and run-off tab; dress the ends.

17. Apply post-weld heat treatment where specified — normalizing where toughness requires it.

18. Inspect: ultrasonics is the primary method on this thickness (Chapter 35).

19. Record joint, operator, WPS revision, consumable and flux batches, and the heat treatment record.

11. When to Use These Processes and When Not To

| Choose electroslag or electrogas when | Choose something else when |
| --- | --- |
| Section thickness makes multi-pass welding uneconomic | Toughness governs and post-weld normalizing is not practical |
| The joint is vertical or can be positioned vertically | The joint cannot be positioned vertically |
| A single continuous pass is achievable without interruption | Production is intermittent or interruption is likely |
| Ingot moulds, machine bases, very heavy structural members | Dynamically loaded structures where the code restricts the process |
| Corrosion-resistant strip cladding with minimum dilution (electroslag strip) | Thin or moderate plate — conventional processes are cheaper and better |
| Storage tank and ship hull vertical seams (electrogas) | Where the equipment, shoes and setup time cannot be justified by the joint count |

13. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Arcing observed in an electroslag weld

Symptom: arc flashes visible at the slag surface; process behaviour changes.

Category: slag bath condition.

Likely causes: slag bath too shallow; flux addition interrupted; voltage too high for the bath depth; slag composition drifted through the weld.

Steps: check flux delivery continuity; increase bath depth to the specified value; reduce voltage; note that arcing means the process is no longer electroslag welding and the deposit it produces is not what was qualified.

Card 2 — Lack of fusion at one plate face

Symptom: UT finds unfused plate face on one side only.

Category: oscillation and alignment.

Likely causes: oscillation not centred on the joint; insufficient dwell at that edge; electrode alignment off-centre; root gap wider on one side.

Steps: check electrode centring and oscillation limits against the joint; increase edge dwell; measure the root gap along the joint length; check whether the joint has moved during welding.

Card 3 — Impact test failure on a completed joint

Symptom: Charpy results below requirement; all NDT acceptable.

Category: inherent grain structure.

Likely causes: coarse columnar weld metal and coarse-grained HAZ from very high heat input and slow cooling; no post-weld normalizing applied; consumable not selected for toughness.

Steps: confirm whether post-weld normalizing was specified and performed; check the consumable against the WPS; recognize that this is not a defect to repair but a property outcome to be addressed by heat treatment or by process selection at design stage (Section 8).

Card 4 — Molten metal escaping at a shoe

Symptom: metal or slag leaking at the shoe face during welding.

Category: containment — immediate safety issue.

Likely causes: shoe not seated against the plate; plate distortion opening a gap; shoe cooling lost causing local melting; clamping released by thermal movement.

Steps: stop safely; do not attempt to reseat a shoe against a live pool; verify cooling flow and shoe condition before restarting; reassess clamping to accommodate thermal movement.

14. Safety Specifics

• Molten metal break-out is the defining hazard: a very large volume of molten metal and slag contained only by water-cooled shoes, in a vertical configuration, above floor level. Break-out is both a severe burn hazard and, if it reaches water, a steam explosion hazard.

• Water and molten metal in proximity. Shoe cooling failure can put water into contact with a large molten pool. Cooling circuit integrity is a safety-critical check, not a maintenance preference.

• The joint is hot for a very long time after welding, given the heat input and section thickness.

• Electroslag has no arc radiation, but the slag bath surface is intensely hot and bright.

• Very high currents with correspondingly heavy conductors.

• Working at height on tall vertical seams, with the equipment climbing the joint.

15. Standards and Qualification

• Process references: ISO 4063 references 721 and 722 for electroslag with strip and wire electrodes; electrogas welding within the same group [S1].

• Consumables: wire, strip and flux per the applicable AWS and ISO specifications for these processes.

• Procedure qualification: as Chapter 31, with impact testing normally required given the toughness issue, and with the post-weld heat treatment condition as a qualification variable.

• Operator qualification: mechanized process — ISO 14732 applies (Chapter 32, Section 9).

• Code restrictions: several structural codes restrict or condition the use of electroslag welding in dynamically loaded structures; the governing code must be checked before selecting the process, at design stage.

16. Worked Example: A Toughness Failure on a Heavy Column Splice

Situation. A fabricator welds heavy column splices by electroslag welding to save time against a multi-pass alternative. The welds pass ultrasonic inspection. Production impact test coupons fail the specified Charpy requirement at the fusion line.

Step 1 — Recognize what the results are telling you. Ultrasonics found no discontinuities and impact testing failed. Those two results are consistent, not contradictory: coarse grain structure is a property, not a discontinuity, and no NDT method detects it (Chapter 35, Section 1).

Step 2 — Identify the mechanism, which is inherent rather than an error. Electroslag welding's very high heat input and very slow cooling produce coarse columnar weld metal and a wide coarse-grained heat-affected zone, and low notch toughness follows directly (Section 8). Nothing went wrong in the sense of a mistake; the process produced its characteristic result.

Step 3 — Establish what was assumed at process selection. The question is whether the toughness requirement was known when electroslag welding was chosen, and whether post-weld normalizing was planned. If the process was selected on cycle time without the toughness requirement being considered, that is the root cause and it sits in planning, not in the welding.

Step 4 — Check the code position. Several structural codes restrict or condition electroslag welding in dynamically loaded structures. If the structure falls into such a category, the process may not have been permissible at all, which changes the disposition question entirely.

Step 5 — Evaluate the available remedies honestly. Post-weld normalizing would restore the grain structure but requires furnace capacity for a heavy column splice and introduces distortion — frequently impractical on an assembled structure. Consumable change addresses the weld metal but not the coarse-grained heat-affected zone, and the failures were at the fusion line. Repair by another process means removing the entire weld.

Step 6 — Decide at the right level. This is an engineering decision about the structure, not a welding decision: either the joints are heat treated, or they are removed and rewelded by a process whose heat input permits the required toughness, or the design is reassessed against the properties actually achieved. Each option has a cost, and the welding department cannot choose among them alone.

Step 7 — Fix the selection process. The lasting correction is that process selection must include the mechanical property requirements, not only the geometry and the schedule. A process-selection check that asks "what does the specification require for toughness, and does this process deliver it as-welded?" would have caught this before a single joint was made — which is exactly the function of the technical review requirement in Chapter 33, Section 4.

17. Known Gaps

• No parameter values are given. These processes are highly equipment- and configuration-specific.

• Thickness capability ranges are described qualitatively. Published capability varies by equipment, material and configuration, and any single figure would mislead.

• Code restrictions on electroslag welding are stated in principle, not quoted. The governing code and its current edition must be checked directly.

• Consumable guide tube variants are named but not developed.

• Electrogas welding is treated more briefly than electroslag, reflecting its narrower application; its parameter development resembles flux-cored arc welding at large scale.
