1. Process Overview: ISO 4063 References 78x

Stud welding joins a fastener — a threaded stud, a shear connector, a pin, an insulation anchor — end-on to a flat surface, in a single automatic cycle lasting from a few milliseconds to a fraction of a second. The stud itself is the electrode; there is no separate filler.

The ISO nomenclature separates the variants [S1]:

| Reference | Process |
| --- | --- |
| 783 | Drawn arc stud welding with ceramic ferrule or shielding gas |
| 784 | Short-cycle drawn arc stud welding |
| 785 | Capacitor discharge drawn arc stud welding |
| 786 | Capacitor discharge stud welding with tip ignition |

Two families sit behind those four numbers: drawn-arc, in which the stud is lifted to draw an arc and then plunged into the resulting pool, and capacitor-discharge, in which stored energy is released in milliseconds through a small ignition tip.

The distinguishing feature of the whole family is that the entire weld is made by a machine cycle, not by an operator's manipulation. The operator positions the gun and pulls the trigger; the sequence, timing and plunge are automatic. Quality is therefore determined by setup, equipment condition and surface condition rather than by manual skill — which changes where troubleshooting must look.

2. Drawn-Arc Stud Welding

The structural variant, used for shear connectors on composite beams, and for heavier threaded studs.

The cycle:

1. The stud is held against the workpiece by the gun, inside a ceramic ferrule.

2. On triggering, current flows and the gun lifts the stud a small controlled distance, drawing an arc.

3. The arc burns for a set time — typically tens to hundreds of milliseconds — melting the stud end and a corresponding pool on the workpiece.

4. At the end of the arc time, the gun plunges the stud into the pool under spring or pneumatic force.

5. Molten metal is displaced outward and forms a fillet of expelled metal around the stud base, contained by the ferrule.

6. Current stops; the joint solidifies with the stud held in place.

The resulting joint is a full cross-section fusion weld across the stud's entire end face, which is why a correctly made stud weld is stronger than the stud shank — the standard acceptance expectation being that the stud will bend or fail in the shank rather than at the weld.

3. Short-Cycle Drawn-Arc Stud Welding

The same lift-and-plunge sequence with a much shorter arc time, at higher current. Its advantages follow from the reduced total energy:

• Thinner base material can be used without burn-through.

• Often no ferrule is required, with shielding gas or no shielding used instead.

• Less distortion and less marking on the reverse face — important on visible panels.

• Faster cycle time.

Its constraint is that the shorter arc gives less tolerance of surface contamination and less time for the pool to develop, so surface preparation matters more.

4. Capacitor-Discharge Stud Welding

An entirely different energy delivery. A capacitor bank is charged and then discharged through the stud in a few milliseconds.

Two ignition arrangements exist, and the ISO numbering separates them [S1]:

• Tip ignition (786): the stud has a small projection — an ignition tip — on its weld face. On contact and discharge, the tip vaporizes almost instantly, establishing the arc, and the stud is immediately driven into the resulting molten layer.

• Drawn-arc capacitor discharge (785): the stud is lifted to draw the arc as in the drawn-arc process, with capacitor-discharge energy.

Characteristics:

• Extremely short cycle — milliseconds — and therefore very low total heat input.

• Very little reverse-side marking, which is why it dominates on thin sheet, appearance panels and cosmetic assemblies.

• Thin base material capability far below the drawn-arc processes.

• The melted depth is very shallow, which means surface condition — plating, oxide, paint, oil — has a proportionally much larger effect than on drawn-arc welding.

• Dissimilar metal combinations are more feasible than with longer-cycle processes, because there is very little time for intermetallic formation (Chapter 27, Section 2).

5. The Ceramic Ferrule and What It Does

The ferrule is a small, single-use ceramic ring placed around the stud base. It does four jobs:

1. Contains the molten metal displaced by the plunge, shaping it into the fillet around the stud base rather than letting it spatter away.

2. Shields the arc and pool from the atmosphere, largely replacing a shielding gas.

3. Concentrates the arc in the joint area.

4. Slows cooling slightly, moderating the very rapid quench into the surrounding cold plate.

It is broken off and discarded after each weld. The fillet it forms is a primary visual acceptance indicator: a complete, uniform fillet all round indicates a correctly made weld, and a partial, one-sided or absent fillet indicates a fault (Section 11).

Where a ferrule is not used — short-cycle and capacitor-discharge work — shielding gas may be used instead, or the cycle may be short enough that atmospheric contamination is not significant.

6. Equipment and Components

| Component | Function | Failure consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Power source | Delivers the weld current: rectifier or inverter for drawn-arc, capacitor bank for CD | Undersized supply gives insufficient current and lack of fusion |
| Stud gun | Holds the stud, executes lift and plunge, controls timing | Worn or dirty mechanism gives inconsistent lift height and plunge — the dominant cause of variability |
| Chuck / collet | Grips the stud and conducts current | Wear causes poor current transfer and inconsistent stud position |
| Foot / leg assembly | Sets the gun square to the surface and holds the lift reference | A gun not held square produces a one-sided weld |
| Ferrule holder | Positions the ferrule concentrically | Off-centre ferrule gives an uneven fillet |
| Control unit | Sets arc time, current, lift and plunge | Setting drift produces gradual quality change with no visible cause |
| Work return clamp | Completes the circuit — often two clamps placed symmetrically | A single asymmetric return causes arc blow, one of the most common stud welding faults |

The symmetric earth return arrangement deserves emphasis. Because the arc is short, central and unmanipulated, magnetic arc blow deflects it consistently to one side and produces a weld fused on one side and unfused on the other. Two work return connections placed symmetrically about the stud location is the standard remedy and is often the difference between a reliable process and a persistently intermittent one.

7. Consumables: Studs, Ferrules and Shielding

Studs are manufactured for the process, with a weld-end geometry designed for it: a flat or slightly chamfered end for drawn-arc, an ignition tip for capacitor-discharge tip-ignition. A stud is not a bolt with the head cut off — the weld-end geometry, the material and often a flux load in the end face are part of the design.

Aluminium studs carry a small flux or aluminium load in the end face in some designs, and are welded with shielding gas rather than a ferrule.

Ferrules are matched to the stud diameter and to the joint configuration — flat surface, fillet to a corner, or through-deck. The wrong ferrule gives the wrong fillet shape and poor containment.

Shielding gas, where used, is inert or an argon-CO₂ mixture depending on the material and variant.

8. Parameters and What Each Controls

| Parameter | Controls | Symptom if wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Weld current | Melting rate and depth | Too low: incomplete fusion, cold weld. Too high: burn-through, excessive expulsion, undercut around the base |
| Arc time | Total energy; pool volume | Too short: insufficient melting, lack of fusion. Too long: burn-through, excessive HAZ, reverse-side marking |
| Lift (arc length) | Arc voltage and stability | Too short: stud shorts into the pool. Too long: arc extinguishes or wanders |
| Plunge depth and damping | How the stud enters the pool and how much metal is displaced | Too shallow: poor fusion and a thin fillet. Too deep: excessive expulsion, undercut, short stud length after welding |
| Plunge speed / damping | Whether the stud bounces or seats cleanly | Uncontrolled plunge causes porosity and inconsistent fillets |
| Gun squareness | Symmetry of the arc and the fillet | Off-square: one-sided fusion and fillet |
| Earth return placement | Magnetic arc balance | Asymmetric return: arc blow and one-sided fusion |

Stud length after welding (burn-off) is a useful indirect check: the process consumes a predictable length of stud, and a stud that is longer than expected after welding indicates insufficient melting, while one that is shorter indicates excessive energy or plunge.

9. Base Material and Surface Condition Requirements

Because the cycle is short and unmanipulated, the process cannot compensate for surface condition the way a manual welder can.

• Rust, scale, paint, primer and oil must be removed from the weld area. Drawn-arc welding tolerates some mill scale; capacitor-discharge tolerates very little, because the melted depth is only a fraction of a millimetre.

• Galvanizing is a specific case: zinc vaporizes, causing porosity, arc instability and zinc fume (Chapter 37, Section 5). Welding through galvanizing is done in some applications with adjusted parameters and studs designed for it, but it narrows the process window substantially and is a common source of intermittent failures.

• Base material thickness must be adequate for the energy: a general working guideline is that the base must be a sufficient fraction of the stud diameter, with capacitor-discharge suiting the thinnest material and drawn-arc requiring more.

• Moisture on the surface causes porosity.

• Curvature and fit: the stud end must meet the surface squarely and completely; welding onto a curved or uneven surface without an adapted arrangement gives partial fusion.

10. Setup and Execution Procedure

Before welding

1. Confirm the specification: stud type, size, material, base material, and the required test regime.

2. Verify base material thickness is adequate for the stud diameter and process variant.

3. Clean the weld area to bare metal over an area larger than the ferrule.

4. Fit the correct chuck and ferrule holder for the stud diameter; fit the correct ferrule type for the joint configuration.

5. Place two work return clamps symmetrically about the weld area to balance the magnetic field.

6. Set current, arc time, lift and plunge per the equipment manufacturer's data and the qualified procedure.

7. Weld and test trial studs before production — this is not optional in stud welding practice, and codes require it. Test them by bending or by the specified method (Section 11).

8. Confirm the gun is held square and the foot assembly is stable on the surface.

Welding

9. Load the stud into the chuck and fit the ferrule.

10. Place the gun square to the surface, with firm, even foot contact.

11. Trigger and hold the gun steady and square until the cycle completes — movement during the cycle is a leading cause of defects, and the cycle is short enough that operators tend to lift too early.

12. Remove the gun after the cycle, break off and discard the ferrule.

13. Inspect the fillet visually on every stud: it should be complete, uniform and continuous all round.

14. Re-test at the frequency the specification requires, and after any interruption, parameter change, material change, or operator change.

After welding

15. Perform the specified proportion of bend or torque tests.

16. Record parameters, trial test results, production test results, and operator.

11. Testing and Acceptance: Bend, Torque and Visual

Stud welding acceptance rests on three methods, and the balance between them is unusual — visual carries more weight here than in most processes, and destructive testing is routine rather than exceptional.

Visual inspection of the fillet. A complete, uniform fillet of expelled metal all round the stud base is the primary indicator of a correct weld. A partial fillet, a fillet on one side only, an undersized fillet or an absent fillet indicates a fault and the stud is rejected without further testing. This check is applied to every stud, and it is quick.

Bend testing. The stud is bent — commonly to a specified angle — by striking or levering it. A correctly welded stud bends in the shank without failure at the weld; a defective one snaps off at the weld interface. This is destructive for the bent stud in principle, though in structural practice studs bent to a moderate angle and showing no failure are often accepted in place, per the governing code. Bend testing is applied to trial studs before production and to a specified proportion of production studs.

Torque testing. For threaded studs, applying a specified torque tests the joint in a manner representing service loading. Used where the stud is loaded in tension or by a fastener.

The important structural point: bend testing on trial studs before production is the process control, because the weld is made by a machine cycle whose settings can be verified before committing to production. A shop that starts production without trial studs has skipped the only pre-production verification the process offers.

12. When to Use Which Variant

| Requirement | Variant |
| --- | --- |
| Structural shear connectors on beams | Drawn-arc with ferrule (783) |
| Heavy threaded studs on structural steel | Drawn-arc with ferrule |
| Thin sheet without reverse-side marking | Capacitor-discharge (785, 786) |
| Appearance-critical panels — no mark on the visible face | Capacitor-discharge |
| Moderate thickness, faster cycle, less distortion than full drawn-arc | Short-cycle drawn-arc (784) |
| Insulation pins on ductwork and thin panels | Capacitor-discharge |
| Aluminium studs | Drawn-arc with shielding gas, studs designed for aluminium |
| Dissimilar metal combinations | Capacitor-discharge — the millisecond cycle limits intermetallic formation |
| Through-deck welding on composite floors | Drawn-arc with a ferrule and parameters qualified for the deck arrangement |

13. Defect Catalog

| Defect | Detection | Cause | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Incomplete fillet / fillet on one side only | Visual | Arc blow from asymmetric earth return; gun not square; ferrule off-centre; uneven surface contact | Place two symmetric earth returns; check gun squareness and foot contact; check ferrule seating |
| No fusion / stud snaps off at the weld | Bend test | Current or arc time too low; contaminated surface; poor earth connection; stud not seated in the chuck | Increase energy per the manufacturer's data; clean the surface; check the return and the chuck |
| Burn-through of the base material | Visual on the reverse | Energy too high for the base thickness; wrong variant for the material | Reduce arc time and current; move to short-cycle or capacitor-discharge |
| Porosity in the weld | Sectioning; bend test failure | Moisture, oil, paint or galvanizing on the surface; damp ferrule; excessive plunge causing entrapment | Clean to bare metal; store ferrules dry; adjust plunge; use studs and parameters qualified for galvanized work |
| Undercut around the stud base | Visual | Excessive energy; excessive plunge; excessive expulsion | Reduce energy and plunge depth |
| Stud too short after welding | Dimensional | Excessive plunge or energy consuming too much stud | Reduce plunge and arc time; verify against expected burn-off length |
| Stud too long after welding | Dimensional | Insufficient melting — the process did not consume the expected length | Increase energy; check for a cold weld even if the fillet looks acceptable |
| Cracking in the weld or HAZ | Bend test; sectioning | Hardenable base material with a very rapid quench; hydrogen from surface contamination | Preheat where the base material requires it; clean thoroughly; select stud material appropriately |
| Intermittent failures on nominally identical welds | Bend test statistics | Variability in surface condition or in the gun mechanism rather than in settings | Check gun lift and plunge consistency; check chuck and foot wear; check surface preparation consistency |

14. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Fillet consistently heavier on one side

Symptom: expelled metal fillet uneven around the stud, same orientation every time.

Category: arc blow or squareness.

Likely causes: single asymmetric work return producing magnetic deflection; gun consistently held off-square; foot assembly worn on one side.

Steps: fit two work returns symmetrically about the weld area; check gun squareness with a square on a test piece; inspect the foot assembly for wear; note that a consistent orientation points at a systematic cause, not a random one.

Card 2 — Studs pass visual, fail bend testing

Symptom: fillets look complete; studs snap at the weld under bending.

Category: energy or surface.

Likely causes: sufficient energy to form a fillet but not to fuse fully — a "cold" weld with a cosmetically acceptable fillet; surface contamination limiting fusion; plunge too shallow leaving a shallow fused zone.

Steps: check stud burn-off length against the expected value — a long remaining stud indicates insufficient melting; increase arc time and current within the manufacturer's data; verify surface cleaning; increase plunge depth. This combination is exactly why bend testing exists alongside visual inspection.

Card 3 — Quality degrading gradually over a shift

Symptom: acceptable at start of shift, increasing rejects later, settings unchanged.

Category: equipment wear or condition.

Likely causes: chuck wear degrading current transfer; gun mechanism becoming sluggish or contaminated with spatter; earth clamp connection deteriorating; power source thermal derating at high duty cycle.

Steps: inspect and clean the chuck and gun mechanism; re-make the earth connections on clean metal; check the duty cycle against the equipment rating; re-test trial studs mid-shift as a routine check rather than only at start-up.

Card 4 — Porosity and instability on coated steel

Symptom: irregular fillets, porosity, spatter, on galvanized or painted material.

Category: surface condition.

Likely causes: zinc vaporizing in the arc; paint or primer decomposing; the process window is narrow on coated material.

Steps: remove the coating locally to bare metal where the specification allows; where welding through coating is required, use studs and parameters qualified for it and expect a narrower window; provide fume extraction for zinc (Chapter 37, Section 5).

15. Safety Specifics

• A very bright, very short arc. The flash is brief but intense; eye protection is required, and the brevity misleads operators into treating it casually.

• Molten metal expulsion at the plunge, contained by the ferrule but not entirely — hot ejected metal and hot ferrule fragments.

• Hot ferrules are broken off immediately after welding and are a burn hazard.

• Zinc fume when welding on galvanized material (Chapter 37, Section 5).

• Capacitor-discharge equipment stores energy and remains hazardous after the supply is disconnected until the bank is discharged.

• High currents in short pulses, with heavy cables and connections.

• Working at height on structural decking, with a heavy gun and cable.

16. Standards and Qualification

• Process references: ISO 4063 references 783, 784, 785 and 786 [S1].

• Structural stud welding is governed in AWS practice by the stud welding provisions of AWS D1.1, which cover stud and ferrule requirements, procedure and operator qualification, pre-production testing and production testing regimes [S2].

• ISO 14555 covers arc stud welding of metallic materials, including procedure and operator qualification and testing requirements.

• Operator qualification applies — the operator sets up and executes a machine cycle, so ISO 14732 principles apply alongside the process-specific requirements (Chapter 32, Section 9).

• Pre-production and production testing regimes are specified by the governing code and are a defining feature of stud welding quality control (Section 11).

17. Worked Example: Intermittent Stud Failures on a Galvanized Deck

Situation. A contractor welds shear connectors through galvanized profiled steel decking onto structural beams. Roughly one stud in twenty fails bend testing. Trial studs at the start of each day pass. Parameters are unchanged and match the qualified procedure.

Step 1 — Read the intermittency. Trial studs pass and production studs fail at a low but consistent rate. That pattern indicates a variable that changes from stud to stud, not a settings error — settings do not vary between studs, and a settings error would fail the trial studs too.

Step 2 — List what varies stud to stud on this application. Decking thickness and the number of layers at the weld point; whether the deck is in intimate contact with the beam flange at that point; the galvanized coating thickness locally; surface contamination such as water, mud or oil from site conditions; the earth return path length and quality; and the operator's squareness and steadiness at each location.

Step 3 — Focus on the through-deck geometry, which is unique to this application. Through-deck welding requires the arc to burn through the deck and fuse into the beam flange beneath. A gap between the deck and the flange at the weld point defeats that entirely: the energy is consumed melting the deck and the stud, and there is nothing to fuse to. Deck-to-flange contact varies from point to point with deck flatness, fixing and beam camber — which matches the intermittent pattern exactly.

Step 4 — Consider the galvanizing contribution. Zinc vaporizing in the arc destabilizes it and introduces porosity, narrowing the process window. It does not by itself produce a one-in-twenty pattern unless coating thickness varies, but it reduces the margin available to absorb the other variations — so it is a contributing factor rather than the root cause.

Step 5 — Check whether water is present. Site decking holds water in the flutes, and moisture at the weld point produces porosity and instability. This also fits an intermittent pattern and is quickly checked by correlating failures with weather and with location on the deck.

Step 6 — Test the hypothesis cheaply. Section a failed stud and an adjacent passing stud through the deck and flange. If the failure shows the deck fused and the flange untouched with a visible gap, the diagnosis is confirmed in one operation.

Step 7 — Correct at the right level. If deck-to-flange contact is the cause, the fix is in deck fixing and flatness control before welding, not in welding parameters — pressing the deck down at the weld location, or fixing the deck more closely, addresses it directly. Increasing energy to burn through a gap is the wrong response: it makes the good welds worse and does not fix the bad ones.

Step 8 — Adjust the test regime to the risk. A one-in-twenty failure rate on a structural shear connection warrants a higher production test frequency until the cause is controlled, and testing concentrated at the locations where deck contact is least certain rather than distributed at random. Testing where the risk is, not uniformly, is the more informative regime.

18. Known Gaps

• No current, arc time, lift or plunge values are given. These are stud-diameter- and equipment-specific and are published by the equipment manufacturer; using generic values risks both lack of fusion and burn-through.

• Base material thickness ratios are described qualitatively. The governing code and the equipment manufacturer state the applicable limits.

• Bend test angles and production test frequencies are set by the governing code and are not stated here.

• Through-deck welding requirements are specific to the deck profile, coating and code, and require their own qualification.

• Aluminium and stainless stud welding are noted but not developed; both require variant-specific consumables and parameters.

1. Why Output Characteristic Is the First Equipment Decision

A welding power source is not simply a supply of current. Its output characteristic — the way its voltage changes as the current drawn from it changes — determines whether the arc is stable and whether the process works at all.

Two characteristics dominate arc welding, and they are near-opposites:

• Constant current (CC), also called drooping, in which output voltage falls steeply as current rises. Current stays approximately constant as the arc length changes.

• Constant voltage (CV), also called flat, in which output voltage stays approximately constant while current varies widely.

Putting a process on the wrong characteristic does not merely degrade the weld — it makes the process uncontrollable. This is why a machine's characteristic is stated before its current rating in any sensible specification, and why "a 400-amp welder" is an incomplete description of a machine.

2. Constant Current: The Drooping Characteristic

The behaviour. As arc length changes, arc voltage changes, but the steep slope of the output curve means the resulting current change is small.

Why manual processes need it. In shielded metal arc and manual gas tungsten arc welding, the arc length is held by a human hand and varies continuously. On a constant-current source, that variation changes the voltage and heat slightly but leaves the current — and therefore the melting rate — nearly unchanged. The weld stays consistent despite an inconsistent hand.

Its consequence for the operator: the machine sets the current, and the welder's arc length affects heat and bead shape but not deposition rate.

Refinements found on modern machines:

• Arc force (dig): momentarily increases current as the arc shortens, preventing the electrode from sticking. Essential for low-current root work with covered electrodes.

• Hot start: a brief current boost at initiation to establish the arc reliably.

• Anti-stick: drops current if the electrode does sit down, so it can be freed without overheating.

3. Constant Voltage: The Self-Regulating Arc

The behaviour. Output voltage stays nearly constant while current varies widely with load.

Why continuous-wire processes need it. In gas metal arc, flux cored and submerged arc welding, wire is fed at a set speed. If the arc lengthens, voltage rises slightly, current falls, the wire burns off more slowly, and the arc shortens back to equilibrium. If the arc shortens, current rises, burn-off accelerates, and the arc lengthens again. The arc length self-regulates, continuously and automatically, without operator intervention.

Its consequence for the operator: on a constant-voltage machine, wire feed speed sets the current. The current knob on a wire machine is the wire feed control; the voltage knob sets arc length and bead shape. This inversion is the single most common source of confusion for welders moving from stick to wire, and it explains why the parameter tables for wire processes list wire feed speed rather than amperage as the primary setting.

Refinements:

• Inductance / arc control: shapes the rate of current rise during short-circuit transfer, trading spatter against pool fluidity (Chapter 39, Section 3).

• Burnback control: sets how long current continues after the trigger releases, controlling the wire stub length at the end of a weld.

• Slope control: on some machines, deliberately introduces a controlled droop into a CV output for short-circuit work.

4. Which Processes Need Which, and the Exceptions

| Process | Characteristic | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SMAW (111) | Constant current | Hand-held arc length varies constantly |
| GTAW (141) | Constant current | As above; plus current control via pedal |
| PAW (153) | Constant current | As GTAW |
| GMAW (131/135) | Constant voltage | Self-regulating arc with fixed wire feed |
| FCAW (114/136) | Constant voltage | As GMAW |
| SAW (121) | Usually constant voltage; constant current used with large-diameter wires | Self-regulation at high deposition; CC gives more penetration control on heavy wire |
| Electroslag (722) | Constant voltage | Continuous feed into a slag bath |
| Stud welding (783) | Purpose-built timed output | Machine cycle, not a sustained arc |

Multi-process machines provide both characteristics and switch between them. The failure mode to know: a machine left in the wrong mode after a process change produces an unusable arc, and the symptom — uncontrollable arc length on a wire process, or wildly varying current on a stick electrode — is often misread as a fault rather than a setting.

5. Open-Circuit Voltage and Why It Is Regulated

Open-circuit voltage (OCV) is the voltage present at the output terminals before an arc is struck. It must be high enough to initiate and re-establish the arc, and it is the voltage a person contacts if they touch the electrode and the work simultaneously.

That dual role is the tension: higher OCV makes striking easier, particularly on alternating current where the arc must re-ignite every half-cycle, and higher OCV increases electric shock risk (Chapter 37, Section 2).

The consequence in practice is that OCV is limited by equipment standards, with lower limits applying in conditions of increased hazard — damp environments, confined spaces, work where the welder's body is in extensive contact with the workpiece. Voltage-reducing devices are fitted to reduce OCV to a safe level between welds and restore it on demand at the moment of striking, and their use is required in some jurisdictions and conditions.

6. Duty Cycle, and What Happens When It Is Exceeded

Duty cycle is the proportion of a defined period — conventionally ten minutes — during which a machine can deliver a stated output without exceeding its thermal limits. A machine rated 300 A at 60 % duty cycle can deliver 300 A for six minutes in any ten, and must rest for four.

Three practical points:

Duty cycle and current trade against each other. The same machine will deliver a lower current at 100 % duty cycle and a higher current at a lower duty cycle. Manufacturers state several points on this curve.

The rating is at a stated ambient temperature. In a hot shop, in summer, or in an enclosure, the achievable duty cycle is lower than the plate rating.

Exceeding it does not usually destroy the machine — thermal protection intervenes. The machine trips and stops welding, typically mid-weld, and that is the observable symptom: welding stops without warning and resumes after a cooling period. It looks like an intermittent electrical fault and is in fact the protection working correctly.

Duty cycle is a real production planning variable. A machine adequate for intermittent manual work is not necessarily adequate for continuous mechanized welding, and the correct comparison is between the process's actual arc-on time and the machine's rating — not between the machine's peak current and the procedure's current.

7. Transformer, Transformer-Rectifier and Inverter

| Type | Principle | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Transformer | Mains-frequency transformer with taps or a moving core | AC output only; simple, robust, heavy; limited control; largely superseded |
| Transformer-rectifier | Transformer followed by a rectifier | DC output, sometimes AC/DC; heavy; robust; limited waveform control |
| Engine-driven generator/alternator | Combustion engine driving a generator | Independent of mains supply; the field and site standard; often provides auxiliary power |
| Inverter | Rectifies mains to DC, switches it at high frequency, transforms at that frequency, rectifies again | Small, light, efficient, and precisely controllable; enables waveform control (Section 8) |

Why the inverter mattered. Transformer size falls as operating frequency rises, so switching at kilohertz frequencies rather than mains frequency shrinks the magnetics dramatically. The result is a machine a fraction of the weight and size of its predecessor, with markedly better energy efficiency — but the more important consequence is control. Because the output is synthesized by fast switching, the output waveform can be shaped in real time, which is what made pulsed transfer, AC balance control, and modern waveform-controlled processes practical.

Inverter limitations worth knowing: sensitivity to input supply quality and to generator waveform on site, sensitivity to dust and moisture ingress in harsh environments, and repair that is a board-level rather than a component-level activity.

8. Waveform Control and What It Made Possible

Waveform control means shaping the current and voltage against time within each transfer event, rather than setting a single average value. Its consequences run through Volume 3:

• Pulsed GMAW — spray transfer at low average current, giving all-position capability (Chapter 39, Section 6).

• Pulsed GTAW — controlled heat input on thin material (Chapter 41, Section 10).

• AC balance and frequency control — independent adjustment of cleaning and penetration on aluminium (Chapter 41, Section 4).

• Controlled short-circuit processes — waveforms that detect the short and reduce current before the bridge ruptures, cutting spatter dramatically and reducing heat input enough to weld thin material and open roots with a wire process. These are proprietary implementations of a shared principle.

• Synergic control — the machine holds pre-programmed relationships between wire feed speed, voltage and waveform for a given wire and gas, so the operator sets one variable and the machine derives the rest.

Two cautions. Synergic programmes are specific to a wire and gas combination, and selecting the wrong programme gives a poor result with correct-looking settings. And proprietary waveform processes must be identified on the WPS by what they are, since a procedure qualified with one is not automatically valid with another — the transfer behaviour is part of the process (Chapter 31, Section 11).

9. Polarity and the AC Options

DCEP (electrode positive) — deeper penetration in consumable-electrode processes; the standard for GMAW and most FCAW; used with most covered electrode classes.

DCEN (electrode negative) — more heat to the work in GTAW, keeping the tungsten cool; used by some self-shielded cored wires; gives higher deposition and lower penetration in wire processes.

AC — required for aluminium GTAW for cathodic cleaning; used in SAW multi-wire arrangements to reduce arc interaction and arc blow; available on some covered electrode classes.

Square-wave AC on inverter machines gives faster polarity reversal, more stable arc re-ignition without continuous high frequency, and adjustable balance and frequency.

The practical rule: polarity is set by the consumable's classification and the process, and running the wrong polarity produces an unstable arc, poor bead, and a deposit that does not meet its classification (Chapter 29).

10. Wire Feed Systems

Covered in operational detail in Chapter 39, Section 8; summarized here as equipment:

| Configuration | Description | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Push | Drive rolls at the feeder push wire through the torch cable | Standard for steel wires over normal cable lengths |
| Pull | Drive motor in the torch pulls the wire | Soft wires, short runs |
| Push-pull | Synchronized drives at both ends | Aluminium, and long cable runs, where push feeding alone deforms soft wire |
| Spool-on-gun | Small spool mounted on the torch | Aluminium and difficult-feeding wires over short lengths |

The equipment principle: feed consistency is a process variable, because on a constant-voltage machine wire feed speed sets current (Section 3). A feeder that cannot hold speed under load cannot hold current, whatever the machine's specification says.

11. Cables, Connections and the Work Return

This is the least glamorous section in the chapter and the source of a large proportion of unexplained welding faults.

Cable sizing. Voltage drop along a cable is proportional to current and length. An undersized or over-long cable drops enough voltage to reduce the current available at the arc, and the machine's panel reading does not show it. Symptoms: low apparent current, poor penetration, unstable arc, and a machine that "isn't as strong as it used to be."

Cable condition. Damaged insulation is a shock hazard; internal strand breakage raises resistance progressively and heats the cable.

Connections. Every connection — at the machine, at the electrode holder or torch, at the work clamp — is a resistance in series with the arc. Loose, dirty or corroded connections heat up, drop voltage and destabilize the arc. Warm connections after welding are a direct diagnostic.

The work return. Three faults recur:

1. Connecting to the bench or the building structure rather than to the workpiece. Current then finds an uncontrolled path, which can arc across bearings, rails, hinges or measuring equipment and cause damage far from the weld.

2. Poor contact at the clamp — clamping to paint, scale, rust or a coated surface.

3. Asymmetric or distant placement, causing arc blow (Chapter 22, Section 13).

Coiled cables act as inductors and can affect arc behaviour, and coiling cable around the body is an electromagnetic exposure issue (Chapter 37, Section 10). Cables should be run out straight, not left coiled on the drum.

12. Cooling Systems

Air-cooled torches are limited by their ability to shed heat, which sets a practical current ceiling for continuous use. Water-cooled torches carry substantially higher current in a smaller, lighter torch body, and are standard for higher-current GTAW, PAW, mechanized GMAW and robotic work.

Failure modes: coolant flow loss destroys the torch quickly; coolant leaks put fluid onto a live assembly; low coolant level and blocked filters reduce cooling without stopping it; and coolant that freezes or grows biological contamination blocks passages. Flow switches that inhibit welding on loss of flow are a standard protective feature and should not be bypassed.

13. Calibration and Verification

Two points, both audit findings in Chapter 33, Section 5:

The panel reading is not a measurement. A machine's displayed current and voltage are indications, and they can drift. Where the WPS specifies parameter ranges and production records claim conformity, the instruments producing those records need to be calibrated and verified.

Voltage measurement location matters. Voltage measured at the machine terminals includes the drop along the cables; voltage at the arc is lower. A WPS parameter range and a production measurement must be taken at consistent, defined points, or the comparison is meaningless — this is a common cause of disputes over recorded heat input.

| Uncalibrated meters | Recorded parameters do not reflect reality; heat input records invalid | Calibrate; define and record measurement points |
| Wrong synergic programme | Poor arc with apparently correct settings | Verify the programme matches the wire diameter, type and gas actually in use |
| Gas solenoid or timing fault | Start and crater porosity | Check pre-flow and post-flow, and hose volume between solenoid and torch |

16. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Machine "not as strong as it used to be"

Symptom: same settings, less penetration, sluggish arc.

Category: circuit resistance.

Likely causes: cable damage or internal strand breakage; loose or corroded connections; poor work return contact; cable too long for the current; extension cables added over time.

Steps: inspect and re-make every connection on clean metal; feel for warm connections and cables after a weld; compare terminal voltage with arc voltage; check total cable length and size against the current; measure output under load rather than trusting the panel.

Card 2 — Welding stops intermittently and resumes after a pause

Symptom: arc stops mid-weld; machine restarts after several minutes.

Category: thermal protection.

Likely causes: duty cycle exceeded; ambient temperature high; airflow blocked by dust or by the machine's position; cooling fan failure; filters blocked.

Steps: compare actual arc-on time and current with the rating; check the machine's ventilation clearance and filters; check fan operation; consider a higher duty-cycle machine for continuous work rather than treating the trip as a fault.

Card 3 — Damage found remote from the welding area

Symptom: pitting on bearings, damaged rollers, failed instruments or bearings in a machine that was welded on.

Category: work return path.

Likely causes: return connected to the bench, the structure or a distant point, so current found a path through bearings and joints.

Steps: connect the return directly to the workpiece as close to the weld as practical; on rotating or jointed assemblies, bond across bearings or use a dedicated return path; treat this as a process control, since the damage is expensive and delayed.

Card 4 — Arc behaviour changed after a wire or gas change

Symptom: unstable arc, spatter, poor bead, with settings unchanged.

Category: synergic programme.

Likely causes: the machine is running a synergic programme for a different wire diameter, wire type or gas than the one now fitted.

Steps: verify the programme selection against the actual wire and gas; note that on a synergic machine the correct settings for a different consumable are not the same numbers, and that the gas change may itself be an essential-variable issue (Chapter 39, Section 19).

17. Safety Specifics

• Open-circuit voltage is present whenever the machine is on (Section 5), and is the shock hazard in most welding electrocutions.

• Isolate before opening any enclosure. Inverters contain charged capacitors that remain hazardous after disconnection until discharged.

• Cable condition is a primary electrical safety item, not a housekeeping one.

• Engine-driven machines add exhaust gas — carbon monoxide — and fuel handling hazards, and must never be run in an enclosed space.

• Water-cooled torches put coolant near live conductors; leaks are an electrical hazard.

• Electromagnetic fields are strongest near cables and around the loop formed by the electrode and return cables; keep cables together and to one side rather than around the body, and note the specific precaution for implanted medical devices (Chapter 37, Section 10).

18. Standards

Equipment safety, performance and rating are covered by the arc welding equipment standards — principally the IEC 60974 series, which addresses power sources, wire feeders, torches, cables and connectors, and the safety requirements including open-circuit voltage limits and voltage-reducing devices. National regulation adds requirements on inspection and testing intervals for portable equipment.

Calibration of welding equipment used for parameter control is addressed within the welding quality-requirement framework (Chapter 33) and in the equipment validation standards referenced there.

19. Worked Example: A Machine That Welded Fine in the Morning

Situation. A fabricator's mechanized GMAW cell produces acceptable welds early in the shift. By mid-afternoon, welds show reduced penetration and increased spatter. Settings are unchanged and verified. The cell is in an enclosed area with a nearby oven for another process.

Step 1 — Note the time dependence and what varies with it. Anything that changes gradually through a shift: machine and cell temperature, ambient temperature, consumable condition, contact tip wear, liner condition, gas cylinder pressure, and duty-cycle accumulation.

Step 2 — Check the thermal path first, because the symptom fits it. An enclosed cell next to an oven will rise in ambient temperature through the day. Duty cycle ratings are stated at a reference ambient; at a higher ambient the machine derates, and a machine near its limit at 20 °C may be over it at 35 °C. Reduced output and a machine running hot are consistent with this.

Step 3 — Check whether the protection has actually operated. If the machine were tripping, welding would stop. If output is merely degrading, the machine may be derating rather than tripping — or the cause may be elsewhere. Checking the machine's temperature and any fault log distinguishes these.

Step 4 — Check the consumable path in parallel, since it also degrades with time. Contact tip wear over a shift's welding produces exactly this pattern: erratic current transfer, more spatter, reduced effective current. Liner loading with debris does the same. Both are cumulative and both reset when replaced.

Step 5 — Use the reset test. Replace the contact tip and liner mid-afternoon without changing anything else. If welds recover immediately, the cause is consumable wear and the fix is a scheduled replacement interval. If they do not, the thermal hypothesis stands.

Step 6 — Check the gas supply as a third candidate. A cylinder approaching empty gives falling and unstable delivery pressure; a manifold serving several cells can drop as demand rises through the day. Both produce degraded shielding, which shows as spatter and porosity rather than reduced penetration — so this fits part of the symptom, not all of it.

Step 7 — Fix at the right level. If it is ambient temperature, the answer is cell ventilation or a higher duty-cycle machine — not reduced production. If it is consumable wear, the answer is a replacement interval set inside the degradation point, tracked like the nozzle interval in Chapter 42, Section 17. In both cases the fix is a scheduled control rather than a reaction, because the degradation is predictable.

20. Known Gaps

• No cable sizing tables are given. Sizing depends on current, duty cycle, length, ambient temperature and installation, and is published in equipment standards and manufacturers' data.

• Open-circuit voltage limits are described in principle, not quoted. They are set by equipment standards and by national regulation and differ by jurisdiction and by hazard condition.

• Proprietary waveform processes are described generically. They are commercially named implementations of shared principles, and this reference set names no products (Volume 1, Chapter 18).

• Duty cycle curves are machine-specific and must be read from the manufacturer's data.

• Calibration intervals and methods are set by the quality system and the applicable standard.

1. How to Use This Chapter

Chapters 38 to 46 each treat one process. This chapter is the cross-process layer: what to do when a weld is wrong and the process is not obviously at fault, and how to choose between the arc processes in the first place.

It follows the same discipline as Volume 1, Chapter 12: work from the largest prerequisite down to the smallest failed layer, and gather evidence before changing anything. The single most expensive habit in arc welding troubleshooting is adjusting a parameter first, because a parameter change destroys the evidence that would have identified the cause and frequently substitutes a worse defect for a visible one.

2. The Diagnostic Sequence for an Arc Welding Problem

Answer each question before moving to the next. A "no" at any step stops the investigation at that layer.

1. Is the correct WPS in force, and does it cover this joint, material, thickness and position? A large proportion of "welding problems" are work being done outside a qualified procedure (Chapter 31, Section 11).

2. Is the welder or operator qualified and current for this work? Including position, thickness, backing and progression (Chapter 32).

3. Is the consumable the one the WPS specifies — classification, diameter, and condition? Including storage and exposure for hydrogen-controlled consumables.

4. Is the shielding gas the one the WPS specifies, by group rather than by trade name?

5. Is the joint preparation and fit-up within tolerance, and is the surface clean? Measure rather than assume; fit-up varies part to part and parameters do not.

6. Is the equipment functioning — cables, connections, work return, feed path, cooling, calibration? (Chapter 46, Section 15.)

7. Are the recorded parameters inside the qualified ranges?

8. Only now: is this a parameter or technique problem?

9. Is the defect real, or is it an inspection or acceptance-criteria question? (Chapter 36, Section 1.)

| Why This Order Is Not Optional Steps 1 to 6 cost minutes and are answerable with records and inspection. Step 8 costs a test coupon and a requalification if it turns out to be wrong. Skipping to step 8 feels faster and is faster only on the occasions when the guess is right — and when it is wrong, the original evidence is gone and the fault recurs after the "fix." |
| --- |

3. Reading the Evidence Before Touching a Setting

Four dimensions of evidence identify most arc welding faults before any parameter is examined:

Timing. Did the defect appear immediately, or after a delay? Immediate cracking is solidification cracking; delayed cracking is hydrogen cracking (Chapter 36, Section 3). This single question resolves the most consequential ambiguity in steel welding.

Location. Weld metal, fusion line, heat-affected zone, or parent plate? Root, fill, or cap? At starts, at stops, or continuous? Each location points at a different mechanism, and "at starts" or "at stops" points directly at gas timing.

Distribution. Uniform along the weld, clustered, or intermittent between parts? Uniform indicates a systematic cause — consumable, gas, parameters. Clustered indicates a local cause — a patch of contamination, a momentary disturbance. Intermittent between nominally identical parts indicates something that varies part to part, which is almost always fit-up or surface condition, not settings.

Correlation. With shift, welder, machine, material batch, consumable batch, weather, or time since a consumable change. A comparison that already exists — one cell out of four, one welder out of six, one batch out of ten — is worth more than any test that has to be set up.

4. Fault Family 1 — Porosity

Symptom: gas cavities in the weld, found by radiography or visible at the surface.

Category: shielding, consumable condition, or surface contamination.

Likely causes:

• Shielding gas: flow too low; flow too high causing turbulence and air entrainment; leak in the gas path; nozzle blocked with spatter; draught; insufficient pre-flow or post-flow; wrong gas group.

• Consumable: damp covered electrodes; damp flux; moisture in a cored wire; contaminated or rusty solid wire.

• Surface: rust, mill scale, oil, grease, paint, primer, galvanizing, moisture, condensation.

• Technique: excessive arc length; excessive stick-out; stick-out too short on self-shielded cored wire (Chapter 40, Section 9).

• Material: hydrogen rejected during solidification in aluminium (Chapter 25, Section 5).

Discriminating evidence: distribution pattern (Section 3); location at starts or stops points at gas timing; worsening when flow is increased confirms turbulence; worm-hole shape indicates a sustained gas source.

Corrective actions: set flow for the nozzle and joint, not higher; leak-check the whole gas path with the torch articulated; clean the nozzle; screen from draughts; control consumable storage; clean the joint to bare metal; verify pre-flow and post-flow; verify stick-out against the consumable's requirement.

Verification: re-weld a coupon under the corrected condition and radiograph it before releasing production.

5. Fault Family 2 — Lack of Fusion and Penetration

Symptom: weld metal not fused to the parent or to a previous pass; or penetration short of the required depth.

Category: energy delivery, joint access, or transfer mode.

Likely causes:

• Short-circuit GMAW used to fill thick section — the single most common cause of serious lack of fusion in modern fabrication (Chapter 39, Section 3).

• Heat input too low: current or wire feed speed too low, travel speed too high.

• Joint access: groove angle too narrow for electrode or torch access, particularly at mid-thickness in deep grooves (Chapter 28, Section 15).

• Technique: arc directed at the pool rather than at the fusion face; incorrect torch or electrode angle; excessive weave leaving cold edges.

• Fit-up: root gap too small, root face too thick for the root process.

• Contamination: oxide or slag on the fusion face; on aluminium, oxide not removed.

• Arc blow deflecting the arc away from one fusion face.

• Vertical-down progression on thick material.

Discriminating evidence: location — sidewall, inter-run, or root. Sidewall at mid-thickness in a deep groove points at access; inter-run points at interpass cleaning or heat input; root points at fit-up or root process.

Corrective actions: change transfer mode (pulsed rather than short-circuit); increase heat input within the qualified range; open the joint preparation; correct angle and weave; correct fit-up; clean fusion faces; reposition the work return.

Verification: ultrasonic or phased array testing, not radiography — this defect family is planar and radiography is unreliable for it (Chapter 35, Section 18).

6. Fault Family 3 — Cracking

Symptom: a crack, in any location.

Category: determined by timing and location before anything else.

| Timing and location | Mechanism | Primary controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Immediate, weld centreline | Solidification (hot) cracking | Reduce travel speed; widen bead; reduce depth-to-width ratio; reduce dilution from high-sulphur parent; eliminate crater terminations |
| Immediate, at every stop | Crater cracking | Crater fill or downslope; run-off tabs |
| Delayed hours to days, HAZ / toe / root | Hydrogen-induced cold cracking | Low-hydrogen consumables with enforced storage; preheat by the hydrogen-control route; maintain interpass; reduce restraint; hydrogen soak |
| During or shortly after welding, stepped, in parent plate below a T-joint | Lamellar tearing | Redesign the joint; through-thickness (Z-quality) plate; buttering; reduce weld volume |
| After PWHT or in high-temperature service, intergranular in coarse-grained HAZ | Reheat (stress-relief) cracking | Control heat input; dress toes; material-specific qualified PWHT cycle |
| Immediate, weld metal, fully austenitic stainless | Solidification cracking without ferrite | Filler that solidifies with ferrite; reduce restraint and heat input |
| Immediate, aluminium 6xxx welded without filler | Solidification cracking near the composition peak | Never weld 6xxx autogenously; use 4043 or 5356 filler |

The discriminating question is always timing. A crack found immediately and a crack found on Monday morning are different mechanisms with different controls, and treating them alike guarantees a wrong corrective action (Chapter 23).

7. Fault Family 4 — Inclusions

Symptom: non-metallic or metallic foreign matter trapped in the weld.

Slag inclusions (301) — slag-producing processes only:

• Causes: inadequate interpass cleaning; groove too narrow for slag release; excessive drag angle pushing slag ahead of the pool; travel too slow; undercut from a previous pass forming a trap; irregular bead profile.

• Actions: clean completely between passes including the groove faces; open the preparation; correct angle and speed; grind out undercut before covering.

Tungsten inclusions (3041) — GTAW and PAW only:

• Causes: electrode contacted pool or filler; current above the electrode's capacity; electrode too small; oxidizing shielding gas; scratch starting.

• Actions: correct electrode type, size and preparation; verify inert gas; replace scratch starting with HF or lift arc; remove the contaminated weld metal — a tungsten inclusion cannot be left in place.

Copper inclusions (3042) — consumable-electrode processes:

• Causes: contact tip damage or melting; copper backing bar melted into the joint.

• Actions: replace the contact tip; check backing arrangement and material.

Oxide inclusions — aluminium in particular:

• Causes: oxide film not removed; contaminated brushes; filler rod end oxidized by withdrawal from the gas envelope.

• Actions: degrease then mechanically clean with dedicated tooling immediately before welding; keep the rod end inside the gas.

8. Fault Family 5 — Profile and Shape

Undercut (501). Causes: current or voltage too high; travel too fast; incorrect work angle; excessive weave; poor wetting from gas selection. Actions: reduce parameters; correct angle; limit weave; add a small active component to the gas for wetting on steel. Significance: a fatigue initiation site, tightly limited in dynamically loaded joints.

Overlap (506). Causes: travel too slow; arc energy too low relative to deposition; incorrect technique. Actions: increase travel speed or reduce deposition rate.

Excess weld metal and oversized fillets. Causes: travel too slow; deliberate oversizing. Actions: weld to the drawing — oversizing costs money, adds heat and distortion, and can violate a heat input limit (Chapter 28, Section 6).

Burn-through and excess penetration. Causes: energy too high for thickness; excessive root gap; wrong transfer mode for thin material; excessive purge pressure. Actions: reduce energy; control fit-up; add backing; reduce purge pressure.

Root concavity. Causes: excessive gap; insufficient root filler; excessive purge pressure. Actions: control fit-up and root technique; vent the purge rather than pressurizing it.

Linear misalignment (507). A fit-up and assembly problem, not a welding one (Chapter 28, Section 12).

Poor restarts. Causes: cold start, slag not removed at the restart, profile discontinuity. Actions: clean the restart area; restart ahead of the crater and run back into it.

9. Fault Family 6 — Spatter and Arc Instability

Treated as a fault family in its own right, because spatter is a leading indicator: it rises before other symptoms appear, and treating it as cosmetic discards a free diagnostic signal (Chapter 36, Section 9).

The control order, applied in sequence [S3][S4]:

1. Identify the transfer mode actually in use and get out of the globular range — into true short-circuit or spray, or use pulsed transfer. Globular transfer is the highest-spatter operating region and the largest single lever.

2. Raise the argon fraction — at least about 80 % argon on steel; avoid pure CO₂, which increases arc force and droplet repulsion.

3. Set inductance for a softer current rise in short-circuit work, so the bridge does not rupture explosively.

4. Service the wire feed path — liner, drive rolls, contact tip. Feed instability modulates arc length and produces spatter before any other symptom is visible.

5. Correct arc blow — reposition or split the work return, use run-off tabs at joint ends, reduce current, or switch to AC where the process permits.

6. Clean the joint — rust, zinc, oil, paint and moisture generate gas that ejects metal.

7. Check stick-out, voltage and polarity against the WPS and the consumable's classification.

What rising spatter is telling you. On a stable production weld, a spatter increase means something changed: gas supply or mixture, wire feed condition, contact tip wear, material surface condition, or the earth connection. Investigating it at that point is cheaper than investigating the porosity it will cause when spatter blocks the nozzle.

On stainless, spatter removal must use stainless-only tooling, or the removal introduces iron contamination and a corrosion problem worse than the spatter (Chapter 24, Section 11).

10. Fault Family 7 — Property Failures With No Visible Defect

The most under-recognized family: the weld passes every non-destructive test and fails a mechanical or corrosion requirement.

| Failure | Mechanism | Where to look |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Low toughness | Excess heat input; interpass maximum exceeded; wrong consumable toughness class; wrong flux type; self-shielded wire run under gas; gas group changed | Recorded heat input and interpass; consumable certificate; gas actually supplied |
| HAZ softening | Heat input above the steel producer's ceiling on Q&T, TMCP or AHSS material | Recorded heat input; material producer's limits; hardness traverse |
| Excess hardness | Cooling too fast: preheat too low, heat input too low, section heavy | Preheat records and measurement method; steel chemistry |
| Sensitization / corrosion failure in stainless | Time in the sensitizing range; grade substitution; repeated repair cycles | Material certificate — is it actually the L grade? Repair history |
| Deposit chemistry out of specification | Excessive dilution; active SAW flux in multi-pass work; wrong filler for the dilution level | Deposit analysis; flux type; recorded current |
| Root corrosion in service | Purge absent, insufficient or unverified | Purge records; borescope of retained spool |

The common thread: none of these is a discontinuity, so none is detectable by radiography, ultrasonics, penetrant or magnetic particle testing. They are found by mechanical testing, by chemical analysis, or in service. This is why procedure qualification tests properties and production control protects them, and why an inspection-only quality strategy misses this entire family (Chapter 31, Section 1).

11. Fault Family 8 — Dimensional and Distortion Problems

Symptom: the assembly is out of tolerance, or moves during or after welding.

Causes: excessive heat input; oversized welds; unbalanced welding sequence; welds placed away from the neutral axis; inadequate or excessive restraint; machining after welding releasing residual stress.

Actions: reduce weld size to the drawing requirement; balance the sequence about the neutral axis; use back-step or skip sequences; pre-set or pre-bend; improve fixturing — while recognizing that restraint converts distortion into residual stress and increases cracking risk on sensitive material (Chapter 22, Section 11).

The recurring root cause in general fabrication is oversized fillet welds, because deposited volume rises with the square of the leg length. A shop with a distortion problem should measure its fillet sizes before changing anything else.

15. Deposition, Cost and Productivity Comparison

The economic comparison between arc processes turns on four quantities, and the one that dominates is usually not the one people quote:

Deposition rate — kilograms of weld metal deposited per hour of arc time. SAW and FCAW lead, GTAW trails by a wide margin.

Duty cycle / operating factor — the fraction of the working day actually spent with an arc established. SMAW is low, because the electrode is consumed in a minute or two and must be changed and the slag removed. Continuous-wire processes are far higher. This factor frequently dominates the comparison, because a process with half the deposition rate and three times the arc-on time deposits more metal per shift.

Deposition efficiency — the fraction of purchased consumable that becomes weld metal. Losses come from stub ends (SMAW), spatter (all consumable-electrode processes), and slag. This is where spatter shows up as a direct cost rather than a cosmetic issue.

Total cost per joint — consumable, labour, gas, power, preparation, cleaning, inspection, and rework. Labour normally dominates in manual processes, which is why a process change that raises consumable cost while reducing arc time usually wins.

The practical conclusion: comparing processes on consumable price per kilogram is the least useful comparison available, and comparing them on deposition rate alone is only slightly better. The comparison that matters includes arc-on time, cleaning time and rework rate.

16. Worked Example: A Defect Rate That Moved Between Processes

Situation. A fabricator moves a structural product from SMAW to gas-shielded FCAW to raise output. Output rises as expected. Within a month, the ultrasonic rejection rate rises from occasional to persistent, with lack of fusion the dominant finding. Management's assessment is that FCAW was the wrong choice and proposes reverting.

Step 1 — Establish what the defect actually is and where. Lack of fusion, and specifically whether it is sidewall, inter-run, or root. The location determines which of several very different causes applies, and reverting the process without knowing this discards the information.

Step 2 — Check whether the joint preparation was changed with the process. This is the most common omission in a process change. A groove designed for a covered electrode's access and slag release is not necessarily suited to a cored wire's torch envelope and travel speed. If the preparation was carried over unchanged, the access geometry may no longer suit the process (Chapter 28, Section 15).

Step 3 — Check the procedure qualification. A process change is a change of essential variable, so a new qualification is required. If the WPS was amended without requalification, the work is unqualified regardless of the defect rate — a separate and more serious finding (Chapter 31, Section 11).

Step 4 — Check heat input and travel speed against the qualified values. The reason for the process change was output, and the most likely informal response to that pressure is increased travel speed. Lack of fusion is the direct consequence of insufficient energy per unit length. Comparing recorded parameters against the qualified range settles it quickly.

Step 5 — Check the wire classification and shielding. A cored wire's usability designator, its shielding designator and the gas actually supplied must match (Chapter 40, Section 8). A mismatch degrades fusion behaviour as well as chemistry.

Step 6 — Check the inspection change, which is easy to miss. Was ultrasonic testing being applied before the process change, or was the previous regime radiographic? If inspection changed at the same time as the process, the rejection rate may reflect better detection rather than worse welding — radiography does not reliably find lack of fusion, and ultrasonics does (Chapter 35, Section 1). This possibility must be eliminated before concluding anything about the process.

Step 7 — Evaluate the reversion proposal honestly. Reverting to SMAW would restore the previous rejection rate. It would also restore the previous output, forgoing the gain the change was made for. And if the actual cause is joint preparation, travel speed or an inspection change, reverting fixes nothing that could not be fixed while keeping the productivity.

Step 8 — Correct in the right order. Requalify properly for the new process; redesign the joint preparation for the process rather than inheriting it; set travel speed within the qualified range and hold it; verify the consumable and gas match; and confirm what changed in the inspection regime. Only if those are all correct and the defect rate persists is the process itself the problem.

Step 9 — Record the general lesson. A process change is a system change: joint preparation, qualification, consumables, gas, inspection method and acceptance criteria all move with it. Changing the process alone and leaving the rest inherited is the most reliable way to convert a productivity improvement into a quality problem.

17. Known Gaps

• The comparison matrix uses relative rankings, not numbers. Deposition rates and costs depend on wire diameter, position, joint, equipment and local prices, and any absolute figures would be misleading across contexts.

• Process selection guidance is engineering guidance, not code permission. Several codes restrict processes for particular applications; the governing code takes precedence over any recommendation here.

• Fault families are organized by symptom, which occasionally splits one mechanism across families — hydrogen cracking appears under cracking and under consumable condition. The cross-references are given rather than duplicating the content.

• Economic comparison is structural rather than quantitative for the reasons in Section 15; a real comparison requires the fabricator's own labour rates, arc-on time measurements and rework rates.

Rolling electrode wheels replacing fixed tips — how overlapping nuggets become a leak-tight seam, the four seam variants and what each is for, and why wheel dressing and cooling govern quality more than the schedule does.
