1. Process Overview: ISO 4063 References 22x

Resistance seam welding replaces the fixed electrode tips of spot welding with rotating wheel electrodes. The workpieces pass between them under force while current flows, and a series of overlapping or adjacent weld nuggets is produced along a continuous line.

The ISO nomenclature distinguishes several distinct configurations [S1]:

| Reference | Process |
| --- | --- |
| 221 | Lap seam welding |
| 222 | Mash seam welding |
| 223 | Prep-lap seam welding |
| 224 | Wire seam welding |
| 225 | Foil butt-seam welding |
| 226 | Seam welding with strip |

All of the physics developed in Volume 1 applies: heat is generated by I²Rt at the interfaces, dynamic resistance evolves through the pulse, force is a coupled process variable, and the weldability lobe concept governs the process window. What changes is that the electrode moves, the heat accumulates, and the joint is continuous.

2. How a Seam Differs From a Row of Spots

Four differences, each with practical consequences:

Heat accumulates. Successive welds are made close together in space and time, so each one is made into material already warmed by the previous one. The result is that a seam's thermal condition drifts as the weld progresses — the first weld of a seam is made cold and the hundredth is not. Schedules that are correct at the start can be too hot by the end.

Shunting is continuous and severe. In spot welding, shunting through an adjacent completed weld is an occasional design consideration (Volume 1). In seam welding the immediately preceding nugget is a permanent low-resistance path a few millimetres away, so a proportion of the current always shunts. This is why seam schedules use higher currents than a comparable spot schedule.

Electrode contact is rolling, not static. The contact patch moves continuously, and the wheel's surface condition at every point around its circumference matters, not just at one tip face.

The joint can be leak-tight, which no row of discrete spots can be. That property is the reason the process exists (Section 10).

3. Continuous, Intermittent and Roll-Spot Modes

| Mode | Current delivery | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Continuous | Current flows without interruption while the wheels rotate | A continuously molten path; used on thin material and at high speed; hardest to control thermally |
| Intermittent (pulsed) | Current pulses with off-times, wheels rotating continuously | The standard mode. Off-time allows cooling and lets the nugget solidify under force; overlap between nuggets is set by pulse timing and wheel speed |
| Roll-spot | Pulses spaced so nuggets do not overlap | A row of discrete spots made with a rolling electrode; faster than spot welding but not leak-tight |

The distinction between intermittent and roll-spot is precisely the distinction between a sealed seam and a fast row of spots, and it is set by the relationship between pulse frequency, wheel speed and nugget size. Getting that relationship wrong is how a seam that must seal is produced with gaps between nuggets that hold pressure under test and leak in service.

4. The Seam Variants: Lap, Mash, Prep-Lap, Wire and Foil

Lap seam (221) — the conventional configuration: two sheets overlapped, welded through the overlap by opposed wheels. The finished joint is the full thickness of both sheets plus any thinning.

Mash seam (222) — the overlap is deliberately small and the wheels apply high force, crushing the overlap down toward the thickness of a single sheet while welding it. The result is a joint approaching parent thickness, which matters where the joint must pass through subsequent forming rolls or where a flush surface is required. Tinplate can and container manufacture is the classic application. It demands much tighter control of overlap and force than lap seam welding.

Prep-lap seam (223) — the sheet edges are prepared or thinned before welding so that the finished joint is closer to parent thickness without the crushing forces of mash seam welding.

Wire seam (224) — a copper wire is fed between the electrode wheel and the sheet, continuously renewing the contact surface. The wire takes the contamination and wear that would otherwise accumulate on the wheel, and is discarded. This is used extensively on coated steels, particularly tin-coated material, where coating pickup on the wheel would otherwise dominate wheel life.

Foil butt-seam (225) and seam welding with strip (226) — configurations in which a foil or strip carries or backs the joint, used for butt configurations where the sheets meet edge to edge rather than overlapping.

5. Equipment and Components

| Component | Function | Failure consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wheel electrodes | Conduct current, apply force, drive or carry the work | Profile wear and contamination change current density directly |
| Wheel drive | Rotates the wheels (driven) or is driven by the work | Speed variation changes overlap and heat input |
| Force system | Applies and maintains electrode force | Force variation moves the process off the lobe |
| Welding transformer and controller | Delivers pulse current and timing | Timing controls overlap; failure changes seal integrity |
| Wheel cooling | Internal water cooling, external flood cooling, or both | The single most important auxiliary system — an overheated wheel changes shape and contaminates rapidly |
| Wheel dressing system | Restores wheel profile in service | Without it, profile drifts continuously through a run |
| Guides and fixtures | Keep the joint aligned under the wheels | Misalignment puts the nugget off the joint |
| Wire feed and take-up (wire seam) | Feeds fresh copper wire to the contact | Interruption stops the process |

External flood cooling is common in seam welding and is more than a refinement: the wheels run continuously in contact with hot material, and without adequate cooling the wheel surface softens, deforms and picks up coating material within a short run.

6. Electrode Wheels: Profile, Material and Dressing

The wheel is the process's consumable and its condition dominates quality.

Profile. Wheel face width and contour set the contact area and therefore the current density. Flat, radiused and crowned profiles are used for different applications. As with spot electrode tips (Volume 1, Chapter 3), face growth from wear reduces current density and progressively weakens the weld — but on a wheel, the wear is distributed around the whole circumference and can be uneven.

Material. Copper alloys selected on the same conductivity-against-hardness trade as spot electrodes, per the RWMA class system.

Dressing. In continuous production, wheels are dressed in service — a dressing tool running against the wheel restores the profile as it wears, either continuously or at intervals. This is the seam-welding equivalent of tip dressing (Volume 1, Chapter 13), and where it is absent, wheel profile becomes a slow-drifting uncontrolled variable that produces exactly the late-in-run failures of Section 17.

Contamination. On coated material, coating constituents transfer to the wheel and alloy with the copper surface, changing its resistance and thermal behaviour. Wire seam welding (Section 4) exists specifically to defeat this, and where it is not used, dressing and wheel change intervals must account for it.

7. Parameters and What Each Controls

| Parameter | Controls | Symptom if wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Current | Heat generation | Too low: undersized nuggets, gaps between nuggets, no seal. Too high: expulsion, surface marking, wheel damage |
| Weld time / pulse duration | Energy per nugget | Too short: undersized nugget. Too long: overheating, expulsion |
| Cool time / off-time | Solidification between pulses; heat accumulation control | Too short: heat accumulates through the seam. Too long: gaps between nuggets, no seal |
| Wheel speed | Nugget spacing with pulse timing; overlap | Too fast: nuggets separate, leak path. Too slow: excessive overlap, heat build-up, distortion |
| Electrode force | Contact resistance, nugget containment, mash reduction | Too low: expulsion, surface burning. Too high: excessive indentation, thinning |
| Wheel face width | Current density | Wide face: reduced density, cold welds |
| Cooling flow and temperature | Wheel condition and workpiece heat removal | Inadequate: wheel deformation and pickup within a short run |

The overlap relationship is the seam-specific control: nugget spacing is set by wheel speed against pulse repetition rate, and the overlap between adjacent nuggets is what determines whether the seam is continuous and sealed. Changing wheel speed without changing pulse timing changes the seal, even though nothing about the individual nugget changed.

8. Materials and Coatings

The material behaviour of Volume 1, Chapter 2 applies directly. Seam-specific notes:

• Low-carbon steel is the standard application and the most forgiving.

• Coated steels transfer coating to the wheel, degrading it progressively. Wire seam welding, more frequent dressing, or increased cooling are the responses.

• Stainless steels have higher resistivity and lower conductivity, so they weld at lower current than carbon steel but retain heat, making cool-time control more critical.

• Aluminium is difficult by seam welding for the same reasons as spot welding — high conductivity requiring very high current, a tenacious oxide, and a narrow window (Volume 1, Chapter 14) — and is a specialist application.

• Thickness combinations and stack-ups behave as in spot welding, with the added consideration that heat accumulation affects the thinner member more.

9. Setup and Execution Procedure

Before welding

1. Confirm the WPS covers the material stack, thickness, coating and seam type — lap, mash and prep-lap are different procedures, not settings.

2. Inspect the wheel profile and surface condition; dress or replace per the established interval rather than on appearance alone.

3. Verify cooling: internal flow, external flood if used, and coolant temperature.

4. Set current, weld time, cool time, force and wheel speed per the WPS.

5. Verify the overlap relationship: confirm that pulse rate against wheel speed gives the intended nugget overlap for a sealed seam.

6. Check joint fit-up and overlap width; for mash seam welding, overlap width tolerance is tight and directly affects the result.

7. Verify alignment of the joint under the wheels through the full travel, including at the start and end of the seam.

8. Run and destructively test setup samples before production, as in spot welding practice.

During production

9. Monitor for surface marking, expulsion and wheel condition.

10. Watch for drift through the seam — the last portion of a long seam is welded into hotter material than the first.

11. Watch for drift through the run — wheel wear and contamination accumulate over hundreds of parts.

12. Sample and test at the established frequency, including at the end of a run, not only at the start.

After welding

13. Inspect for continuity of the seam, surface condition and indentation.

14. Perform leak testing where the application requires it (Section 10).

15. Record parameters, wheel dressing and change events, and test results.

10. Leak-Tightness: What Actually Makes a Seam Seal

A seam is leak-tight when adjacent nuggets overlap sufficiently that there is no continuous unfused path through the joint. Three things follow:

1. Overlap is a geometric requirement, not a strength requirement. A seam can be strong enough with nuggets that barely touch and still leak. The strength test and the leak test are different tests answering different questions.

2. The controlling variables are wheel speed and pulse timing, with nugget size — set by current, time and force — determining how much overlap a given spacing produces.

3. A leak path can be intermittent along the seam, produced by a momentary speed variation, a current fluctuation, or a local surface contamination that shrank one nugget. This is why leak testing samples the whole seam rather than a coupon.

Leak testing methods in order of sensitivity: bubble testing under pressure, pressure decay, and helium mass spectrometry for high-integrity applications (Chapter 35, Section 9). The method must be matched to the leak rate that actually matters for the product — testing to a sensitivity far beyond the requirement rejects sound product, and testing below it passes leaking product.

11. When to Use Seam Welding and When Not To

| Choose seam welding when | Choose something else when |
| --- | --- |
| A leak-tight joint is required in sheet metal | Discrete joints are sufficient — spot welding is simpler and cheaper |
| Long continuous joints in thin sheet at production rate | Access does not allow wheels on both sides |
| Fuel tanks, containers, radiators, drums, filters, silencers | Material is thick — seam welding is a sheet process |
| Mash seam where a near-parent-thickness joint is needed | The joint must be dismantled or is a repair |
| Automated high-volume production | Aluminium in general production — the window is very narrow |
| Coated steels with wire seam welding | Very short joints — setup time dominates |

12. Defect Catalog

| Defect | Detection | Cause | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Leaking seam with acceptable strength | Leak test | Insufficient nugget overlap: wheel speed too high for the pulse rate, or nuggets undersized | Correct the speed-to-pulse-rate relationship; increase current or time to grow the nugget |
| Undersized or absent nuggets | Peel or sectioning | Current too low; excessive shunting; wheel face worn wide; contaminated wheel; force too high | Increase current; dress or replace the wheel; verify force |
| Expulsion and surface burning | Visual | Current too high; force too low; contaminated surfaces; wheel overheated | Reduce current; increase force; clean the material; verify cooling |
| Progressive weakening through a production run | Sample testing at intervals | Wheel profile growth and contamination accumulating | Establish and enforce a dressing interval; consider wire seam welding on coated material |
| Overheating toward the end of a seam | Visual; sectioning | Heat accumulation along the seam | Increase cool time; reduce speed; consider stepped schedules along the seam |
| Excessive indentation or thinning | Dimensional | Force too high; current too high; overlap crushed excessively in mash seam | Reduce force; check mash reduction against specification |
| Seam off the joint | Visual; sectioning | Guide or fixture misalignment; workpiece drift under the wheels | Check alignment through the full travel, not just at the start |
| Sheet separation between nuggets | Sectioning; leak test | Roll-spot spacing used where a continuous seam was required | Correct pulse rate and speed to produce overlap |
| Wheel deformation or pickup | Visual on the wheel | Cooling inadequate; coated material without wire seam or adequate dressing | Verify coolant flow and temperature; increase dressing frequency |

13. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Seams pass strength testing and fail leak testing

Symptom: adequate peel strength; leaks found under test.

Category: nugget overlap.

Likely causes: wheel speed too high relative to pulse rate, leaving gaps; nuggets undersized so that nominal spacing does not produce overlap; intermittent current interruption.

Steps: section a seam and measure actual nugget spacing and diameter; recalculate the speed-to-pulse-rate relationship for the required overlap; check for current dropouts in the controller records; verify that strength and leak requirements are being tested separately, because they are different requirements.

Card 2 — Quality good at the start of a run, poor at the end

Symptom: first parts pass, later parts show undersized nuggets or leaks.

Category: wheel condition.

Likely causes: wheel face growth from wear reducing current density; coating pickup altering the contact; wheel overheating from inadequate cooling; coolant temperature rising through the shift.

Steps: measure the wheel face profile against its initial condition; inspect for pickup; check coolant flow and supply temperature; establish a dressing interval inside the point where degradation begins, and test at the end of runs rather than only at the start.

Card 3 — Overheating and distortion at the end of each seam

Symptom: the last portion of every seam shows excessive heat, marking or distortion.

Category: heat accumulation.

Likely causes: cool time too short for the speed; the material's heat sink saturating along the seam; cooling inadequate to remove accumulated heat.

Steps: increase cool time or reduce wheel speed; consider a stepped schedule that reduces current along the seam; verify workpiece cooling; note that this is inherent to the process and is managed rather than eliminated.

Card 4 — Mash seam joint thicker than specification

Symptom: finished joint thickness above the target; subsequent forming operations fail.

Category: mash seam setup.

Likely causes: force too low for the required reduction; overlap width too great; current insufficient to soften the overlap for crushing; wheel profile wrong for mash seam.

Steps: verify overlap width against specification — this is the tightest tolerance in mash seam welding; check force against the WPS; confirm the wheel profile is the mash configuration; measure the reduction achieved on setup samples before production.

14. Testing and Quality Verification

The methods of Volume 1, Chapter 10 apply, with seam-specific additions:

• Peel testing across the seam, revealing nugget size and spacing.

• Sectioning and metallographic examination, which is the definitive method for measuring nugget overlap — the property that determines leak-tightness.

• Leak testing, per Section 10, on the finished assembly.

• Visual inspection for surface condition, indentation and continuity.

• Sampling frequency must account for drift through a run (Section 12), which means end-of-run sampling, not only start-of-run.

15. Safety Specifics

• Rotating wheels under force present a crushing and drawing-in hazard at the nip point. Guarding at the nip is essential and is the principal mechanical hazard.

• Expulsion ejects molten metal along the length of the seam, not at one point.

• High currents with heavy secondary conductors.

• Water and electricity in proximity through the cooling system.

• Hot workpieces immediately after welding, with the heat spread along the whole seam rather than localized.

• Coating fume where coated steels are welded, with zinc requiring the controls of Chapter 37, Section 5.

• Operator qualification: ISO 14732 for operators and setters of this mechanized process.

17. Worked Example: Leaking Seams Appearing Late in a Production Run

Situation. A manufacturer produces sealed sheet steel vessels with lap seam welds. Setup samples pass strength and leak testing. Leak rejects begin appearing after roughly two hours of production and increase through the shift. Parameters are unchanged and verified against the WPS.

Step 1 — Read the time dependence. Good at start, degrading with cumulative production. That is a wear or thermal accumulation signature, not a settings error — settings did not change and were correct at the start.

Step 2 — Separate the two candidate mechanisms. Wheel profile growth from wear reduces current density and shrinks nuggets, which reduces overlap and opens a leak path. Wheel or coolant heating changes the thermal balance. Both worsen through a shift and both would produce this pattern.

Step 3 — Measure the wheel rather than inferring. Compare the wheel face profile against its condition at setup. Face growth is directly measurable and is the resistance-welding equivalent of the tip mushrooming failure mode of Volume 1, Chapter 13.

Step 4 — Check for coating pickup. If the material is coated, examine the wheel contact surface for transferred coating. Pickup changes contact resistance and heat generation independently of profile, and it accumulates with parts welded rather than with time.

Step 5 — Check the cooling system as it actually is mid-shift. Coolant supply temperature rising through the day, a partially blocked internal passage, or reduced external flood flow will all show at mid-shift and not at start-up.

Step 6 — Confirm the mechanism by sectioning. Section a seam from an early part and one from a late part, and measure nugget diameter and overlap in both. This converts the diagnosis from plausible to demonstrated, and it distinguishes "nuggets got smaller" from "nuggets moved apart."

Step 7 — Correct with an interval, not an adjustment. If wheel condition is the cause, the fix is a dressing or replacement interval set inside the degradation point, not an increase in current to compensate for a worn wheel. Compensating with current masks the wear, drifts the process off its qualified schedule, and eventually fails anyway — the identical argument to the nozzle interval in Chapter 42, Section 17 and the tip-life discipline of Volume 1, Chapter 13.

Step 8 — Move the sampling to where the risk is. Testing only at setup samples the best condition the process will be in all day. Adding end-of-run and mid-run sampling detects drift while it is still recoverable, and is the change that would have caught this before customers did.

• Overlap percentage targets are not stated. Required overlap depends on the leak-tightness requirement and the application standard.

1. Process Overview: ISO 4063 References 24x and the Upset Family

Flash and upset welding join two components end to end across their whole cross-section in a single operation, using resistance heating followed by a forging action. They are the natural process choice where the joint is the full section of a bar, rail, ring, tube or strip, and where a fusion weld would require a groove, multiple passes and filler.

The ISO nomenclature identifies the flash welding variants [S1]:

| Reference | Process |
| --- | --- |
| 241 | Flash welding with preheating |
| 242 | Flash welding without preheating |

Upset (resistance butt) welding belongs to the same group 2 resistance family. Both processes share the defining characteristic that no filler metal is used and no molten pool is retained — everything that melts is expelled.

2. Flash Welding: The Sequence

The cycle has four distinct stages, and understanding them explains everything about the process's behaviour:

1. Clamping. The two components are gripped in heavy conductive clamps that both hold them and carry the welding current. Clamp position sets the initial die opening — the free length of material between the clamps — which governs how much material can be heated and upset.

2. Flashing. The parts are brought into light contact and current is applied. Contact occurs only at isolated high points, so current density at those points is enormous. The bridges melt, vaporize and are expelled violently as sparks — the flash. As each bridge is destroyed, the parts advance slightly and new contacts form. This repeats continuously, at an advance rate that is programmed to accelerate as the ends heat, progressively heating the whole end faces while expelling molten material.

3. Upset. At the moment the end faces are uniformly heated to forging temperature, the parts are driven together rapidly and forcefully. The remaining molten and heavily oxidized material at the interface is squeezed out into the surrounding upset flash, and clean, hot, plastic parent metal from behind the interface is forged together.

4. Post-upset current and hold. Current may continue briefly during upset, and the joint is held under force while it cools.

3. Why Flashing Cleans the Joint

This is the central engineering insight of the process, and it explains why flash welding produces sound joints in materials that would be difficult to fusion weld.

The interface never has to be clean beforehand. Oxide, scale, mill finish and minor contamination are burned away during flashing, and whatever survives is molten and oxidized at the moment of upset — and it is precisely that material that gets extruded out of the joint. The metal that ends up bonded is material from behind the original interface, which was never exposed to the atmosphere.

Three consequences follow:

1. The joint is a solid-state forge weld in its final state, not a fusion weld — molten metal is a stage in the process, not the product.

2. Surface preparation requirements are modest compared with fusion welding, although the clamping surfaces must be clean for current transfer.

3. The upset must be sufficient. If the upset distance is too small, oxidized interface material is not fully expelled and remains as a plane of inclusions across the joint — producing the characteristic flat fracture defect of Section 13.

4. The Upset: Forging Out the Molten Metal

The upset is the quality-determining stage. Its controlled variables:

• Upset distance — how far the parts advance during forging. Too little leaves contaminated interface material in the joint; too much wastes material and can produce excessive flash and grain flow distortion.

• Upset force — must be sufficient to extrude the molten material and forge the parent metal. Insufficient force is the most common root cause of flat fractures.

• Upset speed — must be fast enough that the interface does not cool and oxidize before the forge closes it. A sluggish upset allows oxidation between the end of flashing and the closing of the joint.

• Upset current — current continuing into the upset stage keeps the material hot and plastic through the forging.

The upset flash — the collar of expelled material around the joint — is direct evidence of the process. Its shape and symmetry indicate whether both parts were at the same temperature and whether the upset was concentric, and it is examined for exactly that reason before it is removed.

5. Upset (Resistance Butt) Welding: The Simpler Relative

Upset welding heats the joint without flashing. The parts are held in firm contact under force from the start, and current flows continuously through the contact interface, heating it by bulk resistance until the material reaches forging temperature. The parts are then upset together.

Differences from flash welding:

• No flashing stage, so no expulsion of material during heating and no self-cleaning action — the faying surfaces must therefore be clean and squarely cut before welding.

• Heating is slower and more uniform through the section.

• No sparks, so it is cleaner and quieter in operation.

• Limited to smaller cross-sections in practice, because uniform heating of a large section without flashing is difficult.

• Applications: wire, rod and small-section bar joining, wire mesh, chain, and small ring welding.

6. The Two Compared

| Factor | Flash welding (241/242) | Upset welding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Heating mechanism | Repeated arcing/bridging at isolated contacts | Bulk resistance heating through continuous contact |
| Self-cleaning | Yes — flashing expels contamination | No — faying surfaces must be clean and square |
| Surface preparation | Modest | Critical — square, clean, parallel faces |
| Cross-section capability | Large — rails, rings, tubes, heavy bar | Smaller sections |
| Material loss | Higher — flashing consumes material | Lower |
| Process noise, sparks, fume | High | Low |
| Dissimilar metals | More feasible | Less feasible |
| Typical applications | Rail, ring gears, wheel rims, tube, band saw blades, chain | Wire, rod, small bar, mesh, small rings |

7. Equipment and Components

| Component | Function | Failure consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clamping dies | Grip the parts, carry the current, resist the upset force | Slipping under upset force destroys the weld; poor contact causes local burning at the die |
| Platen and slide | Carries the moving part; provides flashing advance and upset stroke | Misalignment produces an off-square joint; sticking produces a sluggish upset |
| Drive system | Controls flashing advance profile and upset speed and force | The flashing advance profile is a programmed curve, not a constant rate |
| Transformer and controller | Delivers heating current and controls the cycle | Timing and current profile define the process |
| Position and force monitoring | Records the platen displacement and force through the cycle | The upset curve is the primary process record (Section 15) |
| Flash guarding and extraction | Contains sparks and fume | Flash travels a considerable distance and is a fire and eye hazard |
| Cooling | Cools the dies | Overheated dies lose grip and conductivity |

8. Parameters and What Each Controls

| Parameter | Controls | Symptom if wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initial die opening | Length of material heated and available to upset | Too small: insufficient heated length, cold joint. Too large: excessive material loss, buckling |
| Flashing time | Total heat input and heated depth | Too short: insufficiently heated faces, incomplete bonding. Too long: excessive material loss, oversized HAZ |
| Flashing advance profile | How heating develops through the cycle | Too slow: flashing extinguishes and the parts stick. Too fast: metal expelled faster than the heat develops |
| Flashing voltage | Intensity of the flashing action | Too low: unstable flashing, sticking. Too high: excessive burn-off |
| Upset distance | Whether contaminated interface material is expelled | Too small: flat fracture — the characteristic defect |
| Upset force | Whether the forge weld actually forms | Too low: incomplete bonding, flat fracture. Too high: excessive deformation and grain flow distortion |
| Upset speed | Whether the interface stays hot enough to forge | Too slow: oxidation between flashing end and upset |
| Upset current time | Plasticity during forging | Too short: forging into cooling metal |
| Preheat (241) | Initial temperature before flashing | Enables larger sections and reduces flashing time |

9. Materials and Dissimilar Joints

Carbon and low-alloy steels are the principal application, including rail steels, spring steels and tool steels — with post-weld heat treatment normally required for the hardenable grades (Section 11).

Stainless steels are readily flash welded.

Aluminium and copper alloys are more difficult, because high conductivity requires very high current and the oxides behave differently in flashing.

Dissimilar metals are more feasible in flash welding than in fusion welding, because the contact time at high temperature is very short and most of the melted and reacted material is expelled during upset. Flash welding is used for dissimilar combinations that fusion welding handles badly — but the compatibility considerations of Chapter 27 still apply, and intermetallic formation is limited rather than eliminated.

A material-specific caution: the process heats a substantial length of material and cools it in still air under clamping. On hardenable steels this produces a hard, potentially brittle heat-affected zone across the whole section, which is why post-weld heat treatment is routine rather than optional on rail and on tool steel joints.

10. Setup and Execution Procedure

Before welding

1. Confirm the procedure covers the material, section size and any required post-weld heat treatment.

2. Inspect the parts: for upset welding, faces must be square, clean and parallel; for flash welding, faces must be reasonably square but need not be clean.

3. Clean the clamping areas on both parts — die contact carries the full welding current, and contamination there causes local burning.

4. Set the initial die opening per the procedure for the section size.

5. Verify die condition and alignment; check that the parts are coaxial and that faces meet squarely.

6. Set the flashing advance profile, flashing time, voltage, upset distance, upset force and upset current per the procedure.

7. Verify guarding and extraction are in place; flashing produces a substantial spark stream.

8. Weld and destructively test setup samples before production.

Welding

9. Clamp both parts, verifying grip — slippage under upset force is a primary failure mode.

10. Initiate the cycle and allow the programmed sequence to run; the process is machine-executed and is not manually adjusted mid-cycle.

11. Observe the flashing: it should be continuous and intensifying, without extinguishing or sticking.

12. Confirm the upset occurred — the platen displacement record is the evidence.

13. Hold under force through cooling per the procedure.

After welding

14. Examine the upset flash for symmetry and completeness before removing it.

15. Remove flash by the specified method — shearing while hot, machining, or grinding.

16. Apply post-weld heat treatment where required (Section 11).

17. Inspect per the quality plan (Section 15).

18. Record the upset curve — displacement and force against time — with the joint identity.

11. Post-Weld Operations: Flash Removal and Heat Treatment

Flash removal. The upset collar is removed by hot shearing immediately after welding, by machining, or by grinding. Two cautions: hot shearing must not tear into the parent metal, and grinding must not overheat the joint locally or leave a notch at the joint line.

Post-weld heat treatment is normally required on hardenable steels. The process heats a wide band and cools it in air under clamping, producing a hardened structure across the full section. Normalizing or tempering restores toughness. On rail welding this is standard practice and is integrated into the welding operation, frequently by controlled induction or resistance reheating of the joint immediately after welding.

Straightness and alignment must be verified after welding and after flash removal, since the upset and the subsequent cooling both move the parts.

12. When to Use These Processes and When Not To

| Choose flash or upset welding when | Choose something else when |
| --- | --- |
| The joint is the full cross-section of a bar, rail, ring or tube | The joint is a lap, T or fillet configuration |
| High production rate on a repetitive joint | Short-run or one-off work — setup and machine cost dominate |
| Rail joints, ring gears, wheel rims, chain, band saw blades, tube coils | Access is restricted or the parts cannot be clamped rigidly |
| Dissimilar metals that fusion welding handles poorly | The joint must be made in situ with portable equipment (except purpose-built mobile rail welders) |
| No filler metal is wanted and no groove preparation is acceptable | Section size exceeds the machine's upset force capability |
| Contaminated faying surfaces (flash welding's self-cleaning) | The upset collar and material loss are unacceptable |

13. Defect Catalog

| Defect | Detection | Cause | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Flat fracture (oxide plane across the joint, fracture surface flat and featureless) | Bend or fracture testing; UT; metallography | Insufficient upset distance or force — contaminated interface material not expelled; upset too slow allowing re-oxidation | Increase upset distance and force; increase upset speed; verify upset current duration; this is the defining defect of the process |
| Incomplete bonding at the centre or periphery | UT; fracture testing | Uneven heating across the section; die opening wrong for the section; flashing profile not developing heat to the centre | Adjust flashing profile and die opening; consider preheat (241) for larger sections |
| Cracking in the heat-affected zone | MT/PT after delay; UT | Hardenable material air-cooled across a wide heated band without post-weld heat treatment | Apply the specified post-weld heat treatment; control cooling |
| Die burn / local melting at the clamps | Visual | Poor die contact — contamination, worn dies, insufficient clamping force | Clean clamping areas; dress or replace dies; verify clamping force |
| Slipping in the dies during upset | Displacement record; visual | Clamping force insufficient for the upset force; contaminated or worn die faces | Increase clamping force; service dies |
| Misalignment / off-square joint | Dimensional; visual | Parts not coaxial; faces not square; platen alignment | Check part squareness and machine alignment before welding |
| Excessive material loss | Dimensional | Flashing time too long; advance profile too aggressive | Reduce flashing time; adjust the profile |
| Sticking during flashing | Process record; visual | Flashing voltage too low; advance too fast for the heat developed | Increase voltage; adjust the advance profile |
| Notch at the joint after flash removal | Visual; fatigue failure in service | Flash sheared or ground into the parent metal | Control flash removal; dress the joint smoothly |

14. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Flat fractures in destructive testing

Symptom: fracture surfaces flat and featureless across the joint plane, with little deformation.

Category: upset inadequacy — the process's characteristic failure.

Likely causes: upset distance too small; upset force too low; upset speed too slow allowing re-oxidation; upset current stopping too early; die slippage reducing effective upset.

Steps: examine the upset curve for the actual displacement achieved against the setting — die slippage shows here; increase upset distance and force; increase upset speed; verify clamping force is adequate to resist the upset force; re-test.

Card 2 — Uneven upset flash around the joint

Symptom: upset collar heavier on one side or one part.

Category: heating or alignment asymmetry.

Likely causes: unequal die contact between the two parts causing unequal current; parts not coaxial; unequal die opening; different section or material between the two parts.

Steps: check die contact and cleanliness on both sides; check coaxial alignment; measure die opening on both sides; verify both parts are the specified material and section.

Card 3 — Cracking found after welding on rail or tool steel

Symptom: cracks in the heat-affected zone, sometimes delayed.

Category: metallurgy of a hardenable material.

Likely causes: hard structure formed across the whole heated band on air cooling; no post-weld heat treatment applied or applied outside its window; restraint from clamping during cooling.

Steps: verify the post-weld heat treatment was applied and recorded; check the heat treatment parameters against the material; review clamping and release timing during cooling (Chapter 23).

Card 4 — Sticking and unstable flashing

Symptom: flashing extinguishes; parts stick together; cycle aborts.

Category: flashing parameters.

Likely causes: flashing voltage too low; advance rate too fast for the heat developed; contaminated end faces preventing consistent bridging; die contact poor, reducing available current.

Steps: increase flashing voltage; slow the initial advance and re-shape the profile; check die contact and clamping area cleanliness.

15. Testing and Quality Verification

The upset curve is the primary process record. A plot of platen displacement and force against time through the cycle shows the flashing advance, the moment of upset, the distance achieved and the force applied. It is the closest equivalent in this process to the current and force traces of Volume 1, Chapter 11, and it detects die slippage, insufficient upset and timing faults that no post-weld inspection of the finished joint would reveal as clearly.

Destructive testing:

• Bend or fracture testing of setup and sample joints — the standard method, and the one that reveals flat fractures.

• Tensile testing across the joint.

• Metallographic sectioning for bond line examination and heat-affected zone assessment.

• Hardness traverse across the joint, particularly on hardenable materials after heat treatment.

Non-destructive testing:

• Ultrasonic testing across the joint, which is the practical production method on rail and heavy section.

• Visual inspection of the upset flash before removal, and of the joint after.

• Dimensional and straightness checks after flash removal.

16. Safety Specifics

• Flashing produces a violent stream of hot sparks and molten particles travelling a considerable distance. Guarding, screening and clearance of combustibles are mandatory, and this is a genuine fire hazard rather than a nuisance.

• Eye protection against the flash, which is bright as well as hot.

• Fume and particulate from the expelled material require extraction.

• Very high mechanical forces in the upset stroke, with crushing hazards at the dies and platen. Guarding and interlocks at the clamping and upset area are essential.

• Very high currents and heavy secondary conductors.

• Hot components after welding, across a substantial length of material.

• Noise during flashing.

17. Standards and Qualification

• Process references: ISO 4063 references 241 (flash welding with preheating) and 242 (flash welding without preheating) [S1]; upset welding within the same group 2 family.

• Procedure qualification: ISO 15614-13 covers resistance butt and flash welding procedure qualification; product standards govern where they apply — rail welding in particular is covered by dedicated railway standards with their own qualification, testing and acceptance requirements.

• Operator qualification: ISO 14732 for operators and setters of this mechanized process.

• Product-specific regimes: rail, chain and lifting applications each carry their own regulatory and testing frameworks that take precedence over general welding standards.

18. Worked Example: Flat-Fracture Failures on Rail Welds

Situation. A rail welding operation produces flash-welded joints. Routine destructive testing of sample joints shows several with flat, featureless fracture surfaces across part of the joint plane, indicating incomplete bonding. Machine settings match the qualified procedure.

Step 1 — Identify the defect by its signature. A flat, featureless fracture across the joint plane is the classic flash welding flat fracture: oxidized interface material was not fully expelled during upset (Section 13). This identification is immediate and reliable, and it points directly at the upset stage.

Step 2 — Go to the upset curve before anything else. The record shows the displacement actually achieved and the force actually applied, against the settings. Three distinct faults appear here: an upset distance short of the setting (indicating die slippage or a mechanical limit), a force below the setting (indicating a hydraulic or drive fault), or a slow displacement ramp (indicating a sluggish upset that let the interface cool).

Step 3 — Check for die slippage specifically. If displacement fell short while the drive delivered its stroke, the parts moved in the dies. Causes are insufficient clamping force, worn or contaminated die faces, or contamination on the rail clamping surface. Slippage is common and is invisible in the finished joint.

Step 4 — Check the flashing stage, since the upset can only expel what the flashing prepared. If flashing did not heat the full section uniformly, the periphery or the centre may not have reached forging temperature, and no amount of upset force bonds cold metal. Uneven flash collar shape is the visible indicator, and the flashing time and advance profile are the controls.

Step 5 — Check the material and its condition. Rail steel section size, initial temperature and surface condition all affect the heat developed. Cold rail in winter, or a section variation, changes the thermal balance.

Step 6 — Correct the cause, not the setting. If die slippage is confirmed, increasing the upset setting does not fix it — the parts will slip further. Restoring clamping force and die condition does. This distinction matters because increasing the setting produces a record that looks correct while the joint remains defective.

Step 7 — Verify by testing, and check the population. Retest after correction. Then determine which joints were made under the affected condition — the upset curves for the whole period are the evidence, and they can usually be reviewed retrospectively to identify joints with short or slow upsets.

Step 8 — Use the curve as a live control. The upset curve can be evaluated automatically against limits at the moment of welding, rejecting a joint immediately rather than discovering it in periodic destructive testing. On a safety-critical joint made in quantity, that is the control worth engineering — the same argument the process monitoring chapter makes for resistance spot welding (Volume 1, Chapter 11).

19. Known Gaps

• No parameter values are given. Flashing profiles, upset distances and forces are section-, material- and machine-specific, and are established by qualification.

• Rail welding is referenced as an application but its dedicated standards, acceptance criteria and testing regimes are outside this chapter's scope and take precedence where they apply.

• Upset welding is treated more briefly than flash welding, reflecting its narrower application and simpler cycle.

• Dissimilar-metal flash welding is described qualitatively. Feasible combinations and their limits are established by trial and by the compatibility considerations of Chapter 27.

• Machine capability limits — maximum section size against upset force — are equipment-specific.

1. Process Overview: The Two High-Frequency Variants

High-frequency welding produces the longitudinal seam in welded tube and pipe, continuously, at line speeds that make it the dominant process for commodity tubular product. Flat strip is roll-formed progressively into a tube shape with the two strip edges approaching each other, the edges are heated to forging temperature by high-frequency current, and squeeze rolls forge them together — expelling the molten and oxidized material as an internal and external bead.

Two variants deliver the current differently:

High-frequency resistance welding (HFRW) — current is conducted into the strip through sliding contacts placed on each edge upstream of the weld point.

High-frequency induction welding — current is induced in the strip by an encircling work coil, with no physical contact. This appears in the ISO nomenclature as reference 743, high frequency induction welding, alongside induction butt welding (741) and induction seam welding (742) [S1].

Both are solid-state forge welds in their final state, like flash welding (Chapter 49): what melts is expelled, and the bond is made between clean, hot, plastic metal from behind the original surfaces.

2. Skin Effect and Proximity Effect: Why the Current Goes Where It Is Wanted

The process depends entirely on two electromagnetic phenomena, and understanding them explains why it works at all.

Skin effect. Alternating current does not distribute evenly through a conductor's cross-section; it concentrates toward the surface, and the higher the frequency, the shallower the layer it occupies. At the frequencies used in this process — high radio frequencies, far above mains frequency — the current flows in an extremely thin surface layer.

Proximity effect. When two conductors carrying current in opposite directions run close together, the current in each concentrates on the faces nearest the other.

Combined, these two effects mean that current fed into the two strip edges, which converge toward each other, concentrates into the very edge faces that are about to be joined — and into a thin surface layer of them. The result is that a very large amount of energy is deposited exactly where it is needed, in a very small volume, extremely quickly.

Three consequences follow:

1. Heating is confined to a narrow band at the edges. The bulk of the strip stays cool, so the heat-affected zone is narrow and distortion is minimal.

2. Heating is extremely fast, which permits very high line speeds.

3. The process is exquisitely sensitive to the geometry of the converging edges, because that geometry is what determines where the proximity effect concentrates the current (Section 6).

3. High-Frequency Resistance Welding (Contact)

Current is fed through sliding contacts — shoes or wheels — bearing on the strip surface on each side of the open seam, upstream of the weld point. Current flows from one contact, along the edge toward the weld point, across the closing gap at the apex, back along the other edge, and out through the second contact.

Characteristics:

• High electrical efficiency, because current is delivered directly into the strip.

• Suits larger diameters and heavier walls, where induction coupling becomes inefficient.

• The contacts are consumables that wear and must be maintained; contact condition directly affects current delivery and is a common source of variability.

• Contact marking on the strip surface can be an issue on appearance-critical product.

4. High-Frequency Induction Welding

A work coil encircles the formed tube upstream of the weld point. High-frequency current in the coil induces a circulating current in the tube, which is forced by the open seam to flow along one edge, across the apex, and back along the other.

Characteristics:

• No physical contact with the strip, so no contact wear, no contact marking, and no contact maintenance.

• Better suited to smaller diameters and thinner walls, and to product where surface marking is unacceptable.

• Lower electrical efficiency than the contact method, since energy is transferred inductively.

• An impeder — a ferrite core inside the tube — is normally required to increase the impedance of the alternative current path around the inside of the tube, forcing more current along the edges. Impeder condition and position are significant process variables.

5. The Two Compared

| Factor | HF resistance (contact) | HF induction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Current delivery | Sliding contacts on the strip | Encircling work coil |
| Electrical efficiency | Higher | Lower |
| Contact wear and maintenance | Yes — a consumable | None |
| Surface marking | Possible at the contacts | None |
| Diameter range | Better on larger diameters and heavier wall | Better on smaller diameters and thin wall |
| Impeder required | Sometimes | Normally yes |
| Setup complexity | Contact positioning and pressure | Coil positioning and impeder condition |
| Sensitivity to strip surface | Higher — contacts need clean surface | Lower |

6. The Vee: The Master Geometric Variable

The vee is the converging gap between the two strip edges upstream of the weld point, and it is the single most important geometric variable in the process.

Vee angle — the included angle between the converging edges — governs:

• Where the proximity effect concentrates the current. A narrow vee brings the edges close together over a longer distance, spreading the heating; a wide vee concentrates it nearer the apex.

• The heated length of edge and therefore the temperature profile through the wall.

• Process stability. Too narrow a vee causes the edges to arc across prematurely and erratically before the weld point; too wide reduces the proximity effect and requires more power for the same heating.

Vee length — the distance from where the edges begin converging to the weld point — determines the time available for heating and the amount of edge exposed to oxidation before forging.

The apex position relative to the squeeze roll centreline determines whether the forging occurs at the correct temperature.

The practical consequence: vee geometry is set by the forming rolls and the fin pass upstream, not by the welder or the power supply. A vee problem is a roll setup problem, and attempting to correct it with power is the characteristic mistake in this process. This is why a mill's welding quality is largely determined by its forming section.

7. The Tube Mill as a System

High-frequency welding never exists as a standalone operation; it is one station in a continuous mill, and its quality depends on everything upstream:

Uncoiler and strip preparation → accumulator (allowing continuous running through coil changes) → forming section (progressively rolling flat strip into a tubular shape) → fin pass (setting the final edge geometry and vee) → weld station (HF power, contacts or coil, impeder, squeeze rolls) → bead removal (external, and internal where required) → cooling → sizing section → cut-off.

Two systemic consequences:

1. A defect at the weld station frequently originates upstream. Edge condition from slitting, camber in the strip, forming roll wear, and fin pass setting all reach the weld point as vee geometry variation.

2. Coil changes are a transition — a new coil brings a different thickness within tolerance, different surface condition, different edge condition from slitting, and a weld joining the two coils that must itself pass through the mill (Section 18).

8. Equipment and Components

| Component | Function | Failure consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HF power supply | Generates high-frequency current at the required power | Power or frequency variation changes heating directly |
| Contacts (HFRW) | Deliver current to the strip edges | Wear, contamination or pressure loss reduces and destabilizes current delivery |
| Work coil (induction) | Induces current in the tube | Position, condition and cooling affect coupling |
| Impeder | Ferrite core inside the tube forcing current along the edges | A degraded, displaced or overheated impeder reduces edge current substantially — a common and often overlooked fault |
| Squeeze rolls | Apply the forging force that closes the weld | Force and alignment determine whether contaminated material is expelled |
| Fin pass and forming rolls | Set the vee geometry | The origin of most weld quality variation |
| Bead scarfing tools | Remove external and internal weld bead | Tool wear leaves a proud or gouged bead line |
| Seam guidance | Keeps the seam aligned with the weld station | Seam rotation puts the weld point off the vee apex |
| Cooling | Cools coil, contacts, impeder and product | Impeder and coil cooling failures are common causes of drift |
| Weld line monitoring | Records power, speed, temperature or weld line position | The process record for a continuous product |

9. Parameters and What Each Controls

| Parameter | Controls | Symptom if wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HF power | Edge temperature at the weld point | Too low: cold weld, incomplete bonding. Too high: excessive melting, expulsion, internal defects |
| Line speed | Time available for heating; interacts directly with power | Speed and power must be adjusted together; a change to one alone changes the heat |
| Squeeze (forge) pressure | Whether contaminated interface material is expelled | Too low: cold weld with an oxide plane — the characteristic defect. Too high: excessive bead, thinning, work hardening |
| Vee angle and length | Where and how the current concentrates and heats | The dominant geometric variable (Section 6) |
| Apex position relative to squeeze rolls | Whether forging happens at the right temperature | Misposition: forging into metal that is too hot or too cold |
| Impeder condition and position | Edge current concentration | Degraded impeder: reduced edge heating at the same power |
| Contact pressure and position (HFRW) | Current delivery | Poor contact: unstable current, arcing and marking |
| Coil position and gap (induction) | Coupling efficiency | Wrong gap: reduced heating |

Power and speed are coupled. The energy delivered per unit length of weld is what matters, so a line speed change without a corresponding power change alters the weld directly. On a mill that changes speed for product or scheduling reasons, that coupling has to be managed automatically or by procedure.

10. The Weld Line and Its Metallurgy

The finished joint has a characteristic structure that inspection and metallography look for:

The weld line — a narrow band where the two edges met — is visible in a transverse section as a line of altered structure. In a sound weld it shows fine, uniform grain and no continuous inclusion trail.

The upset and flow lines — the forging action turns the grain flow outward toward the bead on both inner and outer surfaces. The shape and symmetry of these flow lines are a direct indicator of forge quality: symmetric outward flow indicates correct heating and forging on both edges, while asymmetric flow indicates uneven heating.

Decarburization and oxide — a continuous oxide trail along the weld line indicates insufficient expulsion, the same mechanism as flash welding's flat fracture (Chapter 49, Section 13).

Heat-affected zone — narrow, because of the skin and proximity effects, and visible as a symmetric hourglass-shaped band either side of the weld line.

Post-weld heat treatment — many product standards require seam normalizing or full-body normalizing to refine the weld line structure and restore toughness, applied in-line immediately after welding by induction heating.

11. Setup and Execution Procedure

Before running

1. Confirm the product specification: material, wall, diameter, and required post-weld treatment and testing.

2. Set the forming and fin pass rolls for the product; verify the vee angle and edge presentation before adjusting anything at the weld station.

3. Verify edge condition from slitting — burrs, camber and edge damage all reach the weld point.

4. Install and verify the impeder: correct type, correct position, cooling flowing.

5. Verify contacts (HFRW) or coil position and gap (induction).

6. Set squeeze roll position and force.

7. Set HF power and line speed together, per the established relationship for the product.

8. Verify bead scarfing tools and internal bead removal where required.

9. Run start-up material and destructively test it — flattening, flaring and metallographic sectioning — before releasing production.

During running

10. Monitor weld line appearance and bead formation continuously; bead symmetry is a live indicator of edge heating symmetry.

11. Monitor power, speed and, where fitted, weld line temperature.

12. Watch for seam rotation and correct it at the guidance rather than at the weld station.

13. Treat every coil change as a transition requiring verification (Section 18).

14. Sample and test at the established frequency.

After running

15. Verify in-line NDT coverage and results (Section 12).

16. Confirm post-weld heat treatment where specified.

17. Record power, speed, squeeze setting, coil identity and test results against product identity.

12. Inspection at Mill Speed

The product is continuous and made at high speed, which changes inspection entirely from batch fabrication:

In-line non-destructive testing is normal and is usually ultrasonic or eddy current, positioned after welding and bead removal, scanning the weld line continuously. It is set up against reference standards containing artificial notches of specified dimensions, and it marks or diverts defective lengths automatically.

Destructive testing on samples at defined intervals and at every transition:

• Flattening test — the tube is flattened between platens with the weld at a specified orientation, and the weld must not open. The standard production check.

• Flaring or expansion test on the tube end.

• Metallographic sectioning of the weld line, examining flow lines, weld line structure and heat-affected zone symmetry (Section 10).

• Hardness traverse across the weld line where the specification requires it.

Hydrostatic testing of finished lengths, where the product standard requires it.

The key structural point: in-line NDT provides continuous coverage but is calibrated to detect specific artificial reference reflectors, and destructive testing at intervals provides the metallurgical evidence that NDT cannot. Both are needed, and a mill relying on either alone has a gap.

13. When to Use Which Variant

| Situation | Variant |
| --- | --- |
| Larger diameter, heavier wall pipe | HF resistance (contact) — higher efficiency at the required power |
| Small diameter, thin wall tube | HF induction — better coupling at small diameter |
| Surface marking unacceptable | HF induction — no contact with the strip |
| Maximum electrical efficiency | HF resistance |
| Minimum consumable maintenance | HF induction — no contacts to wear |
| Stainless and alloy tube where surface condition is critical | HF induction |
| High-volume commodity line pipe | Either, chosen on diameter and mill design |

14. Defect Catalog

| Defect | Detection | Cause | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cold weld / oxide line (weld line with a continuous inclusion trail; opens in flattening test) | Flattening test; metallography; in-line UT | Insufficient heat, insufficient squeeze, or both — contaminated interface material not expelled | Increase power or reduce speed; increase squeeze force; check impeder and vee geometry |
| Penetrator (localized oxide inclusion in the weld line) | In-line UT; metallography | Momentary heat loss — edge contamination, power dip, impeder fault, seam rotation | Investigate the transient cause; check impeder and contacts; check edge condition |
| Excessive expulsion / heavy bead | Visual | Too much power for the speed; excessive squeeze | Reduce power or increase speed; reduce squeeze |
| Asymmetric flow lines | Metallography; bead asymmetry visually | Uneven heating of the two edges — seam rotation, unequal contact or coil coupling, asymmetric vee | Correct seam guidance; check contacts or coil symmetry; check fin pass setting |
| Weld line cracking | Flattening test; metallography | Excessive hardness in a hardenable grade without seam normalizing; hydrogen from contaminated edges | Apply seam normalizing where specified; verify edge cleanliness |
| Gouged or proud bead line | Visual; dimensional | Scarfing tool wear or misalignment; internal bead tool wear | Replace and align scarfing tools; monitor internal bead removal, which is not visible from outside |
| Seam off-position | Visual; weld line location | Seam rotation through the mill; guidance fault | Correct seam guidance upstream; do not compensate at the weld station |
| Inconsistent weld quality after a coil change | Sampling at transition | Thickness, edge condition or surface differences between coils; the coil-joining weld passing through | Verify at every transition; treat coil change as a controlled event (Section 18) |
| Impeder-related heat loss | Falling weld quality at constant power | Impeder degraded, displaced, or overheated through cooling loss | Inspect and replace impeder on a controlled interval; verify impeder cooling |

15. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Flattening tests failing with the weld opening

Symptom: weld opens during the flattening test; metallography shows an oxide line.

Category: cold weld — insufficient heat or forge.

Likely causes: HF power too low for the line speed; squeeze force insufficient; impeder degraded, reducing edge current at the same power; vee geometry wrong, spreading the heating; edge contamination.

Steps: check power and speed together as energy per unit length, not separately; measure squeeze roll setting and force; inspect the impeder — this is the most frequently overlooked cause of gradual heat loss; verify vee angle at the fin pass; check strip edge condition from slitting.

Card 2 — Sporadic in-line ultrasonic indications on an otherwise good run

Symptom: isolated indications along the length; most of the run acceptable.

Category: transient disturbance.

Likely causes: localized edge contamination or damage on the strip; momentary power supply dip; contact arcing (HFRW); brief seam rotation; a coil-joining weld passing through.

Steps: correlate the indications with strip position and with coil transitions; inspect strip edge condition on the coil; review power records for dips; check contact condition; confirm whether the coil-joining welds are being marked and removed as intended.

Card 3 — Quality drifting down over hours at constant settings

Symptom: gradual increase in defect rate with no setting change.

Category: consumable or component degradation.

Likely causes: impeder degradation from heat and wear; contact wear (HFRW); coil damage or cooling loss; scarfing tool wear; forming roll wear altering the vee.

Steps: check impeder condition and cooling first; check contacts and coil; measure the vee angle against setup values; establish component replacement intervals inside the degradation point rather than running to failure.

Card 4 — Asymmetric bead and one-sided flow lines

Symptom: external bead heavier on one side; metallography shows asymmetric grain flow.

Category: heating asymmetry.

Likely causes: seam rotated relative to the weld station; contacts unequal in pressure or position; coil not concentric; fin pass producing unequal edges; strip camber.

Steps: check seam position through the weld station; verify contact or coil symmetry; measure edge geometry from the fin pass on both sides; check strip camber, which is a coil property and will vary between coils.

16. Safety Specifics

• High-frequency electromagnetic fields at significant power. Exposure limits, shielding of the weld station, and the specific hazard to implanted medical devices apply (Chapter 37, Section 10). This is a more substantial consideration here than in arc welding.

• High voltages in the HF power supply.

• Molten metal expulsion at the weld point, continuously along a running line.

• Moving strip and rotating rolls at speed — the dominant mechanical hazard, with entanglement and crushing points throughout the mill.

• Hot product downstream of the weld station.

• Noise from the mill and from the HF supply.

• Scarfing chips and swarf ejected at speed.

17. Standards and Qualification

• Process reference: ISO 4063 reference 743, high frequency induction welding, alongside 741 induction butt welding and 742 induction seam welding [S1]. High-frequency resistance welding belongs to the group 2 resistance family.

• Product standards govern. Welded tube and pipe are made to product specifications — line pipe, structural hollow section, boiler tube, and mechanical tubing standards each specify the permitted processes, the required testing, the acceptance criteria, and any post-weld heat treatment. These take precedence over general welding standards.

• In-line NDT is specified by the product standard, including reference standard notch dimensions and coverage requirements.

• Operator qualification under ISO 14732 principles for a mechanized continuous process.

18. Worked Example: Intermittent Weld Line Defects After a Coil Change

Situation. A tube mill runs consistently for most of a coil. Shortly after each coil change, in-line ultrasonic testing flags a cluster of weld line indications, then the run settles and quality returns to normal. Settings are unchanged across the change.

Step 1 — Note that the pattern is tied to a transition, not to time or wear. Wear-related causes drift gradually; this recurs at a specific event and clears. That points at something that changes at the coil change and then stabilizes.

Step 2 — List what actually changes at a coil change. The coil-joining weld itself passes through the mill; strip thickness changes within tolerance between coils; edge condition from slitting differs between coils; surface condition and residual oil differ; strip camber differs; and the accumulator empties and refills, which can change line tension.

Step 3 — Check the coil-joining weld first. The joint between the trailing end of one coil and the leading end of the next is itself a weld, usually made off-line, and it passes through the forming and welding sections. It is normally marked and the affected length removed. If the marking or removal is not working, that length reaches the product — and it would produce exactly a short cluster of indications immediately after the change.

Step 4 — Check strip thickness and edge condition across the change. A thickness change within specification alters the energy required at constant power and speed, and the mill has to re-establish equilibrium. If the mill has no automatic compensation, that transition period is genuinely under-welded until an operator corrects it — or until the process happens to settle.

Step 5 — Check line tension and speed stability through the accumulator transition. Speed variation changes energy per unit length directly, and the accumulator emptying and refilling is a real disturbance in some mill designs.

Step 6 — Check whether the mill is running with any transition procedure at all. In many cases the answer is that the operator watches and corrects by eye. A defined transition procedure — verify the coil-joining weld is marked and removed, verify thickness, re-check power against the new thickness, sample and test the first product — converts an unmanaged event into a controlled one.

Step 7 — Correct at the transition, not the setting. Increasing power globally to cover the worst case at transitions over-welds the rest of the run. The correct response is transition management: automatic compensation for thickness where the mill supports it, reliable coil-joint marking and removal, and a sampling requirement at every transition.

Step 8 — Confirm the inspection is catching it reliably. The in-line NDT did detect these, which is the system working. The remaining question is whether the marked lengths are actually being removed and segregated, because detection without reliable removal is not protection.

19. Known Gaps

• No parameter values are given. Power, speed, squeeze force and vee angle are product-, mill- and material-specific and are established by qualification and mill experience.

• Frequency ranges are described qualitatively. Operating frequencies vary by equipment generation and application.

• Product standard requirements are referenced, not reproduced. Acceptance criteria, testing extent and heat treatment requirements are specified by the applicable product standard and take precedence.

• In-line NDT reference notch dimensions are specified by the product standard and are not stated here.

• Mill design varies substantially, and the component list in Section 8 describes a typical configuration rather than a universal one.

1. What the Family Shares

Every process in this family generates heat by passing current through the workpieces themselves and applies mechanical force through the electrodes or dies. There is no arc as the working heat source, no filler metal, no shielding gas, and no flux. Volume 1 develops the physics across twenty chapters for spot welding; Chapters 48 to 50 extend it to seam, flash, upset and high-frequency welding.

Four properties follow from that shared basis and apply to the whole family:

Heat is generated where resistance is highest, which is at the interfaces to be joined — so the process is self-locating in a way that no external heat source is.

Force is a process variable, not a fixture requirement. Electrode or die force determines contact resistance, contains the molten metal, and — in the forge processes — performs the joining itself.

The cycle is machine-executed and very short, from milliseconds to a few seconds. Manual skill plays almost no part, and quality is set by machine condition, schedule and material.

Nothing is added. No consumable becomes part of the joint, which removes an entire category of variables — and removes an entire category of remedies, since there is no filler to compensate for a poor fit or a difficult material.
