3. Selection by Joint Geometry

Geometry usually decides the process before any other consideration, and the question that settles it is what shape is the joint:

| The joint is… | Process |
| --- | --- |
| Overlapped sheet, discrete attachment points sufficient | Spot welding |
| Overlapped sheet, needs to be leak-tight | Seam welding (Ch. 48) |
| Overlapped sheet, needs near-parent thickness | Mash seam welding (222) |
| A nut, boss, stud or fastener onto sheet | Projection welding |
| Multiple simultaneous joints at designed locations | Projection welding |
| The full cross-section of a bar, rail, ring or heavy tube, end to end | Flash welding |
| The full cross-section of wire, rod or small bar, end to end | Upset welding |
| A continuous longitudinal seam in tube or pipe, made in a mill | High-frequency welding (Ch. 50) |
| Accessible from one side only | Projection or indirect spot (211) — or a different process family |

4. Selection by Production Volume and Rate

| Volume and rate | Suitability |
| --- | --- |
| Very high volume, repetitive, automotive-scale | The family's core territory. Spot, projection and seam welding are built for it |
| Continuous product measured in kilometres | High-frequency welding — the only member designed for continuous production |
| Moderate volume, repetitive | Well suited, provided tooling and setup can be amortized |
| Low volume, varied joints | Poorly suited. Tooling, electrode design and schedule development cost dominate |
| One-off or repair work | Not suitable. Almost every other family is a better answer |

The family's economics are dominated by setup and tooling amortization, not by consumable cost. There is no consumable in the joint, energy cost per weld is low, and cycle times are very short — but electrodes, dies, wheels and fixtures are engineered per joint, and schedules must be developed and qualified per material stack. That fixed cost is why the family dominates mass production and is rarely the right answer below it.

5. Selection by Material and Thickness

| Material | Behaviour across the family |
| --- | --- |
| Low-carbon steel | The reference case; widest process window throughout the family |
| Coated steels | Coating transfers to electrodes and wheels, dominating consumable life. Wire seam welding (224) exists for this; tip dressing and interval control elsewhere (Volume 1, Ch. 13) |
| Advanced high-strength steels | Narrower window; HAZ softening; higher force requirements (Volume 1, Ch. 2) |
| Stainless steels | Higher resistivity, so lower current than carbon steel, but heat is retained — cooling and cool-time control matter more |
| Aluminium | Functionally a different process — roughly three times the current, a third of the time, a much narrower window, and different equipment demands (Volume 1, Ch. 14) |
| Copper alloys | Very difficult — conductivity is too high for efficient heat generation in the workpiece |
| Dissimilar metals | More feasible in the forge processes (flash, upset, HF) than in the nugget processes, because reacted material is expelled (Ch. 27, Ch. 49) |

Thickness divides the family cleanly: spot, projection and seam welding are sheet processes; flash, upset and high-frequency welding join full sections whose size is limited by machine force capability rather than by heat.

6. Selection by Required Joint Property

| Required property | Process |
| --- | --- |
| Shear strength at discrete points | Spot, projection |
| Leak-tightness | Seam welding with adequate nugget overlap (Ch. 48, Section 10) |
| Full-section strength equal to the parent | Flash, upset, high-frequency — subject to post-weld heat treatment on hardenable materials |
| Near-parent joint thickness | Mash seam (222); flash and upset after flash removal |
| Appearance-critical surface, minimal marking | Projection welding (marking is on the projection side); HF induction on tube |
| Fatigue performance | Full-section forge processes generally outperform discrete nuggets; nugget processes concentrate stress at the nugget edge |
| Multiple joints in one cycle | Projection welding |
| Dissimilar-metal capability | Flash, HF (expulsion limits intermetallic retention) |

7. The Shared Physics, Restated

Stated once, applying to the whole family (Volume 1, Chapter 1 develops it in full):

Heat generation follows I²Rt. Heat scales with the square of current, linearly with resistance and linearly with time. Current is therefore the most powerful variable everywhere in this family.

Resistance is not constant. It evolves through the cycle as surfaces collapse, contact area grows and temperature rises — the dynamic resistance curve — and this is why the process cannot be characterized by a single resistance value.

Force and current are coupled. Force sets contact resistance, so changing force changes heat generation. They cannot be tuned independently, and a schedule is a combination rather than a set of separate settings.

A process window exists in more than one dimension. The weldability lobe — the region of current and time that produces acceptable welds without expulsion — narrows with difficult materials, thin sections, and coating.

Expulsion is the upper boundary. In the nugget processes it is a defect. In the forge processes it is the mechanism — flashing and upset expulsion are how the joint is cleaned (Chapter 49, Section 3).

Shunting diverts current. Adjacent completed welds, contact points and alternative paths all carry current that does not reach the joint. It is occasional in spot welding, continuous in seam welding, and managed by the impeder in high-frequency welding.

8. The Shared Failure Modes

| Failure mode | Where it appears | Common root cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Undersized or absent nugget / cold weld | All | Insufficient current, excessive shunting, worn or contaminated electrodes, excessive force |
| Interfacial or flat fracture | Spot, projection, flash, HF | Insufficient heat or insufficient forge; oxidized interface material not expelled |
| Expulsion where unwanted | Spot, projection, seam | Current too high, force too low, contaminated surfaces, poor fit |
| Progressive degradation through a run | All | Electrode, wheel, die or contact wear and contamination — the family's defining production problem |
| Excessive indentation or thinning | Spot, projection, seam | Force too high, current too high |
| Leak path | Seam | Insufficient nugget overlap |
| HAZ hardening and cracking | Flash, upset, HF, AHSS spot | Hardenable material cooled rapidly without post-weld heat treatment |
| Misalignment / weld off the joint | Seam, HF, flash | Guidance, fixture or alignment fault upstream of the weld |

The single most important shared observation: the dominant production failure in this family is not a schedule error but consumable degradation — electrode tips mushrooming, wheels growing and picking up coating, dies wearing, contacts eroding, impeders degrading. In every chapter of this family, the recurring worked example is the same shape: good at the start of a run, degrading through it, with settings unchanged.

9. The Shared Control Philosophy

Because the cycle is machine-executed and very short, the family's quality control is built on four elements that recur across every chapter:

1. A qualified schedule established by destructive testing on the actual material stack, not calculated.

2. Setup samples tested destructively before production, every time.

3. Consumable interval management — dressing, replacement and inspection intervals set inside the point where degradation begins, rather than reacting to defects.

4. Process monitoring — recording the electrical and mechanical signature of each weld and comparing it against a reference (Volume 1, Chapter 11), which is the only practical way to detect drift on a process producing thousands of joints per shift.

Post-weld inspection alone is structurally inadequate for this family, because the joints are made faster than they can be inspected, most are not accessible for volumetric inspection, and the definitive test is destructive. This is why the family relies on process control and sampling rather than on inspection, more heavily than any other family in this reference set.

12. Decision Walkthrough

1. What is the joint's geometry? Sheet overlap, fastener attachment, full section, or continuous tube seam. This normally eliminates all but one or two processes (Section 3).

2. Must it be leak-tight? If yes and it is sheet, seam welding is the answer and nugget overlap is the controlling requirement.

3. What is the material and thickness? Aluminium and copper narrow the options severely; coated steel changes the consumable strategy (Section 5).

4. What volume and rate? Below the volume that amortizes tooling, look outside this family (Section 4).

5. Is access available on both sides? If not, projection or indirect configurations — or a different family.

6. Is the material hardenable? If so, plan post-weld heat treatment into the process, particularly for the forge processes.

7. How will quality be assured? Establish the schedule by destructive testing, set consumable intervals, and decide the monitoring approach — before production, not after the first defects (Section 9).

8. Confirm against the applicable product standard, which may mandate or exclude specific processes.

13. Worked Example: Choosing a Process for a Sealed Sheet Metal Assembly

Situation. A manufacturer needs to join two formed sheet steel pressings into a sealed enclosure that must hold low pressure without leaking. Production volume is high and continuous. The current design uses spot welds with a sealant bead, and field returns show leaks where the sealant has failed.

Step 1 — Establish the actual requirement. The joint must be leak-tight for the product's life. The current design achieves strength by spot welding and sealing by sealant — two separate mechanisms, with the sealant carrying the requirement that is failing.

Step 2 — Ask whether the welding process can carry the sealing requirement itself. Within this family, seam welding is the member that produces a leak-tight joint (Section 3). That would remove the sealant from the load path entirely rather than improving it.

Step 3 — Check the geometry against seam welding's requirements. Seam welding needs a continuous, accessible joint line with wheel access on both sides, and a consistent overlap. Whether the pressings' flange geometry permits wheel access all round — including at corners and radii — is the decisive feasibility question, and it must be answered on the actual part before anything else.

Step 4 — Check the corners specifically. Wheel electrodes cannot follow a tight radius, and a seam that cannot be closed at the corners is not leak-tight regardless of how good the straight runs are. Real assemblies fail here, and the answer is usually a design change to the flange geometry rather than a welding solution.

Step 5 — Consider mash seam if joint thickness matters. If the enclosure's flange thickness affects assembly or appearance, mash seam welding (222) produces a joint approaching parent thickness — at the cost of much tighter overlap and force control (Chapter 48, Section 4).

Step 6 — Consider the alternatives honestly. Laser seam welding produces a leak-tight seam with access from one side only and no wheel radius limitation, which directly addresses the corner problem — at higher capital cost and with tighter fit-up requirements (Chapter 52). A redesigned mechanical joint with a gasket is also a legitimate answer if the flange geometry cannot be made weldable.

Step 7 — Plan the verification before choosing. Whichever process is chosen, leak testing is now a production requirement, not an option, and its sensitivity must be matched to the pressure the product must hold (Chapter 48, Section 10). Nugget overlap, not strength, is the property being controlled, and sectioning is what measures it.

Step 8 — Plan the consumable strategy. If seam welding is selected, wheel dressing intervals and coating pickup management must be established before production, because the family's characteristic failure is degradation through a run (Section 8) — and on a leak-tight requirement, that degradation shows up as leaks in the field rather than as visible defects on the line.

14. Known Gaps

• No schedules, currents, times or forces appear anywhere in this chapter. Volume 1's position holds for the whole family: a qualified production schedule can only come from destructive testing on the actual material, thickness, coating and equipment combination.

• Machine capability limits — maximum section for flash and upset welding, maximum thickness for spot and seam — are equipment-specific.

• Product standards govern in tube, rail and pressure applications and take precedence over the general guidance here.

• The comparison matrix uses relative rankings, since absolute figures depend on equipment, material and application.

• Aluminium resistance welding is repeatedly flagged as a distinct discipline rather than developed here; Volume 1, Chapter 14 covers it for spot welding.

22. Sources referenced in this chapter

1. Process Overview: ISO 4063 References 52x

Laser beam welding focuses a coherent, monochromatic beam onto the joint, delivering energy at a power density far above any arc process. The ISO nomenclature separates sources [S1]:

| Reference | Process |
| --- | --- |
| 521 | Solid state laser welding |
| 522 | Gas laser welding |
| 523 | Diode laser welding |

That split is a source distinction with metallurgical consequences, not a bookkeeping detail: source type determines wavelength, wavelength determines absorptivity, and absorptivity determines which materials couple efficiently (Section 5). A procedure that says only "laser welding" has omitted a variable that changes the process window substantially on copper and aluminium.

2. Power Density and the Two Welding Modes

Everything about laser welding follows from power density (Chapter 22, Section 2). Below a threshold, the beam heats the surface and heat conducts inward — conduction mode. Above it, the beam vaporizes metal fast enough to open a vapour cavity through the material — keyhole mode.

The transition is not gradual in its consequences: the two modes produce welds of entirely different shape, penetration and defect population, and a process operating near the threshold moves between them unpredictably.

|  | Conduction mode | Keyhole mode |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Surface absorption, heat conduction inward | Vapour cavity through the material; multiple internal reflections |
| Weld shape | Wide, shallow, roughly semicircular | Narrow, deep, nearly parallel-sided |
| Depth-to-width ratio | Below 1 | Well above 1 |
| Energy coupling | Lower — much is reflected | High — the keyhole traps the beam |
| Speed | Lower | High |
| Typical use | Thin sheet, cosmetic seams, hermetic sealing of small components | Structural and deep-penetration welding |
| Characteristic defects | Lack of penetration | Porosity, spiking, humping, root drop-out |

3. Conduction Mode

The beam heats the surface, and the weld pool grows by conduction. It behaves much like a very small, very fast gas tungsten arc weld.

Advantages: a smooth, cosmetically good bead; a stable process without the keyhole's dynamic instability; no keyhole-related porosity; less sensitive to focus position than keyhole welding.

Limitations: shallow penetration; lower coupling efficiency because reflected energy is lost; slower for a given penetration.

Applications: thin sheet, hermetic sealing of small enclosures and medical devices, cosmetic seams, and any joint where a wide shallow fusion zone is preferable to a deep narrow one. Diode lasers (523), whose beam quality does not readily support keyholing but whose wavelength is well absorbed, are frequently used specifically for conduction-mode work.

4. Keyhole Mode

Above the power density threshold, metal vaporizes and the vapour pressure displaces the melt, opening a narrow cavity — the keyhole — that extends into or through the material. The beam enters the keyhole and undergoes multiple internal reflections, depositing energy down its whole depth. This is why coupling efficiency rises sharply on keyhole formation: the keyhole acts as a light trap.

Molten metal flows around the keyhole and solidifies behind it as the beam travels.

What makes the keyhole difficult is that it is a dynamic equilibrium between vapour pressure holding it open and surface tension and hydrostatic pressure closing it. It fluctuates continuously, and those fluctuations are the direct cause of the mode's characteristic defects:

• Keyhole collapse traps vapour at the root, producing porosity.

• Irregular keyhole depth produces spiking — periodic deep excursions of the fusion boundary, often with pores at their tips.

• Melt flow instability at high speed produces humping — periodic bulges and valleys along the bead.

• Root drop-out where full penetration is achieved and surface tension cannot hold the molten root.

5. Laser Sources and Why Wavelength Matters

| Source | ISO ref | Wavelength region | Delivery | Character |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fibre laser | 521 | Near-infrared (around 1 µm) | Optical fibre | High efficiency, excellent beam quality, high power; the current industrial standard |
| Disk laser | 521 | Near-infrared (around 1 µm) | Optical fibre | High power with good beam quality |
| Nd:YAG (rod) | 521 | Near-infrared (around 1 µm) | Optical fibre | Largely superseded by fibre and disk sources |
| CO₂ laser | 522 | Far-infrared (around 10 µm) | Mirrors — cannot use fibre | High power, mature; beam delivery is inflexible; plasma plume absorbs strongly at this wavelength |
| Diode laser | 523 | Near-infrared, various | Fibre | Compact and efficient; beam quality limits keyholing; good for conduction mode and cladding |
| Green and blue diode | 523 | Visible | Fibre | Much higher absorptivity in copper and gold; developed specifically for electrical joining |

Why wavelength decides material capability. Absorptivity — the fraction of incident energy a surface absorbs rather than reflects — depends on both the material and the wavelength. Metals reflect strongly in the infrared, and copper and gold reflect near-infrared radiation very strongly, which historically made them extremely difficult to laser weld: the beam was mostly reflected until the surface melted, at which point absorptivity jumped abruptly and the process became violent and unstable.

Green and blue laser sources address this directly by operating at wavelengths where copper's absorptivity is far higher. This is the technical reason such sources appeared as electrical and battery assembly grew, and it is a genuine capability change rather than an incremental improvement (Chapter 27, Section 8).

The CO₂ wavelength has its own consequence: the metal vapour plume above the keyhole absorbs 10 µm radiation strongly, so CO₂ laser welding requires active plume control with a gas jet, while near-infrared sources are much less affected (Section 8).

6. Beam Delivery and Focusing Optics

Fibre delivery — available to all near-infrared sources — routes the beam through a flexible optical fibre to the processing head. This is what made laser welding practical on robots and multi-station lines, and it is a decisive practical advantage over mirror-delivered CO₂ systems.

Focusing optics determine the beam's shape at the workpiece:

• Focal spot diameter sets power density directly and is the primary determinant of mode.

• Focal position relative to the surface — at, above, or below it — changes penetration and weld shape substantially. Below-surface focus is common for keyhole welding.

• Depth of focus determines how much variation in working distance the process tolerates.

• Beam quality determines how small a spot a given power can be focused into, and therefore what power density is achievable.

Optics contamination is a first-order production problem. Spatter, fume and vapour deposit on the protective cover glass, absorbing energy, heating the optic, distorting the beam and eventually destroying the glass. Cover glass condition monitoring is standard on production systems, and a gradual quality decline with unchanged settings is very often a contaminated optic (Section 17).

7. Equipment and Components

| Component | Function | Failure consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Laser source | Generates the beam | Power drift changes penetration directly |
| Beam delivery (fibre or mirrors) | Transports the beam | Fibre damage; mirror misalignment or contamination |
| Processing head | Collimates and focuses; carries protective optics and gas nozzles | The critical assembly for beam quality at the work |
| Protective cover glass | Shields the focusing optics from spatter and fume | A consumable. Contamination causes progressive power loss and focus shift |
| Cross-jet / air knife | Deflects spatter and fume away from the optics | Without it, cover glass life collapses |
| Shielding gas delivery | Protects the pool; controls the plume | Inadequate shielding gives oxidation and porosity |
| Motion system or robot | Moves beam or part | Positional accuracy is measured against a beam a fraction of a millimetre wide |
| Seam finding / tracking | Locates the joint | Essential — the beam is narrower than the tolerance on most joints |
| Fixturing and clamping | Holds fit-up | The dominant quality variable (Section 10) |
| Process monitoring | Photodiode, camera or interferometric depth sensing | The practical way to detect defects at production speed |

8. Shielding Gas and Plume Control

Shielding gas does two jobs in laser welding, and the second has no equivalent in arc welding:

Protecting the pool from oxidation, as in any fusion process.

Controlling the vapour plume. Metal vapour above the keyhole absorbs and scatters the beam. At the CO₂ wavelength this is severe enough to require active suppression; at near-infrared wavelengths it is milder but still present at high power.

Gas selection reflects both jobs: helium has a high ionization potential and suppresses plume formation effectively, and is the traditional choice for CO₂ laser welding despite its cost. Argon shields well and is cheaper but ionizes more readily, forming a plasma that can block a CO₂ beam. Nitrogen is used on some materials. Near-infrared sources tolerate argon well.

Delivery geometry matters more than in arc welding: coaxial nozzles, off-axis side jets and trailing shields are used, and the gas jet must not disturb the keyhole or blow the pool.

9. Parameters and What Each Controls

| Parameter | Controls | Symptom if wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Laser power | Energy input; whether keyholing occurs | Too low: conduction mode or lack of penetration. Too high: excessive penetration, root drop-out, spatter |
| Travel speed | Energy per unit length | Too fast: lack of penetration, humping, undercut. Too slow: excessive heat, drop-out, distortion |
| Focal position | Power density at the work; weld shape | Wrong focus: mode change, lost penetration; a very sensitive parameter |
| Focal spot size / beam quality | Power density | Larger spot: conduction mode at the same power |
| Shielding gas type and flow | Pool protection and plume suppression | Wrong gas on CO₂: plasma blocking. Excessive flow: pool disturbance |
| Beam oscillation / wobble | Effective spot width; gap bridging; melt stirring | Without it, gap tolerance is minimal |
| Joint gap | Whether there is material to melt | The dominant variable (Section 10) |
| Pulse shaping (pulsed lasers) | Energy delivery profile | Affects cracking and porosity in sensitive materials |

Power, speed and focus interact strongly, and the operating point sits close to a mode boundary. This is why laser welding parameters are developed empirically per joint and are far less transferable between applications than arc welding parameters.

10. The Fit-Up Problem

This is the process's defining practical limitation, and it decides more laser welding projects than any metallurgical consideration.

The mechanism. A focused beam may be a few tenths of a millimetre across. A butt joint with a gap wider than the beam presents nothing for the beam to strike — it passes through, melting the edges inadequately or not at all. There is no filler being added and no wide arc cone to bridge the gap, so the process cannot compensate for a gap the way any arc process can.

The consequences:

• Fit-up tolerances are far tighter than for arc welding — typically a small fraction of the material thickness, and often stated as a fraction of the beam diameter.

• Fixturing and part preparation become the dominant cost and the dominant quality variable. Laser welding installations frequently succeed or fail on their clamping, not on their laser.

• Cut edge quality matters, because the joint edges are the material being melted.

• Seam tracking is essential, because a beam that misses the joint by its own diameter misses it entirely.

The engineered responses:

1. Beam oscillation (wobble) — rapidly scanning the beam across the joint widens the effective interaction zone and improves gap tolerance substantially. Now standard on production systems.

2. Filler wire addition — supplies material to fill a gap, at the cost of a more complex process and tighter wire positioning.

3. Hybrid laser-arc welding — the most complete answer (Section 11).

4. Defocusing — a larger spot bridges more gap, at the cost of power density and penetration.

5. Joint design — lap joints tolerate gaps far better than butt joints, because the beam always finds material.

11. Hybrid Laser-Arc Welding

Hybrid welding combines a laser beam and an arc — usually GMAW — in a single, shared weld pool. It is not two processes in sequence; the interaction is the point.

What each contributes:

| From the laser | From the arc |
| --- | --- |
| Deep keyhole penetration | Filler metal, which fills gaps and adjusts weld metal chemistry |
| High travel speed | Gap bridging tolerance |
| Narrow HAZ, low distortion | Arc stabilization by the laser-generated plume, allowing higher speeds than arc alone |
|  | A wider, better-shaped cap |

Why the combination is more than the sum. The laser's keyhole stabilizes the arc root, allowing the arc to run faster and more stably than it could alone. The arc's filler and broader energy distribution relieve the laser's fit-up intolerance. The result is a process with near-laser penetration and near-arc gap tolerance — which is precisely the combination that pure laser welding lacks.

Its costs: substantially more complex to set up and control, with the relative position of beam and arc, their separation distance, and the lead-lag arrangement all critical; more parameters; higher capital cost; and a qualification exercise covering both sub-processes. ISO 4063 recognizes the hybrid family separately in its nomenclature, and ISO 15609 provides a dedicated part for hybrid procedure specification.

Where it is used: shipbuilding panel lines, heavy plate structural work, and pipeline welding — applications with long seams, real fit-up variation, and a need for both speed and penetration.

12. Remote and Scanner Welding

Remote laser welding uses a scanner head with steerable mirrors at a long working distance, positioning the beam by deflecting it rather than by moving the head. Because the mirrors have very low inertia, the beam can be repositioned between weld locations in milliseconds.

Why it matters commercially: on a part with many short welds — automotive body assemblies in particular — the dominant time cost is moving between welds, not welding. Remote welding collapses that time, and the productivity gain is large enough to have reshaped body-in-white joining strategy.

Its requirements: clear line of sight from the scanner to every weld location, tight part positioning, and clamping that presents the joint correctly without obstructing the beam path.

| Material | Laser welding behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| Carbon and low-alloy steel | Well suited; the fast cooling rate can produce hard martensitic structures, so hardenable grades need attention |
| Stainless steel | Very well suited; the narrow HAZ limits sensitization exposure (Chapter 24) |
| Aluminium | Weldable but demanding: high reflectivity at near-infrared, high thermal conductivity, hydrogen porosity, hot cracking in sensitive alloys, and magnesium loss by evaporation from 5xxx alloys |

Remedies are a deliberate gap between sheets, a dimple or laser-scribed vent path, or welding in a configuration that vents |

14. Setup and Execution Procedure

Before welding

1. Confirm the procedure covers material, thickness, joint type and — explicitly — source type and wavelength.

2. Verify optics: inspect and, if needed, replace the protective cover glass; confirm cross-jet function.

3. Verify focal position and spot size against the procedure; measure rather than assume, since focus is both critical and prone to drift.

4. Verify fit-up on the actual parts — gap, alignment and edge quality — against the procedure's tolerance, not against arc welding intuition.

5. Confirm clamping presents the joint correctly along its whole length and does not obstruct the beam or the gas.

6. Set shielding gas type, flow and nozzle geometry.

7. Verify seam tracking or teaching against the actual joint position.

8. Confirm the enclosure interlocks and beam containment are functional (Section 18).

9. Run and section trial welds — penetration and porosity are not visible from the surface.

Welding

10. Monitor process signals where available: photodiode, camera or interferometric penetration depth.

11. Watch for spatter accumulation on the cover glass and on the nozzle.

12. Watch for surface indications of instability — irregular bead, humping, excessive spatter.

13. Maintain shielding until the metal is cool enough not to oxidize.

After welding

14. Section trial and sample welds to verify penetration and porosity; surface appearance does not indicate penetration in keyhole welding.

15. Apply the specified NDT — radiography and ultrasonics are both used, with the narrow weld geometry posing its own inspection challenges.

16. Record power, speed, focus, gas, optics condition and part identity.

15. When to Use Laser Welding and When Not To

| Choose laser welding when | Choose something else when |
| --- | --- |
| Low distortion and a narrow HAZ are required | Fit-up cannot be controlled — this is the usual disqualifier |
| High travel speed on repetitive joints | Volumes are too low to amortize capital and fixturing |
| Deep penetration in a single pass without filler | Access to the joint line is obstructed |
| Access from one side only | Thick section requiring high deposition — the process adds little or no filler |
| Many short welds on one part (remote welding) | Field or site work — laser welding is an enclosed shop process |
| Hermetic sealing of small components (conduction mode) | Highly reflective material without an appropriate wavelength source |
| Dissimilar or heat-sensitive assemblies needing minimal heat | Manual work — the process is inherently mechanized |
| Long seams with variable fit-up — as hybrid laser-arc | Simple joints where an arc process is adequate and far cheaper |

16. Defect Catalog

| Defect | Detection | Cause | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Keyhole-induced porosity | RT; sectioning | Keyhole instability and collapse trapping vapour; unstable parameters near the mode boundary; zinc vapour in coated lap joints | Stabilize parameters away from the boundary; use beam oscillation; provide a vent path for zinc; adjust focus |
| Spiking (periodic deep fusion excursions, often with pores at the tips) | Sectioning | Keyhole depth fluctuation | Adjust power and speed; oscillation; move away from the unstable operating region |
| Humping (periodic bead bulges) | Visual | Melt flow instability at high travel speed | Reduce speed; adjust focus; beam oscillation |
| Lack of penetration | Sectioning; not visible from the surface | Power too low, speed too high, focus wrong, beam mode dropped to conduction | Verify focal position first — it is the most common cause; verify actual delivered power; check optics contamination |
| Lack of fusion / missed joint | Sectioning; RT | Beam off the joint line; gap too wide; seam tracking error | Verify tracking; measure fit-up; use oscillation or filler |
| Root drop-out | Visual on the root; sectioning | Excessive penetration; too little material to support the molten root | Reduce power or increase speed; support the root |
| Undercut | Visual | Excessive speed; excessive power; poor pool support | Reduce speed; adjust focus |
| Cracking | PT; sectioning | Rapid cooling in hardenable material; hot cracking in sensitive alloys; high restraint | Adjust energy; add filler to modify chemistry; preheat where the material requires it |
| Progressive loss of penetration with unchanged settings | Sectioning; trend monitoring | Cover glass contamination; optics degradation; source power drift | Inspect and replace cover glass on a controlled interval; verify delivered power; check cross-jet function |
| Zinc blow-out in coated lap joints | Visual; sectioning | Zinc vapour trapped between sheets with no escape path | Engineered gap, dimples or scribed vent; different joint configuration |
| Magnesium loss in 5xxx aluminium | Chemical analysis; property testing | Evaporation of magnesium from the pool | Filler addition; energy control |

17. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Penetration falling gradually at unchanged settings

Symptom: sectioned welds show declining penetration over hours or days; parameters verified unchanged.

Category: beam delivery degradation.

Likely causes: protective cover glass contamination absorbing energy and shifting focus; optics contamination further upstream; source power output drift; cross-jet failure allowing spatter onto the optic.

Steps: inspect and replace the cover glass; verify cross-jet function; measure delivered power at the work with a power meter rather than trusting the setpoint; establish a cover glass replacement interval inside the degradation point. This is the laser equivalent of the wheel, nozzle and impeder wear patterns elsewhere in this reference set.

Card 2 — Porosity in keyhole welds on coated steel lap joints

Symptom: gross porosity and blow-through in zinc-coated lap welds.

Category: coating vapour.

Likely causes: zinc boiling below steel's melting point, with vapour trapped at the sheet interface and no escape path.

Steps: introduce a controlled gap between the sheets, or dimples, or a laser-scribed vent path; reconsider the joint configuration so the vapour can escape; note that this is a design problem, not a parameter problem, and that parameter adjustment alone rarely solves it.

Card 3 — Weld quality varies between apparently identical parts

Symptom: some parts weld correctly, others show lack of fusion or missed joints.

Category: fit-up.

Likely causes: joint gap varying beyond the process tolerance; part-to-part dimensional variation; clamping not repeatable; edge quality varying from the upstream cutting process.

Steps: measure the gap on a sample of parts rather than inspecting one; check clamping repeatability; check the upstream cutting process for edge quality and dimensional drift; consider beam oscillation, filler addition or hybrid welding if fit-up cannot be tightened (Section 10).

Card 4 — Erratic penetration and heavy spatter on copper

Symptom: unstable process, alternating between almost no coupling and violent expulsion.

Category: wavelength and absorptivity.

Likely causes: near-infrared source on copper — the beam is largely reflected until melting, when absorptivity jumps abruptly, causing an unstable transition.

Steps: verify the source wavelength against the material; consider a green or blue source for copper (Section 5); surface treatment or coating to raise initial absorptivity; recognize that this is a fundamental source-material mismatch rather than a tuning problem.

18. Safety Specifics

Laser safety differs from arc welding safety in kind, not merely in degree:

• The beam is invisible at the near-infrared and far-infrared wavelengths used for welding. There is no visual warning, and the eye's blink reflex offers no protection.

• Eye damage occurs at very low power compared with the welding beam's power, and near-infrared wavelengths reach the retina — a focused near-infrared beam can cause permanent retinal damage from a stray reflection.

• Reflections are a primary hazard. A specular reflection from a shiny workpiece, a fixture or a tool carries substantial power in an unpredictable direction. This is why laser welding is performed inside interlocked enclosures rather than behind screens.

• Eyewear must be wavelength-specific, and eyewear for one wavelength gives no protection at another. Eyewear is a backup to enclosure, not a substitute.

• Class 4 laser systems — the class covering welding lasers — require formal control: designated laser safety officer, controlled areas, interlocks, warning signage and training. Classification and control requirements are set by the laser safety standards.

• Fume and plume are generated as in any fusion process, with the added consideration that the plume is dense and close to the work.

• Fire risk from a beam that escapes containment or strikes a combustible.

• High voltages in the source power supply.

20. Worked Example: Porosity in a Keyhole Weld at Production Speed

Situation. A manufacturer laser welds a structural steel component in keyhole mode. Sectioned samples show scattered root porosity. The welds look excellent on the surface and pass visual inspection. Increasing power to "make sure of penetration" makes the porosity worse.

Step 1 — Note that surface appearance carries no information here. In keyhole welding, the surface bead can be flawless over a weld with root porosity or lack of penetration. Visual inspection is not a penetration check, and any process relying on it in keyhole mode has an inspection gap (Section 14).

Step 2 — Identify the porosity as keyhole-related from its location. Root porosity, in a keyhole weld, is the signature of keyhole instability and collapse trapping vapour at the bottom of the cavity (Section 4). That is a different mechanism from the shielding-failure porosity of arc welding, and it responds to different controls.

Step 3 — Understand why more power made it worse. Higher power deepens and destabilizes the keyhole, increasing the fluctuation amplitude that traps vapour. The intuition carried over from arc welding — that more energy gives a better weld — is inverted here, and acting on it is the common first mistake.

Step 4 — Check focal position, which is the most sensitive parameter. Focus determines power density and therefore keyhole geometry and stability. A drifted focus — from thermal effects in the optics, a contaminated cover glass, or a working distance change — destabilizes the keyhole at unchanged nominal power. Measuring actual focal position is more informative than any parameter adjustment.

Step 5 — Check the optics and delivered power together. A contaminated cover glass reduces delivered power and shifts focus simultaneously, which produces exactly this combination of symptoms. Measuring power at the workpiece distinguishes a source problem from a delivery problem.

Step 6 — Consider beam oscillation. Oscillating the beam stirs the melt, widens the keyhole and stabilizes it, and it is one of the most effective available remedies for keyhole porosity. It also improves gap tolerance, which is usually welcome for other reasons.

Step 7 — Check the material and the joint. Surface contamination, moisture, and coating vapour all contribute. On a coated lap joint, zinc is the likely dominant cause and requires a vent path rather than a parameter change (Section 17, Card 2).

Step 8 — Establish penetration monitoring rather than relying on sampling. Interferometric depth measurement and other in-process monitoring methods measure keyhole depth in real time. On a repetitive production weld whose penetration cannot be verified visually and whose defects are internal, that measurement is the control worth engineering — the same argument made for the efflux plume in plasma keyhole welding (Chapter 42) and for process monitoring in resistance welding (Volume 1, Chapter 11).

21. Known Gaps

• No parameter values are given. Laser parameters are strongly equipment-, source- and joint-specific, and are established empirically per application.

• Fit-up tolerances are described relatively, not numerically. They depend on beam diameter, oscillation, material and thickness, and are established by qualification.

• Wavelength absorptivity values are described qualitatively. Published absorptivity data is temperature- and surface-condition-dependent.

• The ISO 13919 part structure should be confirmed against current editions, which are revised on their own cycle.

• Proprietary process variants and monitoring systems are described generically, consistent with this reference set's vendor-neutral discipline.

• Laser safety requirements are summarized in principle only and are governed by the applicable standards and national regulation.

1. Process Overview: ISO 4063 References 51x

Electron beam welding accelerates electrons to a large fraction of the speed of light through a high voltage, focuses them magnetically into a narrow beam, and directs that beam at the joint. The electrons' kinetic energy converts to heat on impact, producing the highest power density of any welding process in industrial use.

The ISO nomenclature distinguishes by the atmosphere at the workpiece [S1]:

| Reference | Process |
| --- | --- |
| 511 | Electron beam welding in vacuum |
| 512 | Electron beam welding in atmosphere |
| 513 | Electron beam welding with addition of shielding gases |

The process's signature is deep, narrow, parallel-sided welds made in a single pass at depth-to-width ratios no other process approaches — which is why it is used where thick sections must be joined with minimal distortion and minimal heat-affected zone.

2. How the Beam Makes a Weld

Two features distinguish the mechanism from every other process in this reference set.

Energy is deposited below the surface. Electrons penetrate a short distance into the material before giving up their energy, so heating begins inside the metal rather than on its surface. This is fundamentally different from a laser, which deposits energy at the surface, and it is part of why coupling is so efficient — there is no reflectivity problem at all, on any material.

The keyhole is deep and stable. As with laser keyhole welding (Chapter 52, Section 4), vaporized metal opens a cavity that the beam travels down, and molten metal flows around it and solidifies behind. But because the power density is higher and the vacuum removes any vapour resistance, the keyhole can be extremely deep and comparatively stable — producing welds of very high depth-to-width ratio.

The consequences are consistent: very narrow fusion zone and heat-affected zone; very low total heat input for the depth achieved; very low distortion; and high welding speeds.

3. Why Vacuum Matters

The electron beam requires vacuum for three separate reasons, and they operate at different levels of the machine:

1. The electron gun requires high vacuum to prevent arcing between the high-voltage electrodes and to allow the cathode to emit electrons without oxidizing or being destroyed. This requirement is absolute — the gun is always at high vacuum, in every configuration.

2. The beam scatters on gas molecules. Electrons colliding with air molecules are deflected, so the beam spreads and loses power density as the pressure at the beam path rises. Beam quality therefore degrades progressively as vacuum is reduced.

3. The weld itself benefits. A weld made in vacuum is made in the cleanest possible atmosphere — no oxygen, no nitrogen, no hydrogen. For reactive metals (Chapter 26) this is a metallurgical advantage no gas shielding can equal, and it is one of the reasons EBW is used in aerospace and nuclear work on titanium and refractory metals.

The commercial consequence: the vacuum chamber and its pump-down time are the process's principal constraints, not the welding. A chamber must be large enough for the part, and every cycle includes pumping down and venting. Pump-down time on a large chamber is measured in minutes and dominates the cycle for anything but the longest welds.

4. The Three Vacuum Configurations

| Configuration | Pressure at the work | Penetration | Character |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| High vacuum (511) | Highest vacuum | Maximum | The classic configuration; deepest welds, cleanest metallurgy, longest pump-down |
| Medium / partial vacuum | Intermediate | Reduced | Shorter pump-down; a practical compromise for production |
| Non-vacuum (512) | Atmospheric, with the gun still under vacuum | Substantially reduced | Beam exits through a differentially pumped orifice; working distance is short; no chamber needed |

Non-vacuum EBW deserves specific mention because it changes the process's economics entirely. The gun stays under vacuum and the beam passes out through a series of small apertures with differential pumping between them. Once in air, the beam scatters rapidly — so the working distance is short and penetration is much reduced compared with in-vacuum welding. What it buys is the removal of the chamber and the pump-down cycle, making continuous or high-rate production possible. It sits, in capability, between in-vacuum EBW and laser welding.

Reduced-pressure or local-vacuum systems apply a vacuum only around the joint rather than to the whole part, and are used for very large components — notably in pressure vessel and pipeline applications — where a chamber for the whole assembly would be impractical.

5. Equipment and Components

| Component | Function | Failure consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Electron gun | Emits and accelerates electrons: cathode (filament), grid/bias electrode, anode | Cathode is a consumable with a finite life; its condition affects beam current and stability |
| High-voltage supply | Accelerates the electrons | Voltage determines penetration depth directly |
| Magnetic focusing lens | Focuses the beam | Focus current sets the spot size and therefore power density and depth |
| Deflection coils | Steer and oscillate the beam electromagnetically | Enables beam oscillation, seam tracking and multi-pass patterns (Section 7) |
| Vacuum chamber | Encloses the work at the required pressure | Chamber size limits part size; pump-down dominates cycle time |
| Vacuum pumping system | Achieves and maintains vacuum | Leak or pump failure stops the process; a slow leak degrades beam quality progressively |
| Work manipulator | Moves the part under the beam inside the chamber | Positional accuracy against a beam a fraction of a millimetre wide |
| Viewing / seam locating system | Optical or electron-optical joint location | The joint must be found precisely; the beam is far narrower than most fit-up tolerances |
| X-ray shielding | The chamber walls themselves | Structural — the enclosure is the radiation shield (Section 15) |

6. Beam Parameters and What Each Controls

| Parameter | Controls | Symptom if wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accelerating voltage | Electron energy; penetration depth | Determines the depth regime available |
| Beam current | Total power at a given voltage | Too low: insufficient penetration. Too high: excessive penetration, root drop-out, spatter |
| Focus current | Spot size and therefore power density | The most sensitive parameter. Focus position through the thickness determines weld shape; sharp focus gives maximum depth |
| Travel speed | Energy per unit length | Too fast: lack of penetration, undercut. Too slow: excessive width, drop-out |
| Working distance | Beam divergence at the work | Affects achieved spot size |
| Beam oscillation pattern and amplitude | Weld width, gap tolerance, melt stirring, porosity control | Without oscillation, gap tolerance is minimal and root porosity is more likely |
| Vacuum level | Beam quality at the work | Degraded vacuum: scattered beam, reduced penetration |
| Pulse or slope control | Start and end conditions | Abrupt termination leaves an unfilled keyhole crater |

Voltage and current together set the power, and their ratio affects the shape: high voltage with lower current gives the deepest, narrowest welds. Focus is where most process development effort goes, because it controls the depth-to-width ratio directly and drifts with thermal conditions.

7. Beam Deflection and Its Uses

Because the beam is steered magnetically, it can be moved with essentially no inertia — at frequencies far beyond any mechanical motion system. This capability is used for several distinct purposes and is one of EBW's real advantages over laser welding:

• Beam oscillation in circular, elliptical or figure patterns, which widens the effective weld, stirs the melt, improves gap tolerance, and reduces root porosity by disturbing the keyhole's collapse behaviour.

• Seam tracking by electronically deflecting the beam onto a joint detected by a sensor, without moving the part.

• Multiple welds without moving the part, by deflecting between locations.

• Split beam operation, time-sharing between two locations rapidly enough that both are welded simultaneously in effect.

• Cosmetic pass — a defocused, deflected pass over a completed weld to smooth the surface, done without repositioning anything.

• Preheat and post-heat by scanning a defocused beam over the joint area before and after welding, controlling the thermal cycle in crack-sensitive materials without any separate heating equipment.

That last capability is genuinely distinctive: the process can apply its own preheat and post-weld heat treatment, in vacuum, with the same beam, in the same cycle.

8. Joint Design and Fit-Up

EBW's fit-up requirements are the tightest of any process in this reference set, for the same reason as laser welding (Chapter 52, Section 10) but more severely, because the beam is narrower and no filler is normally added.

Requirements:

• Square butt joints with essentially zero gap are the standard configuration. The beam melts the two faces together; there is nothing to bridge a gap with.

• Machined joint faces are normal, not exceptional. Sheared or flame-cut edges are generally inadequate.

• Alignment tolerance is a fraction of the beam diameter.

• Self-locating joint designs — spigots, interlocking features, shrink fits — are used deliberately so that the joint's own geometry guarantees alignment.

• Cleanliness is critical, and in vacuum any volatile contaminant outgasses and disturbs both the vacuum and the weld.

• Magnetism must be controlled. Residual magnetism in the workpiece deflects the electron beam, and this is a hazard unique to EBW: a magnetized part steers the beam away from the joint, producing a weld that misses. Parts are demagnetized before welding as a routine step.

9. Materials

EBW's vacuum environment and low heat input make it favourable for materials that are difficult elsewhere:

| Material | EBW behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| Titanium and zirconium | Ideal — vacuum provides complete atmospheric exclusion, better than any trailing shield (Chapter 26, Section 5) |
| Refractory metals (tungsten, molybdenum, tantalum, niobium) | Well suited; few alternatives exist |
| Nickel superalloys | Widely used in aerospace; low heat input limits cracking |
| Steels including hardenable grades | Very well suited; extremely fast cooling means hardenable grades may need beam preheat/post-heat (Section 7) |
| Stainless steels | Excellent |
| Aluminium | Weldable; magnesium and zinc evaporation in vacuum is a consideration in some alloys |
| Dissimilar metals | More feasible than fusion alternatives — very short time at temperature limits intermetallic formation (Chapter 27) |
| Materials with volatile constituents | Problematic — zinc, magnesium and cadmium evaporate violently in vacuum, contaminating the chamber and destabilizing the weld |

Copper's reflectivity problem does not exist here, because electrons are absorbed rather than reflected — which is a genuine advantage over near-infrared laser welding on copper (Chapter 52, Section 5).

10. Setup and Execution Procedure

Before welding

1. Confirm the procedure covers material, thickness, joint design and vacuum configuration.

2. Demagnetize the parts — residual magnetism deflects the beam (Section 8).

3. Clean the parts thoroughly with an approved solvent and dry them; anything volatile will outgas in vacuum.

4. Verify joint fit-up: gap, alignment and face quality, against the procedure's tolerance.

5. Load and fixture the part; verify that fixturing does not obstruct the beam and does not introduce magnetic material near the joint.

6. Close the chamber and pump down to the specified pressure; verify the pressure is achieved and stable rather than assuming.

7. Verify gun condition and cathode life status.

8. Locate the joint precisely with the viewing or joint-locating system, and verify the beam's alignment to it — this step is what prevents a weld that misses the joint entirely.

9. Set voltage, current, focus, travel speed and oscillation per the procedure.

10. Where the material requires it, program beam preheat and post-heat passes (Section 7).

Welding

11. Run the weld under the programmed sequence, including any slope-up and slope-down.

12. Where a run-on and run-off tab arrangement is used, start and finish on the tabs.

13. On circumferential welds, program the overlap at the closure — the point where the weld meets its own start is a defect-prone location requiring a controlled overlap and slope-down.

14. Monitor beam current, focus and vacuum through the cycle.

After welding

15. Vent the chamber and remove the part.

16. Inspect: penetration cannot be confirmed visually on a deep weld — sectioning of trial pieces and radiography or ultrasonics of production welds are the methods.

17. Record voltage, current, focus, speed, oscillation, vacuum level and part identity.

11. When to Use EBW and When Not To

| Choose EBW when | Choose something else when |
| --- | --- |
| Deep single-pass penetration with minimal distortion is required | The part is too large for any available chamber |
| The material requires an absolutely clean atmosphere — titanium, zirconium, refractory metals | Production rate requirements cannot absorb pump-down time |
| The heat-affected zone must be minimal on a finished or heat-treated component | Fit-up cannot be machined to near-zero gap |
| Aerospace, nuclear, or vacuum-technology components | The material contains volatile constituents that evaporate in vacuum |
| Welding after final machining, where distortion is unacceptable | Filler metal is needed to fill a gap or modify chemistry |
| Dissimilar combinations where minimal reaction time is wanted | Site or field work — EBW is a fixed-installation process |
| Copper or other highly reflective metals unsuitable for near-infrared lasers | Cost and capital are the deciding factors and a laser will do |

12. EBW Against Laser Welding

| Factor | Electron beam | Laser beam |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Power density | Highest available | Very high |
| Penetration depth | Greatest | Substantial but less |
| Vacuum required | Yes (except non-vacuum configurations) | No |
| Part size limit | Chamber size | None |
| Cycle time overhead | Pump-down | None |
| Beam delivery | Magnetic, inside the chamber only | Fibre — flexible, robot-mounted, long distances |
| Reflectivity problem | None — electrons are absorbed by all metals | Significant on copper and aluminium at near-infrared |
| Beam steering speed | Extremely fast — electromagnetic, no inertia | Fast with scanners; slower with mechanical motion |
| Magnetism sensitivity | Yes — parts must be demagnetized | None |
| X-ray hazard | Yes — inherent | None |
| Atmosphere quality at the weld | Best available — vacuum | Shielding gas only |
| Filler addition | Rarely | Available, and standard in hybrid |
| Fit-up tolerance | Tightest | Very tight, improved by oscillation and hybrid |
| Site/field capability | None | Limited |

The summary judgement: EBW wins on depth, cleanliness and beam agility; laser wins on flexibility, part size, cycle time and installation cost. Laser welding has taken over much of the work EBW once held, and EBW retains the applications where its specific advantages are decisive — depth, vacuum metallurgy, and reactive or refractory materials.

13. Defect Catalog

| Defect | Detection | Cause | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Root porosity | RT; sectioning | Keyhole instability and collapse at the root of a deep weld | Beam oscillation; adjust focus; adjust speed; consider a partial-penetration design with a machined-off root |
| Spiking (periodic root excursions with pores) | Sectioning | Keyhole depth fluctuation in deep welds | Oscillation; parameter adjustment away from the unstable region |
| Missed joint / beam deflection | Sectioning; RT | Residual magnetism deflecting the beam; joint location error; part movement | Demagnetize before welding — this is the EBW-specific cause; verify joint location and beam alignment; check fixturing for magnetic material |
| Lack of penetration | Sectioning | Focus wrong; beam current low; vacuum degraded scattering the beam; cathode aged | Verify focus; verify vacuum level; check cathode condition and life |
| Root drop-out | Visual on the root | Excessive power for the thickness; insufficient root support | Reduce power or increase speed; support the root |
| Undercut / underfill | Visual; sectioning | Excessive speed; excessive power; loss of material from the joint with no filler | Adjust parameters; add filler where the design permits |
| Cracking | PT; sectioning | Very rapid cooling in hardenable or crack-sensitive material; high restraint | Beam preheat and post-heat passes (Section 7); reduce restraint |
| Chamber contamination and unstable weld | Vacuum instability; visual | Volatile constituents (zinc, magnesium, cadmium) evaporating in vacuum | Avoid materials with volatile constituents; clean parts thoroughly; check for outgassing sources |
| Closure defect on a circumferential weld | RT; sectioning | Overlap at the weld closure not properly programmed | Program controlled overlap and slope-down at the closure |
| Progressive loss of penetration | Sectioning; trend | Cathode ageing; vacuum degradation from a slow leak; focus drift | Track cathode life and replace on interval; leak-check the chamber; verify focus |

14. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Weld found off the joint line

Symptom: sectioning shows the weld displaced from the joint; one side unfused.

Category: beam deflection — the EBW-specific failure.

Likely causes: residual magnetism in the workpiece or fixturing deflecting the beam; joint location error; part movement in the fixture; stray magnetic fields near the beam path.

Steps: demagnetize the part and check the fixturing for magnetic material; verify the joint location procedure and the beam-to-joint alignment; check whether any magnetic handling equipment contacted the part; note that this cause has no equivalent in any other process and is frequently overlooked by people new to EBW.

Card 2 — Root porosity in deep welds

Symptom: pores concentrated at the root of full-penetration welds.

Category: keyhole instability.

Likely causes: keyhole collapse at the root; focus position; travel speed; material outgassing.

Steps: apply or increase beam oscillation, which is the most effective control; adjust focus position through the thickness; adjust speed; consider whether a partial-penetration weld with the root machined off is acceptable for the design; verify part cleanliness and outgassing.

Card 3 — Penetration declining over weeks at unchanged settings

Symptom: gradual reduction in weld depth; parameters verified.

Category: gun and vacuum condition.

Likely causes: cathode ageing — emission falls as the filament erodes; vacuum degradation from a developing leak scattering the beam; focus lens drift; high-voltage supply drift.

Steps: check cathode hours against expected life and replace on a controlled interval; leak-check the chamber and verify the pressure actually achieved rather than the setpoint; verify beam current delivered against the setting. This is the same wear-interval discipline that recurs across this reference set.

Card 4 — Cracking in a hardenable steel weld

Symptom: cracks in weld or HAZ after welding.

Category: thermal cycle.

Likely causes: extremely rapid cooling producing hard, crack-susceptible structure; high restraint in a rigidly fixtured part.

Steps: use beam preheat and post-heat passes — defocused scanning before and after the weld — which EBW can do with the same beam in the same cycle (Section 7); review restraint; consider a different material condition or a post-weld heat treatment outside the chamber.

15. Safety Specifics: X-Rays and Vacuum

Two hazards are specific to this process and both are structural rather than procedural:

X-ray generation. When high-energy electrons strike a target, a fraction of their energy is emitted as X-rays. This is not a side effect to be minimized — it is unavoidable physics, and it is why the electron beam welding machine is built as a radiation enclosure. The chamber walls, viewing windows and door seals are the shielding. Consequences:

• The machine must not be operated with shielding compromised, and interlocks preventing this are safety-critical.

• Radiation surveys are performed on installation and after any work affecting the enclosure.

• Higher accelerating voltages produce more penetrating X-rays, so shielding requirements scale with machine voltage.

• Non-vacuum EBW requires particular attention, since the beam exits the gun assembly into the working area.

Vacuum system hazards. Implosion risk on a chamber viewport; pump oil and exhaust management; and the asphyxiation hazard when a chamber is vented with an inert gas rather than air — a vented chamber can be an oxygen-deficient space (Chapter 37, Section 9).

Other hazards: very high voltages in the gun supply; hot components after welding; and fume and vapour deposits inside the chamber requiring controlled cleaning.

16. Standards and Qualification

• Process references: ISO 4063 references 511, 512, 513 [S1].

• Weld quality levels: the ISO 13919 series for electron and laser beam welded joints. As with laser welding, ISO 5817 excludes beam welding from its scope (Chapter 36, Section 11).

• Procedure specification and qualification: ISO 15609-3 for electron beam welding procedure specification, and ISO 15614-11 for procedure qualification of electron and laser beam welding.

• Operator qualification: ISO 14732 for this mechanized process.

• Radiation safety: governed by national radiation protection regulation, with the machine's shielding integrity as the primary control.

• Sector requirements: aerospace and nuclear applications carry additional qualification, inspection and documentation requirements that take precedence.

17. Worked Example: Root Porosity in a Deep Single-Pass Weld

Situation. A manufacturer welds a thick titanium component in high vacuum with full penetration in a single pass. Radiography shows scattered porosity concentrated near the root. The welds are otherwise excellent and the part is high-value with substantial machining already invested.

Step 1 — Recognize the defect as characteristic rather than anomalous. Root porosity in a deep keyhole weld is the process's signature defect, produced by keyhole instability at the root where the cavity is deepest and least stable (Section 2). It is not evidence of a mistake.

Step 2 — Rule out contamination before adjusting the beam. In vacuum, any volatile contaminant on or in the material outgasses into the keyhole. Cleaning procedure, solvent residue, machining fluid trapped in a joint feature, and material cleanliness are all candidates, and they are cheaper to check than a parameter development exercise.

Step 3 — Check the vacuum level actually achieved. A partially degraded vacuum scatters the beam, reducing power density and destabilizing the keyhole. Verifying the achieved pressure — not the setpoint — distinguishes a beam problem from a keyhole dynamics problem.

Step 4 — Apply beam oscillation, which is the primary engineered remedy. Oscillating the beam stirs the melt and disturbs the keyhole's collapse behaviour, and it is the most effective single control for root porosity in both EBW and laser welding. EBW's electromagnetic deflection makes this essentially free to implement — no additional hardware, just programming (Section 7).

Step 5 — Reconsider focus position through the thickness. Focus determines where the keyhole is most stable. Moving the focal plane relative to the joint depth changes the root behaviour, and it is a parameter that can be explored systematically on trial pieces.

Step 6 — Consider the design alternative. If root porosity cannot be eliminated to the required level, a partial-penetration weld with the root region machined away afterwards removes the defective zone entirely. On a high-value machined component this is often the pragmatic engineering answer, and it is worth raising because the design may permit it.

Step 7 — Consider a cosmetic or re-melt pass. A second, defocused pass over the root — where accessible — can re-melt and refine that region, again using deflection rather than additional equipment.

Step 8 — Fix the qualification, not just the part. Whatever combination resolves it — oscillation pattern, focus, cleanliness, design change — belongs in the qualified procedure with the evidence behind it, so the next production run starts from the solution rather than repeating the investigation. On a process with this much setup cost per trial, that record is worth more than in most processes.

18. Known Gaps

• No parameter values are given. Voltage, current, focus and speed are strongly machine- and joint-specific.

• Penetration capability is described qualitatively. Achievable depth depends on machine voltage and power, material and configuration, and any single figure would mislead.

• Vacuum levels are described by regime rather than by pressure. Specific values are machine- and application-dependent.

• X-ray shielding requirements are stated in principle only and are governed by national radiation protection regulation and by the machine's certification.

• Non-vacuum EBW is described in outline; its capability and configuration vary considerably between implementations.

• The ISO 13919 and ISO 15609/15614 part structures should be confirmed against current editions.
