1. Why Beam Welds Fail Differently

Beam welds — laser (Chapter 52) and electron beam (Chapter 53) — share a defect population that arc welding does not produce, and lack several that arc welding does.

What they do not suffer from: slag inclusions (no flux), tungsten inclusions (no electrode), electrode-related defects, and the shielding failures that dominate arc welding porosity. Spatter is present but is a minor issue compared with consumable-electrode arc processes.

What they do suffer from, and arc welding does not:

• Keyhole dynamics defects — porosity, spiking, humping — arising from the instability of a vapour cavity held open by pressure against surface tension.

• The missed joint — a beam narrower than the joint tolerance can miss the joint entirely, producing a weld that is visually acceptable and structurally absent.

• Beam delivery degradation — contaminated optics on a laser, an aged cathode or degraded vacuum on an electron beam — producing progressive loss of penetration at unchanged settings.

• Penetration that cannot be verified visually. A deep keyhole weld's surface appearance is uncorrelated with its root condition, so the defects that matter most are the ones the operator cannot see.

That last point governs the whole chapter: in beam welding, the primary quality question is one the finished surface does not answer.

2. The Diagnostic Sequence for a Beam Welding Problem

1. Is the weld actually on the joint? Sectioning or radiography answers this. A missed joint invalidates every other line of investigation.

2. Is the beam delivering the power it is set to? Measure delivered power (laser) or verify beam current and vacuum (EBW). Optics contamination and cathode ageing are common and silent.

3. Is the focus where the procedure says it is? Focus is the most sensitive parameter in both processes and drifts thermally.

4. Is the fit-up within tolerance on the actual parts? Measure on a sample; do not infer from one part.

5. Is the material and its surface condition as expected? Coatings, contamination and volatile constituents all cause characteristic defects.

6. Which mode is the process actually in? Conduction or keyhole, and how close to the boundary.

7. Only then: are the parameters or the oscillation pattern wrong?

3. Keyhole Instability: The Mechanism Behind Most Beam Defects

The keyhole is a vapour cavity held open by vaporization pressure against surface tension and the hydrostatic head of surrounding molten metal. That balance is dynamic — the cavity fluctuates in depth and shape continuously, at high frequency.

Four defect types trace directly to those fluctuations:

| Fluctuation behaviour | Resulting defect |
| --- | --- |
| Momentary collapse trapping vapour at the root | Root porosity |
| Periodic deep excursions of the cavity tip | Spiking, often with pores at the spike tips |
| Melt flow instability around a fast-moving keyhole | Humping |
| Cavity breaking through with insufficient surface tension to hold the root | Root drop-out |

The controls that stabilize the keyhole are consistent across both processes:

• Beam oscillation, which stirs the melt and widens and stabilizes the cavity. The single most effective control, and essentially free on an electron beam machine where deflection is electromagnetic.

• Focus position through the thickness.

• Operating away from the conduction-keyhole boundary, where the mode itself becomes unstable.

• Travel speed, which sets how much time the melt has to flow around the cavity.

• Reduced pressure or vacuum on laser welding in some implementations, which stabilizes the cavity by removing atmospheric resistance.

4. Porosity in Beam Welds

Three distinct porosity mechanisms operate, and they have different remedies:

Keyhole-collapse porosity. Vapour trapped by a momentarily collapsing cavity, concentrated at or near the root. The remedy is keyhole stabilization (Section 3), not shielding.

Metallurgical / dissolved-gas porosity. Gas dissolved in the melt coming out of solution during solidification — hydrogen in aluminium being the standard case (Chapter 25, Section 5). The remedy is material and surface cleanliness, not beam parameters.

Vaporized-constituent porosity. A constituent of the material boiling at a temperature below the melting point of the bulk — zinc in coated steel being the dominant industrial case, and magnesium in some aluminium alloys. In a lap joint on zinc-coated steel the vapour is trapped between the sheets and blows through the pool violently.

The zinc case deserves separate treatment because it is so common and because the remedy is a design change rather than a parameter change:

• An engineered gap between the sheets, giving the vapour an escape path — commonly produced by dimples, embossed features, or a shim.

• A laser-scribed or machined vent channel.

• Joint reconfiguration so the vapour escapes at an edge.

• Parameter adjustment alone rarely solves it.

Distinguishing the three: location (root-concentrated suggests keyhole collapse), material (aluminium suggests hydrogen), and joint configuration (coated lap joint suggests zinc). Sectioning and examining pore distribution is what separates them.

5. Spiking

What it is: periodic, deep excursions of the fusion boundary below the general penetration depth, producing a saw-tooth root profile in a longitudinal section, frequently with a pore at the tip of each spike.

Why it happens: the keyhole tip oscillates in depth at a characteristic frequency. The deep excursions leave a locally deeper fusion zone, and when the cavity collapses at the bottom of an excursion it traps vapour there.

Why it matters: the spike tips are stress concentrations, the pores are discontinuities, and the resulting root profile is irregular in a way that fatigue-loaded joints do not tolerate.

Controls: beam oscillation; focus position adjustment; travel speed change to move away from the resonant condition; and, where the design allows, partial penetration with the root machined off.

6. Humping

What it is: a periodic bead profile — alternating bulges and valleys along the weld, sometimes with undercut in the valleys — occurring at high travel speed.

Why it happens: at high speed, the molten metal displaced by the keyhole is driven backward in a narrow channel and cannot spread laterally fast enough. Surface tension breaks the elongated molten channel into periodic accumulations, which freeze as humps.

When it appears: above a threshold travel speed for a given power and joint. It is a speed-limiting phenomenon — it sets the practical maximum welding speed for many beam applications, and it is why increasing speed to raise productivity eventually stops working.

Controls: reduce travel speed below the threshold; increase the effective interaction width by beam oscillation or defocusing; adjust power; change joint geometry to support the melt; and in hybrid laser-arc welding, the arc's added material and wider energy distribution raise the humping threshold substantially.

7. Root Drop-Out and Underfill

Root drop-out: molten metal falling out of the root of a full-penetration weld because surface tension cannot support it. Causes: excessive power for the thickness, travel too slow, and no root support.

Underfill: the weld surface below the parent surface, because material was lost — expelled as spatter or vapour — and no filler was added to replace it. This is inherent to autogenous beam welding: the process removes material and adds none.

Controls: reduce energy input; support the root with a backing bar or a joint feature; add filler wire; or, for structural joints, design the joint with excess material at the surface so the finished profile is acceptable after loss.

8. The Missed Joint and Lack of Fusion

The most dangerous beam welding defect, because the weld can look entirely acceptable.

How it happens:

• The beam is offset from the joint line — by a teaching error, seam tracking failure, part positioning variation, or fixture wear.

• On EBW specifically: residual magnetism deflects the beam (Chapter 53, Section 8), which is a cause with no equivalent anywhere else in this reference set.

• The gap exceeds the beam's ability to bridge it, so the beam passes through without melting both faces adequately (Chapter 52, Section 10).

• Part-to-part fit-up variation takes some parts outside the tolerance while others stay inside — producing intermittent failures on nominally identical parts.

Why it is dangerous: a beam offset by its own diameter melts one face and not the other, producing a bead on the surface with no joint underneath. Visual inspection passes it. Only sectioning, radiography or ultrasonics finds it.

Controls: seam tracking with verified accuracy; demagnetization for EBW; fit-up measurement on samples rather than assumption; fixture repeatability verification; and an inspection method actually capable of finding it.

9. Loss of Penetration With Unchanged Settings

A pattern common to both beam processes, and one whose cause is always in the delivery chain rather than in the settings:

| Process | Cause | Check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Laser | Protective cover glass contamination — absorbs power and shifts focus | Inspect and replace on a controlled interval |
| Laser | Upstream optics contamination or damage | Inspect; measure delivered power at the work |
| Laser | Source power output drift | Measure with a power meter, not the setpoint |
| Laser | Cross-jet failure allowing spatter onto optics | Verify cross-jet function |
| EBW | Cathode ageing reducing emission | Track cathode hours; replace on interval |
| EBW | Vacuum degradation scattering the beam | Verify achieved pressure; leak-check |
| EBW | Focus lens or high-voltage supply drift | Verify beam current and focus |
| Both | Working distance change from fixture wear or part variation | Measure |

The discipline that prevents it is the same as for tip dressing in resistance welding, nozzle replacement in plasma welding and wheel dressing in seam welding: replace the degrading component on an interval established inside the degradation point, rather than compensating with power and discovering the limit when compensation runs out.

10. Cracking in Beam Welds

Beam welding's very rapid cooling rate is the driver:

Solidification cracking — the high depth-to-width ratio of a keyhole weld is precisely the geometry that concentrates segregated liquid into a central plane (Chapter 22, Section 6). Beam welds are therefore inherently more susceptible than a wide shallow arc weld in the same material. Controls: filler addition to modify chemistry; oscillation to change the solidification pattern; speed reduction; and material selection for low impurity content.

Hardening and cold cracking — the cooling rate in a beam weld is far higher than in an arc weld, so hardenable steels form more martensite. Controls: beam preheat and post-heat passes on EBW (Chapter 53, Section 7); external preheat; filler addition to modify the deposit; material condition selection.

Hot cracking in aluminium and nickel alloys — as elsewhere, driven by composition and restraint, with the beam weld's rapid solidification and high restraint both unfavourable.

11. Material-Specific Defects

| Material | Beam-specific issue |
| --- | --- |
| Zinc-coated steel | Vapour blow-out in lap joints — a design problem (Section 4) |
| Aluminium | Hydrogen porosity; magnesium loss by evaporation in 5xxx alloys; high reflectivity at near-infrared |
| Copper | Very high near-infrared reflectivity causing unstable coupling — remedied by green or blue sources (Chapter 52, Section 5); no problem at all for EBW |
| Titanium | Requires absolute atmospheric exclusion — trivially satisfied by EBW's vacuum, demanding on laser |
| Materials with volatile constituents | Evaporate violently in EBW's vacuum, contaminating the chamber |
| Hardenable steels | Very rapid cooling; hardening and cracking risk |
| Dissimilar combinations | Short interaction time limits intermetallics, but composition control across a narrow fusion zone is difficult |

12. The Inspection Problem

Beam welds present a genuine inspection difficulty that arc welds do not, and it is worth stating explicitly because inspection plans carried over from arc welding fail here:

The weld is very narrow. A fusion zone a fraction of a millimetre wide is difficult to interrogate — ultrasonic beams must be positioned precisely, and a small misalignment misses the weld entirely. The same narrowness that makes the process attractive makes it hard to inspect.

Planar defects lie along the joint plane. The missed joint and lack of fusion are exactly the defects radiography detects worst (Chapter 35, Section 1), and they are among the most likely in this process.

Surface appearance is uninformative about penetration and root condition.

The defects are internal and often at the root, which is frequently the least accessible part of the joint.

The practical consequences: ultrasonic and phased array methods, set up specifically for the narrow weld geometry, are generally required rather than radiography alone; sectioning of trial and sample welds carries more weight than in arc welding; and in-process monitoring becomes a primary quality tool rather than a refinement (Section 13).

13. In-Process Monitoring

Because the critical properties cannot be verified visually and are expensive to verify destructively, beam welding relies on in-process monitoring more than any other family in this reference set:

| Method | What it measures | What it detects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Photodiode monitoring | Optical emission from the process at selected wavelengths | Keyhole instability, mode change, gross parameter deviation |
| Camera / coaxial vision | Keyhole and pool appearance | Joint tracking, keyhole presence, spatter |
| Interferometric depth measurement | Keyhole depth directly, in real time | Penetration — the property that cannot otherwise be verified without sectioning |
| Plasma / plume sensing | Plume intensity | Coupling changes, shielding problems |
| Back-reflection monitoring | Reflected beam power | Coupling loss, mode change, reflective material behaviour |
| Seam tracking sensors | Joint position ahead of the beam | Missed joint prevention |
| Power measurement at the work | Delivered power | Optics degradation, source drift |

Interferometric depth measurement deserves emphasis: it measures the keyhole depth directly during welding, which is the closest any process in this reference set comes to measuring the property that matters at the moment it is created. On a repetitive production weld whose penetration is otherwise unverifiable, it converts a destructive sampling regime into continuous verification.

The general principle recurs throughout this reference set — Volume 1's process monitoring for resistance welding, the efflux plume in plasma keyhole welding (Chapter 42), the upset curve in flash welding (Chapter 49) — and it applies most strongly here.

14. Master Defect Table

| Defect | Detection | Principal causes | Corrective actions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Root porosity | RT; sectioning | Keyhole collapse; material outgassing; contamination | Beam oscillation; focus adjustment; speed change; cleanliness; partial penetration with root machined |
| Zinc blow-out (coated lap joints) | Visual; sectioning | Zinc vapour trapped between sheets | Engineered gap, dimples or vent path — a design change |
| Hydrogen porosity (aluminium) | RT; sectioning | Moisture and hydrocarbons on the surface; oxide film | Degrease then mechanically clean immediately before welding (Chapter 25) |
| Spiking | Longitudinal sectioning | Keyhole depth oscillation | Oscillation; focus; speed |
| Humping | Visual | Melt flow instability above a speed threshold | Reduce speed; oscillation; defocus; hybrid laser-arc |
| Root drop-out | Visual on root | Excess energy; no root support | Reduce power or increase speed; support the root |
| Underfill | Visual; dimensional | Material loss with no filler | Add filler; design for the loss |
| Missed joint | Sectioning; UT — not visual, not reliably RT | Beam offset; magnetism (EBW); excessive gap; tracking failure | Seam tracking; demagnetize; measure fit-up; verify fixture repeatability |
| Lack of fusion at one face | Sectioning; UT | Beam offset; asymmetric joint presentation | As above |
| Lack of penetration | Sectioning | Focus wrong; delivered power low; vacuum degraded; mode dropped to conduction | Verify focus and delivered power first |
| Progressive penetration loss | Trend across a run | Optics contamination (laser); cathode ageing or vacuum loss (EBW) | Controlled replacement intervals; measure delivered power |
| Solidification cracking | PT; sectioning | High depth-to-width ratio concentrating segregation; restraint | Filler addition; oscillation; speed reduction; material selection |
| Cold cracking | MT/PT after delay | Rapid cooling in hardenable material | Beam preheat/post-heat (EBW); external preheat; filler |
| Chamber contamination (EBW) | Vacuum instability | Volatile constituents evaporating | Material selection; thorough cleaning |
| Closure defect (circumferential welds) | RT; sectioning | Overlap at the weld start not programmed | Controlled overlap and slope-down |

15. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Weld looks perfect, sectioning shows no joint

Symptom: an acceptable-looking bead with the joint unfused beneath it.

Category: missed joint.

Likely causes: beam offset from the joint line; on EBW, residual magnetism deflecting the beam; gap exceeding bridging capability; part positioning or fixture variation; seam tracking not functioning or not enabled.

Steps: verify the beam-to-joint alignment directly; demagnetize on EBW; measure gap and part position on a sample of parts; verify tracking function; and review the inspection plan, because a process capable of this defect requires an inspection method capable of finding it — visual inspection is not one (Section 12).

Card 2 — Porosity that will not respond to parameter changes

Symptom: porosity persists through a systematic parameter exploration.

Category: material or configuration, not beam.

Likely causes: zinc vapour in a coated lap joint with no escape path; hydrogen in aluminium from surface contamination; outgassing from a contaminated or porous material; volatile alloying constituent.

Steps: identify the porosity mechanism by location and material (Section 4); if zinc, implement a vent path — this is a design change and no parameter will substitute; if hydrogen, address cleaning and material condition; recognize that continued parameter adjustment on a material-caused defect is wasted effort.

Card 3 — Periodic humps appeared after a productivity improvement

Symptom: regular bead bulges and valleys following an increase in travel speed.

Category: humping threshold exceeded.

Likely causes: travel speed above the humping threshold for the power, joint and material.

Steps: confirm the correlation with speed by welding trial pieces at a range of speeds; reduce speed below the threshold; alternatively raise the threshold with beam oscillation, defocusing, or hybrid laser-arc welding, which is the standard engineered answer where speed must be retained (Section 6).

Card 4 — Penetration declining week by week

Symptom: gradual reduction in weld depth across a production period.

Category: beam delivery degradation.

Likely causes: laser — cover glass and optics contamination, source drift, cross-jet failure; EBW — cathode ageing, vacuum degradation, focus drift.

Steps: measure delivered power at the workpiece rather than reading the setpoint; inspect and replace consumable optics or cathode; verify achieved vacuum; establish replacement intervals inside the degradation point rather than compensating with power (Section 9).

16. Acceptance Criteria for Beam Welds

A point that causes real disputes: ISO 5817 explicitly excludes beam welding from its scope (Chapter 36, Section 11). Applying it to a laser or electron beam weld is a scope error, and the limits it contains were not derived for this weld geometry.

The applicable family is ISO 13919, covering quality levels for imperfections in electron and laser beam welded joints. Its structure recognizes that beam welds have a different geometry and a different defect population — narrow fusion zones, root defects, and the characteristic keyhole imperfections of this chapter.

Where a product or sector standard governs — aerospace, automotive, pressure — its criteria take precedence over both.

17. Worked Example: Humping That Appeared When the Line Speed Increased

Situation. A manufacturer laser welds a longitudinal seam. To increase output, line speed is raised by a third with laser power increased proportionally to maintain energy per unit length. The welds develop a regular, periodic bulged appearance with undercut between the bulges. Penetration measured at the bulges is acceptable; at the valleys it is marginal.

Step 1 — Identify the phenomenon. Periodic bulges and valleys at high travel speed, with undercut in the valleys, is humping (Section 6). It is a melt-flow instability, not a power problem, and the fact that energy per unit length was held constant is exactly what makes this diagnosis likely — the change was speed, not energy.

Step 2 — Understand why maintaining energy per unit length did not prevent it. Humping depends on the speed at which molten metal is driven backward around the keyhole and on whether it can spread laterally before freezing. It is not governed by energy per unit length. This is the key insight, and it explains why the intuitively correct compensation failed.

Step 3 — Confirm by a speed series. Weld trial pieces at a range of speeds at fixed energy per unit length. If humping appears above a threshold speed and disappears below it, the diagnosis is confirmed and the threshold is now known — which is more useful than the diagnosis alone.

Step 4 — Evaluate the options against the objective. The objective was output. Simply reverting the speed forfeits it. The options that retain speed are: beam oscillation, which widens the effective interaction zone and raises the humping threshold; defocusing, which does the same at the cost of power density and penetration; and hybrid laser-arc welding, which raises the threshold substantially because the arc adds material and distributes energy more widely (Chapter 52, Section 11).

Step 5 — Check the joint geometry. A joint that supports the melt — a lap configuration, or a backing — tolerates higher speed than an unsupported butt joint. If the design permits a change, this is often the cheapest remedy.

Step 6 — Re-examine the marginal penetration at the valleys. Even if the humped appearance were cosmetically acceptable, marginal penetration at the valleys is not. The weld's minimum properties are set by its worst section, not its average, and this must be assessed against the design requirement rather than against the mean.

Step 7 — Requalify at whatever settings are adopted. The speed and power change already took the process outside the qualified range. Whatever combination resolves the humping becomes the new procedure, with its own qualification evidence (Chapter 31, Section 11).

Step 8 — Record the humping threshold as process knowledge. The threshold speed for this joint, material and power is a genuinely useful number that the organization now owns. Recording it prevents the next productivity initiative from rediscovering it the same way.

18. Known Gaps

• No parameter values or thresholds are given. Humping thresholds, oscillation amplitudes and focus positions are joint-, material- and equipment-specific.

• The ISO 13919 part structure and current editions should be confirmed directly, as they are revised on their own cycle.

• Monitoring system capabilities are described generically and vary substantially between implementations; this reference set names no products.

• Ultrasonic inspection techniques for narrow beam welds are specialist and require dedicated procedure development; they are identified here as necessary rather than described.

• Reduced-pressure laser welding is mentioned as a keyhole stabilization approach but not developed.

1. The Three Families as a Single Decision

Arc welding (Volume 3), resistance welding (Volume 1 and Chapters 48–51) and beam welding (Chapters 52–54) are usually treated as separate specialisms with separate equipment, separate people and separate literature. For a process selection decision they are one question, because they compete for the same joints.

The common structure: each family delivers energy to a joint at a characteristic power density, with characteristic requirements for access, fit-up and consumables, at a characteristic capital and operating cost. Selecting between them is a matter of matching those characteristics to what the joint and the business actually require — and the selection errors in Section 13 nearly all come from optimizing one characteristic while ignoring another.

2. The Power Density Spectrum and What It Predicts

Ordering the families by power density predicts most of their behaviour (Chapter 22, Section 2):

| Family | Power density | HAZ width | Distortion | Fit-up tolerance | Penetration per pass |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Oxy-fuel (Ch. 63) | Lowest | Widest | Highest | Most forgiving | Low |
| Arc | Moderate | Moderate | Moderate | Forgiving | Moderate |
| Resistance | High, but localized and brief | Narrow | Low | Moderate — but needs both-side access | Sheet thickness |
| Laser | Very high | Narrow | Low | Tight | High |
| Electron beam | Highest | Narrowest | Lowest | Tightest | Greatest |

The single relationship that this table encodes, and that governs the whole selection: precision and forgiveness are opposite ends of one axis. Every step up in power density buys a narrower HAZ, less distortion and deeper penetration, and costs fit-up tolerance, capital and flexibility. There is no process that is both precise and forgiving, and selection is fundamentally about deciding which of those the application actually needs.

3. Question 1 — What Does the Joint Have to Be?

| The joint is… | Family |
| --- | --- |
| Sheet overlap, discrete attachment sufficient | Resistance spot — or laser stitch welds where one-side access is needed |
| Sheet overlap, leak-tight | Resistance seam — or laser seam |
| A groove in plate requiring filler | Arc — beam processes add little or no filler |
| A deep butt joint in thick section, minimal distortion | Beam — single pass, or arc in many passes |
| Full cross-section of bar or rail, end to end | Resistance flash/upset (Ch. 49) |
| Continuous tube seam at mill speed | High-frequency (Ch. 50) — or laser for precision tube |
| A fastener onto sheet | Resistance projection, or stud welding (Ch. 45) |
| Many short welds on one assembly | Remote laser (Ch. 52, Section 12) or resistance spot |
| Accessible from one side only | Laser or beam — resistance generally needs both sides |
| Requires filler to fill a gap or adjust chemistry | Arc, or hybrid laser-arc |

4. Question 2 — What Is the Fit-Up Capability?

This question eliminates more beam welding projects than any other, and it should be asked early rather than late.

| Achievable fit-up | Viable families |
| --- | --- |
| Gaps and misalignment typical of cut and formed parts | Arc — the process fills what it finds |
| Controlled, but not machined | Arc; laser with oscillation or filler; hybrid laser-arc; resistance |
| Machined or precision-formed, near-zero gap | All families, including EBW |
| Variable between parts | Arc, or hybrid — beam processes fail intermittently on variable fit-up |

Three practical points:

Fit-up is a manufacturing capability, not a drawing statement. The relevant question is what the upstream cutting, forming and fixturing actually deliver on a sample of parts, not what the drawing specifies.

Beam processes convert a fit-up problem into a fixturing and preparation cost. That cost is real and is frequently larger than the welding equipment cost. Laser welding installations that fail commercially usually fail here.

Hybrid laser-arc exists precisely to relax this constraint (Chapter 52, Section 11), and where the objection to laser welding is fit-up rather than anything else, hybrid is the answer to evaluate before abandoning the beam route.

5. Question 3 — What Is the Production Volume?

| Volume | Implication |
| --- | --- |
| One-off, repair, site work | Arc only. Resistance and beam processes are fixed installations with tooling per joint |
| Low volume, varied joints | Arc. Setup and tooling cost dominate elsewhere |
| Moderate volume, repetitive | Arc, mechanized; resistance if the geometry suits; beam if fit-up and cycle time justify it |
| High volume, repetitive | Resistance and beam are in their element; robotic arc also strong |
| Continuous product | High-frequency for tube; laser for continuous seam |

The underlying economics: beam and resistance processes have high fixed cost and low variable cost; arc processes have low fixed cost and high variable cost (labour). The crossover volume is where the fixed cost amortizes, and it moves with labour rates, cycle time and rework rates — which is why the same joint can justify different answers in different plants.

6. Question 4 — What Does Distortion Cost?

Distortion is frequently the hidden driver of a process decision, because its cost appears in downstream operations rather than in welding.

Where distortion cost is high:

• Components machined before welding, where distortion destroys accumulated value.

• Assemblies with tight dimensional tolerances requiring post-weld straightening — a labour cost that is often larger than the welding cost.

• Thin structures prone to buckling.

• Parts where distortion causes fit-up problems at the next assembly stage.

Where beam processes win on this basis alone: if post-weld straightening or machining is a significant labour cost, the low heat input of a beam process can justify itself entirely on distortion reduction, independent of welding speed. This is a real and frequently overlooked justification, and it is one that a comparison based on welding cost per metre will never reveal.

7. Question 5 — What Does the Material Demand?

| Material situation | Family implication |
| --- | --- |
| Reactive metals — titanium, zirconium | EBW (vacuum) is ideal; GTAW with trailing shield and purge is the arc answer; laser is demanding |
| Refractory metals | EBW — few alternatives |
| Copper and highly reflective metals | EBW has no reflectivity problem; laser needs green or blue sources; arc works |
| Heat-treated or thermomechanically processed steels with heat input ceilings | Beam or resistance — low heat input protects properties (Ch. 23, Section 11) |
| Aluminium sheet, high volume | Resistance (narrow window), laser, or FSW (Ch. 57); arc for lower volume |
| Zinc-coated steel lap joints | Resistance spot handles it routinely; laser requires an engineered vent path (Ch. 54, Section 4) |
| Dissimilar metals forming intermetallics | Solid-state (Vol. 6) or resistance forge processes; beam with tight energy control; not conventional arc |
| Thick section, crack-sensitive | Arc with controlled preheat and multi-pass tempering; beam's rapid cooling is unfavourable |
| Materials with volatile constituents | Not EBW — they evaporate in vacuum |

8. Question 6 — What Has to Be Verified, and How?

An under-asked question that materially affects the decision, because verification cost and feasibility differ sharply between families:

| Family | Verification characteristics |
| --- | --- |
| Arc | Well-established NDT methods; weld geometry suits radiography and ultrasonics; surface appearance carries real information; accessible for repair |
| Resistance | Not volumetrically inspectable in production; relies on destructive sampling, process monitoring and consumable interval control (Ch. 51, Section 9) |
| Beam | Narrow weld is difficult to inspect; surface appearance carries no penetration information; missed joint is a real risk; relies on in-process monitoring and sectioning (Ch. 54, Section 12) |

The consequence for selection: a process whose welds cannot be inspected effectively must be controlled by process discipline instead. If an organization does not have — or is not willing to build — the process monitoring, sampling and interval-management discipline that resistance and beam processes require, then selecting one of them on productivity grounds creates a quality system it cannot operate. This is a legitimate and frequently decisive reason to choose arc welding.

9. The Cost Structure, Honestly

| Cost element | Arc | Resistance | Beam |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Capital equipment | Low to moderate | Moderate to high | High |
| Tooling and fixturing per joint | Low | High | High — fit-up dependent |
| Consumables in the joint | Filler, gas, flux | None | Little or none |
| Consumables not in the joint | Tips, nozzles, liners | Electrodes, wheels, dies | Optics, cover glass, cathodes |
| Labour per joint | High | Low | Low |
| Cycle time | Moderate | Very short | Short |
| Energy per joint | Moderate | Low | Moderate |
| Post-weld cleaning | Slag, spatter | Minimal | Minimal |
| Distortion correction | Often significant | Low | Low |
| Inspection cost | Moderate | Sampling and monitoring | Monitoring and sectioning |
| Rework accessibility | Good | Poor | Poor |

The two costs most often left out of a comparison are distortion correction (Section 6) and the cost of building the process control discipline a low-inspectability process requires (Section 8). Including them changes the answer often enough that a comparison omitting them should not be trusted.

11. Where Hybrids and Combinations Win

| Combination | What it solves |
| --- | --- |
| Hybrid laser-arc (Ch. 52, Section 11) | Laser penetration and speed with arc gap tolerance and filler — the standard answer when fit-up blocks a pure laser solution |
| GTAW root + arc fill | Root quality where it matters most, deposition where it matters most |
| Beam root + arc fill | Deep root penetration with economic filling above it |
| Laser + adhesive (weld bonding) | Structural stiffness and sealing beyond what welds alone give, common in vehicle structures |
| Resistance spot + adhesive (weld bonding) | Same, with fatigue and stiffness benefits |
| Laser tack + arc weld | Fast, low-distortion tacking to hold fit-up for a following arc weld |
| Arc for the difficult joints, beam for the repetitive ones | Matching each family to the joints that suit it, rather than standardizing on one |

That last row is the most under-used option: a facility does not have to choose one family. Standardizing on a single process across a mixed product range guarantees that some joints are made by a process poorly suited to them.

12. Decision Walkthrough

1. What does the joint have to be? (Section 3.) Geometry, leak-tightness and filler requirement usually shortlist two families.

2. What fit-up can be delivered on real parts? (Section 4.) This eliminates beam processes if the answer is "variable."

3. What is the volume, and what is the crossover? (Section 5.)

4. What does distortion cost downstream? (Section 6.) This can flip the decision on its own.

5. What does the material demand? (Section 7.)

6. How will the welds be verified, and can the organization operate that regime? (Section 8.)

7. Total the real cost structure, including distortion correction and quality system cost. (Section 9.)

8. Consider hybrids and mixed strategies before committing to a single family. (Section 11.)

9. Check the governing code or product standard, which may mandate or exclude processes regardless of engineering merit.

13. Common Selection Errors

| Error | Why it happens | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Selecting a beam process before verifying fit-up | The welding demonstration is impressive; the fixturing problem appears later | The installation cannot achieve production quality; fit-up cost overruns |
| Comparing on welding cost per metre alone | It is the easiest number to obtain | Distortion correction, inspection and rework are omitted — often the larger costs |
| Standardizing on one family across a mixed product range | Simplifies purchasing and training | Some joints are made by an unsuitable process |
| Assuming resistance welding needs no quality system because it is fast and automatic | The welds look consistent | Consumable degradation goes unmanaged; failures appear in the field |
| Selecting laser welding for a coated lap joint without a vent strategy | The joint looks simple | Zinc blow-out; the remedy is a design change discovered late (Ch. 54, Section 4) |
| Choosing a process the organization cannot inspect or monitor | Productivity drives the decision | An uncontrollable process with no verification route |
| Ignoring code restrictions | Engineering evaluation done independently of the code | A qualified, capable process that is not permitted for the application |
| Using short-circuit GMAW on thick section for out-of-position capability | It is the familiar all-position mode | Lack of fusion; pulsed transfer was the correct answer (Ch. 39, Section 3) |

14. Worked Example: Justifying a Laser Cell Against an Existing Arc Process

Situation. A manufacturer welds a medium-volume steel assembly by robotic GMAW. A laser cell is proposed. The business case compares welding cycle time and consumable cost and shows a marginal, unconvincing return. The engineering team believes the laser is the better process but cannot demonstrate it financially.

Step 1 — Check whether the comparison includes distortion cost. The assembly is currently straightened after welding. That is direct labour, it occupies floor space, and it has its own scrap rate. If laser welding's lower heat input reduces or removes it, the saving belongs in the comparison — and it is often larger than the welding cost difference (Section 6).

Step 2 — Check whether it includes rework and inspection. If the current arc process has a rework rate, the labour, delay and material in that rework is a real cost. Conversely, if the laser process would require in-process monitoring and sectioning that the arc process does not, that cost belongs on the other side of the ledger (Section 8).

Step 3 — Establish the fit-up capability honestly, before going further. Measure gap and alignment on a statistically meaningful sample of production parts. If the answer is "variable beyond the laser's tolerance," the laser cell will not work as proposed and the correct conclusion is either to fix the upstream process, to evaluate hybrid laser-arc, or to stop.

Step 4 — Cost the fit-up work, because it is the hidden capital item. Improving fit-up means better cutting, better forming, better fixturing, or all three. This is frequently a larger investment than the laser itself, and a business case that omits it is not a business case.

Step 5 — Evaluate hybrid laser-arc as the middle option. If the fit-up cost is prohibitive but the distortion and speed benefits are real, hybrid delivers most of the benefit while tolerating the fit-up that exists (Section 11). It should be evaluated explicitly rather than treated as a fallback.

Step 6 — Check the material and joint for laser-specific problems. Coated material in a lap configuration needs a vent strategy; a joint requiring filler for chemistry or gap needs filler addition or hybrid. Discovering either after purchase is expensive.

Step 7 — Assess whether the organization can operate the process. Laser welding requires optics management on an interval, in-process monitoring, seam tracking maintenance, and a quality regime built on sectioning rather than visual inspection. If none of that capability exists, it must be built, and that is a cost and a lead time.

Step 8 — Present the honest conclusion. The comparison may still favour the arc process — and if so, that is a legitimate result, not a failure. What matters is that the decision was made on the full cost structure rather than on welding cycle time, and that the fit-up question was answered before the capital was committed rather than after.

15. Known Gaps

• No costs, rates or crossover volumes are given. They depend on labour rates, utilization, local energy and consumable prices, and rework rates, and any figure here would be misleading.

• Process capability boundaries are described relatively. Actual limits depend on specific equipment.

• Code restrictions are noted as a check but not enumerated; they are numerous and application-specific.

• Solid-state processes (Volume 6) enter this comparison for aluminium and dissimilar joints in particular, and Chapter 73 brings all families into a single framework.

• Weld bonding and hybrid joining are noted but not developed; each has its own qualification and design considerations.

1. Process Overview: ISO 4063 References 42x

Friction welding generates heat by rubbing two components together under pressure, then forges them together while the interface is hot and plastic. Nothing melts in the finished joint — or more precisely, whatever momentarily melts is expelled — so the result is a solid-state weld.

The ISO nomenclature covers the family [S1]:

| Reference | Process |
| --- | --- |
| 421 | Direct drive friction welding |
| 422 | Inertia friction welding |
| 423 | Friction stud welding |
| 424 | Linear friction welding |
| 425 | Radial friction welding |
| 426 | Orbital friction welding |

Friction stir welding, its close relative, is treated separately in Chapter 57 because its mechanism and applications differ substantially.

2. The Mechanism: Heat, Plasticize, Forge

The cycle passes through four physical stages regardless of variant:

1. Rubbing and break-in. Surfaces contact under pressure with relative motion. Initially only asperities touch; friction is high and heating is concentrated at those points. Surface films, oxide and contamination are broken up and swept aside in this stage.

2. Transition to plastic contact. As the interface heats, the material softens, real contact area grows, and the behaviour changes from dry friction to viscous shearing of a thin plasticized layer. Heating becomes uniform across the interface.

3. Steady-state heating. A layer of hot, plastic material forms at the interface and is continuously extruded outward as flash while fresh material is brought into the interface. Axial shortening — the upset or burn-off — proceeds at a steady rate.

4. Forge. Relative motion stops and axial force is applied or increased. The remaining plasticized material is forged, contaminated material is expelled into the flash, and the joint consolidates in the solid state.

The metal that ends up bonded was never at the original interface. It came from behind it, was never exposed to the atmosphere, and was joined under pressure at forging temperature. This is the same principle as flash welding (Chapter 49, Section 3) and high-frequency welding (Chapter 50), and it is why all three are tolerant of surface condition and capable on dissimilar metals.

3. Direct-Drive (Continuous Drive) Friction Welding

One component is held in a rotating chuck driven continuously by a motor; the other is held stationary. The two are brought together under axial force and rubbed until the interface reaches forging condition. Rotation is then stopped by braking, and forge force is applied.

Characteristics:

• Rotational speed is held constant through the heating phase.

• Heating time and upset are the controlled variables, and the cycle can be controlled by time, by upset distance, or by a combination.

• The braking stage matters. How fast rotation stops relative to when the forge force is applied determines whether forging happens into hot, plastic material or into material that has begun to cool.

• Energy is supplied continuously from the motor, so cycle energy is not fixed in advance.

4. Inertia Friction Welding

One component is mounted on a flywheel of known inertia, spun up to a defined speed, and then disconnected from the drive. The stored kinetic energy is the entire energy available for the weld. The parts are pressed together and the flywheel decelerates as its energy is converted to heat at the interface, coming to rest as the weld completes.

Characteristics:

• Total energy is defined before the weld starts — by flywheel inertia and initial speed — which makes the process highly repeatable.

• Speed falls continuously through the weld, so the heating rate and the interface conditions change through the cycle in a characteristic, repeatable way.

• The weld ends when the energy is used, rather than at a time set by a controller.

• The energy signature is inherently recorded in the speed decay curve, which makes verification straightforward.

5. The Two Compared

| Factor | Direct drive (421) | Inertia (422) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Energy source | Motor, supplied continuously | Flywheel, fixed before the weld |
| Speed through the cycle | Constant | Decaying |
| Total energy | Determined by time and force | Determined by inertia and speed — set in advance |
| Repeatability | Good, dependent on control | Excellent — energy is a physical setpoint |
| Cycle time | Generally longer | Generally shorter |
| Control variables | Speed, friction pressure, heating time or upset, braking, forge pressure | Inertia, initial speed, axial pressure |
| Process record | Torque, upset and time traces | Speed decay curve plus upset |
| Typical use | Wide range of general engineering components | Automotive and aerospace production, where repeatability at volume is decisive |

Both are in widespread industrial use, and the choice usually follows the machine base available and the repeatability requirement rather than a metallurgical distinction.

6. Linear, Orbital and Radial Friction Welding

The rotary variants require at least one component to be axisymmetric about the joint. Three variants remove that constraint:

Linear friction welding (424). One component oscillates linearly against the other at high frequency and small amplitude under axial pressure. Because no rotation is involved, non-axisymmetric components can be joined — the process's defining advantage. Its principal industrial application is aerospace: joining blades to discs to form integrally bladed rotors, where the joint geometry is a blade root, not a cylinder.

Orbital friction welding (426). Relative motion follows a small circular orbit rather than rotation about the joint axis, so every point on the interface traces the same small circle. Also suits non-axisymmetric parts, and gives more uniform interface velocity than rotary welding, where velocity varies from zero at the centre to maximum at the periphery.

Radial friction welding (425). A ring is rotated and compressed radially onto the outside of two abutting components, welding them together. Used for pipe joining, where the internal bore must remain unobstructed.

The velocity-distribution point is worth stating for rotary welding: in a solid round bar, the interface velocity is zero at the centre and maximum at the rim, so heating is inherently non-uniform across the face. This is why solid bars of large diameter are more difficult than tubes, and why centre defects are a characteristic rotary friction welding problem (Section 16).

7. Friction Stud Welding

Reference 423 — a stud or pin is rotated and pressed against a surface, welding it end-on. It competes with arc stud welding (Chapter 45) and wins where an arc is unacceptable — in explosive atmospheres, underwater, or where the electrical or thermal effects of an arc cannot be tolerated. It also produces a solid-state joint rather than a fusion joint, which suits some material combinations better.

8. Why the Process Is Self-Cleaning

Surface preparation requirements for friction welding are modest, and the reason is mechanical:

During the rubbing stage, oxide films, mill scale, oil and light contamination are broken up, mixed into the plasticized layer, and extruded outward into the flash. By the forge stage, the material remaining at the interface is clean metal from beneath the original surfaces.

Three consequences:

1. Machined, square faces are needed for geometry and alignment, not for cleanliness.

2. The process is more tolerant of surface condition than any fusion process.

3. Sufficient upset is essential. If the upset is too small, contaminated material is not fully expelled, and it remains as a plane of inclusions at the bond line — producing the same characteristic defect as insufficient upset in flash welding (Chapter 49, Section 13).

Heavy contamination is still a problem — thick grease, paint, and coatings that decompose rather than extrude — and clamping surfaces must be clean for grip and, where relevant, for concentricity.

9. Equipment and Components

| Component | Function | Failure consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Spindle and drive (rotary) | Rotates one component at speed and resists the reaction torque | Speed variation changes heating; insufficient torque capacity stalls the weld |
| Flywheel (inertia) | Stores the weld energy | Its inertia is a process parameter — changing flywheels changes the process |
| Brake (direct drive) | Stops rotation before forging | Braking rate is a controlled variable |
| Chucks and clamping | Grip the components against torque and axial force | Slipping under torque or upset force is a primary failure mode |
| Hydraulic ram | Applies friction and forge pressures | Force accuracy and the transition between the two determine the forge |
| Machine frame | Reacts very high axial and torsional loads | Deflection under load affects upset accuracy |
| Control system | Sequences the cycle and records the traces | The traces are the process record (Section 18) |
| Instrumentation | Torque, axial force, upset displacement, speed, time | Without these, the weld cannot be verified except destructively |

10. Parameters and What Each Controls

Direct drive:

| Parameter | Controls | Symptom if wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rotational speed | Interface velocity and heating rate | Too low: insufficient heating, high torque, possible stall. Too high: overheating, excessive flash, wide HAZ |
| Friction (heating) pressure | Heating rate and torque | Too low: slow, uneven heating. Too high: excessive upset before the interface is uniformly hot |
| Heating time or heating upset | Total heat and heated depth | Too short: cold bond line, unexpelled contamination. Too long: excessive material loss and HAZ |
| Braking rate | When rotation stops relative to forging | Slow braking: interface cools before forging |
| Forge pressure | Expulsion of contaminated material and consolidation | Too low: bond-line defects. Too high: excessive upset and deformation |
| Forge duration | Consolidation and cooling under load | Too short: incomplete consolidation |

Inertia:

| Parameter | Controls |
| --- | --- |
| Flywheel inertia | Total available energy — a physical, discrete parameter |
| Initial speed | Total energy (with inertia) and initial interface velocity |
| Axial pressure | Heating rate, energy conversion rate, and upset |

The inertia process has fewer independent variables, which is a large part of its repeatability advantage.

11. Materials and Dissimilar Combinations

Similar-metal joints: carbon and alloy steels, stainless steels, tool steels, aluminium alloys, copper alloys, nickel alloys and titanium are all routinely friction welded. Hardenable steels require attention to the post-weld cooling and frequently a post-weld heat treatment (Section 14).

Dissimilar joints are a principal reason to choose the process. Because interface temperature is below melting, time at temperature is very short, and reacted material is expelled into the flash, intermetallic formation is limited in a way fusion welding cannot achieve (Chapter 27, Section 2).

Combinations commonly made by friction welding that are difficult or impossible by fusion welding:

• Aluminium to steel — with careful control of upset and time to keep the intermetallic layer thin.

• Copper to aluminium and copper to steel.

• Titanium to steel — feasible in some configurations where fusion welding is not.

• Tool steel to structural steel — the classic application for cutting tool shanks, where an expensive tool material is joined to a cheap shank.

• Stainless to carbon steel.

The controlling principle for dissimilar joints: the intermetallic layer thickness depends on time at temperature. Short cycles and adequate upset keep it thin; long cycles and insufficient upset let it grow and embrittle the joint. This is why dissimilar friction welding parameters are usually shorter and more forceful than similar-metal parameters, and why upset is the critical variable.

12. Joint Design and Geometry Limits

Rotary friction welding requires at least one component to be axisymmetric about the joint axis and to be grippable and rotatable. This is the process's principal geometric limitation.

| Configuration | Suitability |
| --- | --- |
| Bar to bar, tube to tube, bar to tube | Ideal |
| Bar or tube to a flat plate or flange face | Good, provided the plate can be held against torque |
| Large-diameter solid bar | Difficult — velocity is zero at the centre, causing centre defects |
| Tube | Better than solid bar — velocity varies less across a thin wall |
| Non-axisymmetric components | Linear or orbital variants only (424, 426) |
| Very thin sections | Difficult — insufficient stiffness to react the forces |
| Long, slender components | Difficult — buckling under axial force, and runout |

Design points: provide clamping length and a clamping surface that grips; allow for the axial shortening (burn-off) in the component lengths; provide space for the flash; and consider whether the flash must be removed for function, access or appearance (Section 14).

13. Setup and Execution Procedure

Before welding

1. Confirm the procedure covers the material combination, geometry and any post-weld heat treatment.

2. Verify component geometry: face squareness, concentricity, and length allowance for burn-off.

3. Clean the clamping surfaces; interface cleanliness matters less but heavy contamination should be removed.

4. Set the clamping and verify grip — slipping under torque or upset load is a primary failure mode.

5. Set the parameters: for direct drive, speed, friction pressure, heating time or upset, braking and forge pressure; for inertia, flywheel selection, initial speed and axial pressure.

6. Verify the machine's instrumentation is recording torque, force, upset and speed.

7. Weld and destructively test setup samples before production.

Welding

8. Run the cycle; the process is machine-executed and is not adjusted mid-cycle.

9. Observe the flash formation — a uniform, symmetric flash collar curling evenly from both components indicates correct heating and forging.

10. Verify the upset achieved against the setting on the machine record.

11. Confirm the traces — torque, upset, speed — match the expected signature.

After welding

12. Examine the flash for symmetry before removing it (Section 18).

13. Remove flash by the specified method.

14. Apply post-weld heat treatment where required.

15. Inspect per the quality plan.

16. Record the process traces against the component identity.

14. Post-Weld Operations

Flash removal. The upset collar is removed by turning, shearing while hot, or machining. Two points: on a dissimilar joint the flash carries the expelled intermetallic material, so its removal is functionally part of the process; and machining must not leave a notch at the bond line.

Post-weld heat treatment. On hardenable steels, the rapid cooling of a small heated zone in a large cold component produces a hard, potentially brittle heat-affected zone. Tempering or normalizing is common practice and is frequently mandatory. On some dissimilar joints, heat treatment must be chosen carefully because it can promote further intermetallic growth — an important exception to the general rule that heat treatment improves a joint.

Straightness and runout must be verified after welding, particularly on long components.

15. When to Use Friction Welding and When Not To

| Choose friction welding when | Choose something else when |
| --- | --- |
| The joint is axisymmetric — bar, tube, shaft, flange | The geometry is not axisymmetric and linear/orbital machines are unavailable |
| Dissimilar metals that fusion welding handles badly | Volumes are too low to justify machine setup |
| No filler, no gas, no flux is wanted | The joint is a lap, T or fillet configuration |
| Very high repeatability at production volume | The component cannot be gripped or reacted against torque |
| A full cross-section joint stronger than the parent is required | Very large cross-sections exceed machine force capability |
| Tool steel to shank, valve heads to stems, drive shafts, axle assemblies | Site or field work — this is a fixed machine process |
| No arc is acceptable — explosive atmosphere, underwater (friction stud welding) | Flash and axial shortening are unacceptable to the design |

16. Defect Catalog

| Defect | Detection | Cause | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bond-line defect / unbonded region | UT; bend or torsion testing; sectioning | Insufficient upset or forge force — contaminated interface material not expelled; insufficient heating | Increase forge pressure and upset; increase heating; verify clamping is not slipping |
| Centre defect (unbonded region at the axis) | UT; sectioning | Zero interface velocity at the centre of a solid bar; insufficient forge to consolidate it | Increase forge pressure; consider a tube or a centre-relieved geometry; increase heating time |
| Excessive intermetallic layer (dissimilar joints) | Sectioning; metallography; low ductility | Time at temperature too long; insufficient upset to expel reacted material | Shorten the cycle and increase upset; avoid post-weld heat treatment that promotes growth |
| Slipping in the clamps | Upset trace shows short displacement; visible marking | Clamping force insufficient for torque or upset load; contaminated clamping surface | Increase clamping force; clean and inspect clamp faces |
| Asymmetric flash | Visual | Unequal heating between the two components — different materials, different geometry, misalignment | Expected on dissimilar joints; investigate if unexpected on similar materials; check alignment and squareness |
| Cracking in the HAZ | MT/PT; sectioning | Hardenable material cooled rapidly in a large cold component | Apply post-weld heat treatment; control cooling |
| Excessive upset / dimensional error | Dimensional | Forge pressure or heating too high; length allowance wrong | Adjust parameters; correct the burn-off allowance in the component length |
| Runout / misalignment | Dimensional | Component not concentric in the chuck; machine alignment; bending under load | Check chucking concentricity and machine alignment |
| Notch at the bond line after flash removal | Visual; fatigue failure in service | Machining or shearing into the parent metal | Control flash removal; dress smoothly |

17. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Bond-line defects found by ultrasonic testing

Symptom: unbonded areas at the bond line; joints may still pass a simple strength check.

Category: insufficient forge.

Likely causes: forge pressure too low; upset distance too small; heating insufficient so the interface was not uniformly plastic; clamp slipping so the commanded upset was not achieved.

Steps: read the upset trace and compare achieved displacement against the setting — slipping shows here directly; increase forge pressure and upset; increase heating time or pressure; verify clamping force. This is the same diagnostic logic as the flash welding upset curve (Chapter 49, Section 15).

Card 2 — Unbonded region at the centre of a solid bar joint

Symptom: sectioning shows a defect confined to the axis.

Category: velocity distribution.

Likely causes: interface velocity is zero at the axis, so the centre heats by conduction rather than friction; forge pressure insufficient to consolidate the cooler centre.

Steps: increase forge pressure — this is the primary control for centre defects; increase heating time to allow conduction to heat the centre; consider a tubular or centre-relieved geometry if the design allows; recognize that this is a geometric characteristic of rotary friction welding on solid bars, not a machine fault.

Card 3 — Dissimilar joint failing with low ductility

Symptom: brittle failure at the interface; metallography shows a distinct reaction layer.

Category: intermetallic growth.

Likely causes: cycle too long, giving time for the intermetallic layer to grow; upset insufficient to expel reacted material; post-weld heat treatment promoting further growth.

Steps: shorten the heating cycle and increase upset and forge pressure; measure the intermetallic layer thickness on sections to establish the relationship with cycle time; review whether any post-weld heat treatment is promoting growth — on dissimilar joints, heat treatment is not automatically beneficial (Section 14).

Card 4 — Weld quality drifting across a production run

Symptom: gradual change in upset, flash appearance or test results.

Category: machine or clamping condition.

Likely causes: clamp face wear reducing grip; hydraulic pressure drift; brake wear changing the braking rate (direct drive); spindle bearing condition; component length or face squareness varying from the machining operation upstream.

Steps: compare the process traces from early and late in the run — they show which variable moved; inspect clamp faces; verify hydraulic pressures; check incoming component dimensions, since upstream machining variation is a frequent and overlooked cause.

18. Testing and Quality Verification

The process traces are the primary record, and this is one of the process's real advantages: torque, axial force, upset displacement and rotational speed against time form a signature that can be compared against a reference for every weld made. A deviation in the trace identifies the stage at which the cycle went wrong — heating, braking or forging — which post-weld inspection cannot.

Flash appearance is a genuine visual indicator: a uniform, symmetric collar curling evenly from both components indicates correct and symmetric heating and forging. Asymmetry indicates unequal heating, misalignment, or — on dissimilar joints — the expected consequence of different material properties.

Destructive testing:

• Bend and torsion testing of setup and sample joints.

• Tensile testing across the joint.

• Metallographic sectioning for bond-line examination, HAZ assessment and, on dissimilar joints, intermetallic layer measurement.

• Hardness traverse, particularly on hardenable materials.

Non-destructive testing:

• Ultrasonic testing across the bond line — the standard production method, and the one capable of finding centre and bond-line defects.

• Visual inspection of flash before removal.

• Dimensional checks for upset, straightness and runout.

19. Safety Specifics

• Very high rotational energy stored in the spindle or flywheel. A component ejected from a chuck at speed is a severe hazard, and guarding and interlocks are essential rather than advisory.

• Very high axial and torsional forces, with crushing hazards at the clamping and forging area.

• Hot flash ejected radially at the interface, and hot components after welding.

• Noise, particularly in linear friction welding at high frequency.

• Fume and particulate from the flash and from any surface contamination burned off during rubbing.

• Stored energy in the flywheel remains after the cycle in inertia machines.

• Process references: ISO 4063 references 421–426 [S1].

• Procedure and operator qualification: ISO 15620 covers friction welding of metallic materials, including procedure qualification and quality requirements. The general qualification framework of Chapter 31 applies, with the process-specific variables of Section 10.

• Operator qualification: ISO 14732 for this mechanized process (Chapter 32, Section 9).

21. Worked Example: Intermittent Bond-Line Defects on a Dissimilar Joint

Situation. A manufacturer friction welds an aluminium component to a steel shaft. Most joints pass ultrasonic inspection and bend testing. Roughly one in fifteen shows bond-line indications and fails testing. Parameters are unchanged and verified against the qualified procedure.

Step 1 — Read the intermittency. Settings do not vary between parts; something else does. The candidates are component dimensions and face condition from upstream machining, clamping grip, material batch, and machine condition drifting within a run.

Step 2 — Go to the process traces for the failed and passing welds. Comparing the upset displacement, torque and force traces between a failed and a passing joint identifies the stage at which the failures differ. If the failed welds show a shorter achieved upset, the cause is mechanical — slipping or a force shortfall. If they show a normal upset but different torque, the cause is at the interface — face condition or material.

Step 3 — Check clamping first, because it is the most common mechanical cause. Aluminium is soft and grips differently from steel; a clamp force adequate for the steel side may mark or slip on the aluminium side. Slipping reduces the effective upset without any change to the setting, and it varies with surface condition part to part — which fits an intermittent pattern precisely.

Step 4 — Check incoming component dimensions and face squareness. A face that is not square contacts unevenly, heats unevenly, and forges unevenly. Machining variation upstream produces exactly this kind of intermittent behaviour, and measuring a sample of incoming parts is quick.

Step 5 — Consider the dissimilar-joint mechanism specifically. Aluminium-to-steel joints depend on keeping the intermetallic layer thin (Section 11). If the failures show a thicker reaction layer on sectioning, the cause is excessive time at temperature or insufficient upset — and the remedy is a shorter, more forceful cycle rather than more heating.

Step 6 — Section a failed and a passing joint. This distinguishes an unbonded region (mechanical, upset-related) from a brittle intermetallic layer (thermal, time-related). The two have opposite remedies, and guessing between them wastes a production run.

Step 7 — Correct the cause and verify by trace. Whatever the cause, the correction should be visible in the process traces — a longer achieved upset, a different torque signature. Verifying by trace rather than by destructive test alone means the next occurrence is caught at the machine.

Step 8 — Set trace-based limits as a production control. Because every weld generates a full signature, acceptance limits on upset, peak torque and forge force can be applied automatically to every joint. On a safety-relevant dissimilar joint made in volume, that is the control worth building — the same argument made for the upset curve in flash welding and for process monitoring in resistance welding.

22. Known Gaps

• No parameter values are given. Speeds, pressures, times and upsets are material-, geometry- and machine-specific and are established by qualification.

• Machine capability limits — maximum diameter and force — are equipment-specific.

• Intermetallic thickness limits for dissimilar joints are application-specific and are established by qualification and testing rather than by a general rule.

• Linear friction welding is described in outline. It is a specialist aerospace process with substantial proprietary development behind it.

• ISO 15620's current edition should be confirmed, as should any sector standard taking precedence.
