1. Process Overview and ISO 25239

Friction stir welding uses a rotating, non-consumable tool — a profiled pin surrounded by a larger shoulder — plunged into the joint line and traversed along it. Friction and plastic deformation heat the material to a plasticized, but not molten, condition; the tool's rotation stirs material from both sides together; and the shoulder contains it under forging pressure.

The governing standard family is ISO 25239, covering friction stir welding of aluminium in five parts, including Part 4: Specification and qualification of welding procedures and Part 5: Quality and inspection requirements [S1][S2]. Its existence as a dedicated standard family, separate from the fusion welding qualification framework, reflects that the process has its own variables, its own defect population and its own inspection requirements.

In the ISO 4063 nomenclature the visible entries are the friction stir spot welding variants 431 to 435 [S3]; continuous friction stir welding — the process this chapter principally addresses — is governed for aluminium by ISO 25239 rather than by the nomenclature number.

The single most consequential fact about the process: because nothing melts, the two dominant aluminium fusion welding defects — hydrogen porosity and solidification cracking — cannot occur (Chapter 25, Sections 5 and 6). That is why the process took over long aluminium seams so decisively.

2. The Mechanism: Plunge, Traverse, Stir, Forge

1. Plunge. The rotating tool is forced into the joint line. Friction between shoulder and surface, and between pin and material, generates heat. The plunge is force- or position-controlled and generates the highest loads of the cycle.

2. Dwell. A brief pause allows heat to develop and the surrounding material to soften before traverse begins.

3. Traverse. The tool moves along the joint. Material ahead of the pin is plasticized, swept around the pin — predominantly from the advancing side to the retreating side — and consolidated behind it under the shoulder's forging pressure.

4. Consolidation. The shoulder contains the plasticized material and prevents it escaping upward, applying the forging pressure that produces a sound solid-state joint.

5. Retraction, leaving an exit hole where the pin was (Section 12).

The material never melts. Peak temperature is a substantial fraction of the melting temperature, but the joint is made by severe plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization, not solidification.

3. The Tool: Shoulder, Pin and Features

The tool is the process. Its geometry determines material flow, heat generation and defect formation more than any other single factor.

| Feature | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Shoulder | Generates most of the heat by friction on the surface; contains the plasticized material and applies forging pressure; its diameter sets the width of the affected zone |
| Shoulder profile (flat, concave, scrolled) | Controls material containment and flash formation; scrolled shoulders draw material inward and reduce flash |
| Pin (probe) | Stirs material through the thickness; its length sets the penetration depth |
| Pin profile (cylindrical, tapered, threaded, fluted, flatted) | Controls the vertical and circumferential material flow; threads drive material downward, which is critical for root consolidation |
| Pin length | Must be matched to the material thickness — too short leaves an unwelded root; too long strikes the backing bar |
| Tool material | Must retain strength and wear resistance at welding temperature — tool steels for aluminium, and much more demanding materials for steel and titanium |

Tool wear is the process's principal consumable issue, and it differs sharply by material: tools last a very long time in aluminium and are a major cost and technical limitation in steel and titanium, where the required tool materials are expensive and their life is short. This is the main reason FSW dominates aluminium and has spread more slowly to steel.

4. Advancing and Retreating Sides

The weld is not symmetric, and this asymmetry is fundamental rather than incidental.

On one side of the joint, the tool's rotational velocity is in the same direction as the traverse — the advancing side. On the other, it opposes the traverse — the retreating side.

Consequences:

• Material flow is asymmetric. Material is swept from the advancing side around the pin and deposited on the retreating side.

• The advancing side has a sharp, well-defined boundary between the stirred zone and the parent material; the retreating side has a diffuse, gradual boundary.

• Defects concentrate on the advancing side, particularly voids and tunnel defects, because that is where flow is most demanding.

• In dissimilar joints, which material is placed on the advancing side changes the result, and this is a genuine process variable that must be fixed in the procedure.

An engineer looking at a friction stir weld section can identify the advancing side by the sharp boundary, and knowing which side it was is often the first step in diagnosing a defect.

5. The Weld Zones

A friction stir weld section shows four distinct regions — a different structure from any fusion weld:

| Zone | Character |
| --- | --- |
| Nugget / stir zone | Fully recrystallized, very fine equiaxed grains from dynamic recrystallization; frequently shows "onion ring" flow banding |
| Thermo-mechanically affected zone (TMAZ) | Deformed but not fully recrystallized; grains are bent and elongated around the nugget |
| Heat-affected zone (HAZ) | Thermally affected only, no deformation; in heat-treatable aluminium this is where softening occurs |
| Parent material | Unaffected |

The TMAZ has no equivalent in fusion welding, and its presence is one of the identifying features of the process.

Property implication: in heat-treatable aluminium alloys (6xxx, 7xxx, 2xxx) the joint's weakest point is normally in the HAZ, not in the nugget — the nugget's fine recrystallized structure is often stronger than the softened HAZ beside it. The softening mechanism is the same as in fusion welding (Chapter 25, Section 3), but the affected zone is narrower and the peak temperature lower, so the strength retained is generally higher than an equivalent fusion weld. That is a genuine and quantifiable advantage, and it is one of the reasons FSW is specified for structural aluminium.

6. Equipment and the Reaction Force Problem

Friction stir welding generates very high forces, and this shapes the equipment more than any other consideration:

| Force | Consequence |
| --- | --- |
| Axial (downward) force | Very large — the machine and fixture must react it without deflection. This is why FSW machines look like machine tools rather than welding equipment |
| Traverse force | Resists the tool's movement along the joint |
| Side force | Pushes the tool off the joint line |
| Torque | Reaction to the tool's rotation |

Equipment implications:

• Machine stiffness is a process requirement. Deflection under load changes the plunge depth and therefore the weld, so a flexible machine produces a variable weld.

• The backing bar (anvil) must react the axial force along the whole joint, with no gap. It also sets the root condition.

• Clamping must resist the side force and the traverse force, holding the joint closed along its full length.

• Robots need very high payload and stiffness, or force-controlled compensation, to perform FSW — standard welding robots cannot.

• Force control against position control is a fundamental machine capability distinction: force-controlled machines maintain constant axial force and adapt plunge depth, which accommodates thickness variation and machine deflection; position-controlled machines hold depth and let force vary.

7. Parameters and What Each Controls

| Parameter | Controls | Symptom if wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rotation speed | Heat generation and stirring intensity | Too low: insufficient heat, voids, high forces, tool breakage. Too high: excessive heat, flash, surface galling, HAZ softening |
| Traverse speed | Heat input per unit length and productivity | Too fast: insufficient heat, voids and tunnel defects. Too slow: excessive heat, flash, wider softened zone |
| Axial (plunge) force or depth | Forging pressure and shoulder contact | Too low: insufficient consolidation, surface voids, lack of penetration. Too high: excessive flash, thinning, tool or machine overload |
| Tool tilt angle | Shoulder contact geometry and forging at the trailing edge | Incorrect tilt: poor consolidation behind the tool, surface defects |
| Pin length relative to thickness | Root penetration | Too short: unwelded root — the classic root defect. Too long: contact with the backing bar |
| Tool geometry | Material flow | The dominant design variable; changing tools changes the process |
| Dwell time at plunge | Heat before traverse | Too short: cold start defects at the weld beginning |
| Which material is on the advancing side (dissimilar) | Flow and mixing | A fixed procedural variable, not a free choice |

The heat balance is set by rotation and traverse speed together. A useful mental model is that rotation generates heat and traverse consumes it: too hot gives flash, excessive softening and surface galling; too cold gives voids and tunnel defects. The usable window sits between them and is narrower on some alloys than others.

8. Joint Design and Clamping

| Joint type | FSW suitability |
| --- | --- |
| Butt | The primary configuration; requires close abutment along the whole length |
| Lap | Feasible, but the interface can produce hooking defects at the joint edges (Section 14) |
| T-joint | Possible with specialized tools |
| Corner and edge | Possible with adapted configurations |
| Curved and three-dimensional | Possible with robotic or multi-axis machines, subject to force capability |

Fit-up requirements are demanding but different in character from beam welding: FSW does not require a machined gap tolerance so much as close abutment with no gap and rigid clamping. A gap at the joint line means less material for the tool to consolidate, producing voids.

Clamping is a first-order requirement, not a fixture convenience. The parts must be held against the traverse force, the side force pushing them apart, and the axial force, along the entire joint length. Inadequate clamping produces joint opening ahead of the tool, which produces exactly the void defects the process is otherwise free of.

The backing bar reacts the axial force and defines the root. Its material, surface condition and continuity along the joint all affect the root quality, and a gap between the workpiece and the backing bar is a common root defect cause.

9. Materials

| Material | FSW behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| Aluminium alloys | The dominant application. All series weldable including 2xxx and 7xxx, which are difficult or unweldable by fusion (Chapter 25, Section 2) — a decisive capability advantage |
| Magnesium alloys | Well suited |
| Copper | Weldable; high thermal conductivity requires high heat input |
| Steels | Feasible, but requires expensive high-temperature tool materials with limited life; adoption is limited by tool cost |
| Titanium | As steel — tool material is the limiting factor |
| Dissimilar aluminium alloys | Routinely welded, including combinations fusion welding handles badly |
| Dissimilar metals (Al to steel, Al to copper) | Feasible with controlled parameters; solid-state joining limits intermetallic formation (Chapter 27) |
| Aluminium to polymer / composite | Specialist variants exist |

The 2xxx and 7xxx capability deserves emphasis. These high-strength aerospace alloys are crack-sensitive and difficult to fusion weld, which is why aerospace structures were traditionally riveted. FSW makes welded joints in them practical, and that is a structural design capability rather than a process substitution.

10. Friction Stir Spot Welding

The spot variants — ISO 4063 references 431 to 435 [S3] — plunge the tool at a point, dwell, and retract, producing a discrete joint rather than a seam.

| Reference | Variant |
| --- | --- |
| 431 | Friction stir spot welding |
| 432 | Refill friction stir spot welding |
| 433 | Stitch friction stir spot welding |
| 434 | Swept friction stir spot welding |
| 435 | Swing friction stir spot welding |

Refill friction stir spot welding (432) is the significant variant: a separately actuated sleeve and pin allow the material displaced by the plunge to be pushed back in as the tool retracts, eliminating the exit hole. The exit hole is the principal objection to conventional friction stir spot welding, so this variant addresses the process's main weakness directly.

The spot variants compete with resistance spot welding and self-piercing riveting on aluminium sheet, where resistance spot welding's process window is narrow (Volume 1, Chapter 14) and the solid-state nature of FSW avoids it entirely.

11. Setup and Execution Procedure

Before welding

1. Confirm the procedure per ISO 25239-4 covers the material, thickness, joint type and tool [S2].

2. Verify the tool: correct geometry, correct pin length for the thickness, and inspect for wear or damage.

3. Verify the backing bar is continuous, flat and in contact along the whole joint.

4. Clamp the parts, confirming they are held closed along the full joint length against side and traverse forces.

5. Verify joint abutment — no gap along the seam.

6. Set rotation speed, traverse speed, axial force or plunge depth, tilt angle and dwell.

7. Confirm the machine's force monitoring is recording.

8. Weld and section trial pieces before production.

Welding

9. Plunge at the programmed rate, on a run-on tab where the design allows.

10. Dwell for the programmed time.

11. Traverse, monitoring axial force, torque and traverse force.

12. Observe the surface: a smooth, regular surface with a consistent, modest flash indicates correct heat balance. Excessive flash indicates too much heat; a rough or galled surface indicates too little heat or insufficient shoulder contact.

13. Retract at the end of the weld, ideally on a run-off tab so the exit hole lies outside the joint (Section 12).

After welding

14. Inspect the weld surface, the flash and the root where accessible.

15. Section trial welds — root defects and internal voids are not visible from the surface.

16. Inspect per ISO 25239-5 and the quality plan [S1].

17. Record force, torque, speeds, tool identity and tool life count.

12. The Exit Hole and What to Do About It

When the tool retracts, it leaves a hole the size of the pin. This is inherent to conventional FSW and has to be designed for:

| Approach | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Run-off tab | Terminate the weld on a sacrificial tab that is removed afterwards. The standard solution for butt welds |
| Retractable pin tool | The pin retracts progressively during the final traverse, closing the hole as the shoulder passes over |
| Refill variant (432) | For spot welds, the sleeve refills the hole (Section 10) |
| Weld into a region to be machined away | Design the joint so the exit hole falls in material later removed |
| Accept and repair | Fill the hole by another process, with the qualification consequences that entails |
| Circumferential welds | Overlap the start, then run off — the closure region needs specific procedure attention |

The exit hole is a design constraint, and a design that has not accounted for it will discover it late.

13. When to Use FSW and When Not To

| Choose FSW when | Choose something else when |
| --- | --- |
| Long aluminium seams — extrusions, panels, plate | The joint is short, one-off or irregular — setup and fixturing dominate |
| Aluminium alloys that fusion welding handles badly — 2xxx and 7xxx | Access for the tool, backing bar and clamping is unavailable |
| Hydrogen porosity or solidification cracking must be eliminated | The joint is not a straight or simple path and the machine cannot follow it |
| Maximum property retention in heat-treatable aluminium | Steel or titanium, where tool cost and life are limiting |
| Low distortion on long, thin structures | The exit hole cannot be accommodated |
| Dissimilar aluminium alloys or dissimilar metals | Force reaction is impossible — thin, flexible or unsupported structures |
| Shipbuilding panels, rail vehicle bodies, aerospace structures, battery trays | Site or field work — FSW is a machine process |
| No fume, no arc, no gas, no filler is wanted | Very thick sections beyond the machine's force and tool capability |

14. Defect Catalog

| Defect | Detection | Cause | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Void / tunnel defect (continuous cavity, usually on the advancing side) | RT; UT; sectioning | Insufficient heat — traverse too fast or rotation too slow; insufficient axial force; joint gap | Increase rotation or reduce traverse speed; increase axial force; close the joint gap; verify clamping |
| Root defect / lack of penetration | Sectioning; bend testing; not visible from the surface | Pin too short for the thickness; insufficient plunge depth; machine deflection under load; gap between workpiece and backing bar | Verify pin length against actual thickness; increase plunge depth or force; check machine deflection and backing bar contact |
| Kissing bond (surfaces in contact but not bonded) | Difficult — see Section 15 | Oxide layer not sufficiently disrupted at the root; insufficient stirring at that location | Increase heat and stirring at the root; verify pin geometry and length; this defect requires specific inspection attention |
| Surface galling / rough surface | Visual | Insufficient heat; insufficient shoulder contact; incorrect tilt | Increase rotation or reduce traverse; increase axial force; correct tilt angle |
| Excessive flash and thinning | Visual; dimensional | Too much heat; excessive axial force or plunge depth | Reduce rotation, increase traverse, reduce force |
| Hooking (lap joints) | Sectioning | The original interface turned upward at the edges of the stir zone, forming a crack-like feature | Tool geometry selection; joint configuration; recognize as a lap-joint-specific limitation |
| Wormhole | RT; sectioning | Insufficient consolidation, generally cold conditions | Increase heat input; increase force |
| Exit hole in the joint | Visual | Weld terminated in the joint rather than on a tab | Use run-off tabs, retractable pin, or design the termination out (Section 12) |
| Tool wear or breakage | Visual on the tool; force trace change | Excessive force, cold conditions, wrong tool material for the workpiece | Monitor tool life; adjust parameters; select appropriate tool material |
| HAZ softening | Hardness traverse; tensile testing | Inherent to heat-treatable alloys | Minimize heat input; design to reduced HAZ properties (Chapter 25, Section 3) |
| Joint line remnant | Sectioning | Original oxide layer not fully dispersed, remaining as a faint line | Increase stirring; verify surface preparation; assess against the acceptance criteria |

15. The Kissing Bond Problem

This defect deserves separate treatment because it is the process's most difficult quality issue and has no close analogue elsewhere.

What it is: a region where the two surfaces are in intimate contact but not metallurgically bonded — typically at the root, where an oxide layer was flattened and pressed together but not disrupted and dispersed by the stirring action.

Why it is difficult:

• It has essentially no volume. There is no cavity, no inclusion, no gap — the surfaces are touching. Volumetric NDT methods depend on a reflector or a density difference, and a kissing bond presents almost neither.

• Ultrasonic detection is unreliable for the same reason: the interface transmits sound almost as well as sound metal.

• Radiography cannot detect it at all — there is no thickness or density variation.

• It may pass a routine bend test while failing under fatigue or under a different loading direction.

• It reduces fatigue performance substantially even where static strength appears acceptable.

How it is managed — and the honest answer is that it is managed by prevention and by qualification rather than by inspection:

1. Process control — parameters, pin length and force that ensure adequate stirring at the root, established and locked by qualification.

2. Force and torque monitoring, since the conditions that produce kissing bonds usually show as a deviation in the process signature.

3. Destructive sampling, including bend testing in the direction that opens the root, and metallographic examination.

4. Fatigue testing during qualification, because static testing may not reveal it.

5. Specialized ultrasonic techniques developed for the purpose, with the honest caveat that detection reliability is limited.

The general principle this illustrates: a process whose critical defect is not reliably detectable must be controlled by process discipline, which is the same conclusion reached for resistance welding (Chapter 51, Section 9) and beam welding (Chapter 54, Section 12).

16. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Tunnel defect along the advancing side

Symptom: a continuous cavity running along the weld, found by radiography or sectioning.

Category: insufficient heat or consolidation.

Likely causes: traverse speed too high or rotation too slow — the material was not plastic enough to flow around the pin; axial force too low; joint gap; clamping allowing the joint to open ahead of the tool.

Steps: increase rotation speed or reduce traverse speed to raise heat input; increase axial force; check joint abutment and clamping along the whole length — a gap ahead of the tool starves it of material; verify pin and shoulder geometry against the procedure.

Card 2 — Root defects on a full-penetration weld

Symptom: sectioning shows unwelded material at the root; the surface is perfect.

Category: penetration.

Likely causes: pin length too short for the actual thickness — including thickness variation within tolerance; insufficient plunge depth; machine deflection reducing effective depth under load; a gap between the workpiece and the backing bar.

Steps: measure actual material thickness across a sample and compare with pin length; check plunge depth achieved under load, not commanded; check machine deflection and backing bar contact; consider force control rather than position control to compensate for deflection and thickness variation.

Card 3 — Excessive flash and a thinned weld

Symptom: heavy flash on both sides; weld surface below the parent surface.

Category: excessive heat or plunge.

Likely causes: rotation too high or traverse too slow; axial force or plunge depth excessive; incorrect shoulder profile for the application.

Steps: reduce rotation, increase traverse speed, reduce axial force; consider a scrolled shoulder, which draws material inward and reduces flash; verify plunge depth.

Card 4 — Weld quality changed after a tool change

Symptom: parameters unchanged; results differ after fitting a replacement tool.

Category: tool geometry or condition.

Likely causes: replacement tool geometry differs — pin length, thread form, shoulder profile; wear on the previous tool had shifted the process and the new tool restored it; tool not seated or concentric.

Steps: verify the replacement tool against the drawing, particularly pin length; check concentricity and seating; recognize that the tool is a process variable and that changing it is a process change, not a maintenance action — tool identity belongs in the weld record (Section 11).

17. Testing and Quality Verification

ISO 25239-5 sets quality and inspection requirements for friction stir welding of aluminium [S1], and the practical regime combines:

Process monitoring — axial force, torque, traverse force, rotation and traverse speed recorded through the weld. As in friction welding (Chapter 56, Section 18), this signature is the most informative record available and detects deviations that post-weld inspection may not.

Visual inspection — surface finish, flash, weld width and the presence of the exit hole. Surface appearance genuinely indicates the heat balance, though it says nothing about the root.

Radiography — effective for voids and tunnel defects; cannot detect kissing bonds.

Ultrasonic testing — effective for voids; limited for kissing bonds (Section 15).

Destructive testing — bend testing (including root-opening orientations), tensile testing, macro and micro sectioning, and hardness traverses. Metallographic sectioning is the definitive method for root defects and joint line remnants.

Fatigue testing during qualification, particularly where kissing bonds are a credible risk.

18. Safety Specifics

• Very high forces in a machine-tool-like installation: crushing hazards at the tool, fixture and clamping, with guarding and interlocks essential.

• Rotating tool at speed, with entanglement and contact hazards.

• Hot workpiece and tool after welding; the material reaches a substantial fraction of its melting temperature.

• Flash is hot and can be sharp.

• No arc, no fume, no gas, no radiation — a genuine occupational health advantage over every arc process, and one of the reasons the process is favoured in enclosed production environments.

• Noise from the machine and the process.

• Stored energy in a heavily loaded machine structure.

19. Standards and Qualification

• Governing standard family: ISO 25239 for friction stir welding of aluminium, with Part 4 covering welding procedure specification and qualification and Part 5 covering quality and inspection requirements [S1][S2]. Further parts address vocabulary, joint design and operator qualification.

• Process references: ISO 4063 references 431–435 for the friction stir spot variants [S3].

• Procedure qualification variables include tool geometry and identity, rotation and traverse speeds, axial force or plunge depth, tilt angle, material and thickness, joint type, clamping and backing arrangement, and — for dissimilar joints — which material sits on the advancing side.

• Operator qualification is addressed within the ISO 25239 family and by ISO 14732 principles for mechanized processes.

• Acceptance criteria come from ISO 25239-5 and from the product or sector standard. ISO 5817 does not apply — it covers fusion welds, and this is a solid-state process.

20. Worked Example: Root Defects on a Full-Penetration Butt Weld

Situation. A manufacturer friction stir welds aluminium extrusions into panels. Welds pass visual inspection with excellent surface appearance. Sectioning of samples reveals intermittent unwelded regions at the root. Parameters match the qualified procedure and the machine reports no faults.

Step 1 — Note that surface appearance is uninformative about the root. A perfect FSW surface is produced by the shoulder, which never contacts the root. This is directly analogous to keyhole beam welding, where the surface says nothing about penetration (Chapter 54, Section 1), and it means visual inspection cannot be part of the root quality argument.

Step 2 — Check pin length against actual thickness, first. The pin must reach close to the far surface to consolidate the root. Extrusion thickness varies within its tolerance, and a pin length set for nominal thickness will leave an unwelded root on material at the thick end of the tolerance band. Measure the actual material, not the drawing.

Step 3 — Check the plunge depth achieved under load. On a position-controlled machine, deflection of the machine and fixture under the very high axial force reduces the effective plunge depth. The commanded depth and the achieved depth are different numbers, and the difference varies with force. Force-controlled machines compensate for this automatically, which is a strong argument for force control on full-penetration work.

Step 4 — Check backing bar contact along the whole joint. A gap between the workpiece and the backing bar lets the material deflect downward under the tool, so the pin does not reach through. This produces intermittent root defects that correlate with position along the joint rather than with time — a distinctive and diagnostic pattern.

Step 5 — Check clamping and joint abutment. Material that can move or a joint that opens ahead of the tool both starve the root of material.

Step 6 — Distinguish an unwelded root from a kissing bond. Sectioning shows the difference: an unwelded root has a visible gap or unbonded interface; a kissing bond shows surfaces in contact. The two have different remedies and, critically, different detectability — if the defect is a kissing bond, the inspection strategy itself needs revisiting (Section 15).

Step 7 — Correct and lock the controls. Set pin length against measured thickness with an allowance; move to force control if deflection is the cause; verify backing bar continuity as a setup step; and add root-opening bend tests to the sampling regime so the root is being tested in the direction that reveals the defect.

Step 8 — Use the force trace as the production control. The conditions producing root defects — reduced effective plunge, backing gaps, thickness variation — generally show as deviations in the axial force trace. Setting limits on that trace and rejecting welds that fall outside them converts a destructive sampling regime into per-weld verification, which is the recurring conclusion for processes whose critical defects are internal and hard to inspect.

21. Known Gaps

• No parameter values are given. Rotation and traverse speeds, forces and tool geometries are alloy-, thickness- and machine-specific and are established by qualification per ISO 25239-4.

• Tool designs are described functionally. Specific geometries are extensively patented and proprietary, and this reference set names no products.

• Kissing bond detection capability is stated honestly as limited. No general claim about detection reliability would be defensible.

• FSW of steel and titanium is described in outline. Tool material development is the limiting factor and is an active field.

• ISO 25239 part scopes and editions should be confirmed directly; the standard family addresses aluminium specifically, and other materials may be governed by other documents or by contract.

• The ISO 4063 number for continuous friction stir welding is not asserted here; the visible entries in the preview used are the spot variants 431–435, and ISO 25239 is the governing document for the continuous process on aluminium.

1. Process Overview: ISO 4063 References 41x

Ultrasonic metal welding joins two metal parts by applying high-frequency lateral vibration under moderate clamping force. The vibration is applied parallel to the interface — a scrubbing action — rather than perpendicular to it, and this distinction is fundamental.

The ISO nomenclature covers the family [S1]:

| Reference | Process |
| --- | --- |
| 411 | Ultrasonic hot welding |
| 412 | Ultrasonic spot welding |
| 413 | Ultrasonic seam welding |
| 414 | Ultrasonic torsion welding |

The process is dominant in electrical and electronic joining — battery tabs and busbars, wire harness splices, terminal connections, and foil stacks — where the requirement is a low, stable electrical resistance across a joint between thin, highly conductive, often dissimilar metals. That is a combination almost every other process in this reference set handles badly.

2. The Mechanism: Scrub, Disperse, Bond

The cycle lasts from a few tens of milliseconds to a second or two:

1. Clamp. The parts are pressed together between a vibrating sonotrode (horn) and a fixed anvil under a controlled force.

2. Oscillate. The sonotrode vibrates laterally at ultrasonic frequency with an amplitude measured in tens of micrometres. The relative motion between the two parts occurs at their interface.

3. Scrub and disperse. The lateral motion breaks up and disperses surface oxides and contamination, exposing clean metal. Asperities on the two surfaces deform and interlock.

4. Bond. Clean metal in intimate contact under pressure bonds in the solid state. Localized plastic deformation and a modest temperature rise assist, but the joint forms below the melting point.

5. Hold. Vibration stops and force is maintained briefly.

The bond is metallurgical and solid-state. Metallographic sections show interlocked, deformed material at the interface with dispersed oxide, and — with sufficient energy — genuine metallurgical continuity across it.

3. Why It Is Not a Thermal Process

The interface warms, and that warmth assists bonding, but heat is a consequence rather than the mechanism, and treating it as thermal leads to wrong conclusions:

• Peak temperature stays well below melting for the materials involved. Nothing melts, so there is no solidification, no porosity from dissolved gas, and no solidification cracking.

• The heat-affected region is very small, which is why the process can join components with heat-sensitive contents — a battery cell being the standard case, where excessive heating damages internal materials.

• Dissimilar metals are far more tractable than in fusion welding, because time at temperature is measured in milliseconds and intermetallic formation is correspondingly limited (Chapter 27, Section 8).

• Surface preparation requirements are modest, because the scrubbing action performs the cleaning — the same self-cleaning principle as friction and flash welding, delivered by lateral rather than rotary motion.

4. Equipment and Components

| Component | Function | Failure consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Generator | Converts mains power to high-frequency electrical energy at the working frequency | Frequency drift or power limit changes the delivered energy |
| Converter (transducer) | Converts electrical energy to mechanical vibration, usually piezoelectric | Degradation reduces amplitude progressively |
| Booster | Amplifies or reduces the vibration amplitude mechanically | Selects the amplitude range available |
| Sonotrode (horn) | Delivers vibration to the workpiece; its face carries the gripping pattern | A consumable — face wear changes grip and energy transfer |
| Anvil | Reacts the force and grips the lower part; also patterned | As sonotrode — wear changes the process |
| Force system | Applies and maintains clamping force | Force variation changes coupling directly |
| Controller | Controls energy, time, amplitude, force and collapse distance | Determines which control mode governs the weld (Section 7) |
| Fixturing | Positions and supports the parts | Poor support absorbs energy that should reach the interface |

The stack — converter, booster and sonotrode — is a tuned mechanical resonator. Its components are designed to resonate together at the working frequency, and they are not interchangeable across frequencies or arbitrary combinations. A stack that is out of tune delivers reduced amplitude, heats itself, and can fail.

5. The Stack: Converter, Booster, Sonotrode

Two practical consequences of the resonant stack:

Amplitude is set by the stack, not only by the controller. The booster's gain ratio and the sonotrode's design multiply the converter's motion. Changing a booster changes the achievable amplitude range, which is a process change rather than a maintenance action.

Stack condition degrades. Sonotrode faces wear, cracks develop at stress concentrations, and joints between stack components loosen. Symptoms are reduced weld quality at unchanged settings, stack heating, and unusual noise — and a cracked sonotrode can fail suddenly.

6. Knurl Patterns and Tooling

The sonotrode and anvil faces are patterned — knurled, serrated or textured — and this is functional rather than cosmetic:

• The pattern grips the workpiece, so that the sonotrode's motion is transmitted into the upper part rather than sliding across its surface. Without grip, the vibration scrubs the tool against the part instead of scrubbing the two parts against each other.

• The anvil pattern grips the lower part so it does not move with the upper one.

• Pattern geometry affects marking on the workpiece surface — deeper, coarser patterns grip better and mark more.

• Pattern wear is the principal consumable issue. As the knurl rounds off, grip falls, energy transfer into the interface falls, and weld quality declines progressively at unchanged settings. This is the process's version of the wear pattern that recurs throughout this reference set.

Tooling is application-specific: pattern, face size and material are selected for the parts, and tool changes are process changes.

7. Parameters and What Each Controls

| Parameter | Controls | Symptom if wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Amplitude | Scrubbing displacement per cycle; the primary energy control | Too low: insufficient oxide dispersal, weak bond. Too high: excessive deformation, part damage, tool marking, fatigue of thin parts |
| Clamping force | Coupling between tool and part, and interface pressure | Too low: tool slips on the surface instead of driving the interface. Too high: excessive deformation, suppressed relative motion at the interface |
| Weld time / energy / collapse | Total scrubbing delivered | Too little: incomplete bonding. Too much: over-welding, thinning, cracking of thin parts |
| Frequency | Fixed by the stack | Not a production variable |
| Trigger force / pre-force | When welding starts relative to clamping | Affects consistency |
| Hold time | Consolidation after vibration stops | Too short: bond disturbed before it sets |

Control modes matter here and differ from most welding processes. A weld can be controlled by time, by delivered energy, or by collapse distance (the thickness reduction of the stack). Energy and collapse control are generally more robust than time control, because they compensate for variation in coupling — and collapse control in particular tracks the physical result rather than the input.

The force-amplitude relationship is the central interaction. Force must be high enough to couple the tool to the part but not so high that it suppresses the relative motion at the interface that does the welding. That window is the process's core, and it narrows for difficult combinations.

8. Materials and the Thin-to-Thick Rule

Well suited:

| Material | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Aluminium | Excellent; the oxide that makes fusion welding difficult is dispersed by scrubbing |
| Copper | Excellent; the reflectivity and conductivity problems that hamper laser and resistance welding do not apply |
| Nickel, and nickel-plated materials | Widely used for battery tabs |
| Gold, silver | Electronics applications |
| Aluminium to copper | A signature application — the intermetallic problem of fusion welding is largely avoided (Chapter 27, Section 8) |
| Aluminium to nickel, copper to nickel | Battery and electrical joining |

Poorly suited:

| Material | Reason |
| --- | --- |
| Hard, high-strength steels | Do not deform readily under the available energy |
| Thick sections | Energy cannot be delivered through the bulk |
| Brittle materials | Fracture rather than deform |

The thin-to-thick rule. The vibration must be transmitted through the upper part to reach the interface. A thick upper part absorbs and damps the vibration before it arrives. The process therefore works best with a thin part on top and a thicker part beneath — a foil, tab or thin sheet welded to a substantial substrate. Attempting to weld a thick part on top of a thin one is a common setup error and produces poor, inconsistent results for a reason that no parameter change addresses.

9. Joint Design

Lap joints only. The process requires two surfaces in face-to-face contact with the tool able to reach the upper surface and the anvil the lower. Butt joints are not made this way.

Design considerations:

• Access for sonotrode above and anvil below.

• Support: the lower part must be rigidly supported by the anvil, or energy is absorbed in flexing the assembly rather than in scrubbing the interface.

• Surface marking is inevitable where the tools grip, and its acceptability must be considered — this is a real constraint on appearance-critical and thin parts.

• Multiple foils can be welded in a stack, which is why the process suits battery cell tab stacks; but the number of layers is a process variable with a limit.

• Weld area is set by the sonotrode face size, so a larger joint means a larger tool and more power, not a longer weld time.

10. The Variants: Spot, Seam, Torsion, Wire Splicing

Ultrasonic spot welding (412) — the standard configuration, producing a discrete joint the size of the sonotrode face.

Ultrasonic seam welding (413) — a rotating sonotrode wheel traverses the joint, producing a continuous seam. Used for foil and thin sheet, including hermetic seals in some applications.

Ultrasonic torsion welding (414) — the sonotrode applies torsional rather than lateral vibration, producing a circular scrubbing motion. This suits round components and gives a more uniform relative motion distribution than lateral vibration on a circular joint.

Ultrasonic wire splicing — a specific and commercially important configuration in which multiple wire strands are compacted and welded into a solid splice within a shaped anvil. It dominates automotive wire harness manufacture, where the alternative is crimping.

Ultrasonic hot welding (411) — vibration combined with applied heat, extending the range of materials and thicknesses.

11. Setup and Execution Procedure

Before welding

1. Confirm the procedure covers the material combination, thicknesses and layer count.

2. Verify the thin part is on top (Section 8).

3. Inspect the sonotrode and anvil faces for pattern wear and damage — this is the primary consumable check.

4. Verify the stack is correctly assembled and torqued, and that booster and sonotrode match the intended amplitude.

5. Set amplitude, force and the control mode (time, energy or collapse) per the procedure.

6. Confirm the fixture supports the lower part rigidly beneath the anvil.

7. Verify part cleanliness — modest requirements, but heavy grease or thick coatings still interfere.

8. Weld and destructively test setup samples, including a peel test and, where the application is electrical, a resistance measurement (Section 15).

Welding

9. Position the parts against the anvil and cycle the machine.

10. Monitor the process feedback: delivered energy, collapse distance and weld time. On a well-instrumented machine all three are recorded per weld.

11. Watch for surface marking beyond the acceptable level.

12. Sample and test at the established frequency, including at the end of a run.

After welding

13. Inspect the weld surface and the marking.

14. Verify electrical resistance where the joint is an electrical connection.

15. Record energy, collapse, force, amplitude, tool identity and tool cycle count.

12. When to Use Ultrasonic Welding and When Not To

| Choose ultrasonic welding when | Choose something else when |
| --- | --- |
| Electrical joints in aluminium, copper or nickel needing low, stable resistance | The joint is thick, or the upper part is thick |
| Battery tabs, busbars, terminals, foil stacks | Materials are hard, strong or brittle |
| Aluminium to copper or other intermetallic-forming pairs | A butt joint is required |
| Heat-sensitive components — cells, electronics | Tool access above and below is unavailable |
| Very short cycle times at high volume | Surface marking is unacceptable |
| Wire harness splicing | The joint must be leak-tight over a large area |
| No filler, no flux, no gas, no fume is wanted | The parts cannot be rigidly supported |

13. Defect Catalog

| Defect | Detection | Cause | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Weak or unbonded joint | Peel test; electrical resistance | Insufficient energy or amplitude; force too low (tool slipping) or too high (interface motion suppressed); worn tool pattern; thick part on top | Increase energy/amplitude; optimize force within its window; replace worn tooling; verify part orientation |
| High or unstable electrical resistance | Resistance measurement | Incomplete bonded area; oxide not fully dispersed; intermetallic growth in Al-Cu joints over time | Increase energy within limits; verify bonded area by sectioning; assess long-term stability by ageing tests |
| Over-welding: thinning, cracking of the upper part | Visual; dimensional; peel test | Excessive energy, amplitude or collapse | Reduce energy and amplitude; use collapse control to limit deformation |
| Excessive surface marking | Visual | Coarse tool pattern; excessive force; excessive energy | Finer pattern; reduce force; assess acceptability at design stage |
| Tool sticking to the workpiece | Visual; process interruption | Material transfer to the tool face; excessive energy; wrong pattern | Clean or replace tooling; adjust parameters; consider tool coating |
| Progressive quality decline through a run | Sample testing at intervals | Tool pattern wear reducing grip and energy transfer | Establish a tool replacement or refurbishment interval inside the degradation point |
| Cracking of thin foils | Sectioning; visual | Excessive amplitude; too many layers; unsupported foil flexing | Reduce amplitude; support the stack; reduce layer count |
| Inconsistent results between nominally identical parts | Statistics | Fixture support varying; part flatness varying; surface condition varying | Check fixture and part support; check incoming part condition |
| Stack fault: reduced amplitude, heating, noise | Machine feedback; audible | Cracked sonotrode; loose stack joint; degraded converter | Inspect and replace stack components; check torque on stack joints |

14. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Joints weaken gradually over a production run

Symptom: acceptable at start of shift, failing peel tests later; settings unchanged.

Category: tooling wear.

Likely causes: sonotrode and anvil pattern wear reducing grip, so less of the applied motion reaches the interface; material build-up on the tool faces.

Steps: inspect the tool faces against a new tool; clean built-up material; establish a replacement or re-knurling interval based on cycle count rather than on defect occurrence; if the machine records delivered energy against collapse, look for the trend — a worn tool typically shows the same energy producing less collapse.

Card 2 — Electrical resistance acceptable at manufacture, rising in service

Symptom: joints pass resistance testing initially; field returns show high resistance and heating.

Category: intermetallic growth in a dissimilar joint.

Likely causes: aluminium-copper interfaces form intermetallic phases that are both brittle and more resistive, and that grow over time — accelerated by the joint's own resistance heating, which is self-reinforcing (Chapter 27, Section 8).

Steps: assess the as-made bonded area by sectioning — a small bonded area concentrates current and accelerates the mechanism; increase bonded area where the design allows; qualify with accelerated ageing tests rather than initial resistance alone, since initial resistance does not predict service life on this couple.

Card 3 — Inconsistent welds with no obvious cause

Symptom: apparently random variation between nominally identical parts.

Category: support and coupling.

Likely causes: the lower part not rigidly supported by the anvil, so energy is absorbed in flexing; part flatness varying; fixture wear; part surface condition varying.

Steps: check anvil support directly under the weld location; check part flatness on a sample; verify the thin part is on top; check incoming surface condition and any coating variation.

Card 4 — Upper part cracking or thinning

Symptom: the top foil or tab is cracked, torn or excessively thinned at the weld.

Category: over-welding.

Likely causes: energy or amplitude too high; collapse not limited; too many layers for the parameters; unsupported foil flexing during the cycle.

Steps: reduce amplitude and energy; switch to collapse control so the deformation is bounded physically; improve support; reduce the number of layers or increase the tool face area to spread the energy.

15. Testing and Quality Verification

Destructive:

• Peel test — the standard production check, revealing bonded area and bond quality.

• Tensile-shear test.

• Metallographic sectioning — measures the actual bonded area, which is the property that determines both strength and electrical resistance, and reveals intermetallic layers on dissimilar joints.

Non-destructive:

• Electrical resistance measurement — for electrical joints this is the functional test and is frequently applied to every weld in production.

• Visual inspection of marking and deformation.

• Process data: delivered energy, collapse distance, peak power and time, recorded per weld. Because the cycle is very short and fully machine-controlled, this data is complete and is the practical basis for per-weld verification.

The structural point: ultrasonic welds are small, numerous and not amenable to conventional volumetric NDT. The regime that works is per-weld process data plus destructive sampling plus, for electrical joints, resistance measurement — the same pattern as resistance welding (Chapter 51, Section 9).

16. Safety Specifics

• Noise. The working frequency is above the audible range, but sub-harmonics and machine noise frequently are not, and ultrasonic welding installations can produce genuinely uncomfortable and harmful noise levels. Enclosure and hearing protection are common requirements.

• Crushing hazard at the sonotrode and anvil, which close under force on a short cycle — guarding and two-hand controls are standard.

• Vibration exposure if the tool or fixture is contacted during operation.

• Tool failure: a cracked sonotrode can fail energetically.

• No fume, no arc, no radiation, no gas — the process has an unusually clean occupational profile, which is part of its appeal in electronics and battery manufacture.

• Battery-specific hazards where cells are being welded: short-circuit risk, thermal runaway, and the electrical hazards of live assemblies. These frequently dominate the risk assessment and are outside the welding process itself.

17. Standards and Qualification

• Process references: ISO 4063 references 411, 412, 413, 414 [S1].

• Procedure qualification follows the general framework of Chapter 31 with process-specific variables: amplitude, force, energy or collapse, control mode, tooling pattern and identity, material combination, thickness and layer count, and part orientation.

• Operator qualification: ISO 14732 for this mechanized process.

• Application standards dominate. Battery, electrical and electronic assembly standards typically specify the joint requirements — resistance, strength, ageing performance — and take precedence over general welding standards, which have little to say about this process's actual acceptance criteria.

18. Worked Example: Rising Resistance on Battery Tab Welds

Situation. A manufacturer ultrasonically welds nickel-plated tabs to battery cells. Production welds pass peel testing and initial resistance measurement. Field data shows a small proportion of packs developing elevated joint temperatures after months in service.

Step 1 — Recognize that the failure is in service, not at manufacture. The joints passed both tests applied at production. Whatever is happening develops over time, which points to a growth or degradation mechanism rather than a manufacturing defect that was missed.

Step 2 — Identify the credible mechanisms. Two dominate: bonded area smaller than it appears, so the joint carries current through a small area and heats; and intermetallic growth at a dissimilar interface, raising resistance progressively with a self-reinforcing thermal feedback (Chapter 27, Section 8).

Step 3 — Section joints from the affected population and from a good one. Sectioning measures the actual bonded area and reveals any intermetallic layer. This distinguishes the two mechanisms directly, and it is the only method that does.

Step 4 — Question whether the production tests measure what matters. A peel test measures strength, which correlates only loosely with bonded area. An initial resistance measurement on a cold joint may pass even with a small bonded area, because the resistance difference at low current is small. Neither test targets the property that governs service life, which is bonded area and its stability.

Step 5 — Check the process data for the affected units. If energy, collapse and peak power are recorded per weld, the affected joints can be compared against the population. A systematic difference — lower collapse for the same energy, for instance — points at tooling wear at the time those units were made.

Step 6 — Check tooling history against production date. If the affected units cluster around a period late in a tool's life, tool pattern wear is the likely cause: worn knurls transfer less energy to the interface, producing a smaller bonded area at the same settings, with strength that may still pass a peel test.

Step 7 — Correct the process and the test regime together. Set a tool replacement interval inside the degradation point; use collapse or energy control rather than time control so the process compensates for coupling variation; and change the acceptance test to one that measures bonded area, whether by a sectioning sampling regime or by a resistance measurement at a current high enough to be sensitive.

Step 8 — Qualify against ageing, not against initial condition. For aluminium-copper and similar couples, qualification should include accelerated thermal ageing, because the initial measurement does not predict the service behaviour. This is a qualification design point rather than a production one, and it is the durable fix.

19. Known Gaps

• No parameter values are given. Amplitude, force and energy are material-, thickness- and tooling-specific and are established by qualification.

• Frequencies are not stated numerically; they are fixed by the equipment and vary by application scale.

• Tool pattern designs are application-specific and largely proprietary.

• Acceptance criteria come from application standards — battery, electrical and electronic assembly — rather than from welding standards, and are not reproduced here.

• Intermetallic growth rates for dissimilar couples are material- and temperature-specific and must be established by testing.

• Ultrasonic welding of plastics is a large adjacent field using the same equipment principles and entirely different mechanisms; it is outside this reference set's scope (Chapter 21, Section 9).

1. Process Overview: ISO 4063 Reference 441

Explosion welding uses a controlled explosive charge to accelerate one metal plate — the flyer — across a small standoff gap onto a stationary base plate. The two collide at high velocity and at a small angle, and a solid-state bond forms across the entire collision area in microseconds.

The ISO nomenclature lists it as reference 441, explosion welding, alongside 442, magnetic pulse welding (Chapter 62) [S1]. Both belong to the same physical family: high-velocity impact welding, in which the joint is made by a collision rather than by heating.

The process exists for one dominant reason: it joins metal combinations that no fusion process can join, over large areas, in a single operation.

2. The Mechanism: Acceleration, Collision, Jetting

1. Setup. The flyer plate is positioned above the base plate at a controlled standoff distance, either parallel or at a small initial angle. An explosive layer of controlled thickness and detonation velocity is placed on the flyer's upper surface, usually over a protective buffer layer.

2. Detonation. The charge is initiated at one point and the detonation front travels across the plate at a defined velocity.

3. Progressive acceleration. As the detonation front passes each point, the flyer plate beneath it is accelerated downward. The collision point therefore travels across the plate, and it is this progressive, angled collision — not a flat simultaneous impact — that makes the process work.

4. Collision and jetting. At the collision point, the pressure momentarily exceeds the strength of both metals by orders of magnitude, and they behave hydrodynamically. A thin jet of material from both surfaces is squirted forward ahead of the collision point (Section 3).

5. Bonding. Immediately behind the collision point, the freshly exposed, jet-cleaned surfaces are pressed together at enormous pressure and bond in the solid state.

The whole event lasts microseconds, and the bond forms without bulk heating — the plates are cold before and, apart from a very thin interface region, cold afterwards.

3. The Jet: Why the Interface Ends Up Clean

The jet is the process's cleaning mechanism and the reason it works on oxide-covered, contaminated surfaces:

At the collision point, material from the surfaces of both plates is expelled forward as a fine, high-velocity stream. That stream carries away the surface oxide, contamination and the outermost layer of both metals. What is left immediately behind the collision point is virgin metal — never exposed to the atmosphere — pressed together at pressures far above the yield strength of both materials.

Two consequences follow:

1. Surface preparation requirements are modest. Surfaces must be flat, parallel and free of heavy contamination; they do not need to be metallurgically clean, because the jet cleans them.

2. Jetting is a necessary condition. If the collision geometry does not produce a jet, no cleaning occurs and no bond forms. This is why the process has a defined weldability window (Section 5) rather than simply a minimum energy.

4. The Wavy Interface and What It Means

A properly made explosion weld shows a characteristic wavy interface in cross-section — a regular, periodic waveform along the bond line, often with small vortices at the wave crests.

What produces it: the interaction between the travelling collision point and the jet creates an instability analogous to wave formation on a fluid surface. The waves are frozen into the interface as it bonds.

Why it matters:

• The waves are the standard visual evidence of a sound weld. Metallographic examination of an explosion weld looks first for a regular, continuous wave pattern.

• They increase the bonded area and mechanically interlock the two metals.

• Wave amplitude and wavelength vary with the parameters, and their character indicates where in the weldability window the weld was made.

• A flat interface is not necessarily unbonded, but it indicates conditions at the edge of the window.

• Excessive melting at the wave vortices — visible as pockets of solidified material, often intermetallic on dissimilar joints — indicates too much energy, and those pockets are brittle and are a defect.

The metallographic signature is therefore genuinely diagnostic: waves present and regular with minimal vortex melting indicates a weld made in the middle of the window.

5. The Weldability Window

Explosion welding has a well-defined operating window bounded on all sides, and it is one of the clearest examples in this reference set of a process that fails in both directions.

| Boundary | What happens outside it |
| --- | --- |
| Minimum collision velocity / pressure | Insufficient pressure to bond — no weld |
| Minimum collision angle | No jetting — the interface is not cleaned, so no bond forms |
| Maximum collision angle | Jetting becomes unstable |
| Maximum energy / velocity | Excessive melting at the interface, producing continuous melted layers and, on dissimilar joints, brittle intermetallic layers |
| Material limits | Both materials must have sufficient ductility and impact resistance to survive the collision without fracturing |

The window is plotted in the literature as collision velocity against collision angle, and welding parameters are chosen to sit inside it with margin. Both boundaries matter: too little energy gives no bond, and too much gives a brittle melted interface — which on a dissimilar joint is precisely the intermetallic layer the process was chosen to avoid.

6. Equipment and Materials of the Process

There is no machine in the conventional sense. The process consists of:

| Element | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Base plate | The stationary component, supported on a substantial anvil — sand, steel or concrete |
| Flyer plate | The component accelerated onto the base |
| Standoff | Spacers setting the gap; determines acceleration distance and impact velocity |
| Explosive | Selected for detonation velocity — the critical property — and applied at a controlled thickness |
| Buffer layer | Protects the flyer's upper surface from the explosive |
| Initiator | Starts the detonation at a defined point |
| Anvil / support | Reacts the impact; its stiffness affects the result |
| Facility | An outdoor site or a purpose-built chamber with the necessary licensing and separation distances |

Detonation velocity is the key explosive property, because it sets the velocity of the travelling collision point and therefore the collision angle. Explosives are selected and, where necessary, diluted with inert material to achieve the required detonation velocity for the combination being welded.

7. Parameters and What Each Controls

| Parameter | Controls | Symptom if wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Explosive detonation velocity | Collision point velocity, and therefore collision angle | Outside the window: no jetting, or unstable jetting |
| Explosive load (mass per unit area) | Flyer velocity and kinetic energy | Too low: no bond. Too high: excessive melting, plate damage |
| Standoff distance | Acceleration distance and impact velocity | Too small: insufficient velocity. Too large: instability, plate deformation |
| Initial plate angle | Collision angle at the start | Sets where in the window the weld begins |
| Flyer plate thickness | Mass to accelerate; energy required | Interacts with explosive load |
| Surface flatness and parallelism | Consistency of collision conditions across the area | Variation moves parts of the weld outside the window |
| Support / anvil stiffness | Reaction of the impact | Poor support causes plate deformation and inconsistent bonding |

8. Materials and Combinations

The process's defining capability is dissimilar-metal joining across large areas, including combinations impossible by fusion welding.

| Combination | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Titanium to steel | A signature application; no practical fusion route exists (Chapter 27, Section 9) |
| Aluminium to steel | The standard route for structural transition joints |
| Copper to aluminium | Electrical transition joints |
| Copper to steel | Electrical and process equipment |
| Stainless to carbon steel | Clad plate for pressure vessels |
| Nickel alloys to steel | Corrosion-resistant clad plate |
| Zirconium, tantalum, niobium to steel | Chemical process equipment |
| Three-layer combinations | An interlayer is used where the two target metals cannot be directly bonded — for example a compatible intermediate metal between titanium and steel |

Material requirements: both metals must have sufficient ductility and impact toughness to survive the collision. Brittle materials fracture rather than bond, which excludes some hard and brittle alloys. There is no requirement that the two have similar melting points, thermal expansion or metallurgical compatibility in the fusion sense — which is exactly why the process succeeds where fusion welding cannot.

9. Products: Clad Plate, Transition Joints, Tube-to-Tubesheet

Explosion-clad plate is the largest-volume product: a corrosion-resistant or specialized alloy layer bonded to a structural carbon steel backing plate, over areas measured in square metres. The clad plate is then formed, cut and welded into pressure vessels, heat exchangers and process equipment by conventional means — with the cladding's own welding handled as a separate operation.

Transition joints are the process's most strategically valuable product (Chapter 27, Section 10). A bimetallic block, ring or strip is manufactured by explosion welding under factory conditions and supplied as a component. A fabricator then makes two similar-metal welds — one to each side — using ordinary qualified procedures.

Why this matters: it converts an impossible dissimilar weld into two routine welds, and it moves the difficult joint into a controlled factory environment where it is inspected and certified as a product. Common commercial combinations are exactly the pairs that fusion welding handles worst: aluminium-to-steel, titanium-to-steel, copper-to-aluminium and copper-to-steel.

Tube-to-tubesheet explosion welding is a specialist variant using a small explosive charge inside a tube end to expand and weld it into a tubesheet, used in heat exchanger manufacture and repair.

10. Setup and Execution

The process is executed by specialist licensed operators at a licensed facility, and this chapter describes it for understanding rather than as an instruction:

1. Plates are prepared: surfaces machined or ground flat and parallel, and cleaned of heavy contamination.

2. The base plate is placed on its anvil support.

3. Standoff spacers are set to the specified gap, and the flyer plate is positioned.

4. A buffer layer is applied to the flyer's upper surface.

5. The explosive is spread to a controlled thickness over the buffer.

6. The initiator is placed at the specified point.

7. The area is cleared to the required separation distance and the charge is initiated.

8. Plates are recovered, cleaned, and flattened if required.

9. The bond is inspected — ultrasonic testing over the whole area, plus destructive testing of edge coupons (Section 14).

10. Edges, where bonding conditions differ, are trimmed off.

The edge effect is worth stating: at the initiation edge the collision conditions have not yet stabilized, and at the far edge the plate is unsupported. Both edges are routinely trimmed away, and the plate is manufactured oversize for that reason.

11. When to Use Explosion Welding and When Not To

| Choose explosion welding when | Choose something else when |
| --- | --- |
| The metals cannot be fusion welded to each other | The metals can be fusion welded — this is a specialist route |
| Large-area cladding is required | The joint is a conventional seam or fillet |
| A transition joint would convert one impossible weld into two routine ones | Volumes are very small and no standard transition product exists |
| Titanium, zirconium, tantalum or similar clad onto steel | Either material lacks the ductility to survive the collision |
| Very large plate areas in a single operation | A facility, licence and specialist supplier are unavailable |
| Corrosion-resistant clad plate for pressure equipment | The component geometry is complex — the process needs flat or simple surfaces |
| Copper-to-aluminium electrical transitions | The part is finished and cannot be subjected to the impact |

12. Defect Catalog

| Defect | Detection | Cause | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unbonded area | Ultrasonic testing over the full area | Insufficient explosive load; standoff wrong; collision angle outside the jetting window; surface contamination too heavy; local flatness variation | Adjust explosive load and standoff into the window; improve plate flatness and cleanliness |
| Excessive interface melting | Metallography — continuous melted layer at the interface | Energy too high — the upper boundary of the window | Reduce explosive load or adjust detonation velocity |
| Brittle intermetallic layer (dissimilar joints) | Metallography; low ductility in testing | Excessive melting at a dissimilar interface producing intermetallic compounds | Reduce energy; consider an interlayer of a compatible intermediate metal |
| Flat (waveless) interface | Metallography | Conditions at the low-energy edge of the window | Increase energy within the window; assess bond strength by testing |
| Edge unbonding | UT at the plate edges | Initiation and terminal edge effects — inherent | Trim edges; manufacture oversize |
| Plate cracking | Visual | Material insufficiently ductile for the impact; energy too high | Material selection; reduce energy; consider an interlayer |
| Plate distortion / bowing | Dimensional | Impact and residual stress | Flatten after welding; account for it in the process design |
| Surface damage on the flyer's upper face | Visual | Buffer layer inadequate | Improve the buffer; machine the surface afterwards where required |

13. Troubleshooting

Because the process is a single non-repeatable event executed by specialists, troubleshooting is largely a matter of parameter selection before the shot and metallographic diagnosis afterwards:

If a plate shows unbonded areas: examine whether they are edge-related (inherent, trim them), distributed (parameter or standoff problem), or localized (surface flatness or contamination at that location). The distribution pattern identifies the cause.

If the interface shows continuous melting: energy was above the window's upper boundary. On a dissimilar combination this is the most consequential error, because the melted layer is likely to be intermetallic and brittle — the joint may test acceptably in shear and fail in bending or fatigue.

If the interface is flat with no waves: the weld was made near the lower boundary. Bond strength should be verified by testing rather than assumed from the absence of visible defects.

If plates crack: the material's ductility under impact is the limit, and the answer is material selection or an interlayer, not parameter adjustment.

14. Testing and Quality Verification

Ultrasonic testing over the entire bonded area is the standard non-destructive method and is the primary acceptance test for clad plate. It maps bonded and unbonded regions directly, and acceptance criteria specify permissible unbonded area, its size and its distribution.

Destructive testing on coupons cut from the plate edges (which are trimmed anyway):

• Shear test of the bond.

• Bend test, which reveals brittle interfaces that a shear test may not.

• Metallographic sectioning — wave form, wave regularity, melted regions, intermetallic layers.

• Tensile test through the thickness (ram tensile) where the specification requires it.

• Chisel test as a workshop check.

Acceptance criteria are set by the applicable product standard — clad plate for pressure equipment is covered by material specifications that state bond quality requirements, permissible unbonded area and test regimes.

15. Safety Specifics

Explosion welding is an explosives operation, and its hazards are governed by explosives regulation rather than by welding safety practice:

• Licensed explosives handling, storage and use is a legal requirement, with licensed personnel.

• Separation distances and exclusion zones for blast, noise and fragments.

• Blast overpressure and noise affecting the surrounding area, which is why the process is performed at remote sites or in purpose-built chambers.

• Fragments from the plates, spacers and support.

• Fume from the detonation products.

• Ground vibration, which is a planning constraint near other structures.

• Misfire management, a specific explosives-handling discipline.

The practical consequence for a fabricator: this is not an in-house process. It is bought as a manufactured product — clad plate or transition joints — from a licensed specialist supplier, and the fabricator's responsibility is specification, incoming inspection and correct subsequent welding.

16. Standards and Qualification

• Process reference: ISO 4063 reference 441 [S1].

• Product standards govern. Explosion-clad plate is supplied to material specifications that define bond quality, testing and acceptance. The purchase specification is where the requirements live.

• Transition joints are supplied as manufactured components with their own certification, and the fabricator's qualification concerns the two similar-metal welds made to each side, not the bimetallic interface.

• Explosives regulation governs the operation itself.

• Subsequent welding of clad plate is its own discipline: welding the cladding, welding the backing steel, and handling the transition at the clad-to-base boundary each require their own qualified procedures, and the dilution considerations of Chapter 27 apply directly.

17. Worked Example: Specifying a Transition Joint for an Aluminium-to-Steel Structure

Situation. A designer needs to connect an aluminium superstructure to a steel hull. Fusion welding aluminium to steel is not viable (Chapter 27, Section 7). The fabricator has no experience of dissimilar joining and asks how to proceed.

Step 1 — Confirm the fusion route is genuinely closed. Aluminium and iron form brittle intermetallic compounds whenever they are melted together; this is thermodynamics, not a process limitation to be optimized around. A structural fusion weld between them is not an acceptable design.

Step 2 — Identify the available routes. Explosion-welded transition joints; friction stir welding (Chapter 57); mechanical fastening; adhesive bonding; or a bolted connection with isolation. For a structural marine connection carrying load and exposed to seawater, the transition joint is the established answer and is a standard commercial product for this exact application.

Step 3 — Understand what the transition joint does for the fabricator. It converts one impossible weld into two routine ones: an aluminium-to-aluminium weld on one side and a steel-to-steel weld on the other, both made with the fabricator's existing qualified procedures and existing welders. The difficult interface was made and certified in a factory.

Step 4 — Specify the joint properly. The specification must cover the material combination and grades on each side; the section dimensions; the bond quality requirement and test regime; the certification required; and any interlayer if the supplier uses one.

Step 5 — Address the welding heat input constraint, which is the item most often missed. When the fabricator welds to the aluminium side, heat conducted into the bimetallic interface can damage it — excessive temperature at the bond line promotes intermetallic growth in exactly the layer the joint depends on. Suppliers state maximum interface temperatures and minimum distances from the interface for welding. This constraint must be in the fabricator's WPS, and it is a real and enforceable requirement.

Step 6 — Address galvanic corrosion. An aluminium-steel connection in a marine environment is a galvanic cell (Chapter 27, Section 11). The transition joint solves the metallurgical problem and does not by itself solve the corrosion problem — coating, sealing and detailing to prevent electrolyte retention at the joint remain necessary.

Step 7 — Plan incoming inspection. The transition joint arrives with certification. The fabricator should verify the certification, verify dimensions, and — depending on criticality — perform incoming ultrasonic verification of the bond.

Step 8 — Record the reasoning. The decision not to fusion weld, and the constraints attaching to the transition joint, are engineering knowledge that must survive into the fabrication documentation. A transition joint welded without the interface temperature limit being observed will fail, and the failure will look inexplicable to anyone who does not know the constraint existed.

18. Known Gaps

• No parameters are given. Explosive selection, load, standoff and geometry are combination-specific, are established by specialist suppliers, and are inappropriate to publish in a general reference.

• Weldability window boundaries are described qualitatively. Published windows exist per material combination and must be taken from the specialist literature.

• Acceptance criteria for clad plate are set by material and product specifications and are not reproduced here.

• Interface temperature limits for transition joints are supplier-specific and must be obtained with the product.

• This chapter does not enable anyone to perform the process. It is described for specification, selection and inspection purposes; the operation itself requires licensed explosives capability.
