1. Process Overview: ISO 4063 Reference 48 and the Roll Bonding Family

Cold pressure welding joins metals at room temperature, with no applied heat at all, purely by plastic deformation under pressure. No arc, no flame, no resistance heating, no friction heating — the only energy input is mechanical work, and any temperature rise is an incidental consequence of that work rather than the mechanism.

The ISO nomenclature places cold pressure welding in group 4 with the other pressure welding processes; roll welding, in which the deformation is applied by rolling rather than by dies, belongs to the same family, and coextrusion welding is listed as reference 493 [S1].

The processes are used where any heating would be unacceptable, where the metals form intermetallics on melting, or where a continuous bonded strip or plate is required in bulk.

2. The Mechanism: Film Breakup and Virgin Metal Contact

Clean metal surfaces brought into intimate contact bond spontaneously — metallic bonding requires no activation energy. The reason two pieces of metal placed together do not weld is that every metal surface in air carries an oxide film, and it is the film, not the metal, that is in contact.

Cold pressure welding works by defeating that film mechanically:

1. Surface preparation removes the existing oxide and leaves a hard, brittle, freshly formed thin oxide over clean metal (Section 4).

2. Deformation. The parts are pressed together and forced to deform substantially. As the metal beneath the surface flows plastically, the surface area increases dramatically.

3. Film fracture. The oxide film is hard and brittle relative to the metal beneath it. It cannot stretch with the expanding surface, so it fractures into islands.

4. Virgin metal extrusion. Clean metal from beneath is extruded through the gaps between the oxide fragments.

5. Bonding. Where virgin metal from one part meets virgin metal from the other under pressure, a metallic bond forms instantly.

The oxide is never removed from the joint — it remains as dispersed fragments within the bond. The bond forms in the areas between them, which is why the degree of deformation determines the bonded fraction and therefore the joint strength.

3. The Threshold Deformation

This is the process's defining characteristic and the fact that governs every design decision around it.

Below a threshold amount of deformation, no bond forms at all. Not a weak bond — no bond. The surface expansion has been insufficient to fracture the oxide film and extrude virgin metal through it.

Above the threshold, bond strength rises rapidly with further deformation, as the bonded fraction increases.

The threshold is material-specific and is expressed as a percentage reduction in thickness or area. It is typically substantial — for aluminium it is a large fraction of the original thickness, and for harder metals it is higher still. This has direct consequences:

• The joint is visibly and permanently deformed. A cold pressure weld is not a subtle joint; the material at the joint has been squeezed to a fraction of its original thickness, and the design must accommodate that.

• Insufficient deformation produces a complete failure, not a marginal one, which is a useful property: the process tends to fail obviously.

• Design must provide for the deformation — the flash, the dimensional change and the space to contain them.

• Hard materials require deformations that may be unachievable with practical equipment, which is what limits the process's material range.

4. Why Surface Preparation Is the Entire Process

In every other process in this reference set, surface preparation is one variable among several. In cold pressure welding it is the dominant variable, and a process that fails almost always failed here.

The requirement: the surfaces must be degreased and then mechanically cleaned to produce a clean, hard surface. The standard method is scratch brushing with a rotating stainless steel wire brush of specified wire diameter and stiffness, which removes the existing thick oxide and leaves a hardened, freshly abraded surface carrying only a very thin new oxide.

Why the sequence matters:

• Degrease first, then brush. Brushing a greasy surface drives contamination into the metal, and hydrocarbon contamination prevents bonding completely — it is not displaced by deformation the way oxide is.

• The brushed surface is deliberately hardened, so the thin oxide on it is brittle and fractures readily under deformation. A soft, polished surface is worse, not better.

• Time between preparation and welding must be short, because the oxide regrows. The permitted interval is short — minutes to hours depending on the metal and the environment.

• Do not touch the prepared surfaces. Fingerprints are hydrocarbon contamination.

• The brush is dedicated to the material and is itself a controlled item; a brush that has been used on another material transfers contamination.

The single most common cause of cold pressure welding failure is inadequate or stale surface preparation, and it is worth stating as bluntly as that, because operators unfamiliar with the process reasonably assume that a process using this much force must be tolerant of a slightly dirty surface. It is not.

5. Cold Pressure Butt Welding

The dominant industrial application, used for joining wire, rod and bar end to end.

The cycle:

1. The two ends are cut square and prepared.

2. Each is gripped in a die that clamps close to the end, leaving a controlled short length protruding.

3. The dies are driven together, upsetting the protruding material and forcing it to flow radially outward as flash.

4. Several successive upsets may be applied, with the flash trimmed between them, to accumulate the required deformation.

5. The flash is trimmed off, leaving a joint with little or no remaining upset.

Applications: aluminium and copper wire and rod joining in wire drawing plants and cable manufacture, where a joint must pass through subsequent drawing dies; and joining of wire in continuous processing lines. The joint must survive the same drawing reduction as the parent wire, which is a demanding requirement that this process meets.

6. Cold Pressure Lap and Spot Welding

Two overlapping sheets are pressed between shaped punches that force a locally very large deformation — commonly reducing the combined thickness of both sheets to a small fraction of the original.

Applications: sealing and joining of thin non-ferrous sheet, container and packaging closures, electrical connections, and any application where heating is unacceptable.

Characteristics: the joint is visibly indented on both faces; the process is fast and needs no consumables; and the strength depends directly on the deformation achieved.

7. Roll Bonding

Two or more metal strips are passed together through a rolling mill under sufficient reduction to bond them across their whole width, producing clad strip or plate in a continuous process.

Cold roll bonding achieves the bond by deformation alone, at room temperature, and requires a large reduction in a single pass — commonly a majority of the combined thickness. Surface preparation before the mill is the same scratch-brushing discipline as Section 4, applied continuously in line.

Hot roll bonding applies heat as well, which lowers the deformation required and allows diffusion to contribute (Chapter 61). It is used for thicker clad products.

Post-bond annealing is frequently applied after cold roll bonding, both to restore ductility after the heavy deformation and to allow diffusion across the interface to strengthen the bond further.

Products: clad strip for coinage, cookware bases (aluminium or copper cores in stainless), bimetallic strip for thermostats, electrical contact strip, and heat exchanger cladding.

Roll bonding competes with explosion welding (Chapter 59) for clad product: roll bonding is continuous, high-volume and suited to strip and thinner plate; explosion welding is a batch process suited to thick plate and to combinations too dissimilar for rolling.

8. Equipment and Components

| Component | Function | Failure consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dies / punches | Grip the parts and apply the deformation | Die geometry sets the deformation; wear changes it progressively |
| Clamping mechanism | Holds the parts against the upsetting force | Slipping reduces achieved deformation without changing the setting |
| Force system (mechanical, hydraulic or pneumatic) | Delivers the upsetting force | Force capacity limits the material and section that can be joined |
| Rolling mill (roll bonding) | Applies the reduction | Roll force, gap and condition determine the bond |
| Scratch brushing station | Prepares the surfaces | The most critical element in the whole process |
| Flash trimming | Removes the upset flash | Trimming into the parent metal leaves a notch |

For wire butt welding the equipment is frequently a small hand-operated or bench machine, which understates how process-critical the preparation is.

9. Parameters and What Each Controls

| Parameter | Controls | Symptom if wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deformation (upset distance or reduction ratio) | Whether a bond forms at all | Below threshold: no bond. Excessive: material damage, excessive flash, cracking |
| Die geometry and grip length | How the deformation is distributed | Wrong grip length: buckling instead of upsetting |
| Clamping force | Whether the parts move in the dies | Slipping reduces effective deformation |
| Number of upset stages | Accumulated deformation | Some materials require multiple stages with flash trimming between |
| Surface preparation quality and freshness | Whether virgin metal can meet virgin metal | Inadequate or stale preparation: no bond, regardless of deformation |
| Roll force and gap (roll bonding) | Reduction achieved | Insufficient reduction: no bond across the width |
| Post-bond anneal | Ductility and diffusion bonding | Omitted where needed: brittle, weak bond |

Note the pattern: two parameters — deformation and surface preparation — dominate absolutely, and both are threshold variables rather than continuous ones. This makes the process unusually binary in its behaviour, which is both its main difficulty and, once controlled, its main virtue.

10. Materials

Well suited — soft, ductile, face-centred cubic metals:

| Material | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Aluminium | The classic application; excellent |
| Copper | Excellent |
| Silver, gold, lead, tin | Very readily cold welded |
| Nickel | Feasible with higher deformation |
| Aluminium to copper | A significant application — no melting, so no intermetallics form (Chapter 27, Section 8) |

Poorly suited:

| Material | Reason |
| --- | --- |
| Steels | Require deformation levels that are impractical for most equipment |
| Hard and high-strength alloys | Insufficient ductility; fracture rather than flow |
| Materials with tenacious, thick or ductile oxide | The film does not fracture cleanly |
| Any material that work-hardens rapidly | The required deformation cannot be reached before cracking |

The aluminium-to-copper capability deserves emphasis. Because there is no melting and no significant heating, intermetallic phases do not form at the time of welding — the dominant failure mechanism for this couple in every fusion process. The joint's long-term behaviour still depends on service temperature, since diffusion continues slowly in service, but the as-made joint is free of the brittle layer that fusion welding produces immediately.

11. When to Use These Processes and When Not To

| Choose cold pressure welding when | Choose something else when |
| --- | --- |
| Any heating is unacceptable — heat-sensitive assemblies, explosive atmospheres, no power available | The material is steel or another hard alloy |
| Aluminium or copper wire and rod joining | The deformation and flash cannot be accommodated by the design |
| Aluminium to copper electrical joints without intermetallics | Surface preparation cannot be controlled |
| Continuous clad strip production (roll bonding) | The joint must be made in a contaminated environment |
| No consumables, no fume, no gas, no arc is wanted | High strength across a thick section is required |
| Sealing and joining thin non-ferrous sheet | The parts cannot be gripped and deformed |
| Joints that must survive subsequent drawing or forming | Appearance at the joint matters and deformation is unacceptable |

12. Defect Catalog

| Defect | Detection | Cause | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| No bond at all | Pulls apart by hand or in the first test | Deformation below the threshold, or inadequate/stale surface preparation | Increase deformation; re-establish the preparation discipline (Section 4) |
| Partial bonding / low strength | Tensile or twist test; sectioning | Deformation marginal; preparation inconsistent; contamination on part of the surface | Increase deformation; verify brushing coverage and freshness |
| Contamination-related failure | Bond surfaces clean and shiny on separation | Grease or oil not removed before brushing, or surfaces touched afterwards | Degrease before brushing; handle with clean gloves; enforce the time limit before welding |
| Cracking of the parent material | Visual | Deformation beyond the material's ductility; work hardening; too few upset stages | Use multiple staged upsets with trimming between; select a more ductile temper |
| Buckling instead of upsetting | Visual | Grip length too long for the section; die geometry wrong | Reduce protruding length; correct die selection |
| Slipping in the dies | Short achieved deformation | Clamping force insufficient; die faces worn or contaminated | Increase clamping force; service die faces |
| Notch at the joint after flash trimming | Visual; failure in service | Trimming cut into the parent metal | Control trimming; dress smoothly |
| Roll bonding: unbonded areas across the width | Ultrasonic; peel test | Reduction insufficient; strip surface preparation inconsistent across the width; roll force variation | Increase reduction; verify brushing across the full width; check mill condition |
| Bond degrading in service (Al-Cu) | Resistance rise; sectioning | Diffusion at service temperature slowly forming intermetallics | Limit service temperature; qualify with ageing tests |

13. Troubleshooting

If nothing bonds at all, check in this order: was the surface degreased before brushing; was it brushed with a correct, dedicated brush; how long between brushing and welding; was the achieved deformation measured (not the setting); and did the parts slip in the dies. In practice the answer is nearly always one of the first three.

If bonding is intermittent, look for what varies between parts: brushing coverage, elapsed time before welding, handling between preparation and welding, incoming material surface condition, and die wear. Intermittency in this process points at preparation consistency far more often than at force.

If bonds are weak but present, deformation is marginal. Measure the achieved deformation and compare with the threshold for the material; increase it, using staged upsets if a single stage cracks the material.

If the material cracks, the required deformation is at or beyond the material's ductility. Options are a softer temper, multiple staged upsets with trimming between, or accepting that the material is unsuitable for the process.

14. Testing and Quality Verification

The joint has no fusion zone, no heat-affected zone and no discontinuity in the conventional sense, so the testing regime is functional rather than volumetric:

Destructive:

• Tensile test — for wire and rod butt welds, the standard check, with the expectation that a sound joint breaks in the parent metal rather than at the weld.

• Twist and bend tests — sensitive to partial bonding.

• Drawing test — for wire joints, drawing the joint through the production dies is the functional test that matters.

• Peel test — for lap and roll-bonded joints.

• Sectioning — measures deformation achieved and reveals unbonded regions.

Non-destructive:

• Visual and dimensional — verifying the deformation achieved, which is directly measurable and is the process's primary indicator.

• Ultrasonic testing for roll-bonded plate over the bonded area.

• Electrical resistance for electrical joints.

The most useful production control is measuring the deformation achieved, because it is the variable that determines whether a bond exists and it is measurable on every joint without destroying it.

15. Safety Specifics

• High mechanical forces with crushing hazards at the dies; guarding and two-hand control are standard.

• Rotating wire brushes at the preparation station — a significant hazard in their own right, ejecting wire fragments; guarding and eye protection are required.

• Flash and trimmed material are sharp.

• Rolling mills carry their own substantial machinery hazards, including entanglement at the roll bite.

• No fume, no arc, no radiation, no gas, no heat — the process has essentially no welding-specific occupational health hazards, which is one of the reasons it is chosen for hazardous environments.

• Suitability for explosive atmospheres is a genuine and specific advantage: with no arc and no heat, cold pressure welding can be performed where any thermal process would be prohibited.

16. Standards and Qualification

• Process references: cold pressure welding within ISO 4063 group 4; 493 coextrusion welding is separately listed [S1].

• Product standards govern for clad strip and plate produced by roll bonding, specifying bond quality and test regimes.

• Wire and cable industry practice governs cold pressure butt welding of wire, where the functional requirement — surviving subsequent drawing — is the acceptance criterion.

• Procedure qualification follows the general framework of Chapter 31 with the process-specific variables of Section 9: deformation, die geometry, surface preparation method and time limit, and material and temper.

• The surface preparation procedure is a qualification variable, not a work instruction detail, and should be documented with the brush specification and the maximum permitted interval before welding.

17. Worked Example: Intermittent Failures on Cold-Welded Wire Splices

Situation. A wire drawing plant joins aluminium rod ends by cold pressure butt welding before drawing. Most joints survive drawing. Roughly one in twenty breaks at the joint in the drawing die, stopping the line. Machine settings are unchanged.

Step 1 — Recognize the failure mode's significance. A joint that survives handling but fails in the drawing die was bonded, but only partially — enough for handling loads, not enough for the drawing reduction. That points at marginal bonded area rather than at no bond.

Step 2 — Establish whether the deformation achieved is consistent. Measure the upset achieved on a sample of joints rather than reading the machine setting. Die wear, clamping slip and rod diameter variation all reduce achieved deformation without changing the setting.

Step 3 — Examine the surface preparation discipline directly, by watching it. The questions are concrete: is the rod degreased before brushing; is the brush dedicated, and is it worn; is the brushing covering the whole end face; how long elapses between brushing and welding; do operators handle the prepared ends. Any of these varying between operators or through a shift produces exactly a one-in-twenty pattern.

Step 4 — Check the elapsed time specifically. Oxide regrowth is time-dependent. If the practice is to prepare several rod ends and then weld them in sequence, the last one welded has a substantially older prepared surface than the first. This is a common and easily overlooked cause of intermittent failure, and the remedy — prepare and weld one at a time — costs nothing.

Step 5 — Check the incoming rod condition. Rod that has been stored in a humid environment, or that carries drawing lubricant residue from a previous operation, presents a different surface to the brush. Batch-to-batch variation in incoming condition produces intermittency that looks like process variation.

Step 6 — Check die condition and clamping. Worn dies grip less well and slip; slipping reduces the achieved upset invisibly.

Step 7 — Correct with controls rather than force. Increasing the upset setting compensates for a preparation problem only partially and at the cost of more flash and more material. The durable fixes are: prepare and weld immediately, one joint at a time, with a stated maximum interval; a dedicated brush with a replacement interval; degreasing before brushing as a mandatory step; and measurement of achieved upset as a routine check.

Step 8 — Use the drawing die as the acceptance test it already is. The line already tests every joint functionally, at the point of failure. Recording which joints fail against operator, shift, rod batch and time since brush change turns that into diagnostic data at no extra cost — and on a process this sensitive to preparation, that correlation is usually what identifies the cause.

18. Known Gaps

• No threshold deformation values are given. They are material- and configuration-specific and are established by trial; published figures vary with test method.

• Surface preparation time limits are not stated numerically and depend on material, environment and humidity.

• Brush specifications — wire diameter, stiffness, speed — are established by the equipment supplier and by trial.

• Roll bonding reduction requirements are product- and material-specific and are proprietary to producers.

• Coextrusion welding (493) is named but not developed.

• Long-term behaviour of aluminium-copper cold welds in service depends on service temperature and time, and requires application-specific qualification.

1. Process Overview: ISO 4063 Reference 45x

Diffusion welding joins two surfaces by holding them in contact under pressure at elevated temperature, in a controlled atmosphere or vacuum, for a period long enough for atoms to diffuse across the interface until it ceases to exist as a distinguishable boundary.

The ISO nomenclature lists 451, hot isostatic pressure welding within the group 4 pressure welding family [S1]; diffusion welding generally belongs to the same group.

Three characteristics distinguish it from every other process in this reference set:

• Nothing melts, and there is no macroscopic deformation. Unlike friction, cold pressure and impact welding, the parts do not change shape appreciably.

• The cycle is measured in hours, not seconds.

• The finished joint can be metallurgically indistinguishable from the parent metal — no fusion zone, no heat-affected zone, no deformed zone, and in a well-made joint no visible interface at all.

That last property is the reason the process exists: it produces joints with parent-metal properties in geometries and materials no other process can serve.

2. The Mechanism: Contact, Creep, Diffusion

Two clean metal surfaces held together at temperature will bond, because the atoms do not distinguish between "my crystal" and "the other crystal." The obstacles are that real surfaces touch only at asperities, and that oxide films separate the metal.

Diffusion welding overcomes both by time, temperature and pressure acting together:

• Pressure brings the surfaces into intimate contact by deforming asperities, and is kept low enough that the parts do not change shape macroscopically.

• Temperature — typically a substantial fraction of the melting temperature — softens the material so asperities creep into contact, and provides the atomic mobility for diffusion.

• Time allows creep to close the remaining voids and diffusion to eliminate the interface.

The three trade against each other: higher temperature or pressure shortens the time required; lower temperature or pressure lengthens it. The choice is bounded by what the material and the part can tolerate.

3. The Three Stages in Detail

Stage 1 — Asperity deformation and initial contact. Under pressure at temperature, the high points on both surfaces deform plastically and by creep. Contact area grows from a small fraction of the nominal area to a large one. Voids remain between the contacting regions, forming a network along the interface.

Stage 2 — Void shrinkage by creep and diffusion. The remaining voids shrink. Material creeps into them and atoms diffuse along grain boundaries and through the lattice to fill them. The interface becomes a series of isolated, shrinking pores rather than a continuous void network.

Stage 3 — Interface elimination. Grain boundaries migrate across the original interface, and the remaining micro-voids are eliminated. In a fully completed bond the original interface is no longer identifiable metallographically, and grains span what was once the joint.

Incomplete bonding means the cycle stopped at stage 1 or 2 — a line of residual voids along the interface, or a continuous flat interface with grains on either side that never migrated across it. Both are detectable metallographically and both reduce properties, particularly in fatigue and in the through-thickness direction.

4. Why Surface Condition Dominates

Because there is no melting, no macroscopic deformation, no scrubbing and no jetting, nothing in this process removes surface contamination or oxide. Everything present on the surfaces at the start is still there at the end, either dissolved into the material or trapped at the interface.

The consequence is a set of surface requirements more demanding than any other process in this reference set:

• Flatness and parallelism must be sufficient that the applied pressure produces intimate contact across the whole area. A gap that pressure cannot close is a permanent void.

• Surface finish is specified — smooth enough that asperities are small and close readily, but not so polished that the surfaces cannot key together. Machining or lapping to a specified roughness is normal.

• Cleanliness is absolute. Degreasing, chemical cleaning, and often etching immediately before assembly. Handling with clean gloves.

• Oxide removal immediately before assembly for metals whose oxide is stable — and this is the process's central difficulty on aluminium and titanium, whose oxides reform instantly (Section 5).

• Time between preparation and loading must be short, with assembly sometimes performed in a controlled atmosphere.

The general rule: if a fusion process would tolerate a surface, diffusion welding probably will not.

5. Interlayers and Why They Are Used

A thin foil or coating of a different metal placed between the surfaces — an interlayer — is used routinely, for several distinct reasons:

| Purpose | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Reduce required temperature, pressure or time | A softer interlayer deforms more readily and diffuses faster |
| Break up stable oxide | Some interlayers dissolve or disrupt the oxide film that would otherwise block bonding |
| Bridge dissimilar metals | An interlayer compatible with both avoids a direct interface that would form brittle intermetallics (Chapter 27) |
| Accommodate thermal expansion mismatch | A ductile interlayer absorbs the strain from differential expansion during heating and cooling |
| Fill minor surface irregularities | A soft foil conforms to imperfections that rigid surfaces cannot close |

The trade-off: the interlayer becomes part of the joint. Its properties — strength, corrosion resistance, melting point, and the phases it forms with both parents — are now the joint's properties in that region, and must be assessed as such rather than treated as a process aid.

Transient liquid phase bonding is the related process in which the interlayer melts at the bonding temperature, wets the surfaces, and then solidifies isothermally as its melting-point-depressing element diffuses away into the parents. The joint ends up with a composition close to the parent and a melting point above the bonding temperature — which is why it can serve at temperatures above the one at which it was made. It sits between diffusion welding and brazing (Chapter 66) and is used extensively in nickel superalloy repair.

6. Hot Isostatic Pressure Welding

Reference 451 [S1] applies pressure isostatically — via a gas, usually argon, at high pressure in a heated vessel — rather than through a mechanical ram.

Why it matters:

• Pressure is applied uniformly from all directions, so complex shapes and internal surfaces are bonded as effectively as flat ones. A mechanical press can only push along one axis.

• No dies or fixtures are needed to transmit pressure, so parts of arbitrary shape can be processed.

• It is the same equipment used for densifying castings and powder consolidation, so the capability often already exists in an organization for other reasons.

• The parts must be encapsulated or the interfaces sealed, so that the pressurizing gas acts on the outside of the assembly rather than entering the joint — a canned or sealed assembly is the standard arrangement.

7. Equipment and Components

| Component | Function | Failure consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Furnace or heated press | Provides and controls temperature over hours | Temperature uniformity across the part is critical — cold regions do not bond |
| Vacuum or controlled atmosphere system | Prevents oxidation during the long cycle | Loss of vacuum or atmosphere purity oxidizes the interface and prevents bonding |
| Pressure system | Mechanical ram, or isostatic gas pressure | Pressure uniformity determines bonding uniformity |
| Tooling and fixtures | Position the parts and transmit pressure | Must survive the cycle temperature without reacting with the parts |
| Instrumentation | Temperature, pressure, time, atmosphere | The cycle record is the process evidence |
| Cleaning and preparation facility | Machining, lapping, chemical cleaning | The determining capability (Section 4) |

Cycle time dominates the economics. Heating a large mass to temperature, holding for hours, and cooling under control means cycles measured in many hours or a full day, with the furnace occupied throughout.

8. Parameters and What Each Controls

| Parameter | Controls | Symptom if wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Temperature | Atomic mobility and creep rate | Too low: incomplete bonding whatever the time. Too high: grain growth, property loss, distortion, unwanted phase formation |
| Pressure | Asperity contact and void closure | Too low: voids remain. Too high: macroscopic deformation of the part — which defeats the process's purpose |
| Time | Extent of diffusion and void elimination | Too short: stage 1 or 2 bonding with residual voids. Too long: grain growth, cost |
| Atmosphere / vacuum quality | Whether surfaces stay clean during the long hold | Poor vacuum: oxidation during the cycle; no bond |
| Surface finish and flatness | Initial contact area | Beyond tolerance: permanent unbonded regions |
| Interlayer material and thickness | Bonding kinetics and joint properties | Wrong choice: brittle phases or a weak joint |
| Heating and cooling rates | Distortion and residual stress | Too fast: distortion, cracking on dissimilar joints |

The three primary parameters are interchangeable within limits, and process development consists largely of finding the combination that achieves full bonding without exceeding the deformation, grain growth or property-loss limits of the material.

9. Materials and Combinations

Well suited:

| Material | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Titanium and its alloys | The premier application — titanium's oxide dissolves into the metal at bonding temperature, which removes the film problem that blocks most other metals |
| Nickel superalloys | Aerospace components; transient liquid phase bonding widely used |
| Refractory metals | Few alternatives |
| Stainless steels | Feasible; oxide stability requires attention |
| Copper | Readily bonded |
| Dissimilar combinations | A principal reason to choose the process, generally with an interlayer |

Difficult:

| Material | Reason |
| --- | --- |
| Aluminium | The oxide is extremely stable, does not dissolve into the metal, and reforms instantly. Requires interlayers or special surface treatment; a well-known difficulty |
| Materials with stable, non-dissolving oxides generally | The film blocks diffusion and nothing in the process removes it |
| Materials that grain-coarsen at bonding temperature | The cycle degrades the parent properties |

The titanium case is worth understanding, because it explains why the process is so strongly associated with that metal: at diffusion bonding temperatures, titanium dissolves its own oxide into the bulk metal. The film that would block bonding simply disappears into the material. Almost no other structural metal does this, and it is why titanium diffusion bonding is a production process while aluminium diffusion bonding is a research and specialist activity.

10. Diffusion Bonding With Superplastic Forming

A combined process of real industrial significance: superplastic forming and diffusion bonding (SPF/DB).

Certain alloys — notably some titanium alloys — exhibit superplasticity at elevated temperature: they can be stretched to very large strains without necking, like a thermoplastic. The temperature at which they are superplastic is close to the temperature at which they diffusion bond.

The combined process exploits this: sheets are selectively bonded together in a pattern by diffusion bonding, then gas pressure is applied to inflate the unbonded regions, which stretch superplastically into a die. The result is a complex, hollow, internally stiffened structure made in one operation from flat sheet — with integral internal ribs where the bonds were.

It is used for aerospace structures, and it produces geometries that could not be assembled by any conventional joining route.

11. Joint Design

| Consideration | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Surface accessibility for preparation | Both surfaces must be machinable, cleanable and inspectable before assembly |
| Pressure transmission | Mechanical pressure must reach the interface; complex geometry favours isostatic pressure |
| Flatness and conformity | The surfaces must be capable of intimate contact under the available pressure |
| Thermal expansion | On dissimilar joints, expansion mismatch generates stress during heating and cooling — a ductile interlayer or a matched pair is needed |
| No filler is added | The joint has no reinforcement and no fillet |
| Assembly must be held in position | Fixturing must survive the cycle without reacting with the parts |
| Part distortion | Long exposure at temperature under load can creep the whole part, not just the joint |

12. Setup and Execution Procedure

Before bonding

1. Confirm the procedure covers the materials, interlayer, cycle and part geometry.

2. Machine or lap the surfaces to the specified finish and flatness; verify by measurement.

3. Clean thoroughly: degrease, chemical clean, and etch where specified; handle only with clean gloves thereafter.

4. Assemble immediately, with the interlayer if used, minimizing the time in air.

5. Fixture the assembly to maintain alignment and transmit pressure; verify fixture materials will not react with the parts at temperature.

6. For isostatic processing, encapsulate or seal the assembly.

7. Load into the furnace; establish vacuum or atmosphere and verify it before heating.

Bonding

8. Heat at the controlled rate to the bonding temperature.

9. Apply the specified pressure.

10. Hold for the specified time, monitoring temperature uniformity, pressure and atmosphere throughout.

11. Cool at the controlled rate, releasing pressure per the procedure.

After bonding

12. Remove and, where encapsulated, remove the can.

13. Inspect: ultrasonic testing of the bonded area; sectioning of trial pieces (Section 16).

14. Verify dimensions — creep during the cycle can change them.

15. Record the full cycle: temperature at each thermocouple, pressure and atmosphere against time. This record is the process evidence, and a bond cannot be shown to have been made correctly without it.

13. When to Use Diffusion Welding and When Not To

| Choose diffusion welding when | Choose something else when |
| --- | --- |
| Parent-metal properties are required across the joint | A fusion or solid-state alternative can meet the requirement |
| No macroscopic deformation is acceptable | Cycle time of hours cannot be accommodated |
| Titanium or nickel superalloy components | The material is aluminium, unless a qualified interlayer route exists |
| Large or complex bonded areas, including internal surfaces (with isostatic pressure) | Surfaces cannot be machined, cleaned and assembled cleanly |
| Dissimilar combinations with a suitable interlayer | Volumes are high and cycle cost matters |
| Multiple joints made simultaneously in one furnace cycle | The part cannot tolerate the temperature and time |
| Combined with superplastic forming for hollow structures | Inspection of the bonded area would be impossible |
| Internal passages and channels that cannot be welded from outside | A simpler process meets the need |

The multiple-joints point is a genuine economic argument: a single furnace cycle can bond many joints, or many assemblies, simultaneously. The cycle is long but it is not per-joint, which changes the economics substantially for assemblies with many internal interfaces — heat exchanger cores being the standard example.

14. Defect Catalog

| Defect | Detection | Cause | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unbonded region / residual voids | Ultrasonic; sectioning | Insufficient time, temperature or pressure; surface flatness beyond tolerance; contamination | Extend the cycle or raise temperature/pressure within limits; improve surface flatness and finish |
| Continuous flat interface with no grain migration | Metallography | Stage 2 bonding only — the cycle stopped before interface elimination | Extend hold time; raise temperature |
| Oxide layer at the interface | Metallography; poor bond strength | Surfaces oxidized before or during the cycle; poor vacuum or atmosphere; time in air before loading | Verify vacuum and atmosphere; shorten the interval between preparation and loading; consider an interlayer |
| Contamination-related non-bonding | Bond surfaces clean on separation | Hydrocarbon residue from handling or cleaning | Enforce the cleaning and handling procedure |
| Macroscopic deformation of the part | Dimensional inspection | Pressure too high, or creep over the long hold at temperature | Reduce pressure; reduce temperature and extend time; support the part |
| Grain growth and property loss | Metallography; mechanical testing | Temperature too high or hold too long for the material | Reduce temperature; use an interlayer to shorten the cycle |
| Brittle intermetallic layer (dissimilar joints) | Metallography; low ductility | Direct contact between incompatible metals; interlayer wrong or too thin | Select a compatible interlayer; reduce time at temperature |
| Cracking on cooling (dissimilar joints) | Visual; NDT | Thermal expansion mismatch generating stress | Ductile interlayer; controlled cooling rate; design for the mismatch |
| Non-uniform bonding across a large area | Ultrasonic mapping | Temperature or pressure non-uniformity across the part | Verify furnace uniformity with multiple thermocouples; verify pressure distribution; consider isostatic pressure |

15. Troubleshooting

Unbonded regions distributed across the area point at insufficient cycle parameters — time, temperature or pressure — or at overall surface condition.

Unbonded regions in a specific location point at local flatness, local contamination, or local temperature or pressure non-uniformity. Mapping the unbonded regions against the furnace's known temperature distribution and against the pressure path frequently identifies the cause immediately.

An oxide layer visible at the interface points at atmosphere quality during the cycle, or at time in air between preparation and loading. Both are verifiable from records.

Deformation of the part means pressure or temperature exceeded what the geometry could withstand over the hold time; the remedy is a longer, cooler, lower-pressure cycle, or better support.

Failure on a dissimilar joint requires metallography before anything else, to distinguish an unbonded interface from a bonded but brittle one — the two have opposite remedies.

16. Testing and Quality Verification

The cycle record is the primary evidence. Because the joint is made over hours inside a furnace with no observable event, the temperature, pressure and atmosphere traces are what demonstrate that the intended conditions were achieved at every point on the part.

Non-destructive:

• Ultrasonic testing — the principal method, mapping bonded and unbonded areas. Its limitation is the same as for friction stir welding's kissing bond (Chapter 57, Section 15): a bonded-looking interface with no metallurgical continuity presents little reflector, so detection of marginal bonding is limited.

• Radiography — poor for this defect type, since an unbonded interface has essentially no thickness.

• Dimensional inspection for creep distortion.

Destructive:

• Metallographic sectioning — the definitive method. It shows the interface condition, grain migration across it, residual voids, oxide layers and interlayer behaviour.

• Tensile, shear and bend testing of representative coupons processed in the same cycle.

• Fatigue testing during qualification, since marginal bonding shows in fatigue before it shows in static strength.

Coupons processed in the same furnace load as the production parts are the standard evidence route, and their placement within the load matters — coupons should sample the least favourable positions, not the most convenient ones.

17. Safety Specifics

• High-temperature furnaces with the associated burn and thermal hazards.

• High-pressure vessels in hot isostatic pressing — a stored-energy hazard governed by pressure equipment regulation, with the vessel and its closure as safety-critical items.

• Inert gas asphyxiation — argon used for atmosphere or pressurization is heavier than air and accumulates; a vessel or furnace chamber being purged or vented is an oxygen-deficient space (Chapter 37, Section 9).

• Chemical cleaning and etching hazards — acids, solvents and their disposal, which are a substantial part of the process's actual risk profile.

• Vacuum system hazards, including implosion risk on viewports.

• Long unattended cycles, requiring alarm and monitoring arrangements for out-of-hours operation.

18. Standards and Qualification

• Process reference: ISO 4063 reference 451, hot isostatic pressure welding, within the group 4 pressure welding family [S1].

• Procedure qualification follows the general framework of Chapter 31, with the process-specific variables of Section 8: temperature, pressure, time, atmosphere, surface preparation specification, interlayer material and thickness, and fixturing.

• The surface preparation specification is a qualification variable of the first rank, not a work instruction, and must be documented with the finish, flatness, cleaning method and maximum time before loading.

• Sector standards dominate. Aerospace and nuclear applications, which are the principal users, impose their own qualification, process control and documentation requirements that take precedence.

• Acceptance criteria come from the product specification; fusion welding acceptance standards do not apply.

19. Worked Example: Unbonded Regions in a Diffusion-Bonded Heat Exchanger Core

Situation. A manufacturer diffusion-bonds a stack of etched plates into a compact heat exchanger core. Ultrasonic inspection shows unbonded regions concentrated toward one edge of the core. The cycle record shows temperature and pressure within specification.

Step 1 — Map the unbonded regions against the physical assembly. Their concentration at one edge is the key evidence: a parameter problem would produce uniform or random distribution, while a localized pattern points at a local condition. This distinction should be established before any parameter is questioned.

Step 2 — Check temperature uniformity, not just temperature. "Within specification" usually means the control thermocouple was within specification. A large furnace load has a temperature distribution, and the part's edge may have been cooler than the control point throughout the hold. Additional thermocouples placed at the extremes of the load are how this is established, and their absence is itself a finding.

Step 3 — Check pressure distribution. With mechanical pressure, the load path through the fixture determines the pressure at each point on the interface, and a fixture that is not perfectly flat or that deflects delivers less pressure at the edges. Pressure-sensitive measurement or a witness assembly reveals it. Isostatic pressure would remove this failure mode entirely (Section 6), which is a real argument for the HIP route on parts like this.

Step 4 — Check flatness of the plates, particularly at the edges. Etched plates can bow, and stacking bowed plates concentrates contact at the centre and opens gaps at the edges — producing exactly the observed pattern. Measuring incoming plate flatness is quick and is frequently the answer.

Step 5 — Check cleaning coverage. Chemical cleaning of a stack of etched plates may be less effective at the edges, or handling may contaminate the edges preferentially. Sectioning an unbonded region and examining the interface for oxide or contamination distinguishes a contamination cause from a contact cause, and this distinction determines the remedy.

Step 6 — Recognize the inspection limitation. Ultrasonic testing maps gross unbonded areas but is limited on marginally bonded regions where the surfaces are in contact but not metallurgically joined (Section 16). The bonded area may be smaller than the inspection suggests, so sectioning a representative core is worth the cost on a first article.

Step 7 — Correct the cause. If it is temperature uniformity: instrument the load properly, change the load arrangement, or extend the hold to allow the cool region to complete. If it is pressure distribution: correct the fixture, or move to isostatic pressure. If it is plate flatness: control the incoming plates. If it is cleaning: revise the cleaning and handling procedure.

Step 8 — Fix the evidence chain, not just the part. The cycle record showed compliance while the part was non-compliant, which means the record was not measuring the right thing. Adding thermocouples at the load extremes, and including sacrificial coupons at the least favourable positions in every load, makes the record actually evidential — which on a process with no observable event and a cycle measured in hours is the only quality control available.

20. Known Gaps

• No temperatures, pressures or times are given. They are material- and geometry-specific and are established by qualification; published values vary widely.

• Surface finish and flatness requirements are described qualitatively and are specified per application.

• Interlayer selection is material-pair-specific and is established by development and testing.

• Transient liquid phase bonding is introduced but not developed; it has substantial literature of its own and sits at the boundary with brazing (Chapter 66).

• Aluminium diffusion bonding is identified as difficult rather than described; the routes that exist are specialist.

• Superplastic forming is described in outline; the forming discipline is a field in its own right.

• Acceptance criteria come from product and sector specifications and are not reproduced.

1. Process Overview: ISO 4063 Reference 442

Magnetic pulse welding discharges a large stored electrical charge through a coil placed around or beside a workpiece. The resulting intense, rapidly changing magnetic field induces opposing currents in the workpiece, and the interaction between the field and those induced currents produces a repulsive force that accelerates the workpiece across a small gap onto a mating part. The two collide at high velocity and weld in the solid state.

The ISO nomenclature lists it as reference 442, magnetic pulse welding, immediately after 441, explosion welding [S1] — and that adjacency is metallurgically correct: both are high-velocity impact welding processes, differing only in how the flyer is accelerated.

The whole event takes tens of microseconds. There is no heat source, no consumable, no shielding gas, no flux, and — critically — no melting.

2. The Mechanism: Field, Force, Flight, Collision

1. Charge. A capacitor bank is charged to a high voltage.

2. Discharge. The bank is discharged through a coil in microseconds, producing a very large, rapidly rising current.

3. Field and induced current. The coil current creates an intense magnetic field. That changing field induces an opposing eddy current in the nearby conductive workpiece.

4. Repulsive force. The coil's field and the workpiece's induced current interact to produce a repulsive Lorentz force — the same principle as an induction launcher — driving the workpiece away from the coil.

5. Flight. The workpiece — the flyer — accelerates across the standoff gap, reaching a very high velocity over a very short distance.

6. Collision and jetting. The flyer strikes the mating part at a small angle. Pressure at the collision point far exceeds both materials' strength, they behave hydrodynamically, and a jet of surface material is expelled ahead of the collision point, carrying away oxide and contamination.

7. Bonding. Immediately behind the collision point, jet-cleaned virgin metal is pressed together at enormous pressure and bonds in the solid state.

3. Why It Is Explosion Welding by Another Driver

The physics from the collision onward is identical to explosion welding (Chapter 59), and the same three features appear:

Jetting cleans the interface. No surface preparation to metallurgical cleanliness is required, because the jet removes the surface layers of both parts at the moment of impact.

The bond line is characteristically wavy. A properly made magnetic pulse weld shows the same periodic wave pattern in cross-section, and the same diagnostic reading applies: regular waves indicate a weld made inside the window; a flat interface indicates the low-energy edge; melted pockets at wave vortices indicate excessive energy.

A weldability window exists, bounded on all sides. Too little impact velocity or too small a collision angle gives no jetting and therefore no bond; too much energy produces interface melting and, on dissimilar joints, the brittle intermetallic layer the process was chosen to avoid.

What differs from explosion welding:

| Factor | Explosion welding | Magnetic pulse welding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Driver | Chemical explosive | Capacitor discharge |
| Facility | Licensed explosives site or chamber | Ordinary factory floor |
| Repeatability | Good, shot to shot | Excellent — an electrical parameter |
| Cycle time | Batch, with setup | Seconds — production rate |
| Area | Very large plates | Small, localized joints |
| Geometry | Flat plates, cladding | Tubular and overlapping configurations |
| Automation | No | Yes, readily |
| Consumables | Explosive per shot | Coil wear only |

The practical summary: magnetic pulse welding brings impact welding into a production factory, at the cost of being limited to small, localized, mostly tubular joints.

4. Equipment and Components

| Component | Function | Failure consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Capacitor bank | Stores the discharge energy | Its capacitance and charge voltage set the available energy |
| Switching (spark gap or solid state) | Releases the charge in microseconds | Switching speed determines the current rise rate and therefore the force |
| Coil | Converts the current pulse into the magnetic field | The principal consumable — it experiences the reaction force of every shot |
| Field shaper | Concentrates the field into the working zone | Determines where and how the force is applied (Section 5) |
| Fixturing | Positions the parts and holds the standoff gap | Standoff accuracy is a primary process variable |
| Control system | Sets charge voltage, timing and interlocks | The record of charge energy per shot is the process evidence |
| Safety enclosure and interlocks | Contains the discharge event | Required — the discharge is energetic and the coil can fail |

The coil is the component that limits the process. Every discharge produces a reaction force on the coil equal and opposite to the force on the workpiece, so the coil experiences a violent mechanical impulse on every shot. Coil life is finite, coil design is the principal engineering effort in an installation, and coil failure is the characteristic maintenance event.

5. The Coil and the Field Shaper

The coil must carry an extremely large current for a few microseconds while withstanding the reaction force. Coils are made of high-strength, high-conductivity material and are frequently reinforced. Their geometry — usually a single or few turns around the workpiece — determines the field distribution and therefore where the force is applied.

The field shaper is a separate conductive insert placed between the coil and the workpiece. It carries induced current from the coil's field and re-concentrates that field into a smaller, precisely defined region at its inner surface.

Why it matters practically:

• It concentrates the force where the joint is, improving efficiency.

• It defines the weld zone geometry precisely.

• It protects the coil by taking the mechanical and electrical duty at the working surface — the field shaper is a cheaper, replaceable item, and coil life improves substantially with one.

• It allows one coil to serve several part sizes by changing only the field shaper.

Field shapers are consumables and their wear changes the process, so their condition and replacement interval belong in the process control.

6. Parameters and What Each Controls

| Parameter | Controls | Symptom if wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Charge energy (voltage) | Impact velocity | Too low: no bond — below the window. Too high: interface melting, part damage, intermetallics on dissimilar joints |
| Standoff gap | Acceleration distance and therefore impact velocity, and the collision angle | A primary variable. Too small: insufficient velocity. Too large: instability, excessive deformation |
| Coil and field shaper geometry | Where the force acts and the weld zone location | Determines the joint configuration; changing it is a process change |
| Discharge frequency / pulse shape | Force profile and skin depth in the flyer | Set by the equipment and circuit |
| Flyer wall thickness | Mass to accelerate | Too thick: insufficient velocity for the available energy |
| Flyer conductivity | How much current is induced, and therefore how much force | Poor conductors cannot be flyers (Section 8) |
| Overlap length | Bonded area | Too short: insufficient joint area; too long: outer regions outside the window |
| Part alignment and concentricity | Uniformity of the collision around the joint | Eccentricity: partial bonding around the circumference |

Charge energy and standoff together set the impact conditions, and they are the two variables that process development principally works with. As in explosion welding, both boundaries of the window matter, and dissimilar joints require operating below the melting threshold rather than simply above the bonding threshold.

7. Joint Configurations

The process's geometry is dictated by how the force can be applied:

| Configuration | Description | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tube to tube (compression) | Coil around an outer tube drives it inward onto an inner tube or rod | The primary configuration — driveshafts, tubular structures, fluid connections |
| Tube to rod / fitting | Outer tube compressed onto a solid or fitted insert | Hydraulic and pneumatic fittings, electrical terminals |
| Tube expansion | Coil inside a tube drives it outward into a surrounding component | Tube-to-tubesheet, tube into fitting |
| Sheet lap (flat) | Flat coil drives one sheet onto another | Feasible but less efficient than tubular; a smaller share of applications |
| Sealed joints | The bond is continuous around a circumference | Pressure-tight fluid connections |

Tubular joints dominate because a coil encircling a tube produces a uniform inward force around the whole circumference, which is exactly the geometry the process wants. Flat joints require a flat coil and are less efficient because the field cannot wrap the workpiece.

8. Materials and the Conductivity Requirement

The flyer must be a good electrical conductor. The force depends on the current induced in it, and a poor conductor develops insufficient current. This is a hard physical constraint, not a process preference.

| Role | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Flyer (accelerated part) | Good conductor — aluminium and copper are ideal; steel is a poor flyer |
| Target (stationary part) | Any material with sufficient strength and ductility — steel, stainless, titanium, even some non-conductors in specific configurations |

This asymmetry shapes the applications: aluminium or copper is driven onto steel, not the reverse. Where a steel flyer is unavoidable, a conductive driver ring of aluminium or copper can be placed over it to carry the induced current and transmit the force mechanically.

Combinations of interest:

| Combination | Significance |
| --- | --- |
| Aluminium to steel | A major application — no fusion route exists (Chapter 27, Section 7) |
| Aluminium to copper | Electrical joints without the intermetallics that dominate fusion and even ultrasonic joints over time |
| Copper to steel | Electrical and process applications |
| Aluminium to stainless | Structural and process |
| Aluminium to titanium | Specialist |
| Similar-metal joints | Feasible, though usually cheaper by other processes |

Why the dissimilar capability is real rather than marginal: the joint forms in microseconds with no bulk heating. Intermetallic formation requires time at temperature, and there is essentially none. Provided the energy is kept below the interface-melting threshold, the intermetallic layer is extremely thin or absent — which is precisely what fusion welding cannot achieve on these couples at any parameter setting.

9. Magnetic Pulse Forming and Crimping — the Adjacent Processes

The same equipment performs three related operations, and distinguishing them matters because they are often confused:

Magnetic pulse forming — the workpiece is accelerated into a die and permanently deformed, but no second part is welded. A metal forming operation.

Magnetic pulse crimping — one part is driven onto another to produce a mechanical interference joint, with no metallurgical bond. Fast, useful and structurally different from a weld: it relies on friction and interlocking, not on a bond.

Magnetic pulse welding — the impact velocity and collision angle are inside the weldability window, so jetting occurs and a metallurgical bond forms.

The important consequence: a magnetic pulse joint is not necessarily a weld. The same machine, same coil and similar-looking result can produce a crimp rather than a weld if the energy or standoff falls outside the welding window. Verifying that the joint is actually welded — by sectioning for the wavy interface, and by testing — is therefore a real acceptance requirement rather than a formality.

10. When to Use Magnetic Pulse Welding and When Not To

| Choose magnetic pulse welding when | Choose something else when |
| --- | --- |
| Dissimilar metals — aluminium to steel, copper to aluminium — in a tubular or overlapping joint | The joint is not tubular or overlapping |
| Intermetallic formation must be avoided | Neither part is a good conductor |
| No heat is acceptable — heat-sensitive assemblies, coated or pre-finished parts | Large bonded areas are required — use explosion welding |
| Production rate and repeatability are required | The parts cannot be held to consistent standoff and concentricity |
| A sealed, pressure-tight circumferential joint is needed | Volumes are too low to justify the capital and the coil development |
| No consumables, no fume, no gas, no arc | Very thick flyer sections exceed the available energy |
| Electrical joints where resistance stability matters | The joint must be inspected volumetrically by conventional methods |

11. Defect Catalog

| Defect | Detection | Cause | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| No bond — mechanical crimp only | Sectioning (no wave pattern); pull-off test | Energy below the window; standoff too small; collision angle outside the jetting range | Increase charge energy; adjust standoff; verify against the qualified window |
| Partial bonding around the circumference | Sectioning at several positions; leak test | Part eccentricity; coil or field shaper wear; non-uniform standoff | Improve concentricity and fixturing; replace worn field shaper |
| Interface melting / intermetallic layer | Metallography | Energy above the upper window boundary | Reduce charge energy — this is the failure mode that defeats the process's purpose on dissimilar joints |
| Flat (waveless) interface | Metallography | Conditions at the low-energy edge of the window | Increase energy within the window; verify bond strength by testing |
| Flyer cracking or tearing | Visual | Energy too high for the material's ductility; standoff too large | Reduce energy; check material temper |
| Excessive deformation of the flyer | Dimensional | Energy too high; standoff too large | Reduce energy and standoff |
| Target deformation or collapse | Dimensional | Insufficient internal support for a compression joint | Support the inner part; use a mandrel |
| Progressive quality decline | Sample sectioning | Coil or field shaper wear changing the field distribution | Track shot count; replace the field shaper on interval; monitor coil condition |
| Coil failure | Immediate, sometimes energetic | Fatigue from repeated reaction impulses; overload | Coil life management; do not exceed rated energy |
| Leaking joint | Leak test | Partial bonding around the circumference | As partial bonding above |

12. Troubleshooting

If joints pull apart with a clean, unbonded interface, the process produced a crimp rather than a weld. Check charge energy and standoff against the qualified window, and verify the coil and field shaper condition. This is the most common outcome of a process drifting out of the window, and it is dangerous precisely because the joint looks and initially behaves like a good one.

If bonding is partial around the circumference, the collision conditions varied around the joint. Causes are eccentricity between the two parts, non-uniform standoff, and field shaper wear. Sectioning at four positions around the joint maps it directly.

If a dissimilar joint is brittle, section it and look for an intermetallic layer. If one is present, the energy was above the window's upper boundary — the remedy is less energy, which is counter-intuitive to anyone accustomed to fusion processes.

If quality declines gradually, the coil or field shaper is wearing. This is the process's version of the wear pattern that recurs throughout this reference set, and the answer is a shot-count-based replacement interval rather than energy compensation.

13. Testing and Quality Verification

The joint has no fusion zone and is often hidden inside a tubular assembly, so verification is a real challenge and the regime reflects that:

Destructive:

• Metallographic sectioning — the definitive method, showing the wavy interface, bonded length, and any melted or intermetallic layer. This is the only method that distinguishes a weld from a crimp with certainty.

• Pull-off and torsion testing — a sound weld should fail in the parent material, not at the interface.

• Burst or proof pressure testing for fluid joints.

• Peel testing where geometry allows.

Non-destructive:

• Leak testing for sealed joints — functional and directly relevant.

• Ultrasonic testing, with the same limitation as other solid-state processes: an unbonded but contacting interface presents a poor reflector.

• Electrical resistance for electrical joints.

• Process data — charge energy per shot, recorded automatically, which is the per-joint record available for every part.

The practical regime is per-shot energy recording plus destructive sampling plus, for fluid joints, leak testing of every part. The same conclusion as every low-inspectability process in this reference set: control the process, sample destructively, and use the functional test where one exists.

14. Safety Specifics

• Very high stored electrical energy in the capacitor bank. This is the dominant hazard: the bank holds lethal energy even after the supply is disconnected, and discharge and isolation procedures before any access are safety-critical.

• High voltages during charging.

• Energetic mechanical event. The coil experiences the reaction of every shot; coil failure can be violent, and enclosure is required.

• Noise — the discharge is loud.

• Strong pulsed magnetic fields — a specific and serious hazard to implanted medical devices such as pacemakers, and a hazard to magnetic media and nearby electronics. Exclusion zones apply.

• Flying parts if fixturing fails during the impulse.

• No fume, no arc, no radiation, no gas, no heat — like the other solid-state processes, the occupational health profile is otherwise clean.

15. Standards and Qualification

• Process reference: ISO 4063 reference 442, magnetic pulse welding [S1].

• Dedicated welding standards are limited. The process is comparatively young in industrial terms, and qualification generally proceeds under the general framework of Chapter 31 with process-specific variables, or under the customer's or sector's own requirements.

• Qualification variables: charge energy, standoff gap, coil and field shaper geometry and identity, overlap length, material combination and thickness, flyer temper, and part concentricity and fixturing.

• Acceptance criteria come from the product specification. Fusion welding acceptance standards do not apply — there is no fusion zone.

• A qualification must demonstrate that the joint is welded rather than crimped (Section 9), by metallography, and must establish the window boundaries in both directions.

• Electrical safety for the capacitor installation is governed by electrical equipment regulation.

16. Worked Example: Qualifying an Aluminium-to-Steel Tubular Joint

Situation. A manufacturer needs to join an aluminium tube to a steel shaft in a driveshaft assembly. Fusion welding is not viable. Magnetic pulse welding is proposed. The task is to qualify it.

Step 1 — Confirm the configuration suits the process. A tubular compression joint with aluminium outside and steel inside is the process's ideal geometry: aluminium is an excellent flyer, steel is a suitable target, and the coil can encircle the joint. This is the configuration the process was made for.

Step 2 — Establish the weldability window in both directions, which is the core of the qualification. Weld a matrix of samples across a range of charge energies and standoff gaps, and section each. The results define: the lower boundary, below which no bond forms (crimp only); the upper boundary, above which the interface melts and intermetallics appear; and the region between, where a regular wavy interface forms.

Step 3 — Section and read the interfaces properly. For each sample, record whether waves are present and regular, whether melted pockets appear at wave vortices, and — critically for this couple — whether an intermetallic layer is present and how thick it is. This is the measurement that matters for an aluminium-steel joint, and it is why metallography rather than mechanical testing must lead the qualification.

Step 4 — Set the operating point with margin from both boundaries. Not just above the bonding threshold: the upper boundary matters more here, because exceeding it produces the brittle intermetallic layer that the process was chosen to avoid. An operating point comfortably below the melting threshold and comfortably above the bonding threshold is what a robust process needs.

Step 5 — Test mechanically and functionally at the operating point. Torsion testing to the assembly's service requirement; pull-off testing; and fatigue testing, because a driveshaft joint is fatigue-loaded and static strength does not predict fatigue performance on a joint with a wavy, partially intermetallic interface.

Step 6 — Establish the concentricity and standoff tolerance. Deliberately test at the extremes of the fixturing tolerance to confirm the joint remains inside the window across the whole production tolerance band. A process qualified only at nominal conditions will fail intermittently in production when parts sit at their tolerance limits.

Step 7 — Establish the coil and field shaper life. Run a life trial and section joints at intervals through it to find where the process drifts out of the window. Set the replacement interval inside that point. This becomes the production maintenance control.

Step 8 — Define the production control. Charge energy recorded per shot with limits; standoff and concentricity verified at setup and by fixture maintenance; field shaper replaced on shot count; destructive sampling at a defined frequency including sectioning; and, if the joint must be pressure-tight, leak testing every part. Because the joint is inside the assembly and cannot be inspected volumetrically, this control set is the quality system — there is no inspection route that substitutes for it.

17. Known Gaps

• No parameter values are given. Charge energy, standoff and coil geometry are entirely application-specific and are established by the window-mapping exercise of Section 16.

• Weldability window boundaries must be determined per material pair and geometry; no general values exist.

• Coil and field shaper designs are proprietary and are the principal engineering content of an installation.

• Standards coverage is genuinely thin for this process, and this chapter says so rather than implying a framework that does not exist.

• Intermetallic thickness limits are application-specific and established by testing.

• Sheet lap configurations are described briefly; they are less developed industrially than tubular joints.
