1. Process Overview: ISO 4063 References 31x

Oxyfuel gas welding burns a fuel gas with oxygen at a torch to produce a flame hot enough to melt the workpiece. Filler metal is added by hand as a bare rod. There is no electricity involved anywhere in the process.

The ISO nomenclature distinguishes by fuel gas [S1]:

| Reference | Process |
| --- | --- |
| 311 | Oxyacetylene welding |
| 312 | Oxypropane welding |
| 313 | Oxyhydrogen welding |

Its industrial role has shifted almost entirely: as a welding process it has been displaced by arc processes in nearly every application, while as a heating, cutting, brazing and straightening process it remains in universal daily use. This chapter covers the welding process and identifies honestly where it still earns selection.

2. The Flame: How Heat Is Generated

Combustion occurs in two stages, and the distinction between them is the basis of flame control:

The inner cone — the small, sharply defined, bright cone at the tip. Here the fuel gas reacts with the oxygen supplied through the torch in a primary reaction. This is where the useful heat is, and the hottest point is just beyond the tip of the inner cone. Welding is performed with the inner cone tip held a small distance from the pool, not touching it.

The outer envelope — the larger, softer flame surrounding and extending beyond the inner cone. Here the products of the primary reaction complete their combustion with oxygen drawn from the surrounding air. This region is cooler but contributes substantial total heat, and — importantly — it shields the weld pool from the atmosphere by consuming the oxygen around it.

Two consequences follow:

• The process has an inherent shielding mechanism in the outer envelope, which is why no separate shielding gas is used.

• Power density is low (Chapter 22, Section 2), because the heat is spread over a comparatively large area. This is the process's defining characteristic and the source of both its weaknesses and its remaining advantages.

3. The Three Flame Settings

The ratio of oxygen to fuel gas is adjusted at the torch, and the three resulting settings are three different tools, not three degrees of the same one.

| Setting | Ratio | Appearance | Metallurgical effect | Use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Neutral | Balanced | Sharply defined inner cone; no feather | Neither adds nor removes carbon; the pool is chemically undisturbed | Steel, stainless, cast iron, copper — the general-purpose setting |
| Carburizing (reducing) | Excess fuel | A feathery secondary cone extends beyond the inner cone | Adds carbon to the pool; reducing atmosphere | Hardfacing, some cast iron work, and where a reducing atmosphere is wanted |
| Oxidizing | Excess oxygen | Shorter, sharper, noisier inner cone | Oxidizes the pool; produces a protective oxide skin on some alloys | Brass and bronze, where the oxide skin suppresses zinc evaporation |

Setting the flame correctly is the process control, and it is done by eye. The standard method is to establish a carburizing flame with a visible feather, then reduce fuel (or increase oxygen) until the feather just disappears — that is neutral. From there, further oxygen gives an oxidizing flame.

Why it matters metallurgically: welding steel with a carburizing flame raises the carbon content of the weld metal, hardening and embrittling it. Welding with an oxidizing flame oxidizes the pool and burns out alloying elements. Neither error is visible in a finished weld until it is tested, and both are the direct consequence of an incorrectly set flame — which is why flame setting is the first thing to check when an oxyfuel weld tests badly.

The oxidizing flame on brass is the exception that illustrates the principle: the excess oxygen forms a thin oxide film on the pool surface that suppresses zinc evaporation (Chapter 26, Section 8), reducing both porosity and zinc fume. The setting is chosen deliberately for that chemical effect.

4. Fuel Gases Compared

| Fuel | Flame temperature | Heat distribution | Use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Acetylene | Highest of the common fuels | Concentrated in a small, intense inner cone | The only common fuel used for welding steel; also cutting, brazing, heating |
| Propane | Lower | More heat in the outer envelope, less in the cone | Cutting, heating, brazing — poor for welding steel |
| Propylene | Intermediate | Between acetylene and propane | Cutting and heating |
| Natural gas | Low | Diffuse | Heating; some cutting |
| Hydrogen | Moderate | Clean, carbon-free | Underwater cutting; specialist work where no carbon can be introduced |

Why acetylene dominates welding. Welding requires localized melting, which requires a concentrated heat source. Acetylene's high flame temperature and concentrated inner cone provide it; propane's heat is spread through the outer envelope, which suits heating and cutting — where broad preheat is wanted — but cannot produce a controlled weld pool in steel.

The corollary is often misunderstood on site: a propane set is not a welding set. It cuts and heats perfectly well and cannot weld steel.

5. Equipment and Components

| Component | Function | Failure consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cylinders (oxygen, fuel) | Store the gases | See Section 15 — acetylene has specific storage and use requirements |
| Regulators | Reduce cylinder pressure to working pressure | Incorrect or faulty regulation; acetylene has a strict maximum working pressure |
| Flashback arrestors | Stop a flame travelling back up a hose toward the cylinder | Required safety equipment, fitted at the regulator and often at the torch |
| Non-return (check) valves | Prevent gas flowing backward into the other line | Prevent the mixed-gas condition that causes flashback |
| Hoses | Convey the gases; colour-coded and with different thread handedness | Oil contamination on the oxygen side is a fire hazard |
| Torch (blowpipe) | Mixes the gases and delivers them to the tip | Mixer condition affects flame stability |
| Tips (nozzles) | Size the flame to the work | Tip size selection is the principal "parameter" of the process |
| Tip cleaners | Clear the orifice | A partially blocked tip gives an unstable, misdirected flame |
| Lighter / striker | Ignites the flame | Never use a match or lighter held in the hand |

Two torch types exist: injector (low-pressure) torches, which use the oxygen flow to draw in fuel gas at low pressure, and equal-pressure (positive-pressure) torches, which take both gases at similar pressures. The torch and the fuel supply must match.

6. Consumables

Filler rods are bare — no covering, no flux built in — because the flame's outer envelope provides the shielding. Steel rods are supplied to the relevant filler metal specification, commonly with a copper coating for corrosion protection in storage.

Flux is used separately where the material requires it — cast iron, aluminium, and brazing operations — applied by dipping the heated rod into powdered flux or by brushing it onto the joint. Flux residues are corrosive and must be removed completely after welding, which is a real disadvantage of the process on aluminium and a reason it is rarely used there now.

Gases per Chapter 30, Section 10.

7. Parameters and Technique

The process has few numeric settings and a great deal of technique:

| Variable | Controls | Symptom if wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tip size | Heat delivered — the primary "setting" | Too small: cannot establish a pool. Too large: burn-through, excessive HAZ |
| Gas pressures | Flow through the selected tip | Set to the tip manufacturer's data |
| Flame setting | Pool chemistry (Section 3) | Carburizing on steel: hard, brittle weld. Oxidizing: burnt, weak weld |
| Cone-to-work distance | Heat input at the pool | Too close: cone touches the pool, disturbing it. Too far: heat wasted |
| Torch angle | Heat direction and penetration | Affects penetration and pool control |
| Travel speed | Heat input per unit length | Too slow: excessive heat, burn-through, wide HAZ |
| Rod feeding | Deposit volume | Rod added to a cold pool gives lack of fusion |

The dominant characteristic is heat spread. Because power density is low, the whole area around the joint heats up, giving a wide heat-affected zone, substantial distortion, and slow travel. Every technique element is about managing that.

8. Forehand and Backhand Welding

Two techniques, with a genuine and instructive difference:

Forehand (leftward) welding — the torch points in the direction of travel, ahead of the rod. The flame preheats the joint ahead of the pool. Gives a wider, shallower weld with a good appearance; preferred on thin material.

Backhand (rightward) welding — the torch points back at the completed weld, with the rod ahead. The flame plays on the solidifying weld metal, slowing its cooling. Gives deeper penetration, faster travel and less gas consumption, and the post-heating effect slows the cooling rate, which is metallurgically beneficial on thicker or more hardenable material.

The backhand post-heating effect is worth noting because it is a rare case of a technique choice having a direct metallurgical consequence: it functions as a built-in post-heat, reducing hardness and cracking risk on material that would otherwise cool quickly.

9. Materials

| Material | Suitability |
| --- | --- |
| Low-carbon steel, thin section | The classic application — sheet, thin-wall tube, small-diameter pipe |
| Higher-carbon and alloy steels | Possible, but the wide HAZ and slow cooling are usually undesirable |
| Cast iron | A genuine strength — the slow, broad heating and slow cooling suit cast iron's requirements (Chapter 26, Section 10), and oxyfuel is a traditional cast iron repair method |
| Copper and copper alloys | Feasible; brass welded with an oxidizing flame (Section 3) |
| Aluminium | Possible with flux, but flux residues are corrosive and hard to remove; largely abandoned in favour of GTAW and GMAW |
| Stainless steel | Possible but rarely appropriate — the wide HAZ promotes sensitization and distortion (Chapter 24) |
| Titanium and reactive metals | Not suitable — no atmospheric exclusion |
| Thick section | Not suitable — heat input and time become prohibitive |

10. Setup and Execution Procedure

Before welding

1. Inspect cylinders, regulators, hoses, flashback arrestors and torch. Check for damage and leaks.

2. Verify oxygen equipment is free of oil and grease (Section 15).

3. Secure cylinders upright; acetylene cylinders must be used and stored upright (Chapter 30, Section 11).

4. Select the tip size for the material thickness from the manufacturer's data.

5. Set regulator pressures for the selected tip.

6. Purge the hoses individually before lighting.

7. Prepare the joint: clean, and set fit-up.

8. Verify preheat where required — on cast iron in particular (Chapter 26, Section 10).

Lighting and flame setting

9. Open the fuel valve slightly and light with a friction striker, never a match or lighter held in the hand.

10. Add oxygen until the flame reaches the required setting.

11. Set the flame deliberately: establish a carburizing flame with a visible feather, then reduce it until the feather just disappears for a neutral flame; adjust further only if a carburizing or oxidizing flame is wanted (Section 3).

12. Verify the flame is stable and the inner cone is sharply defined; a soft or fluttering cone indicates a blocked tip or a pressure problem.

Welding

13. Hold the inner cone tip a short distance from the surface, not touching.

14. Establish the pool before adding filler; adding rod to a cold surface produces lack of fusion.

15. Feed the rod into the leading edge of the pool, keeping the hot rod end within the flame envelope.

16. Maintain the technique — forehand or backhand — per the material and thickness (Section 8).

17. Watch the pool, not the flame.

18. At the end, withdraw slowly to avoid a crater, and shut down in the correct order.

Shutdown

19. Close the fuel valve first, then oxygen — this order prevents a backfire.

20. Close cylinder valves, release regulator pressure and bleed the lines when finished.

After welding

21. Remove flux residues completely where flux was used — this is not optional; residues are corrosive.

22. Inspect and record.

11. Related Operations: Braze Welding, Heating, Straightening

These are where oxyfuel equipment does most of its industrial work today:

Braze welding — depositing a brazing filler (commonly a copper alloy) into a groove without melting the parent metal, giving a joint that looks like a weld but is made at a much lower temperature. Widely used on cast iron and on dissimilar or thin material where fusion welding would crack or burn through (Chapter 66).

Heating for forming and bending — local heating to allow bending, straightening or shaping.

Flame straightening (heat straightening) — controlled local heating and cooling to remove distortion from welded or damaged structures. A genuine skill, and one of the most valuable uses of oxyfuel equipment in fabrication.

Preheating for welding (Chapter 34, Section 5), with the caveat that torch heating is difficult to control and evidence.

Flame cleaning and descaling.

Cutting — Chapter 64.

12. When to Use Oxyfuel Welding and When Not To

| Choose oxyfuel welding when | Choose something else when |
| --- | --- |
| No electrical supply is available and no generator is practical | Any arc process is available — it will be faster and better |
| Cast iron repair, where slow, broad heating and slow cooling are wanted | Distortion matters — the HAZ is very wide |
| Thin sheet, tube and small-diameter pipe repair in the field | The material is thick |
| One set of equipment must weld, braze, cut, heat and straighten | The material is stainless, aluminium, titanium or another material needing atmospheric exclusion or narrow HAZ |
| Braze welding is the appropriate joint | Production rate matters at all |
| Very small-scale, artistic or restoration work | Code work where the process is not permitted |
| Training in pool control — it teaches puddle management directly | A qualified procedure requires a process the code recognizes for the application |

The honest summary: oxyfuel welding survives as a welding process principally for cast iron repair, thin-section field repair, and situations without power. Its equipment survives universally for cutting, heating, brazing and straightening. Recommending it for general fabrication would be wrong.

13. Defect Catalog

| Defect | Detection | Cause | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hard, brittle weld metal in steel | Hardness testing; cracking; bend test | Carburizing flame adding carbon to the pool | Set a neutral flame correctly (Section 3) |
| Burnt, weak, oxidized weld | Visual — dirty, scummy pool; poor mechanical results | Oxidizing flame on steel | Set a neutral flame |
| Porosity | RT; visual | Contaminated surface; dirty rod; unstable flame; incorrect flame setting | Clean the joint and rod; check tip condition and pressures |
| Lack of fusion | RT; sectioning | Rod added before the pool was established; tip too small; travel too fast | Establish the pool first; select the correct tip size |
| Burn-through | Visual | Tip too large; travel too slow; excessive dwell | Smaller tip; increase travel speed; use forehand technique on thin material |
| Excessive distortion | Dimensional | Inherent — low power density means a wide heated zone | Reduce heat input where possible; sequence and restrain; accept that this is a process characteristic |
| Wide, soft heat-affected zone | Hardness traverse; metallography | Inherent to the process | Accept, or select a higher power density process |
| Corrosion after welding (fluxed work) | Service failure; visual corrosion at the joint | Flux residues not removed | Remove residues completely — mechanically and by washing per the flux manufacturer's instruction |
| Backfire (a sharp pop, flame goes out or relights) | Audible | Tip touching the work; tip overheated; blocked tip; incorrect pressures | Shut down, allow the tip to cool, clean the tip, check pressures |
| Flashback (flame burns back into the torch or hose) | A squealing or hissing sound; flame inside the equipment | Mixed gases in a hose; reverse flow; incorrect pressures; blocked tip | Immediate shutdown; do not reuse equipment until inspected; check arrestors and check valves — this is a safety event, not a quality one |

14. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Steel welds are cracking and testing hard

Symptom: brittle weld metal; cracks in the weld or at the toes; high hardness.

Category: flame setting.

Likely causes: carburizing flame raising the carbon content of the deposit; excessive heat and slow cooling in a hardenable steel.

Steps: check the flame setting by the feather method and re-set to neutral (Section 3); check the fuel and oxygen pressures against the tip data; verify the filler rod is the correct one; on a hardenable steel, consider whether the process is appropriate at all.

Card 2 — Flame will not hold a stable neutral setting

Symptom: the flame drifts, flutters, or the cone is soft and undefined.

Category: equipment.

Likely causes: partially blocked tip; damaged tip seat; incorrect regulator pressures for the tip; acetylene withdrawal rate too high for the cylinder, drawing acetone; regulator fault.

Steps: clean the tip with the correct cleaner size; inspect the tip seat; verify pressures against the tip manufacturer's data; check the acetylene withdrawal rate against the cylinder's limit — this is a real and under-recognized cause of unstable flames on small cylinders (Chapter 30, Section 11).

Card 3 — Repeated backfires

Symptom: sharp popping; flame extinguishing and relighting.

Category: tip condition and technique.

Likely causes: tip touching the work; tip overheated from working in a corner or on a confined joint; blocked or damaged tip; pressures too low for the tip.

Steps: shut down and let the tip cool; clean and inspect the tip; verify pressures; adjust technique to keep the cone off the work. Distinguish a backfire from a flashback, which is a serious safety event (Section 15).

Card 4 — Corrosion appearing at joints months after welding

Symptom: corrosion localized at and around welded joints on fluxed work.

Category: flux residue.

Likely causes: flux residues left on the joint after aluminium or cast iron welding, or after brazing.

Steps: establish whether flux was used and what removal was performed; residues from most fluxes are hygroscopic and corrosive and must be removed completely by the method the flux manufacturer specifies; treat this as a process step with a verification requirement, not as cleaning-up.

15. Safety Specifics

Oxyfuel work presents hazards that are different in kind from arc welding, and several have killed people:

• Acetylene is unstable above a limited pressure. It is dissolved in acetone within a porous mass inside the cylinder. Three consequences: it must never be used above its rated maximum working pressure; cylinders must be used and stored upright, or liquid acetone can be drawn into the hose; and there is a maximum withdrawal rate, above which acetone is drawn out with the gas and the cylinder can overheat.

• Oxygen is not flammable but makes everything else burn violently. Oil or grease in contact with high-pressure oxygen can ignite spontaneously. Oxygen equipment, hands, gloves and clothing must be free of hydrocarbons. Oxygen must never be used to blow down clothing, ventilate a space, cool a person, or power tools.

• Flashback — the flame burning back into the torch, hose or regulator — can cause a hose or cylinder fire or explosion. Flashback arrestors and non-return valves are required equipment, and a flashback event means the equipment must be inspected before reuse.

• Cylinder handling: secured upright, valve caps fitted for transport, never dropped, never lifted by the valve, never used as rollers.

• Hot work: the process is an open flame, so hot work permits, combustible clearance, fire watch during and after, and far-side checks all apply (Chapter 37, Section 8).

• Eye protection: filtered goggles or a face shield of the appropriate shade — the flame is bright and the work is incandescent, though the radiation hazard is lower than an arc.

• Fume: from the material, any coating, and the flux. Zinc-bearing materials and galvanizing are specific hazards (Chapter 37, Section 5).

• Confined spaces: leaking fuel gas accumulates; oxygen enrichment from a leaking oxygen line makes everything in the space violently flammable, and oxygen enrichment is not detectable by smell.

16. Standards and Qualification

• Process references: ISO 4063 references 311, 312, 313 [S1].

• Procedure specification and qualification: ISO 15609-2 covers welding procedure specification for gas welding; procedure qualification follows the general framework of Chapter 31.

• Welder qualification: ISO 9606-1 and the applicable code cover gas welding as a process (Chapter 32).

• Equipment standards govern regulators, hoses, torches, flashback arrestors and their inspection and maintenance intervals.

• Code acceptance varies. Many modern codes restrict or exclude oxyfuel welding for structural and pressure applications, and its permitted use must be checked before it is selected.

17. Worked Example: Choosing a Process for a Remote Pipeline Repair

Situation. A small-diameter, thin-wall carbon steel line in a remote location requires a repair. No electrical supply exists, the site is a considerable walk from vehicle access, and the repair must be completed in one visit. The options under consideration are oxyfuel welding, an engine-driven arc welding set, and a battery-powered inverter.

Step 1 — Establish the code position first. Whether the line is a coded installation determines whether the process choice is an engineering decision at all. If a code governs, its list of permitted processes and its qualification requirements decide the matter, and oxyfuel welding is excluded by many of them.

Step 2 — Assess the material and thickness against the process. Thin-wall small-diameter carbon steel is genuinely within oxyfuel welding's capability — it is close to the process's remaining core application. Thick wall or a higher-strength grade would not be.

Step 3 — Weigh the portability advantage honestly. Oxyfuel equipment is heavy — two cylinders — but requires no power and no fuel beyond the gas. An engine-driven set is heavier still and needs fuel and access. A battery inverter is light but is limited in duty cycle and total energy, which matters for a repair of any size.

Step 4 — Consider what else the visit requires. If the repair also needs cutting out the damaged section, preheating, or straightening, oxyfuel equipment does all of those with the same kit. An arc set requires separate cutting provision. This multi-function argument is frequently the deciding factor for remote work and is the reason oxyfuel kits remain on maintenance vehicles.

Step 5 — Consider the weld quality requirement. Oxyfuel welding on thin-wall pipe produces a sound weld in competent hands, with a wider heat-affected zone and more distortion than an arc weld. Whether that matters depends on the service and the inspection requirement — and on a pressure line it very likely does.

Step 6 — Consider the welder. Oxyfuel pipe welding is a declining skill. A welder qualified and current in the process is required, and in many organizations that qualification simply no longer exists in the workforce (Chapter 32, Section 8). This practical constraint frequently settles the question regardless of the engineering merits.

Step 7 — Consider the hot work and gas hazards on a remote site. Fuel and oxygen cylinders carried to a remote location, an open flame in vegetation or near a hydrocarbon line, and a fire watch requirement in an isolated place — these are real considerations, not paperwork, and they may argue for the arc option despite its logistical cost.

Step 8 — Reach a reasoned conclusion. For a small, non-coded, thin-wall repair with a qualified welder and manageable fire risk, oxyfuel is a legitimate and practical answer. For a coded pressure line, the process choice is dictated by the code, and the correct answer is very likely an engine-driven arc set with a qualified procedure and welder — with the extra logistics being the cost of doing it correctly.

18. Known Gaps

• No tip sizes, pressures or flow rates are given. These are equipment-specific and are published by the torch and tip manufacturer.

• Acetylene pressure and withdrawal rate limits are described qualitatively. The numeric limits are set by equipment standards and by national regulation.

• Flame temperatures are described comparatively rather than numerically, since published values vary with measurement conditions.

• Flame straightening is named but not developed — it is a substantial skill with its own literature.

• Code permissions vary widely and must be checked directly; nothing here should be read as establishing that the process is acceptable for a given application.

1. Why Cutting Belongs in a Welding Reference

Cutting is not a joining process, and it belongs here for a specific and practical reason: the cut edge is the joint face.

Everything a welding engineer cares about at the root of a joint — fit-up, squareness, cleanliness, metallurgical condition of the fusion faces — is determined by the cutting operation that produced those faces. Root defects investigated as welding problems frequently originate at the cutting machine, and a fabricator who separates cutting from welding organizationally usually separates them diagnostically too, with the result that the cause is never found.

Three specific links:

1. Cut squareness and dimensional accuracy determine the root gap and included angle achieved (Chapter 28, Section 12).

2. Cut surface condition — dross, oxide, roughness — determines whether the fusion faces are clean.

3. The cut edge's metallurgical condition — hardened, oxidized, or nitrogen-enriched depending on the process — affects cracking and fusion (Section 9).

2. Process Overview: ISO 4063 Group 8

ISO 4063 group 8 covers cutting and gouging [S1]. The three thermal processes that dominate industrial plate cutting:

| Process | Mechanism | Materials |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Oxy-fuel cutting | Chemical oxidation of the metal in a jet of pure oxygen | Carbon and low-alloy steels only |
| Plasma cutting | Melting and mechanical ejection by a constricted, high-velocity plasma jet | Any electrically conductive metal |
| Laser cutting | Melting, or oxidation, or vaporization, with ejection by an assist gas | Most metals, plus non-metals |

A fourth process — waterjet — is not thermal and is included in Section 6 for comparison, because its defining advantage is precisely the absence of the thermal effects the other three produce.

3. Oxy-Fuel Cutting: The Oxidation Mechanism

Oxy-fuel cutting is chemically distinct from the other two, and the distinction determines everything about where it can be used.

The mechanism:

1. A preheat flame (Chapter 63) heats a spot on the steel to its ignition temperature — the temperature at which it will burn in oxygen, which is below its melting point.

2. A jet of pure oxygen is directed at that spot through a central orifice in the nozzle.

3. The steel burns in the oxygen stream — an exothermic oxidation reaction producing iron oxide and a great deal of heat.

4. The oxygen jet's kinetic energy blows the molten oxide out of the kerf.

5. The heat of the reaction preheats the metal ahead, so the cut is self-sustaining and the preheat flame's job becomes maintaining the reaction rather than driving it.

The three conditions the material must satisfy, which together define the process's material limitation:

• The metal's ignition temperature must be below its melting point, or it melts rather than burns.

• The oxide's melting point must be below the metal's, or the oxide forms a solid crust that stops the reaction.

• The oxide must be fluid enough to be blown away.

Carbon and low-alloy steel satisfies all three. Stainless steel, aluminium, copper and cast iron do not — stainless because chromium oxide is refractory and forms a protective crust; aluminium for the same reason with its own oxide; copper because of conductivity and oxide behaviour. This is not a matter of trying harder or using more oxygen; the chemistry does not permit it.

Characteristics: very low equipment cost; portable; capable of very thick sections — into hundreds of millimetres; slow compared to plasma and laser on thin plate; wide kerf and a substantial heat-affected zone.

4. Plasma Cutting

The mechanism: an arc is struck between an electrode and the workpiece and constricted through a nozzle orifice, exactly as in plasma arc welding (Chapter 42, Section 2) but at higher gas flow and with the deliberate objective of blowing the molten metal out of the kerf rather than containing it. The plasma jet melts the metal and its kinetic energy ejects it.

Because it melts rather than oxidizes, it cuts any electrically conductive metal — stainless, aluminium, copper, nickel alloys and carbon steel alike. That is its decisive advantage over oxy-fuel.

Variants:

• Conventional plasma — air or oxygen plasma, general purpose.

• High-definition / precision plasma — additional constriction and gas management producing a narrower, squarer, higher-quality cut, closing much of the gap to laser cutting.

• Underwater plasma — cutting with the plate submerged, which dramatically reduces noise, fume and radiation, and reduces distortion. A genuine and under-used option for production cutting.

Characteristics: fast on thin and medium plate — considerably faster than oxy-fuel; narrower kerf and smaller HAZ than oxy-fuel; a characteristic bevel angle on the cut edge from the swirling plasma jet, which must be accounted for in programming; very high noise and fume in air; and an upper thickness limit well below oxy-fuel's.

5. Laser Cutting

Three mechanisms, selected by the assist gas:

| Mode | Assist gas | Mechanism | Use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fusion (clean) cutting | Nitrogen (inert) | Beam melts, high-pressure gas ejects the melt | Stainless and aluminium — leaves an oxide-free edge, weldable and paintable without cleaning |
| Oxidation (flame) cutting | Oxygen | Beam initiates, oxidation reaction contributes energy | Carbon steel — faster and thicker capability, but leaves an oxide layer on the edge |
| Vaporization | Inert | Material vaporized directly | Thin material and non-metals |

Characteristics: the narrowest kerf and the smallest heat-affected zone of the three thermal processes; excellent dimensional accuracy and edge squareness; very high speed on thin material; capable of fine detail and small holes no other thermal process can produce; high capital cost; thickness capability well below oxy-fuel; and reflectivity limits on copper and aluminium at near-infrared wavelengths, exactly as in laser welding (Chapter 52, Section 5).

The nitrogen-cut edge matters to the welding engineer: a nitrogen-assisted laser cut leaves a bright, oxide-free edge that can be welded without further preparation, whereas an oxygen-assisted cut leaves an oxide layer that should be removed before welding.

6. Waterjet, as the Non-Thermal Comparison

Abrasive waterjet cutting uses a high-pressure water stream carrying abrasive particles to erode through the material. It is included here for one reason: it produces no heat-affected zone at all.

Where that matters: materials whose properties would be damaged by heat; hardened materials that must not be tempered or re-hardened; components where any metallurgical change at the edge is unacceptable; and materials that cannot be thermally cut at all.

Its costs: slow compared with thermal processes; high consumable cost (abrasive); taper on thicker sections; wet process with abrasive handling and disposal.

For a welding engineer, waterjet is the answer when the cut edge metallurgy (Section 9) is the governing requirement.

| Materials | Carbon and low-alloy steel only | Any conductive metal | Most metals and non-metals |

8. Cut Edge Quality and How It Is Characterized

Cut quality is a defined, measurable property, and ISO 9013 provides the classification system for thermally cut surfaces — quantifying the characteristics that matter [S2]:

| Characteristic | What it is | Why it matters to welding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Perpendicularity / angularity tolerance | Deviation of the cut face from square | Determines the included angle and root face actually achieved (Chapter 28) |
| Mean height of the profile (roughness) | Surface roughness of the cut face | Rough faces trap contamination and affect fusion |
| Drag lines | The curved striations left by the cut front | Their curvature indicates speed and quality; heavy drag indicates cutting too fast |
| Top edge condition | Rounding or melting of the top edge | Affects fit-up and joint geometry |
| Dross adhesion | Resolidified material clinging to the bottom edge | Must be removed before welding — it is contamination directly on the fusion face |
| Kerf width | Material removed | Affects dimensional accuracy and nesting |
| Heat-affected zone depth | Metallurgically altered material at the edge | Section 9 |

Specifying cut quality is a real engineering decision rather than a purchasing detail: a joint requiring tight fit-up for laser welding (Chapter 52, Section 10) needs a far tighter cut quality specification than one to be arc welded with a filled groove, and the cutting process must be selected accordingly.

9. The Metallurgy of a Cut Edge

This section is the reason this chapter exists in a welding reference, because these effects cause weld failures that are attributed to welding.

The hardened cut edge. Thermal cutting heats a thin layer at the cut face to high temperature and then quenches it into the surrounding cold plate — a very rapid cooling rate. In hardenable steels this forms martensite at the cut edge (Chapter 22, Section 8). Consequences:

• The edge is hard and brittle, and may crack.

• It is susceptible to hydrogen cracking during subsequent welding (Chapter 23, Section 4), because it is exactly the hard microstructure that mechanism requires.

• It is difficult to machine and can damage tooling.

• Preheating before cutting reduces the effect, and is standard practice on higher-carbon and higher-strength steels.

• Removing the hardened layer by grinding or machining before welding is specified in some codes for higher-strength materials.

Nitrogen pickup on plasma-cut edges. Air plasma cutting introduces nitrogen into the melted edge layer. Nitrogen in steel promotes porosity in a subsequent weld and can embrittle. This is a documented cause of porosity in welds made on air-plasma-cut edges without preparation, and the remedies are to remove the affected layer, or to use an oxygen or nitrogen plasma gas rather than air where edge quality matters.

Oxide layers. Oxy-fuel and oxygen-assisted laser cutting leave an oxide scale. On carbon steel it is generally removed by the welding arc but contributes to porosity if heavy. On stainless steel, plasma cutting leaves a heavily oxidized edge that must be removed before welding or the joint's corrosion resistance is compromised (Chapter 24, Section 10).

Distortion. Thermal cutting puts heat into the plate and induces residual stress. Cutting thin parts from a plate, or cutting long narrow strips, produces measurable distortion — and the parts are then presented to the welding operation out of shape.

The practical rule for a welding engineer: know how the joint faces were cut, and specify the edge preparation required before welding. Treating cut edges as "ready to weld" without asking is where a substantial share of unexplained root defects originates.

10. Gouging Processes

Gouging removes metal in a groove rather than cutting through, and it is used for back-gouging (Chapter 28, Section 5), removing defective welds for repair, and preparing joints.

| Process | Character |
| --- | --- |
| Air carbon arc gouging | A carbon electrode strikes an arc to melt the metal and a compressed air jet blows it away. Fast, effective, works on most metals — and produces extreme noise, very high fume, and violent ejection of molten metal (Chapter 37, Section 11). It also leaves a carburized, hardened layer on the gouged surface that must be ground away before welding |
| Oxy-fuel gouging | A special nozzle produces a shallow groove. Carbon steel only |
| Plasma gouging | Adapted torch and parameters; cleaner than carbon arc, works on all conductive metals |
| Mechanical (grinding, machining, milling) | Slower but leaves a clean, unaltered surface with no metallurgical damage |

The carbon arc gouging carburization point is important and frequently missed: carbon from the electrode enters the molten surface layer. If that layer is welded over without removal, the weld metal picks up carbon, hardens, and may crack. Grinding the gouged surface to bright metal is a required step, not a cosmetic one.

11. Bevelling and Joint Preparation by Cutting

Most groove preparations in plate fabrication are produced by thermal cutting rather than by machining:

• Single-torch bevelling produces a single bevel face.

• Multi-torch heads produce V, X, K and Y preparations in one pass, with two or three torches set at the required angles.

• Plasma and laser bevelling heads tilt the torch under CNC control, producing bevels and even variable-angle preparations along a contour.

• Machining — milling or edge planing — is used where cut quality or metallurgy demands it.

The link to welding is direct: the included angle, root face and squareness achieved by the bevelling operation are exactly the dimensions Chapter 28, Section 4 identifies as controlling root fusion. A bevelling head out of adjustment produces a systematic fit-up error across every part it cuts, which then appears as a systematic welding defect.

12. Equipment and Consumables

| Process | Key consumables | Wear consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Oxy-fuel | Nozzles; gases | Worn or blocked nozzle: poor cut, drag lines, dross |
| Plasma | Electrode and nozzle (consumable set); gases | The dominant consumable cost. Worn consumables progressively degrade cut angle, kerf width and dross — and consumable life is a real production variable |
| Laser | Protective optics; assist gas; nozzles | Contaminated optics reduce power and shift focus, exactly as in laser welding (Chapter 54, Section 9) |

Plasma consumable life management is the direct equivalent of the wear-interval discipline that recurs throughout this reference set: cut quality declines progressively as the electrode and nozzle wear, and the correct response is a replacement interval established inside the degradation point rather than compensation by parameter adjustment.

15. Defect Catalog: Cut Quality Problems

| Defect | Detection | Cause | Corrective action | Welding consequence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Dross on the bottom edge | Visual | Speed too fast or too slow; wrong gas pressure; worn consumables; standoff wrong | Optimize speed; replace consumables; correct gas | Must be removed — contamination directly on the fusion face |
| Heavy drag lines / lost cut | Visual | Travel speed too high; insufficient power or oxygen | Reduce speed; increase power/oxygen | Rough face, poor fit-up |
| Bevelled (non-square) edge | Measurement | Plasma jet swirl (inherent, compensated in programming); worn nozzle; standoff wrong; torch not perpendicular | Compensate in the program; replace consumables; verify standoff and squareness | Wrong included angle and root face (Chapter 28, Section 12) |
| Rounded top edge | Visual | Speed too slow; excessive preheat; standoff too high | Increase speed; reduce preheat | Fit-up error, gap variation |
| Rough cut face | Roughness measurement per ISO 9013 | Worn consumables; incorrect parameters; contaminated plate surface | Replace consumables; correct parameters | Trapped contamination; poor fusion |
| Hardened cut edge | Hardness traverse; cracking | Rapid quench into cold plate on hardenable steel | Preheat before cutting; remove the hardened layer by grinding | Hydrogen cracking risk in the subsequent weld |
| Nitrogen-enriched edge | Porosity in the subsequent weld | Air plasma cutting | Remove the affected layer; use a different plasma gas | Porosity in the weld |
| Oxide scale on the edge | Visual | Oxy-fuel or oxygen-assisted cutting | Remove before welding, especially on stainless | Porosity; on stainless, corrosion |
| Dimensional error | Measurement | Kerf compensation wrong; machine calibration; thermal distortion of the plate | Verify kerf compensation and machine accuracy | Fit-up error across every part |
| Plate distortion | Dimensional | Thermal input from cutting; part geometry; cutting sequence | Optimize cutting sequence; consider waterjet for critical parts | Parts presented to welding out of shape |

16. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Cut quality declining over a shift on a plasma machine

Symptom: increasing dross, increasing edge bevel, wider kerf; parameters unchanged.

Category: consumable wear.

Likely causes: electrode and nozzle wear — the process's normal and predictable degradation; gas quality or flow drift; standoff drift from torch height control.

Steps: inspect the consumable set against a new one; check pierce count against the expected life; verify gas flow and purity; check torch height control calibration. Set a replacement interval inside the degradation point rather than adjusting parameters to compensate.

Card 2 — Porosity in welds made on plasma-cut edges

Symptom: porosity along the joint, particularly at the root, on plate cut by air plasma.

Category: cut edge chemistry.

Likely causes: nitrogen pickup in the cut edge layer from air plasma cutting, released into the weld pool.

Steps: confirm the cutting process and plasma gas used; grind the cut faces to bright metal before welding and re-test; consider a different plasma gas or laser cutting with nitrogen assist for edges to be welded; note that this cause is invisible unless the cutting process is part of the investigation (Section 9).

Card 3 — Cracking at the cut edge on high-strength steel

Symptom: cracks visible on the cut edge, or cracks initiating at the edge during welding.

Category: cut edge hardening.

Likely causes: martensite formed at the cut edge by rapid quenching into cold plate; hardenable steel; no preheat before cutting.

Steps: measure hardness at the cut edge; preheat before cutting on hardenable grades; remove the hardened layer by grinding before welding; check whether the material grade's own guidance requires either measure.

Card 4 — Systematic fit-up error across all parts

Symptom: root gap or included angle consistently wrong across a whole batch.

Category: cutting setup.

Likely causes: bevelling head angle out of adjustment; kerf compensation incorrect in the program; torch not perpendicular; machine calibration drift.

Steps: measure the cut faces against the drawing on a sample; check bevelling head angles and torch squareness; verify kerf compensation; recognize that a systematic error across all parts is a machine or program cause, not a variable one — and that the welding department will experience it as a welding problem.

17. Safety Specifics

• Oxy-fuel cutting carries the full set of oxyfuel hazards (Chapter 63, Section 15): acetylene pressure and withdrawal limits, oxygen and hydrocarbon incompatibility, flashback protection, cylinder handling.

• Plasma cutting in air is the noisiest common process in fabrication, routinely requiring hearing protection; it also produces very high fume rates and intense ultraviolet radiation. Underwater plasma cutting reduces all three dramatically and is a legitimate control measure.

• Air carbon arc gouging produces extreme noise, very high fume, and violent ejection of molten metal over a substantial distance.

• Laser cutting carries the laser hazards of Chapter 52, Section 18: invisible beam, reflection hazard, enclosure and interlocks, wavelength-specific eyewear.

• Fume from coatings — painted, primed, galvanized or plated material — is a significant hazard in all thermal cutting and is frequently worse than in welding because more material is vaporized.

• Hot work controls apply: molten metal and sparks travel a long way, particularly from gouging; permits, combustible clearance, fire watch during and after, and far-side checks (Chapter 37, Section 8).

• Falling cut parts — the offcut and the part both drop when the cut completes.

• Waterjet carries a severe injection injury hazard from the high-pressure stream, plus abrasive handling and noise.

18. Standards

• Process references: ISO 4063 group 8 covers cutting and gouging [S1].

• Cut quality classification: ISO 9013 — thermal cutting, classification of thermal cuts, geometrical product specification and quality tolerances [S2]. This is the standard that lets a cut quality requirement be specified and verified rather than argued about.

• Weld preparation requirements referencing cut edges are set by the welding code — including any requirement to remove hardened or affected layers before welding.

• Equipment and safety standards govern oxy-fuel, plasma and laser cutting equipment.

• Laser safety per IEC 60825 and ISO 11553 (Chapter 52, Section 19).

19. Worked Example: Root Defects Traced to the Cutting Process

Situation. A fabricator experiences persistent root defects — a mixture of incomplete penetration and porosity — on a butt-welded structure. Welder qualifications, WPS, consumables and gas have all been verified as correct. The welding parameters are within the qualified range. The rejection rate is consistent across welders and shifts.

Step 1 — Note what the consistency implies. A defect rate that is consistent across welders and shifts is not a technique problem. Something systematic upstream is affecting every joint equally, and the investigation should look for a systematic input.

Step 2 — Measure the joint preparation on parts as they arrive at welding. Not on the drawing — on the actual parts. Included angle, root face, root gap, edge squareness and edge condition, measured on a sample of a dozen parts.

Step 3 — Compare against the WPS requirement. If the root face is thicker than specified, or the included angle narrower, or the gap smaller, incomplete penetration follows directly and no welding adjustment corrects it (Chapter 28, Section 12). The measurement usually settles this in minutes.

Step 4 — Examine the cut edge condition, since porosity is also present. Two candidates: heavy oxide scale from oxy-fuel or oxygen-assisted cutting, and nitrogen enrichment from air plasma cutting (Section 9). Establishing which cutting process and which gas were used is a question for the cutting department, and it is the question a welding-only investigation never asks.

Step 5 — Check whether the edges are prepared before welding. Many fabricators weld directly onto cut edges. Whether that is acceptable depends on the cutting process, the material and the code. If air-plasma-cut edges are being welded without grinding, the porosity has an explanation.

Step 6 — Check the bevelling setup at the cutting machine. If the preparation dimensions are out, the cause is at the bevelling head — torch angles, kerf compensation, torch squareness or machine calibration. A single setup error there produces a systematic error on every part, which is exactly the pattern observed.

Step 7 — Test the hypothesis cheaply. Take a small batch, prepare the cut faces by grinding to bright metal and correcting the root face by machining, and weld them under the same procedure. If the defects disappear, the cause is confirmed without any further investigation of the welding process.

Step 8 — Fix it at the right department, and connect the two. The corrective action is at the cutting machine — bevelling setup, cut quality specification, and an edge preparation requirement before welding. The deeper fix is organizational: cut quality must be specified against ISO 9013 [S2] and verified as an incoming requirement at welding, so that the two operations are connected by a specification rather than by an assumption.

20. Known Gaps

• No cutting parameters are given. Speeds, currents, pressures and consumable selections are equipment- and thickness-specific and are published by the equipment manufacturer.

• Thickness capability ranges are described comparatively, since they depend heavily on equipment.

• ISO 9013's quality classes and tolerance values are not reproduced; the standard is the source, and this chapter identifies what it classifies and why that matters.

• Waterjet cutting is covered only as a comparison, not developed.

• Code requirements for removing hardened cut edges vary and must be checked in the governing code.

• Underwater cutting for marine and salvage work is a distinct discipline outside this chapter's scope.

Welding used to make and restore material rather than to join it — the thermal management problem that governs additive builds, dilution control as the whole objective in cladding, and why a weld deposit built layer on layer behaves differently from a weld deposited in a groove.

1. Two Applications of One Idea

This chapter covers two families that share a single principle: a welding process used to deposit metal rather than to join two parts.

Additive manufacturing builds a component from nothing, layer by layer, from wire or powder.

Surfacing — cladding, hardfacing, buttering and weld repair — deposits a layer onto an existing component to give it a surface property it does not have, or to restore material it has lost.

The processes are the same ones from Volume 3 and Chapter 52. What changes is the objective, and that change alters which variables matter: in joining, penetration into the parent is desirable; in surfacing it is usually the enemy (Section 9), and in additive building there is no parent at all after the first layer.

2. Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing: Process Overview

Wire arc additive manufacturing (WAAM) deposits successive weld beads to build up a three-dimensional shape. The heat source is normally GMAW, FCAW, or GTAW/PAW with wire feed (Volume 3), mounted on a robot or a CNC gantry.

Where it fits among additive processes:

| Family | Feedstock | Deposition rate | Resolution | Part size |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Powder bed fusion | Fine powder in a bed | Low | High | Limited by the machine's build chamber |
| Powder-fed directed energy deposition | Powder blown into a melt pool | Moderate | Moderate | Large |
| WAAM | Welding wire | Highest by a wide margin | Lowest | Very large — effectively unlimited |

WAAM's proposition is therefore specific: large parts, high deposition rate, low feedstock cost, poor surface finish and dimensional resolution. It is not a competitor to powder bed fusion for small precise parts; it is a competitor to large castings and forgings, and to machining large parts from solid billet where the material removed is a substantial fraction of the billet.

The economic argument that drives its adoption is the buy-to-fly ratio: machining a large aerospace or energy component from a forging can remove the great majority of the purchased material. Depositing a near-net shape and machining only the finished surfaces changes that ratio dramatically, and on expensive alloys — titanium, nickel — that is the whole business case.

3. The Thermal Accumulation Problem

This is the central technical difficulty of WAAM and the source of most of its defects.

In conventional welding, the workpiece is a large heat sink that absorbs and conducts away the heat of each pass. In an additive build, each new layer is deposited onto a small, already-hot structure whose thermal mass grows slowly and whose ability to conduct heat away is limited by its own geometry.

The consequences accumulate as the build grows:

• Interpass temperature rises continuously unless deliberately managed.

• Cooling rates fall, changing the microstructure from layer to layer.

• The melt pool becomes larger and more fluid at the same parameters, so wall width grows and the deposit slumps.

• The upper layers of a tall thin wall may become too hot to support their own melt pool.

• Properties vary through the build height — a genuine problem for a structural part.

The controls:

| Control | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Interpass temperature limits with forced dwell | Wait between layers until the temperature falls; the simplest and most common control, at the cost of build time |
| Active cooling | Forced gas, water-cooled substrate, or even submerged deposition |
| Parameter adaptation through the build | Reducing current or increasing travel speed in upper layers to compensate |
| Deposition path strategy | Alternating direction, and distributing deposition around the part so no region accumulates heat continuously |
| Substrate heat sinking | A thick, cooled substrate for the early layers |

Interpass temperature control is not a refinement in WAAM; it is the primary process control, and a build made without it will vary in geometry and properties from bottom to top.

4. Deposition Strategy and Path Planning

The path the torch follows determines the geometry, the thermal history and the defect population:

| Strategy | Description | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single-bead wall | One bead per layer, stacked | The simplest geometry; wall thickness fixed by bead width |
| Multi-bead / overlapping | Adjacent overlapping beads per layer | Wider sections; overlap ratio determines whether inter-bead voids form |
| Alternating direction | Reverse the travel direction each layer | Compensates for the start and stop height differences that otherwise accumulate |
| Contour plus infill | Perimeter beads then filling | Better outer surface |
| Oscillation / weaving | Weaving to widen the bead | Fewer passes for a given width, with more heat |

Two geometric problems recur:

Start and stop effects. Each bead starts cold and ends with a crater. Over dozens of layers these accumulate into a height difference at the ends of a wall — which is why alternating direction each layer is standard practice.

Overhangs and unsupported geometry. Molten metal is held only by surface tension. Steep overhangs slump, and features that a powder-bed process could build with support structures cannot be built this way. WAAM part design must therefore be designed for the process, favouring self-supporting geometry, and this is a design constraint rather than a programming one.

5. Materials and Properties in Additive Builds

Materials used are the standard welding consumables: steels, stainless steels, nickel alloys, titanium, aluminium and bronze — because the feedstock is welding wire, the material range is the welding wire range (Chapter 29).

Properties differ from wrought material in specific, predictable ways:

Anisotropy. Grains grow epitaxially from the layer beneath, so columnar grains can extend through several layers in the build direction. Mechanical properties then differ between the build direction and the deposition direction — commonly with lower ductility in the build direction. This is a first-order design consideration and must be established by testing in both orientations.

Layer-to-layer variation. As thermal conditions change up the build (Section 3), microstructure changes with them.

Reheating. Each layer is heat-treated by the layers deposited above it. This can be beneficial — refining and tempering the structure below, exactly as in multi-pass welding (Chapter 22, Section 12) — and it means the top layer, never reheated, is metallurgically different from the rest and is usually machined away.

Titanium requires full atmospheric protection through the whole build, not just at the arc — trailing shields, local enclosures or full chambers — because every layer is at temperature long enough to react (Chapter 26, Section 5).

Post-build heat treatment is common: stress relief to control distortion during machining, and in some cases hot isostatic pressing (Chapter 61, Section 6) to close internal porosity and homogenize the structure.

6. Distortion, Residual Stress and Machining Allowance

Every layer contracts as it cools while restrained by the layers beneath, so residual stress accumulates through the build, and it can be very high.

Consequences:

• The part distorts during building, and the distortion accumulates.

• It distorts again when removed from the substrate, as the substrate's restraint is released. This can be dramatic on long parts.

• It distorts again during machining as material removal redistributes the remaining stress (Chapter 22, Section 10).

Controls: substrate design and clamping; deposition sequence balanced about the part's neutral axis; interpass temperature control; post-build stress relief before machining — normally essential rather than optional; and generous machining allowance so that distortion can be machined out.

Machining allowance is a design decision, and under-specifying it is a common and expensive error: a near-net shape with insufficient allowance becomes scrap when it distorts.

7. Equipment for Additive Deposition

| Element | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Welding power source | Standard, but with good low-current control and pulse or controlled-transfer capability for stable small beads |
| Motion system | Robot or CNC gantry with the working envelope for the part; positional repeatability directly determines geometric accuracy |
| Wire feed | Standard, with consistency a priority (Chapter 39, Section 8) |
| Shielding | Local shielding for most materials; enclosure or chamber for titanium |
| Substrate and clamping | Thick, rigid, and clamped to resist distortion; frequently sacrificial and machined off |
| Thermal monitoring | Interpass temperature measurement — the primary process control (Section 3) |
| Path planning software | Slicing, path generation, and — increasingly — thermal simulation |
| In-process monitoring | Layer height measurement, arc data logging, thermal imaging |

8. Surfacing, Cladding and Hardfacing

The second family: depositing material onto an existing component.

| Application | Objective |
| --- | --- |
| Corrosion-resistant overlay (cladding) | Give a cheap substrate an expensive alloy surface — stainless or nickel alloy on carbon steel pressure equipment |
| Hardfacing | Give a component a wear-resistant surface |
| Repair / restoration | Replace material lost by wear, corrosion or damage; restore dimensions |
| Buttering | Deposit a compatible layer on a joint face before making a dissimilar joint (Section 12) |

All four deposit weld metal onto a surface, and all four are dominated by one variable: dilution.

9. Dilution: The Controlling Variable in Cladding

Dilution is the proportion of the deposit that came from the melted parent metal rather than the consumable (Chapter 22, Section 9):

Dilution (%) = (Area of melted parent metal ÷ Total deposit cross-sectional area) × 100

Why it is the whole problem in cladding. The purpose of a corrosion-resistant overlay is to present a surface of a specified chemical composition. If the deposit is diluted by 40 % with carbon steel from the substrate, the surface chemistry is not the consumable's chemistry — it is a mixture, and it may not meet the corrosion specification at all. The overlay looks perfect and fails its chemical analysis.

The consequences:

• Overlay is specified by the chemistry achieved at a stated depth, not by the consumable used. Acceptance is by chemical analysis of the deposit surface.

• Multiple layers are commonly required, because the first layer is heavily diluted and the second, deposited onto the first, is diluted only by already-alloyed material. Two-layer overlays are standard where a specification must be met with margin.

• Every process and parameter choice in cladding is aimed at reducing dilution.

How dilution is reduced:

| Method | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Lower current / lower heat input | Less parent melted |
| Higher deposition rate at the same heat | More consumable per unit of parent melted — the principle behind strip and metal powder cladding |
| Strip electrodes | Wide, shallow deposits with inherently low dilution (Chapter 43, Section 7) |
| Weaving or oscillation | Spreads the heat and reduces penetration at any point |
| Higher electrode extension | Resistive preheating melts more wire for the same arc energy |
| Bead overlap control | Depositing onto previously deposited metal rather than parent |
| Process selection | Section 10 |

10. Cladding Processes Compared

| Process | Dilution | Deposition rate | Application |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SAW strip cladding (122) | Low | Very high | The standard for large-area vessel internals |
| Electroslag strip cladding (721) | Lowest | Highest | Where minimum dilution and maximum rate are both needed (Chapter 44, Section 9) |
| GMAW / FCAW | Moderate | High | General cladding and repair, flexible and portable |
| GTAW with wire | Low | Low | Precision work, small areas, thin overlays |
| PTA (plasma transferred arc, powder) — ISO 152 | Low, and well controlled | Moderate | Hardfacing — the dominant process for valve seats and precision wear surfaces |
| Laser cladding | Very low | Moderate | Precision overlay with minimal heat input and distortion; growing rapidly |
| Oxyfuel with powder | Very low | Low | Small-scale hardfacing, field repair |

Note that the two lowest-dilution options — laser cladding and PTA — are also the two with the most precise heat control, which is not a coincidence: dilution is a direct function of how much parent metal the process melts.

11. Hardfacing Consumables and Wear Mechanisms

Hardfacing consumable selection is driven by the wear mechanism, and selecting on hardness alone is the classic error:

| Wear mechanism | Description | Consumable direction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Abrasion | Hard particles cutting or ploughing the surface | High-hardness deposits with hard carbides — chromium carbide and complex carbide types |
| Impact | Repeated blows | Tough, work-hardening deposits — austenitic manganese types. A hard, brittle deposit spalls |
| Combined impact and abrasion | Both | A compromise, or a tough underlayer beneath a hard surface layer |
| Metal-to-metal wear / galling | Sliding contact | Cobalt-based or specific alloy types with anti-galling properties |
| Erosion | Particle or fluid impingement | Hardness with the right carbide morphology |
| Corrosion plus wear | Both | Cobalt-based or nickel-based alloys |
| High temperature | Wear at elevated temperature | Cobalt-based alloys retaining hardness hot |

The critical selection principle: hardness and toughness trade against each other. A hardfacing deposit selected for maximum hardness on a component subject to impact will crack and spall, and the surface will be lost faster than a softer, tougher deposit would have worn. Identifying the actual wear mechanism before selecting the consumable is the whole of good hardfacing practice.

Check cracking — a network of fine transverse cracks in a hard deposit — is expected and acceptable in many hardfacing applications, because the deposit is too hard to accommodate contraction strain any other way. It is not acceptable where the cracks would propagate into the substrate or where the component is fatigue-loaded, and distinguishing acceptable check cracking from a genuine defect requires knowing which situation applies.

12. Buttering and Its Distinct Purpose

Buttering deposits a layer of a chosen filler onto a joint face before the joint is welded (Chapter 27, Section 4). Its purposes are distinct from cladding:

• Dissimilar joints: butter the carbon steel side with a high-alloy or nickel filler, then make the closing weld between the buttered layer and the other parent. This isolates the dilution problem into a controlled operation.

• Post-weld heat treatment conflicts: butter and heat-treat the carbon steel component separately, then make the closing weld without subjecting the austenitic side to a heat treatment that would harm it.

• Lamellar tearing prevention: butter a plate surface with ductile weld metal so the contraction strain is absorbed by weld metal rather than by the susceptible plate (Chapter 23, Section 9).

• Repair of a damaged or contaminated surface before welding to it.

13. Setup and Execution Procedure

For additive building

1. Confirm the material, the build path programme and the required properties, including orientation-dependent properties (Section 5).

2. Prepare and clamp the substrate rigidly; verify it is thick enough to resist distortion.

3. Set parameters including the interpass temperature limit and the dwell or cooling strategy.

4. Verify shielding — enclosure or chamber for titanium.

5. Build, monitoring interpass temperature at each layer and logging arc data.

6. Monitor layer height against the programme; deviation accumulates.

7. Apply post-build stress relief before removing from the substrate where the procedure requires it.

8. Remove from the substrate; expect and measure distortion.

9. Machine to final dimensions with the specified allowance.

10. Inspect, including testing in both orientations for a structural part.

For cladding and hardfacing

1. Confirm the specification: the chemistry required at a stated depth for corrosion overlay, or the wear mechanism and hardness for hardfacing.

2. Prepare the surface: remove all previous deposit, corrosion products, scale and contamination to sound parent metal.

3. Verify preheat where the substrate or the consumable requires it — many hardfacing consumables require substantial preheat to avoid cracking.

4. Set parameters for minimum dilution consistent with fusion (Section 9).

5. Deposit the first layer, controlling overlap between beads.

6. Deposit further layers where the specification requires the chemistry to be met with margin.

7. Control interpass temperature — both minimum and maximum.

8. Apply post-weld heat treatment where specified.

9. Verify by chemical analysis at the specified depth for corrosion overlay, and by hardness for hardfacing.

10. Inspect for cracking, lack of fusion and disbonding.

15. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Overlay fails chemical analysis despite a perfect appearance

Symptom: corrosion-resistant overlay looks flawless; chemical analysis at the specified depth shows iron content above the limit.

Category: dilution.

Likely causes: heat input too high; single layer where two were needed; excessive penetration; bead overlap insufficient so the analysis point sits over heavily diluted metal.

Steps: measure dilution on a section; reduce current and increase electrode extension; increase bead overlap; deposit a second layer — this is the standard answer where the specification must be met with margin; consider a lower-dilution process such as strip or laser cladding (Section 10).

Card 2 — Hardfacing deposit spalling off in service

Symptom: hard deposit breaking away in pieces under impact loading.

Category: consumable selection.

Likely causes: a consumable selected for maximum hardness applied to a component subject to impact; insufficient preheat causing cracking during deposition; no tough underlayer.

Steps: identify the actual wear mechanism (Section 11) rather than assuming abrasion; select a tougher, work-hardening consumable for impact, or deposit a tough underlayer beneath a hard surface layer; verify preheat against the consumable manufacturer's requirement, which for hard deposits is frequently substantial.

Card 3 — Additive build wall growing wider and slumping with height

Symptom: wall thickness increases up the build; upper layers sag.

Category: thermal accumulation.

Likely causes: interpass temperature rising through the build; no dwell or cooling; parameters unchanged from the first layer.

Steps: measure interpass temperature at each layer and impose a limit with forced dwell; reduce current or increase travel speed in upper layers; consider active cooling; recognize this as the process's fundamental control problem rather than a parameter error (Section 3).

Card 4 — Build distorts badly when removed from the substrate

Symptom: the part springs out of shape as the clamps are released.

Category: residual stress.

Likely causes: accumulated contraction stress through the build; no stress relief before removal; substrate too thin or clamping too rigid, storing stress.

Steps: apply stress relief before removing from the substrate; review the deposition sequence for balance; increase machining allowance so the distortion can be machined out; accept that a degree of distortion is inherent and must be designed for.

16. Testing and Quality Verification

For corrosion-resistant cladding:

• Chemical analysis of the deposit at a specified depth — the primary acceptance test, because the specification is a chemistry requirement.

• Ultrasonic testing for disbonding and lack of fusion at the interface.

• PT for surface cracking.

• Thickness measurement.

• Corrosion testing where specified.

For hardfacing:

• Hardness testing of the deposit surface, at the specified depth.

• Visual and PT for cracking, with the acceptable check-cracking criterion defined.

• Metallography for microstructure and carbide distribution.

• Bond integrity by UT.

For additive builds:

• Dimensional inspection, before and after machining.

• RT and UT for internal porosity and lack of fusion.

• Mechanical testing in both orientations — essential given the anisotropy (Section 5).

• Metallography through the build height, since properties vary with height.

• Witness coupons built alongside the part, in the same thermal environment, as the standard evidence route.

17. Safety Specifics

• The arc process hazards of Volume 3 apply throughout — radiation, fume, electrical, hot metal.

• Fume exposure is high in cladding and hardfacing, because deposition is continuous and prolonged; hardfacing consumables frequently contain chromium, nickel, cobalt and manganese in significant quantity, requiring the controls of Chapter 37, Section 5.

• Additive builds run for hours or days, so exposure is cumulative and enclosure with extraction is normal.

• Hot components for extended periods, with high interpass temperatures maintained deliberately.

• Titanium builds in enclosures carry inert gas asphyxiation risk (Chapter 37, Section 9).

• Automated cells carry the robot and machinery hazards of Chapter 69.

• Grinding and machining of hardfacing deposits generates dust containing the deposit's alloying elements — cobalt and chromium dust are specific hazards.

18. Standards and Qualification

• Process references: the deposition processes themselves are the ISO 4063 arc and beam processes of Volume 3 and Chapter 52; 152 is powder plasma arc welding, the PTA process used for hardfacing, and 721 is electroslag strip cladding [S1].

• Consumables: AWS A5.13 and A5.21 cover surfacing consumables; the standard filler metal specifications cover the rest (Chapter 29).

• Procedure qualification: the general framework of Chapter 31 applies, with overlay-specific requirements: qualification of cladding typically requires chemical analysis of the deposit and bond integrity testing rather than the transverse tensile and bend tests used for joints.

• Additive manufacturing standards — the ISO/ASTM 52900 series covers additive manufacturing generally, with directed energy deposition addressed within it; the field's standards are developing and should be checked for current scope.

• Sector requirements dominate for additive structural parts — aerospace, energy and pressure applications each impose their own qualification regimes, and these are where the substantive requirements live.

19. Worked Example: Cracking in a Hardfaced Wear Surface

Situation. A maintenance workshop hardfaces the wear surfaces of crushing equipment components. The deposit is applied with a high-hardness chromium carbide consumable. Deposits crack during application and pieces spall off within weeks of return to service. The workshop increases preheat, which reduces the cracking during deposition but does not prevent the spalling in service.

Step 1 — Separate the two symptoms. Cracking during deposition and spalling in service are different failures with different causes, and treating them as one produced the partial fix already attempted.

Step 2 — Address the deposition cracking first, since it is already partly understood. A high-hardness carbide deposit has almost no ductility and cannot accommodate contraction strain except by cracking. Preheat reduces it, which is why the change helped. Fine transverse check cracking is expected and often acceptable in this class of deposit — the question is whether the cracks are confined to the deposit or propagating into the substrate, which sectioning or PT after grinding answers.

Step 3 — Establish the actual wear mechanism, which the service failure points at. Crushing equipment subjects surfaces to heavy impact as well as abrasion. A chromium carbide deposit is selected for abrasion resistance and is hard and brittle. Under impact it fractures and spalls, and the surface is lost far faster than a softer, tougher deposit would have worn away (Section 11).

Step 4 — Recognize the selection error. The consumable was chosen on hardness, which is the classic hardfacing mistake. Hardness is the correct criterion for pure abrasion and the wrong one for impact. The evidence — spalling rather than wearing — is diagnostic of exactly this error.

Step 5 — Select against the mechanism. For combined impact and abrasion the established approaches are a tougher, work-hardening deposit — austenitic manganese types, which harden in service under impact — or a layered system: a tough underlayer that absorbs impact strain, with a harder surface layer on top for abrasion resistance.

Step 6 — Check the substrate and the preparation. Repeated hardfacing on the same component leaves previous deposit that must be removed completely before rehardfacing. Building a new deposit onto old, cracked hardfacing carries the old cracks forward, and this is a common maintenance shortcut.

Step 7 — Check the preheat and interpass requirements against the consumable. Whatever consumable is selected, its manufacturer states preheat and interpass requirements. Hard deposits generally require substantial preheat and controlled cooling, and these are not optional.

Step 8 — Record the wear mechanism as the selection basis. The durable fix is that the workshop's hardfacing procedure states the wear mechanism the component experiences, and selects the consumable from that. A procedure that specifies a consumable without recording why will be applied to the next component with a different wear mechanism and will fail again.

20. Known Gaps

• No parameters or dilution values are given. Both are process-, material- and application-specific and are established by qualification.

• Hardfacing consumable selection is described by mechanism, not by product. Specific alloy selection requires the consumable manufacturer's data and, frequently, trial in service.

• Additive manufacturing standards are developing, and the current scope of the ISO/ASTM 52900 family and its directed energy deposition parts should be confirmed directly.

• Acceptable check cracking criteria are application-specific and are stated in the component specification.

• Powder-based additive processes are named only for comparison and are outside this reference set's scope.

• Thermal simulation and path optimization software is a developing field and is not addressed.
