1. Process Overview: What Brazing Is and Is Not

Brazing joins two components using a filler metal that melts above 450 °C but below the melting point of the parent metals, drawn into a closely fitted joint by capillary action.

Three defining characteristics distinguish it from welding:

1. The parent metal is not melted. It is heated, and it must be wetted by the filler, but it stays solid throughout.

2. The filler is distributed by capillary action into a narrow gap, not deposited into a groove.

3. The joint's strength comes from the joint geometry — the bonded area and the clearance — rather than from the filler's own bulk strength.

The 450 °C boundary is the conventional dividing line: above it is brazing, below it is soldering (Chapter 67). The distinction is not arbitrary — it correlates with the filler families used, the strengths achievable and the applications.

Brazing is not a weaker substitute for welding. A correctly designed brazed joint can be stronger than the parent metal, because the joint area can be made as large as the design requires — and a lap joint of sufficient overlap will fail in the parent material rather than in the joint.

2. The Mechanism: Wetting, Capillary Action, Solidification

1. Heating. The assembly is heated until the joint area reaches the filler's flow temperature. The parent metal is heated, not the filler directly — this is a critical technique point, because filler melted by direct flame impingement rather than by contact with hot parent metal will ball up and fail to flow.

2. Fluxing or atmosphere protection. Surface oxides are removed and prevented from reforming (Section 6). Wetting cannot occur through an oxide film, and this is where most brazing failures originate.

3. Wetting. The molten filler spreads across the clean parent surface rather than balling up. Wetting is a surface-energy phenomenon and requires a chemically clean, oxide-free surface at temperature.

4. Capillary flow. Surface tension draws the molten filler into the narrow joint gap — against gravity if necessary, which is why a correctly designed brazed joint can be fed from below or from one side and fill completely.

5. Solidification. The filler solidifies, forming a metallurgical bond with both parents. Some diffusion occurs at the interface, and in some systems this produces an interface stronger than the filler itself.

3. Joint Clearance: The Single Most Important Variable

Capillary force varies inversely with gap width, and the strength of a brazed joint depends strongly on the gap. This produces a relationship that is unlike anything in welding:

• Too tight a gap and the filler cannot enter — flow is obstructed and the joint is unfilled.

• Too wide a gap and capillary action is weak or absent — the filler does not fill the joint, and where it does, the thick filler layer has the filler's own low bulk strength rather than the joint's much higher constrained strength.

• The optimum is a specific, narrow range, typically measured in hundredths of a millimetre, and it is filler-system-dependent.

Why a thin filler layer is stronger. A thin layer of filler constrained between two much stronger parent surfaces cannot deform freely — the parents restrain it triaxially. Its effective strength in that constrained state is far higher than its bulk tensile strength. As the layer thickens, the constraint weakens and the joint's strength falls toward the filler's own. This is why brazed joint strength falls as clearance increases, and it is the single most counter-intuitive fact about the process for someone coming from welding.

The clearance must exist at brazing temperature, not at room temperature. Thermal expansion changes the gap during heating, and this matters enormously in dissimilar-metal assemblies: a steel tube inside a brass fitting has a different clearance hot than cold, and the design must produce the correct clearance at temperature. Getting this wrong — designing the clearance cold and finding it closes or opens on heating — is a standard and expensive design error.

4. Joint Design for Brazing

Lap joints are the standard configuration, because they provide the area that gives strength and the parallel faces that capillary action requires.

| Design factor | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Configuration | Lap, not butt. A butt joint offers only the cross-sectional area, which is rarely enough |
| Overlap length | Set to give the required strength; a common design rule is an overlap of several times the thinner member's thickness, so the joint is stronger than the parent |
| Clearance | Per the filler system, at brazing temperature (Section 3) |
| Filler placement | Pre-placed as rings, shims, paste or wire, or fed by hand; pre-placement is standard for furnace and induction brazing |
| Venting | The joint must be able to expel air and flux as the filler flows in, or a gas pocket blocks the flow |
| Fixturing | Parts held in position through heating and cooling without over-restraining |
| Fillet | A visible fillet at the joint edge is the standard visual evidence that the filler flowed through |

The venting requirement is frequently overlooked. Filler flowing into a blind gap compresses the air ahead of it, and the trapped gas stops the flow. Designs must provide an escape path — a vent hole, a deliberate gap, or a flow direction that pushes the air out.

5. Filler Metals

| Family | Character | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Silver-based (silver brazing) | Lowest brazing temperatures, excellent flow and wetting, good strength; expensive | The general-purpose family: steel, stainless, copper, brass, tool joints, refrigeration |
| Copper-phosphorus | Self-fluxing on copper — the phosphorus reduces copper oxide, so no flux is needed on copper-to-copper joints | Copper pipework, refrigeration, electrical — a major commercial application |
| Copper | Used in furnace brazing of steel, flows extremely freely | High-volume furnace brazing of steel assemblies |
| Nickel-based | High-temperature and corrosion-resistant service; requires high brazing temperature and usually vacuum or controlled atmosphere | Aerospace, turbine components, heat exchangers |
| Aluminium-silicon | For brazing aluminium; the narrow gap between filler melting point and parent melting point makes temperature control critical | Aluminium heat exchangers, automotive radiators |
| Gold- and palladium-based | High reliability, vacuum-compatible | Electronics, vacuum, medical, aerospace |

Two properties matter most in selection:

The melting range. Fillers have a solidus (where melting begins) and a liquidus (where melting completes). A eutectic filler melts at a single temperature and flows freely and quickly; a filler with a wide melting range becomes pasty first and can be manipulated, which is useful for filling wider gaps but risks liquation — where the low-melting constituent flows away first, leaving a high-melting residue behind that never flows.

Cadmium. Some traditional silver brazing alloys contain cadmium to lower the melting point and improve flow. Cadmium fume is acutely and severely toxic (Chapter 37, Section 5), and cadmium-free alloys have largely displaced them. Any brazing operation should establish whether a cadmium-bearing alloy is in use before anything else — this is a health question with immediate consequences.

6. Fluxes and Atmospheres

Wetting requires a clean, oxide-free surface at brazing temperature, and there are two routes to it:

Flux — a chemical applied to the joint that dissolves existing oxide and prevents reformation during heating. Fluxes are formulated for specific temperature ranges and filler systems, and using a flux outside its active temperature range is equivalent to using no flux at all: it will be exhausted before the filler melts, or not yet active when it does.

Flux residues are corrosive and must be removed after brazing — usually by hot water washing, sometimes chemically. Residues left in a joint cause corrosion in service, and this is a common cause of delayed failure.

Controlled atmosphere or vacuum — furnace brazing under a reducing atmosphere (hydrogen or dissociated ammonia), an inert atmosphere, or vacuum removes the need for flux entirely.

| Route | Advantages | Limitations |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flux | Simple, portable, works with any heating method | Residues must be removed; flux fume; limited temperature range |
| Reducing atmosphere furnace | No flux, no residue, clean joints, high volume | Furnace required; not all materials suit hydrogen |
| Vacuum furnace | Cleanest of all; essential for reactive and high-alloy materials | Highest cost; batch process |
| Self-fluxing filler | Copper-phosphorus on copper needs no flux at all | Only on copper; not on steel or on copper-to-steel joints, where flux is still required |

The copper-phosphorus exception is worth stating precisely because it is frequently over-generalized: it is self-fluxing on copper-to-copper joints only. Brazing copper to steel or brass with the same filler requires flux, and phosphorus-bearing fillers must not be used on ferrous or nickel-bearing parents at all, because they form brittle phosphides.

7. Heating Methods Compared

| Method | Character | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Torch | Manual, portable, flexible; heating is local and operator-dependent | Repair, site work, low volume, large or varied assemblies |
| Furnace | Whole assembly heated uniformly; atmosphere or vacuum control; filler pre-placed | High volume, complex assemblies, many joints at once, flux-free work |
| Induction | Rapid, localized, highly repeatable, easily automated | High volume, small localized joints — the standard for production tube and fitting joints |
| Resistance | Current passed through the joint; fast and localized | Small assemblies, electrical components |
| Dip | Assembly immersed in molten salt or molten filler | Aluminium assemblies, multiple joints at once |
| Infrared / laser | Highly localized, precise | Small precision assemblies, electronics |

Two selection principles:

Uniform heating matters more than fast heating. A joint heated unevenly has filler flowing toward the hot region and away from the cold one, leaving the cold region unfilled. Furnace and induction methods control this well; torch brazing depends on the operator's technique to achieve it.

The heating method determines whether flux is needed. A furnace or vacuum route allows flux-free brazing with no residue problem — which is a substantial quality advantage, not merely a convenience, because flux residue removal from complex internal passages is frequently impossible.

8. Braze Welding: The Exception to Capillary Action

Braze welding deposits a brazing filler into a groove or fillet, exactly like a weld bead, without relying on capillary action and without melting the parent metal.

Why it exists: it gives a joint that looks and functions like a weld, at a much lower temperature than fusion welding — which matters where the parent metal cannot tolerate welding temperatures.

Its main application is cast iron (Chapter 26, Section 10): braze welding avoids the high-carbon melting, the hard heat-affected zone and the cracking that fusion welding of cast iron risks. It is a standard cast iron repair method and frequently the best one.

It is also used on thin sheet, on dissimilar joints, and on galvanized steel where the lower temperature limits zinc loss.

It is not brazing in the capillary sense — no narrow gap, no capillary flow, and the strength comes from the deposit and the bond area rather than from a constrained thin layer.

9. Materials and Combinations

| Material | Brazing behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| Copper and copper alloys | Excellent; the classic application, with copper-phosphorus self-fluxing on copper |
| Carbon and low-alloy steel | Excellent with silver or copper fillers |
| Stainless steel | Good, but the chromium oxide requires an aggressive flux or a controlled atmosphere; vacuum brazing is common |
| Aluminium | Demanding — the filler's melting point is close to the parent's, so temperature control is critical; specialized fluxes or vacuum |
| Nickel alloys | Good with nickel-based fillers, usually in vacuum |
| Cast iron | Braze welding is the standard route (Section 8) |
| Titanium, zirconium | Specialist, vacuum only |
| Dissimilar metals | A major strength of the process — parent metals are not melted, so no fusion-zone intermetallics form and no dilution occurs |
| Carbide to steel | The standard method for attaching cutting tool tips |
| Ceramic to metal | Possible with active brazing alloys — an application no welding process can serve |

The dissimilar-metal capability deserves emphasis. Because neither parent melts, the incompatibilities that dominate fusion welding of dissimilar metals (Chapter 27) largely do not arise. Thermal expansion mismatch remains a real issue — it stresses the joint during cooling and in service — but the metallurgical incompatibility does not. Brazing is therefore often the correct answer for a dissimilar joint that welding cannot make.

10. Setup and Execution Procedure

Before brazing

1. Confirm the procedure: filler, flux or atmosphere, heating method, temperature and time.

2. Verify the joint clearance at brazing temperature, accounting for differential expansion (Section 3).

3. Clean the joint surfaces thoroughly — degrease, then remove oxide mechanically or chemically. Brazing will not wet a contaminated surface, and this is the leading cause of failure.

4. Apply flux where used, covering the whole area the filler must wet.

5. Pre-place the filler where the method requires it, or prepare hand-fed filler.

6. Assemble and fixture, verifying alignment and that vent paths are clear.

7. Confirm the flux's active temperature range matches the filler's flow temperature.

Brazing

8. Heat the parent metal, not the filler. Distribute the heat so the whole joint reaches temperature together.

9. Watch the flux: it will typically go through visible stages as it heats, and its behaviour indicates the joint temperature — a genuinely useful indicator in torch brazing.

10. Bring the joint to flow temperature and touch the filler to the hot parent metal, away from the flame if torch brazing. If the filler does not melt on contact, the parent is not hot enough — melting the filler with the flame instead is the classic error and produces a ball of filler sitting on an unwetted surface.

11. Allow capillary action to draw the filler through; a complete fillet appearing on the far side is the evidence that it flowed through the whole joint.

12. Remove heat as soon as flow is complete — overheating burns the flux, oxidizes the joint and can erode the parent metal.

13. Allow to cool without disturbing the joint until the filler has solidified.

After brazing

14. Remove flux residues completely — hot water washing while still warm is usual; residues are corrosive (Section 6).

15. Inspect the fillets on all accessible sides.

16. Test per the quality plan.

11. When to Braze Rather Than Weld

| Braze when | Weld when |
| --- | --- |
| The parent metals cannot be fusion welded to each other — dissimilar combinations | A fusion weld is straightforward and the joint suits it |
| The parent metal is damaged by welding temperatures — cast iron, heat-treated components, thin sections | The joint must operate at high temperature, above the filler's capability |
| Thin sections where welding would burn through | Maximum joint strength at elevated temperature is required |
| Many joints must be made simultaneously — furnace brazing an assembly | The joint geometry cannot provide a lap and a clearance |
| Distortion must be minimized — uniform heating, no localized melting | Clearance cannot be controlled |
| Complex internal joints a welder cannot reach | Flux residues could not be removed from the finished assembly |
| Carbide tips, ceramic-to-metal, or other combinations welding cannot join | The service environment attacks the filler |
| A neat, unmachined joint is wanted | The joint is a butt configuration in thick section |

12. Defect Catalog

| Defect | Detection | Cause | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Incomplete filling / voids in the joint | RT; leak test; sectioning | Clearance too tight or too wide; insufficient heat; uneven heating; no vent path; insufficient filler | Correct clearance at temperature; heat uniformly to flow temperature; provide venting; verify filler quantity |
| Poor or no wetting (filler balled up on the surface) | Visual | Surface contamination or oxide; flux exhausted or outside its range; parent not at temperature; filler melted by direct flame | Clean thoroughly; verify flux range against filler; heat the parent, not the filler |
| Flux entrapment | RT; sectioning; corrosion in service | Flux unable to escape ahead of the advancing filler; excessive flux; no vent path | Provide venting; use the correct flux quantity; consider a flux-free atmosphere route |
| Corrosion at the joint after months in service | Visual; leak | Flux residues not removed | Remove residues completely; consider flux-free brazing where removal is impractical |
| Parent metal erosion | Sectioning; dimensional | Overheating; excessive time at temperature; filler dissolving the parent | Reduce temperature and time; select a filler less aggressive to the parent |
| Liquation (filler separating, low-melting fraction flowing away) | Visual; residue at the joint entry | Filler with a wide melting range heated too slowly | Heat faster through the melting range, or select a eutectic filler |
| Cracking in the joint | Visual; PT | Thermal expansion mismatch on dissimilar joints; restraint during cooling; brittle phases | Reduce restraint; control cooling; verify filler compatibility — for example, avoid phosphorus-bearing fillers on ferrous and nickel parents |
| Brittle joint on steel or nickel | Testing; metallography | Phosphorus-bearing filler used on a ferrous or nickel-bearing parent, forming brittle phosphides | Use a phosphorus-free filler on these parents |
| Overheated, oxidized joint | Visual — burnt flux, discolouration | Too much heat, too long | Control temperature and time |
| Joint fails at low load | Testing | Clearance too wide, so the filler layer is thick and has only its bulk strength (Section 3) | Correct the clearance; this is the most under-recognized brazing failure |

13. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Filler balls up and will not flow into the joint

Symptom: molten filler sits on the surface as a bead rather than wetting and flowing.

Category: wetting failure.

Likely causes: surface contamination or oxide not removed; flux exhausted, wrong for the temperature, or not covering the whole area; the parent metal is not at flow temperature and the filler was melted by the flame; parent surface oxidized during heating.

Steps: clean the joint properly — degrease then remove oxide; verify the flux's active range against the filler's flow temperature; touch the filler to the hot parent away from the flame and only proceed when it melts on contact; check heating uniformity.

Card 2 — Joint filled at the entry, empty further in

Symptom: sectioning shows filler at the joint entrance and voids further along.

Category: capillary flow obstruction.

Likely causes: no vent path, so trapped air stopped the flow; clearance too tight; clearance too wide at some point along the joint; uneven heating so the far region was colder; insufficient filler.

Steps: check for a vent path and add one; measure clearance along the joint length, including at temperature; check heating uniformity — the far region must be at temperature too; verify filler quantity.

Card 3 — Brazed joints leaking after several months in service

Symptom: joints pass leak testing at manufacture, leak later.

Category: flux residue corrosion.

Likely causes: flux residues not removed, corroding the joint from the inside; entrapped flux in the joint that cannot be washed out.

Steps: establish what flux was used and what removal was performed; wash while still warm per the flux manufacturer's instruction; where residues cannot be reached — internal passages, complex assemblies — the answer is a flux-free route (furnace, vacuum, or self-fluxing filler on copper), not better washing (Section 6).

Card 4 — Joints fail at loads well below the design value

Symptom: brazed joints fail at low load, in the filler layer.

Category: clearance.

Likely causes: clearance too wide, so the thick filler layer has only its bulk strength rather than the much higher constrained strength of a thin layer (Section 3); insufficient overlap length.

Steps: measure the actual filler layer thickness on a section — this is the direct evidence; correct the clearance to the filler system's specified range at brazing temperature; check the overlap length against the design requirement; recognize that this failure is a design and fit-up problem, not a brazing technique problem.

14. Testing and Quality Verification

Non-destructive:

• Visual inspection of the fillets on all accessible sides. A complete fillet on the far side is the primary evidence that the filler flowed through the whole joint, and its absence is a rejection.

• Leak testing — the functional test for fluid-carrying joints, and frequently applied to every joint.

• Radiography for internal voids, where geometry allows.

• Ultrasonic testing for bonded area, with the limitations common to thin bonded layers.

• Proof or pressure testing.

Destructive:

• Peel and shear testing of representative joints.

• Sectioning and metallography — the definitive method for filler layer thickness, void content, wetting quality, erosion of the parent, and interface condition.

• Torque or tensile testing to the functional requirement.

The visual fillet check deserves emphasis because it is cheap, immediate, and genuinely diagnostic: capillary action fills a joint from the entry outward, so filler appearing at the far side means it traversed the whole joint. No other non-destructive check on a hidden joint gives that information as directly.

15. Safety Specifics

• Cadmium in some traditional silver brazing alloys. Cadmium fume is acutely and severely toxic and small exposures can cause serious lung injury (Chapter 37, Section 5). Establish whether cadmium-bearing alloys are in use; substitute cadmium-free alloys; where they must be used, mandatory local exhaust ventilation and specific controls apply.

• Fluoride-bearing fluxes produce irritant and toxic fume. Local exhaust ventilation is required, not advisable.

• Flux is corrosive to skin and eyes; handling controls apply.

• Zinc from brass parents or fillers (Chapter 26, Section 8).

• Oxyfuel hazards where torch brazing is used (Chapter 63, Section 15).

• Hot components — brazed assemblies retain heat, and furnace-brazed assemblies are hot for a long time.

• Furnace atmospheres: hydrogen is flammable; vacuum furnaces vented with inert gas create oxygen-deficient spaces (Chapter 37, Section 9).

• Beryllium in some copper alloys being brazed (Chapter 26, Section 8).

16. Standards and Qualification

• Process references: brazing occupies ISO 4063 group 9 alongside soldering and braze welding [S1]; the preview used did not display the complete group 9 numbered list, so this chapter describes the methods by category.

• Filler metals: AWS A5.8 covers brazing filler metals; ISO 17672 covers brazing filler metals internationally. AWS A5.31 and the corresponding ISO standards cover brazing fluxes.

• Procedure and operator qualification: ASME Section IX includes brazing qualification (its scope covers welding, brazing and fusing); ISO 13585 covers qualification testing of brazers and brazing operators; ISO 18279 covers imperfections in brazed joints.

• Qualification variables for brazing differ from welding: filler metal, flux or atmosphere, joint clearance, overlap, heating method, brazing temperature and time, parent materials, and joint design.

• Sector standards — aerospace, medical, refrigeration and pressure applications each impose their own requirements.

17. Worked Example: Leaking Brazed Joints in a Heat Exchanger

Situation. A manufacturer furnace-brazes a compact heat exchanger with many internal joints. Assemblies pass pressure testing at manufacture. A proportion develop leaks within the first year in service. The failures are internal and cannot be repaired.

Step 1 — Establish that this is a service degradation, not a manufacturing escape. The units passed pressure testing, so the joints were sound enough to hold pressure at manufacture. Something changed over months in service.

Step 2 — List the credible mechanisms. Flux residue corrosion, if flux was used; corrosion from the service fluid attacking the filler; thermal fatigue from cycling, driven by expansion mismatch; and marginal joints that held a static pressure test but not thermal cycling.

Step 3 — Establish whether flux was used at all. In furnace brazing under a controlled atmosphere or vacuum, flux is unnecessary, and its absence removes the residue mechanism entirely. If flux was used — as it may be on aluminium — then residue trapped inside internal passages cannot be washed out, and it is the leading candidate (Section 6).

Step 4 — Section failed units. Metallography at the leak location distinguishes the mechanisms directly: corrosion products and a corroded filler layer indicate flux residue or service-fluid attack; a fatigue crack through the filler indicates thermal cycling; and a partially filled joint with a small bonded area indicates a marginal joint that pressure testing passed.

Step 5 — Check the joint filling quality across the population. If sectioning shows incomplete filling, the pressure test was simply not sensitive enough to find it — a partially filled joint can hold a static test comfortably and fail under thermal cycling. This points at clearance, venting or heating uniformity in the furnace (Sections 3, 4 and 7).

Step 6 — Check the furnace temperature uniformity. In a furnace-brazed assembly with many joints, joints in the coolest part of the load may not have reached flow temperature properly. This is the furnace-brazing equivalent of the temperature uniformity issue in diffusion bonding (Chapter 61, Section 19), and it produces exactly a proportion of units failing rather than all of them.

Step 7 — Check the expansion mismatch if the assembly is dissimilar. Thermal cycling of a dissimilar assembly stresses every joint on every cycle. This is a design consideration that brazing does not eliminate, and it requires either matched materials, a compliant joint design, or a filler with sufficient ductility.

Step 8 — Correct where the evidence points, and change the test. If joint filling is the cause, the fixes are clearance, venting and furnace uniformity, verified by sectioning first articles. And in every case the acceptance test should change: a static pressure test does not represent the service condition, and a thermal cycling test or a more sensitive leak test (helium mass spectrometry rather than pressure decay) is what would have caught these units before shipment.

18. Known Gaps

• No clearance values are given. They are filler-system-specific and are published by the filler manufacturer and in the brazing standards; using a generic figure is exactly the error Section 3 warns against.

• No temperatures or times are given. They are filler- and material-specific.

• Flux selection is filler- and temperature-specific and must come from the flux manufacturer's data.

1. Process Overview and the 450 °C Boundary

Soldering joins components with a filler metal that melts below 450 °C, drawn into the joint by capillary action, without melting the parent materials. It is mechanically identical to brazing (Chapter 66) and distinguished from it only by that temperature boundary — which sits in the ISO nomenclature's group 9 alongside brazing and braze welding [S1].

The boundary is conventional but not arbitrary: it separates two families of filler alloys, two ranges of achievable strength, and two largely separate industrial disciplines.

Soldered joints are weak compared with brazed or welded joints. Solder alloys have low melting points and correspondingly low strength, and a soldered joint typically carries a small fraction of the parent metal's strength. That is usually irrelevant, because soldering is chosen for electrical continuity or for sealing, not for structural strength — and where strength is needed, the joint is designed with mechanical retention and the solder provides only the electrical or sealing function.

2. The Mechanism: Wetting, Intermetallic Formation, Solidification

1. Cleaning. Flux removes oxide from both the component surface and the solder, and prevents reformation during heating.

2. Heating. The joint is heated to the solder's melting temperature. As in brazing, the components are heated and the solder is melted by contact with them, not by direct application of the heat source to the solder.

3. Wetting. Molten solder spreads across the clean metal surface. Wetting is the visible evidence that the surface was clean and at temperature.

4. Intermetallic formation. At the interface, the solder and the base metal react chemically to form an intermetallic compound layer (Section 3). This reaction is what makes the joint metallurgical rather than merely adhesive.

5. Capillary flow into the joint gap.

6. Solidification. The bulk solder solidifies. The joint must not be disturbed during solidification — movement produces a disturbed joint with a dull, grainy, cracked appearance and poor properties.

3. The Intermetallic Layer: The Joint's Real Interface

This is the most important concept in soldering and the one that distinguishes a superficial understanding from a working one.

A soldered joint is not solder stuck to metal. At the interface, the solder reacts with the base metal to form a thin layer of intermetallic compound — typically copper-tin compounds on a copper substrate. That layer is the actual bond. Without it there is no metallurgical joint, only mechanical adhesion.

Three consequences govern joint reliability:

A thin intermetallic layer is necessary and good. It demonstrates that a metallurgical reaction occurred. A joint with no intermetallic layer has not properly wetted and will fail.

A thick intermetallic layer is brittle and bad. Intermetallic compounds are hard and brittle. As the layer thickens, the joint becomes progressively more brittle and more prone to fracture at the interface under mechanical or thermal stress.

The layer keeps growing after manufacture. Intermetallic growth is diffusion-controlled, so it continues at service temperature throughout the product's life, and it accelerates with temperature. A joint that is sound at manufacture can become brittle after years in service — and this is a genuine, documented reliability mechanism rather than a theoretical concern.

What controls it: peak temperature and time at temperature during soldering, and service temperature and time afterwards. This is why soldering profiles specify time above liquidus as tightly as they specify peak temperature — excessive time at temperature grows the layer just as excessive temperature does. It is also why reworking a joint repeatedly is limited: each rework cycle adds to the accumulated thermal exposure and thickens the layer further.

4. Two Disciplines: Electronics and Mechanical

Soldering divides into two industrial worlds that share physics and almost nothing else:

|  | Electronics soldering | Mechanical / plumbing soldering |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Electrical connection plus mechanical retention | Sealing — a leak-tight joint |
| Joint size | Very small, very numerous | Larger, fewer |
| Volume | Thousands of joints per assembly, automated | Manual, joint by joint |
| Alloys | Tin-based, tightly specified | Tin-based, often with different requirements |
| Flux | Rosin or no-clean, residue-controlled | Aggressive acid fluxes acceptable in some applications |
| Standards | Highly developed and prescriptive (IPC family) | Plumbing and pressure codes |
| Failure mode | Intermittent electrical failure, often thermal-cycling driven | Leaks |
| Inspection | Automated optical, X-ray, electrical test | Visual, pressure test |
| Rework | A defined, controlled process with limits | Remake the joint |

The two disciplines rarely inform each other, and a practitioner from one is frequently wrong about the other. The most consequential difference is flux: an acid flux acceptable in plumbing is destructive on an electronic assembly, where residues corrode fine conductors and cause leakage currents and failures that appear months later.

5. Solder Alloys

| Family | Character | Application |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tin-lead (eutectic and near-eutectic) | Excellent wetting, low melting point, sharp eutectic melting, forgiving, well-understood | The historical standard; now restricted in most consumer electronics (Section 6) |
| Tin-silver-copper (SAC) | The dominant lead-free electronics family; higher melting point; good reliability | Lead-free electronics |
| Tin-copper | Simpler, cheaper lead-free alloy | Wave soldering, plumbing |
| Tin-silver | Good strength and thermal fatigue resistance | Electronics, some mechanical |
| Tin-antimony | Higher temperature capability | Plumbing and refrigeration |
| Bismuth-bearing | Low melting point | Heat-sensitive assemblies, step soldering |
| Indium-bearing | Very low melting point, good on difficult surfaces | Specialist, cryogenic, optical |
| Lead-free plumbing solders | Lead prohibited in potable water systems | Potable water plumbing — a legal requirement, not a preference |

The eutectic point matters. A eutectic alloy melts and freezes at a single temperature, giving a sharp transition and a bright, well-formed joint. A non-eutectic alloy has a pasty range between solidus and liquidus, during which it can be shaped — useful in plumbing wiped joints — but during which movement produces a disturbed joint.

6. The Lead-Free Transition and What It Changed

The restriction of lead in electronics and in potable water plumbing changed the process substantially, and the changes are worth stating because they explain much of modern soldering practice:

• Higher process temperatures. Lead-free alloys melt higher than tin-lead eutectic, so soldering temperatures rose. Components, boards and everything else had to tolerate the increase.

• Narrower process windows. The gap between "hot enough to wet properly" and "hot enough to damage the component" narrowed.

• Poorer wetting. Lead-free alloys wet less readily, making surface cleanliness and flux performance more critical.

• Different joint appearance. Lead-free joints are duller and grainier than tin-lead joints. This changed the visual acceptance criteria, and inspectors trained on tin-lead joints reject sound lead-free joints for appearance.

• Faster intermetallic growth at the higher temperatures, making time-at-temperature control more important (Section 3).

• Tin whiskers — fine conductive filaments growing spontaneously from tin surfaces over time, which lead additions previously suppressed. A recognized long-term reliability risk in high-reliability applications, and one reason some sectors retain exemptions permitting tin-lead.

In plumbing, lead-free solders became a legal requirement for potable water systems, with the practical consequences of higher working temperature and different flow behaviour.

7. Fluxes

Flux removes oxide, prevents reformation during heating, and reduces the molten solder's surface tension so it flows.

| Type | Activity | Residue | Use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rosin (R, RMA) | Mild | Non-corrosive; often left in place | Electronics |
| No-clean | Mild | Formulated to leave benign residue | Electronics — the volume standard, chosen to avoid a cleaning step |
| Water-soluble | More active | Must be washed off completely | Electronics where cleaning is performed |
| Acid / activated (zinc chloride, ammonium chloride) | Aggressive | Corrosive — must be removed | Plumbing and sheet metal only. Never on electronics |

The flux rule that matters most: an aggressive flux gives better wetting and leaves a residue that will corrode the joint if not removed. On a plumbing joint the residue can be washed off. On an electronic assembly it cannot be reliably removed from beneath components, and it will cause corrosion and leakage failures months later. Using plumbing flux on electronics is a classic and destructive error.

No-clean flux is not "no residue" — it leaves a residue designed to be benign. It can still cause problems under high-voltage or high-impedance conditions, and it can interfere with conformal coating adhesion.

8. Heating Methods

| Method | Application |
| --- | --- |
| Soldering iron / station | Manual electronics work, rework, repair |
| Wave soldering | Through-hole electronics at volume: the board passes over a wave of molten solder |
| Reflow soldering | The dominant surface-mount process: solder paste is printed onto pads, components placed, and the whole assembly passed through a controlled thermal profile in an oven |
| Vapour phase | Reflow using a condensing vapour, giving very uniform, temperature-limited heating |
| Selective soldering | Automated, localized soldering of specific joints on a populated board |
| Torch | Plumbing, sheet metal, larger mechanical joints |
| Induction, resistance, hot plate | Production mechanical joints |
| Dip | Small assemblies, tinning |

The reflow profile is the process control in electronics soldering, and it has four defined stages: preheat, soak (allowing flux activation and temperature equalization across a board with components of very different thermal mass), reflow above liquidus, and cooling. Time above liquidus and peak temperature are the two most tightly controlled parameters, because they determine both whether the joint forms and how thick the intermetallic layer becomes (Section 3).

9. Electronics Soldering Processes

Through-hole with wave soldering: component leads pass through plated holes; the board passes over a molten solder wave; capillary action fills the barrel. Joint quality is judged partly by barrel fill — the extent to which solder rose through the hole.

Surface mount with reflow: solder paste (solder powder plus flux in a carrier) is printed through a stencil onto the pads, components are placed onto the wet paste, and the assembly is heated through a controlled profile. The paste collapses, flux activates, solder melts, and surface tension self-centres the components onto their pads — a genuinely useful self-correcting effect.

Rework is a defined process with limits: each thermal cycle adds intermetallic growth and stresses the board and components. Standards limit the number of rework cycles permitted at a location, and exceeding them is a real reliability concern rather than a paperwork limit.

10. Mechanical and Plumbing Soldering

Copper pipework is the classic application: capillary fittings with a controlled clearance, heated with a torch, with solder drawn into the joint by capillary action.

Practical points:

• The joint must be clean — abrasive cleaning of both pipe end and fitting socket, then flux applied to both.

• Heat the fitting, not the solder. Solder touched to the hot joint should melt on contact and be drawn in; melting it with the flame is the same error as in brazing (Chapter 66, Section 10).

• A complete ring of solder at the fitting mouth is the evidence that capillary action filled the joint.

• Do not disturb the joint while it solidifies.

• Remove flux residues — acid fluxes will corrode the joint and the pipe.

• Potable water systems require lead-free solder by law in most jurisdictions.

• Water in the pipe prevents the joint reaching temperature — a very common practical problem, remedied by draining or by a temporary plug.

Sheet metal and mechanical soldering — including wiped joints in lead work and soldering of tinplate — uses the same principles with the joint designed to hold mechanically while the solder seals.

11. Joint Design

The brazing principles of Chapter 66, Section 4 apply, with soldering-specific emphasis:

• Lap or socket configurations, never butt — the solder's low strength requires area.

• Controlled clearance for capillary action.

• Mechanical retention where load must be carried. In electronics this is the through-hole or the pad area; in mechanical work it is the socket fit or a crimp. The solder is not expected to carry the primary load in a well-designed joint.

• Thermal considerations: a joint attached to a large thermal mass — a ground plane in electronics, a large fitting in plumbing — is difficult to bring to temperature, and this is a leading cause of cold joints.

• Access for heating and for inspection.

12. Setup and Execution

Electronics (manual)

1. Verify the correct solder alloy and flux for the assembly, and the tip temperature setting.

2. Clean the tip and tin it; a dirty or oxidized tip transfers heat poorly.

3. Ensure the joint surfaces are clean and, where applicable, fluxed.

4. Heat the joint — pad and lead together — not the solder.

5. Apply solder to the heated joint; it should melt on contact and flow to form a concave fillet.

6. Remove the solder, then the iron; do not move the joint while it solidifies.

7. Inspect: a good joint is shiny (tin-lead) or matte but smooth (lead-free), concave, with a visible fillet wetting both pad and lead.

8. Clean residues where the flux type requires it.

Plumbing

1. Cut the pipe square and deburr.

2. Clean the pipe end and the fitting socket abrasively to bright metal.

3. Apply flux to both surfaces.

4. Assemble.

5. Heat the fitting, distributing the heat around it.

6. Touch solder to the joint away from the flame; when it melts on contact and is drawn in, feed the required amount.

7. Look for a complete ring at the joint mouth.

8. Allow to solidify undisturbed; then wipe and wash off flux residues.

9. Pressure test.

13. Defect Catalog

| Defect | Detection | Cause | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cold joint (dull, grainy, poorly wetted) | Visual; electrical intermittency | Insufficient heat; joint attached to a large thermal mass; solder melted by the iron rather than by the joint | Increase heat or dwell; preheat large thermal masses; heat the joint, not the solder |
| Disturbed joint (cracked, crazed surface) | Visual | Joint moved during solidification | Hold the joint still until solidified; improve fixturing |
| Dewetting / non-wetting | Visual — solder retracts or balls up | Contamination; oxidized surface; flux exhausted or wrong; surface finish incompatible | Clean; verify flux type and activity; check the component's solderability and shelf life |
| Insufficient fill / poor barrel fill | Visual; X-ray | Insufficient heat; insufficient solder; hole or clearance wrong; flux inadequate | Increase heat and dwell; verify hole-to-lead clearance |
| Excess solder / bridging | Visual; electrical short | Too much solder; stencil aperture too large; profile wrong | Reduce solder volume; correct stencil design |
| Voids in the joint | X-ray | Flux volatiles trapped during reflow; paste volume; profile | Adjust the reflow profile — particularly the soak stage; adjust paste volume |
| Tombstoning (a chip component standing on one end) | Visual | Unequal wetting forces at the two ends during reflow — unequal pad thermal mass or paste volume | Balance pad design and thermal mass; correct paste volume and profile |
| Thick, brittle intermetallic layer | Sectioning; brittle failure at the interface | Excessive peak temperature or time above liquidus; excessive rework; high service temperature over time | Control the reflow profile; limit rework cycles; consider service temperature in the design (Section 3) |
| Flux residue corrosion | Corrosion; leakage current; delayed failure | Corrosive flux residue not removed; acid flux used on electronics | Use the correct flux class; remove residues per the flux type; never use plumbing flux on electronics |
| Tin whiskers | Microscopy; intermittent shorts after long service | Spontaneous filament growth from tin surfaces, unsuppressed in lead-free finishes | Finish selection; conformal coating; a recognized risk in high-reliability applications (Section 6) |
| Thermal fatigue cracking | Failure after thermal cycling in service | Expansion mismatch between component and board cycling the solder joint | Joint design; underfill; compliant leads; alloy selection for fatigue resistance |
| Leak in a plumbing joint | Pressure test | Incomplete capillary fill; water in the pipe preventing temperature; joint disturbed; contamination | Drain the pipe; clean and flux properly; heat the fitting; remake the joint |

14. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Joints look dull and grainy; are they cold joints?

Symptom: matte, grainy joint surfaces on a lead-free assembly.

Category: possibly nothing — an inspection criteria problem.

Likely causes: lead-free solder joints are normally duller and grainier than tin-lead joints (Section 6). An inspector trained on tin-lead will reject sound lead-free joints on appearance.

Steps: confirm the alloy in use; compare against lead-free acceptance criteria and reference images, not tin-lead ones; distinguish a normal lead-free matte surface from a genuine cold joint by checking wetting and fillet shape rather than by shine alone. This is a real and common false-rejection cause.

Card 2 — Joints failing intermittently after months in service

Symptom: electrical intermittency appearing in the field; joints looked acceptable at manufacture.

Category: interface degradation or fatigue.

Likely causes: intermetallic layer growth in service embrittling the interface (Section 3); thermal fatigue cracking from expansion mismatch under cycling; flux residue corrosion; tin whiskers shorting adjacent conductors.

Steps: section failed joints and measure the intermetallic layer thickness; examine for fatigue cracks in the solder; check the flux type and cleaning process; check the service temperature profile against the design assumption; note that none of these are manufacturing escapes — they are reliability mechanisms that manufacture-time inspection cannot detect.

Card 3 — Solder will not flow into a plumbing joint

Symptom: solder melts but is not drawn into the fitting.

Category: temperature or cleanliness.

Likely causes: water in the pipe absorbing the heat, so the joint never reaches temperature; joint not cleaned to bright metal; flux not applied to both surfaces; heat applied to the pipe rather than the fitting; fitting clearance wrong.

Steps: drain the line or use a temporary plug — water is the most common cause and is frequently not suspected; clean both surfaces abrasively; flux both; heat the fitting and test by touching solder to the joint away from the flame.

Card 4 — Voids found by X-ray under area-array components

Symptom: X-ray shows voids within the solder joints beneath BGA-type components.

Category: reflow profile and paste.

Likely causes: flux volatiles unable to escape during reflow; paste volume; profile soak stage too short or too fast; pad or via design allowing solder to be drawn away.

Steps: adjust the reflow profile — the soak stage governs volatile escape; check paste volume and stencil design; check for vias in pads drawing solder away; establish the void acceptance criterion from the applicable standard, since some voiding is normal and acceptable and over-rejecting is its own cost.

15. Testing and Quality Verification

Electronics:

• Automated optical inspection (AOI) — the volume standard for visible joints.

• X-ray inspection — essential for area-array components whose joints are hidden beneath the package; the only way to see them.

• Electrical test — in-circuit and functional testing, which finds electrical failures that inspection may not.

• Cross-sectioning — the definitive method for intermetallic thickness, void content and wetting quality; used for process qualification and failure analysis.

• Solderability testing of components and boards before assembly, which prevents a large class of wetting failures.

• Thermal cycling and accelerated life testing for reliability qualification — the only way to assess the fatigue and intermetallic mechanisms of Section 3.

Mechanical and plumbing:

• Visual — the complete solder ring at the joint mouth.

• Pressure and leak testing.

• Sectioning for qualification.

16. Safety Specifics

• Lead in tin-lead solders: a cumulative toxin. Controls are hygiene-based — no eating or drinking at the bench, hand washing, and control of lead-bearing dust and residues — plus ventilation. Lead fume at soldering temperatures is limited, but lead dust and residue transfer to hands and surfaces is the real exposure route.

• Flux fume is the dominant occupational health issue in electronics soldering. Rosin-based flux fume is a recognized respiratory sensitizer that can cause occupational asthma, and once a person is sensitized the condition is permanent. Local exhaust ventilation at the soldering point is a requirement, not a comfort measure, and this is one of the clearest cases in this reference set where the control must be engineered rather than left to the individual.

• Acid flux fume in plumbing work is irritant and corrosive.

• Burns from irons, molten solder and hot workpieces.

• Molten solder splash in wave soldering and dip operations.

• Torch hazards in plumbing work — open flame in confined spaces, near combustible building materials, with hot work controls required (Chapter 37, Section 8). Soldering pipework in a wall cavity or ceiling void is a genuine and recurring fire cause.

17. Standards and Qualification

• Process classification: soldering sits in ISO 4063 group 9 with brazing and braze welding [S1].

• Electronics standards are highly developed and prescriptive. The IPC family dominates: IPC J-STD-001 for requirements for soldered electrical and electronic assemblies, and IPC-A-610 for acceptability of electronic assemblies. These define workmanship criteria, class levels by reliability requirement, rework limits and inspection criteria in detail, and they are the operative documents in the electronics industry.

• Operator certification to those standards is a formal, examined qualification and is widely required contractually.

• Plumbing and pressure applications are governed by national plumbing codes and by pressure equipment requirements, including the legal prohibition of lead-bearing solder in potable water systems.

• Solder alloy specifications — including ISO 9453 for soft solder alloys — define compositions.

• ASME Section IX covers brazing but soldering is generally outside welding qualification frameworks; the electronics and plumbing regimes govern instead.

18. Worked Example: Intermittent Electronic Failures Traced to Joint Quality

Situation. A manufacturer's product returns show intermittent faults appearing after six to eighteen months in the field. Assemblies pass all production tests including AOI, X-ray and functional test. Returned units frequently test as functional on the bench, then fail again in service.

Step 1 — Read the pattern. Intermittent, appearing after months, and not reproducible on the bench — the signature of a mechanical intermittency that depends on temperature or vibration, not of a component failure. A cracked or embrittled solder joint that opens under thermal expansion and closes again fits precisely.

Step 2 — Recognize what production testing can and cannot see. AOI checks appearance, X-ray checks internal geometry, and functional test checks the assembly at bench temperature. None of them detects a joint that is sound now and will embrittle later (Section 3), and none reproduces the thermal cycling of service.

Step 3 — Section returned joints and measure the intermetallic layer. This is the decisive measurement. A thick intermetallic layer, with fracture running through it, confirms the mechanism. A fatigue crack through the bulk solder points instead at thermal cycling and expansion mismatch. The two have different remedies.

Step 4 — If intermetallic growth is confirmed, examine the thermal history. Peak reflow temperature and time above liquidus; the number of reflow passes the assembly received; the number of rework cycles at the failing locations; and the service temperature the product actually experiences. Each adds to the accumulated exposure that grows the layer.

Step 5 — Check the rework history specifically. Rework locations receive additional thermal cycles, and standards limit the permitted number for exactly this reason. If failures cluster at reworked locations, the rework limit is being exceeded or not tracked.

Step 6 — If thermal fatigue is confirmed instead, examine the design. Expansion mismatch between component and board under cycling is a design and materials issue: component package selection, board material, joint standoff, underfill for area-array parts, and alloy fatigue resistance are the levers.

Step 7 — Change the qualification, which is where the real gap is. Production tests verify manufacture; they do not verify reliability. Accelerated thermal cycling to the product's actual service profile is the test that would have revealed this before shipment, and its absence — not any manufacturing defect — is the root cause of the field failures.

Step 8 — Correct the process within its window. Tighten the reflow profile toward the lower end of its acceptable peak temperature and time above liquidus; enforce and record rework limits; and re-qualify by thermal cycling rather than by bench test. The manufacturing process was never out of control — it was operating at the wrong end of a window whose consequences appear only in service.

19. Known Gaps

• No temperatures, profiles or clearances are given. They are alloy-, component- and application-specific, and in electronics they are governed by the component manufacturers' limits and the IPC standards.

• IPC acceptance criteria are not reproduced. They are extensive, class-dependent and are the operative documents; this chapter identifies them rather than summarizing them.

• Intermetallic thickness limits are application- and alloy-specific and are established by reliability testing.

• Tin whisker mitigation is a developing field with its own standards and is not developed here.

• Plumbing code requirements vary by jurisdiction and govern where they apply.

• The ISO 4063 group 9 numbered list is not reproduced, as the preview used did not display it.

1. The Question This Chapter Answers

Every other chapter in this reference set assumes a weld is being made and asks how to make it well. This chapter asks the prior question: should this joint be welded at all?

It is the question most likely to be skipped, because the answer is usually assumed at the point the drawing is produced. The consequence of skipping it is expensive: a welded joint in a material combination that welding handles badly, in a geometry welding cannot reach, at a volume that does not justify the process, is a problem the whole rest of this reference set exists to manage — and that need not have existed.

2. The Five Families

| Soldering | Filler melting below 450 °C, same mechanism | Chapter 67 |

4. Decision Criterion 1 — Must the Joint Be Permanent?

If the joint must be demountable — for maintenance, replacement, transport or end-of-life recycling — mechanical fastening is the only family that provides it. Everything else is permanent, and cutting a welded, brazed or bonded joint apart destroys the components.

This criterion frequently settles the question outright and should be asked first because it is the cheapest to answer.

Partial exceptions: soldered electronic joints can be reworked within limits (Chapter 67, Section 9), and some adhesive systems can be released by heating — but neither is a general demountability route.

5. Decision Criterion 2 — What Are the Materials?

| Combination | Welding | Brazing | Soldering | Mechanical | Adhesive |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Same metal, weldable | Best choice | Possible | If load permits | Possible | Possible |
| Aluminium to steel | No (Ch. 27, §7) — except solid-state or transition joint | Yes | Limited | Yes | Yes |
| Copper to aluminium | Problematic | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Metal to plastic | No | No | No | Yes | Yes |
| Metal to ceramic or glass | No | Specialist (active brazing) | Specialist | Yes | Yes |
| Metal to composite | No | No | No | Yes (with care) | Yes — the standard route |
| Carbide to steel | No | Yes — the standard route | No | Possible | Possible |
| Heat-treated component | Damaged by welding | Possibly damaged | Yes | Yes | Yes |

The rule that emerges: as material dissimilarity increases, the viable families shift from welding toward brazing, mechanical fastening and adhesive bonding. Welding is the strongest option and the least tolerant of dissimilarity; adhesive and mechanical are the most tolerant and the weakest per unit area.

6. Decision Criterion 3 — What Load and What Service?

| Requirement | Family implications |
| --- | --- |
| Full parent-strength structural load | Welding |
| High load with a large joint area available | Welding, brazing, or adhesive with sufficient area |
| Fatigue-loaded | Adhesive distributes stress best; welding requires attention to toe geometry; mechanical fastening concentrates stress at holes |
| Peel or cleavage loading | Poor for adhesive — adhesives are strong in shear and weak in peel; mechanical or welded is better |
| Impact loading | Welding, mechanical; brittle adhesives and hard brazed joints perform poorly |
| Elevated service temperature | Welding first, then brazing. Soldering and adhesive are both limited, and adhesive is usually the binding constraint |
| Cryogenic | Welding with appropriate materials; adhesive systems are limited |
| Corrosive environment | Welding with a compatible filler; adhesive can seal a dissimilar joint against galvanic attack |
| Electrical conductivity required | Welding, brazing, soldering, mechanical |
| Vibration | Adhesive damps; mechanical fasteners loosen; welded joints crack at stress raisers |

Two limits deserve stating clearly:

Adhesive service temperature is the most common reason adhesive bonding is eliminated. Structural adhesives have a defined upper service temperature above which strength falls sharply, and it is far below what a welded joint tolerates.

Peel loading destroys adhesive joints. An adhesive joint loaded in shear over a large area can be very strong; the same joint loaded in peel fails at a small fraction of that load. Joint design for adhesive bonding is largely about converting peel into shear.

7. Decision Criterion 4 — What Does Heat Do to This Assembly?

| Situation | Consequence |
| --- | --- |
| Heat-treated or hardened components | Welding and brazing temper or anneal them locally (Chapter 23, Section 11) |
| Thermomechanically processed or advanced high-strength steels | Heat input limits apply; excess heat destroys the properties the mill created |
| Assemblies containing electronics, seals, plastics or lubricants | Welding and brazing are generally excluded; soldering may be too hot |
| Tight dimensional tolerances | Welding distortion may be unacceptable; mechanical and adhesive add none |
| Pre-painted or pre-coated components | Welding and brazing destroy the coating locally and generate hazardous fume (Chapter 37, Section 5) |
| Explosive or flammable environment | No hot process is permitted; mechanical, adhesive, or cold pressure welding (Chapter 60) |
| Assemblies already containing adhesive or sealant | Heat degrades them |

The pre-coated component case is worth highlighting because it drives real industrial decisions: an assembly built from pre-painted or pre-galvanized components can be mechanically fastened or bonded without damaging the coating, whereas welding requires either post-weld coating repair or a different build sequence.

8. Decision Criterion 5 — What Does the Geometry Allow?

| Geometry | Family implications |
| --- | --- |
| Access from both sides | All families |
| Access from one side only | Welding (most arc and beam processes), adhesive, blind fasteners; not resistance spot welding |
| No access after assembly | Adhesive applied before closure; brazing filler pre-placed; not welding |
| Very thin material | Adhesive, soldering, mechanical; welding risks burn-through |
| Large area to be joined | Adhesive — it bonds an area, not a line |
| Long continuous seam | Welding, adhesive |
| Complex internal passages | Brazing in a furnace — many hidden joints at once |
| Joint must be sealed | Welding, brazing, soldering, adhesive; mechanical needs a gasket |
| Dimensional adjustment needed at assembly | Mechanical — the only family with adjustment |

9. Decision Criterion 6 — Volume, Cost and Rate

| Volume | Family implications |
| --- | --- |
| One-off, repair, site work | Welding (arc), mechanical |
| Low volume | Welding, mechanical, brazing (torch) |
| Medium volume | Any, with the tooling amortization considered |
| High volume | Resistance welding, mechanical (automated), adhesive (dispensed), brazing (furnace or induction) |
| Continuous production | Specialized welding processes (Chapter 50), adhesive |

Cost structure differs fundamentally:

• Welding: low equipment cost for arc, high labour, low consumable — or the inverse for resistance and beam.

• Brazing: furnace and fixture cost amortized over many joints per cycle; filler is expensive (silver-bearing alloys particularly).

• Mechanical: low process cost, but the fasteners themselves are a per-joint material cost and add weight, and hole preparation is an operation.

• Adhesive: low equipment cost, high surface preparation cost, and cure time is a production constraint requiring fixturing or handling strength before the assembly can move.

Cure time is the constraint most often underestimated in adhesive bonding: parts must be held in position until the adhesive develops handling strength, which consumes fixtures and floor space in a way welding does not.

10. Decision Criterion 7 — What Must Be Verified?

| Family | Verification |
| --- | --- |
| Welding | Best-established NDT of any family, with mature methods and codes (Chapter 35) |
| Brazing | Visual fillet, leak test, radiography; limited internal verification |
| Soldering | Visual, X-ray for hidden joints, electrical test |
| Mechanical | Simple and reliable — count, torque, visual |
| Adhesive | The family's weakness. No reliable NDT exists for bond strength; a well-formed bond and a weak one look identical |

The adhesive verification problem is genuinely limiting. Ultrasonic methods detect voids and disbonds but cannot measure adhesion, and a joint with a perfect-looking bond line and inadequate surface preparation — the dominant failure cause — is not detectable. Adhesive bonding is therefore controlled by process discipline and destructive sampling, exactly like resistance welding (Chapter 51, Section 9) and friction stir welding's kissing bond (Chapter 57, Section 15).

For safety-critical adhesive joints, this frequently drives the decision toward a hybrid joint (Section 13), where a mechanical or welded element provides verifiable load capacity and the adhesive provides stiffness, sealing and fatigue performance.

| Flow-drill screws | Form their own hole and thread; one-side access |
| Clinching | Sheets locally deformed to interlock, no fastener at all; cheap, no consumable |
| Crimping | Deformation of one part around another; standard for electrical terminations |
| Press and shrink fits | Interference joints |

Why mechanical methods matter in this comparison: they join any material combination, add no heat, are immediately verifiable, and — for SPR and clinching — are fast and automated. Their costs are the fastener weight and cost, the stress concentration at holes, and their unsuitability for sealing without a gasket.

12. Adhesive Bonding in Outline

| Family | Character |
| --- | --- |
| Epoxy | High strength, good temperature resistance; the structural standard |
| Polyurethane | Tough, flexible, good impact; used for glazing and panel bonding |
| Acrylic | Fast curing, tolerant of imperfect surface preparation |
| Cyanoacrylate | Very fast, low strength, poor durability |
| Silicone | Flexible, sealing, high temperature; low strength |
| Anaerobic | Threadlocking, retaining |

The three facts that govern adhesive joints:

1. Surface preparation determines the joint. Degreasing, abrasion and — for durability — chemical treatment or priming. The dominant failure mode is adhesive failure at the interface caused by inadequate preparation, and it is not detectable by inspection.

2. Design for shear, not peel (Section 6).

3. Durability, not initial strength, is the design question. Adhesive joints degrade with moisture, temperature and time, and a joint that tests strong at manufacture may not survive years of humid service. Accelerated ageing testing is the qualification that matters.

13. Hybrid Joining

Combining families frequently outperforms either alone, and these combinations are established industrial practice rather than novelties:

| Hybrid | What it achieves |
| --- | --- |
| Weld bonding (resistance spot welding + adhesive) | Spot welds give verifiable load capacity and hold the parts during cure; adhesive gives stiffness, fatigue performance and sealing between the spots. Standard in vehicle structures |
| Rivet bonding (self-piercing rivets + adhesive) | Same logic for materials that cannot be spot welded — the standard for aluminium and mixed-material bodies |
| Bolt bonding | Bolts provide verifiable capacity and clamping during cure |
| Brazed and mechanically retained | Mechanical interlock carries load; braze seals and conducts |
| Weld plus sealant | Weld carries load; sealant closes crevices against corrosion |

The recurring logic of hybrid joining: it pairs a verifiable, discrete load path with a distributed, sealing, fatigue-resistant one, and it directly answers the adhesive verification problem of Section 10 — the discrete elements can be counted and inspected, so the joint has a demonstrable minimum capacity even if the adhesive's contribution cannot be measured.

14. The Decision Walkthrough

1. Must it be demountable? If yes: mechanical. (Section 4)

2. What are the materials? Dissimilar or non-metallic combinations move the decision away from welding. (Section 5)

3. What load, and what service temperature? High load and high temperature favour welding; low temperature and distributed load open up adhesive. (Section 6)

4. What does heat do to this assembly? Heat-sensitive contents, coatings or heat-treated material may exclude the hot processes. (Section 7)

5. What does the geometry allow? Access, thickness and sealing requirements. (Section 8)

6. What volume and rate? (Section 9)

7. How will it be verified? If the answer is "it cannot be," consider a hybrid. (Section 10)

8. Would a hybrid outperform any single family? (Section 13)

9. Check the governing code or standard, which may mandate or exclude families regardless of engineering merit.

10. Only now, select the specific process within the chosen family — Chapter 73 for welding.

15. Common Selection Errors

| Error | Consequence |
| --- | --- |
| Assuming welding by default | A joint fights the process for the product's whole life; the alternative was never evaluated |
| Fusion welding dissimilar metals that form intermetallics | Brittle joint; the metallurgy was decided at the drawing stage (Chapter 27) |
| Designing an adhesive joint in peel | Fails at a fraction of its shear capacity |
| Ignoring adhesive service temperature | The joint's limit is the adhesive's, not the structure's |
| Under-specifying adhesive surface preparation | The dominant adhesive failure mode, and undetectable by inspection |
| Using mechanical fasteners in a fatigue-loaded joint without considering the holes | Holes are fatigue initiation sites |
| Welding pre-coated components without a coating strategy | Coating damage, hazardous fume, and a repair operation |
| Choosing a family the organization cannot verify | An uncontrollable joint with no evidence route |
| Ignoring cure time in production planning | Fixtures and floor space consumed; throughput below plan |
| Treating a hybrid as unnecessary complexity | Forgoing the combination that solves both the verification and the fatigue problem |

16. Worked Example: A Mixed-Material Vehicle Structure

Situation. A vehicle structure is being designed with aluminium extrusions, aluminium sheet, high-strength steel sheet and some composite panels. The body shop's existing capability is resistance spot welding of steel. The question is how to join the structure.

Step 1 — Recognize that no single family serves this. The joints fall into distinct categories — steel to steel, aluminium to aluminium, aluminium to steel, composite to metal — and each has different viable families. A single-process answer will be wrong for at least some of them.

Step 2 — Steel to steel. Resistance spot welding remains the right answer: existing capability, high rate, adequate strength (Volume 1). Weld bonding — adding adhesive — should be evaluated, because it improves stiffness, fatigue performance and sealing at modest additional cost, and the spot welds hold the parts during cure (Section 13).

Step 3 — Aluminium to aluminium. Resistance spot welding of aluminium is possible but has a narrow process window and heavy electrode wear (Volume 1, Chapter 14). The alternatives are self-piercing rivets, friction stir welding for long extrusion seams (Chapter 57), laser welding, and adhesive. For long straight extrusion joints, FSW is strong; for sheet assembly, SPR with adhesive is the industry-standard answer.

Step 4 — Aluminium to steel. Fusion welding is excluded (Chapter 27, Section 7). The viable routes are self-piercing rivets, adhesive, rivet bonding (both together), cold metal transfer brazing onto coated steel, and magnetic pulse welding for tubular joints (Chapter 62). For sheet-to-sheet, rivet bonding is the established answer.

Step 5 — Composite to metal. Only adhesive and mechanical apply. Adhesive is preferred structurally because fastener holes in composite are damaging stress concentrations; mechanical elements are often added anyway for verifiable capacity and for peel resistance.

Step 6 — Address galvanic corrosion, which the material mix guarantees. Aluminium in contact with steel in the presence of moisture is a galvanic cell (Chapter 27, Section 11). Adhesive serves a second function here: a continuous adhesive layer between the two metals acts as an insulating barrier, which is a genuine engineering reason for rivet bonding beyond its structural merits.

Step 7 — Address the verification problem. Adhesive contribution cannot be verified non-destructively (Section 10). The hybrid answer resolves it: the rivets or spot welds provide a countable, inspectable minimum load path, so the joint's demonstrable capacity does not depend on the adhesive, while the adhesive delivers the stiffness, fatigue and sealing benefits.

Step 8 — Plan the process capability honestly. The body shop currently has resistance spot welding only. Adding SPR, adhesive dispensing with surface preparation control, and possibly FSW is a substantial capital and capability programme with a long lead time — and the surface preparation and adhesive process control is the hardest part to build, not the equipment. That should be stated at the design stage, not discovered during industrialization.

Step 9 — Record the joining strategy as a design deliverable. A mixed-material structure needs an explicit joining strategy document — which family for which joint category, and why — because the decisions interact with material selection, corrosion protection, assembly sequence and repair strategy. Leaving it implicit is how a structure ends up with joints that cannot be made economically.

17. Known Gaps

• Mechanical fastening and adhesive bonding are outlined, not developed. Each is a substantial engineering discipline with its own standards, design methods and literature.

• No strength, temperature or cost values are given. All are material-, product- and supplier-specific.

• Adhesive selection requires the adhesive manufacturer's data and application-specific testing, particularly for durability.

• Design methods for adhesive and bolted joints — stress analysis, joint efficiency, bolt group design — are outside this reference set.

• Code requirements may mandate or exclude families for specific applications and must be checked.

• Recycling and end-of-life separation is an increasingly significant selection criterion, particularly for mixed-material structures, and is noted rather than developed.

What automation actually changes — it removes the welder's continuous correction, so every variation the welder used to absorb must now be engineered out or sensed, and fixturing and part tolerance become the quality system.
