1. What Automation Removes, and What That Costs

A manual welder is a continuous, adaptive control system. Watching the pool, they correct for a gap that varies along the joint, for a part that is a millimetre out of position, for a plate thicker than the drawing says, for distortion developing as the weld progresses, and for a tack that stands proud. None of these corrections is recorded anywhere, and most are not consciously noticed.

Automation removes that control system and replaces it with a machine that repeats a programmed path exactly. The consequence is the single most important fact about welding automation:

Everything the welder was silently absorbing must now be either engineered out of the process or sensed and compensated for by the machine.

This explains why robot welding cells succeed or fail on things that look peripheral to welding:

• Part tolerance — because the robot cannot see that the part is different from the last one.

• Fixture repeatability — because the robot goes where it was taught, not where the joint is.

• Tack weld consistency — because a large tack changes the joint geometry the robot arrives at.

• Consumable condition — because nobody is watching the arc.

What automation gives in return: consistency, higher arc-on time, repeatable heat input, complete process data on every weld, and the removal of a welder from a hazardous position. These are real and substantial. But they are only realized if the variation problem is solved first, and a cell installed without solving it produces defects consistently instead of good welds consistently.

2. Levels of Automation

| Level | Description | Human role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Manual | Welder holds and manipulates the torch | Continuous adaptive control |
| Semi-automatic | Wire fed automatically, torch manipulated by hand (conventional GMAW/FCAW) | Torch manipulation and adaptation |
| Mechanized | Machine moves the torch or the work; an operator watches and adjusts during welding | Monitoring and intervention |
| Automatic | Machine performs the weld; the operator loads, starts and unloads | Setup and loading |
| Robotic | Programmable multi-axis manipulator, capable of complex paths and multiple parts | Programming, setup, maintenance |
| Adaptive / autonomous | Sensing and closed-loop correction during welding | Programming, exception handling |

The distinction between mechanized and automatic matters for qualification (Section 18): the operator's role differs, and so does what the operator must be qualified to do.

3. The Cell as a System

A welding robot is one component of a system, and the system's weakest element determines its output:

| Element | Function | Failure consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Robot manipulator | Positions and moves the torch | Reach and access limits determine which joints are weldable at all |
| Positioner | Moves the part | Determines whether joints can be presented in the flat position |
| Fixture | Locates and holds the part | The dominant quality variable (Section 6) |
| Power source and wire feed | Delivers the process | Must communicate with the robot controller |
| Torch and consumables | Delivers the arc | Contact tip and nozzle wear silently degrade quality (Section 10) |
| Torch cleaning station | Removes spatter, sprays anti-spatter, cuts the wire | Not optional in production |
| TCP calibration device | Verifies the tool centre point | Without it, a bent torch goes undetected |
| Seam finding / tracking | Locates the actual joint | The compensation for part variation (Section 7) |
| Fume extraction | Removes fume from an enclosed cell | Required — the cell concentrates fume |
| Safety enclosure and interlocks | Protects personnel | Mandatory |
| Controller and data logging | Coordinates and records | The process record (Section 16) |

4. Robots: Types, Capability and Reach

| Type | Character | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Six-axis articulated | The standard welding robot; six degrees of freedom give torch orientation flexibility | General welding |
| Seven-axis / redundant | An extra axis to reach around obstructions | Complex assemblies, restricted access |
| Gantry-mounted | Robot on a linear gantry, extending the work envelope | Large structures |
| Collaborative (cobot) | Force-limited, operable without full guarding under an assessed risk | Low-volume, high-mix work where programming ease matters more than speed |
| Dedicated / hard automation | Purpose-built for one joint at very high rate | Very high volume, single product |

Selection criteria that actually matter: reach and work envelope against the part; payload including torch, cable and any sensing package; repeatability; and — the one most often underestimated — whether the torch can physically reach every joint at a usable angle, which is an access study rather than a specification comparison.

Collaborative robots deserve a specific note. Their advantage in welding is not primarily safety — a welding arc requires screening regardless of whether the robot is force-limited — but programming accessibility: they can be hand-guided through a path, which makes short-run programming practical for a fabricator who could not justify a conventional cell. That is what has driven their adoption in low-volume, high-mix shops.

5. Positioners and Coordinated Motion

A positioner rotates and tilts the workpiece, and its purpose is specific and important: to present every joint in the flat or horizontal position.

Why that matters:

• Deposition rate is highest in the flat position, and out-of-position welding restricts the process to lower-deposition modes (Chapter 39, Section 11).

• Weld quality is generally best in the flat position.

• The programme is simpler and more robust.

| Type | Axes | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Turntable | 1 | Rotating circular or symmetrical parts |
| Headstock-tailstock | 1 | Long parts between centres |
| Tilt-rotate | 2 | General purpose — the workhorse |
| Skyhook / drop-centre | 2 | Large parts with access below |

Coordinated motion — the positioner moving simultaneously with the robot, under one controller — is the capability that makes continuous welding of a complex three-dimensional seam possible while keeping the joint at the optimum orientation throughout. Without it, the part is repositioned between welds and each weld is a separate operation with its own start and stop.

6. Fixturing: The Real Determinant of Success

This section is placed here deliberately, because fixturing is where robot welding projects are won or lost, and it is consistently under-budgeted relative to the robot.

What the fixture must do:

1. Locate the part repeatably — the robot welds where it was taught, so the part must be in the same place every time. Repeatability, not accuracy, is the requirement.

2. Hold the joint closed and in position against welding forces and against distortion as the weld progresses.

3. Resist distortion — but not so rigidly that it locks in unacceptable residual stress on crack-sensitive material (Chapter 22, Section 11).

4. Present the joint accessibly without obstructing the torch or the gas.

5. Provide reliable earth return, without which arc blow and inconsistent current follow (Chapter 46, Section 11).

6. Load and unload quickly, since fixture cycle time is often the cell's real constraint.

7. Tolerate spatter and heat without its own accuracy degrading.

The recurring failure: a cell specified around a robot's cycle time and delivered with a fixture that does not locate repeatably. The robot then welds accurately to the wrong place, and the cell produces consistent defects.

Part tolerance is the fixture's input. A fixture cannot make an out-of-tolerance part correct; it can only locate it. If incoming parts vary beyond the joint tolerance, either the upstream processes must be improved or the cell must sense the variation (Section 7). Choosing neither is the third and most common option, and it does not work.

7. Seam Finding and Seam Tracking

Two distinct capabilities, frequently confused:

Seam finding (touch sensing) locates the joint before welding. The wire or nozzle is used as a probe, touching the part at defined points; the controller compares the found position with the taught position and shifts the programme accordingly. It is cheap — requiring no additional hardware — and it compensates for part-to-part positional variation. It does not compensate for variation along the joint.

Seam tracking follows the joint during welding:

| Method | Principle | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Through-arc (arc sensing) | The torch weaves, and the current variation indicates the joint's position | No extra hardware; works only on joints with sidewalls (fillets, grooves); cannot see ahead |
| Laser vision | A laser stripe projected ahead of the arc, viewed by a camera, measuring the joint's actual position and geometry | Sees ahead; measures gap and mismatch; enables adaptive control (Section 8); cost and cleanliness requirements |
| Tactile / mechanical | A probe follows the joint | Simple, robust, physically obstructive |

When each is appropriate:

• Consistent parts, consistent fixture: neither is needed. This is the cheapest and most robust cell.

• Part-to-part variation, consistent within a part: touch sensing.

• Variation along the joint — from distortion during welding, or from a large fabricated assembly: tracking.

• Variable gap requiring parameter change: laser vision with adaptive control.

The important engineering point: sensing is a compensation for variation, and it costs money, cycle time and complexity. Reducing the variation at source is usually cheaper and always more robust. Sensing should be selected because the variation genuinely cannot be economically removed — not as a substitute for engineering it out.

8. Adaptive Control

Adaptive control goes beyond tracking: the system measures the joint and changes the welding parameters in response.

| Measured | Adapted |
| --- | --- |
| Joint gap | Wire feed speed, weave width, number of passes |
| Joint cross-sectional area | Deposition rate |
| Root opening | Root pass parameters |
| Position along the joint | Torch position and angle |
| Arc signals | Detection of process deviation |

Where it earns its cost: large fabrications where fit-up genuinely varies along a joint — shipbuilding, heavy structures, pipe — and multi-pass welding where the fill volume must match the actual groove.

Where it does not: small, well-fixtured parts where the correct answer is a better fixture.

9. Programming Methods

| Method | Character |
| --- | --- |
| Teach pendant (online) | The operator jogs the robot to each point and records it. Simple, requires no CAD, occupies the cell for the whole programming time |
| Hand guiding | Physically moving the robot through the path — the collaborative robot's advantage |
| Offline programming (OLP) | The programme is generated from CAD in software, simulated, and downloaded. The cell keeps producing during programming |
| Automatic path generation | Software generates welding paths from the CAD model's weld definitions |
| Parametric / template | Families of similar parts programmed from a template with dimensional variables |

The economic argument for offline programming is not programming speed but cell utilization: teaching a complex part online can take hours or days during which the cell produces nothing. For high-mix production this is frequently the deciding factor in whether automation is viable at all.

The catch: an offline programme assumes the real cell matches the model. Discrepancies between the modelled and actual fixture, part and robot must be resolved by calibration, and a poorly calibrated cell makes offline programmes that need extensive touch-up — which forfeits the benefit.

10. Torch, Consumables and Maintenance in an Automated Cell

In manual welding, the welder notices a worn contact tip because the arc feels wrong. In an automated cell nobody is watching, so consumable degradation continues until it produces defects.

| Item | Failure mode | Control |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Contact tip | Bore wear causing erratic current, arcing inside the tip, spatter | Scheduled replacement by arc-time or part count |
| Nozzle | Spatter build-up disturbing gas flow, causing porosity | Automated cleaning station; scheduled replacement |
| Liner | Wear causing feed instability | Scheduled replacement |
| Gas diffuser | Spatter blockage | Cleaning and replacement |
| Torch alignment (TCP) | A collision bends the torch; the robot then welds accurately to the wrong place | Automatic TCP verification at defined intervals |
| Anti-collision device | Protects the torch in a crash | Verify function; a triggered device must be reset and TCP re-verified |
| Wire supply | Bulk drums run out or tangle | Level monitoring; drum handling discipline |
| Gas supply | Cylinder change, manifold drift | Monitoring; leak checks |

The scheduled replacement principle recurs throughout this reference set — tip dressing in resistance welding (Volume 1, Chapter 13), nozzle life in plasma welding (Chapter 42), wheel dressing in seam welding (Chapter 48), cover glass in laser welding (Chapter 54). In an automated arc cell it applies to the contact tip and nozzle, and the interval must be established from a life trial and enforced by count rather than by inspection.

Automatic torch cleaning stations — which ream the nozzle, spray anti-spatter and cut the wire to a consistent stick-out — are standard equipment for a reason: they address the two things that most degrade an unattended cell's output.

11. Process Selection for Automation

| Process | Automation suitability |
| --- | --- |
| GMAW (131/135) | The dominant robotic arc process — continuous wire, no slag, high deposition, controllable |
| GMAW pulsed | All-position capability at controlled heat; standard in modern cells |
| Metal-cored (133/138) | High deposition, minimal slag; good for automation |
| FCAW (136) | Good, but slag removal between passes is an obstacle to unattended multi-pass welding |
| GTAW (141) | Used where quality justifies the speed penalty — orbital, tube, precision (Chapter 70) |
| SAW (121) | Inherently mechanized; robot-mounted for some applications |
| Laser and hybrid (52x) | Inherently automated; highest precision requirement (Chapter 52) |
| Resistance spot (21x) | The most automated welding process of all (Volume 1, Chapter 6) |
| SMAW (111) | Not automatable — electrode changing makes it impractical |

The slag consideration is worth stating: any slag-producing process requires interpass cleaning, which either needs a person or an additional automated operation. This is a real constraint on unattended multi-pass FCAW and a significant reason GMAW and metal-cored wire dominate robotic welding.

12. Parameters and Their Control

The welding parameters are those of the process chapters; automation changes how they are managed:

• Parameters are stored in the programme, so the same values are used every time — the consistency benefit.

• Parameters can vary along the joint under programme control: ramping current around a corner, changing at a thickness transition, adapting to a sensed gap.

• Start and stop sequences — pre-flow, hot start, crater fill, burnback, post-flow — are programmed rather than manual, and they are where a large share of automated weld defects occur.

• Every weld's actual parameters can be recorded, giving a complete process record (Section 16).

• Parameter drift is invisible without monitoring, because nobody is watching.

Corner and start-stop treatment deserves emphasis. A manual welder naturally slows and adjusts at a corner. A robot travelling at programmed speed around a corner deposits more metal per unit length on the inside and less on the outside unless the programme handles it. Corners, starts and stops are the characteristic locations of automated welding defects.

13. Setup and Execution Procedure

Cell setup

1. Verify the WPS and confirm the programme's parameters match it.

2. Verify the TCP — a bent torch invalidates every taught point.

3. Verify torch condition: contact tip, nozzle, liner, diffuser; check the cleaning station.

4. Verify gas: correct mixture, flow, no leaks with the torch articulated through its range.

5. Verify wire: correct classification and diameter, correctly loaded, feed path serviced.

6. Verify the fixture: locators, clamps, earth return connection, and freedom from spatter build-up.

7. Load a part and verify fixture location repeatability — load and unload several times.

8. Run the programme dry, without arc, to verify path, clearances and reach.

9. Weld a first-off part and inspect it against the acceptance criteria.

Production

10. Monitor arc data and any deviation alarms.

11. Maintain the consumable replacement schedule by count, not by symptom.

12. Inspect at the established frequency, and specifically after any consumable change, collision, programme edit or material batch change.

13. Record parameters, part identity and any interventions.

After a collision or intervention

14. Re-verify the TCP before restarting — this is the step most often skipped and most often the cause of a subsequent batch of misplaced welds.

15. Verify the first part after any intervention.

14. Defect Catalog for Automated Welding

| Defect | Detection | Automation-specific cause | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Weld consistently offset from the joint | Visual; UT | Part not located as taught (fixture wear, spatter build-up on locators, part variation); TCP drift after a collision | Verify TCP; check and clean fixture locators; check incoming part variation; add touch sensing |
| Weld misses the joint entirely at one location | Visual; UT | Distortion during welding moving the joint away from the taught path | Seam tracking; revise the welding sequence to control distortion; add tacking |
| Variation in weld size along a joint | Visual; dimensional | Gap variation with no adaptive control; speed variation at corners | Adaptive control; programme corner treatment; improve fit-up |
| Defects concentrated at starts and stops | Visual; RT | Start and crater sequences not optimized; gas timing | Programme hot start, crater fill, burnback and gas timing; use run-on/run-off where possible |
| Porosity appearing progressively | RT; visual | Nozzle spatter build-up disturbing gas flow; nobody watching | Automatic nozzle cleaning; scheduled nozzle replacement |
| Erratic arc, spatter, current variation | Arc data; visual | Contact tip wear; liner wear; feed instability (Chapter 39, Section 8) | Scheduled tip and liner replacement by count |
| Burn-through at a thin section | Visual | Programme uses one parameter set across a varying thickness | Programme parameter changes at thickness transitions |
| A whole batch defective | Inspection after the fact | An undetected change — collision, programme edit, consumable change, material batch — with no first-off verification | First-off inspection after every intervention; process monitoring with deviation alarms |
| Arc blow, inconsistent current | Visual; arc data | Earth return through the fixture degraded by spatter or wear | Maintain and inspect the earth return path as a scheduled item |
| Collision damage | Immediate | Part not present, part misloaded, fixture obstruction, programme error | Part-present sensing; anti-collision device; dry-run new programmes |

15. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Welds offset on every part after a collision

Symptom: all welds displaced by a consistent amount following a crash.

Category: TCP.

Likely causes: the torch was bent in the collision, so the tool centre point no longer matches the taught points. The robot is repeating its programme accurately; the torch is not where the controller thinks it is.

Steps: verify and re-establish the TCP using the calibration device; inspect the torch neck for damage and replace if bent; re-verify a first-off part; make TCP verification a mandatory step after every anti-collision trigger — this is the single most valuable procedural control in a robot cell.

Card 2 — Quality degrading gradually through a shift

Symptom: acceptable early, increasing porosity and spatter later; programme unchanged.

Category: consumable wear.

Likely causes: contact tip bore wear; nozzle spatter build-up restricting gas flow; liner loading with debris.

Steps: check arc-time since the last tip change against the established interval; inspect the nozzle and verify the cleaning station is functioning; establish replacement intervals by count and enforce them — in an unattended cell there is no operator to notice the arc degrading (Section 10).

Card 3 — Intermittent defects on nominally identical parts

Symptom: most parts good, some with lack of fusion or misplaced welds; no pattern in time.

Category: part or fixture variation.

Likely causes: incoming part dimensional variation exceeding the joint tolerance; fixture locating inconsistently; spatter build-up on locators; clamping sequence varying; tack welds varying in size and position.

Steps: measure incoming part variation on a sample; load and unload one part repeatedly and measure the resulting joint position; clean and inspect locators; check tack weld consistency, which is a frequent and overlooked source; then decide between improving the input variation and adding sensing (Sections 6 and 7).

Card 4 — Cell producing far below its planned output

Symptom: the cell works but does not achieve the cycle time the business case assumed.

Category: system, not robot.

Likely causes: load and unload time dominating; fixture cycle time; programming time on the cell for new parts; consumable changes and cleaning; first-off inspection; rework of defects.

Steps: measure where the time actually goes over a full shift rather than assuming; arc-on time as a percentage of shift time is the diagnostic figure, and it is frequently far below what the business case assumed; address the largest contributor — which is usually loading, programming or rework rather than welding speed.

16. Quality Assurance in an Automated Cell

Automation changes the quality strategy fundamentally:

What improves: parameter consistency; complete process data on every weld; repeatable travel speed and torch position; controlled heat input; and elimination of welder-to-welder variation.

What worsens: nobody is watching the arc; consumable degradation is silent; a fault produces defective parts continuously rather than being noticed and corrected; and a programme or TCP error affects every part until it is found.

The regime that works:

1. First-off inspection after every intervention — programme change, consumable change, collision, fixture adjustment, material batch change. This is the highest-value control in an automated cell.

2. Process data monitoring with limits — current, voltage, wire feed speed and gas flow recorded per weld and compared against limits, with alarms. This is what replaces the welder's eyes.

3. Scheduled consumable replacement by count, not by symptom.

4. Periodic TCP verification and after every collision.

5. Sampling inspection at a frequency matched to the consequence of a batch of defective parts.

6. Traceability linking each part to its programme revision, parameters and consumable batch (Chapter 33, Section 6).

The structural point: an automated cell makes defects consistently as readily as it makes good welds. The quality system's job is to detect a change quickly, because the cost of a change going undetected is the entire production between the change and its discovery.

17. Safety Specifics

• Robot motion is the primary hazard. An industrial robot moves fast, with force, and without warning. Physical guarding with interlocks is the standard control, and the safety requirements are governed by the industrial robot safety standards — ISO 10218 for robots and robot systems, with ISO/TS 15066 addressing collaborative applications.

• Collaborative operation is not automatically safe. A force-limited robot may be safe to contact, but a welding torch, arc, hot part and spatter are not — a collaborative welding application requires a risk assessment addressing the process hazards, not just the robot's forces, and normally still requires arc screening and fume control.

• Arc radiation is contained by the cell enclosure, which must be UV-opaque and must protect anyone outside it (Chapter 37, Section 3).

• Fume accumulates in an enclosed cell and must be extracted at a rate matched to the deposition rate.

• Entry procedures for programming, maintenance and clearing faults: lockout, teach-mode speed limits, enabling devices, and — critically — the discipline that a person inside the cell is never protected by the interlocks they bypassed to get there.

• Stored energy in the robot's axes, particularly on vertical axes that can fall when brakes are released.

• Hot parts and spatter in a cell where the operator loads immediately after welding.

18. Standards and Qualification

• Robot and cell safety: ISO 10218 (robots and robot systems for industrial environments — safety requirements) and ISO/TS 15066 for collaborative applications.

• Operator qualification: ISO 14732 covers qualification testing of welding operators and weld setters for mechanized and automatic welding [S2]. This is the applicable standard, not the manual welder standard — the competence being tested is setup, verification and process monitoring, not manipulation (Chapter 32, Section 9).

• Procedure qualification: as Chapter 31. The WPS applies to the process regardless of who or what holds the torch; automation does not remove the requirement.

• Quality system: ISO 3834 applies fully, and its equipment maintenance, calibration and traceability requirements are more consequential in an automated cell, not less (Chapter 33).

• Acceptance criteria: unchanged — ISO 5817 or the applicable code (Chapter 36).

The qualification point most often missed: a shop that automates and disbands its welder qualification programme has substituted one requirement for another, not eliminated it. Operators must be qualified under ISO 14732, and the procedures must still be qualified.

19. Worked Example: A Robot Cell That Never Achieved Its Planned Output

Situation. A fabricator installs a welding robot cell justified on a cycle time calculation. A year later, output is roughly half the plan. Weld quality is acceptable. Management concludes the robot is too slow and considers a second cell.

Step 1 — Measure where the time actually goes. Over a full shift, record: arc-on time, part loading and unloading, fixture operations, programme changes and teaching, consumable changes and torch cleaning, first-off inspection, waiting for parts, and rework. Arc-on time as a percentage of shift time is the key figure, and it is almost always far lower than the business case assumed.

Step 2 — Test the assumption in the business case. Cycle time calculations are typically built from welding speed and weld length. They frequently ignore loading, fixture cycles, programming, consumable maintenance and inspection — which together commonly exceed the welding time.

Step 3 — Examine loading and unloading. If the cell has a single fixture, the robot is idle during every load. A two-station arrangement, where the operator loads one side while the robot welds the other, can roughly double output with no change to the robot at all — and it is a far cheaper intervention than a second cell.

Step 4 — Examine programming time. If the cell handles a high mix and each new part is taught online, the cell is idle for hours during teaching. Offline programming moves that work off the cell (Section 9) and is frequently the single largest available gain in a high-mix shop.

Step 5 — Examine consumable and cleaning stoppages. Frequent tip changes, manual nozzle cleaning and wire changes all consume cell time. An automatic torch cleaning station, bulk wire supply and a proper replacement schedule reduce them.

Step 6 — Examine rework. Time spent reworking defective parts is time the cell's output does not include. If rework is significant, the fixture and part tolerance question (Section 6) is costing output as well as quality.

Step 7 — Reconsider the second-cell decision on the evidence. If arc-on time is a small fraction of shift time, a second cell doubles the capacity of the element that is not the constraint, and output will not double. Fixing the actual constraint is cheaper and faster.

Step 8 — Record the general lesson. A welding robot's cycle time is not a cell's output. The business case for automation must be built on shift output including loading, programming, maintenance and inspection, and where it is not, the shortfall is discovered a year later and attributed to the robot.

20. Known Gaps

• No cycle times, costs or utilization figures are given. They are entirely application-specific.

• Robot programming languages and controller specifics are vendor-dependent and are not covered; this reference set names no products.

• Sensor and adaptive control implementations vary substantially between suppliers and are described functionally.

• ISO 10218 and ISO/TS 15066 editions should be confirmed; robot safety standards are under active revision.

• Collaborative welding applications are a developing area, and the risk assessment approach for them is application-specific.

• Vision-based part identification and autonomous programming are developing capabilities not covered here.

1. Why Pipe Welding Is Its Own Discipline

A butt weld between two pipes is geometrically a butt weld and practically a different problem from a butt weld in plate, for four reasons:

The weld travels through every position. On a fixed horizontal pipe, one continuous weld passes through overhead at the bottom, vertical up both sides, and flat at the top. A single set of parameters cannot be correct throughout (Section 2).

The root is usually inaccessible. In most pipe joints the inside cannot be reached, inspected or repaired after welding. The root pass must be correct first time, and everything about pipe welding practice follows from that.

The inside atmosphere must be controlled. On any material that oxidizes, the root's back face requires purging (Section 8).

The joint is closed and self-restraining. A pipe joint restrains its own contraction circumferentially in a way a plate butt weld does not.

2. Position, and the 6G Problem

Pipe welding positions are defined in Chapter 28, Section 9. The key distinction:

| Position | Pipe | Welding position |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1G | Rotated | Flat throughout — the easy case |
| 2G | Fixed vertical | Horizontal throughout |
| 5G | Fixed horizontal | Passes through overhead, vertical and flat |
| 6G | Fixed at 45° | All positions, continuously changing — the benchmark test |
| 6GR | 6G with a restriction ring | The most demanding standard test |

Why 5G and 6G are hard, stated physically: the molten pool is held by surface tension against gravity, and the direction of gravity relative to the pool changes continuously as the weld progresses around the circumference. At the bottom, the pool must be held up against gravity; at the sides, it tends to sag downward across the joint; at the top, gravity assists.

The consequence: the parameters and technique that produce a correct weld overhead will produce an excessively fluid, sagging pool at the top. Either the welder adapts continuously — which is exactly what a skilled pipe welder does — or the machine must be programmed to change its parameters by position (Section 6).

This is why 6G is the benchmark welder test (Chapter 32, Section 5): a welder who completes a 6G weld has demonstrated pool control through every orientation in one continuous joint.

3. Manual Pipe Welding Practice

Established practice, worth stating because orbital welding automates it:

Root pass options:

• GTAW root (141) — the highest-quality option, giving precise pool control and a smooth internal profile; requires purging; the standard for stainless, alloy and high-quality carbon steel work.

• Cellulosic SMAW root (E6010/E6011) — deep penetrating, fast-freezing, forgiving of an open root, welded downhill at speed; the pipeline standard for carbon steel, and explicitly not low-hydrogen (Chapter 38, Section 4).

• Consumable insert — a preplaced ring fused into the root, giving a consistent root profile (Section 9).

Fill and cap: SMAW with low-hydrogen electrodes, FCAW, or GMAW — chosen on deposition rate and code permission.

Direction: uphill welding gives higher deposition and penetration and is used where strength governs; downhill is fast and is standard on thin-wall pipeline work with cellulosic electrodes, where the technique is qualified for it.

The root pass is where the quality is decided, and the fill and cap cannot correct a defective root that they have buried.

4. Orbital Welding: Process Overview

Orbital welding mechanizes the rotation: the pipe stays fixed and the welding head rotates around it, carrying the torch through the full circumference under programme control.

The process is almost always GTAW (141/142), for the reasons that make GTAW the manual root process: precise pool control, no slag, no spatter, and a clean internal profile.

What mechanization delivers:

• Repeatability far beyond manual welding.

• Parameters that change by position under programme control, correctly and identically on every joint (Section 6).

• Access in restricted spaces — a compact head fits where a welder's hands and helmet cannot.

• Complete process records for every joint.

• Consistency independent of welder skill and fatigue — significant on installations with hundreds or thousands of joints.

What it requires:

• Excellent joint preparation — machined ends, consistent fit-up.

• Consistent material — wall thickness variation directly affects the result.

• Programme development for each pipe size, wall and material combination.

• A trained operator who can set up, verify and judge the result (Section 18).

5. Orbital Equipment Types

| Head type | Description | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Enclosed (closed) head | A small chamber clamps around the pipe and encloses the joint; filled with inert gas | Tube welding, high purity; small diameters; superb shielding; autogenous |
| Open head | The torch rotates on a guide ring or track around the pipe, unenclosed | Larger diameters; wire feed capability; accessible for observation |
| Track-mounted (band) systems | The head travels on a band clamped around the pipe | Large diameter pipeline and process pipe |
| Tube-to-tubesheet heads | Purpose-built for welding tubes into a tubesheet | Heat exchanger manufacture |

The enclosed head's advantage is shielding. By enclosing the joint in an inert atmosphere, it eliminates the shielding problems that dominate open-air welding of reactive and oxidation-sensitive materials — which is why it dominates high-purity tube welding (Section 11).

Wire feed is available on open heads and larger systems, allowing filled grooves; enclosed head welding of thin-wall tube is usually autogenous — no filler at all, the joint being fused directly.

6. Sector Programming: The Core of Orbital Control

This is the technical heart of orbital welding and the direct answer to the position problem of Section 2.

The circumference is divided into sectors — typically four or more — and each sector has its own parameter set:

| Sector | Position | Typical parameter direction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start / overhead | Bottom | Higher current to establish and hold the pool against gravity |
| Vertical up (both sides) | Sides | Reducing current; pool tends to sag |
| Flat / top | Top | Lowest current; gravity assists, so less energy is needed to maintain the pool |
| Overlap / downslope | Return to start | Controlled overlap onto the start, with current downslope to close the pool |

Parameters varied by sector: current (peak and background if pulsed), pulse timing, travel speed, wire feed speed where used, and arc voltage or arc length control.

Two further controls are standard:

Pulsed current is used almost universally in orbital GTAW. The peak establishes penetration and the background lets the pool partially solidify, giving control against gravity that steady current cannot (Chapter 41, Section 10).

Arc voltage control (AVC) measures arc voltage and adjusts the electrode height to maintain a constant arc length — compensating for pipe ovality, run-out, and electrode wear through the weld. Without it, arc length varies around the circumference and the weld varies with it.

The overlap at the closure is a defect-prone location and is programmed deliberately: the weld overlaps its own start by a controlled distance with a current downslope, so the pool closes rather than terminating abruptly.

7. The Root Pass and How It Is Controlled

The governing fact: in most pipe joints the root cannot be inspected, dressed or repaired after welding. The root pass is the joint.

What determines it:

| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| End preparation | Machined, square, consistent land and bevel; hand-cut ends are a leading cause of root defects |
| Fit-up: root gap and alignment (hi-lo) | Gap variation changes penetration directly; misalignment produces incomplete fusion on the low side |
| Wall thickness consistency | Variation within tolerance changes the heat required |
| Root parameters | Current, travel speed, pulse |
| Purge | Determines whether the root oxidizes (Section 8) |
| Consumable insert, where used | Provides consistent root geometry and filler (Section 9) |

Fit-up tolerance for orbital welding is tighter than for manual welding, because the machine cannot adapt. A manual welder compensates for a varying gap; an orbital head welds the programme it was given. This is why orbital installations invest in end preparation machining, and why a project that specifies orbital welding without specifying end preparation will not achieve it.

8. Purging in Pipe Welding

Covered generally in Chapter 30, Section 7 and Chapter 24, Section 10; the pipe-specific practice:

Why it matters: the root's inside face is exposed to whatever atmosphere is inside the pipe. On stainless, duplex, nickel and titanium, oxygen in that atmosphere oxidizes the hot root — producing heat tint at best and sugaring at worst, both of which destroy corrosion resistance at exactly the surface in contact with the process fluid.

Practice:

• Purge to a measured residual oxygen level, not to a time. An oxygen analyser on the purge exhaust is standard for critical work, and the required level is specified — with the tightest requirements in high-purity work.

• Contain the purge volume with dams, soluble film barriers or purpose-made devices. On a long or large pipe, purging the entire volume is slow and expensive; containing a short length around the joint is far faster and uses far less gas.

• Vent, do not pressurize. The purge must flow through and out, and excessive pressure blows the root out or produces root concavity.

• Maintain until cool. Hot stainless continues to oxidize after the arc stops.

• Gas selection: argon generally; nitrogen-bearing mixtures for duplex where austenite formation at the root is wanted; hydrogen-bearing forming gas on austenitic stainless for a bright root — never on ferritic steel or titanium.

Soluble dams deserve a specific note: water-soluble film barriers allow a short purge volume to be established and then dissolve and flush away when the system is filled — solving the problem of removing a dam from a completed pipe run. They must be fully removed, and a dam left in a system is a real and recurring installation defect.

9. Consumable Inserts and Backing

Consumable inserts are preplaced rings of filler metal fitted into the joint root before welding. The root pass fuses the insert, the pipe ends and the joint together.

Advantages: a consistent, repeatable root geometry independent of fit-up variation; a controlled filler addition at the root; a smooth internal profile; and improved tolerance of small fit-up variations.

Costs: the insert is a consumable; it requires its own preparation dimensions; and it must be correctly seated — an insert that is not fully seated produces a defect worse than no insert.

Backing rings are permanent metal rings inside the joint that support the root. They give a reliable root but leave a crevice and a stress concentration inside the pipe, so they are prohibited in corrosive service, in hygienic applications, and in fatigue-loaded joints. In clean-service piping they are generally not acceptable.

11. High-Purity and Hygienic Welding

A distinct discipline within pipe welding, where the requirement is not strength but the condition of the internal surface.

Why the internal surface governs: in pharmaceutical, biotech, food and semiconductor systems, the process fluid contacts the pipe's inside surface. Any feature that traps material, resists cleaning, or corrodes is a contamination risk. Consequences:

• The root must be smooth and fully penetrated, with no concavity, no excess penetration, no crevices.

• Heat tint must be minimal, and is specified against colour standards.

• No backing rings, no crevices, no dead legs.

• Autogenous welding is standard on thin-wall tube: no filler, so no filler-related contamination.

• Surface finish of the tube itself is specified — mechanically polished or electropolished — and the weld must not spoil it.

• Purge oxygen levels are specified very tightly.

• Every weld is documented, frequently with a weld log, coupon and internal borescope record.

The inspection regime is correspondingly specific: borescope examination of the internal surface of every weld, or of a sampled proportion, with acceptance judged against colour and profile criteria. This is one of the few applications where visual inspection of an internal surface is the primary acceptance method, and it is why enclosed-head orbital welding with tightly controlled purging dominates the sector.

12. Setup and Execution Procedure

Before welding

1. Confirm the WPS for the material, diameter and wall thickness, and confirm the operator's qualification.

2. Prepare the pipe ends by machining — square, correct land, correct bevel where used, and clean.

3. Clean the internal and external surfaces at the joint; on stainless, use stainless-only tooling.

4. Align and fit up, checking root gap and hi-lo alignment around the whole circumference, not at one point.

5. Fit consumable insert if used, verifying it is fully seated.

6. Set up the purge: install dams, connect gas, purge and verify the oxygen level with an analyser.

7. Fit the orbital head, verifying electrode condition, electrode position and head alignment on the pipe.

8. Load the programme for this diameter, wall and material; verify it against the WPS.

9. Weld a coupon — a test joint on the same material and preparation — and examine its root before welding production joints. On high-purity work this is a standard requirement at the start of every shift and after any change.

Welding

10. Start the cycle; the head executes the programmed sector sequence.

11. Monitor arc voltage, current and rotation for deviation.

12. Maintain the purge throughout and until the joint has cooled.

13. Verify the closure overlap completed correctly.

After welding

14. Inspect the outer surface and, where accessible, the root by borescope.

15. Record the weld: joint number, operator, programme, parameters, purge verification, material and consumable heat numbers.

16. Perform the specified NDT.

13. When to Use Orbital Welding and When Not To

| Choose orbital welding when | Choose manual welding when |
| --- | --- |
| Many identical joints — an installation with hundreds or thousands | Few joints, or all different |
| Consistency and documentation are required | Field conditions are uncontrolled |
| High-purity or hygienic requirements | Fit-up cannot be machined |
| Restricted access where a welder cannot reach | Joints are irregular, repairs, or tie-ins |
| Thin-wall tube where manual control is difficult | Very large diameters beyond head capability |
| Skilled pipe welders are unavailable | Access for the head is obstructed |
| Radiation or hazardous environments limiting human exposure | The work is one-off or exploratory |

Most real installations use both: orbital welding for the repetitive prefabricated spools and the accessible field joints, manual welding for tie-ins, repairs and awkward locations. Planning which joints go which way is a real engineering decision at the design stage, and it affects the piping layout — because a joint that must be manually welded needs access for a welder.

14. Defect Catalog

| Defect | Detection | Cause | Corrective action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Root oxidation / sugaring | Borescope; visual on accessible roots | Purge absent, insufficient, not verified, lost during welding, or stopped before cooling; leaking dam | Purge to a measured oxygen level; contain the volume; maintain until cool; verify dam integrity |
| Lack of root penetration | RT; borescope | Root gap too small; land too thick; current too low; wall thicker than programmed | Correct end preparation and fit-up; verify wall thickness; adjust the root sector programme |
| Root concavity | RT; borescope | Excessive purge pressure; gap too large; insufficient filler | Vent the purge properly; correct fit-up; add filler or use a consumable insert |
| Excess penetration / icicles | RT; borescope | Current too high; gap too large; travel too slow | Adjust the sector programme; correct fit-up |
| Incomplete fusion on one side | RT; UT | Hi-lo misalignment; head not centred; electrode offset | Improve alignment; verify head centring and electrode position |
| Defect at the closure overlap | RT | Overlap and downslope not programmed correctly; start conditions not re-established | Programme a controlled overlap with downslope |
| Variation in weld appearance around the circumference | Visual | Sector programme not correctly developed for position; AVC not functioning | Develop the sector programme on coupons; verify AVC |
| Tungsten inclusion | RT | Electrode contacted the pool; electrode contaminated or worn; current above the electrode's rating | Verify electrode type, size and condition; check head alignment (Chapter 41, Section 16) |
| Weld quality varying between joints | Inspection | Wall thickness or fit-up varying between joints; electrode wear through a series; purge inconsistent | Verify incoming material; establish electrode replacement interval; verify purge on every joint |
| Dam left in the system | Found on flushing, or never found | Soluble dam not fully dissolved or a physical dam not removed | Procedural control on dam removal and verification |

15. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Root oxidation appearing on some joints and not others

Symptom: borescope shows discoloured or sugared roots on a proportion of joints.

Category: purge.

Likely causes: purge verified on the first joint and assumed thereafter; dam leaking or displaced; purge stopped before the joint cooled; purge volume too large to be displaced in the time allowed; gas supply interruption.

Steps: verify the oxygen level on every joint, not once per session; check dam fit and integrity; extend the purge until the joint is cool; reduce the purge volume with dams so it can be displaced reliably; check the gas supply and connections. Intermittency here nearly always means the purge is being assumed rather than measured (Section 8).

Card 2 — Root penetration varying between joints with identical settings

Symptom: some joints fully penetrated, others not; programme unchanged.

Category: input variation.

Likely causes: wall thickness variation within the material tolerance; root gap variation from hand-prepared ends; land dimension varying; electrode wear reducing energy through a series of welds.

Steps: measure wall thickness on a sample of pipe; measure fit-up on several joints around the circumference; verify the ends are machined, not hand-cut; establish an electrode replacement interval. This is the orbital equivalent of the fit-up variation problem in every mechanized process (Chapter 69, Section 6).

Card 3 — Defects concentrated at the weld closure

Symptom: RT shows porosity or lack of fusion at the point where the weld meets its start.

Category: closure programming.

Likely causes: overlap distance too short; no current downslope, so the pool terminated abruptly; start conditions leaving a step that the overlap cannot fuse through.

Steps: programme a controlled overlap onto the start with a downslope; review the start sequence, since a poor start makes the closure harder; examine a coupon sectioned at the closure to see what is actually happening there.

Card 4 — Welds acceptable on coupons, defective in production

Symptom: coupon welds pass; installed joints fail inspection.

Category: field conditions.

Likely causes: coupons prepared and fitted on the bench with better fit-up than field joints; purge easier to establish and verify on a short coupon than on an installed run; head alignment easier on the bench; ambient conditions differ.

Steps: prepare coupons under field conditions rather than bench conditions — same fit-up method, same purge arrangement, same access; this is what makes a coupon representative, and a coupon that is not representative provides false assurance.

16. Testing and Quality Verification

| Method | Application |
| --- | --- |
| Borescope / internal visual | The primary acceptance method for high-purity work — root profile and colour |
| Radiography | The standard volumetric method for pipe welds |
| Ultrasonic / PAUT / AUT | Increasingly standard on pipeline girth welds; superior for planar defects; encoded records (Chapter 35, Section 7) |
| Penetrant testing | Surface examination on austenitic material |
| Hydrostatic / pneumatic testing | System-level proof — not a weld quality test (Chapter 35, Section 9) |
| Coupon welds | Welded alongside production under the same conditions and sectioned |
| Purge verification records | Oxygen level per joint — a process record that substitutes for inspection of an inaccessible surface |
| Weld logs | Joint-by-joint records of operator, programme, parameters, material heats and inspection results |

The weld log deserves emphasis in pipe work: an installation with thousands of joints, many of them inaccessible after commissioning, depends entirely on the record to demonstrate that each was made correctly. This is the traceability requirement of Chapter 33, Section 6 in its most demanding form.

17. Safety Specifics

• Argon asphyxiation. A purged pipe or vessel is an oxygen-deficient atmosphere, and argon is heavier than air and accumulates in low points. This has killed people, including on pipe installations where a purged line was entered. Purged volumes must be labelled and isolated, and confined space procedures apply (Chapter 37, Section 9).

• Working in restricted spaces — pipe racks, trenches, vessel interiors — combining confined space, shock and fume hazards.

• Working at height on installed pipework.

• Arc radiation in enclosed and reflective spaces.

• Hot pipework after welding, in locations where people move past it.

• Enclosed head equipment is compact and clamps around the pipe — a pinch hazard.

• Grinding and cutting during preparation and repair.

18. Standards and Qualification

• Process references: ISO 4063 references 141 and 142 for the GTAW processes used [S1].

• Procedure qualification: ASME Section IX, the ISO 15614 family, or the applicable piping code (Chapter 31). Pipe qualification carries diameter as a variable in addition to thickness and position (Chapter 32, Section 4).

• Operator qualification: ISO 14732 for orbital welding operators and weld setters [S2] — the competence is setup, purge verification, programme selection and result judgement, not manipulation. Manual pipe welders qualify under ISO 9606-1 or the code, and 6G is the benchmark test (Chapter 32, Section 5).

• Piping codes govern: process piping, power piping and pipeline codes each specify materials, qualification, inspection extent and acceptance.

• High-purity standards: the bioprocessing and semiconductor sectors have their own detailed requirements covering surface finish, weld acceptance, documentation and inspection, and these are more prescriptive than general welding standards.

19. Worked Example: Root Oxidation in a Pharmaceutical Installation

Situation. A contractor installs 316L process pipework using enclosed-head orbital welding. Borescope inspection finds unacceptable root discolouration on a proportion of joints. The orbital equipment is new, the operators are certified, and the programmes were developed on coupons that passed.

Step 1 — Confirm what the discolouration means. Heat tint on the root indicates the root was hot in the presence of oxygen. On 316L in pharmaceutical service, that is a corrosion resistance loss on the product-contact surface, and it is rejectable (Chapter 24, Section 10). The question is where the oxygen came from.

Step 2 — Check whether purge oxygen was measured on every joint or once per session. This is the single most productive question. Verifying the purge once and assuming it thereafter is common practice and is the leading cause of exactly this pattern — most joints are fine and some are not, depending on how well the purge happened to be established each time.

Step 3 — Check the purge volume and dam arrangement. A long run purged end to end takes a long time to reach the required oxygen level, and the operator under time pressure will start welding before it does. Containing a short volume with dams around the joint makes reaching the level fast and reliable, and it is the standard answer.

Step 4 — Check whether the purge was maintained until cool. Stopping the purge when the arc stops leaves hot metal exposed. On thin-wall tube the cooling time is short but not zero, and this is a frequent and easily corrected cause.

Step 5 — Check for leaks in the purge path. Dams that do not seal, fittings, open branches and valves left open all admit air. On an installed system with multiple branches this is a real and hard-to-find problem, and a systematic check of the purge boundary before each joint is the control.

Step 6 — Check why the coupons passed. Coupons welded on the bench with a short, well-sealed purge volume are far easier to purge than an installed run. The coupon was not representative (Section 15, Card 4), which is why it gave false assurance. Coupons should be prepared under installation conditions.

Step 7 — Check the closure and start regions specifically. These are where the joint is hottest for longest and where a marginal purge shows first. If discolouration is concentrated there, the purge is marginal rather than absent.

Step 8 — Correct the procedure, and verify the population. The corrective action is a purge procedure with measured oxygen verification per joint, contained purge volumes, maintenance until cool, and a recorded value in the weld log. Then every joint welded under the previous practice must be assessed — which on an inaccessible installed system is expensive, and is exactly why the verification requirement exists.

20. Known Gaps

• No parameters or sector programmes are given. They are diameter-, wall-, material- and equipment-specific and are developed on coupons.

• Purge oxygen level requirements are not stated numerically. They are specified by the application standard, and high-purity requirements are far tighter than general process piping.

• Piping code requirements are referenced, not reproduced, and the applicable code governs.

• High-purity sector standards are named by category rather than by number, as they vary by sector and jurisdiction.

• Pipeline field welding — with its own productivity-driven practices, mechanized systems and AUT inspection regimes — is a large discipline treated only in outline here.

• Tube-to-tubesheet welding is named as an application but not developed.

1. Why Environment Is a Process Variable

Every parameter and technique in this reference set assumes a normal shop or site environment: ambient temperature and pressure, breathable air, a dry workpiece, and unrestricted access.

Remove any of those and the process changes fundamentally — not in degree but in kind:

| Environment | What changes |
| --- | --- |
| Underwater | Cooling rate, arc stability, hydrogen availability, visibility, diver limits |
| Pressure (hyperbaric) | Arc characteristics, gas density, physiological limits |
| Confined | Fume and gas accumulation, shock risk, access, rescue |
| Live plant / in-service | Heat sink from flowing contents, burn-through risk, ignition risk |
| Radioactive | Personnel exposure time limits, remote operation, contamination control |
| Explosive atmosphere | Ignition sources prohibited entirely |
| Extreme cold | Material toughness, preheat requirement, equipment behaviour |

This chapter covers each, and the common thread is that the environment usually cannot be changed, so the process and the procedure must be.

2. Underwater Welding: The Three Approaches

| Approach | Description | Quality achievable |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wet welding | Welded directly in the water, no enclosure | Lowest — but fast, cheap and flexible |
| Cofferdam / dry chamber at ambient pressure | A structure excludes water from the joint, open to the surface | Approaching surface quality |
| Hyperbaric dry welding (habitat welding) | A sealed chamber excludes water; the interior is at ambient water pressure, gas-filled | Highest — approaching surface quality, and the route for structural and pressure work |

The choice is essentially between cost and quality, and the decision is usually made by the code and the criticality of the joint rather than by preference: structural repairs on offshore structures and pipelines requiring full properties are habitat-welded; non-critical attachments, temporary repairs and salvage work are wet-welded.

3. Wet Welding: The Mechanism and Its Consequences

The arc burns inside a gas bubble formed by the vaporization and decomposition of the surrounding water and the electrode covering. The bubble is unstable, forms and collapses continuously, and the arc burns within it.

Three consequences dominate, and every characteristic of wet welding follows from them:

1. Extremely rapid quenching. Water conducts heat away from the weld far faster than air. The cooling rate is enormously higher than a surface weld — the equivalent of quenching every weld immediately. The consequence is a hard, martensitic heat-affected zone in any hardenable steel (Chapter 22, Section 8), with low toughness and high cracking susceptibility.

2. Abundant hydrogen. Water dissociates in the arc, so the weld metal is exposed to a high concentration of hydrogen throughout. Combined with the hard microstructure from the quench and the restraint of a structural joint, all three ingredients of hydrogen cracking are present in abundance (Chapter 23, Section 4).

3. Arc instability and visibility. The bubble is unstable, the water is turbid, and the diver's visibility is frequently near zero.

The resulting joint properties: lower strength, substantially lower toughness, higher hardness, higher porosity, and a real risk of hydrogen cracking. Wet welds are therefore restricted by code and by engineering judgement, and they are qualified and accepted against criteria appropriate to what the process can achieve rather than against surface-welding criteria.

Material limitation is severe. Carbon equivalent governs (Chapter 23, Section 3): low-carbon-equivalent steels can be wet welded with acceptable results; higher-carbon-equivalent steels harden and crack. This makes material identification a prerequisite, and welding an unidentified steel underwater is a genuine hazard.

4. Wet Welding Consumables and Practice

Electrodes are specially manufactured and waterproofed — the covering sealed against water ingress, which would otherwise destroy it before it reached the joint. Consumable selection is limited to those qualified for the purpose.

Practice:

• Ferritic electrodes are used for most work, with the hardness and hydrogen consequences of Section 3.

• Austenitic (nickel-bearing) electrodes are used in some applications because the austenitic weld metal holds hydrogen in solution and is more tolerant of the hydrogen problem — at the cost of a dissimilar joint's own issues (Chapter 27).

• Drag technique is standard: the electrode is dragged along the joint in contact with the work, since maintaining a precise arc length blind in turbid water is impractical.

• Temper bead and multi-pass techniques are used deliberately, because each pass tempers the hard heat-affected zone of the previous one (Chapter 22, Section 12) — the same principle as temper bead welding on the surface (Chapter 34, Section 12), applied here to counteract the quench.

5. Hyperbaric Dry Welding

The joint is enclosed in a habitat — a chamber sealed against the structure and filled with gas at the ambient water pressure, displacing the water. The welder works inside, in a dry gas atmosphere.

Why it produces good welds: the water is gone, so the quench rate is normal, the hydrogen source is removed, visibility is good, and conventional processes and consumables can be used. The resulting welds can meet the same requirements as surface welds, which is why this is the route for structural and pressure-retaining repairs.

The pressure effects that remain, and they are real:

• Gas density rises with pressure, changing arc characteristics substantially. Arc voltage rises, the arc constricts, and parameters developed at surface pressure do not transfer. Procedures must be qualified at the working depth, or at least at a representative pressure.

• The chamber atmosphere must support the welder physiologically and the process metallurgically — usually a helium-oxygen mixture at depth, which itself affects the arc.

• Diver physiology governs everything: saturation diving, decompression, shift lengths, and communication difficulty in a helium atmosphere.

• Habitat installation is a substantial marine engineering operation in its own right, and it dominates the cost.

6. Habitat Welding

The habitat is fitted around the joint and sealed to the structure, water is displaced with gas, and the interior is drained and dried. Practical points:

• Sealing to an irregular structure is the principal engineering challenge, particularly on a corroded or damaged member.

• The atmosphere is monitored for oxygen, carbon dioxide, contaminants and welding fume, with the fume issue significant in a small sealed volume.

• Fire risk in an oxygen-controlled chamber is a serious consideration; oxygen levels are controlled partly for this reason.

• Preheat and interpass control are achievable, which is a further reason the resulting welds can meet surface standards.

• The joint must be dried thoroughly — residual moisture is a hydrogen source, and this is a controlled step rather than an assumption.

7. Diver and Equipment Safety

Underwater welding combines diving hazards with electrical hazards, and the combination is unforgiving:

• Electric shock. The diver is immersed in a conductive medium in contact with the workpiece. DC is used, not AC, because AC's continuous zero crossings and physiological effects make it far more dangerous in water. Direct-current electrode negative is standard, and the welding circuit is fitted with a positive-action safety switch controlled by the surface, so the circuit is energized only when the diver requests it and is de-energized immediately otherwise.

• Equipment insulation must be maintained rigorously; damaged insulation in water is directly hazardous.

• Hydrogen and oxygen accumulation. The arc dissociates water into hydrogen and oxygen. In an enclosed or inverted space — under a structure, inside a compartment, at the top of a habitat — this mixture accumulates and is explosive. Underwater welding explosions from trapped gas are a documented and recurring cause of serious injury, and venting enclosed volumes is a standard requirement.

• Diving hazards — decompression, entrapment, differential pressure, visibility, currents — govern the operation and are managed under diving regulation.

• Communication with the surface and the safety switch operator is safety-critical.

8. Underwater Cutting

| Method | Character |
| --- | --- |
| Oxy-arc cutting | A tubular electrode carries oxygen; the arc preheats and the oxygen jet cuts. The workhorse method for steel |
| Exothermic cutting rods | A rod containing reactive metals burns fiercely once ignited, cutting almost any material including concrete; needs oxygen but no external arc once burning |
| Shielded metal arc cutting | Melting and washing away with an electrode |
| Abrasive waterjet | Non-thermal, no ignition risk |
| Mechanical | Saws, shears, grinders |

The gas accumulation hazard applies to cutting even more strongly than to welding, because cutting generates large volumes of gas rapidly. Cutting into an enclosed volume — a tank, a compartment, a void — that contains hydrocarbons or trapped gas has caused fatal explosions, and the controls are the same as for hot work on any container of unknown contents (Chapter 37, Section 8).

9. Inspection Underwater

Inspection is as constrained as welding:

• Visual inspection by diver or ROV, with cleaning of marine growth first — which is itself a substantial operation.

• Magnetic particle inspection underwater, using specially formulated inks.

• Ultrasonic testing underwater, with couplant supplied by the water itself in some configurations.

• ACFM (alternating current field measurement) — widely used offshore because it detects and sizes surface-breaking cracks through marine growth and coatings, reducing the cleaning requirement significantly.

• Radiography is possible but the safety and logistics are severe.

The inspection constraint feeds back into the process decision: a weld that cannot be adequately inspected must be made by a process and to a procedure that gives confidence without inspection — which is another argument for habitat welding on critical joints.

10. Confined Space Welding

Welding inside vessels, tanks, pipes, trenches, compartments and voids concentrates every hazard (Chapter 37, Section 9):

• Fume and gas accumulate with no natural dilution.

• Shielding and purge gases displace oxygen, and argon and CO₂ are heavier than air and pool in the bottom of a space.

• Shock risk increases — damp conditions, extensive body contact with the workpiece, and no room to recoil.

• Heat accumulates, causing heat stress that degrades judgement about every other hazard.

• Escape and rescue are difficult, and rescuer fatalities are a documented pattern.

The controls are procedural and non-negotiable: permit-controlled entry, atmosphere testing before and continuously during, forced ventilation, an attendant outside, rescue arrangements established before entry, and — specific to welding — isolation of gas supplies during breaks, because a leaking torch left inside will fill the space while nobody is watching.

11. Elevated Temperature and Live-Plant Welding

Welding on equipment that is hot, or that cannot be shut down:

• The workpiece is a heat sink or a heat source, changing the thermal cycle from the qualified condition in either direction.

• Preheat may be provided by the process fluid — or the fluid may be quenching the joint (Section 12).

• Heat stress on personnel limits working time.

• Thermal expansion of the structure during welding changes fit-up and restraint.

• Insulation removal exposes hot surfaces and may expose hazardous insulation materials.

12. In-Service Welding on Operating Pipelines

A specific and technically demanding case: welding onto a pipeline that continues to carry product. It is done to install branch connections and repair sleeves without shutting down the line, and it presents two competing risks that must be balanced against each other:

Risk 1 — Burn-through. The pipe wall is thinned by the welding heat while internal pressure acts on it. If the remaining wall cannot contain the pressure, it fails. This risk decreases with lower heat input.

Risk 2 — Hydrogen cracking. The flowing contents remove heat from the joint rapidly — a substantial quench — producing a hard heat-affected zone. Combined with hydrogen, this risk increases with lower heat input, because lower heat input means faster cooling.

The two risks push in opposite directions, and the procedure must find heat input that is low enough to avoid burn-through and high enough to avoid an unacceptably hard heat-affected zone. This is one of the clearest examples in this reference set of a genuinely two-sided process window, and it is why in-service welding procedures are developed with thermal analysis rather than by extrapolating from ordinary practice.

The controls:

• Wall thickness assessment before welding, by ultrasonic measurement, to establish what remains.

• Flow conditions — flow rate, pressure, product — recorded, because they determine the quench rate. Some procedures require flow to be reduced but not stopped: stopping flow removes the burn-through cooling benefit, and full flow maximizes the quench.

• Low-hydrogen consumables, without exception.

• Heat input controlled within a qualified band, with the band established for the specific wall thickness and flow condition.

• Temper bead or controlled deposition sequences to temper the hard heat-affected zone.

• Delayed inspection for hydrogen cracking (Chapter 35, Section 12).

• Procedure qualification representing the actual thermal conditions, not a bench coupon.

13. Radioactive and Contaminated Environments

Nuclear plant maintenance and decommissioning:

• Personnel dose limits determine the maximum time a welder can spend at the joint, which frequently makes manual welding impossible.

• Remote and automated welding is therefore the standard approach, with equipment designed for remote deployment and retrieval.

• Contamination control — everything entering the area must be decontaminated or disposed of.

• Equipment must survive radiation, which degrades polymers, electronics and optics.

• Material may be activated, and welding on activated material generates activated fume and swarf.

• Access is frequently through small penetrations, driving miniaturized equipment.

• Qualification and documentation requirements are the most stringent of any sector.

14. Explosive and Flammable Atmospheres

Where a flammable atmosphere may be present — process plant, fuel storage, mines, grain handling — no ignition source is permitted, and every welding process except the cold ones is an ignition source.

The hierarchy of responses:

1. Eliminate the atmosphere — purge, gas-free, isolate, and verify by testing with a calibrated instrument, then re-test at intervals, because conditions change.

2. Hot work permit with gas testing, continuous monitoring, isolation and a fire watch.

3. Move the work to a safe area.

4. Use a cold process — mechanical fastening, adhesive, or cold pressure welding (Chapter 60), which generates no heat and no arc and is one of the few processes usable in such an atmosphere.

The recurring fatal error is welding on a container assumed to be empty. A vessel that held flammable product retains vapour in seams, scale and residue, and it explodes when heated. A container of unknown history is treated as dangerous, and the controls are cleaning, purging or inerting, and gas testing (Chapter 37, Section 8).

15. Cold and Remote Environments

• Material toughness falls with temperature, and ferritic steels have a ductile-to-brittle transition. Welding and handling structures below their transition temperature risks brittle fracture, and codes impose minimum temperatures for welding and for handling.

• Preheat requirements increase, and preheat is harder to achieve and maintain in wind and cold.

• Condensation and ice on the workpiece are hydrogen sources; a warm-through to remove moisture is essential.

• Consumable storage is harder — the cold-weather site failures of Chapter 40, Section 17 are the direct example.

• Equipment behaviour changes: gas regulators, hoses, hydraulics and batteries all perform differently in extreme cold.

• Personnel — dexterity, judgement and endurance all degrade, and PPE for cold conflicts with PPE for welding.

• Remote logistics dominate: equipment, consumables, power and repair capability must all be brought in and must work first time.

18. Standards and Qualification

• Underwater welding: AWS D3.6M, Underwater Welding Code, is the principal standard. It defines weld classes by the properties achievable and required — recognizing explicitly that wet welds and hyperbaric dry welds sit in different classes — and it covers procedure and welder-diver qualification.

• Welder-diver qualification is qualification as both a welder and a diver, under the code and under diving regulation.

• Procedure qualification must represent the environment: depth and pressure for hyperbaric work, water for wet welding, and flow and wall thickness for in-service work.

• In-service pipeline welding is governed by pipeline codes with dedicated provisions, and by industry recommended practice for hot tapping and in-service welding.

• Confined space entry is governed by occupational safety regulation, not by welding standards.

• Diving operations are governed by diving regulation, which takes precedence over welding standards on every question of diver safety.

• Nuclear work is governed by the sector's own qualification and documentation regimes.

19. Worked Example: Repairing a Corroded Section of an Operating Pipeline

Situation. An operating gas pipeline has a corroded external area with wall loss. Shutting the line down is commercially unacceptable. A repair sleeve is proposed, welded onto the line in service.

Step 1 — Establish the remaining wall thickness by measurement. Ultrasonic thickness measurement over the affected area determines what is actually there. This is the input to every subsequent decision, and estimating it is not acceptable — the burn-through calculation depends on it directly.

Step 2 — Recognize the two-sided risk. Low heat input reduces burn-through risk and increases hydrogen cracking risk; high heat input does the opposite (Section 12). The procedure must find a window between them, and the window is narrower the thinner the remaining wall.

Step 3 — Establish the flow condition and control it. Flowing product cools the pipe, which reduces burn-through risk and increases the quench. Some in-service procedures specify reduced flow — enough to keep the burn-through margin, not so much as to maximize the quench. Flow rate, pressure and product must be recorded and controlled during welding, not merely noted.

Step 4 — Establish the material's weldability. Pipeline steel carbon equivalent and wall thickness determine hardenability. Older lines may have material of uncertain specification, and welding an unidentified pipeline steel in service compounds every risk. Material verification is a prerequisite.

Step 5 — Qualify the procedure for the actual conditions. A bench coupon does not represent a pressurized, flowing pipe. Qualification must represent the thermal condition — commonly by a flow loop or an equivalent thermal simulation — with hardness survey and, where the code requires, delayed cracking assessment.

Step 6 — Specify the consumables and sequence. Low-hydrogen consumables without exception, with verified storage. A temper bead or controlled deposition sequence so that each pass tempers the previous pass's heat-affected zone (Section 12).

Step 7 — Plan the inspection, including the delay. Hydrogen cracking is delayed (Chapter 23, Section 4). Inspecting immediately after welding examines a joint before the mechanism has operated, so a specified delay before final inspection is a technical requirement rather than a formality — and on a live pipeline, arranging to return is a logistical commitment that must be planned at the outset.

Step 8 — Address the ignition and containment risks separately. Welding on a pipeline containing flammable product carries an ignition risk if burn-through occurs, and the procedure must address what happens if it does — which is why burn-through avoidance is a safety control here and not only a quality one.

Step 9 — Record the reasoning. In-service welding is a specialist engineering activity whose procedures are specific to wall thickness, flow, product and material. Recording the basis — the measurements, the calculation, the qualification — is what allows the next repair to start from evidence rather than from a repeat of the whole exercise.

20. Known Gaps

• No parameters, heat input limits or wall thickness thresholds are given. In-service welding limits in particular are calculated per case and must not be taken from a general reference.

• AWS D3.6M weld classes are named but their requirements are not reproduced; the code is the source.

• Diving regulation and practice are outside this reference set's scope entirely and take precedence on every question of diver safety.

• In-service welding methodology — thermal analysis, burn-through calculation, flow requirements — is a specialist field with its own recommended practices, referenced rather than reproduced.

• Nuclear welding requirements are sector-specific and are not detailed.

• Hyperbaric procedure development at depth requires facilities and expertise that only specialist contractors hold.
