1. Why Welding Generates a Data Problem

Welding is a special process (Chapter 31, Section 1): the product cannot be fully verified by inspection, so confidence comes from controlling the inputs and from evidence that those controls were in force when the weld was made.

That evidence is data, and the volume is substantial. A single production weld may need to be connected to a procedure revision, a qualification record, a welder's current qualification, a consumable batch, a parent material heat, a preheat measurement, a set of parameters, a heat treatment cycle, an inspection result and a disposition.

Multiply by the number of welds in a fabrication, and the reason welding quality systems are records-heavy becomes clear: the records are not documentation of the quality system, they are the quality system.

The failures throughout this reference set are, over and over, failures to connect records:

• A welder's certificate in date, with no continuity record proving the qualification is live (Chapter 32, Section 8).

• A consumable substitution that reached the shop floor with no goods-in check against the WPS (Chapter 29, Section 13).

• A drawing revision that changed a thickness without triggering a WPS review (Chapter 31, Section 15).

• A gas supply change reaching the arc without engineering review (Chapter 39, Section 19).

• A cracked joint with no way to identify which other joints share the affected consumable batch.

Every one of these is a data problem before it is a welding problem.

2. The Core Records and How They Relate

| Record | Contains | Links to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PQR / WPQR | Evidence of a qualification test | The WPS it supports |
| WPS | Production instruction with parameter ranges | Its PQR; the joints it is used on; approved consumables and gases |
| Welder / operator qualification | Person, process, ranges, validity, continuity | The welds they made |
| Consumable batch record | Classification, batch, certificate, storage history | The welds it was used on |
| Material record | Grade, heat number, certificate | The parts it became |
| Weld record | Joint identity, welder, WPS revision, date, parameters | Everything above, plus inspection and heat treatment |
| Heat treatment record | Cycle, thermocouple positions, chart | The joints treated |
| Inspection record | Method, operator, result, acceptance criteria | The joint and the disposition |
| Non-conformance and disposition | What was wrong, what was decided, what was done | The joint, and the corrective action |
| Equipment calibration | Instrument, date, result, due date | The measurements taken with it |

The relationships are the point. Any one record in isolation answers little; the connections are what allow a question to be answered — and the questions that matter in practice are of the form "which welds are affected by *this*?"

3. Procedure and Qualification Management

What a system must do:

• Hold every WPS with its revision history, and know which revision was current on any given date.

• Link each WPS to its supporting PQR and show the qualified ranges.

• Support the question "is this WPS valid for this joint?" — material group, thickness, diameter, position, process — as a check rather than a judgement.

• Flag when a drawing or specification change takes work outside an existing qualification, which is the failure of Chapter 31, Section 15.

• Prevent use of a superseded revision at the workstation (Chapter 33, Section 5).

• Maintain the approved consumable and gas list attached to each WPS.

The check that prevents the most expensive failures is the one at work allocation: before a joint is assigned, does a valid WPS exist that covers this material, thickness, position and process, and is the assigned welder qualified for it? Making that check a system function rather than a supervisor's recollection is the single highest-value item in this chapter.

4. Personnel Qualification and Continuity Management

What a system must do:

• Hold each qualification with its ranges, not just its certificate date.

• Track continuity from production weld records — the mechanism that invalidates certificates silently (Chapter 32, Section 8).

• Warn before expiry and before continuity lapses, rather than reporting them afterwards.

• Support the allocation check of Section 3.

• Hold the welding coordinator's appointment and competence evidence (Chapter 32, Section 10).

Continuity is the case where a database genuinely changes the outcome. Continuity is derived from production activity, so a system that already holds the weld records can compute it automatically. A paper system requires someone to compile it, which means it is compiled at audit time rather than maintained — and by then, a lapse has already been running.

5. Consumable and Material Control

What a system must do:

• Record goods-in verification against the approved list for the WPS.

• Hold batch identity and certificates.

• Track storage conditions and exposure for hydrogen-controlled consumables — issue and return from ovens and quivers (Chapter 29, Section 10).

• Link batch to weld, which is what bounds the affected population when a batch problem appears.

• Record material heat numbers through cutting and forming into parts and into welds.

The bounding question is the whole point. When a consumable batch is found defective, or a welder's qualification is found to have lapsed, or a heat treatment furnace is found out of calibration, the question is always "which welds are affected?" With linked records the answer is a list; without them it is the whole period. The cost difference between those two answers is the business case for the entire system (Chapter 33, Section 6).

6. Weld Mapping and Joint Identification

For any fabrication with more than a handful of welds, every weld needs an identity that connects the drawing to the physical joint to the records.

• Weld numbering on the drawing, carried onto the fabrication and into the records.

• Weld maps — drawings marked with each weld's identity, process, WPS and inspection requirement.

• Isometrics in piping, where each weld on each spool is numbered and logged (Chapter 70, Section 16).

• Progress and status by weld: fitted, welded, inspected, accepted, released.

In pipework, the weld log is the deliverable, sometimes more scrutinized than the welds themselves — because on a completed installation with inaccessible joints, the record is the only remaining evidence.

7. Weld Data Monitoring

Modern welding equipment can record the actual parameters of every weld, and this changes what is knowable:

| Process | Recorded | Detects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Arc welding | Current, voltage, wire feed speed, gas flow, arc time, calculated heat input | Parameter excursions, arc-on time, consumable drift, gas problems |
| Resistance welding | Current, force, displacement, resistance curve (Volume 1, Chapter 11) | Nugget formation deviation, electrode wear, expulsion |
| Friction welding | Torque, upset, speed, force (Chapter 56, Section 18) | Insufficient upset, clamp slippage |
| Flash welding | Upset curve (Chapter 49, Section 15) | Short or slow upset |
| Beam welding | Power, focus, speed, keyhole depth (Chapter 54, Section 13) | Penetration deviation, optics degradation |
| Friction stir | Axial force, torque, traverse force (Chapter 57, Section 17) | Plunge depth, backing gaps, thickness variation |
| Orbital | Sector parameters, arc voltage, rotation (Chapter 70) | Programme deviation, electrode wear |

Two uses, of very different value:

Recording — keeping the data as evidence. Useful for investigation and for demonstrating compliance.

Monitoring with limits — comparing each weld against acceptance limits in real time and flagging deviations immediately. This is the use that changes outcomes, because it detects a problem at the weld rather than at inspection, and it is the mechanism that has recurred in the worked examples throughout this reference set.

8. What the Data Actually Proves, and What It Does Not

This section is deliberately placed before the enthusiasm of Section 9, because overstating what monitoring proves is a real and consequential error.

What weld data proves:

• That the equipment delivered the recorded parameters.

• That those parameters were, or were not, inside the qualified range.

• That the arc was established for the recorded time.

• That a deviation occurred at a recorded moment.

What weld data does not prove:

• That the weld is sound. Correct parameters delivered to a joint with a gap, a contaminated surface, misaligned parts, or the wrong material produce a defective weld with a perfect data record.

• That the joint was fused. A robot welding accurately to a misplaced part records exemplary parameters (Chapter 69, Section 14).

• That the material was correct.

• That the fit-up was correct — the variable that no arc data sees.

• That the weld meets its mechanical properties, which no in-process measurement determines.

The honest formulation: weld data monitoring is a necessary-condition check. Data outside limits means something is wrong. Data inside limits means one class of problems is absent — and says nothing about the others.

The practical consequence: monitoring supplements inspection and process control; it does not replace them. A shop that reduces inspection because it has monitoring has misunderstood what the monitoring measures.

9. Deviation Detection and Alarms

Where monitoring genuinely earns its place:

Real-time alarms on a parameter excursion allow the weld to be stopped, marked or rejected at the moment it happens — rather than being buried under subsequent passes or shipped.

Trend detection finds progressive degradation before it produces defects: contact tip wear showing as rising voltage variability, electrode wear in resistance welding showing as a changing resistance curve, optics degradation showing as falling delivered power. This is the mechanism that converts the scheduled-replacement discipline from a guess into a measurement.

Statistical process control applied to welding parameters detects a shift in the process before it exits the limits.

Correlation between a defect found in inspection and the recorded data for that weld — and, crucially, for every other weld with the same signature. This is what turns one found defect into a bounded population.

The design question for alarms is what happens when one fires. An alarm that produces a log entry nobody reads is worse than no alarm, because it creates a false sense of control. An alarm must have a defined response: stop, mark, notify, or reject.

10. Equipment Calibration and Configuration Management

• Calibration records for every instrument used to control or record a welding variable — including the welding machine's own meters where they produce records (Chapter 46, Section 13), preheat thermometers, gas flow meters and heat treatment recorders.

• Recall management so that an instrument out of calibration is withdrawn.

• The retrospective question: when an instrument is found out of calibration, which measurements did it make since it was last verified? This is another bounding question, and it needs the same record linkage.

• Configuration management for programmed equipment: robot programmes, orbital programmes, resistance welding schedules and synergic programme selections are all controlled documents whose revision must be known.

Programme revision control is frequently the weakest link in an automated shop: robot programmes edited on the shop floor without revision control leave no way to know what was actually run on a given day.

11. Inspection and Non-Conformance Records

• Inspection results by weld, with method, operator, acceptance criteria and result.

• Inspector qualification linked to the method performed (Chapter 35, Section 13).

• Non-conformances with the disposition — repair, accept-as-is, reject — and the authority for it.

• Repair records, including repair count at a location, which codes limit (Chapter 36, Section 13).

• Corrective action addressing the cause, with effectiveness verification (Chapter 33, Section 11).

Repair count tracking deserves specific mention: a location repaired repeatedly accumulates thermal cycles and degrades, and codes limit repeats for that reason. Tracking it requires the repair to be linked to the joint identity rather than logged as a separate event.

12. Traceability End to End

Traceability is the property that lets a chain be followed in either direction:

Forward — from a material heat or consumable batch to every weld it went into. Used when a batch problem is found.

Backward — from a failed weld to everything that made it. Used in failure investigation.

The chain: material heat → part → joint → weld → welder, WPS revision, consumable batch, parameters → heat treatment → inspection → disposition → assembly → product → customer.

The chain is only as strong as its weakest link, and the weak link is usually at a transformation: where plate becomes parts and identity must be transferred by marking, or where a spool becomes part of an assembly.

How much traceability is appropriate is set by the contract and the product standard, and it ranges from batch-level for general fabrication to individual weld identification with a marked location on an as-built drawing for pressure and safety-critical work (Chapter 33, Section 6).

13. Integration and the Practical Architecture

Systems in use range from a spreadsheet to a fully integrated platform, and the honest position is that the level of sophistication matters far less than whether the links exist and are maintained.

| Level | Character | Adequate for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Paper and spreadsheets | Cheap, flexible, manual linkage that decays | Small shops with few procedures and stable personnel |
| Dedicated welding management software | WPS/PQR/welder management with the checks built in | Most fabricators; the common step up |
| Welding software plus equipment data capture | Adds actual parameter records per weld | Automated and high-volume production |
| Integration with ERP/MES | Welding data connected to production planning and material management | Large operations |
| Full digital thread | Design through as-built, with the model carrying weld data | Aerospace, nuclear, large projects |

The practical failure mode of sophisticated systems is that they are implemented as document repositories — a place to store PDFs — rather than as linked databases. A repository holds records; it does not answer "which welds are affected?" The value is in the links, not the storage.

14. Data Quality and the Failure Modes of Digital Systems

Digitizing does not automatically improve control, and these failure modes are common:

| Failure | Consequence |
| --- | --- |
| Data captured but never used | Cost with no benefit; a false sense of control |
| Alarms with no defined response | Ignored; worse than no alarm |
| Records not linked | The bounding question cannot be answered — a repository, not a system |
| Manual data entry at the point of work | Under time pressure it is skipped or falsified; automated capture is far more reliable |
| Recording the setpoint rather than the actual value | The record proves nothing about what happened |
| Uncalibrated instruments feeding the system | Precise records of wrong values (Chapter 46, Section 13) |
| Programme edits without revision control | No way to know what was run |
| Over-alarming | Alarm fatigue; real deviations lost in noise |
| Believing the data proves soundness | Section 8 |

The single most valuable design principle is to capture automatically what can be captured automatically, and to require manual entry only where there is no alternative. Data a person must remember to enter, on a shop floor, under time pressure, is the data least likely to be there when it matters.

15. Decision Reference: What to Digitize First

For an organization improving its welding data management, in order of value returned:

1. WPS and qualification register with validity checking — prevents the most expensive class of failure (Section 3).

2. Welder qualification with automatic continuity tracking — prevents the most common audit finding (Section 4).

3. Consumable control from goods-in to weld — bounds a batch problem and enforces the hydrogen discipline (Section 5).

4. Weld identification and mapping — makes every subsequent record connectable (Section 6).

5. Inspection and non-conformance linked to the weld (Section 11).

6. Calibration with recall and retrospective bounding (Section 10).

7. Automatic weld parameter capture (Section 7).

8. Monitoring with limits and defined alarm responses (Section 9).

9. Trend analysis for consumable and equipment degradation (Section 9).

10. Integration with production and material systems (Section 13).

Items 1 to 4 deliver most of the value, cost the least, and are achievable without specialized equipment. Item 7 onward requires capable equipment and delivers most where volume is high and inspection is hard.

16. Worked Example: A Fabricator With Excellent Records That Could Not Answer the Question

Situation. A fabricator is notified by a consumable supplier that a batch of flux-cored wire had a manufacturing fault affecting diffusible hydrogen content. The fabricator holds complete records: goods-in certificates, WPSs, qualification records, welder certificates, inspection reports, all filed and retrievable. The customer asks which delivered products contain welds made with the affected batch.

Step 1 — Note that the records exist and the question still cannot be answered. This is the distinction between a repository and a linked system (Section 13). Every individual record is present and correct; none of them connects a consumable batch to a specific weld.

Step 2 — Establish what links do exist. Goods-in records show when the batch was received. Stores issue records may show which department drew it. Production records show what was welded in that period. Between them there may be a partial reconstruction, but the resolution is a date range and a department, not a list of welds.

Step 3 — Bound the population by date, which is the only route available. Every joint welded with flux-cored wire in the period between the batch's issue and its exhaustion is potentially affected. That is a far larger population than the true one, and every joint in it must be treated as suspect.

Step 4 — Assess the technical exposure. Elevated diffusible hydrogen raises hydrogen cracking risk (Chapter 23, Section 4), and the risk is greatest on thicker sections, higher-strength material, higher restraint and lower preheat. The affected population can be risk-ranked by those factors, which is the only way to make the response proportionate.

Step 5 — Decide the response. Options are delayed magnetic particle inspection on the higher-risk joints, engineering assessment, or rework. The cost is driven entirely by the size of the population — which is driven entirely by the absence of the link.

Step 6 — Recognize the size of the cost. With batch-to-weld linkage the answer would have been a list of specific joints. Without it, the response covers weeks of production across multiple products. That difference is the entire business case for traceability, and it is rarely visible until the day it is needed.

Step 7 — Fix the link, not the filing. The corrective action is not more records; it is a link between consumable batch and weld record, captured at the point of issue rather than reconstructed later. In practice this is a batch identity recorded on the weld record when the consumable is drawn — a small operational change with a large consequence.

Step 8 — Test the system with the question. The useful audit of a welding data system is not whether records exist but whether it can answer: *which welds used consumable batch X; which welds did welder Y make in the period their continuity lapsed; which welds were measured with the thermometer found out of calibration; which welds were made under WPS revision 3 before it was superseded.* A system that cannot answer these has records but not traceability.

17. Known Gaps

• No software products are named, consistent with this reference set's vendor-neutral discipline (Volume 1, Chapter 18).

• Data formats and interfaces for welding equipment are not standardized across manufacturers, which is a real practical obstacle to integration and is stated rather than solved here.

• Statistical methods for welding process control are referenced in principle; their application requires statistical expertise beyond this chapter.

• Retention periods for welding records are set by contract, code and regulation and vary widely.

• Cyber security of connected welding equipment and production systems is a real and growing consideration not addressed here.

• Machine learning applied to weld data is an active field; nothing is claimed for it here, and the limits in Section 8 apply to any analysis of the same data regardless of method.

1. What This Chapter Consolidates

Process selection is treated in every process chapter of this reference set from the inside — what a process does well, what it does badly, and where its window closes. Chapters 47, 55 and 68 treat selection within a family, between families, and above the welding family respectively. This chapter is the consolidation: one route from a drawing to a defensible answer, referring outward to the chapters that hold the detail.

It is deliberately a screening framework, not a scoring model. Weighted scoring models are attractive because they produce a number, but the number conceals what is actually happening: most process selections are decided by one or two hard constraints that eliminate everything else, and the remaining choice is made on cost and capability. A scoring model that lets a strong score on productivity outvote a hard material incompatibility gives a confidently wrong answer. Screens applied in order do not do this.

2. The Order the Decisions Must Be Taken In

The order matters because early screens are eliminating and late screens are optimizing. Running them in the wrong order produces the classic failure: a process is selected on productivity and cost, and the material or access constraint that rules it out is discovered during industrialization.

| Order | Screen | Nature | Chapter for detail |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Joining family | Eliminating | 68 |
| 2 | Material | Eliminating | 23–27 |
| 3 | Thickness and joint geometry | Eliminating | 22, 28, 55 |
| 4 | Access and position | Eliminating | 28, 69, 70 |
| 5 | Volume and rate | Optimizing | 55, 76 |
| 6 | Quality level and verification | Constraining | 33–35 |
| 7 | Capability and cost of change | Optimizing | 76 |

Screens 1–4 answer *what is possible*. Screens 5–7 answer *what is sensible*. If screens 1–4 leave nothing, the joint design must change — that is a legitimate and important outcome, and it is the outcome most often suppressed because it means going back to the designer.

3. Screen 1 — The Joining Family

Answered in full in Chapter 68. Summarized here as the four questions that eliminate welding:

| Question | If yes | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Must the joint be demountable in service? | Mechanical fastening | Welding eliminated |
| Are the materials metallurgically incompatible, or is one non-metallic? | Adhesive, mechanical, or brazing | Fusion welding usually eliminated |
| Is the assembly intolerant of the heat a weld applies? | Adhesive, mechanical, soldering, or a solid-state process | Fusion welding eliminated; solid-state may survive |
| Is the required electrical or thermal continuity absent from the alternatives? | Welding, brazing or soldering retained | Adhesive eliminated |

A joint that survives this screen is a welded joint, and the remaining screens select the welding process.

4. Screen 2 — The Material Constraint

The material eliminates processes in three distinct ways, and conflating them causes errors.

Way 1 — the material is not weldable by the process at all. Aluminium cannot be welded by processes that cannot break or displace its oxide; magnesium and zinc-rich alloys behave badly in high-heat-input processes; refractory and reactive metals require shielding that most processes do not provide.

Way 2 — the material's cracking mechanisms constrain the thermal cycle. Hardenable steels require a controlled cooling rate, which sets a heat-input floor or a preheat requirement (Chapter 23). Austenitic stainless steels require a heat-input ceiling to limit sensitization and distortion (Chapter 24). Nickel alloys require restraint and heat-input control against ductility-dip and reheat cracking (Chapter 26).

Way 3 — the material requires a filler that only some processes can deliver. Dissimilar joints and overmatched or undermatched fillers require a process that accepts filler in the required form; autogenous processes cannot use a filler at all unless a shim, insert or pre-placed wire is possible.

| Material group | Processes that work | Processes to avoid | Governing chapter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Carbon and C-Mn steel | Nearly all | — | 23 |
| High-strength low-alloy | Most, with hydrogen and heat-input control | Uncontrolled high-hydrogen consumables | 23, 34 |
| Quenched and tempered | Controlled heat input; low hydrogen mandatory | High heat input; unpreheated | 23, 34 |
| Austenitic stainless | GTAW, GMAW, PAW, laser, resistance | Oxyfuel; high-heat-input multipass without control | 24 |
| Duplex stainless | Controlled heat input, both floor and ceiling | Autogenous without solution anneal; laser without filler | 24 |
| Aluminium alloys | GMAW, GTAW (AC), FSW, laser, resistance, EBW | Oxyfuel; SMAW (rarely justified) | 25 |
| Nickel alloys | GTAW, GMAW pulsed, SMAW, PAW | High-heat-input; high-restraint multipass without control | 26 |
| Titanium and reactive | GTAW with trailing/backing shield, EBW, laser, FSW, resistance | Any process without complete inert protection | 26 |
| Copper and alloys | GTAW/GMAW with preheat, EBW, FSW, resistance (limited) | Processes without power to overcome conductivity | 26 |
| Cast iron | SMAW with Ni fillers, brazing | Most high-heat-input fusion routes | 26 |
| Dissimilar metals | Depends entirely on the pair — see the pair, not the process | Assuming a process transfers between pairs | 27, 68 |

The material screen is the most frequently underestimated. A process that welds one grade in a family very well may be unusable on another grade in the same family.

5. Screen 3 — The Thickness and Joint-Geometry Constraint

Thickness governs through three separate mechanisms: whether the process can deposit or penetrate the section at all; whether the process's heat input is appropriate to the section; and whether the joint preparation the process needs can be made.

| Section | Processes in window | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Foil, < 0.5 mm | Resistance, laser, micro-GTAW, ultrasonic, soldering | Most arc processes burn through |
| Sheet, 0.5–3 mm | Resistance, laser, GMAW short-circuit, GTAW, FSW, mechanical | The most contested range; see Chapter 55 |
| Plate, 3–20 mm | GMAW, FCAW, SMAW, SAW, GTAW root + fill, laser-hybrid | Most arc processes are comfortable |
| Heavy, 20–100 mm | SAW, FCAW, ESW/EGW, narrow-gap GMAW, EBW | Deposition rate governs |
| Very heavy, > 100 mm | ESW, EBW (vacuum), narrow-gap multipass | Very few options |

Joint geometry then screens further. Butt, fillet, lap and edge joints are not equally available to every process: resistance spot welding requires a lap; FSW requires a rigidly backed joint accessible to a rotating tool; beam processes require a fit-up tolerance often an order of magnitude tighter than arc processes; brazing requires a controlled capillary gap.

The fit-up question is the one most often deferred and most often decisive. A process whose gap tolerance the fabrication route cannot hold is not a candidate, however attractive its other properties. Chapter 55 develops this comparison; the short form is that beam processes buy speed and low distortion with fit-up discipline, and arc processes buy fit-up tolerance with heat input.

6. Screen 4 — Access and Position

| Access condition | Effect | Chapter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Both sides accessible | All processes available | — |
| One side only | Requires single-sided capability: backing, consumable insert, controlled root, or a one-sided process | 28, 70 |
| Two-sided simultaneous required | Resistance spot, some pressure processes | 01–20 |
| Confined or remote | Limits equipment size; may force manual or orbital | 70, 71 |
| Position other than flat | Excludes SAW and ESW; constrains transfer modes | 28, 39 |
| Fixed pipe | Orbital or manual all-position | 70 |
| Underwater, radioactive, vacuum, altitude | Specialist envelope | 71 |

The position constraint is frequently the one that eliminates the highest-productivity candidate. Submerged arc welding is the fastest way to lay a large volume of weld metal and cannot be used out of position at all; that single fact reroutes a large fraction of structural fabrication to flux-cored and gas-metal arc processes and drives the use of positioners.

7. Screen 5 — Production Volume and Rate

Volume does not eliminate processes; it changes which ones are economic. The mechanism is the trade between fixed cost (equipment, tooling, programming, qualification) and variable cost (labour, consumables, cycle time), developed with numbers in Chapter 76.

| Volume | Typical economic answer | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One-off, repair | Manual arc — SMAW, GTAW, GMAW | Zero fixed cost dominates |
| Low, varied | Manual or semi-automatic, flexible fixturing | Setup cost per part dominates |
| Medium, families of parts | Mechanized or robotic with quick-change tooling | Programming amortizes across the family |
| High, stable | Fully automated, dedicated tooling; beam and resistance processes become viable | Cycle time dominates; fixed cost amortizes |
| Very high, single part | Special-purpose machines; process integrated into the line | Every second of cycle is capitalized |

The common error is running this screen before the eliminating screens: a business case is built on the productivity of a process that a later screen rules out, and the business case survives the elimination because it has already been approved.

8. Screen 6 — Quality Level and Verification

Quality requirements act on process selection in two ways.

First, the acceptance level constrains the achievable imperfection population. ISO 5817 quality level B is not a label applied to a finished weld; it is a requirement that must be designed into the process, because some processes cannot reliably meet it in some configurations. [S1]

Second, and more decisively, the verification method must be compatible with the process and the joint. This is the constraint that most often reroutes a selection late:

| If the joint requires | Then the process must | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Volumetric NDT (RT or UT) | Produce a geometry the method can interrogate | Excludes some lap and partial-penetration configurations |
| Full penetration verified | Allow the root to be inspected or the penetration to be proven | Single-sided welds need a qualified root procedure |
| No verification possible (resistance, brazing, adhesive, some beam) | Be controlled by monitoring and process discipline | Drives ISO 3834-2 style process control, Chapter 33 |
| Destructive sampling only | Support a sampling plan and a stable process | High-volume resistance and beam processes |

The rule that runs through this reference set: where the weld cannot be inspected, the process must be monitored. Chapters 11, 36, 47, 54 and 72 each state a version of it. It is a selection criterion, not only a quality criterion, because a process that cannot be monitored and cannot be inspected is not usable on a joint whose failure matters.

9. Screen 7 — Existing Capability and Cost of Change

The last screen is the one written down least and decided most: what can this fabricator actually do, and what would it cost to be able to do something else?

| Capability element | Question | Lead time to acquire |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Equipment | Owned, available, capable at the duty cycle required? | Weeks to months |
| Qualified procedures | Does a qualified WPS cover this range? | Weeks (existing PQR) to months (new test) |
| Qualified personnel | Welders or operators qualified in the process, position and range? | Weeks to months |
| Consumable supply | Available, with the required certification and storage? | Days to weeks |
| Inspection capability | Method, qualified personnel, procedure, acceptance criteria? | Weeks |
| Coordination | Competent welding coordination for the process (ISO 14731)? | Months |
| Maintenance and calibration | Can the process be kept in its window? | Ongoing |

A capability gap is not a reason to select a worse process; it is a cost and a lead time to be entered into the comparison honestly. The failure mode is the opposite of the obvious one: fabricators do not usually select processes they cannot run — they select processes they *nearly* can run, and absorb the gap as quality cost.

| Conflict | Resolution |
| --- | --- |
| Material says A, volume says B | Material wins. Change the material or change the design, not the metallurgy. |
| Access says A, productivity says B | Access wins, unless the assembly sequence or fixture can be changed to create access — which should be considered explicitly. |
| Quality says A, cost says B | Quality wins where it is a code or safety requirement. Where it is an internal specification, question the specification. |
| Capability says A, everything else says B | This is the only conflict resolvable by investment. Quantify the gap; do not absorb it silently. |
| Two candidates survive all screens | Decide on cost, then on risk, then on flexibility — in that order (Chapter 76). |

There is one asymmetry worth stating: it is much cheaper to change the joint design than to force a process outside its window. When all candidates fail, the correct output of this framework is a design change request, and the framework has done its job.

12. Process Families That Are Commonly Confused

| Confusion | Distinction | Chapter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FCAW-G against FCAW-S | Gas-shielded (136) needs shielding gas and is not for wind; self-shielded (114) is | 40 |
| Metal-cored against flux-cored | 138 is metal-cored, behaving like a solid wire with higher deposition; 136 is flux-cored, producing slag | 21, 40 |
| Spray against pulsed spray | Spray needs high current and argon-rich gas and is flat/horizontal; pulsed achieves spray-like transfer at lower mean current, all positions | 39 |

| Brazing against braze-welding | Brazing fills a capillary gap; braze-welding fills a groove like a weld with a brazing filler | 66 |
| Projection against spot welding | Projection welding puts the current concentration into the part geometry rather than the electrode | 14 |

Each confusion in this table has caused real procedure errors — most commonly a WPS that cites a process number the shop does not actually run.

13. The Five Most Common Selection Errors

Error 1 — selecting on productivity before feasibility. Running screen 5 before screens 2–4. Symptom: an industrialization programme that discovers a metallurgical or access constraint after capital has been committed.

Error 2 — transferring a process across a material change without re-selecting. "We weld this steel with X, so we will weld the new grade with X." Symptom: cracking, or an unexpected qualification failure.

Error 3 — ignoring the verification constraint. Selecting a process whose welds cannot be inspected to the level the contract requires, then discovering at inspection release. Symptom: a request to change acceptance criteria late.

Error 4 — designing fit-up the fabrication route cannot hold. Specifying a beam process on parts made by a route with a tolerance stack larger than the beam's gap tolerance. Symptom: chronic lack of fusion or underfill, blamed on the welding process.

Error 5 — leaving the decision undocumented. The process is selected, the reasoning is not recorded, and when the joint, material or volume changes nobody knows which of the original constraints still applies. Symptom: the same selection argument repeated every few years with different conclusions.

14. Documenting the Decision

The record does not need to be long. It needs to survive personnel changes and answer the question a future engineer will ask: *why this process, and what would change the answer?*

A sufficient record contains:

1. The joint identification — drawing, weld number or joint category.

2. Materials, grades and thicknesses, with the condition of supply.

3. Service conditions that constrain the choice: load, temperature, environment, fatigue.

4. The applicable code or specification and the quality level.

5. The processes considered and, for each rejected one, the screen that eliminated it.

6. The selected process, with the reference WPS or the qualification route planned.

7. The verification method and acceptance criteria.

8. The conditions under which this decision should be revisited — for example a change of grade, thickness, volume band or supplier.

Item 5 is the one that carries the value. A list of what was rejected and why is far more useful later than a statement of what was chosen.

15. Worked Example A — A Pressure Vessel Longitudinal Seam

The joint. Longitudinal seam, 32 mm C-Mn pressure vessel plate, 2.4 m long, full penetration, shop fabrication, code-stamped vessel with full radiography.

Screen 1 — family. Permanent, pressure-retaining, code-governed. Welding, unambiguously.

Screen 2 — material. C-Mn pressure vessel plate. Weldable by all arc processes. Section and grade set a preheat and hydrogen control requirement per the code and the carbon equivalent (Chapter 23). No process eliminated; hydrogen control constrains consumable choice, not process choice.

Screen 3 — thickness and geometry. 32 mm, straight seam, both sides accessible before the shell is closed. Heavy-plate band: SAW, FCAW, narrow-gap GMAW, SMAW are candidates. Deposition rate matters over 2.4 m of a thick section.

Screen 4 — access and position. Shop, on rolls, flat position achievable. This is the key enabler: SAW becomes available. Both sides accessible allows a double-V or double-U preparation with back gouging, which halves the deposited volume against a single-sided preparation.

Screen 5 — volume. A vessel shop making these regularly. SAW's fixed cost — flux handling, tractor or column-and-boom, procedure development — amortizes readily.

Screen 6 — quality and verification. Full radiography. SAW produces a sound, smooth weld well suited to RT interpretation, and the process is stable enough that RT findings are usually a genuine surprise rather than routine. Slag inclusions are the imperfection to control (Chapter 43).

Screen 7 — capability. If the shop is a code shop it has SAW, a qualified WPS covering the thickness range, and qualified operators under ISO 14732 or ASME Section IX. If not, this is a substantial capability gap and the honest answer is FCAW or SMAW with a longer cycle.

Decision. SAW, double-sided with back gouging, in the flat position on rolls, with a matching-strength wire/flux combination selected for low hydrogen and the required impact properties. Revisit if: the seam becomes circumferential and out of position; the material changes to a low-alloy grade with tighter heat-input limits; or the vessel becomes too small to rotate.

16. Worked Example B — A High-Volume Sheet Assembly

The joint. 1.2 mm to 1.5 mm coated steel lap joint, structural, in a subassembly produced at 400,000 per year, appearance not critical, joint is not accessible after assembly.

Screen 1 — family. Permanent, structural, metal-to-metal, no demountability requirement. Welding, or a hybrid with adhesive.

Screen 2 — material. Coated steel sheet. The coating governs: it changes resistance welding electrode life and produces porosity and spatter in arc processes (Chapters 13, 36). It does not eliminate a family; it constrains parameters and consumable wear management.

Screen 3 — thickness and geometry. Sheet lap. Squarely in the resistance spot welding band, and in the laser band if a stitch or seam replaces the discrete nugget.

Screen 4 — access. Two-sided access is available at the assembly station even though the joint is inaccessible afterwards. Two-sided access at the station is what keeps resistance spot welding available — one-sided access would eliminate it and force laser or a mechanical route.

Screen 5 — volume. 400,000 per year justifies full automation, dedicated tooling and either technology.

Screen 6 — quality and verification. This is the decisive screen. The joint cannot be inspected after assembly, and neither resistance spot welds nor laser stitches can be verified non-destructively at production rate with confidence. Both processes therefore require monitoring plus a destructive sampling plan (Chapters 10, 11, 54). Neither is eliminated, but both inherit a process-control obligation that must be costed.

Screen 7 — capability. A body shop typically has resistance spot welding capability, gun and transformer infrastructure, dressing and tip-change routines, and destructive test facilities. Laser needs beam sources, safety enclosure to IEC 60825 and ISO 11553, fit-up discipline the pressing route may not hold, and different skills.

Decision. Resistance spot welding, with electrode wear management and a monitored process, unless the joint's fatigue or stiffness requirement is not met by discrete nuggets — in which case adhesive-bonded weld-bonding is the next candidate (Chapter 68), not a change of welding process. Revisit if: the access becomes one-sided; a grade change moves the material into a resistance window that electrode life cannot sustain economically; or the stiffness requirement changes.

17. Worked Example C — A One-Off Repair on an Unknown Material

The joint. A cracked bracket on a machine of unknown provenance, out of production, no drawings, no material certificate. Site conditions, machine down.

Screen 0 — identify the material, or accept that you are guessing. This is the step most often skipped under time pressure and the one that causes the repair to fail. Spark test, hardness, magnetism, a portable analyser if available; if it is cast, treat it as cast iron until proven otherwise (Chapter 26).

Screen 1 — family. Under time pressure, a bolted doubler or a bonded and bolted repair is often the better engineering answer and is frequently dismissed without consideration. Include it explicitly.

Screen 2 — material. If unidentified, the choice must be a tolerant one. A nickel-based SMAW consumable tolerates cast iron and many unknown ferrous materials, deposits a soft crack-tolerant weld metal, and does not require the exact preheat regime a matching consumable would.

Screen 3 and 4 — geometry and access. Site, any position, likely poor access. This eliminates almost everything except SMAW and GTAW.

Screen 5 — volume. One. Fixed cost must be zero. Nothing automated.

Screen 6 — quality. Almost certainly visual and dye penetrant only. That should be stated, together with what it does and does not prove.

Screen 7 — capability. Whatever is on the truck.

Decision. SMAW with a nickel-based or otherwise tolerant electrode, crack ends drilled and the crack fully excavated and verified by penetrant before welding, short runs with peening and interpass temperature control, penetrant inspection after. State the limitation in writing: this is a repair of unknown-material, unqualified provenance, appropriate to restoring function, and its life is not predictable. That statement is the professional part of the job, and omitting it is the most common failure in repair welding.

18. Known Gaps

• No parameter values are given anywhere in this framework. Parameters are material-, equipment- and joint-specific and belong to a qualified WPS, not to a selection framework.

• Cost figures are not given. Chapter 76 gives the cost structure and the comparison method; the numbers are regional, time-dependent and must be gathered locally.

• Code-mandated process restrictions exist in many application codes and override this framework wherever they apply. The applicable code must be read.

• Hybrid and emerging processes — laser-arc hybrid, additive-assisted joining, hybrid mechanical-adhesive routes — are covered thinly and are moving quickly.

• Automation feasibility is treated in Chapter 69 but not integrated into the screening logic here as a formal screen; on high-volume work it deserves to be one.

• Repair-specific selection for in-service equipment, including welding on live or contained equipment, is a specialist field with its own codes that this reference set does not develop.

1. How to Use This Index

This chapter is a lookup, not a narrative. It is entered from an observed condition — a radiograph, a macro-section, a visual finding, a leak, a fracture — and exits to a mechanism, a corrective action and a chapter reference.

It does not replace the process-specific troubleshooting chapters (36, 47, 54 and the resistance chapters in Volume 1). Those chapters give the diagnosis in context, with the process behaviour that makes a cause plausible or implausible. This index gives the map: what the condition can be, across all processes, and where to go.

Two cautions before the tables.

A defect name is not a diagnosis. "Porosity" is an observation. The corrective action depends entirely on whether the gas is hydrogen, nitrogen, carbon monoxide, or shielding-gas entrainment, and those have different sources and different fixes. Every table in this chapter therefore carries a mechanism column, and the mechanism is what the corrective action attaches to.

Not every imperfection is a defect. ISO 6520-1 classifies imperfections; ISO 5817 and its companions set the levels at which an imperfection becomes unacceptable for a given quality level. [S1] [S2] An imperfection within the acceptance level is a recorded observation, not a nonconformity, and treating it as one wastes repair welding on sound joints — itself a source of damage.

2. The Classification This Index Follows

ISO 6520-1 classifies geometric imperfections in fusion welds into six groups by a three- or four-digit reference number. [S1] The groups are:

| Group | Title | Typical members |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Cracks | 100 series — longitudinal, transverse, crater, branching |
| 2 | Cavities | 200 series — gas pores, blowholes, shrinkage, crater pipe |
| 3 | Solid inclusions | 300 series — slag, flux, oxide, metallic |
| 4 | Lack of fusion and penetration | 400 series |
| 5 | Imperfect shape and dimension | 500 series — undercut, excess metal, misalignment, sagging |
| 6 | Miscellaneous | 600 series — arc strike, spatter (602), torn surface, grinding mark |

Where a process is outside ISO 6520-1's scope — resistance welding, solid-state processes, brazing, soldering — the imperfections have their own vocabulary and are indexed in Sections 10–13.

3. The Diagnostic Method — Before the Tables

The tables are only useful if the observation feeding them is accurate. The method that runs through this reference set has four steps, and skipping any of them is how a shop ends up repeatedly correcting the wrong variable.

Step 1 — Establish what is actually there, and where. Location within the weld is the single most powerful discriminator. Root against cap, centreline against fusion line, first pass against later passes, start against middle against crater. A crack at the fusion line in the last pass and a crack on the centreline in the root pass have almost nothing in common.

Step 2 — Establish when it formed. During solidification, immediately after, hours later, or in service. Hydrogen cracking may appear up to 48 hours after welding and this delay is diagnostic (Chapter 23). A crack found on the first inspection after a weekend is not the same defect as one found on the bench.

Step 3 — Establish the distribution. Isolated, clustered, uniform along the weld, at every start, on one shift only, on one machine only, after a consumable batch change. Distribution in time and across the shop is often more informative than the metallurgy. A defect that appears on one of six identical stations is a machine problem, whatever the metallurgy says.

Step 4 — Only then, reach for the cause table. And when the table gives several candidate causes, order the investigation by what is cheap to check and what changed recently, not by what is most interesting.

Spatter — the cross-process treatment

Spatter is classified as an imperfection (602) and is usually acceptable in itself, but it matters for four reasons that have nothing to do with the acceptance criterion:

1. It is a leading indicator. A process that has started to spatter has usually left its intended droplet-transfer mode, and the same departure produces fusion and porosity defects that are much harder to see.

2. It causes secondary damage. Removal by grinding damages the surface (604, 613); spatter on a machined face, a sealing surface or a coated surface is a rework cost far above the welding cost.

3. It destroys consumables and hardware. Nozzle clogging changes shielding, which causes porosity — spatter therefore causes defects indirectly and with a delay.

4. On coated and galvanized material it indicates the coating is being vaporized in the arc, which is simultaneously a porosity and a fume-exposure issue.

Diagnosis order for GMAW spatter — check in this sequence (developed in Chapters 30 and 39):

| Order | Variable | What it does | Why this order |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Transfer mode | Globular transfer is the highest-spatter regime; short-circuit and spray are lower | The largest single effect; check the operating point is in the intended mode |
| 2 | Shielding gas composition | Spray transfer needs an argon-rich gas (roughly ≥ 80 % Ar); CO₂-rich gas raises spatter markedly | The second-largest effect and often the cheapest to change |
| 3 | Inductance / waveform | Controls short-circuit clearing violence | Directly sets short-circuit spatter |
| 4 | Wire feed path | Erratic feed causes erratic transfer | Liner, drive rolls, tension, tip wear — cheap to check, commonly the cause |
| 5 | Arc blow | Deflects the arc, disrupting transfer | Return-lead position, magnetized parts, DC in a fixture |
| 6 | Surface condition | Oil, rust, coating, moisture disrupt the arc and gasify | Last because it is the most often blamed and the least often the whole cause |

For resistance welding, spatter (expulsion) has a different meaning entirely: it indicates the nugget has exceeded the containment capacity of the electrode force and the surrounding solid metal, and it is a parameter-window indicator, treated in Chapters 01 and 10–13. Expulsion is not merely cosmetic there — it removes metal from the nugget, degrades the electrode, and marks the upper edge of the process window.

For SAW, spatter is largely absent because the flux blanket contains the arc; its appearance indicates flux coverage failure. For beam processes, spatter indicates keyhole instability and is a leading indicator of porosity and spiking (Chapter 54).

14. The Discriminator Tables — Telling Similar Defects Apart

| Confusable pair | Discriminator that resolves it |
| --- | --- |
| Solidification crack vs hydrogen crack | Timing and location. Solidification: hot, immediate, centreline, weld metal. Hydrogen: cold, delayed up to 48 h, usually HAZ or high-strength weld metal, hard microstructure present |
| Hydrogen crack vs reheat crack | When relative to PWHT. Reheat cracking appears after PWHT or service at temperature, in the coarse-grained HAZ, intergranular |
| Lamellar tearing vs HAZ crack | Location and shape. Lamellar tearing is stepped, in the parent metal, parallel to the surface, under a through-thickness loaded joint |
| Porosity vs slag inclusion (radiograph) | Shape. Pores are rounded with sharp density contrast; slag is irregular and less dense |
| Slag inclusion vs lack of fusion | Orientation and shape. Lack of fusion is planar and follows a fusion face; slag is volumetric and irregular |
| Tungsten inclusion vs porosity | Density on a radiograph. Tungsten is denser than steel and appears light; pores appear dark |
| Incomplete penetration vs lack of root fusion | Whether the root faces were melted. Penetration is a depth deficiency; root fusion is a bonding deficiency at a melted-or-not boundary |
| Undercut vs shrinkage groove | Which side and which mechanism. Undercut is melted parent not refilled at the toe; the root shrinkage groove is a contraction feature |
| Expulsion vs surface pit (resistance) | Expelled metal present. Expulsion leaves evidence outside the weld |
| Interfacial fracture vs undersize nugget | Nugget size measurement. A full-size nugget can still fracture interfacially in high-strength steel; that is a different problem from a small nugget |
| FSW wormhole vs porosity | Continuity and location. A wormhole is continuous along the weld on the advancing side; porosity is discrete |
| Beam keyhole porosity vs gas porosity | Size, shape and position. Keyhole porosity is large, irregular and root-biased |

15. Corrective Action Against Containment

A corrective action fixes the cause. A containment action protects the customer while the cause is being found. Confusing the two is the most common failure in industrial defect response, and it produces two symptoms: problems that recur, and inspection regimes that grow permanently.

| Step | Action | Timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Contain — quarantine suspect product, define the suspect window by date, batch, machine and shift | Immediately |
| 2 | Assess — is the imperfection outside the acceptance level for the applicable quality level? | Before any repair decision |
| 3 | Disposition — accept, repair, rework, downgrade or scrap, recorded against the applicable code | With the authority the code requires |
| 4 | Investigate — mechanism, then cause, using the discriminators above | In parallel with 1–3 |
| 5 | Correct — change the variable that caused it | After the cause is established, not before |
| 6 | Verify — evidence that the corrected process no longer produces the imperfection | Before releasing the containment |
| 7 | Standardize — update the WPS, the work instruction, the maintenance interval or the training | Before closing |
| 8 | Close the containment — return inspection to its normal level, deliberately and with a record | Explicitly, or it never happens |

Step 8 is skipped often enough to be worth naming. Inspection added as containment tends to become permanent, and a shop can accumulate a decade of containment inspection that nobody can justify or remove.

Repair welding is itself a hazard. A repair applies a second thermal cycle to a region that has already had one, in a more restrained condition, often with worse access. Repair procedures must be qualified, repair counts must be limited by the applicable code, and repeated repair of the same location is a signal that the cause has not been found.

16. What to Do When the Cause Cannot Be Identified

Sometimes the tables do not converge. The professional response is a structured one, not a guess.

1. Re-verify the observation. A surprising number of unresolvable defects are misidentified. Take a macro-section. Have a second qualified inspector look.

2. Establish what changed. Consumable batch, parent material heat, gas supplier, operator, shift, machine, maintenance event, ambient conditions, a software or parameter update. A defect that started has a start date.

3. Bound it. Which welds have it and which do not. The boundary is usually informative.

4. Run the cheap checks anyway. Gas flow at the nozzle rather than at the regulator, tip and liner condition, earth return, electrode condition, consumable storage. These are cheap enough to check without a hypothesis.

5. Design a test that separates the surviving hypotheses. One variable, on test coupons, with sections. Two variables changed together prove nothing.

6. Record the unresolved case. An honest "cause not established, contained by X" is a better record than a plausible cause that was never confirmed — because the plausible cause will be believed the next time and will send the next investigation the wrong way.

17. Worked Example — A Porosity Problem That Was Not a Gas Problem

The observation. A fabricator welding 8 mm structural steel with gas-shielded flux-cored wire began finding porosity on radiography. It appeared on one of four identical welding stations. The porosity was clustered, not uniform.

Step 1 — the observation. Confirmed on the radiographs and on a sectioned coupon: rounded pores in groups, weld metal, mid-thickness passes, with sound weld between the groups.

Step 2 — distribution. Clustered means an intermittent source (Section 5). One station only means a machine or a local condition, not a consumable batch or a material heat — a consumable problem would have appeared on all four stations drawing from the same store.

Step 3 — what changed. Nothing recorded. The station had not been serviced recently, which was itself the finding: the other three stations had been, and this one had been missed.

Step 4 — cheap checks. Gas flow measured at the nozzle, not the flowmeter, was correct at rest. Nozzle and tip were spattered but not blocked. Liner was contaminated.

Step 5 — the separating test. Welding a coupon while watching the gas flow at the nozzle during welding showed the flow was correct at rest and fell intermittently during welding. The gas hose had been chafing against a fixture and had a partial split that opened under the movement of the torch during welding and closed at rest.

Why the shop had been going round in circles. Every check had been made with the torch stationary. The fault only existed in motion. The team had replaced the wire batch twice and changed the gas cylinder once, neither of which could have helped, and had begun to suspect the consumable supplier.

Corrective action. Hose replaced and re-routed clear of the fixture. Standardization: hose condition and routing added to the station's preventive maintenance check, and the check made a moving one — flow verified at the nozzle during a test weld, not at rest.

The general lesson. The distribution pointed at an intermittent, station-local source before any hypothesis about gas chemistry was needed. Steps 2 and 3 of the diagnostic method did the work; the metallurgy did none of it.

18. Known Gaps

• No acceptance limits are quoted. ISO 5817, ISO 10042, ISO 13919, ISO 18279, IPC J-STD-001, AWS D1.1 and ASME Section VIII each set their own, and they differ. The applicable document must be read.

• Cause lists are not exhaustive. Each table gives the causes that account for most occurrences, not every possible cause.

• Corrective actions are directional, not parametric. "Reduce heat input" is a direction; the value belongs to a qualified procedure.

• Detection probability is not quantified. The likelihood of finding a given imperfection with a given method depends on size, orientation, technique and personnel, and is outside this reference set.

• Service-induced damage — creep, fatigue, corrosion, hydrogen damage in service — is mentioned only where it is confusable with a fabrication defect. Fitness-for-service assessment is a separate discipline.

• Statistical defect analysis — control charting of defect rates, sampling theory for destructive testing — is treated only in outline in Chapter 33.

1. Why This Chapter Exists and What It Will Not Do

Welding is governed by three large standards systems — ISO (with EN as its European adoption), AWS, and ASME — that developed independently, use different vocabulary for the same physics, and are not interchangeable. A welding engineer moving between them is not translating a language; they are moving between legal frameworks that happen to describe the same processes.

This chapter maps the territory. It does not provide an equivalence table that lets a document written to one system be substituted for a document written to another. Such tables exist commercially and are useful as starting points, but treating one as an authority is how a qualification gets rejected at audit. The relationship between, for example, an ISO 9606-1 welder qualification and an ASME Section IX performance qualification is not equivalence; it is overlap with different boundaries, different essential variables and different administration.

The honest statement to make to a client is: "This qualification was made to standard X. To satisfy standard Y, the following specific gaps must be closed." Chapter 31 develops the qualification detail; this chapter gives the structural map that makes such a statement possible.

2. The Three Systems and How They Are Structured

| System | Origin and scope | Structure | Legal force |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ISO | International; adopted in Europe as EN ISO | Horizontal standards by subject — one for process nomenclature, one for procedure qualification, one for welder qualification, and so on — referenced by application codes | Voluntary unless invoked by a contract, a directive, or a national regulation |
| EN | European; largely superseded by EN ISO adoptions, some EN-only standards remain | As ISO where adopted; harmonized standards give presumption of conformity to EU directives | Harmonized standards carry weight under EU directives (e.g. the Pressure Equipment Directive) |
| AWS | United States; American Welding Society | A mix: application codes (D-series), consumable specifications (A5-series), definitions, symbols, safety | Voluntary unless invoked; D1.1 is widely adopted into US building codes |
| ASME | United States; Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code | A vertical code: construction rules by book (Section VIII, I, III...) with welding qualification centralized in Section IX | Adopted into law by many US states and other jurisdictions for pressure equipment |

The structural difference matters more than the content difference. ISO is horizontal, ASME is vertical, AWS is mixed. An ISO-based fabricator assembles compliance from a set of independent standards; an ASME-based fabricator works inside a single code that references one qualification book for everything. This is why a fabricator experienced in one system often finds the other confusingly organized rather than confusingly written.

3. The First Rule — The Contract Decides

Before any cross-reference question is worth asking, one thing must be established: which document governs this job?

| Source of the requirement | Typical wording | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purchase order or contract | "Fabrication to AWS D1.1" | Governing — this is the usual answer |
| Client specification | A company standard referencing others | Governing, and often adds requirements above the code |
| Regulation | Jurisdictional adoption of ASME, or an EU directive | Mandatory, not negotiable by contract |
| Design code | The code the design was performed to | Usually governs fabrication too |
| Fabricator's own system | ISO 3834 level, internal procedures | Applies in addition, never instead |

Where two documents conflict, the contract's precedence clause decides; where there is none, the more stringent requirement is the safe reading, and the conflict should be raised in writing rather than resolved silently. A conflict resolved silently by a welding engineer becomes a nonconformity discovered by an auditor.

5. Procedure Specification and Qualification

| Function | ISO | AWS D1.1 | ASME Section IX |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The specification document | WPS per ISO 15609 | WPS | WPS |
| The qualification record | WPQR per ISO 15613/15614 | PQR | PQR |
| The preliminary document | pWPS per ISO 15607 | — | — |
| The general rules | ISO 15607 | Clause 4 | Article I–II |
| Qualification by test | ISO 15614 series | Clause 4 Part B | Article II |
| Qualification by pre-production test | ISO 15613 | — | — |
| Qualification by tested consumables | ISO 15610 | — | — |
| Qualification by previous experience | ISO 15611 | — | — |
| Qualification by standard procedure | ISO 15612 | — | — |
| Prequalified — no test required | — | Clause 5 (prequalified WPS) | Not available |

This is the single most consequential structural difference in the whole chapter, and it runs in two directions.

ISO offers five qualification routes; ASME offers one. ISO 15607 sets out qualification by procedure test (15614), pre-production test (15613), tested consumables (15610), previous experience (15611) and standard welding procedure (15612). [S2] ASME Section IX recognizes qualification by test, full stop — there is no prequalification and no experience route. A fabricator moving from ISO to ASME who has been relying on 15610 or 15611 has no qualification at all under ASME and must test.

AWS D1.1 offers prequalification, which ISO does not. D1.1 Clause 5 allows certain combinations of process, base metal, consumable, joint detail and parameter ranges to be used without a qualification test, provided every prequalification condition is met exactly. [S3] This is a substantial commercial advantage on structural steelwork and has no ISO counterpart. It is also frequently misapplied: prequalification is conditional on every listed condition, and a single deviation — a joint detail outside the tabulated geometry, a base metal not in the approved list — voids it and returns the WPS to the qualification-by-test route.

Essential variables do not map. Each system defines its own list of variables whose change requires requalification, with different thresholds. Thickness qualification ranges, position coverage, heat input limits and material grouping all differ. There is no shortcut here; the applicable standard's variable table must be read against the actual WPS.

6. Personnel Qualification

| Function | ISO | AWS | ASME |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Manual and partly mechanized welders | ISO 9606-1 (steel), -2 (Al), -3/-4/-5 (Ni, Cu, Ti/Zr) | D1.1 Clause 6 Part C | Section IX, Article III |
| Operators and setters of mechanized/automatic equipment | ISO 14732 | D1.1 | Section IX, Article III |
| Welding coordination personnel | ISO 14731 | — (no direct counterpart) | — (no direct counterpart) |
| Inspection personnel | ISO 9712 (NDT), national schemes for welding inspectors | AWS CWI (QC1) | Owner/AI framework, SNT-TC-1A for NDT |

Three structural differences matter.

ISO 14731 has no direct AWS or ASME counterpart. It defines welding coordination tasks and responsibilities and requires a competent, named person to hold them. [S4] The American system distributes the equivalent responsibility across the Authorized Inspector, the fabricator's quality programme and the CWI, rather than defining a coordination role. A European fabricator's Responsible Welding Coordinator has no ASME equivalent to point at, and an American fabricator entering ISO 3834 usually has to create the role.

Qualification validity is administered differently. ISO 9606-1 ties continued validity to demonstrable continuity of work in the qualified range, with a periodic confirmation interval; ASME Section IX ties it to the welder having used the process within a defined period. The practical effect is similar; the record-keeping obligations are not.

Coverage rules differ. Both systems define what a test coverage in one position, thickness and material qualifies for elsewhere, and the ranges are not the same. Chapter 32 develops the ISO ranges; the ASME ranges must be read from Section IX's own tables.

Consumable classification is where cross-system substitution is most often attempted and most often done badly. The two systems classify on overlapping but not identical property sets: mechanical property levels, impact test temperatures, hydrogen levels, chemical composition limits and position capability are all defined with different thresholds and different test conditions.

The rule that survives contact with an auditor: a consumable is qualified for a job by its own classification against the standard the contract invokes, evidenced by the manufacturer's certificate. A cross-reference chart from a supplier's catalogue is a purchasing aid, not evidence of compliance. Where a contract invokes AWS and only an ISO-classified consumable is available, the correct action is to obtain a manufacturer's certificate showing the AWS classification, not to argue equivalence.

ISO 14175 deserves separate mention because its gas group designations (I, M1, M2, M3, C, R, N, O, Z with numeric subdivisions) are widely used on European WPSs and have no compact AWS equivalent; AWS documents typically specify gas composition directly. [S5] A WPS moving from ISO to AWS should convert the gas group designation into an explicit composition.

8. Material Grouping

| System | Grouping scheme | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ISO | ISO/TR 15608 groups and sub-groups | Determines qualification coverage across materials |
| ASME | P-Numbers, with Group Numbers; F-Numbers for consumables; A-Numbers for weld metal analysis | Determines qualification coverage |
| AWS D1.1 | Approved base metal tables, with prequalified base-metal/consumable combinations | Determines prequalification eligibility |

These schemes group materials by weldability characteristics so that a qualification on one material covers others. They do not correspond. An ISO/TR 15608 group and an ASME P-Number are both weldability groupings, but the boundaries differ, and a qualification's coverage therefore differs.

The ASME triplet is worth understanding as a set: P-Number groups the base metal, F-Number groups the filler by usability characteristics, and A-Number groups the deposited weld metal by chemical composition. A change to any of them may be an essential variable depending on the process. This three-way split has no ISO equivalent.

ISO 5817 levels are not a quality scale to be picked freely. B is the most stringent, D the least; the applicable level comes from the application standard or the contract, and selecting it is a design decision that has to account for loading, consequence of failure and service conditions. [S6] The most common misuse is a drawing note saying "weld quality to ISO 5817" without a level, which specifies nothing.

ISO 5817 explicitly excludes beam welding, which is why ISO 13919 exists. A laser or electron-beam weld assessed against ISO 5817 is being assessed against the wrong document. [S6] [S7]

AWS and ASME acceptance criteria are embedded in the application code, not in a separate quality-level standard. This is the vertical-against-horizontal structure again: a D1.1 fabricator finds acceptance criteria in D1.1; an ISO fabricator finds them in ISO 5817 at a level the application standard specifies.

10. Non-Destructive Testing

| Function | ISO | ASTM/ASME/AWS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Method selection | ISO 17635 | Application code |
| Radiographic testing | ISO 17636 series | ASME Section V Article 2 |
| Ultrasonic testing | ISO 17640, ISO 11666 (acceptance) | ASME Section V Article 4; AWS D1.1 Clause 8 |
| Phased array / TOFD | ISO 13588, ISO 10863 | ASME Section V Article 4 appendices |
| Penetrant testing | ISO 3452 series, ISO 23277 (acceptance) | ASME Section V Article 6 |
| Magnetic particle | ISO 17638, ISO 23278 (acceptance) | ASME Section V Article 7 |
| Visual testing | ISO 17637 | ASME Section V Article 9 |
| Personnel qualification | ISO 9712 | SNT-TC-1A / CP-189 |

ISO separates the technique standard from the acceptance standard — ISO 17640 tells you how to perform ultrasonic testing, ISO 11666 tells you what is acceptable. ASME Section V gives the method and the construction code gives the acceptance. The separation is a common source of incomplete specifications: citing ISO 17640 alone specifies a technique with no acceptance criterion.

ISO 17635 is the entry point for method selection, mapping joint type, material, thickness and quality level to the appropriate method. [S8] It is the document to reach for when a contract specifies a quality level but not an inspection method.

11. Quality Management of Welding

| Level | ISO 3834 part | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Comprehensive | ISO 3834-2 | Full requirements; typical for pressure equipment and safety-critical structures |
| Standard | ISO 3834-3 | Intermediate |
| Elementary | ISO 3834-4 | Basic |
| Selection guidance | ISO 3834-1 | How to choose the level |
| Conformity demonstration | ISO 3834-5 | What documents must be conformed to |
| Implementation guidance | ISO 3834-6 | How to implement |

ISO 3834 has no direct AWS or ASME counterpart. The American system achieves comparable control through the ASME Quality Control System and stamp certification, the Authorized Inspector, and AWS certification programmes for fabricators — but these are certification schemes tied to a code, not a standalone quality-requirements standard that any fabricator can implement. [S9]

The relationship to ISO 9001 is worth stating precisely, because it is often confused: ISO 9001 is a general quality management system standard and does not address welding-specific requirements. ISO 3834 supplements it for welding. A fabricator certified to ISO 9001 alone has not demonstrated welding quality requirements; a fabricator certified to ISO 3834 has, and the two are commonly held together.

Structural steel fabrication in Europe adds EN 1090-2 with its execution classes EXC1–EXC4, which invoke ISO 3834 levels and set out execution requirements. This is the nearest European structural analogue to AWS D1.1's role.

12. Symbols and Drawing Representation

| Function | ISO | AWS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Welding symbols | ISO 2553 | AWS A2.4 |
| Terms and definitions | ISO 25901 series | AWS A3.0 |
| NDT symbols | ISO 2553 | AWS A2.4 |

ISO 2553 and AWS A2.4 use similar symbol shapes and are not interchangeable in one critical respect: the arrow-side/other-side convention relative to the reference line. ISO 2553 provides for both a dual reference line (a continuous line with a dashed identification line) and, in its later editions, a system where the dashed line may be omitted; AWS A2.4 places arrow-side information below the reference line and other-side information above it — the opposite of the ISO dashed-line convention in the configuration most engineers first learn.

The practical consequence is that a weld can be placed on the wrong side of a joint by an engineer reading a drawing in the convention they were trained in. The defence is that every drawing states which standard its symbols follow, in the title block, and that this is checked when drawings cross between organizations. This is a real and recurring error, not a theoretical one.
