15. The Transfer Problem — What Does Not Carry Across

When work moves between systems, the following do not transfer and must be addressed explicitly:

| Item | Why it does not transfer | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Procedure qualification | Different essential variables, different test requirements, different ranges | Requalify, or demonstrate the existing PQR meets every requirement of the target standard |
| Welder qualification | Different test pieces, coverage rules and continuity administration | Requalify to the target standard |
| Non-test qualification routes | ISO 15610/15611/15612 have no ASME equivalent | Requalify by test |
| Prequalified WPS | AWS D1.1 Clause 5 has no ISO equivalent | Qualify by test under ISO |
| Consumable classification | Different property thresholds and test conditions | Obtain a certificate to the required classification |
| Material grouping | P-Numbers and ISO/TR 15608 groups differ | Re-derive the coverage from the target standard's tables |
| Acceptance criteria | Different limits, sometimes for the same imperfection | Assess against the target standard's limits |
| NDT acceptance | Method standards and acceptance standards pair differently | Specify both, from the target system |
| The coordination role | ISO 14731 has no direct US counterpart | Map the tasks onto the target system's roles explicitly |
| Drawing symbols | Convention differs | State the symbol standard on every drawing |

What does transfer is the underlying engineering: the metallurgy, the process physics, the defect mechanisms, the diagnostic method. That is most of this reference set, and it is why the process and materials chapters are written without reference to a governing system.

16. Worked Example — A European Fabricator Quoting to an ASME Scope

The situation. A fabricator holding ISO 3834-2 certification and EN 1090-2 EXC3, with a mature set of EN ISO 15614-1 qualified procedures and EN ISO 9606-1 qualified welders, is invited to quote for pressure vessels to ASME Section VIII Division 1 with a U stamp.

What they have that helps. A quality system, competent welding coordination, calibrated equipment, traceable material and consumable control, trained inspectors, and — most importantly — the engineering capability. None of this is wasted.

What does not transfer, and must be built:

1. The ASME Quality Control System and certificate of authorization. This is the gateway, not a formality: a written QC manual accepted by the review process, with an Authorized Inspection Agency contracted and an AI accepted into the shop. Long lead time; this is the item that decides whether the quote is realistic.

2. Procedure qualification to Section IX. Existing EN ISO 15614-1 WPQRs are not ASME PQRs. Some may be usable as evidence supporting a Section IX qualification if the original test happened to satisfy Section IX's requirements, but this must be demonstrated variable by variable and is often easier to redo than to argue. Any procedure relying on ISO 15610, 15611 or 15612 has no path at all and must be tested.

3. Welder performance qualification to Section IX Article III. Requalification, with test coupons and ranges per Section IX's own tables.

4. Material grouping re-derivation. Coverage must be re-derived on P-Numbers rather than ISO/TR 15608 groups.

5. Consumable certification. AWS A5-series classification certificates for the consumables to be used, not ISO classifications with a cross-reference chart.

6. Acceptance criteria. Section VIII Division 1 criteria, not ISO 5817 levels. The mapping is not one-to-one.

7. NDT. ASME Section V methods with Section VIII acceptance, and NDT personnel qualified under a written practice per SNT-TC-1A rather than ISO 9712.

8. The coordination role. The Responsible Welding Coordinator's tasks must be mapped onto the QC manual's defined roles; ASME will not recognize the ISO 14731 title but will require the functions to be assigned.

9. Drawings and symbols. If drawings are produced in-house to ISO 2553, either convert to AWS A2.4 or state the standard unambiguously and confirm the client accepts it.

What the quote must include. The cost and, more importantly, the lead time of items 1–3. The common commercial error is quoting the fabrication and treating the certification path as an overhead already in place. It is neither quick nor certain.

The honest position to state to the client: "We hold ISO 3834-2 and EN 1090-2 EXC3 with qualified procedures and personnel under the EN ISO system. ASME Section VIII work requires a separate certification path and requalification of procedures and personnel under Section IX. We estimate X months to that position. Our engineering capability, quality system and inspection capability transfer; the qualification records do not."

17. How to Keep a Standards Register Current

Standards are revised, and a WPS citing a withdrawn edition is a finding waiting to happen. A minimal register that works:

| Field | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Standard number and title | Identification |
| Edition/year held | The version the work was done to |
| Current edition | Checked periodically against the publisher's catalogue |
| Where it is invoked | Which WPSs, procedures, drawings and contracts cite it — this is the field that makes a revision actionable |
| Owner | Who checks it |
| Last checked | Date |
| Impact assessment | What changed, and what has to be updated |

The field that carries the value is where it is invoked. Without it, a revision notice produces a shrug; with it, it produces a list of documents to review. An annual review cycle is usual, with a shorter cycle for the small number of standards that govern the fabricator's main product.

When a standard is revised, the contract usually still governs the edition it cited. New work moves to the new edition; work in progress under an old contract normally does not, unless the contract says otherwise or a regulator requires it. This should be decided deliberately and recorded, not left to whoever prints the next WPS.

18. Known Gaps

• This chapter maps structure, not content. It does not reproduce any standard's requirements, tables, variable lists or acceptance limits.

• No equivalence claims are made, and none should be inferred. Where two documents are listed side by side, that indicates comparable function, not interchangeability.

• Editions are not stated for every standard. Standards are revised; the edition invoked by the contract is what governs, and the current edition must be checked against the publisher's catalogue.

• National deviations to EN ISO adoptions, and jurisdictional amendments to ASME adoption, are not covered and can be significant.

• Japanese (JIS), Chinese (GB), Russian (GOST) and Indian (IS) systems are not covered. They are substantial systems with their own structures and are outside this reference set's scope.

• Classification society rules for shipbuilding and offshore are noted only in Section 14 and have their own qualification and approval frameworks.

• Commercial cross-reference charts — consumable equivalence tables in particular — are widely available and are useful for purchasing. They are not compliance evidence and this chapter deliberately does not reproduce one.

1. What This Chapter Does and Does Not Provide

This chapter gives a cost structure and a comparison method. It does not give cost figures, rates, or prices, for three reasons that are worth stating plainly rather than hiding behind:

1. Rates are local and dated. Labour rates, energy prices, consumable prices and equipment costs vary by region, by year and by supplier, and a number printed in a reference set is wrong somewhere and out of date everywhere.

2. Productivity figures are configuration-specific. A deposition rate depends on the wire, the diameter, the position, the joint, the equipment and the operator. A single number would be a fiction.

3. A wrong number is worse than no number, because it will be used. Estimating tools built on borrowed figures produce confident answers that nobody can defend when they are challenged.

What this chapter does provide is the structure into which locally-gathered numbers are placed, the relative comparisons that hold across most situations, and the errors that make estimates wrong even when the numbers are good.

2. Where the Money Actually Goes

The single most useful fact in welding economics is the shape of the cost breakdown, because it is counter-intuitive and it directs improvement effort correctly.

| Cost element | Typical share of total welded-joint cost | Comment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Labour and overhead | The dominant share, usually the majority | Includes the welder, the welder's supervision and the facility burden |
| Filler metal and flux | Modest | Visible, easily measured, and therefore over-attacked |
| Shielding gas | Small | Often confused with a large cost because cylinders are visible |
| Electrical energy | Small | Usually the smallest line |
| Equipment depreciation | Small to moderate | Depends heavily on utilization |
| Joint preparation, fit-up, tacking | Often larger than the welding itself | Frequently omitted from the estimate entirely |
| Inspection and NDT | Moderate to large on code work | Scales with quality level, not with weld volume |
| Rework and repair | Highly variable; can dominate on a bad job | Usually invisible until it is measured |
| Distortion correction | Frequently underestimated | Straightening, machining allowance, fixturing |

The practical consequence: a programme to reduce consumable price by ten percent attacks a small slice of the total; a programme to raise arc time by ten percentage points attacks the largest one. Yet consumable price is negotiated annually in most shops, and arc time is measured in very few.

3. The Cost Model

The cost of a welded joint decomposes cleanly. Every term below is measurable locally.

Weld metal required — cross-sectional area of the joint (from the preparation geometry) multiplied by length, multiplied by density. This is set by the *designer*, not by the welding department.

Arc time — weld metal required, divided by deposition rate, divided by deposition efficiency.

Total labour time — arc time divided by the operating factor (arc time as a fraction of the welder's paid time). This single division is where most of the cost lives.

Labour cost — total labour time multiplied by the fully burdened labour rate.

Consumable cost — weld metal required divided by deposition efficiency, multiplied by consumable price; plus flux consumption for SAW and ESW; plus gas flow rate multiplied by gas time multiplied by gas price.

Energy cost — arc power multiplied by arc time divided by power source efficiency, multiplied by energy price.

Preparation cost — cutting, bevelling, cleaning, fit-up and tacking labour and consumables.

Quality cost — inspection, NDT, documentation, and the expected cost of repair (repair rate multiplied by repair cost).

Amortized fixed cost — equipment, tooling, fixturing, programming and qualification, divided across the expected production quantity.

The model is not difficult. What makes estimates wrong is not the arithmetic; it is the values put into the operating factor, the preparation cost and the quality cost — Sections 4, 6 and 8.

4. Arc Time and Duty Cycle — The Dominant Variable

The operating factor (also called duty cycle or arc-on time) is the fraction of a welder's paid time during which an arc is burning. It is the largest single lever in welding economics and the one least often measured.

| Working arrangement | Character of the operating factor |
| --- | --- |
| Manual SMAW, site work, varied positions | Lowest — electrode changes, slag removal, repositioning, scaffolding, waiting |
| Manual SMAW, shop | Low |
| Semi-automatic GMAW/FCAW, shop | Moderate — continuous wire removes electrode changes |
| Mechanized, single operator | Higher |
| Robotic cell, single station | Higher still, but limited by load/unload |
| Robotic cell with two stations or a positioner | Highest — welding continues while the operator loads |

Where the non-arc time actually goes — and this is what a measurement exercise reveals:

| Activity | Typical relationship to the weld |
| --- | --- |
| Fetching material, consumables, tools | Unrelated to welding; pure loss |
| Fit-up and tacking | Necessary, often larger than welding time |
| Repositioning the work or the welder | Reducible by positioners and fixtures |
| Slag removal and interpass cleaning | Process-dependent — a real reason to prefer a slagless process on multipass work |
| Electrode changes | SMAW only, and a major reason continuous-wire processes win on productivity |
| Waiting — for crane, inspection, drawings, instructions | Organizational, and often the largest single block |
| Grinding and dressing | Partly rework, partly process |
| Documentation | Scales with quality level |

The uncomfortable finding that a time study usually produces is that the largest single block of non-arc time is organizational — waiting for a crane, a drawing, an inspector, or a decision. That is not a welding problem and cannot be fixed by a welding process change, which is precisely why it survives so long: nobody in the welding department owns it.

How to measure it honestly. Direct observation over full shifts, or arc-on time logged by the power source (Chapter 72). Logged arc-on time is objective and cheap once the equipment supports it, and it is one of the strongest arguments for welding data monitoring on a pure cost basis rather than a quality basis. Measure over enough shifts to cover normal variation; a single observed day is a performance, not a measurement.

5. Deposition Rate and Deposition Efficiency

Two different quantities, frequently confused, both needed.

Deposition rate is mass of weld metal deposited per unit of arc time. It rises with current, with wire feed speed, with wire diameter, with multiple wires, and with electrode extension in cored-wire processes. It falls out of position.

Deposition efficiency is the mass ending up in the weld divided by the mass of consumable used. Losses go to slag, spatter, fume, stub ends and, in cored wires, the non-metallic core content.

| Process | Deposition rate character | Deposition efficiency character | Main loss route |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SMAW (111) | Low; limited by electrode length and changes | Lowest of the arc processes | Stub ends and coating — a substantial fraction of the electrode is never deposited |
| GMAW solid wire (135) | Moderate to high | Highest of the common arc processes | Spatter; efficiency falls as spatter rises |
| Metal-cored (138) | Higher than solid at the same current | High | Spatter, small core loss |
| FCAW gas-shielded (136) | High | Moderate | Slag-forming core content |
| FCAW self-shielded (114) | High | Lower than gas-shielded | Larger slag-forming and shielding core content |
| SAW (12x) | Highest for a single arc; multi-wire higher still | Effectively complete for the wire | Flux is a separate consumable cost |
| GTAW (141) | Lowest | Very high | Almost none — filler is placed deliberately |
| ESW/EGW (72/73) | Very high in a single pass | High | Flux/gas |

Two economic consequences follow, and they pull in opposite directions.

First, the productivity ranking of arc processes is broadly stable: GTAW is the slowest and SAW the fastest, with GMAW/FCAW between them and SMAW low. That ranking survives most situations, which is why it drives so much process selection.

Second — and this is the one that gets missed — spatter is a direct cost, twice. It reduces deposition efficiency, so more consumable is bought per kilogram deposited; and it produces removal labour, which lands in the operating factor as non-arc time and sometimes as surface damage requiring further repair (Chapter 74). A process running in globular transfer is paying for both. This is the economic argument for the transfer-mode discipline set out in Chapters 30 and 39, and it is usually stronger than the quality argument in a shop where spatter is being tolerated.

6. Joint Preparation — The Variable Decided by the Designer

Weld metal volume scales with the groove cross-section, and groove cross-section scales roughly with the square of thickness for a constant included angle. The consequences are large and the decision is made on a drawing, usually without a cost calculation.

| Preparation choice | Effect on volume | Effect elsewhere |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reducing the included angle | Large reduction | Risks lack of sidewall fusion; requires process capability and often mechanization |
| Double-sided preparation instead of single | Roughly halves the volume at a given thickness | Requires access to both sides and back gouging |
| U-preparation instead of V on thick sections | Substantial reduction | More expensive to machine |
| Narrow-gap techniques | Largest reduction on heavy sections | Requires specialized equipment, procedure development and confidence in sidewall fusion |
| Fillet leg size | Volume scales with the square of the leg | An oversized fillet is the most common and most expensive drawing error in fabrication |
| Partial instead of full penetration | Large reduction | Only where the design permits it |

Oversized fillets deserve emphasis because the error is so common and so invisible. A fillet specified one size larger than required costs disproportionately more weld metal, disproportionately more arc time, more distortion and more heat input — for no structural benefit. Welders also tend to overweld fillets slightly as insurance, compounding it. Measuring actual fillet sizes against drawing requirements is one of the highest-return audits available in a structural shop, and it usually finds systematic overwelding.

The general point: the largest cost reductions in welding are usually available at the drawing, not at the arc. A welding engineer who is not consulted during design is being asked to optimize the small end of the problem.

7. Consumable Cost Against Consumable Consequence

Consumable price is a small share of total cost (Section 2), which means selecting a consumable on price is almost always a false economy if the cheaper one costs anything in arc time, spatter, slag removal, repair rate or operating factor.

| Consumable decision | Price effect | Consequence effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cheaper wire, more spatter | Small saving | Lower efficiency, more cleaning, possible surface damage — usually a net loss |
| Larger diameter wire where the joint allows | Slightly cheaper per kg | Higher deposition rate — usually a net gain |
| Metal-cored instead of solid | Higher price per kg | Higher deposition rate, less spatter, fewer passes — often a net gain |
| Higher-argon gas mixture | Higher gas price | Lower spatter, better transfer, less cleaning — usually a net gain on quality-sensitive work |
| Low-hydrogen consumable where required | Higher price and storage cost | Avoids hydrogen cracking — not a trade at all where the material requires it |
| Longer electrode extension (cored wires) | None | Higher deposition rate through resistive preheating — free, within the procedure's limits |

The one place price discipline genuinely pays is consumable waste: stub loss, unused opened packets, flux over-recovery losses, wire left on part-used spools, and consumables scrapped by poor storage. That is a stores and handling problem, not a purchasing problem.

8. The Cost of Quality

Quality cost has three parts, and confusing them makes the trade impossible to see.

| Part | Contents | Behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prevention | Procedure development, qualification, training, maintenance, calibration, fixture accuracy, process monitoring | Rises with investment; reduces the other two |
| Appraisal | Inspection, NDT, documentation, destructive sampling | Set by the quality level and the contract |
| Failure | Repair, rework, scrap, delay, concessions, warranty, and the reputational cost | Falls as prevention rises — but only after a lag |

Two facts govern the trade.

Appraisal cost scales with quality level, not weld volume. Moving a joint from a lower to a higher ISO 5817 level, or from visual to full volumetric inspection, can multiply the inspection cost of a weld that takes the same time to make. This is why quality-level selection is an economic decision as well as an engineering one, and why a blanket "level B everywhere" specification is expensive in a way that is rarely quantified.

Failure cost is where the money is and where the measurement is worst. Repair welding costs far more than the original weld — excavation, re-preparation, a qualified repair procedure, re-welding in worse access under worse restraint, re-inspection, and the schedule impact. Most shops do not have a reliable repair rate figure because repairs are absorbed into the welder's time rather than booked. A shop that cannot state its repair rate cannot make any quality economics argument, in either direction — which is why measuring it is the first step, before any improvement is proposed.

9. Distortion and Rework as a Cost Line

Distortion costs money in four ways, and only the first is usually visible:

1. Straightening labour — flame straightening, pressing, mechanical correction.

2. Machining allowance — extra material and extra machining time provided to absorb the movement.

3. Fit-up difficulty downstream — a distorted subassembly makes the next joint harder, which raises its cost and its defect rate.

4. Scrap — parts that cannot be brought back into tolerance.

The prevention levers are set out in Chapter 34: heat input, welding sequence, restraint, pre-setting, balanced welding and joint design. All of them cost something at the point of welding — a sequence that controls distortion is usually slower than one that does not — which is why distortion control loses arguments in shops that measure welding time and do not measure straightening time. Booking straightening labour separately is the change that makes the argument winnable.

10. Capital, Tooling and Programming

| Fixed cost element | Amortizes over | Risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Power sources and feeders | Many jobs; long life | Low; utilization is the variable |
| Positioners and manipulators | Many jobs | Low, and they raise the operating factor across everything |
| Dedicated fixtures | One part or family | High — dies with the part |
| Robot cells | Many parts if flexible; one if not | Moderate to high |
| Programming and path development | One part, but reusable within a family | Underestimated in almost every case |
| Procedure qualification | Range of thickness/material covered | Moderate; the ISO route chosen matters (Chapter 31) |
| Beam sources and enclosures | Many parts | High capital, high utilization requirement |

Programming and fixture development are the systematically underestimated items in automation business cases. The equipment quotation is a firm number from a supplier; the programming, fixture iteration, procedure development and debug time is an internal estimate made by someone with an incentive for it to be small. Chapter 69 develops what robotic implementation actually involves.

Qualification cost interacts with the ISO route chosen. ISO 15610 through 15613 can, where permitted by the contract, avoid the cost of a full ISO 15614 procedure test. Under ASME, no such route exists (Chapter 75). This is a real cost difference between working under the two systems and belongs in the estimate.

11. Automation Economics

The automation decision is a fixed-against-variable trade, and it turns on four things — of which cycle time is only one.

| Factor | Favours automation | Favours manual |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Volume and stability | High volume, stable design | Low volume, changing design |
| Part accuracy | Accurate, repeatable parts | Variable fit-up |
| Joint accessibility | Simple, accessible, repeatable paths | Complex, obstructed |
| Consistency requirement | High, or unverifiable welds | Tolerant |
| Labour availability | Scarce or expensive skilled welders | Available |
| Working conditions | Hazardous, hot, awkward positions | Benign |
| Product life | Long | Short |

The condition that most often defeats an automation case is part accuracy. A robot repeats a path; it does not compensate for a joint that is not where the program says it is unless seam tracking and adaptive control are fitted, and those add cost and complexity. Automating a joint fed by parts with an uncontrolled tolerance stack converts a fit-up problem into a defect problem at higher speed. The correct sequence is: control the incoming part accuracy first, then automate. Reversing it is the most expensive mistake in this chapter.

The second most common defeat is variety. A cell that must be reprogrammed and refixtured frequently spends its capacity on changeover, and the business case built on cycle time evaporates.

12. Comparing Processes — The Method

To compare two processes for a specific joint honestly:

1. Fix the joint. Same material, thickness, length, position, access and quality requirement. If the processes require different preparations, use each process's own correct preparation — this is a real difference between them, not a variable to normalize away.

2. Calculate weld metal required for each, from each process's preparation geometry. Beam and narrow-gap processes often win here before anything else is counted.

3. Obtain deposition rate and efficiency locally — from procedure trials, supplier data for the specific consumable and configuration, or measured production. Not from a textbook.

4. Estimate the operating factor for each, in this shop, for this work. This is where borrowed figures do the most damage, and where a measured number from your own shop is worth more than a published one from anywhere.

5. Add preparation, fit-up and tacking for each. Beam processes shift cost here; arc processes shift it to welding.

6. Add inspection cost appropriate to each process's verification requirement (Chapter 73, screen 6). Processes whose welds cannot be inspected carry monitoring and destructive sampling cost instead.

7. Add an expected repair cost using each process's realistic repair rate in this shop, not its theoretical capability.

8. Add distortion and straightening — this is where high-heat-input processes lose ground they gained on deposition rate.

9. Amortize fixed costs over the honest expected quantity, not the optimistic one.

10. Sum, and then test the answer's sensitivity to the two or three most uncertain inputs. If the ranking flips within the uncertainty, the honest conclusion is that the processes are comparable and the decision should be made on risk, flexibility and capability rather than on cost.

Step 10 is what separates an estimate from a number. An answer that reverses when the operating factor assumption moves by a few points has not decided anything, and saying so is more useful than presenting the point estimate.

13. Comparing Processes — The Relative Picture

Ordinal comparisons that hold in most situations. They rank; they do not quantify.

| Process | Deposition rate | Consumable efficiency | Operating factor achievable | Fixed cost | Distortion | Inspection burden |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SMAW | Low | Low | Low | Lowest | Moderate | Standard |
| GMAW | Moderate–high | High | Moderate–high | Low | Moderate | Standard |
| FCAW-G | High | Moderate | Moderate | Low | Moderate–high | Standard |
| FCAW-S | High | Moderate–low | Moderate | Lowest (no gas) | High | Standard |
| SAW | Highest | Highest | High | Moderate | High (heat input) | Standard |
| GTAW | Lowest | High | Low | Low | Lowest | Standard |
| PAW | Low–moderate | High | Moderate | Moderate | Low | Standard |
| Laser | n/a (low volume) | n/a | Highest | High | Lowest | High — fit-up and monitoring |
| EBW | n/a | n/a | Moderate (vacuum cycle) | Highest | Lowest | High |
| Resistance spot | n/a | n/a | Highest | Moderate–high | Lowest | Destructive sampling + monitoring |
| FSW | n/a | n/a (no consumable) | High | High | Very low | Difficult — process control |

Reading the table correctly matters. The high-productivity processes on the left of the deposition column carry their cost somewhere else — fixed cost, fit-up discipline, distortion, or an inspection burden that cannot be discharged by inspection at all. The processes that look expensive per metre of weld are often the cheapest per finished, accepted assembly. That is the whole reason to run the method in Section 12 rather than compare deposition rates.

14. The Seven Most Common Estimating Errors

Error 1 — using arc time instead of total time. Dividing by an operating factor of 1.0. Produces an estimate that can be off by a factor of several, always in the optimistic direction.

Error 2 — omitting preparation, fit-up and tacking. Frequently comparable to or larger than the welding time itself, and routinely left out because it is done by a different person.

Error 3 — using a published deposition rate as an achieved rate. Published rates are for a specific configuration, usually flat position, at the top of the current range.

Error 4 — assuming zero repairs. Every process has a repair rate in every shop. A zero assumption is a decision to be wrong.

Error 5 — ignoring distortion and straightening. Booked elsewhere, so invisible in the welding estimate — and the reason low-heat-input processes are undervalued.

Error 6 — amortizing fixed cost over an optimistic volume. The most common way an automation business case is made to work on paper.

Error 7 — comparing processes at different quality outcomes. A cheaper process producing a higher defect rate is not cheaper; it has moved cost from the welding line to the repair line, where nobody is looking for it.

15. Where the Improvement Actually Is

Ranked by the size of the prize in a typical fabrication shop:

| Rank | Lever | Why it is first |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Reduce weld metal required — joint design, fillet size discipline, preparation geometry | Attacks every downstream cost at once: arc time, consumable, distortion, inspection |
| 2 | Raise the operating factor — material flow, positioners, fixtures, removing waiting | Attacks the largest cost element |
| 3 | Reduce repair rate | Removes cost that is currently invisible |
| 4 | Raise deposition rate within the process — wire size, extension, transfer mode, parameters within the qualified range | Cheap, fast, no capital |
| 5 | Change process | Effective but slow, capital-intensive and constrained by Chapter 73's screens |
| 6 | Reduce consumable price | Attacks a small share of cost, and risks a net loss |

The ranking is stable enough to be worth trusting as a starting hypothesis, and it is close to the reverse of the order in which shops usually attack the problem.

16. Worked Example — Reducing the Cost of a Structural Fillet Weld

The situation. A structural shop welds long fillet welds on stiffeners, semi-automatically with gas-shielded flux-cored wire, in the horizontal position. Management asks for a ten percent cost reduction and the purchasing department has begun negotiating wire price.

What was measured first. Three things, over two weeks: actual fillet leg sizes against the drawing; operating factor by observation; and repair rate from the inspection records.

What the measurements showed.

• Fillet legs were consistently above the drawing requirement, by a margin welders described as "making sure".

• Operating factor was low, and the largest non-arc block was repositioning the work — the stiffeners were welded on trestles, requiring the welder to walk and to weld some runs in an awkward position.

• Repair rate was low, and almost entirely at starts and stops.

What was done, in order of the ranking in Section 15.

Lever 1 — weld metal required. Fillet size was addressed two ways: the drawing requirement was reviewed by the designer and confirmed correct (it was), and gauges were provided with training on measuring rather than judging. Because fillet volume scales with the square of the leg, bringing consistently oversized welds back to size was the largest single saving available, and it required no capital.

Lever 2 — operating factor. A simple rotating fixture was made so the stiffener assemblies could be turned to bring every fillet into the flat or horizontal position without the welder moving. This removed walking time, removed the awkward-position runs, and — as a second-order effect — allowed a higher deposition rate because the flat position permits parameters the awkward position did not.

Lever 3 — repair rate. Start-and-stop defects were addressed by run-off tabs where the geometry allowed and by a revised start technique in the work instruction.

Lever 4 — deposition rate. With the work now in position, the wire diameter and the parameters were reviewed within the qualified range of the existing WPS, and a higher deposition operating point adopted. Note the sequence: this was possible only because lever 2 had already been done. Attempting it first would have failed, because the awkward position would not support it.

Lever 6 — wire price. The purchasing negotiation continued, and delivered a small saving on a small line.

The outcome that mattered. The reduction came almost entirely from levers 1 and 2, neither of which involved welding technology, consumables, or capital beyond a simple fixture. The purchasing negotiation that started the whole exercise contributed least.

The general lesson. The improvement was found by measuring, not by proposing. Nobody in the shop had believed the fillets were oversized, and the operating factor had never been measured at all.

17. Worked Example — The Automation Case That Did Not Pay

The proposal. A fabricator making a medium-volume welded assembly proposed a robot cell to replace two semi-automatic welding stations, justified on cycle time.

How the business case was built. Robot cycle time from the supplier's simulation, against the current manual arc time, over the current annual volume, amortizing the quoted equipment cost.

What was wrong with it — four things.

First, it compared robot cycle time against manual arc time, not against manual total time — and then, inconsistently, applied the resulting saving to total labour. The comparison mixed two different time bases (Error 1, Section 14).

Second, it omitted fixture development. The assembly was located by hand at the manual stations with the welder compensating for variation. A robot requires the parts to be located repeatably, which required fixtures that did not exist and, as it turned out, a tolerance improvement in two upstream pressed components.

Third, it omitted programming and debug. The quoted figure covered installation and basic programming; developing and proving paths for the full part family took substantially longer, and each subsequent variant needed its own.

Fourth, and decisively, it assumed the incoming parts were accurate enough. They were not. The manual welders had been absorbing a fit-up variation nobody had quantified, because absorbing it was part of their job and nobody had ever written it down.

What happened. The cell was installed and ran below its projected utilization for its first year, producing lack-of-fusion defects traceable to fit-up rather than to the welding parameters. The eventual fix was upstream: tolerance improvement on the pressed parts and a redesigned fixture. Once that was done, the cell performed close to the original projection.

The two lessons.

The first is the one in Section 11: control part accuracy before automating, not after. The manual process had been concealing a fit-up problem, and automation revealed it in the most expensive possible way.

The second is about the business case itself. The case was not dishonest; it was built by people who did not know what the manual welders were compensating for, because that compensation had never been measured. The most important input to an automation case is an honest description of what the current manual process is actually doing — including the parts of it nobody has written down.

18. Known Gaps

• No cost, price or rate figures are given, for the reasons in Section 1. The structure is provided; the numbers must be gathered locally.

• No deposition rate values are given. Ordinal comparisons only. Actual rates must come from procedure trials or specific consumable data for the exact configuration.

• Operating factor values are not given. The character of the ranking is given; the values must be measured in the shop concerned, and published figures vary widely because they measure different things.

• Energy cost modelling is simplified. Power source efficiency, standby consumption and demand charges are real and are not developed.

• Life-cycle and sustainability costing — embodied carbon, end-of-life, recyclability — is increasingly required and is not covered.

• Fume extraction, ventilation and personal protective equipment costs are part of the true cost of a welding operation and are treated only in outline.

• Learning-curve effects on new processes and new products are real, sometimes large, and are not modelled here.

• Currency, inflation and regional variation make any absolute figure short-lived; this is the reason for the approach taken, not a limitation of it.

1. How This Glossary Works

This is a working glossary, not a standards dictionary. Formal definitions are held in ISO 25901 and AWS A3.0, and where a term has a formal definition this glossary is consistent with it but is worded for use rather than for precision of law. [S1] [S2] Where the two systems define a term differently, the difference is stated.

Chapters 15 and 18 hold the resistance-welding-specific vocabulary from the original reference set. This chapter supplements them across the full process range and does not repeat what they cover in detail.

Cross-references give the chapter where a term is developed, not merely mentioned. A term with no chapter reference is defined here and not developed elsewhere.

2. Terms That Mean Different Things in Different Processes

These are the traps. Each of these words is used confidently in two different senses by people who assume they are talking about the same thing.

| Term | Meaning in one context | Meaning in another | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Spatter | Arc processes: droplets expelled from the arc or pool, ISO 6520-1 code 602 (Ch. 36, 39) | Resistance welding: expulsion — molten metal ejected from the nugget, indicating the top of the process window (Ch. 01, 12) | In arc welding it is mostly an efficiency and cleanliness issue; in resistance welding it marks a parameter limit and removes metal from the joint |
| Duty cycle | Equipment rating: percentage of a ten-minute period a power source may deliver a current (Ch. 46) | Production: operating factor, the fraction of paid time with an arc burning (Ch. 76) | A shop can hit an equipment duty cycle limit and a low operating factor simultaneously; they are unrelated |
| Penetration | Arc: depth of fusion into the parent metal (Ch. 22) | Resistance: proportion of sheet thickness consumed by the nugget (Ch. 01) | Different measurements, different acceptance bases |
| Weld nugget | Resistance: the fused zone of the spot weld (Ch. 01) | Beam/arc: occasionally used loosely for the fusion zone | Use "fusion zone" for arc and beam |
| Heat input | Arc: energy per unit length, from current, voltage and travel speed, with a thermal efficiency factor (Ch. 22) | Resistance: total energy from current, resistance and time (Ch. 01) | The formulae and the units differ |
| Electrode | SMAW: the consumable, filler and coating in one (Ch. 38) | GTAW/PAW: the non-consumable tungsten (Ch. 41) | Resistance: the copper alloy tool that applies force and current (Ch. 03) |
| Flux | SMAW/FCAW: within or on the consumable (Ch. 38, 40) | SAW: a separate granular consumable (Ch. 43) | Brazing/soldering: a chemical cleaning agent (Ch. 66, 67) |
| Backing | Arc: material supporting the root (Ch. 28) | Resistance: not used | A backing bar, backing gas and backing strip are three different things |
| Root | Butt joint: the bottom of the preparation (Ch. 28) | Fillet: the point of intersection of the fusion faces | Root penetration means different things in each |
| Leg | Fillet weld: the distance from the root to the toe along a fusion face | Not used elsewhere | Fillet size may be specified by leg or by throat; they are not the same |
| Efficiency | Thermal: fraction of arc energy entering the workpiece (Ch. 22) | Deposition: fraction of consumable ending in the weld (Ch. 76) | Both are called "efficiency" in the same conversation |
| Qualification | Procedure: WPQR/PQR proving a procedure (Ch. 31) | Personnel: proving a welder (Ch. 32) | Both abbreviate to "qualification" and neither implies the other |
| Standard | A published document | ISO 3834-3, one of the three named levels | "Standard quality requirements" is a level, not a generic description |
| Level | ISO 5817: B, C or D acceptance level (Ch. 36) | ISO 3834: quality requirement level (Ch. 33) | Both are "levels" and both apply to the same job |

| Pulse | GMAW: current pulsing for controlled transfer (Ch. 39) | Resistance: multiple current pulses within a weld schedule (Ch. 01) | Magnetic pulse welding: an electromagnetic discharge (Ch. 62) |

3. A — C

Acceptance criteria. The limits that separate an acceptable imperfection from a rejectable defect, set by the application code or by a quality-level standard such as ISO 5817. Not a property of the weld; a property of the contract. (Ch. 36, 74, 75)

AC (alternating current). In GTAW on aluminium, the polarity reversal provides the cathodic cleaning that breaks the oxide film; the balance between electrode-positive and electrode-negative time is an adjustable parameter. (Ch. 25, 41)

Adaptive control. A control system that measures a process signal — arc voltage, seam position, pool image — and adjusts a parameter during welding. Distinct from monitoring, which records without adjusting. (Ch. 69, 72)

Arc blow. Deflection of the welding arc by magnetic fields, from the return current path, from residual magnetism in the workpiece, or from nearby ferromagnetic mass. Causes erratic transfer, spatter and fusion defects; corrected by return-lead position, demagnetization, or AC. (Ch. 22, 39)

Arc efficiency. See thermal efficiency.

Arc strike. An arc initiated outside the joint, ISO 6520-1 code 601. Produces a small, rapidly quenched region on the parent metal that is a crack initiation site in hardenable steels. Prohibited by most codes. (Ch. 23, 74)

Arc time. Time during which an arc is burning. Distinguished from total labour time by the operating factor. (Ch. 76)

Autogenous weld. A weld made without filler metal. Common in GTAW, orbital GTAW, laser and electron beam. The weld metal composition is the parent composition, which constrains where autogenous welding is acceptable — in duplex stainless steel, for example, it disturbs the phase balance. (Ch. 24, 41, 70)

Backing. Material placed at the root to support the pool. May be permanent (left in place), temporary (removed), or gaseous (a backing or purge gas). (Ch. 28, 41)

Backing gas. Inert gas on the root side, protecting it from oxidation. Essential for stainless steel, titanium and nickel alloys. Its adequacy is measured by residual oxygen, not by flow rate or time. (Ch. 24, 26, 70)

Back gouging. Removing the root of a first-side weld, usually by arc-air gouging or grinding, to sound metal before welding the second side. Standard practice on double-sided full-penetration welds. (Ch. 28, 64)

Base metal / parent metal. The material being joined. ISO usage prefers "parent metal"; AWS usage prefers "base metal". Identical meaning. (Ch. 23–27)

Bead. A single run of weld metal.

Braze welding. Joining with a brazing filler metal deposited into a groove or fillet as in welding, rather than drawn into a capillary gap. Not brazing, despite the filler. (Ch. 66)

Brazing. Joining with a filler metal melting above 450 °C, drawn into a close-fitting joint by capillary action, without melting the parent metal. (Ch. 66)

Burn-through. Collapse of the weld pool through the joint, leaving a hole. (Ch. 36)

Buttering. Depositing a layer of weld metal on one or both fusion faces before making the joint. Used for dissimilar joints, for lamellar tearing prevention, and to provide a compatible surface. (Ch. 23, 27)

Carbon equivalent (CE). A single number combining the alloying elements' contributions to hardenability, used to assess cold cracking susceptibility and to set preheat. Note that the formula is not unique: the classic IIW form and the form in AWS D1.1 Annex B differ, the latter including a silicon term. A carbon equivalent value is meaningless without stating the formula used. Pcm is a separate parameter used for low-carbon high-strength steels. (Ch. 23, 34)

Cathodic cleaning. Oxide removal by ion bombardment during the electrode-positive part of an AC cycle. The mechanism that makes AC GTAW work on aluminium. (Ch. 25, 41)

Cladding. Depositing a surface layer, usually for corrosion resistance. Distinguished from hardfacing, which targets wear. (Ch. 65)

Cold cracking. See hydrogen-assisted cracking.

Consumable insert. A pre-placed ring or strip of filler metal at the root of a joint, melted into the root pass. Used in orbital and pipe welding to control root profile. (Ch. 70)

Contact tip. The current-transfer component in GMAW/FCAW guns. Wear changes electrical contact and wire position and is a common root cause of erratic arcs, spatter and copper inclusions. A scheduled consumable. (Ch. 39, 74)

Crater. The depression at the end of a weld run, where the pool solidifies without further filling. The concentration of shrinkage there makes it a crack site; crater-fill functions and run-off tabs address it. (Ch. 36, 39)

Creep. Time-dependent deformation under load at elevated temperature. Governs material and consumable selection for high-temperature service and drives PWHT requirements in creep-resistant steels. (Ch. 26)

4. D — F

Deposition efficiency. Mass of weld metal deposited divided by mass of consumable used. Losses to spatter, slag, fume, stub ends and core content. (Ch. 76)

Deposition rate. Mass of weld metal deposited per unit of arc time. Not the same as travel speed and not the same as productivity. (Ch. 76)

Dilution. The proportion of parent metal in the deposited weld metal. Critical in cladding, surfacing and dissimilar-metal welding, where high dilution can destroy the intended deposit composition. (Ch. 27, 65)

Distortion. Dimensional change caused by non-uniform heating and cooling. Categorized as longitudinal and transverse shrinkage, angular distortion, bowing, buckling and rotational distortion. (Ch. 34)

Ductility-dip cracking. Intergranular cracking in a temperature range below the solidus, in reheated weld metal of some austenitic and nickel alloys. Distinct from solidification and hydrogen cracking. (Ch. 26)

Duplex stainless steel. A steel with an approximately balanced austenite-ferrite microstructure. Requires heat input control at both ends — a ceiling to limit intermetallic precipitation and a floor to ensure sufficient austenite reformation on cooling. One of the few materials with a genuinely two-sided heat-input window. (Ch. 24)

Duty cycle. See Section 2 — two distinct meanings.

Electrode extension. The energized length of consumable between the contact tip and the arc. Resistive preheating over this length raises deposition rate, markedly so in cored wires. (Ch. 40)

Electroslag welding (ESW). A process in which current passes through a molten slag pool, which melts the parent and filler by resistance heating. Not an arc process once established. Very high deposition, vertical position, heavy sections, coarse microstructure. (Ch. 44)

Essential variable. A variable whose change beyond a defined limit requires a welding procedure to be requalified. Defined differently by ISO 15614, AWS D1.1 and ASME Section IX; the lists do not correspond. (Ch. 31, 75)

Expulsion. Resistance welding: ejection of molten metal from the weld under excessive current, time or insufficient force. Marks the top of the process window. (Ch. 01, 12)

Ferrite number (FN). A measure of ferrite content in austenitic and duplex stainless weld metal, obtained magnetically. Used to control solidification cracking in austenitic welds (a small ferrite content helps) and phase balance in duplex. Predicted from composition by constitution diagrams. (Ch. 24)

Filler metal. Metal added to the joint. May be wire, rod, strip, powder, a consumable insert, or the core of a covered electrode.

Fillet weld. A weld of approximately triangular section joining two surfaces at an angle. Specified by leg or by throat. Volume scales with the square of the leg — the basis for Chapter 76's warning about oversizing. (Ch. 28, 76)

Fit-up. The dimensional relationship of the parts before welding: gap, alignment, root face, angle. The variable that most often defeats a process change, particularly to beam processes. (Ch. 28, 55, 73)

Fusion line / fusion boundary. The boundary between weld metal and the heat-affected zone. A preferential site for several cracking mechanisms and for lack of fusion. (Ch. 22)

Fusion zone. The region that was molten and resolidified. Preferred term for arc and beam welds; "nugget" is the resistance welding term.

5. G — I

Globular transfer. GMAW droplet transfer in which droplets larger than the wire diameter detach irregularly under gravity. The highest-spatter transfer regime, and generally a mode to pass through rather than operate in. (Ch. 39)

Groove. The prepared opening between parts to be welded. Groove geometry sets weld metal volume and therefore cost. (Ch. 28, 76)

Hardfacing. Surfacing to resist wear. (Ch. 65)

HAZ (heat-affected zone). Parent metal whose microstructure has been altered by the welding thermal cycle without melting. Where much of welding metallurgy's difficulty lives: hardening, softening, grain growth, liquation, sensitization and reheat cracking all occur here. (Ch. 23–27)

Heat input. See Section 2. In arc welding, energy per unit length of weld, calculated from current, voltage and travel speed and multiplied by a process thermal efficiency factor. Controls cooling rate, and therefore microstructure, hardness, toughness, distortion and several cracking mechanisms. (Ch. 22)

Hot cracking. Umbrella term for cracking at high temperature during or shortly after solidification. Includes solidification cracking and liquation cracking. (Ch. 23, 24, 26)

Hydrogen-assisted cracking (HAC). Also cold cracking or delayed cracking. Requires four conditions together: diffusible hydrogen, a susceptible microstructure, tensile stress, and a temperature range near ambient. Removing any one prevents it, which is why the controls are preheat, low-hydrogen consumables and consumable handling, restraint reduction, and post-weld hydrogen release. May appear up to 48 hours after welding — the delay is diagnostic. (Ch. 23, 34)

Imperfection. A deviation from the intended weld. Becomes a defect only when it exceeds the acceptance criteria applicable to the job. The distinction is not pedantic: it determines whether repair welding is required, and unnecessary repair does harm. (Ch. 74)

Impeder. In high-frequency tube welding, a ferrite core inside the tube that increases the impedance of the unwanted current path. A wear item. (Ch. 50)

Interpass temperature. The temperature of the joint immediately before the next pass is deposited. Has a minimum where cooling rate must be controlled and a maximum where excessive heat input or grain growth must be avoided. Both may apply on the same joint. (Ch. 34)

Intermetallic. A compound of two metals with its own crystal structure, usually hard and brittle. The reason many dissimilar-metal fusion joints fail, and the reason solid-state processes succeed where fusion does not — a shorter time at temperature grows a thinner intermetallic layer. (Ch. 27, 57, 67)

6. J — M

Joint preparation. The shaping and cleaning of the fusion faces before welding. Sets weld metal volume, access for the arc, and defect risk. (Ch. 28)

Keyhole. A vapour-filled cavity through the material, held open by vapour pressure and traversed along the joint. The mechanism of deep-penetration laser, electron beam and keyhole-mode plasma welding. Its stability governs the characteristic beam-process defects. (Ch. 42, 52, 53, 54)

Kissing bond. A solid-state joining defect in which the faying surfaces are in intimate contact but not metallurgically bonded, usually because an oxide film was not disrupted. Very difficult to detect by any NDT method — the reason solid-state processes rely so heavily on process control. (Ch. 57, 61)

Lack of fusion. Absence of union between weld metal and parent, or between passes. Planar, tight and preferentially detected by ultrasonic rather than radiographic testing — an asymmetry that can hide a chronic problem in an RT-only shop. (Ch. 74)

Lamellar tearing. Stepped cracking in the parent plate beneath a joint loaded in the through-thickness direction, initiating at elongated non-metallic inclusions. Prevented by through-thickness tested plate, buttering, or joint redesign. (Ch. 23)

Liquation cracking. Cracking in the partially melted zone where grain boundaries have locally melted. (Ch. 24, 26)

Macrograph / macro-section. A polished and etched cross-section, examined at low magnification, revealing weld profile, penetration, fusion, HAZ extent and many defects. The most informative single test in welding and the most under-used. (Ch. 35)

Martensite. A hard, supersaturated microstructure formed by rapid cooling of austenite in steel. Its formation in the HAZ is the "susceptible microstructure" of hydrogen cracking. (Ch. 23)

Metal-cored wire. A tubular wire with a metallic core, ISO 4063 process 138. Behaves broadly like a solid wire with a higher deposition rate and little slag. Distinct from flux-cored wire (136), which produces slag. Confusing the two is a common procedure error. (Ch. 40)

Monitoring. Recording process signals without adjusting them. Distinguished from adaptive control. The compensating measure wherever the weld cannot be inspected. (Ch. 11, 72)

7. N — P

NDT (non-destructive testing). Examination without damaging the part: visual, penetrant, magnetic particle, radiographic, ultrasonic, eddy current and others. Method selection is governed by ISO 17635 and by what the joint geometry allows. (Ch. 35)

Nugget. Resistance welding: the fused, resolidified zone. Its diameter is the primary acceptance measure. (Ch. 01)

Operating factor. The fraction of a welder's paid time during which an arc burns. The dominant variable in welding cost and the least often measured. (Ch. 76)

Overlap. Weld metal extending onto the parent surface without fusing to it, ISO 6520-1 code 506. A stress raiser and a common consequence of excessive deposition at too low a travel speed. (Ch. 74)

Peening. Mechanical working of a weld surface, usually to redistribute residual stress. Permitted, restricted or prohibited depending on the code, the pass and the material. (Ch. 34)

Porosity. Gas-filled cavities in the weld metal, ISO 6520-1 group 2. Its distribution — uniform, clustered or linear — is the diagnostic key, not its quantity. (Ch. 36, 74)

Positioner. Equipment that moves the work to bring joints into a favourable position. One of the highest-return investments in welding productivity because it raises the operating factor and permits higher-deposition positional parameters simultaneously. (Ch. 69, 76)

Post-weld heat treatment (PWHT). Heating after welding to relieve residual stress, temper hardened microstructure, restore corrosion resistance, or achieve required properties. Required by many codes above a thickness threshold. Carries its own risks — reheat cracking, distortion, property change. (Ch. 34)

Preheat. Heating before welding to reduce cooling rate. The principal control against hydrogen cracking, derived from carbon equivalent, thickness, hydrogen level and restraint. Not a comfort measure; a calculated requirement. (Ch. 34)

Prequalified WPS. An AWS D1.1 provision allowing certain combinations to be used without a qualification test, conditional on every prequalification requirement being met exactly. No ISO equivalent exists. (Ch. 31, 75)

Purging. Displacing air from the root side with inert gas. Adequacy is measured by residual oxygen concentration. (Ch. 24, 26, 70)

pWPS (preliminary WPS). The draft procedure taken into qualification testing under the ISO system. No ASME or AWS equivalent term. (Ch. 31)

8. Q — S

Qualification. See Section 2 — procedure and personnel qualification are distinct and neither implies the other. (Ch. 31, 32)

Quality level. ISO 5817 (steel, nickel, titanium), ISO 10042 (aluminium), ISO 13919 (beam): levels B (most stringent), C and D, specifying acceptance limits for each imperfection type. Selected by the application standard or the contract, not by the welding department. (Ch. 36)

Reheat cracking. Also stress relief cracking. Intergranular cracking in the coarse-grained HAZ of creep-resistant steels during PWHT or high-temperature service. Timing relative to PWHT is the diagnostic discriminator against hydrogen cracking. (Ch. 26)

Residual stress. Stress remaining after welding, arising from constrained thermal contraction. Can approach yield magnitude. Contributes to cracking, distortion, stress corrosion cracking and fatigue behaviour. (Ch. 34)

Restraint. The degree to which the joint is prevented from moving during welding and cooling. Raises residual stress and is a contributing factor in most cracking mechanisms. Frequently the variable that makes a procedure that worked on a test coupon fail on the real structure — a coupon is a low-restraint condition. (Ch. 23, 34)

Root face. The unbevelled portion of the joint face at the root. Together with the root gap, controls root penetration and burn-through. (Ch. 28)

Root gap. The separation between root faces before welding. (Ch. 28)

Run-off tab / run-on tab. An extension piece at the ends of a joint so that starts and craters fall outside the finished weld. (Ch. 36, 43)

Sensitization. Chromium carbide precipitation at grain boundaries in austenitic stainless steel in a critical temperature range, depleting adjacent chromium and reducing corrosion resistance. Controlled by low-carbon or stabilized grades and by heat input limitation. (Ch. 24)

Shielding gas. Gas protecting the arc and pool from atmosphere. Classified by ISO 14175 into groups I (inert), M1/M2/M3 (mixed oxidizing), C (carbon dioxide), R (reducing), N, O and Z. Composition affects transfer mode, penetration profile, spatter, fume and mechanical properties. (Ch. 30)

Short-circuit transfer. GMAW mode in which the wire contacts the pool and the resulting short is cleared, transferring metal. Low heat input, all-position, suited to thin material and root passes. Spatter is governed by how violently the short clears — controlled by inductance or waveform. (Ch. 39)

Slag. Non-metallic residue from flux or from the electrode coating or core. Protects the cooling weld and must be removed before the next pass. (Ch. 38, 40, 43)

Solidification cracking. Cracking at the centreline during solidification, caused by low-melting films at the last-freezing region under transverse strain. Promoted by deep narrow beads (high depth-to-width ratio) and by sulphur and phosphorus. (Ch. 23, 24, 36)

Spatter. See Section 2 for the two distinct meanings. In arc welding, ISO 6520-1 code 602: droplets expelled from the arc or pool. Matters as a leading indicator of a process outside its intended transfer mode, as a cause of secondary damage during removal, and as a direct cost through reduced deposition efficiency and cleaning labour. Controlled in the order: transfer mode, gas composition, inductance/waveform, wire feed path, arc blow, surface condition. (Ch. 22, 30, 36, 39, 47, 74, 76)

Spray transfer. GMAW mode in which small droplets detach at high frequency and cross the arc without shorting. Requires current above a transition value and an argon-rich shielding gas — roughly 80 % argon or more; not available in pure CO₂. Low spatter, high deposition, flat and horizontal positions unless pulsed. (Ch. 39)

Stringer bead. A bead deposited without significant transverse oscillation, as opposed to a weave bead.

Stub end. The unused remainder of a covered electrode. A significant contributor to SMAW's low deposition efficiency. (Ch. 38, 76)

9. T — Z

Tack weld. A short weld holding parts in position before welding. Frequently treated as unimportant and frequently a defect source: tacks are short, fast-cooling welds often made without preheat, and they are then welded over. Codes commonly require tacks to be made by qualified welders to a qualified procedure and to be removed or fused into the weld. (Ch. 28)

Temper bead technique. A controlled deposition sequence in which later passes temper the HAZ of earlier ones, used where PWHT is impossible — typically in-service repair. (Ch. 34)

Thermal efficiency. The fraction of arc energy entering the workpiece. Differs by process and is applied as a factor in heat input calculation. Standardized values are given in the relevant heat-input standard, and using a different value changes a heat input compliance assessment. (Ch. 22)

Throat. The effective load-carrying dimension of a fillet weld, measured from the root to the weld face. Related to but not equal to the leg. (Ch. 28)

Toe. The junction of the weld face and the parent surface. The site of undercut, overlap, and — because of the geometric stress concentration — the usual fatigue initiation site. Toe angle and toe dressing therefore matter to fatigue life. (Ch. 34, 74)

Transfer mode. The mechanism by which molten metal crosses the arc in GMAW: short-circuit, globular, spray or pulsed spray. Determines heat input, positional capability, spatter and penetration profile. The first thing to check on any GMAW problem. (Ch. 39)

Travel speed. The rate at which the arc advances along the joint. Together with current and voltage, determines heat input.

Undercut. A groove melted into the parent at the weld toe and not filled, ISO 6520-1 code 5011/5012. A stress concentration and a fatigue initiation site. (Ch. 74)

Underfill. Insufficient weld metal, leaving the weld face below the parent surface, ISO 6520-1 code 511. (Ch. 74)

Weave. Transverse oscillation of the arc during travel. Widens the bead, increases heat input per unit length, and is restricted by some codes and procedures.

Weld map. A drawing or record identifying each weld in an assembly by a unique number, tying it to its procedure, welder, consumable, inspection and result. The backbone of traceability. (Ch. 72)

Weldability. Not a single property. The ease with which a material can be joined by a given process to produce a joint meeting the service requirement. Depends on the material, the process, the joint, the procedure and the requirement — which is why "is this material weldable?" is not answerable as asked. (Ch. 23–27)

WPQR / PQR (welding procedure qualification record). The record of the qualification test and its results. ISO uses WPQR; AWS and ASME use PQR. (Ch. 31)

WPS (welding procedure specification). The document instructing how a weld is to be made: process, materials, consumables, joint, parameters, preheat, technique, position. The central document of welding fabrication. (Ch. 31)

Two unit traps worth naming. Resistance welding time in "cycles" depends on the mains frequency, so a schedule transferred between a 50 Hz and a 60 Hz plant changes duration unless converted. 1. Why This Chapter Exists

Every chapter in this reference set ends with a Known Gaps section. That discipline serves the reader working within a single chapter, but it scatters the limits across seventy-seven documents, which means a reader can finish the set without ever seeing the shape of what is missing.

This chapter collects them. It exists because a reference work that does not state its boundaries invites misuse: the reader assumes that anything not mentioned is either unimportant or covered elsewhere, and neither is safe. The most dangerous failure mode of any technical reference is a confident reader who does not know what the reference does not know.

It also exists because the honest limits of welding engineering are themselves engineering content. Knowing that a preheat temperature must be calculated from the actual material, thickness, hydrogen level and restraint — and cannot be read from a table in a general reference — is not a deficiency in the reader's knowledge. It is the knowledge.

2. The Four Kinds of Gap

Not all gaps are the same, and treating them alike leads to the wrong response.

| Type | Nature | Correct response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Deliberately excluded | The information exists but belongs in a qualified, job-specific document | Go to the WPS, the qualification record, the supplier's data |
| 2. Contractual or regulatory | The answer depends on which document governs, and that is not knowable in general | Establish the governing document first |
| 3. A separate discipline | The subject is real and adjacent but is its own field | Go to that field's literature or a specialist |
| 4. Genuine uncertainty | The subject itself is not settled, or sources disagree | Test, or proceed with a stated assumption and a margin |

Type 1 accounts for most of the gaps in this set, and the exclusion is a deliberate safety decision, not a shortcoming.

3. Gap Type 1 — Deliberately Excluded, Because the Value Belongs to a Qualified Document

No welding parameters are given anywhere in this reference set. No currents, voltages, travel speeds, wire feed speeds, gas flow rates, electrode forces, weld times, beam powers, focal positions, rotation speeds or forge pressures. This is the largest single exclusion and it is absolute.

The reason is not caution for its own sake. A parameter is only meaningful as part of a qualified procedure for a specific material, thickness, joint, position, equipment and requirement. A parameter lifted from a general reference:

• has not been qualified for the material actually being welded;

• was developed on different equipment with different calibration;

• assumes a joint preparation and fit-up that may not match;

• carries no evidence, so it cannot be defended at an audit or in an investigation; and

• will be believed, because it is printed.

A number in a reference set is used as though it were qualified. That is why none are given.

Similarly excluded:

| Excluded | Where it belongs |
| --- | --- |
| Parameter values of any kind | The qualified WPS |
| Preheat temperatures | Calculated per the applicable standard from actual CE, thickness, hydrogen and restraint |
| Acceptance limits | ISO 5817 / 10042 / 13919 / 18279, or the application code |
| Consumable selection by trade designation | The consumable classification and the manufacturer's certificate |
| Vendor names, product names, brand designations | Supplier literature |
| Cost, price and rate figures | Gathered locally, into the structure in Chapter 76 |
| Deposition rates as values | Procedure trials for the actual configuration |
| Operating factor values | Measured in the shop concerned |
| Detection probability for NDT | Method-, technique- and personnel-specific |
| Specific material property values | Material standards and mill certificates |
| Qualification coverage ranges as tables | ISO 15614 / ASME Section IX / AWS D1.1 tables |
| Essential variable lists | The applicable qualification standard |

The one category of number this set does give is ordinal comparison — which of two processes deposits faster, which produces more distortion, which has the tighter fit-up requirement. Those rankings are stable and useful. Absolute values are neither.

4. Gap Type 2 — Excluded Because It Is Contractual, Regulatory or Jurisdictional

A large class of questions has no general answer because the answer is whatever the governing document says.

| Question | Why it has no general answer |
| --- | --- |
| Is this weld acceptable? | Depends on the acceptance criteria the contract invokes and the quality level specified |
| Is this procedure qualified? | Depends on which qualification standard governs and its essential variables |
| Is PWHT required? | Set by the application code, by thickness, material and service |
| How many repairs are allowed? | Set by the code; some permit none in the same location |
| Who may approve a concession? | Set by the contract and, on code work, involves the Authorized Inspector or equivalent |
| Is this welder qualified for this joint? | Depends on the qualification standard's coverage rules |
| Must this be inspected, and by what method? | Application code, quality level, ISO 17635 or the code's own requirements |
| Is hot work permitted here? | Jurisdictional regulation and the site permit system |
| What is the exposure limit for this fume? | National occupational exposure regulation |
| Can I substitute this consumable? | Contract, code, and the consumable's own classification |

The recurring instruction throughout this set — establish which document governs before answering — is the content, not an evasion. A welding engineer who answers an acceptance question without knowing the governing code has not answered it.

Specifically not covered:

• National deviations to EN ISO adoptions.

• Jurisdictional amendments to ASME adoption, which vary by state, province and country.

• Occupational health and safety regulation, which is national and changes.

• Environmental and emissions regulation.

• Classification society rules for marine and offshore.

• Nuclear regulatory requirements.

• Customer-specific specifications, which frequently exceed code requirements and are proprietary.

5. Gap Type 3 — Excluded Because It Is a Separate Discipline

These subjects are real, adjacent, and would each require their own reference set.

| Subject | Relationship to welding | Where it lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Structural design and analysis | Determines the loads the joint must carry and often the weld size | Structural engineering; design codes |
| Fracture mechanics and fitness-for-service | Determines whether a known flaw is acceptable in service | BS 7910, API 579, fracture mechanics literature |
| Fatigue design of welded joints | Weld toes govern fatigue life; detail classification decides it | Design codes, IIW fatigue recommendations |
| Physical metallurgy | Underlies everything in Volume 2 | Metallurgy textbooks |
| Corrosion engineering | Determines material and consumable selection for service | Corrosion literature; NACE/AMPP |
| Creep and high-temperature design | Governs power plant and process equipment | High-temperature design codes |
| Adhesive bonding | A joining family outlined in Chapter 68 | Adhesives engineering |
| Mechanical fastening design | A joining family outlined in Chapter 68 | Machine design; bolted joint literature |
| Forming, machining and fabrication upstream | Determines the fit-up the welding process receives | Manufacturing engineering |
| Non-destructive testing technique development | Chapter 35 selects methods; it does not teach them | NDT qualification schemes |
| Robot programming and industrial control | Chapter 69 covers the welding aspects only | Automation engineering |
| Software, networks and data architecture | Chapter 72 covers what to record, not how to build the system | Information systems |
| Occupational hygiene | Fume, noise and radiation measurement and control | Industrial hygiene |
| Failure analysis | Overlaps heavily with Chapter 74 but is a formal discipline | Failure analysis literature |
| Statistics and experimental design | Underlies process capability and any parameter optimization | Statistical literature |
| Training and competence development | Chapters 31 and 32 cover qualification, not pedagogy | Training organizations |

The most consequential of these for a welding engineer is fatigue. A large proportion of in-service welded joint failures are fatigue failures initiating at weld toes, and the governing variables — detail geometry, toe angle, residual stress, misalignment — are welding variables, but the assessment method is not a welding method. Chapter 34 treats the welding side; the assessment belongs to design.

6. Gap Type 4 — Genuine Uncertainty in the Subject Itself

Some things are not settled. Presenting them as settled would be the worse error.

| Subject | Nature of the uncertainty |
| --- | --- |
| Carbon equivalent formulae | Several formulae exist, giving different values for the same steel, and they were derived for different material ranges. See Section 7. |
| Preheat prediction | Multiple methods exist, based on different variables, and they do not agree. Standards give methods; none is universal. |
| Heat input thermal efficiency factors | Standardized values exist but real efficiency varies with configuration; a compliance calculation is only as good as the factor used |
| Acceptance of interfacial fracture in AHSS resistance welds | Conventional button-pull acceptance was developed on milder steels; high-strength grades can fracture interfacially at full nugget size. The acceptance basis is contested |
| Kissing bonds in solid-state welds | Detection remains unreliable; the industry response is process control, which is a mitigation, not a solution |
| Spatter prediction | Qualitatively well understood; not quantitatively predictable from first principles for a given setup |
| Fume composition and health effects | Active research; exposure limits change, and some classifications have been revised in recent years |
| Residual stress magnitude and distribution | Measurable and modelable, but prediction for a real structure remains difficult and model-dependent |
| Hydrogen behaviour in high-strength steels | Thresholds are not sharp; susceptibility to delayed cracking in the newest grades is an active subject |
| Additive manufacturing by arc processes | Qualification frameworks are still developing; standards are newer than the practice |
| Machine learning applied to weld quality | Claims are numerous; validated, generalizable, production-proven implementations are fewer |

Where this set has encountered such an area, it has said so in place rather than picking a side.

7. Points Where Authoritative Sources Disagree

Three are worth stating explicitly because they can produce a defensible-looking calculation that another engineer will reject.

The carbon equivalent formula. The classic IIW carbon equivalent and the form given in AWS D1.1 Annex B are not identical — the latter includes a silicon term. Applying one formula's value to the other's threshold is an error, and a CE value quoted without its formula is not usable. [S1] Chapter 23 presents both forms rather than selecting one. The related parameter Pcm was developed for low-carbon high-strength steels and is not interchangeable with CE.

ISO 4063 process numbers across editions. The 2023 edition revised the nomenclature, and some numbers used confidently in older documents no longer mean what the reader assumes. The distinction between 136 (flux-cored, active gas) and 138 (metal-cored, active gas), and between 132 (flux-cored, inert gas) and 114 (self-shielded), is a live source of procedure error. [S2] A WPS citing an ISO 4063 number should state the edition.

Quality level applicability. ISO 5817 explicitly excludes beam welding; ISO 13919 covers it; ISO 10042 covers aluminium arc welds. A beam weld assessed to ISO 5817 has been assessed against a document that says it does not apply. [S3] [S4] This is a common specification error rather than a disagreement between sources, but the effect is the same.

Where such conflicts exist, this reference set's practice has been to present both positions and identify the discriminating condition, rather than to resolve them by assertion.
